summary: Polya's method for solving mathematical problems: four phases and a list of questions, shown in classroom examples and a dictionary of heuristic terms.

unitSummaries.Unit 1: Why Polya wrote the book, what heuristic is for, and the four-phase list of questions the rest of the book explains.
unitSummaries.Unit 2: How a teacher can help a student by asking general, natural questions, and why imitation and practice are how the student learns.
unitSummaries.Unit 3: The four phases of solving a problem, each shown with an example, and the teacher's method of asking questions.
unitSummaries.Unit 4: Three longer worked examples (construction, proof, rate) showing the questions of the list used in a classroom dialogue.
unitSummaries.Unit 5: A short dialogue between a student and himself that puts the four phases and their questions into plain first-person steps.
unitSummaries.Unit 6: Analogy, auxiliary elements and auxiliary problems as tools for finding a way in, and what makes a bright idea.
unitSummaries.Unit 7: Looking back at a result, carrying out a plan, the parts of a condition, and decomposing and recombining a problem.
unitSummaries.Unit 8: Going back to definitions, Descartes's plan, how determination and hope drive a solution, and checking that all the data were used.
unitSummaries.Unit 9: Testing a guess, drawing figures, generalizing, using a related problem solved before, and what heuristic and heuristic reasoning are.
unitSummaries.Unit 10: Solving a related problem first, induction and mathematical induction, the inventor's paradox, and looking at the unknown.
unitSummaries.Unit 11: Modern heuristic, notation, Pappus's analysis and synthesis, pedantry and mastery, practical problems, and problems to find versus problems to prove.
unitSummaries.Unit 12: Progress, puzzles, indirect proof, routine problems, the rules of discovery, style and teaching, and separating the parts of a condition.
unitSummaries.Unit 13: Setting up equations, signs of progress, specialization, subconscious work and symmetry.
unitSummaries.Unit 14: Old and new terms, testing by dimension, the future mathematician, the intelligent reader, varying the problem and finding the unknown.
unitSummaries.Unit 15: Why proofs matter, what proverbs teach about method, and working backwards from the unknown.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: How the four phases, the questions and the dictionary entries fit together, and which to use in which situation.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
concepts.title: A taste of discovery
concepts.question: Why should a learner solve even a modest problem by their own means?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Solve problems by your own means, even modest ones, and treat a mathematics course as a chance to taste discovery.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A taste for mental work, which may grow into a hobby, a tool of your profession, your profession or a great ambition.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya says there is a grain of discovery in the solution of any problem. If the problem challenges your curiosity and calls on your inventive powers, solving it yourself brings the tension and triumph of discovery. You cannot know you like something you have never tasted.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student who treats the course as credit to earn and forget after the exam never tastes this. One who finds a problem as much fun as a crossword, or hard thinking as good exercise as a fast game of tennis, may not forget the pleasure easily.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A solution copied from someone else brings no triumph, because the discovery was not yours.

card.rule: Solve problems that challenge your curiosity by your own means, and let the pleasure of finding the answer win you a taste for mental work.
card.limits: The problem must challenge your curiosity and call on your own powers; a handed-over answer gives no triumph.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
concepts.title: The teacher's opportunity
concepts.question: What should a mathematics teacher do with class time instead of drilling routine operations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Challenge students' curiosity with problems that fit their knowledge, and help them solve those problems with stimulating questions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Students who can think for themselves instead of only following routine.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Filling the allotted time with drill in routine operations kills interest and hampers intellectual development, so the teacher wastes a great opportunity. Problems matched to what students know awaken their curiosity, and questions let them do the solving.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher with a week for fractions could set thirty near-identical exercises. Instead she sets one puzzle her class has the knowledge to crack, and when they stall she asks a question rather than giving the answer.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a problem far beyond the class's knowledge does not fit it, so it cannot challenge their curiosity.

card.rule: Set problems proportionate to your students' knowledge and help with stimulating questions rather than filling the time with routine drill.
card.limits: Our reading: the problem must fit what the students know, or it stops challenging them.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
concepts.title: Asking how a solution was invented
concepts.question: Beyond whether a solution works, what question did Polya as a student keep asking?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look beyond whether a solution is correct and ask how anyone could have invented it, and how you could do the same.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understanding the motives and procedures of solution so that you can invent or discover things by yourself.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A solution can appear to work and be correct and still not show how it was found. As a student, Polya was disturbed by this gap, and trying to explain the motives and procedures of solution to others finally led him to write the book.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Polya recalls listening to lectures and reading books in mathematics and physics, taking in the solutions and facts presented, while a question kept coming back: how can people discover such things?

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: asking is only a start; it helps only if you go on to study how solutions are actually found.

card.rule: Ask not only whether a solution is correct but how it could have been invented, and how you could invent such things yourself.
card.limits: Our reading: the question is a start, not an answer.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
concepts.title: The two faces of mathematics
concepts.question: In what two ways can mathematics be presented, and which one does the study of problem solving show?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you study mathematics, look at how it is made as well as at the finished proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing the experimental side of mathematics, which the study of methods of solution, called heuristic, brings out.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Presented in Euclid's way, mathematics looks like a systematic, deductive science. Mathematics in the making, while it is being invented, looks experimental and inductive. Polya says mathematics has two faces, and the study of problem solving shows the second.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A neat proof in a textbook shows the first face. The scribbled guesses, tests and false starts of whoever first found it belong to the second.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The second face does not replace the first: mathematics is the rigorous science of Euclid and also something else.

card.rule: Look at mathematics both as a finished deductive system and as an experimental science in the making.
card.limits: The experimental face adds to the Euclidean one; it does not replace it.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
concepts.title: The book's sequel
concepts.question: What did the author finish after the first printing, and how does it relate to this book?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a book's later prefaces to see what the author has added since the first printing and how later work continues the line of thought.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Placing the book inside the author's larger project, so you know where to go next.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The seventh-printing preface says a promise made in the first preface has now been kept, at least in part. The author's later work, Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning, continues the line of thinking begun in this book.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The first preface announced a more extensive book on the way to completion. The seventh preface reports the promise partly kept.

card.rule: Read later prefaces to see how an author's later work continues the book.
card.limits: Our reading: the preface says the later work continues this one; it does not say it replaces it.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: Mathematics as fun, not detested
concepts.question: What problem with mathematics teaching does the second-edition preface describe, and what does Polya hope for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat mathematics as more than a route to jobs and science: as something that may be fun and may open a vista of high-level mental activity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Breaking a cycle in which teachers who learned to detest mathematics teach the next generation to detest it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The preface cites a 1956 study that called mathematics the least popular subject: future teachers learn in elementary school to detest it, then return to teach a new generation to detest it. Polya hopes his edition will convince some readers that mathematics may be fun.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil taught by a teacher who detests the subject picks up the same dislike, and may one day pass it on as a teacher.

card.rule: Do not treat mathematics only as a necessary avenue to jobs; it may be fun and a vista of mental activity at the highest level.
card.limits: Polya still calls mathematics a necessary avenue to engineering jobs and scientific knowledge, and only hopes to convince some readers.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: The four phases of solving
concepts.question: In what order does the list say to work, and what are its four phases?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Work a problem in four phases, in order: understand it, devise a plan, carry out the plan, then look back.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Getting from a problem to a checked solution without skipping a phase.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The list is divided into four headed parts, each with its own questions. First, understand the problem. Second, find the connection between the data and the unknown to reach a plan. Third, carry out the plan. Fourth, examine the solution obtained.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Sharing a taxi fare among friends: first make sure what you must find; then choose how to share; then do the sums; then check that the shares add up to the whole fare.

card.rule: Work in four phases: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back.
card.limits: Our reading: the list gives questions to ask, not a machine, and the plan phase may send you to auxiliary problems first.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: Understanding the problem
concepts.question: Before planning, which three things about a problem should you be able to name?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before planning anything, say what the unknown, the data and the condition are.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing exactly what is asked and what you have.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The list's first phase asks what the unknown is, what the data are and what the condition is. A plan later connects the data to the unknown, so you need to be able to name both. In everyday words: the unknown is what you must find, the data are what you are given, and the condition ties them together.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tank holds 120 litres and a tap adds 8 litres a minute; how long to fill it from empty? The unknown is the time, the data are 120 and 8, and the condition ties them: rate times time must equal the volume.

card.rule: Before planning, name the unknown, the data and the condition.
card.limits: Naming the parts does not solve the problem; it only prepares the plan.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: Devising a plan
concepts.question: How does the list suggest you find a connection between the data and the unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To find a plan, look for a connection between data and unknown by recalling a related problem you have solved, starting from the unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A plan of the solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Many problems are related to ones solved before. The list asks whether you have seen this problem, or one like it, and urges you to look at the unknown and think of a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown. If you find one, could you use its result, its method, or an added auxiliary element?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked for the floor area of an L-shaped room, you may recall finding the area of a rectangle: the unknown is the same kind. Could you split the L into rectangles and use that method?

card.rule: Look for a connection to a related problem you have solved, starting from the unknown.
card.limits: A matching earlier problem may not exist; the list then sends you to auxiliary problems.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: Carrying out the plan and looking back
concepts.question: What does the list ask you to do while carrying out a plan, and after you have a solution?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check each step as you carry out the plan, then examine the finished solution by checking the result and the argument.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A solution you can trust.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Carrying out the plan is the third phase, and the list asks you to check each step: can you see that it is correct, can you prove it? The fourth phase, looking back, asks whether you can check the result and the argument.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student finds that 20 tiles of 15 cm fit along a 3 m wall. She checks each step as she goes, then tests the count by laying 20 tiles end to end.

card.rule: Check each step while you work, then examine the result and the argument.
card.limits: Checking steps does not finish the job: looking back is a separate fourth phase.

concepts.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
concepts.title: How the book is built
concepts.question: What are the book's four parts, and how should each be used?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the four parts differently: Part I for the list in use, Part II as a dialogue, Part III by consulting, Part IV to try problems.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Getting the most from the book while solving your own problems or helping students.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The introduction says the Dictionary is condensed and sometimes subtle, so it should not be read too quickly. Reading about points that come from your own experience with problems or students has a much better chance to be profitable.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A reader stuck on a puzzle meets the word analogy in the list and looks up the matching article instead of reading the Dictionary straight through.

card.rule: Read Part I, the dialogue and the problems as written, and consult the Dictionary when a point arises in your own work.
card.limits: Our reading: reading the Dictionary cold from start to end is likely to be less useful than visiting it with a question.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
concepts.title: Help the student, but only just enough
concepts.question: How much help should a teacher give, and in what manner, so that the student still does real work?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Help the student by putting yourself in his place and offering a question or a step that could have occurred to him, giving neither too much nor too little.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: The student gets as much experience of independent work as possible, with a reasonable share of the effort left to him.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A student left alone with no help, or too little, may make no progress at all. A teacher who helps too much leaves nothing for the student to do. Help that follows the student's own likely thinking sits between these two.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil is stuck on how many 30-pence pencils can be bought with 3 pounds. Instead of announcing the division, the teacher asks what the pupil is trying to find. The pupil could have asked that himself.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author admits this is not easy: no formula gives the right amount of help for every student, so the teacher has to judge each case.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you help someone with a problem, offer one question instead of the next step.

card.rule: Help naturally and in measure: ask a question or point to a step the student could have thought of himself.
card.limits: The right amount of help differs from student to student and no formula fixes it. Naturalness is the aim, not a script, so judge each student's case afresh.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
concepts.title: Stock questions set off mental operations
concepts.question: Why does a teacher keep asking the same few questions, and what are they meant to set going in the student?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When helping, use the stock questions and suggestions of the list, in whatever wording fits, so that each one sets off the mental operation it points to.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Help that is effective yet natural: the student's attention goes to the part of the problem that matters, and he does the thinking.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A question and a suggestion can aim at the same effect, so they tend to provoke the same mental operation. The list gathers and arranges questions that typically help in discussing problems.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the question What is the unknown? It can be reworded as What is required?, What do you want to find? or What are you supposed to seek? The suggestion Look at the unknown! does the same job.

blocks.label: Look-alike
blocks.text: Treating the list as phrases to recite. The point is the action behind each phrase, so the wording may vary.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Stuck on any problem, ask yourself in your own words what you are supposed to find.

card.rule: Choose the wording freely: what counts is the mental operation the question or suggestion provokes.
card.limits: A question is not magic words. If the student cannot see the action behind it, nothing is set going. The list is a stock of helpful moves, not a guarantee.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
concepts.title: General in scope, plain in sense
concepts.question: Why are the list's questions usable on every kind of problem, and why does the author call them plain common sense?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask the list's questions about any problem, whatever its subject; they only put into general words what a serious solver would do anyway.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: General direction that fits all sorts of problems, algebraic or geometric, theoretical or practical, serious or a mere puzzle, while leaving the work to the solver.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions are natural, simple and obvious, so a person seriously concerned with a problem would come to them anyway. Their use is not restricted to a subject.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A hungry person thinks of familiar ways of getting food. Someone facing a construction of a triangle thinks of familiar ways of constructing one. Both follow the advice to think of a familiar problem with a similar unknown.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Generality has one restriction, and it is not about subject matter: some questions of the list fit only problems to find, not problems to prove.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you face a small everyday problem, ask what is unknown and what ways you know of finding something like it.

card.rule: Use the general questions on any problem, but check whether the problem is one to find or one to prove.
card.limits: Subject matter is no limit, but the kind of problem is: some questions suit only problems to find, and a problem to prove needs different questions.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
concepts.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
concepts.title: Imitation and practice build the skill
concepts.question: What two aims does a teacher have in putting these questions, and how does a student come to make them his own?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the list's questions to students as often as you can do so naturally, and give them plenty of opportunity for imitation and practice.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Two aims: to help the student solve the problem at hand, and to develop his ability to solve future problems by himself, until he puts the right question to himself at the right moment.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Solving problems is a practical skill, like swimming, learned by imitation and practice. A question that is helpful again and again gets noticed, and the student begins to ask it himself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Learning to swim, you copy what others do with hands and feet to keep your head up, and you finally learn by practising swimming. Learning to solve problems goes the same way.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a question forced in where it does not arise naturally loses the unobtrusive quality the book values; the book asks for them only as often as natural.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one question from the list and ask it on three different problems this week.

card.rule: A skill is learned by watching it done and doing it: use the questions often, and make them the student's habit.
card.limits: Hearing a question is not enough; the student must practise it and succeed with it. Forcing it in unnaturally is also unwelcome.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: The four phases of solving a problem
concepts.question: What four phases does the work of solving a problem pass through, and in what order?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Work in four phases: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, then look back at the finished solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the solver a short map of the work, so that each helpful question is asked at the point where it belongs.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes that our view of a problem keeps shifting: it is incomplete at the start and different once some progress is made. Naming four phases groups the questions of his list in a convenient way.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Finding the diagonal of a box: first see what is asked and what is given; then plan to use right triangles; then work out the lengths; finally test the formula that came out.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the phases name where the attention is, not four sealed rooms. The author says we change our point of view again and again, so going back to an earlier phase is normal.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take any problem from last week and write which phase each line of your work belongs to.

card.rule: Work in four phases: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, then look back at the finished solution.
card.limits: The four phases are a convenient grouping of the work and of the questions, not a fixed timetable.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Why no phase should be left out
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a solver leaves out one of the four phases?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not leave out any phase unless a really good idea has already given you the whole solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid wasted effort and avoidable mistakes, and keep the benefit that comes from reviewing a result.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A lucky idea is welcome, but without one the skipped phase causes trouble. Checking each step prevents many mistakes, and reconsidering the finished solution keeps some of the best effects of the work.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two pupils get the same word problem. One starts adding numbers at once and has to start again; the other first says what is asked and finishes in half the time.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The warning is about skipping without a good idea. When a bright idea really does show the whole solution, using it is fine.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: next time you want to start calculating at once, first say aloud what is being asked.

card.rule: Do not leave out any phase unless a really good idea has already given you the whole solution.
card.limits: A bright idea may let you jump ahead; absent one, each phase protects something specific.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Understand the problem and want its solution
concepts.question: Why must a solver both understand a problem and want to solve it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make sure you understand the question and also want its answer before you set to work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid the foolish and sad case of answering what you did not understand or working toward an end you do not desire.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that answering a question you do not understand is foolish, and working for an end you do not want is sad. He adds that a lack of understanding or interest is not always the student's fault.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher gives a problem that is too hard and dull, so the pupils lose interest. A better chosen, natural and interesting problem wins their attention.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: When a pupil lacks interest, the cause may lie in the problem or its presentation. The author asks the teacher to choose the problem well.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: before starting, say in one sentence why you would like the answer.

card.rule: Make sure you understand the question and also want its answer before you set to work.
card.limits: Understanding is necessary but the author wants desire as well; lack of either may be the problem's fault, not the solver's.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Unknown, data and condition
concepts.question: Which three principal parts of a problem should a solver be able to point out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before planning, name the unknown, the data and the condition of the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Check that the statement of the problem is really understood before any planning starts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The unknown is what you are asked to find; the data are what you are given; the condition links the two. The author says a teacher can seldom afford to miss asking about them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A school trip problem: find the cost per child. The unknown is that cost; the data are the total bill and the number of children; the condition says the cost times the number of children equals the bill.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Only the principal parts are named this way. Naming them does not solve the problem; it only shows what the problem consists of.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: for the next problem you meet, write three short lines headed Unknown, Data and Condition.

card.rule: Before planning, name the unknown, the data and the condition of the problem.
card.limits: Naming the three parts is a check of understanding, not a solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Draw a figure and choose notation
concepts.question: How can a figure and well-chosen letters help a solver study the parts of a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the problem has a figure, draw it and mark the unknown and the data; if names are needed, choose suitable letters.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the solver look at the principal parts attentively, repeatedly and from various sides.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: To choose a sign for an object you have to think about that object. The author says that paying attention to the choice of signs obliges the student to consider the things the signs stand for.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the garden problem, draw a rectangle, write 12 m along one side and mark the other side with a letter w for the unknown width.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The advice about a figure applies when a figure is connected with the problem. Letters are introduced when names for the objects are necessary, not as a ritual.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: for the next word problem, draw a quick sketch and put one letter on each quantity.

card.rule: If the problem has a figure, draw it and mark the unknown and the data; if names are needed, choose suitable letters.
card.limits: Draw and label only when a figure exists or names are needed; the gain comes from the attention the labelling demands.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Is it possible to satisfy the condition?
concepts.question: What kind of answer is wanted to the question whether the condition can be satisfied?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether the condition can be satisfied, and accept a provisional guess for an answer at this stage.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Start the solver thinking about whether the problem is reasonable, without demanding a proof yet.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The question belongs to the preparatory stage. The author says we should not expect a definitive answer there, only a provisional one: a guess that later work can confirm or change.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked for three whole numbers that add to 10 and are each larger than 4, a pupil says: probably not, because three such numbers already add to at least 15.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A provisional answer can be wrong. It is a first view of the problem, and it must not stand in for the later phases.

card.rule: Ask whether the condition can be satisfied, and accept a provisional guess for an answer at this stage.
card.limits: A guess made early is not a verdict; later work decides.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Making a problem concrete and asking the first questions
concepts.question: How does the teacher in the first example make the box problem concrete and test whether pupils understand it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make the problem concrete, then ask: unknown, data, notation, condition, and whether the condition determines the unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring the pupils to understand the problem, and show some interest in it, before any planning.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A concrete setting turns a bare statement into something pupils can see and estimate. The author's problem, the diagonal of a box, is made concrete by treating the classroom as the box.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The teacher treats the room as a box and asks for the diagonal of the room. The pupils name the unknown, the three data, the letters, and the condition. They answer yes to whether the condition fixes the unknown.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The discussion needs pupils who already know the theorem of Pythagoras and its plane applications. Without that knowledge the problem cannot be discussed profitably.

card.rule: Make the problem concrete, then ask: unknown, data, notation, condition, and whether the condition determines the unknown.
card.limits: The method needs pupils with the background the problem uses; interest alone is not enough.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: The idea of a plan is the main achievement
concepts.question: What is a plan, and why does the author call the idea of a plan the main achievement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Aim first at the idea of a plan: know, at least in outline, which calculations or constructions will give the unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach the idea of the solution, which is the hardest and most valuable part of the work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The road from understanding to a plan may be long and winding, and the idea may come slowly or in a flash. The teacher's best help is a quiet nudge toward a bright idea, using questions that tend to provoke one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To cost the paint for two walls 4 m wide and 2.5 m high at 3 pounds per square metre, a pupil plans: area of one wall, double it, multiply by the price.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Questions and suggestions help but cannot work magic. When a plan does not come, the solver must look for other approaches, as the following ideas show.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: before computing, say your plan in one sentence, such as find the area, then multiply by the price.

card.rule: Aim first at the idea of a plan: know, at least in outline, which calculations or constructions will give the unknown.
card.limits: The author says questions very often help, but they cannot help always.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Start from what you know: a related problem
concepts.question: Why does a good idea need past knowledge, and which question starts the search?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start the search for a plan with the question: Do you know a related problem?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Collect the materials that good ideas are built from: facts and problems you already know.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Good ideas rest on formerly acquired knowledge. Remembering alone is not enough, but no good idea comes without recalling some pertinent facts. The author compares this to a house: materials alone do not build it, yet it cannot be built without them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil asked for the cost of 7 notebooks at 3 pounds each recalls an earlier problem about 5 pens at 2 pounds each. Both ask for the cost of several equal items.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Remembering is not a plan. With little knowledge of the subject a good idea is hard to find, and with none it is impossible.

card.rule: Start the search for a plan with the question: Do you know a related problem?
card.limits: A related problem is only raw material; it has still to be used.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Look at the unknown
concepts.question: How can a solver choose the few useful problems out of the many that are somewhat related?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When too many problems seem related, look at the unknown and recall a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pick, out of many loosely related problems, the few that are really useful.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Many problems share some point with the present one. The unknown is an essential common point, so a problem with the same or a similar unknown is a promising choice. If one is recalled, the solver is lucky but should deserve the luck by exploiting it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil must find the time a trip takes. The unknown is a time, so he recalls an earlier problem whose unknown was also a time, and asks whether he can use it.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Recalling a problem is not a solution; the solver must still use it. The question also cannot always succeed.

card.rule: When too many problems seem related, look at the unknown and recall a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown.
card.limits: A match of unknowns suggests a good problem to try; it does not guarantee that it can be used.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Vary the problem when recall fails
concepts.question: What can a solver do when no related problem helps?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If no related problem helps, change the problem: restate it, or try a related problem that you can solve first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find another point of contact between the problem and what you already know.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions about related problems cannot help always. When they do not, the author says we must vary, transform or modify the problem. Means include generalization, specialization, analogy and dropping part of the condition.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Unable to plan a table for 12 guests, a host first plans for 2 guests, then for 3. The easier problem is a related problem solved first to help with the original.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author gives only the list; the details belong elsewhere. Variation also brings the danger of drifting from the original problem.

card.rule: If no related problem helps, change the problem: restate it, or try a related problem that you can solve first.
card.limits: Variation is a way to find new contact; it needs a check that you are still on the original task.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Did you use all the data?
concepts.question: How does a solver find the way back after wandering among related problems?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you have wandered among related problems, ask: Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring you back to the original problem when experiments have taken you far from it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Applying known problems, trying modifications and solving helper problems can carry us so far that we are in danger of losing the original. The author says this question brings us back to it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A taxi costs 3 pounds plus 2 per km, and a 5-pound tip is added for a 6 km ride. A pupil gets 15 and stops. The tip is a datum she has not used, so the full cost is 20.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The question points to the original problem. It does not say how to use a missing datum.

card.rule: When you have wandered among related problems, ask: Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition?
card.limits: It only shows what is missing; finding how to use it is still the solver's job.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Leading pupils to the idea by graded hints
concepts.question: How does the teacher in the box example lead pupils from a general question to the decisive idea?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When pupils are silent, repeat the question with some modification and move step by step to more explicit hints.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the pupils themselves introduce the decisive auxiliary element, with as much help as needed and no more.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The teacher begins with: do you know a related problem; then asks about the same unknown, then a similar unknown, and finally points to a triangle in the figure. Each step gives a little more, so the pupils keep a share of the discovery.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the box example the diagonal is a length. The pupils recall finding a side of a right triangle. The teacher asks whether the figure has a triangle, and a right triangle with the diagonal as hypotenuse is drawn.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Even a fairly explicit hint may not break the pupils' torpor. The teacher must have a whole range of more and more explicit hints ready.

card.rule: When pupils are silent, repeat the question with some modification and move step by step to more explicit hints.
card.limits: Hints grow more explicit only as far as needed; silence is a signal to try again in other words.

The long diagonal x runs from the far left bottom corner up to the near right top corner. A shaded right triangle has x as hypotenuse, the upright edge c as one leg and a diagonal across the bottom face as the other leg.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Check that pupils see far enough ahead
concepts.question: What should the teacher check before pupils go into actual calculations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before calculating, check that the new element holds the unknown and that its other parts are known or can be found.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure a plan exists before the calculation starts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The decisive idea, such as drawing a triangle, is not yet a plan. The teacher should convince himself that the pupils see far enough ahead, and then say: now I see you have a plan.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The pupils have drawn a right triangle. The teacher asks whether it contains the unknown, and whether both legs are known. One leg is given, and the other is the hypotenuse of a second right triangle.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A bright idea can still leave gaps. The teacher can only judge by asking, and the pupils must see the chain for themselves.

card.rule: Before calculating, check that the new element holds the unknown and that its other parts are known or can be found.
card.limits: A helpful idea is not yet a plan until its chain of steps is seen.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Carry out the plan with patience
concepts.question: Why is carrying out a plan easier than finding it, and what is its main danger?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Carry out the plan patiently, examining the details one after another until no obscure corner remains.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure the details fit the outline and that no error has a place to hide.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Devising a plan takes knowledge, good mental habits, concentration and some luck. Carrying it out mainly asks for patience. The plan is an outline, so every detail has to be examined until all of it is clear.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil with a plan to cost a party goes through each line of the bill, adding it up and writing the sub-total, so no unclear item remains where an error could be hidden.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The outline does not do the work for you: the details still have to be examined one by one.

card.rule: Carry out the plan patiently, examining the details one after another until no obscure corner remains.
card.limits: A plan gives the outline; the details still have to be examined.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Check each step: seeing and proving
concepts.question: How can a solver become honestly convinced that a step is correct?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check each step until you are honestly convinced of it, by seeing it clearly or by proving it from formal rules.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid many mistakes by making sure every step is sound before building on it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A step can be accepted by concentrating until it is so clear no doubt remains, or by deriving it according to formal rules. The author calls the first insight and the second formal proof, and leaves further discussion to philosophers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil sees at a glance that 3 rows of 7 chairs is 21, then also proves it by writing 7 + 7 + 7 = 21.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Seeing is not proving: a step may look clear and still fail to be proved. The author says the main point is honest conviction.

card.rule: Check each step until you are honestly convinced of it, by seeing it clearly or by proving it from formal rules.
card.limits: Honest conviction is the goal; a trusted authority is not a source of it.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Carrying out the box plan
concepts.question: How do two right triangles combine into a formula for the diagonal of the box?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Work through the chain, name the auxiliary unknown, and combine the results; do not press for a proof the class cannot yet give.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach the formula for the diagonal while keeping the pupils confident and in charge of the details.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let x be the diagonal and y the diagonal of the face with sides a and b. The big triangle gives \(x^2 = y^2 + c^2\); the small gives \(y^2 = a^2 + b^2\). Eliminating y leaves \(x^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2\), so x is the square root of that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With a = 3, b = 4 and c = 12 the face diagonal is y = 5 and the box diagonal is x = 13, since 9 + 16 + 144 = 169.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A question such as can you prove this is a right triangle may be too hard before a good start in solid geometry. It can become the main difficulty and hide the main idea.

card.rule: Work through the chain, name the auxiliary unknown, and combine the results; do not press for a proof the class cannot yet give.
card.limits: The teacher may leave the proof question for later, unless the class is well prepared.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Look back at the completed solution
concepts.question: Why look back at a solution that is already finished?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the solution is written down, reconsider and reexamine the result and the path that led to it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Consolidate your knowledge and develop your ability to solve problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Students often close the book once the argument is neatly written. They miss an instructive phase. The author holds that no problem is completely exhausted: something always remains to be done, and at least our understanding of a solution can always be improved.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After finding the cost per child on a school trip, a pupil asks what she learned from the route, whether a shorter route existed, and what other problems it might solve.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author does not ask for endless reworking. He asks for a real look back, which interests pupils most after an honest effort.

card.rule: When the solution is written down, reconsider and reexamine the result and the path that led to it.
card.limits: Looking back works best after real effort; it adds to the solution, it does not replace it.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Check the result and the argument
concepts.question: Which questions help a solver verify a result and its argument?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check the result and the argument, derive the result in a different way, and look for a short argument you can see at a glance.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain well-founded confidence that the solution is right, since errors are possible even after careful work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Errors are always possible, especially in long arguments. A rapid, intuitive test of the result or of the argument should not be overlooked. A second, different derivation adds conviction, and a short argument that can be seen at a glance is preferred.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Five boxes of 12 pencils give 60. A second derivation: ten boxes make 120, and half of that is 60.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Not every check is available for every problem. The author asks for the quick intuitive ones; a heavy re-derivation is saved for difficult and important cases.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Try it: after your next calculation, find a second way to get the answer.

card.rule: Check the result and the argument, derive the result in a different way, and look for a short argument you can see at a glance.
card.limits: Choose checks in proportion to the difficulty and importance of the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Use the result or method elsewhere
concepts.question: How can the look back show that a problem is connected with others?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In the look back, ask whether you can use the result, or the method, for some other problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show that problems are connected, and prepare the pupil to do equally well another time.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: One of the teacher's first duties is not to leave the impression that problems have little connection with each other or with anything else. Looking back is a natural moment to find links, especially after an honest effort. Pupils are then eager to see how else the effort could pay.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A pupil who found how long a 60-litre tank takes to fill at 5 litres a minute asks about emptying a 90-litre pool at 15 litres a minute. The same method gives 12 and 6 minutes.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The link is interesting only after a real effort. A pupil who has not done the work will not feel the pull.

card.rule: In the look back, ask whether you can use the result, or the method, for some other problem.
card.limits: The question pays most after real effort; it needs a solved problem to build on.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Testing a formula: all data, symmetry, analogy
concepts.question: Which simple tests can a formula in letters pass or fail?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Test a result in letters by asking: are all the data in it, does it respect the symmetry of the problem, and does it match the analogous plane result?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain confidence in the result from a different source than the derivation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem in letters has an advantage over one in numbers, since its result can be tested in several ways. A yes to each question adds confidence, and a no would show a serious flaw.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The box formula \(\\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}\) uses all of a, b and c, stays the same when they are swapped, and looks like the rectangle formula \(\\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A formula that passes is not proved by that, only better supported. The tests need a problem in letters, not just numbers.

card.rule: Test a result in letters by asking: are all the data in it, does it respect the symmetry of the problem, and does it match the analogous plane result?
card.limits: Passing the tests adds confidence; it does not replace the derivation.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Testing a formula: limits, growth and scale
concepts.question: What should happen to the diagonal when a measure vanishes, grows, or all are scaled?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Test a formula by letting one measure shrink to zero or grow, and by scaling all measures or changing units.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Link the formula to other facts, so it is better supported and better remembered.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If the height shrinks to zero, the box flattens to a rectangle and the diagonal should be that of the rectangle. If the height grows, the diagonal grows. Scaling every measure by one factor scales the diagonal by the same factor.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With c = 0 the formula gives \(\\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), the rectangle's diagonal. Multiplying a, b, c by 12 multiplies the root by 12.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Passing all these tests supports the formula as experimental evidence; it is not a proof. A failed test shows a flaw.

card.rule: Test a formula by letting one measure shrink to zero or grow, and by scaling all measures or changing units.
card.limits: These tests support a result; they do not prove it.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Rechecking touchy points and reusing the result
concepts.question: How is the box result checked and then used for a new problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recheck the touchy points of the argument, and find uses by giving the abstract elements a concrete meaning.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend rechecking effort where it matters, and turn a solved problem into a tool for new ones.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Usually it is enough to pick out the touchy points of an argument for rechecking, not every step. For uses, students give concrete meanings to the abstract elements, such as the classroom for the box. The distance from the centre of a box to a corner is half its diagonal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A building top is 21 yards long and 16 wide, a pole 8 yards high stands at its centre, and cables run from 2 yards below the pole's tip to the four corners. The edges are 10.5, 8 and 6, so each cable is 14.5 yards.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Some uses are weak, and a better use needs a different problem.

card.rule: Recheck the touchy points of the argument, and find uses by giving the abstract elements a concrete meaning.
card.limits: Uses vary in value, and rechecking is selective, not total.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: A second approach: by analogy
concepts.question: How can a teacher reach the same idea by way of an analogous problem instead of the unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If recalling by the unknown does not work, ask for a simpler analogous problem and see whether it can be used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find another point of contact with what the pupils know, and let even slow pupils contribute part of the idea.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The box problem is about a solid; an analogous problem lives in the plane, concerning the diagonal of a rectangle. In the first approach the contact came through the unknown. Here analogy provides the contact, and the idea is essentially the same.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Asked how many unit cubes fill a 3 by 4 by 5 block, a class first recalls how many unit squares fill a 3 by 4 grid, 12, and uses the same layering idea for 60 cubes.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: An analogous problem is another route to the idea, not a better one.

card.rule: If recalling by the unknown does not work, ask for a simpler analogous problem and see whether it can be used.
card.limits: The analogue helps only if it is simpler or already familiar.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: From general questions to specific ones
concepts.question: Where does a teacher start, and how does the teacher move when a question gets no response?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Begin with a general question from the list and come down gradually to more specific ones, only as far as needed.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the student as great a share of the work as possible.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each step down gives the student a little more help and so takes a little less of the work. Starting general means the student does the most thinking. Coming down by degrees stops at the first question that gets a response.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tutor helps with a savings puzzle: what is the unknown, do you know a related problem, a problem with the same unknown, could a total-cost problem help here?

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The method is not a script. The list is a first list and could be improved, and the steps may be varied.

card.rule: Begin with a general question from the list and come down gradually to more specific ones, only as far as needed.
card.limits: Going down more than needed gives the secret away; stopping too early may leave the pupil stuck.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Simple, natural, general and short
concepts.question: What qualities should the teacher's starting suggestions have, and how rigidly should they be used?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the starting suggestions simple, natural, general and few, and use them with elasticity rather than as a rigid routine.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Let the questions become the pupil's own mental habit, rather than a teacher's trick for one problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Simple and natural suggestions are unobtrusive. General ones apply to problems of all sorts, so they build ability and not a special technique. A short list can be repeated often under varying circumstances, so it may be assimilated as a habit.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tutor uses three questions in arithmetic, geometry and puzzles: what is the unknown, do you know a related problem, can you check the result.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says his list is a first list. He also warns a reader to prepare the examples and to try the method with caution.

card.rule: Keep the starting suggestions simple, natural, general and few, and use them with elasticity rather than as a rigid routine.
card.limits: Rigid, mechanical procedure is necessarily bad in these matters; the method must allow elasticity.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
concepts.title: Why a special hint is a bad question
concepts.question: What is wrong with the question: could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prefer a general, natural question, such as the one about a related problem, to a special hint that hands over the method.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Help where help is needed, and help in a way that is instructive for future problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives objections to a hint such as the Pythagoras one. If a pupil is not near the solution, the hint may be missed, so it fails where help is most needed. If it is understood, it gives the secret away. And it is too special to teach anything for future problems.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tutor stuck on a perimeter puzzle says: use the formula for a rectangle. The pupil copies it, finishes this puzzle and cannot do the next.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Judge a hint by the situation. The objections do not apply to the general questions of the author's own procedure.

card.rule: Prefer a general, natural question, such as the one about a related problem, to a special hint that hands over the method.
card.limits: A good hint is judged by what the pupil can do with it next time.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Name the unknown, the data and the condition
concepts.question: Before trying any method, can you say what you must find, what you are given and what must hold?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before you work on a problem to find something, say what the unknown is, what the data are and what the condition is.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To be sure you understand the problem, so that you know exactly what is asked and what you have to start from.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each part has a different job: the unknown is the target, the data are the material, the condition ties them together. Saying them in turn makes you read the statement closely instead of guessing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The problem is to inscribe a square in a triangle. The unknown is a square. The condition puts all four corners on the outline of the triangle, two on the base and one on each other side.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Naming the three parts does not make the problem easy, and does not tell you whether the condition can be met at all.

card.rule: Name the unknown, the data and the condition before you try to solve anything.
card.limits: Naming the parts is a start, not a method: it will not tell you whether a solution exists or how to reach it.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: When you are unsure, try a related problem first
concepts.question: What can you do when you are unsure that a problem can be solved as it stands?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot solve the problem you were given, or are unsure it can be solved, solve a related problem first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep moving on a problem that you cannot attack directly, and to gather something that helps with the original.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A related problem is a nearby problem that is easier to handle. What you learn from it can bring the original within reach.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The student of the square problem says he thinks the square can be drawn but is not sure. The teacher suggests solving a related problem before going further.

card.rule: If the problem as given is too hard to start, solve a related problem first.
card.limits: A related problem helps only if it really bears on the original; a problem picked at random is no stepping stone. The next ideas show one way to choose.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Keep part of the condition and drop the rest
concepts.question: How can you make a hard condition easier while still working on the same kind of unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep only a part of the condition, drop the other part, and aim at the easy part first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To get a version of the problem that you can start on, with the same kind of unknown as the original.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A condition often speaks about several things at once. A part of it speaks about fewer of them and so is easier to satisfy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The square must have all four corners on the outline of the triangle. A part of that condition concerns fewer than four corners, so the student keeps some corners on the outline and drops the others, and draws a figure.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The part you keep is easier but is usually not the whole problem; you still have to come back to what you dropped.

card.rule: Keep a part of the condition, drop the other part, and satisfy the part that is easy.
card.limits: The reduced problem is a stepping stone. It will usually have many answers, so it does not replace the original; you must still come back to the part you dropped.

media.alt: A large triangle with a horizontal base and a pointed top. A square stands on the base with its two top corners at different heights relative to the sides: its upper left corner touches the left side of the triangle while the upper right corner floats inside, so only three corners lie on the outline.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Ask how far the unknown is now determined
concepts.question: After dropping part of the condition, how can you find what is still undecided?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After keeping only part of the condition, ask how far the unknown is determined, and draw a figure of what you have.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To see what is still free, because what is free points to what the dropped part of the condition must settle.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The kept part pins down some features of the unknown and leaves others open. Seeing exactly which ones are open turns a vague difficulty into a definite question.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With three corners on the triangle's outline the student draws figures and sees that the square can vary. Its fourth corner is not yet where it should be, so the question becomes how that corner can move.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: If the kept part already fixes the unknown completely, nothing is left to vary; our reading is that the part you dropped then did not matter.

card.rule: Ask how far the unknown is determined by the part you kept, and see what can vary.
card.limits: A figure shows what can vary but does not by itself say how to fix it. The answer is not found by this question alone; it only sharpens the next one.

media.alt: A triangle with a square on its base, one top corner touching the left side, as before, and a second, much smaller square tucked into the bottom left corner with the same arrangement. The two squares show that three corners on the outline do not fix a single square; the fourth corner moves.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Draw many cases and watch where the free corner goes
concepts.question: How can drawing several cases show the shape of the answer to a construction problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the kept part leaves a point free, draw several cases, small and large, and ask where the free point seems to go.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To guess the locus of the free point, meaning the set of positions it takes as the figure varies, since the dropped part of the condition can then be used to pick out one position.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An experiment turns a vague freedom into something visible: the marked points either scatter or fall into a pattern that can be named.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The teacher asks the student to draw more squares with three corners on the outline, small ones and large ones, and to say what seems to be the locus of the fourth corner.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The drawing suggests a pattern; it does not prove it. A guess still has to be tested.

card.rule: Draw several varying cases and look for the path the free point follows.
card.limits: A pattern in a few drawings is a guess, not a proof. The guess has to be tested and then used with the part of the condition you set aside.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: For a proof, name the hypothesis and the conclusion
concepts.question: What do you write down first when asked to prove a statement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a problem to prove, state the hypothesis and the conclusion, draw a figure, and choose suitable letters for the objects.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To have in exact words what may be assumed and what has to be shown, ready to be checked against the figure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem to prove has two parts as a problem to find has: what you may use and what you must reach. In letters they can be read off the figure.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two angles lie in different planes. Each side of one is parallel to the matching side of the other and points the same way. The hypothesis says this in letters; the conclusion is that the two angles are equal.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Writing both parts in notation does not itself give the proof; it only makes the next steps possible.

card.rule: Name the hypothesis and the conclusion, draw a figure and introduce notation.
card.limits: Stating both parts is a beginning. Leaving out any piece of the hypothesis, such as the same direction, can make the proof impossible.

media.alt: Two separate angles, each drawn as a pair of rays from a vertex. The upper one has vertex A' with rays toward C' and B'; the lower has vertex A with rays toward C and B. Matching rays slope the same way, as if parallel and equally directed. No triangle or joining line is drawn.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Look at the conclusion and recall a familiar theorem
concepts.question: How can the conclusion you must reach lead you to a tool you already know?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look at the conclusion, recall a familiar theorem with the same or a similar conclusion, and ask whether you could use it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To bring in a result you already have, one that does part of the job, instead of building everything from nothing.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A theorem that ends as your goal ends shows what facts would be enough, so it turns a vague goal into a list of things to establish.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The goal is that two angles are equal. The student recalls that corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal. The teacher confirms that it is a related theorem proved before and asks whether it could be used; the student thinks so but does not yet see how.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A theorem you recall may not fit the figure as it stands, and you may not yet see how to use it.

card.rule: Look at the conclusion and recall a theorem with a similar conclusion.
card.limits: A recalled theorem is only a candidate. It may not fit your figure yet, and it may not be the best one to choose; keep looking if it does not help.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Add an auxiliary element and set a new aim
concepts.question: What can you do when the theorem you want is about objects your figure does not contain?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the theorem you want to use is about objects missing from your figure, introduce an auxiliary element, and make proving what the theorem needs your new aim.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To join the problem to a theorem you know, through a smaller step that is easier to reach than the original goal.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The auxiliary element makes the figure fit the theorem. The new aim is a step: once it is proved, the original conclusion follows at once.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The theorem is about congruent triangles but the figure has no triangles. The student joins B to C and B' to C', choosing the points so that AB = A'B' and AC = A'C'. The new aim is that the two triangles are congruent; then the angles are equal immediately.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The new aim still has to be proved, and it may call for the same question again, with a further aim.

card.rule: Add what the theorem needs to the figure, and take its requirement as your new aim.
card.limits: A new aim is only a means. It may itself need a theorem, an auxiliary element or both, so the process can repeat before the proof is finished.

media.alt: The same two angles as before, now completed into triangles: the upper angle with vertex A' and the lower with vertex A, each with a dotted segment joining the free ends of its two rays (C' to B' and C to B). The dotted segments are the added auxiliary lines that create two triangles.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Check that you have used the whole hypothesis
concepts.question: How can the part of the hypothesis you have not used lead to the missing step?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you are stuck, ask whether you used the whole hypothesis, and whether it says more about the objects than you have used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find an overlooked fact that connects the pieces of the figure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A hypothesis often holds several facts. If you use only one, a link can stay hidden in the others.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The student has used only that AB and A'B' are parallel. The teacher asks whether that is all he knows about these lines; they are also equal, so the segments are parallel and equal. This is a familiar configuration: a parallelogram. He joins A to A', B to B' and C to C'.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A configuration that looks familiar is a guess until it is proved.

card.rule: Ask whether you have used the whole hypothesis and all it tells you.
card.limits: Recognising a familiar shape is a guess until proved. Two of the parallelograms in the figure can be proved at once; the third still has to be shown.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Work with letters first, numbers last
concepts.question: When a problem gives numbers, at what point do you put them in?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the statement suggests it, set the numerical values aside, work with letters for the data, and substitute the numbers only at the end.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To get a general expression for the unknown, which shows how it depends on the data and can be checked before any number is used.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Letters keep the connections between quantities visible. A number put in too early can hide a connection, or fix a quantity that really changes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The vessel problem gives a = 4 ft, b = 3 ft, r = 2 cu ft per minute and y = 1 ft. The teacher disregards the values for now and expresses the unknown in terms of a, b, r and y, and only then substitutes.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: This is a suggestion from the statement, not a law; some problems are easier with numbers.

card.rule: Work with letters first and put in the numerical values last.
card.limits: The order is advised when the statement suggests it. A letter that stands for a changing quantity should stay a letter until the end.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Restate the unknown until you reach a definition
concepts.question: How do you turn a wordy unknown into something you can write and work with?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Restate the unknown in other words, again and again, until you reach a definition you can write in notation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To replace a loose phrase by a precise symbol that can be linked to the data.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each restatement strips away loose wording. The last one is a definition, and a definition can be written with symbols.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The rate at which the surface is rising becomes the rate at which the depth increases, then the rate of change of the depth y. The derivative is the rate of change of a function, and y depends on the time t, so the unknown is written dy/dt.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The restatements must mean the same thing; a wrong turn gives a wrong unknown.

card.rule: Keep restating the unknown until you reach a definition you can write in symbols.
card.limits: Restating changes the words, not the problem. Each version must mean the same as the last, and the chain stops when you reach a definition.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Find connections between quantities, step by step
concepts.question: How do you link the unknown to the data when no direct link can be seen?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot see how the unknown is linked to the data, look for simpler connections between related quantities, name any quantity you lack, and use each link as a stepping stone.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To build a chain of relations from the data to the unknown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Quantities in one figure depend on one another, so each link is a relation you can write. Chaining them gives a relation between the quantities you care about.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The volume V of water in the cone depends on the depth y. V is the volume of a cone of height y, whose radius x is not known, so the student calls it x and writes V = (1/3)πx²y. By similar triangles x : y = a : b, so x = ay/b and V = πa²y³ divided by 3b².

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A relation is a stepping stone only if it brings you nearer the unknown; keep the goal in view.

card.rule: Link the unknown to the data through simpler connections, one stepping stone at a time.
card.limits: Many connections can be found; only those that lead toward the unknown help. Do not lose sight of the goal while collecting them.

concepts.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
concepts.title: Keep the goal in view and differentiate
concepts.question: Once you have a relation between depth and volume, how do you reach the rate you want?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the unknown in view; when you have a relation between related quantities, differentiate it to get a relation between their rates.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To connect the rate you want with the rate you are given.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If V depends on y and both change with time t, then differentiating the relation with respect to t links dV/dt and dy/dt, the data rate and the unknown rate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From V = πa²y³ divided by 3b² the student gets dV/dt = (πa²y²/b²) times dy/dt. This links the inflow rate dV/dt = r to the unknown dy/dt, with a, b and y.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The student is expected to know the simplest rules of differentiation, and the numbers go in only at the end.

card.rule: Differentiate the relation between the quantities to link their rates.
card.limits: Differentiation applies when the quantities are functions of time. The relation found still contains y, so the answer holds at one moment, with y given its value at the end.

concepts.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
concepts.title: Understanding the problem in two passes
concepts.question: What should you do first with a problem, and what do you gain before any plan exists?

blocks.label: Rule
