blocks.text: Start from the statement of the problem. First picture the problem as a whole, vividly, leaving details aside. Then start again from the statement and go through its principal parts one by one, in turn and in combinations, relating each detail to the others and to the whole.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To understand the problem, become familiar with it and fix its purpose in your mind, and to prepare and clarify the details that are likely to play a role later.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, careful attention to the whole and then to the parts gives you a problem so clear that you can set it aside for a while without fear of losing it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An invented case: asked to plan a school trip within a budget, you first picture the trip as a whole. Then you list the unknown (date and place), the data (group size, budget) and the conditions (the cost limit), and ask how each bears on the others.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the second pass is for a statement already clear in your mind. If the statement is still hazy, return to the first pass before sorting parts.

card.rule: Start from the statement: see the whole problem first, then examine its principal parts one by one and in combinations.
card.limits: The first pass deliberately ignores details, and the second begins only once the statement is clear. Neither solves the problem. Principal parts: hypothesis and conclusion in a problem to prove; unknown, data and conditions in a problem to find.

concepts.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
concepts.title: Hunting for a helpful idea
concepts.question: How do you look for a helpful idea, and what do you do with one that is only partly formed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Consider your problem from various sides and seek contacts with what you already know. When an idea comes, even an incomplete one, examine it, follow it as far as it seems reliable, and then look again at the changed situation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To perceive a helpful idea: one that shows you the whole way, or part of it, and suggests how to proceed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, emphasizing different parts and looking at details in new ways may reveal a new meaning, and recalling what helped in similar past situations may reveal something familiar and useful.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An invented case: a cook's sauce keeps splitting. She changes what she attends to (heat, speed, order of adding) and recalls a similar sauce that held. That suggests adding the oil more slowly, a partial idea she tries and then re-examines.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says you are lucky to have any idea, and that some ideas lead astray. The search starts when the parts are clearly arranged and memory seems responsive.

card.rule: Look at the problem from several sides, seek contact with earlier knowledge, and follow each promising idea as far as it leads before looking again.
card.limits: No idea is guaranteed, and some ideas mislead. Do not begin hunting until the principal parts are distinctly arranged. An incomplete idea is a start, not a solution; after following it you reconsider the new situation.

concepts.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
concepts.title: Carrying out the plan
concepts.question: How do you turn a lucky idea into a solution you can trust at every step?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Make your grasp of the idea secure, carry through in detail the operations you recognised as feasible, and convince yourself that each step is correct by formal reasoning, by intuitive insight, or by both.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A presentation of the solution in which each step is correct beyond doubt.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, checking in a sensible order keeps a long solution under control: if the problem is complex, separate great steps from small steps, each great step being made of several small ones, and check the great ones first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An invented case: a budget model has five sections and many cell formulas. You first check that each section does its job, then go down into the formulas inside each section.

card.rule: Carry out the planned steps in detail, justify each one by reasoning or insight, and check the great steps before the small ones.
card.limits: This phase begins only once you have a plan to carry out. If the problem is not complex, you need not divide steps into great and small. Our reading: a failure in a great step makes the checking of its small steps beside the point.

concepts.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
concepts.title: Looking back at the solution
concepts.question: What should you do with a finished, correct solution, and what does that practice give you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Starting from a complete and correct solution, look at it from various sides: simplify and shorten its parts, try to see the whole at a glance, improve it, and scrutinize both the method and the result for use on other problems.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find a new and better solution or new facts, and to build your ability to solve problems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, surveying and scrutinizing your solutions as a habit gives you knowledge that is well ordered and ready to use, and develops your ability.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An invented case: a team finishes a route plan for deliveries that works. They try to cut steps, see whether the plan can be explained in one sentence, and note the method for the next schedule.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author says you may find a better solution, not that you will. It starts only from a solution complete and correct in each detail.

card.rule: Once the solution is complete and correct, simplify and shorten it, then scrutinize its method and result for use on other problems.
card.limits: Looking back needs a complete, correct solution first. The rewards are possibilities: a better solution or new facts may appear, and sometimes nothing new does. Our reading: the lasting value lies in the habit rather than in any single review.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Analogy: sameness of relations
concepts.question: What makes two things analogous, as opposed to merely similar?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Call two systems analogous when the same relations hold among their parts, and say so by giving the parts a shared name.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To state an analogy exactly enough that it can be used in a solution, not just felt.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Similar objects agree in some respect; analogous objects agree in how their parts relate. A shared term lets one sentence describe both systems, so the common pattern becomes visible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Each side of a rectangle is parallel to exactly one other side and perpendicular to the rest. Each face of a rectangular box does the same with faces. Call both a bounding element, and one sentence covers both: each bounding element is parallel to one other and perpendicular to the others.

card.rule: Name the relations the two systems share, and give their parts one common name.
card.limits: A shared name only helps if the relation really is the same in both systems; a catchy word can hide a difference.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Analogy at every level of precision
concepts.question: How good does an analogy have to be before it is worth using in solving a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Accept analogies of any quality as possible clues, and note how clear each one is before leaning on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep every source of help open, from a vague likeness to an exact mathematical match.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book says analogy appears in everyday speech, trivial conclusions, art and the highest science. It ranges from vague or incomplete to mathematically exact, and every sort may help discover a solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tenant compares a landlord's rent rise to a shop raising prices. The likeness is vague, but it suggests asking what each side gains. A mathematician compares two systems with exact matching relations. Both comparisons can start a line of thought.

card.rule: Do not dismiss a rough analogy; use it as a lead, and know how rough it is.
card.limits: The book welcomes all sorts as aids to discovery. Our reading: a vague analogy is a lead to test, not a result to trust.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Look for a simpler analogous problem
concepts.question: What can you do when a problem is too hard to attack directly?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the problem is hard, look for a simpler problem that is analogous to it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn one hard question into two connected questions, of which the easier can be answered first.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two questions can be easier than one if they are intelligently connected. The simpler problem has the same pattern but fewer demands, so you can get a result or a method from it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find the centre of gravity of an even solid tetrahedron needs heavy knowledge. The analogous problem in the plane asks for the centre of gravity of an even triangle. Now there are two questions, but the triangle is much easier.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Luck is involved: the book says we may consider ourselves lucky when such a problem turns up.

card.rule: Replace a hard problem by an analogous easier one, and connect the two on purpose.
card.limits: The simpler problem must really be analogous; otherwise its answer says nothing about the original.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Lay the original aside and solve the analogue
concepts.question: Once you have chosen a simpler analogous problem, what should you do with the original?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Set the original aside for a while and solve the simpler analogous problem completely.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To obtain a finished solution that can serve as a model or a source of results.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Attention divided between two problems helps nobody. The book solves the triangle fully, using a plausible principle: if the parts of a system each have their centres in one plane, so does the whole. That principle is all the triangle needs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Slice a triangle into thin strips parallel to one side. Each strip balances at its midpoint, and all midpoints lie on the line from the opposite vertex to the middle of that side. So the centre lies on that median. The same holds for the other two sides, so it is where the three medians meet.

card.rule: Work the simple problem to the end, naming the principle you lean on.
card.limits: The book flags that the principle used is plausible and mechanical, and asks for a purely geometric check (see the later idea on checking independently).

media.alt: A triangle with base AB and apex C, cut into many thin horizontal strips parallel to AB. A dotted line runs through the middles of all the strips, from C down to the point M, the midpoint of AB. It shows that the strips' balance points all lie on the median from C.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Imitate the analogue's method point by point
concepts.question: Once the simpler problem is solved, how can its solution guide the original?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take the finished analogue as a model, and repeat its steps in the original, translating each part.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To solve the original by following a route already proved to work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The triangle solution becomes a plan. Each ingredient has a counterpart, so the steps carry over almost word for word, which makes the original problem feel fairly easy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The triangle was cut into strips parallel to a side. Cut the tetrahedron into strips parallel to an edge AB. Their midpoints lie in a plane through the midpoint M of AB and the opposite edge CD. The tetrahedron has six such planes, one per edge, and each holds the centre, so they meet in one point.

card.rule: Translate the model solution step by step: sides become edges, medians become median planes.
card.limits: A step may have no counterpart; then the model must be changed (see the idea on using method, result or both).

media.alt: A tetrahedron drawn with vertices A, B and D visible and a fourth vertex C hidden at the right. M marks the midpoint of the base edge AB. A shaded planar region joins M, the apex D and the opposite edge, showing a median plane of the solid, the counterpart of a median of a triangle.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Use the analogue's result as a ready-made fact
concepts.question: Can you use an analogue without copying how it was solved?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take the finished result of the simpler problem and use it as a fact inside the original, without caring how it was obtained.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To get a fact you can build on, even when the analogue's route does not carry over.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A result is a block you can place. The book proves that six median planes of the tetrahedron share a point by using the fact that the three medians of a triangle share a point, not by imitating its proof.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the three median planes through one corner D. They cut the base triangle in its three medians, which meet in one point. So the three planes share a line through D and that point. The same goes for A, B and C, and the six planes then have a common point.

card.rule: Look in the analogue's results for a fact that fits a part of your problem.
card.limits: The fact must apply to the figure inside your problem, so check that the right triangle or sub-case is really there.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Method, result, or both
concepts.question: When you borrow from a simpler analogous problem, what exactly can you take?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask what to borrow from the analogue: its method, its result, or both; and rework it if it does not carry over.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To get the most from a solved analogue, and to avoid stalling when it does not fit directly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book separates two uses. Under imitation the steps are copied point by point; under use of a result the finished fact is placed in the original. A solution may use both. When the analogue cannot be used at once, reconsider and vary its solution until a form is found that extends.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the centre-of-gravity problem, the triangle's strip method was copied to get the six median planes, and its result about three medians meeting was used to show those six planes share a point. Both uses appear in one solution.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book warns that complications may arise in harder cases, so a clean fit is not promised.

card.rule: Decide which of method and result the original needs, and rework the model if neither fits.
card.limits: Harder problems bring complications the example does not show, so expect to vary the solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Verify the key fact by an independent route
concepts.question: If a solution rests on a plausible outside assumption, how do you make it solid?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a solution relies on an assumption borrowed from another field, confirm the key fact by a separate argument inside your own field.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To complete the solution, so it stands without leaning on the outside assumption.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The centre-of-gravity proof uses a principle from mechanics. That makes the result plausible, but the geometric claim that the medians meet is still unproved. The book therefore asks for a check by pure geometry, independent of mechanical assumptions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the triangle, the mechanical argument says the three medians meet at the centre. To complete it, show by geometry alone that three medians meet at one point. For the tetrahedron, do the same for the six median planes, using the simpler triangle result.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Where no independent route is available, say the result is plausible rather than proved.

card.rule: List the facts your solution took on trust, and prove each by a route that does not use that trust.
card.limits: A check by another route is stronger than a repeated argument along the same route.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Forecast the result by analogy
concepts.question: How can an analogy tell you what the answer is likely to be before you prove it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before proving, guess the result or some of its features from a known analogous case, and treat the guess as plausible, not certain.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To aim the work at a likely target and to have something definite to test.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Plausible forecasts are often based on analogy. The book notes the triangle's centre of gravity is also the centre of its three vertices, so it conjectures the tetrahedron's centre is the centre of its four vertices. This is an inference by analogy. It would be foolish to take it as certain, but more foolish still to disregard it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A rod balances at the middle of its two ends, a triangle at the centre of its three corners. A student guesses that a four-cornered solid balances at the centre of its four corners, marks it as a guess, and then tests it on one numerical example before relying on it.

card.rule: Guess by analogy, label the guess as a guess, and test it.
card.limits: The book says such conjectures may or may not be confirmed by experience and stricter reasoning.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Weigh an analogical conclusion
concepts.question: What makes one analogical conclusion stronger than another?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Trust a conclusion more when it rests on more parallel cases, and still more when the analogies are clear-cut and systematically arranged.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To decide how much weight a forecast by analogy deserves.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book says many parallel cases give a stronger conclusion than a few. But quality counts more than quantity: clear analogies outweigh vague likenesses, and instances arranged systematically outweigh a random collection.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The tetrahedron guess is backed by the triangle. Adding the rod (a straight segment of even density) gives a third case in a clear series: segment, triangle, tetrahedron. That series is more convincing than three unrelated cases.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Many cases that share only a vague likeness do not add up to strong support.

card.rule: Prefer clear, ordered cases to many loose ones.
card.limits: Cases that look alike by chance count for little, however numerous.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Line the cases up in a table
concepts.question: How can counting the parts of several analogous figures reveal a hidden regularity?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List the same counts for each figure in the series, arrange them in a table, and look for a pattern.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find regularities that make the analogy more than a feeling.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The segment has 2 endpoints. The triangle has 3 vertices and 3 sides. The tetrahedron has 4 vertices, 6 edges and 4 faces. Counting the whole interior as one more element gives rows 2, 1; 3, 3, 1; 4, 6, 4, 1. The book notes this is a section of Pascal's triangle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A square has 4 vertices, 4 sides and 1 interior. A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces and 1 interior. Such counts form a table that you can compare with the triangle's row to see whether a pattern holds.

card.rule: Tabulate the parts by dimension for each case and compare the rows.
card.limits: Our reading: a pattern in a table is a clue, and still needs a reason before it counts as a proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Follow the pattern: simplicity as a guide
concepts.question: Why does a neat regularity make a conjecture seem likely, and how far can that go?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When cases show a beautiful regularity, take it as a reason to suspect the next case; extend it as far as the pattern runs, and still test it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a pattern in a series into a definite conjecture that can be tested.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A rod's centre of gravity divides the segment between its endpoints in the ratio 1 to 1, a triangle's divides the vertex-to-midpoint line 2 to 1. So the tetrahedron's divides vertex-to-face-centre 3 to 1. The book says the feeling that simple order cannot deceive guides discoverers, as expressed in the Latin saying simplex sigillum veri.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A rod gives 1 to 1, a triangle 2 to 1, so a tetrahedron is predicted at 3 to 1. For vertices (0,0,0), (4,0,0), (0,4,0), (0,0,4) the vertex-average (1,1,1) sits three quarters of the way to the face-centre, which is 3 to 1.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a feeling of harmony is a guide and not a proof.

card.rule: Extend the numbers of the series by their regularity, and test the extension.
card.limits: The book says it appears extremely unlikely that such regularity would fail, not that it cannot fail.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Precise analogies: shared laws and isomorphism
concepts.question: How exact can an analogy become in mathematics, and what are the exact forms called?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In mathematics, an analogy can be exact: shared laws between two systems, a one-to-one match that keeps relations (isomorphism), or a one-to-many match that keeps them (homomorphism).

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To name the sharpest forms of analogy so they can be used with confidence.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book lists three exact cases. First, two systems whose relations obey the same laws, such as rectangle sides and box faces. Second, a one-one correspondence preserving relations, called isomorphism. Third, a one-many correspondence preserving relations, called merohedral isomorphism or homomorphism.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our example: the seven weekdays and the numbers 0 to 6 match one to one, and the relation next day matches adding 1 around the cycle. That is isomorphism. Many calendar dates map to one weekday, preserving next day; that is a one-many match, as in homomorphism.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book does not explore the advanced uses, so this card stops at the definitions.

card.rule: Check the type of correspondence between the systems and name it.
card.limits: The book says merohedral isomorphism is important in advanced study, such as group theory, and need not be discussed in detail.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: What an auxiliary element is
concepts.question: What is an auxiliary element, and what forms can it take?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Name each addition you make to a problem as an auxiliary element: something introduced in the hope that it furthers the solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make the growth of your picture of the problem a deliberate tool and not an accident.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book notes there is much more in our conception of a problem at the end of our work than at the start. We add elements as we go. Such an element is called auxiliary if we add it in the hope of furthering the solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In geometry it may be a new line in the figure, an auxiliary line. In algebra it may be an auxiliary unknown. In proofs it may be an auxiliary theorem, whose proof we undertake to promote the solution of the original problem.

card.rule: Add elements on purpose, and say what each one is for.
card.limits: Our reading: the label describes the hope behind the addition, so an element is auxiliary only while it is there to serve the original problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Two good reasons to add an element
concepts.question: When is it a good idea to add something to the problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Add an element when it lets you use a known related problem, or when you go back to a definition and need its parts visible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make a recollected result or a definition actually usable in the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If you recall a solved problem about triangles but your figure has no triangle, you must introduce one by adding lines. Likewise, a definition cannot be used concretely unless its elements appear: explaining a circle by its centre and radius means drawing them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A figure shows two lines meeting a circle and you need the fact about equal radii. Draw the centre and the two radii. Without them the definition of a circle stays a statement, and the book calls such a definition without a drawing lip-service.

card.rule: Ask whether adding an element makes a known result or a definition usable.
card.limits: The book says these are among the best reasons but not the only ones.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Have a reason; do not add wantonly
concepts.question: Why should an added element always have some reason behind it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Add an element only for some reason, even a hunch, and never wantonly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep the figure or setup useful and to avoid clutter that hides the solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book allows elements added to make the problem fuller, more suggestive or more familiar, before we know how they will be used. We may just feel it is a bright idea to see the problem that way. Still, there should be some reason, and elements must not be added without one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver adds a midpoint to a segment because it is a natural, familiar point, hoping it will suggest something. That is a reason, though a vague one. Adding ten random lines hoping one will help has no reason.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A weak reason can still fail, and the added element may be wasted.

card.rule: Before adding, say why: what does it connect to or make visible?
card.limits: The reason may be only a hope; the book does not demand a proof that the element will work.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Ask whether all the data is used
concepts.question: How can a missing piece of the data tell you what to add?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check each datum against your figure; a datum that does not appear in it tells you what to introduce.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make sure the figure represents the whole problem, and to find where an auxiliary element is needed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book's construction problem gives an angle, the altitude from its vertex, and the perimeter of the triangle. Notation and a figure easily place the angle and altitude. Asking whether all the data is used shows that the perimeter is missing, so it must be introduced into the figure.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Construct a triangle given one angle, the altitude from the vertex of that angle, and the perimeter. After placing the angle and altitude, the perimeter p appears nowhere. That gap tells the solver to find a way to show a length equal to p in the figure.

card.rule: Count the data; put the missing item into the figure by an auxiliary element.
card.limits: Our reading: finding a missing datum does not tell you how to place it; that takes further thought.

media.alt: A triangle at the upper right with its apex A, a small arc marking the given angle there, and an upright altitude h from A to the base. A long slanted line labelled p extends down and to the left from the triangle's left side, an awkward attempt to show the perimeter.

A triangle with apex A, an angle arc at A and altitude h to the base. The base line is extended far to the right as a long horizontal segment labelled p, starting at the triangle's left corner. This second attempt also fits the perimeter unevenly onto the figure.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Let symmetry guide where the element goes
concepts.question: How can a symmetry of the problem help you place an auxiliary element?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If two unknowns play the same role, place the new element so that it treats them alike.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To choose a natural, balanced placement and avoid clumsy ones.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The triangle has unknown sides b and c, with a opposite the given angle, and a + b + c equals the perimeter p. Sides b and c are interchangeable, so a good figure should treat them the same way. Attempts that favour one are clumsy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Extend side a to the right by the length b and to the left by the length c. The whole segment then has length b + a + c = p, treating both unknowns alike. This is the placement the book keeps.

card.rule: Ask which parts are interchangeable and keep your addition balanced between them.
card.limits: Our reading: symmetry guides the choice but does not guarantee a solution.

media.alt: A small triangle with apex A, angle arc at A, altitude h, and sides b and c. Its base a is extended on the left by a length equal to b to a point E and on the right by a length equal to c to a point D. Dashed lines join A to E and to D.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Prefer simple, familiar elements
concepts.question: What kind of auxiliary element is a good first try, and what can it reveal?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Introduce elements that are simple and familiar, such as an isosceles triangle, and look at what relations they reveal.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a placement into a relation you can use, in this case a known angle.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: With the length p laid out as the segment ED, the book adds lines AD and AE. Each is the base of an isosceles triangle, a simple and familiar figure. The isosceles triangles show that angle DAE equals half the given angle plus 90 degrees, a simple relation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Triangle ABD is isosceles (BD equals BA), so its angle at D is half of B. Triangle ACE is isosceles, so its angle at E is half of C. Then angle DAE = 180 - B/2 - C/2, which equals 90 + half the given angle, since B + C = 180 minus that angle.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Luck is involved, so the familiar element may not reveal anything useful.

card.rule: Add the elements that bring in familiar shapes, then see what angles or lengths they reveal.
card.limits: The book calls this fortunate: we have been quite lucky.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Explain the motive of a conspicuous step
concepts.question: Why should a surprising auxiliary line come with an explanation of why it was drawn?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you teach or write, show the motive and purpose of an auxiliary step instead of letting it appear from nowhere.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To let students and readers learn about reasoning and invention, not just check that the steps are valid.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book says an intelligent student or reader wants not only to check each step but to know why it was taken. A tricky auxiliary line that appears abruptly and solves the problem leaves readers disappointed, as if cheated. Remarks or carefully chosen questions can explain the motive, though that takes time and effort.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A textbook proof draws a mysterious line and the result follows. A better one says: we need a triangle to use a known result, so we add one, and here is why this line makes it. The reader learns where such lines come from.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Not every audience has the time for it; the book says only that it may be worth while.

card.rule: Give the reason for each conspicuous step in a solution you present.
card.limits: The book admits it takes a lot of time and effort, but says it may be worth while.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: An auxiliary problem is a means, not an end
concepts.question: What is an auxiliary problem, and why does the book say it takes a refined intelligence to use one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem resists a direct attack, pose a separate problem whose only job is to help with the original.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To go around an obstacle that cannot be overcome directly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An auxiliary problem is considered not for its own sake but because its consideration may help solve another problem, the original one. The original is the end; the auxiliary problem is a means. The book contrasts an insect that tries the same windowpane again and again with a person who goes around an obstacle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student cannot solve a long equation directly. She sets it aside and poses a smaller question whose answer will let her return to the equation. The small question is not what she wants; it is the way back to what she wants.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Time spent on an auxiliary problem is time not spent on the original, so it needs a reason.

card.rule: Make the means into a clearly stated problem of its own, keeping the original as the end.
card.limits: The book calls it an important task to learn, or to teach, how to handle auxiliary problems intelligently.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Introduce an auxiliary unknown
concepts.question: How can a new unknown turn a hard-looking equation into an easy one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a part of the equation repeats in a simple way, name it with a new unknown and solve the new equation first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To change a problem into one you already know how to solve, then return to the original unknown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The equation x to the fourth minus 13 x squared plus 36 equals zero looks hard. Observe that x to the fourth is the square of x squared. Setting y equal to x squared gives y squared minus 13 y plus 36 equals zero, a quadratic. Its unknown y is the auxiliary unknown.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Solving the quadratic gives y = 4 or y = 9. Then x squared is 4 or 9, so x = 2, -2, 3 or -3. Our fresh case: x to the fourth minus 5 x squared plus 4 equals zero gives y = 1 or 4, so x = 1, -1, 2 or -2.

card.rule: Name the repeating part by a new letter, solve for it, then go back for the original unknown.
card.limits: Remember to return to x: the solution for y is not yet the answer.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: What you can gain: result, method or both
concepts.question: What can an auxiliary problem give back to the original?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Plan what you will take from the auxiliary problem: its result, its method, or both.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To judge whether an auxiliary problem is worth the effort of solving.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the equation example, the result of the auxiliary problem (y = 4 or 9) gives every possible x. In the box-diagonal example, the auxiliary problem is a rectangle diagonal, a plane problem analogous to but simpler than the solid one, so its method is instructive. Looking closely we can use both its method and its result.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find the diagonal of a box with three edges meeting at a corner, first find the diagonal of a rectangle with two edges meeting at a corner. The method, a right triangle, carries over, and the result becomes one side of a new right triangle.

card.rule: Before investing in an auxiliary problem, ask which of its method and result you expect to use.
card.limits: Our reading: some auxiliary problems turn out to give neither, which is why the book also warns about risk.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Weigh the risk before choosing one
concepts.question: What does an auxiliary problem cost, and how should you decide whether to try one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Count the time and effort an auxiliary problem will take from the original, and choose one for a good reason.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To avoid sinking effort into a detour that gives nothing back.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The time and effort given to an auxiliary problem are taken from the original. If the investigation fails, they may be lost. So judgment is needed in choosing. Good reasons: it looks more accessible, or instructive, or has aesthetic appeal. Sometimes it is chosen only because it is new, when all approaches to the original seem exhausted.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student stuck on a proof for an hour tries a special case, because it looks more accessible than the general one. If the special case is solved quickly, she gains a method. If not, an hour is spent for nothing.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A failed auxiliary problem costs time that cannot be recovered.

card.rule: Pick an auxiliary problem that looks accessible or instructive, and keep an eye on the cost.
card.limits: The book allows novelty as a reason when you are tired of the original, but that is the weakest ground.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: No infallible way to find one
concepts.question: Is there a sure method for discovering a suitable auxiliary problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect no sure recipe; use the helpful questions, such as looking at the unknown and varying the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep trying sensible questions without expecting a guarantee.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book says that the discovery of the solution often depends on the discovery of a suitable auxiliary problem. There is no infallible method, just as there is none for the solution itself. However, some questions and suggestions are frequently helpful. One is to look at the unknown. Another is variation of the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student stuck on finding a missing side asks: what is the unknown, and what do I know of problems with this kind of unknown? She also varies the problem by changing a number, hoping to meet a problem she can solve.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book promises no guarantee.

card.rule: Look at the unknown and vary the problem to generate candidate auxiliary problems.
card.limits: The questions are frequently helpful, not always.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Equivalent problems and convertible reduction
concepts.question: When are two problems equivalent, and why is an equivalent auxiliary problem especially useful?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Call two problems equivalent when solving each solves the other; reducing one to the other in this way is a convertible reduction.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To switch to a version of a problem that is easier or more foreseeably easier without losing anything.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two problems are equivalent if the solution of each involves the solution of the other. Take theorem A, in an equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees, and theorem B, in an equiangular triangle each angle is 60 degrees. Each follows from the other, so proving A is equivalent to proving B.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove A we may introduce B as an auxiliary problem. B is a little easier, and we can foresee that: B speaks only about angles and is more homogeneous than A, which speaks about both angles and sides. The passage from A to B is called a convertible (bilateral, equivalent) reduction.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Equivalence needs checking; similar-looking problems are not always equivalent.

card.rule: When possible, replace the problem by an equivalent one that looks simpler.
card.limits: Convertible reductions are in a certain respect more desirable, but non-equivalent auxiliary problems may be useful too.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Chains of equivalent problems
concepts.question: How can a sequence of equivalent problems lead from an unsolved problem to an easy one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot solve A, find an equivalent B, then an equivalent C, and continue until the last problem has a known or immediate solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To pass from the original to an easy problem without losing or gaining any solutions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Suppose A is equivalent to B, B to C, and so on to a last problem L whose solution is known. Each problem is equivalent to the one before, so L is equivalent to A, and the solution of A follows from L. The book notes that Greek mathematicians noticed such chains, as in a passage of Pappus.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book's equation chain runs: x to the fourth minus 13 x squared plus 36 equals 0; then, through intermediate forms, the square of (2 x squared minus 13) equals 25; then 2 x squared minus 13 equals plus or minus 5; then x squared equals (13 plus or minus 5) over 2; finally x equals 3, -3, 2 or -2.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book notes its example differs from Pappus's chain: all problems here share the same unknown and differ only in the condition.

card.rule: Make each link a small, clearly purposeful step, and keep every link equivalent.
card.limits: One non-equivalent link breaks the guarantee for the whole chain.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Check that each reduction stays equivalent
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a step narrows or widens the condition, and how do you guard against it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: At every step ask whether the new condition is equivalent to the original: narrowing loses solutions, widening admits false ones.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep the final answer exactly the set of solutions of the original problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Equivalent conditions are satisfied by the same objects. A narrower condition loses solutions; a wider one admits improper, adventitious solutions with no link to the problem. If we narrow and then widen, we may lose track of the original problem completely. So check each new condition's nature.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Dividing x squared equals 3 x by x gives x equals 3 and loses the solution 0 (a narrowing). Squaring both sides of the square root of (x + 2) equal to x gives x + 2 = x squared, with roots 2 and -1; -1 is a false solution (a widening).

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Checking candidate answers in the original condition catches false ones but cannot recover lost ones.

card.rule: After each transformation, ask: Is it equivalent to the original condition?
card.limits: The book says this matters even more for systems of equations and for conditions not given by equations, as in construction problems.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Unilateral reduction: more or less ambitious
concepts.question: What is a unilateral reduction, and why is it riskier than a convertible one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When two problems are not equivalent, work out which is more ambitious, and expect any move to the other kind to carry more risk.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To use non-equivalent auxiliary problems knowingly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let A and B both be unsolved. If solving A would give B in full, but solving B would not give A in full, then A is the more ambitious and B the less ambitious problem. A step from the original to either a more or a less ambitious problem is called a unilateral reduction, and the book says both are more risky than a convertible reduction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A planner wants a menu for every day of a month (A). Solving it gives a menu for any single day (B), but a menu for one day does not give the month. So A is more ambitious than B. Moving from A to B, or from B to A, is unilateral.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A unilateral step can still be the best move, but it needs more care.

card.rule: Decide which problem would give the other, and note that this lopsided link is the price.
card.limits: Our reading: the label describes a relation between problems, not a verdict that the step is wrong.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: A less ambitious problem as a stepping stone
concepts.question: How can a less ambitious auxiliary problem help with the original?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Solve a less ambitious special case, then add a supplementary remark that carries the result to the original.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To get a foothold on a problem that is too big to attack at once.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the book's box-diagonal example, a box with length a, width b and height c would, if solved, give the flat case by putting c equal to 0, a rectangle with length a and width b. So the flat case is less ambitious. With some luck, its solution combined with a suitable supplementary remark gives the original.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The rectangle diagonal is the special case. The supplementary remark is that the box diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the rectangle diagonal and the height c. So the diagonal squared equals a squared plus b squared plus c squared. With a=1, b=2, c=2 it is 3.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The supplementary remark may be the hard part.

card.rule: Pick a special case, solve it, then ask what extra step reaches the original.
card.limits: The book says with some luck: the stepping stone may not lead across.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: A more ambitious problem can be easier
concepts.question: Why might a harder-looking, more ambitious problem still be easier to solve?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Consider replacing the problem by a more ambitious one; it may be more accessible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find a path when the special case gives too little to work with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A unilateral reduction to a more ambitious problem may also succeed. The book says the more ambitious problem may be more accessible, and calls this the inventor's paradox. It points to Generalization and to Induction and Mathematical Induction for examples.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our example: asked to prove a fact about the sum of the first 5 odd numbers, a student proves it for the first n odd numbers. The general statement carries a pattern that the single case hides. The book gives no such example in this article.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A more ambitious problem can be harder; the paradox is that it sometimes is not.

card.rule: Try generalising the problem when the special case offers no foothold.
card.limits: The book says such a reduction may be successful, not that it always is.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: Bolzano: state the rules able people already follow
concepts.question: What did Bolzano claim, and not claim, about the rules of investigation he set out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you write down a method, state clearly the procedures able people already follow, and do not promise novelty.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make unconscious good practice explicit so that others can learn and apply it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Bolzano (1781 to 1848) was a logician and mathematician who devoted an extensive part of his logic, the Wissenschaftslehre, to heuristic. He writes that he does not think he can present any procedure not already perceived by talented people, and he promises nothing quite new. He aims to put clearly the ways that able people follow without being conscious of them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A cook writes down the habits of a skilled chef who never noticed them: taste early, season in stages, rest the meat. None is new, but writing them in clear words lets a beginner follow them.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Making unconscious practice explicit may not fully capture it.

card.rule: Aim to make existing good practice explicit and usable.
card.limits: Bolzano is modest: he doubts he will fully succeed, and hopes only that the little presented may please some people and have some application.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: A bright idea is a sudden advance
concepts.question: What is a bright idea, and how did Aristotle describe the quality behind it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recognise a bright idea as a sudden advance toward the solution, a quick guess at the essential connection.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To name an experience everyone knows so that it can be discussed, noticed and valued.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Bright idea, good idea or seeing the light is a colloquial expression for a sudden advance toward the solution. Conceiving one is an act of sagacity. The book quotes Aristotle, who defined sagacity as hitting by guess upon the essential connection in an inappreciable time.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Aristotle's first example: seeing a person talk with a rich man in a certain way, you guess at once that the person is trying to borrow money. The book calls this not bad but trivial: not much sagacity is needed and the idea is not very bright.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: A quick guess may be wrong; sagacity is the quality of hitting the connection, not just guessing.

card.rule: Look for the essential connection, and judge how bright an idea is by how much it explains.
card.limits: Our reading: the brightness depends on how hard the connection was to see.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
concepts.title: The moon: a bright idea in its setting
concepts.question: Why does the book rate Aristotle's moon example as impressive?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To judge an idea fairly, put it back in its time and see what the thinker knew and lacked.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To appreciate how much a leap of imagination achieved, not just how simple the answer looks.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Aristotle's second example: noticing that the bright side of the moon always faces the sun, you perceive why: the moon shines by the sun's light. The book asks us to imagine a person who had no wristwatches or street lights, who watched the sky for time and travel, and who saw the full moon as a flat disc.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: He found that the bright side of the moon is always toward the sun. Then he saw that the moon's changing shapes resemble a ball lit from one side. He conceived sun and moon as round bodies, one giving light and one receiving it, and rearranged his conceptions instantly: a leap of imagination.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the same rearrangement can look trivial to someone who already holds the answer.

card.rule: When judging a discovery, recover what was known then and how the pieces were rearranged.
card.limits: The book calls this a flash of genius.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Test a numerical result against the real world
concepts.question: Does my numerical answer fit what could actually be observed?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare a numerical result with observed numbers or with a commonsense estimate before you trust it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Trust in the solution, and solidity in what you know.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Problems that arise from practical needs aim at facts, so an answer that clashes with observable facts is probably wrong.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student reports a boat 16,130 feet long and a captain aged 8 years 2 months who is known to be a grandfather, and is not troubled.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author reads such neglect as indifference toward artificial problems, not as stupidity. Our reading: a comparison with the world cannot catch a wrong number that still looks believable.

card.rule: Compare a numerical result with observed numbers or with a commonsense estimate before you trust it.
card.limits: It works only for quantities that can be set beside something observable; an invented quantity has nothing to be compared with.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Test a letter formula on special cases
concepts.question: What happens to my formula when a letter takes a value for which I already know the answer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Test a result in letters by specialization: give the letters values for which you know the answer and see whether the formula agrees.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch a wrong formula before you rely on it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A formula in letters must fit the cases it contains, so a known case that disagrees shows the formula is wrong.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A square frustum has lower side a, upper side b and height h, with volume \(\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3}h\). If b equals a the solid is a prism and the formula gives \(a^2h\). If b is 0 it is a pyramid and the formula gives \(a^2h/3\).

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a formula can pass a few special cases and still be wrong elsewhere, so passing raises trust without proving anything.

card.rule: Test a result in letters by specialization: give the letters values for which you know the answer and see whether the formula agrees.
card.limits: Special cases help only when you know the true answer for them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Test a result by its dimension
concepts.question: Does my formula have the right dimension: length, area or volume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check that the expression has the dimension the quantity should have: a cube of a length for a volume, a square for an area.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch a formula whose terms cannot belong together.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A volume is a cube of a length, so any correct volume formula must come out as a length cubed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The frustum volume \(\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3}h\) has terms \(a^2\), \(ab\), \(b^2\), each a length squared, times h, a length, so the whole is a cube of a length.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The test cannot see a wrong pure number, such as a factor of 3 where 2 belongs, because numbers carry no dimension. Our reading.

card.rule: Check that the expression has the dimension the quantity should have: a cube of a length for a volume, a square for an area.
card.limits: It says nothing about numerical constants.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Test a result by varying the data
concepts.question: When one datum grows, does my result move the way the situation says it should?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Vary the data in your head: if a quantity grows, check that the result grows or shrinks as the situation demands.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch a formula that moves the wrong way.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A correct result responds to a change in the data in the direction the problem itself dictates.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the frustum volume, if any one of the positive quantities a, b or h increases, the value of the expression increases, as a larger solid should.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The test says nothing about how big the change should be. Our reading: a formula can move the right way and still be wrong.

card.rule: Vary the data in your head: if a quantity grows, check that the result grows or shrinks as the situation demands.
card.limits: It needs a clear expectation of the direction, and some quantities have none.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Test intermediate results and prepare problems for testing
concepts.question: Can I test the steps on the way, and can I put the numbers into letters first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Apply the tests to intermediate results as well as the final one, and turn a problem in numbers into a problem in letters so that the tests become possible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a mistake close to where it was made, with more tests available.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Letters allow specialization, dimension and variation tests that a bare number does not, and a checked step is a safe base for the next.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A box has edges 3, 4 and 12. The face diagonal is 5 and the box diagonal is 13. Written with letters l, b and h, the same working shows a face diagonal \(\sqrt{l^2+b^2}\), which has the dimension of a length and grows with each edge.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: turning numbers into letters costs extra work, so it pays when the result will be reused or the numbers hide a pattern.

card.rule: Apply the tests to intermediate results as well as the final one, and turn a problem in numbers into a problem in letters so that the tests become possible.
card.limits: A one-off numerical answer that is easy to compare with the world may not need letters.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Vary the order when you re-check an argument
concepts.question: If I must go through an argument again, how do I avoid repeating my earlier slip?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you check an argument step by step, avoid plain repetition; at least change the order of the steps or their grouping.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A re-check that can find what the first pass missed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Plain repetition is boring, teaches little and strains attention, and where you stumbled once you are likely to stumble again in the same circumstances.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student re-adds a column of figures downward, gets the same total, and feels sure. Adding the same figures upward, or in pairs, gives a new path through the same sum.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The advice is to vary, not to skip the re-check. If the whole argument must be re-run, the variation is the minimum.

card.rule: When you check an argument step by step, avoid plain repetition; at least change the order of the steps or their grouping.
card.limits: It applies when you decide a full re-run is needed; the next idea says to pick a weak point first.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Examine the weakest point first
concepts.question: Which point of my argument is the weakest, and have I tested it first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pick out the weakest point of the argument and examine it first; the question Did you use all the data? helps you find such points.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A check that costs less effort and is more interesting.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: It takes less effort and is more interesting to start where the argument is most likely to break than to go through every step evenly.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver finds the height of a ladder against a wall and realises one given length was never used. That unused datum is the first place to look, since a good solution normally needs every datum.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: a datum that was never used is a hint, not a proof of error, because a problem can contain a redundant datum.

card.rule: Pick out the weakest point of the argument and examine it first; the question Did you use all the data? helps you find such points.
card.limits: If no weak point stands out, go back to a step-by-step check with variation.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Knowledge rests on tests as well as on proofs
concepts.question: According to the author, what does our knowledge of mathematics rest on besides formal proofs?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat each successful test of a result as widening the experimental base on which your knowledge stands.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Solid knowledge that is more than a chain of formal proofs.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, everyday knowledge is tested and strengthened by experience, and mathematical knowledge too has a broad experimental basis that each tested result widens.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author notes that natural sciences test by careful experiments and measurements, combined in the physical sciences with mathematical reasoning.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author calls whether mathematics could rest on formal proofs alone a philosophical question he does not debate; this card reports his stated view only.

card.rule: Treat each successful test of a result as widening the experimental base on which your knowledge stands.
card.limits: This is the author's own claim, offered without extended argument.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
concepts.title: Look for a second derivation of a result
concepts.question: Can I reach the same result a second way, or see it at a glance?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Even after a satisfactory solution, try to derive the result differently and, if the first route was long, look for a clearer one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Greater conviction, and often a clearer and shorter route.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author compares two derivations to perceiving an object through two senses, as one wants to touch what one has seen; two proofs are safer than one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Having found the lateral surface of a frustum of a cone by subtracting a small cone's surface from a large one, we may ask whether the result can be seen at a glance, and set out to find a clearer argument.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book notes that when a solution is long and involved we naturally suspect a less roundabout one; that suspicion is a hint, not a guarantee that one exists. Our reading.

card.rule: Even after a satisfactory solution, try to derive the result differently and, if the first route was long, look for a clearer one.
card.limits: Time is limited, and the author says the search is more likely to pay for an experienced solver with an advanced problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
concepts.title: Find the geometric meaning of each part of a result
concepts.question: What does each piece of my formula mean in the figure?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To see a result intuitively, look for the geometric meaning of each part of it in turn.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A clearer view of why the result holds.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A part of a formula that you can read as a length, a mean or a perimeter stops being a symbol and starts being something you can see.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the lateral surface of a cone frustum with base radii R and r and height h, the formula is \(\pi(R+r)\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}\). The root is the slant height; \(\pi(R+r)\) is the mean of the two base perimeters, and the perimeter of the mid-section.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the method needs a formula with parts that have a plain meaning; some parts may offer none, and then you move to another part.

card.rule: To see a result intuitively, look for the geometric meaning of each part of it in turn.
card.limits: It does not promise an interpretation for every part.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
concepts.title: See the whole result in a different light
concepts.question: After reading the parts, can I restate the whole result as a familiar rule?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the interpreted parts together and restate the whole result in words, then compare it with a familiar statement.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To see the result almost at a glance and to find a shorter proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Once each part has a meaning, the whole formula reads as a statement, and a statement can resemble one you already know.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The frustum surface reads: area equals perimeter of the mid-section times slant height. This echoes the trapezoid rule, area equals middle-line times altitude.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says we then feel near a short direct proof; it does not say the proof is yet found. Our reading: the analogy points the way and needs work.

card.rule: Put the interpreted parts together and restate the whole result in words, then compare it with a familiar statement.
card.limits: An analogy can mislead if the likeness is only in form.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
concepts.title: Study the result itself to find a better proof
concepts.question: What new aspect of my result could suggest a shorter proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you are not satisfied with a derivation, study the result: find a new reading of one part, then of another, until the whole looks different.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new proof that is clearer than the first.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Small advances accumulate: a new reading of one small part, then of another, may lead to seeing the whole result differently, and that view may suggest a new proof.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The frustum example is typical. We read the slant height, then the mean perimeter, then the mid-section, then the whole formula, each step small.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book admits the search can fail, and that luck plays a part when we are 'lucky enough' to find a new conception of a part. Our reading.

card.rule: When you are not satisfied with a derivation, study the result: find a new reading of one part, then of another, until the whole looks different.
card.limits: It is slow and may not find a shorter route at all.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
concepts.title: Experts and beginners find shorter routes differently
concepts.question: Who is better placed to find the shorter route, and what should a teacher do?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Teach students at least once or twice how to solve a problem more shortly and how to find, in the result itself, signs of a shorter solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Students who can improve their own long solutions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, an experienced mathematician may mobilise too much knowledge and frame an unnecessarily involved argument, yet is better placed to appreciate a new reading of a small part.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Even in very elementary classes, students can present an unnecessarily complicated solution; then the teacher shows the shorter way.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author's view of experts and beginners is a general observation, not a rule; individuals will differ. Our reading.

card.rule: Teach students at least once or twice how to solve a problem more shortly and how to find, in the result itself, signs of a shorter solution.
card.limits: The advice assumes there is a shorter route to be found.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Exploit your success
concepts.question: Having solved a problem, what else can its result or its method solve?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After solving a problem, ask whether the result or the method can be used for some other problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: More from every discovery, and possibly something better than the first problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author counts even a modest solution found by your own means as a discovery, and a discovery may have more behind it than the problem that led to it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student who found a formula for a box's diagonal asks next which other questions the same formula answers, such as the radius of a sphere around the box.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book warns that the search for new problems is unlimited in theory but in practice is seldom carried far.

card.rule: After solving a problem, ask whether the result or the method can be used for some other problem.
card.limits: It does not say every success leads to something worth pursuing.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Derive new problems by the main means of variation
concepts.question: Which means can I use to turn one solved problem into others?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: From a solved problem, derive others by generalization, specialization, analogy, and decomposing and recombining.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A supply of new problems from one starting point.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each new problem can serve as a starting point for more, so the supply is unlimited in theory.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From the problem of the diagonal of a box, the book derives problems by each of these means, such as the cube with a given edge by specialization.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: In practice we seldom carry the process far, because the problems obtained this way tend to be inaccessible.

card.rule: From a solved problem, derive others by generalization, specialization, analogy, and decomposing and recombining.
card.limits: The process needs the solver to stop when problems become too remote.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Find problems that are both interesting and accessible
concepts.question: When I vary a problem, how do I find a new one that is both worth solving and within reach?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When deriving new problems, aim for ones that are both interesting and accessible; expect that this takes experience, taste and good luck.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: New problems that reward the effort of solving them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, problems that are easy because they follow from the old solution tend to be uninteresting, while the interesting ones tend to be inaccessible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the box example, adding a new notion to the problem leaves it easy to solve because the notion is easily removed; the book calls some of the resulting problems interesting.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: easy and interesting are not opposites; the author says only that the combination is not easy to find.

card.rule: When deriving new problems, aim for ones that are both interesting and accessible; expect that this takes experience, taste and good luck.
card.limits: No rule is given that guarantees the combination.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Look around after a good problem
concepts.question: Where should I look for further good problems once I have found one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Having found a good problem, look around for more nearby; good problems grow in clusters like certain mushrooms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A richer harvest from each find.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says good problems and mushrooms of certain kinds have something in common: they grow in clusters, so a find makes more nearby likely.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After solving the box-diagonal problem, the book lists neighbours: the sphere around a box, the pyramid on a rectangle, and the distance between two points given by coordinates.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book does not promise that the neighbours are all worth solving; some were easy and some merely interesting.

card.rule: Having found a good problem, look around for more nearby; good problems grow in clusters like certain mushrooms.
card.limits: It does not tell how large a cluster is.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Add a notion that is easy to remove
concepts.question: Can I make a new problem by adding a notion that can later be stripped off?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To make an easy new problem from a solved one, add some new notion that is easily eliminated, then fall back on the original problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: New solvable problems that exercise the old solution in a fresh dress.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because the added notion is easily added and easily eliminated, the new problem is scarcely different from the old one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Given the three dimensions of a box, find the diagonal. Add a circumscribed sphere and ask its radius, which is half the diagonal: for edges 3, 4 and 12 the diagonal is 13 and the radius 6.5.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book notes the new problems are easy but their interest depends on the notion added; coordinates make the distance problem important.

card.rule: To make an easy new problem from a solved one, add some new notion that is easily eliminated, then fall back on the original problem.
card.limits: If the notion cannot be removed easily, the new problem is not easy.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Swap the unknown with one of the data
concepts.question: Can I treat the old unknown as given and one of the old data as unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To get an easy new problem from a solved one, regard the original unknown as given and one of the original data as the unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new problem solved by the same relation, without new work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The solution of the original problem is a relation among the unknown and the data; if all but one of its quantities are known, the last follows from the relation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A box has length 2, breadth 3 and diagonal 7. Its height h satisfies \(2^2+3^2+h^2=7^2\), so \(h^2=36\) and h is 6.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book contrasts this pattern with the add-a-notion pattern; they are different ways to get new problems.

card.rule: To get an easy new problem from a solved one, regard the original unknown as given and one of the original data as the unknown.
card.limits: It works only if you can solve the relation for the quantity that is now unknown.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Derive problems by generalization, specialization and analogy
concepts.question: Which derived problems follow at once from the solution, and which do not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Derive problems from a solved one by generalization, specialization and analogy, and expect only the specialization to be solvable at once.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know which derived problems your solution already covers.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A specialization is a case of the problem solved, so its solution is a case of yours; a generalization or analogy changes the problem too much for that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From the box diagonal, a generalization asks the diagonal given three edges and the three angles between them. A specialization is the cube with given edge, whose diagonal is the edge times the root of 3. Analogies include the regular octahedron.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says all these are interesting, but only the specialization can be solved immediately from the solution of the original problem.

card.rule: Derive problems from a solved one by generalization, specialization and analogy, and expect only the specialization to be solvable at once.
card.limits: Even a specialization can be easy and dull, as the earlier idea warns. Our reading.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Let an element of the problem vary
concepts.question: What happens if I treat a fixed element of the problem as variable?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Derive new problems by letting a fixed element vary, and ask which values of the varying quantity are critical.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new and richer problem, with its own interesting values.

blocks.label: Why it works
