blocks.text: A moving element passes through special positions where something changes, and those positions pose questions with exact answers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A cube has a sphere with the same center. As the radius grows, the sphere touches the faces, then the edges, then passes through the vertices. For edge 2 the three radii are 1, root 2 and root 3.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the critical values can be found only if the moments are well defined; the book names three here.

card.rule: Derive new problems by letting a fixed element vary, and ask which values of the varying quantity are critical.
card.limits: It needs a figure that changes in an ordered way.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Solve problems of your own invention
concepts.question: Have I ever solved a problem I invented myself?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give students the chance to invent problems from one solved: the teacher may show how and leave part of the invention to them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Mathematical experience that is complete.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, a student who never solved a problem of his own invention has incomplete mathematical experience; showing how problems derive from a solved one provokes curiosity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After describing the growing sphere, the teacher may ask: what would you try to calculate, and which value of the radius is particularly interesting?

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The author leaves part of the invention to the students; he does not say every invention will be good. Our reading.

card.rule: Give students the chance to invent problems from one just solved: the teacher may show how and leave part of the invention to them.
card.limits: It needs time in class that may not exist.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Plausible arguments to plan, strict arguments to carry out
concepts.question: Which kind of argument may I accept while devising the plan, and which when carrying it out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use provisional and plausible reasoning freely while devising the plan, but accept only conclusive, strict arguments when carrying it out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A final solution that stands on rigorous argument alone.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Plausible arguments work like scaffolding for a bridge: they support the work while it is built, and when it is advanced they are taken off and the bridge must stand by itself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student guesses from a few cases that a pattern holds, uses the guess to find the idea of a proof, and then proves it step by step without relying on the cases.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Anything that leads to the right idea is right in devising; but the book does not allow plausible reasoning to remain in the final argument.

card.rule: Use provisional and plausible reasoning freely while devising the plan, but accept only conclusive, strict arguments when carrying it out.
card.limits: A step that still rests on a plausible guess is scaffolding left in the bridge.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Check each step while carrying out the plan
concepts.question: Can I see clearly that each step of my plan is correct?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Carrying out your plan, check each step by asking: can you see clearly that the step is correct?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A solution in which every step has been examined.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Conceiving a plan is different from carrying it through, and carrying it through means examining each step in turn.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver working a long calculation stops after each line and asks whether the line follows from the previous one, before writing the next.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book does not say a check is needed after the plan is complete only; each step is examined when it is met.

card.rule: Carrying out your plan, check each step by asking: can you see clearly that the step is correct?
card.limits: Checking does not replace understanding the plan as a whole.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Work out the details in proper order
concepts.question: In what order should I work out and write down the details of a complex plan?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Work out the details in proper order: do not check minor details before the major steps are sound, and expect the orders of inventing, working out and writing down to differ.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A complex solution without omitted details or lost connections.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A break in the main line makes any check of a secondary detail useless, and the order of invention, of working out and of the final exposition may each be different.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver of a long problem first confirms that the main steps lead from data to unknown, and only then checks the arithmetic of a secondary calculation.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book does not set a single fixed order for all problems; it asks for a reasonable one that omits no detail.

card.rule: Work out the details in proper order: do not check minor details before the major steps are sound, and expect the orders of inventing, working out and writing down to differ.
card.limits: In a simple problem, the main line and the details may be too few to need ordering.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Argue from the data to the unknown, step by step
concepts.question: In what direction do Euclid's arguments run, and why does that make checking easy?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In the Euclidean way every argument runs from the data toward the unknown, or from the hypothesis toward the conclusion, and each new element or assertion is examined once.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A complete, detailed check of an argument.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each new element or assertion has to be correctly derived from the data or from steps already correct, so the whole argument is correct if each step is, including the last one, the unknown or the conclusion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A proof by Euclid builds a construction from the given points, checking each new point as it is made; the last new element to be checked is the unknown.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says nothing in this order needs to look ahead or back, which is exactly why it suits checking but not teaching.

card.rule: In the Euclidean way every argument runs from the data toward the unknown, or from the hypothesis toward the conclusion, and each new element or assertion is examined once.
card.limits: It does not show where the argument is going.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: The Euclidean order checks well but explains poorly
concepts.question: For what purpose is the Euclidean exposition recommended, and for what is it not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the Euclidean way to examine an argument in detail, especially your own; do not rely on it alone to convey an argument to someone who has not heard of it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Both a checked argument and a reader who understands its main line.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The Euclidean order shows each point well but hides the source, purpose and connection of the whole, because it often proceeds in the opposite order to the natural order of invention.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A reader of a pure Euclidean proof can see that each step is correct and yet have trouble seeing why the argument is what it is.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book recommends the Euclidean way without reservation for detailed checking, but not without reservation for conveying.

card.rule: Use the Euclidean way to examine an argument in detail, especially your own; do not rely on it alone to convey an argument to someone who has not heard of it.
card.limits: It suits an author who already surveyed the argument on large lines.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: What to ask of students and what to present
concepts.question: How much Euclidean exposition should students write and teachers present?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Encourage students to examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner, without enforcing it rigidly; present intuitive sketches before details.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Students who check carefully and also see the main idea.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author, the Euclidean presentation is useful after a discussion in which students, guided by the teacher, found the main idea independently, and an intuitive sketch can come before the details.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher guides the class until the students find the main idea of a proof themselves, and only afterwards sets the details out in the Euclidean order.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: These are the author's recommendations and he says nothing of this kind should be too rigidly enforced.

card.rule: Encourage students to examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner, without enforcing it rigidly; present intuitive sketches before details.
card.limits: The advice depends on class time and the aims of the lesson.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: See it and prove it
concepts.question: Can I both see that a statement is true and prove that it is?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Wishing to satisfy yourself that a proposition is true, try to see it intuitively and to give a formal proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Conviction by two different ways of perceiving the truth.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Intuitive insight and formal proof are two ways of perceiving the truth, comparable to sight and touch; the conscientious mathematician, like a shopper judging a fabric, wants both.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Anyone who has understood the terms can see that two straight lines parallel to a third are parallel to each other; yet the proof in Euclid's eleventh book needs a long, careful preparation.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Either way can lag behind the other: a statement you grasp at once may need a long proof, and a proof may leave you with no picture.

card.rule: Wishing to satisfy yourself that a proposition is true, try to see it intuitively and to give a formal proof.
card.limits: Both directions are useful, but neither replaces the other.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Sometimes intuition runs ahead, sometimes proof does
concepts.question: In which cases is intuition ahead of formal reasoning, and in which is formal reasoning ahead?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In checking a step, sometimes intuition is ahead and sometimes formal reasoning is; do the exercise both ways.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A check that does not depend on one way of seeing alone.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Intuition may rush far ahead of proof, as with parallel lines, and formal manipulation may get far ahead of intuition, as with planes dividing space.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Three random lines divide the plane into 7 parts, which we see at once; five random planes divide space into 26 parts, which almost no one sees, yet it is rigidly proved.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: neither way is superior; each can mislead when it runs alone.

card.rule: In checking a step, sometimes intuition is ahead and sometimes formal reasoning is; do the exercise both ways.
card.limits: A formal proof can exist while intuition has no picture of it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Name the condition apart from the unknown and the data
concepts.question: In a problem to find, which part is the condition?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a problem to find, name the unknown, the data and the condition separately; the condition is a principal part.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A problem whose parts you can examine one by one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book lists the condition with the unknown and the data as the principal parts of a problem to find, so a question about each part opens the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Find a number whose double, increased by 3, is 17. The unknown is the number, the data are 3 and 17, and the condition is that twice the number plus 3 equals 17.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the entry is short; it names the condition as a principal part and leaves its detailed treatment to the entries it points to.

card.rule: In a problem to find, name the unknown, the data and the condition separately; the condition is a principal part.
card.limits: It applies to problems to find; problems to prove have a hypothesis and a conclusion instead.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Redundant, contradictory and insufficient conditions
concepts.question: What does it mean for a condition to be redundant, contradictory or insufficient?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Call a condition redundant if it has superfluous parts, contradictory if its parts oppose one another so that nothing satisfies it, and insufficient if it does not fix the unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Judge whether a problem is well posed before you try to solve it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A condition that is contradictory has no solution at all; one that is redundant carries parts you do not need; one that is insufficient leaves the unknown free.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Find x with x greater than 5 and x less than 3 is contradictory. Find x with x equal to 4 and x equal to 2 plus 2 is redundant. Find x with x greater than 5 is insufficient to give one number.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the book gives the first two definitions and the third in the sentence on equations; the examples here are ours.

card.rule: Call a condition redundant if it has superfluous parts, contradictory if its parts oppose one another so that nothing satisfies it, and insufficient if it does not fix the unknown.
card.limits: A redundant condition is harmless but may hide a datum that was never needed.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Count equations against unknowns
concepts.question: What does the number of equations, compared with the number of unknowns, say about a condition?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a condition is a set of linear equations, compare their number with the number of unknowns: more is redundant or contradictory, fewer is insufficient, equal is usually sufficient.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A quick judgment of whether the condition can fix the unknowns.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each independent equation removes one degree of freedom, so equal numbers usually fix the unknowns, with exceptions when equations repeat or conflict.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 there are two equations and two unknowns, giving x = 3 and y = 2.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: counting is a first test only; it does not look inside the equations.

card.rule: When a condition is a set of linear equations, compare their number with the number of unknowns: more is redundant or contradictory, fewer is insufficient, equal is usually sufficient.
card.limits: Counting equations is a first test, not a proof that the unknowns can be found.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: A corollary is a gratuity of a theorem
concepts.question: What is a corollary, and how do I find one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After finding a theorem, examine it for further theorems that come easily out of it; those are corollaries.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: More results for little extra work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A corollary is a theorem we find easily in examining another theorem found, so it costs little beyond the theorem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Having proved that the angles of a triangle add to two right angles, one easily gets that the angles of a four-sided figure add to four right angles by cutting it into two triangles.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book gives only the definition and the origin of the word; the example here is ours.

card.rule: After finding a theorem, examine it for further theorems that come easily out of it; those are corollaries.
card.limits: A corollary comes only as easily as the theorem allows.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: A problem is a gap you can bridge from either side
concepts.question: From which side can I start bridging the gap between the data and the unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Picture the unsolved problem as a gap between the data and the unknown, and start building the bridge from either side.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A connection between data and unknown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each bank offers a place to begin, so if the work from one side stalls you can try the other.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Looking at the unknown, we recall a familiar problem with the same unknown. Looking at the data, we ask what useful thing we can derive from them.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says that starting from the unknown is usually preferable, yet starting from the data has chances of success and must often be tried.

card.rule: Picture the unsolved problem as a gap between the data and the unknown, and start building the bridge from either side.
card.limits: Neither start is certain; if one stalls, try the other.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: Usually start from the unknown, but try the data too
concepts.question: Which start is usually preferable, and why not drop the other?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Starting the reasoning from the unknown is usually preferable; yet starting from the data has chances of success and must often be tried.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A second route when the first stalls.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: According to the author it appears that starting from the unknown is usually preferable, but the alternative start deserves illustration because it often succeeds.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book gives an example where a stranded solver is rescued by the question: could you derive something useful from the data?

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The advice is a tendency, not a rule: it appears usually preferable, not always.

card.rule: Starting the reasoning from the unknown is usually preferable; yet starting from the data has chances of success and must often be tried.
card.limits: Our reading: if both starts fail, change the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: Set up the example: unknown, data, condition, figure
concepts.question: How do I begin a geometric problem: what are the data, the unknown and the condition?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Begin by asking what the data, the unknown and the condition are, and draw a figure that shows them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A figure that holds everything the problem says.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions bring the parts of the problem into the open, and a figure of the data and then of the required relations lets you see the structure.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Three points A, B and C are given. Draw a line through A that passes between B and C and is at equal distances from B and C. The data are the three points, the unknown is a line, and the condition says the line passes through A, between B and C, equidistant from them.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The figure suggested by the definition of the distance of a point from a line shows right angles; that is an inference from the definition, as the book notes.

card.rule: Begin by asking what the data, the unknown and the condition are, and draw a figure that shows them.
card.limits: The figure may still be too empty to reveal a solution.

media.alt: Three isolated dots on a blank field, labelled A on the left, B at the top and C at the lower right. Nothing joins them: it shows only the given data, three points in position, before any line or relation is drawn.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: When the figure is too empty, ask for an auxiliary element
concepts.question: What do I do when my figure does not connect the unknown to the data?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the figure is still too empty and the unknown is not connected to the data, look for an auxiliary line or other addition.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A figure rich enough to show the solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An unknown that is only loosely tied to the data cannot be pinned down; an auxiliary element can supply the missing tie.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the three-point example, the unknown line is not well connected with A, B and C, so the figure needs some addition, and a fairly good student can be stranded.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says there are various things to try, but the best question to refloat the student is the one about the data.

card.rule: If the figure is still too empty and the unknown is not connected to the data, look for an auxiliary line or other addition.
card.limits: Adding elements at random can clutter the figure.

media.alt: A long horizontal line starts at the dot A. Two short segments stand at right angles to it, one rising above the line toward the upper side and one dropping below it further right; each ends in a dot for B and C. It shows the unknown line with perpendicular distances.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: Use all the data: with two points, join them
concepts.question: Have I used each datum, and what can I do with just two points?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask what you have not yet used among the data, and derive something from it; with two points alone, join them by a straight line.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new element that brings the unused data into the figure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The points B and C have not been used enough, and the one thing you can do with two points is to join them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the example, joining B and C gives a new figure that can be laid over the figure of the unknown line.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The step is easy, but the book notes that what is gained appears only after the two figures are put together.

card.rule: Ask what you have not yet used among the data, and derive something from it; with just two points, join them by a straight line.
card.limits: Joining two points helps only when the line they define matters to the problem.

media.alt: Three dots on a blank field: an unlabelled point A on the left, and B near the top right joined to C at the lower right by a thick straight segment. The only new element compared with the plain data figure is the segment BC.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: Put the figures together and look
concepts.question: What do I see when I lay the figure of the data over the figure of the relations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the figure of the data and the figure of the required relations together and study what the combination shows.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A solution that appears in a flash.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each figure holds part of the problem; laid over one another, the parts can meet and show a link that neither shows alone.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the three-point example, the figure with the required line and the perpendiculars from B and C is laid over the figure in which B and C are joined.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says the solution may appear in a flash, not that it will.

card.rule: Put the figure of the data and the figure of the required relations together and study what the combination shows.
card.limits: It depends on seeing what the combined figure shows, which takes practice.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
concepts.title: If stuck, restate the problem or go back to definitions
concepts.question: What can I do when neither start works?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When stuck, ask whether you could restate the problem, even differently, and go back to the definitions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new view of the problem when direct attempts stall.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Restating the problem is a way of varying it, and the definitions of its terms can introduce new elements to work with.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the example, the definition of distance from a point to a line led to the right angles in the figure.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book gives these only as suggestions: Could you restate the problem? Could you restate it still differently?

card.rule: When stuck, ask whether you could restate the problem, even differently, and go back to the definitions.
card.limits: Restating does not by itself solve the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Split a whole into parts and join the parts anew
concepts.question: What do decomposing and recombining do to my view of a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Examine an object or a problem by looking at its details one after another, then recombine the parts into a whole you see differently.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A view of the problem that is more definite than the first impression.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A first impression of the whole is seldom definite enough; attending to a detail, then another, then to combinations of details, ends in seeing the whole again, but differently.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: You examine an object whose purpose and origin puzzle you. You have an impression of the whole, a detail strikes you, then another, various combinations of details present themselves, and finally you see the whole again, but differently.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book warns that going into detail may lose you in details.

card.rule: Examine an object or a problem by looking at its details one after another, then recombine the parts into a whole you see differently.
card.limits: Too many or too minute details become a burden on the mind.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Understand the whole first and decompose only as far as needed
concepts.question: How far should I go into detail, and when should I begin?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: First understand the problem as a whole; then decompose gradually, and not further than you need.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Details that serve the main point, not drown it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We cannot say beforehand which details will matter, so understanding the whole first lets us judge which points to examine, and each examined point helps judge the next.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student who starts working at details before understanding the problem as a whole follows, in the book's words, a foolish and bad habit; the man who cannot see the forest for the trees is the image.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book admits teachers cannot expect all students to act wisely in this respect.

card.rule: First understand the problem as a whole; then decompose gradually, and not further than you need.
card.limits: Some problems need detail from the outset, but the book's rule is whole first.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Begin with the unknown, the data and the condition
concepts.question: Where do I start when I go into detail in a problem to find?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To go into detail, begin with the questions: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A start that works in almost every problem to find.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The unknown, the data and the condition are the principal parts, and almost always the reasonable place to begin.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the box problem we ask what is the unknown, the diagonal; what are the data, three edges; what is the condition, the diagonal joins opposite corners. Next we look at each datum alone.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book says almost all cases, not all: other starts exist.

card.rule: To go into detail, begin with the questions: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?
card.limits: The entry says to go further only if needed.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Three formal ways to recombine a problem to find
concepts.question: What can I keep and what can I change when building a new problem from the old?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build a new problem from a proposed one by keeping the unknown and changing the rest, keeping the data and changing the rest, or changing both unknown and data.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A new problem that is more accessible than the old.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: These three cases are the neatly placed classification of the most usual and useful combinations; simpler problems need only these.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book lists: (1) keep the unknown, change data and condition; (2) keep the data, change unknown and condition; (3) change both unknown and data.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The cases (1) and (2) overlap; one can keep both unknown and data and change only the form of the condition.

card.rule: Build a new problem from a proposed one by keeping the unknown and changing the rest, keeping the data and changing the rest, or changing both unknown and data.
card.limits: Difficult problems may need hidden and original combinations beyond these.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Keep the unknown, change the data and the condition
concepts.question: How do I make a related problem that has the same unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look at the unknown and try to recall a solved problem with the same or a similar unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A related problem closer to the proposed one, so it is more likely to help.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem more closely related to the proposed problem has a better chance of being useful, so change as little as feasible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A good method omits something without adding anything: keep the unknown, keep only a part of the condition, drop the other part and add no new clause or datum.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book suggests this as a tendency to prefer; it does not claim it always works.

card.rule: Look at the unknown and try to recall a solved problem with the same or a similar unknown.
card.limits: If recollection fails and invention fails, move to another case.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Keep the data and seek a new, useful unknown
concepts.question: What makes a new unknown worth deriving from the data?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keeping the data, look for a new unknown that is both more accessible than the original and useful for finding it; settle for less if need be.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A stepping stone between the data and the original unknown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The new unknown should be easier to get from the data than the original, and when found should help in the search for the original; a stone mid-creek is nearer than the far bank and helps me on toward it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the diagonal of a box, the diagonal of a face is a new unknown: with it we can get the diagonal of the solid, and it is easy to obtain.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: In practice we may content ourselves with less: something that has some chance of being useful, or an unknown closely connected with the original.

card.rule: Keeping the data, look for a new unknown that is both more accessible than the original and useful for finding it; settle for less if need be.
card.limits: A new unknown may be accessible but useless, or useful but out of reach.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Change both unknown and data only when milder changes fail
concepts.question: When should I change both unknown and data, and what is the risk?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Change both the unknown and the data when milder changes have failed, so that the new unknown and the new data are nearer to each other.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A problem within reach, even at the cost of drifting from the original.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A change this big risks losing the original problem altogether, so it is a last resort, to be accepted when it promises success.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book's triangle example: to construct a triangle from its base a, height h and apex angle, we draw BC equal to a and ask only for the apex A. The unknown changed from a triangle to a point, and the datum a became two points B and C, while h and the angle stayed.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: We do not like to deviate so far, because we sense the danger of losing the original problem.

card.rule: Change both the unknown and the data when milder changes have failed, so that the new unknown and the new data are nearer to each other.
card.limits: It is not the first thing to try.

media.alt: A triangle with horizontal base BC and apex A at the top. A solid vertical segment h falls from A to the base, which carries the letter a. Dashed lines join A to B and to C, and a small arc at A marks the angle between them. The apex is the unknown point.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Keep only part of the condition and describe what is left
concepts.question: What if I keep only one part of the condition and ask how far the unknown is then determined?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Separate the parts of the condition, keep only one, drop the other, and ask how the unknown can then vary; the answer is a locus or a set of objects.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A weakened problem whose answer is a simple set, from which the full answer comes by intersection.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Weakening the condition leaves the unknown less restricted; describing how it can vary is a new problem, and the solution of the original lies where the two partial answers meet.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Construct a triangle with a given side a, the altitude h on it and the angle opposite. Fix the side BC and ask where the apex can lie: on a parallel at distance h from BC for one part, and on a circular arc through B and C for the other. The apex is where they cross.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book notes that if the unknown is not a point, the new problem is to describe a certain set of objects.

card.rule: Separate the parts of the condition, keep only one, drop the other, and ask how the unknown can then vary; the answer is a locus or a set of objects.
card.limits: The pattern needs a condition that splits into parts that each have a describable set of solutions.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: Separate the condition in a puzzle
concepts.question: How can separating the parts of a clue help me solve a word puzzle?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a puzzle, ask what is unknown and what the condition is, split the condition into parts, and run through the objects that fit one part to see which fit the other.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A candidate list that is checked against the second part.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The meaning and the spelling are two parts of one condition; many words fit the first part alone, and the right one is among them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The clue is 'Forward and backward part of a machine (5 letters)'. One part: a five-letter word for a machine part. The other: spelled backward it gives a machine part again. Lever, screw, wheel, shaft, hinge and motor fit the first part; our reading is that rotor fits both.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: Our reading: the method needs a list of candidates that is not too long to test.

card.rule: In a puzzle, ask what is unknown and what the condition is, split the condition into parts, and run through the objects that fit one part to see which fit the other.
card.limits: The method needs a candidate list that is not too long.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
concepts.title: The same method for problems to prove
concepts.question: How does decomposing and recombining work when I must prove a statement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a problem to prove, take the hypothesis and the conclusion as the principal parts, separate the parts of the hypothesis, and recombine in three ways.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A related theorem close to the one to be proved.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The principal parts of a problem to prove play the part that unknown, data and condition play in a problem to find, and the three recombinations are analogous.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Keep the conclusion and change the hypothesis: recall a theorem with the same or similar conclusion, or keep part of the hypothesis and check whether the conclusion remains.

blocks.label: When it fails
blocks.text: The book gives only a few short remarks for problems to prove.

card.rule: In a problem to prove, take the hypothesis and the conclusion as the principal parts, separate the parts of the hypothesis, and recombine in three ways.
card.limits: Treated at length for problems to find; here only analogous remarks.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: What a definition does
concepts.question: What is a definition, and what must you already know for it to work?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a definition as a statement of a term's meaning in other terms that you are expected to know well.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Grasp a new term by building it from words you already understand.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A definition can only pass meaning along if the words it uses are familiar. The new term is explained by the old ones, so unfamiliar words inside it block the transfer.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The book's definition of the parabola names three new terms (parabola, focus, directrix) and expects the reader to know all the other words it uses.

card.rule: Read a definition as a statement of a term's meaning in other terms that you are expected to know well.
card.limits: Our reading: if you do not know the words a definition is built from, it fails for you. First get those words, then the new term.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Primitive and derived terms
concepts.question: Which terms does mathematics leave undefined, and how are the others defined?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take a few starting terms as primitive and undefined, and define every other term from primitive or earlier defined terms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Build a whole vocabulary without going round in circles.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Every definition needs terms already known, so something must be accepted at the start. Derived terms then rest on the primitive ones and on terms defined before them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Point, straight line and plane are accepted as primitive and not formally defined. Bisector of an angle, circle and parabola are derived and are formally defined.

card.rule: Take a few starting terms as primitive and undefined, and define every other term from primitive or earlier defined terms.
card.limits: Primitive does not mean unexplained to a beginner; it means not formally defined inside the system.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Reading a definition: the parabola
concepts.question: What exactly does the definition of a parabola say, and which parts does a point have to satisfy?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take a definition apart into the thing defined, the property that defines it and the setting it assumes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be able to use the definition later without misremembering it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: When you use a definition you need every part of it. Splitting it up shows which part tells you whether a given point belongs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A parabola is the locus of points at equal distance from a fixed point (the focus) and a fixed straight line (the directrix), with all elements in one fixed plane.

card.rule: Take a definition apart into the thing defined, the property that defines it and the setting it assumes.
card.limits: This is one definition among several possible for some notions; for other notions the parts differ.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Dictionary versus mathematical definitions
concepts.question: How does a mathematician's definition differ in spirit from a dictionary entry, though they look alike?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take a technical definition as creating the meaning, and do not test it against ordinary speech.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid arguing about a technical term from everyday usage.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A dictionary writer records the current meaning and states it neatly. A mathematician is not mainly concerned with ordinary meaning, so the definition itself sets the meaning.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: What circle or parabola may mean in everyday speech matters little to the mathematician; the mathematical definition creates the mathematical meaning.

card.rule: Take a technical definition as creating the meaning, and do not test it against ordinary speech.
card.limits: This holds for technical terms. For an ordinary word you do want the current meaning, which is what a dictionary reports.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Going back to definitions
concepts.question: When a problem is full of technical terms, what does going back to definitions tell you to do?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Replace each technical term by the facts its definition states, and work with those.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the problem concrete and workable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A technical term hides relations behind a single word. The definition states those relations, so substituting it puts the real content in front of you.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A problem about a parabola is rephrased by what a parabola is: points at equal distance from a focus and a directrix.

card.rule: Replace each technical term by the facts its definition states, and work with those.
card.limits: It needs a definition you can state correctly and completely; a half-remembered one gives a wrong restatement.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Using the definition to eliminate a term
concepts.question: Beyond remembering a definition, what must you do to remove a technical term from a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Introduce suitable elements, state the relations the definition gives them, and rewrite the problem without the term.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: End with a restatement free of the technical term.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Remembering the definition is not enough; the term goes only when its meaning has been put to work. The elements you add carry the relations the definition gives.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To remove parabola, the book draws the segment from P to the focus F and the perpendicular from P to the directrix d, then uses the definition: the two are equal.

card.rule: Introduce suitable elements, state the relations the definition gives them, and rewrite the problem without the term.
card.limits: Adding elements and relations changes how you see the problem, so expect a restatement, not a copy.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Worked example: the parabola problem
concepts.question: How does the teacher's dialogue turn a problem full of unfamiliar terms into a plain one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Name the unknown, data and condition, go back to the definition, draw the figure, and state the problem plainly.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach a plain restatement that no longer sounds pompous.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The first statement used technical terms that were unfamiliar. After the definition is used, only familiar things remain, so the problem is deflated.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Given a line c, a point F and a line d, find the point P on c that is at equal distance from F and from d, which restates finding where c meets the parabola.

card.rule: Name the unknown, data and condition, go back to the definition, draw the figure, and state the problem plainly.
card.limits: It worked because the student knew the definition; a student who knew nothing of it could not carry out the substitution.

media.alt: A U-shaped parabola curve opens upward with a point F inside it. A sloping straight line c crosses the curve at a point P on its right branch. A dotted segment joins P to F, and a dashed vertical segment drops from P to a horizontal line d, meeting it at Q.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Definition or known theorem?
concepts.question: For a problem about a derived notion, when must you use its definition and when might a theorem serve?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use either the definition of the notion or a theorem about it; if you know only the definition, use that.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring real knowledge of the notion to bear on the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The basic axioms do not mention a derived notion such as the parabola. Any argument about it must therefore rest on its definition or on theorems about it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Geometry rests on axioms, definitions and theorems. The parabola is not in the axioms, which deal only with primitive terms.

card.rule: Use either the definition of the notion or a theorem about it; if you know only the definition, use that.
card.limits: At the start you cannot tell which will be better, but one of the two has to be used.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Choosing among several definitions
concepts.question: If a notion has several definitions, how do you choose which to go back to?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List the definitions you know and choose the one that fits the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Pick the definition that suggests a method.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Different definitions of one notion highlight different features. The right feature can suggest the route to a solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sphere can be defined as the points at a given distance from a given point, or as the surface a circle sweeps when it revolves about a diameter. Archimedes preferred the second for finding the sphere's surface area.

card.rule: List the definitions you know and choose the one that fits the problem.
card.limits: Many definitions may exist; no single one is best for every problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Checking an argument by its definitions
concepts.question: How can going back to definitions help you decide whether an argument holds?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Wait for the moment the argument uses the notion's meaning or a theorem about it; if that moment does not come, distrust it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spot arguments that talk about a notion without using it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If the arguer never says something substantial about the notion, you cannot know he understood it. An argument that does not use an essential notion cannot be sound.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Someone presents a new solution for the area of the sphere's surface. You listen for the moment he uses the sphere's definition or a theorem; if it never comes, the solution is no good.

card.rule: Wait for the moment the argument uses the notion's meaning or a theorem about it; if that moment does not come, distrust it.
card.limits: The check is aimed at essential notions; a passing mention of a minor term does not need this test.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: The power of a word lies in the facts
concepts.question: Why does the book call it sound to look for facts behind words?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look behind a word to the ideas and facts it stands for, not to its sound.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid being fooled by mere words.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We hardly think without words, signs or symbols, so words have power. That power comes from the ideas they recall and, in the end, the facts under those ideas.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The mathematician seeks the actual relations of mathematical objects behind technical terms; the physicist seeks definite experiments; the common person wants hard facts.

card.rule: Look behind a word to the ideas and facts it stands for, not to its sound.
card.limits: The advice is to look through words, not to do without them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Descartes and rules found in practice
concepts.question: What did Descartes plan, what became of it, and how did his rules arise?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Notice the rules you actually use when you invent a solution, and collect them as a method.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Build a general method for solving problems from your own practice.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Descartes reports that, inventing things on his own as a young man, he saw by degrees that he was following certain rules. A method can start as a description of what works.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Descartes planned a universal method for solving problems but left his Rules for the Direction of the Mind unfinished; fragments were printed after his death.

card.rule: Notice the rules you actually use when you invent a solution, and collect them as a method.
card.limits: Our reading: rules noticed in your own success are a starting point; they do not by themselves make a complete method, as his unfinished work shows.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Determination follows hope
concepts.question: Why does the book say solving problems is not purely intellectual, and what moves determination?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect serious problems to need will power, and expect your determination to rise and fall with hope and disappointment.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep going through the ups and downs of a hard problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: To solve a serious scientific problem you need will power that can outlast years of toil. Determination goes up when the solution seems near and down when no way out is visible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: When you hold a method with some confidence and it is suddenly blocked, you feel depressed and your determination wavers.

card.rule: Expect serious problems to need will power, and expect your determination to rise and fall with hope and disappointment.
card.limits: The book describes a usual pattern; a dip is not by itself a sign that the problem is hopeless.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Match determination to the outlook
concepts.question: How should a scientist match effort to the promise of a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take up a problem if it has some interest, work seriously if it is instructive, and give your whole self when the promise is great.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend your will where it pays.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A scientist should have some hope to start with and some success to go on, so determination has to be apportioned wisely to outlook.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A problem with some interest is taken up; one that seems instructive gets serious work; one of great promise gets your whole personality.

card.rule: Take up a problem if it has some interest, work seriously if it is instructive, and give your whole self when the promise is great.
card.limits: Our reading: the outlook is a judgment made in advance and can be wrong, so it should be revised.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Seek little successes
concepts.question: What should you do when you cannot solve the proposed problem, and why seek small successes?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not despise little successes; if the proposed problem resists, solve a related problem first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep hope and determination alive on a hard problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Determination follows hope and success, and little successes feed both. A related problem you can solve gives a foothold.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Stuck on the proposed problem, you first solve some related problem that you can handle.

card.rule: Do not despise little successes; if the proposed problem resists, solve a related problem first.
card.limits: The related problem is a step, not the goal; the proposed problem still has to be solved.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: A student without desire has not understood
concepts.question: What is almost always behind silly blunders or exasperating slowness, and what should a teacher do first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before helping with the work, stir the student's curiosity and give some desire to solve the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get the student to understand the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A student with no wish to solve a problem has no wish to understand it properly, so has not understood it. Blunders and slowness follow.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student makes silly blunders; the teacher first arouses interest in the problem, not more drill.

card.rule: Before helping with the work, stir the student's curiosity and give some desire to solve the problem.
card.limits: The book says almost always, not every time; other causes are possible.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Teaching problem solving educates the will
concepts.question: What does a student learn about persistence by solving problems that are not too easy?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give students problems that are not too easy, so they practise the struggle for a solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Educate the will along with the mind.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In struggling with such problems a student learns to persevere through failure, to value small advances, to wait for the essential idea and to concentrate hard when it comes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Problems that resist for a while teach a student to hold on, to notice progress, to wait and then focus.

card.rule: Give students problems that are not too easy, so they practise the struggle for a solution.
card.limits: Problems that are far too hard do not teach this; the book asks for problems not too easy.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Diagnosis versus a grade
concepts.question: What does diagnosis mean in teaching, and how does it differ from a grade?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Describe a student's work by its good and bad points, not by a grade alone.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know what to improve in the student's work.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A grade characterizes work only crudely. A teacher wanting to improve the work needs a closer characterization, as a physician needs a diagnosis to improve health.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A paper marked 6 out of 10 says little; a note on what was done well and badly tells the student what to fix.

card.rule: Describe a student's work by its good and bad points, not by a grade alone.
card.limits: The word is a technical term in education here; a grade still has some use.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Faults in understanding and in planning
concepts.question: Which faults are typical when students understand the problem and when they devise a plan?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look for incomplete understanding, and for the two opposite planning faults: rushing without a plan or waiting clumsily for an idea.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Name the fault so the right help can follow.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Students show characteristic behavior in each phase. Naming the fault tells you what to work on.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student starts calculating at once with no plan; another sits and waits for an idea, unable to do anything to hasten it.

card.rule: Look for incomplete understanding, and for the two opposite planning faults: rushing without a plan or waiting clumsily for an idea.
card.limits: The two planning faults are opposites, so advice that cures one can feed the other.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Faults in carrying out and in checking
concepts.question: Which faults are most frequent when carrying out the plan and when looking at the result?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Watch for carelessness in carrying out the plan and for failure to check the result at all.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch the faults that cost correct answers.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Students who lack patience to check each step slip, and those who do not check the result accept errors.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student gets an answer, drops the pencil and does not review it.

card.rule: Watch for carelessness in carrying out the plan and for failure to check the result at all.
card.limits: These are the book's observations of typical student behavior, not an exhaustive list.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Treat the fault with the list's questions
concepts.question: Once a fault is diagnosed, how does the book say a teacher can try to cure it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Diagnose the fault first, then insist on the questions of the list that aim at it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Cure the fault, not just the wrong answer.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Because faults are tied to phases, a teacher who has diagnosed one can press the questions that belong to that phase.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student who never checks results is asked, again and again, whether the result can be checked.

card.rule: Diagnose the fault first, then insist on the questions of the list that aim at it.
card.limits: The book speaks of some chance to cure; this is not a guarantee.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.section: Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Did you use all the data?
concepts.question: What does asking whether you used all the data check, and what does a no tell you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether you used all the data and the whole condition; an unused item points to a missing element.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find the weak spot in your conception of the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: As your knowledge is mobilized, your conception of the problem grows. The question tests whether it is now adequate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A puzzle gives three numbers and your solution used two. The third is a clue to what is still missing.

card.rule: Ask whether you used all the data and the whole condition; an unused item points to a missing element.
card.limits: It applies cleanly only to well-posed problems; see the limits.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.section: Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Worked example: the diagonal of a box
concepts.question: How did the question lead from a stuck face diagonal to the diagonal of the box?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When your expression lacks one of the data, build a figure that brings the missing datum in.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach the decisive step that you had not yet found.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A face diagonal uses only two edges, a and b. The third edge, c, is missing, so the conception is incomplete.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The problem asks for the diagonal of a rectangular box with edges a, b and c. A student finds the diagonal of a face, then stops.

card.rule: When your expression lacks one of the data, build a figure that brings the missing datum in.
card.limits: The question points to a gap; the student still has to find the figure that fills it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.section: Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Checking a proof with the hypothesis
concepts.question: How does asking whether a proof used the whole hypothesis help you check it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If every part of a hypothesis is essential, ask where the proof uses each part; any part left unused means the proof is wrong.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Check a proof for hidden gaps.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If dropping any part of the hypothesis makes the theorem false, a proof that does not use that part must be wrong.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A theorem has a three-part hypothesis, all essential. Ask: where does the proof use the first part, the second, the third?

card.rule: If every part of a hypothesis is essential, ask where the proof uses each part; any part left unused means the proof is wrong.
card.limits: It holds only when each part is essential; a redundant part may be unused without harm.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.section: Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Essential notions as well as data
concepts.question: Besides data and conditions, what else must your conception of the problem include to be complete?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Also ask whether you have taken into account all the essential notions in the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make your conception of the problem complete.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A conception is also incomplete if you fail to realize the meaning of an essential term, even when every number was used.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A proof of a statement about convex sets uses every given number but never uses what convex means; the conception is incomplete.

card.rule: Also ask whether you have taken into account all the essential notions in the problem.
card.limits: Only essential notions matter for this test.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.section: Did You Use All the Data?
concepts.title: Limits: perfectly stated problems
concepts.question: For which problems does use all the data hold without change, and what do you do when in doubt?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask use everything only of perfectly stated, reasonable problems; if in doubt, ask whether the condition can be satisfied.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid forcing every datum into a badly posed problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A perfectly stated problem to find has all necessary data, no superfluous datum, and a condition that is neither contradictory nor redundant. Only then must every datum be used.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Textbook problems are supposed to be perfectly stated, but one should not rely on that when there is the slightest doubt.

card.rule: Ask use everything only of perfectly stated, reasonable problems; if in doubt, ask whether the condition can be satisfied.
card.limits: Practical problems are rarely perfectly stated.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Examine a vivid guess: neither believe it nor bin it
concepts.question: Should you trust a vivid guess, throw it away, or do something else with it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat a guess that comes after real understanding as worth testing: do not accept it as proven, and do not dismiss it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep useful ideas alive without being fooled by them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says a guess that arrives after you have attentively considered and really understood a problem you care about usually holds at least a fragment of the truth, though seldom the whole.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a shopkeeper notices that sales dip in rainy weeks and suspects the rain is the cause. She neither announces a law nor ignores the pattern; she compares the rainy and dry weeks of the past year.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time a hunch strikes you, write it as one sentence and add one fact that would show it is wrong.

card.rule: A guess earns a test: not belief, and not dismissal.
card.limits: The author's praise is for guesses that follow real understanding of a problem you care about. A snap guess made without that effort has no such claim on your attention.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: A wrong guess is useful; no idea at all is the real loss
concepts.question: Is a wrong guess a waste, and what does the author count as really bad?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Value an idea for what examining it can teach, and prefer a wrong idea that you examine to having none.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep your thinking moving instead of freezing for fear of being wrong.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author observes that many a guess has turned out wrong but was useful in leading to a better one. He says no idea is really bad unless we are uncritical, and that what is really bad is to have no idea at all.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a gardener guesses that her tomatoes wilt for lack of water. Extra water changes nothing, but checking the soil to test the guess shows the roots are rotting, which leads her to the true cause.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Recall a recent wrong guess of yours and write what testing it taught you.

card.rule: A wrong guess that you examine beats having no guess at all.
card.limits: The saving condition is being critical. A guess held uncritically is the bad case, so the author's praise covers examined guesses, not stubborn ones.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Don't let a suspicion grow without examination
concepts.question: What went wrong with Mr. Jones, and how do you keep your own suspicions from going the same way?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Once you suspect something, look for signs against it as well as for it, and do not let it harden unexamined.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To stop a suspicion from becoming a belief that no evidence can change.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the author's story, Mr. Jones missed a raise and suspected his director. The suspicion was fair, since some signs pointed that way. The fault was that he then became blind to opposite signs. In theoretical matters, the author says, good ideas thrive on critical examination.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a tenant sees a ceiling stain and decides the upstairs bath leaked. She ignores that the stain grows only after storms and that her neighbour is away. A fair look at both signs would point to the roof.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick one suspicion you hold now and write down one sign that points against it.

card.rule: A suspicion is allowed; refusing to examine it is the fault.
card.limits: The author writes chiefly about theoretical matters, and he does not ask you to doubt everything you think.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: State the guess; a problem to find becomes a problem to prove
concepts.question: What changes when you put a guess into words as a definite statement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put your guess into words as a full statement, so that it can be proved or disproved.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a vague problem to find into a definite statement you can test.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author asks us to have the courage to state a guess. In his example, the problem is to find the quadrilateral of greatest area for a given perimeter, and the obvious guess is the square. Stated as a claim, the problem changes: we no longer have a problem to find but a problem to prove, a theorem to prove or disprove.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: asked to find the cheapest way to cover a floor, a builder writes the guess as a claim, namely that tiling in large sheets costs least, and now has something to prove or disprove.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a guess you hold and write it as one sentence beginning: Of all ... the ...

card.rule: Say the guess as a definite claim, and then you have something to prove or disprove.
card.limits: Stating the guess does not prove it. Our reading: a clear statement can still be false, and the author treats the next step as work still to be done.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: If the claim is hard, prove a weaker part first
concepts.question: How can a hard claim be approached when you cannot yet prove it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot prove the full claim, prove a more accessible part or weaker version of it first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make progress when the whole claim is out of reach.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the author's example, the claim that the square beats all quadrilaterals is hard to attack. He reasons that if the square is best among all quadrilaterals, it must also be best among rectangles. That weaker claim is only a part of the problem, but it is easier to reach. He says we should have the courage to restate it in more detail.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: you doubt that a certain bridge design suits every river. Before testing all rivers, you test it on narrow rivers only, which is a weaker, easier claim.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For a claim you cannot yet prove, write the narrowest version of it that you could check today.

card.rule: When the whole claim is out of reach, prove a weaker part of it first.
card.limits: A proved part is not the whole. The author notes that the rectangle statement is weaker than the quadrilateral one, so the original problem remains open.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Restate the claim in algebra and check it
concepts.question: How does writing the rectangle claim in algebra turn it into something you can check by calculation?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put a claim into algebra with letters for the sizes, and rewrite it until you reach a form you can check.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make a claim exact enough to prove or refute by calculation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let a and b be the adjacent sides of a rectangle, so its area is \(ab\) and its perimeter is \(2a+2b\). A square with that perimeter has side \(\frac{a+b}{2}\), so its area is \(\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2\). The claim becomes: this exceeds \(ab\). Multiplying out turns it into \(a^2-2ab+b^2>0\), that is \((a-b)^2>0\), which holds unless \(a=b\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take a = 4 and b = 9. The rectangle has area 36 and perimeter 26. The square with perimeter 26 has side 6.5 and area 42.25, which is 6.25 more, and \(\frac{(a-b)^2}{4}=\frac{25}{4}=6.25\) agrees.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take two numbers with the same sum, such as 6 and 6 versus 3 and 9, and compare the product of each pair.

card.rule: The square beats the rectangle unless the rectangle is already a square.
card.limits: The strict inequality fails when a = b: then the two areas are equal. A proof for rectangles also leaves the claim for all quadrilaterals unproved.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Spell out what a guess means, then check it
concepts.question: How do you turn a hazy clue into a guess you can check, step by step?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a guess tempts you, write down concretely what it would mean, and check it against another piece of evidence.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make a hazy clue testable by spelling out its consequences.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The crossword clue is: do the walls again, back and forth, with seven letters. Repetition suggests the word starts with RE, so the author writes RE followed by blanks and checks the R against a crossing word. Then back and forth suggests the word may read the same both ways, so the pattern becomes RE, three blanks, ER, with the third letter equal to the fifth.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author's two guesses give two patterns. The first leaves five blanks. The second fixes the first two and last two letters, so only three places remain, and the third and fifth must match. He adds that the fourth letter is very likely a vowel.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you guess at a puzzle answer, write the pattern with blanks before you try to fill it.

card.rule: Spell out what the guess means, then test it against something else.
card.limits: A guess that survives one check is not proved. The author says only that if no reason against it is found, we come back to the original word.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Draw the figure on paper when details pile up
concepts.question: When is a figure on paper better than a figure held in your head?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem has many details to examine one after another, draw the figure on paper.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep every detail in view without relying on memory.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A figure may be imagined or traced on paper. The author allows that imagining is sometimes enough. But when we must look at several details one by one, we cannot picture them all at once in our imagination, while on paper they are all present together. A detail kept only in the mind may be forgotten.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: planning furniture for a room, you must weigh door swing, window light, and radiator position together. A quick sketch holds all three, where a mental picture drops one as soon as you attend to another.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Sketch a problem you are now working on, with every given detail written next to its place.

card.rule: Put many details on paper so that none depends on memory.
card.limits: The author grants that imagining without drawing can be desirable on certain occasions, and a drawing is a help to reasoning, not a replacement for it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Assemble unknown and data in one figure, then take it apart
concepts.question: In a construction problem, what goes into the first figure, and how do you then use it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Draw a figure containing the unknown and all the data arranged as the condition prescribes, then examine each part separately.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To understand the problem distinctly before looking for the solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: For a problem of geometric construction, the author starts with a figure that contains the unknown and the data, put together as the condition says.
