To understand the problem, we consider each datum and each part of the condition separately, then reunite the parts and view the condition as a whole.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: to construct a triangle from a base, the angle at one end of the base, and a height, draw a triangle with the base and the angle marked and the height shown as a dotted line. Look at each given in turn, then at all of them together.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For your next fitting or building task, draw the whole arrangement first and add each given measurement beside its place.

card.rule: Put unknown and data in one figure, study the parts, then see the whole.
card.limits: The figure is for understanding, not for solving by itself. The author notes we would scarcely handle the details without a figure, yet drawing it does not settle that a solution exists.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Assume what is required as already done
concepts.question: Is it legitimate to draw a figure that supposes the problem is already solved?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Draw a hypothetical figure that supposes the condition satisfied in all its parts, without committing to its truth.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To see how the unknown must relate to the data, before knowing that it can be found.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author asks whether it is unwarranted to draw a figure in which the unknown already has the required relations. He says it is not, as long as we do not confuse mere possibility with certainty. A judge may question the defendant while considering that he did the crime, without committing to it. The recommendation: draw a hypothetical figure that supposes the condition satisfied in all its parts.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: to find a point equally far from three towns, sketch the three towns and a point marked O, supposing it is at the same distance from each. The sketch is a supposition and settles nothing, but the supposed distances now show where O must lie.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For a goal you want to reach, write the situation as if it were already achieved, then list what must be true in it.

card.rule: Suppose the condition satisfied, draw it, and keep the supposition open.
card.limits: The hypothetical figure is a possibility only. If you start treating it as certain, you have confused possibility with certainty, and the problem may turn out to have no solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Exact or free-hand: the logic is the base
concepts.question: Must a figure be drawn exactly, and how far can you trust what it seems to show?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For reasoning, a careful free-hand figure is usually enough; trust the logical connections, not the look of the drawing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To work fast without being misled by the picture.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says exact and free-hand figures both have uses. For the purpose of reasoning, carefully drawn free-hand figures are usually good enough and far quicker, provided they do not look absurd: straight lines should not wave, and circles should not look like potatoes. The figure is a help, never the basis of a conclusion; the logical connections are the real basis.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a student sketches a circle with a chord by hand. The circle is slightly oval, but the argument uses only that the chord's endpoints lie on the circle. The drawing's flaw does not touch the reasoning.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Redraw a figure of yours with a different shape and check that your argument still holds.

card.rule: Draw quickly and carefully by hand, and base the argument on logic.
card.limits: A careless figure can mislead. The author says an inaccurate figure can occasionally suggest a false conclusion, and the protection is to vary the figure.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Build the figure in the convenient order
concepts.question: Does the order in which you construct the parts of a figure matter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: The relations among the parts matter, not the order of construction, so build in the most convenient order.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To draw a figure easily even when the problem states the relations in an awkward direction.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says it is important that the elements stand in the required relations, but it is unimportant in which order they are constructed. So choose the most convenient order. His example: to draw two angles, alpha and beta, with alpha equal to three times beta, do not start from an arbitrary alpha; choose a fairly small beta and construct alpha from it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Choose beta as 20 degrees. Then alpha, three times beta, is 60 degrees, easy to construct. Starting from a 60 degree alpha and trying to find beta by construction is the awkward direction.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time a figure seems hard to start, ask which part, if chosen first, makes the rest easy to draw.

card.rule: Start with the part that makes the rest easy to construct.
card.limits: The freedom concerns the order of drawing, not the relations: the finished figure must still show every required relation between its parts.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Do not let the figure suggest a special case
concepts.question: What should you avoid when drawing a figure meant to stand for a general case?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not let your figure show relations that the problem does not require, such as equal sides or right angles.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep your reasoning general rather than tied to a special case.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says your figure should not suggest undue specialization. Lines should not look equal or perpendicular unless the problem requires it, and triangles should not look isosceles or right-angled by accident. For a general triangle, he suggests drawing one with angles of 45, 60 and 75 degrees, or one not very different from it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Compare angles 70, 60, 50 with 75, 60, 45. In the first, the smallest gap between angles is 10 degrees. In the second, every gap is 15 degrees, including the gap of 15 between 75 and a right angle.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you sketch a triangle for a proof, check that no two sides or angles look equal by accident.

card.rule: Draw the general triangle as neither right-angled nor isosceles.
card.limits: A figure that really must be isosceles or right-angled should show that. The 45, 60, 75 triangle suits only a general case.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Use line styles and colours to show roles
concepts.question: How can you make the different roles of lines in a figure easy to tell apart?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give lines different weights, patterns or colours to show their different roles.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep the structure of a busy figure readable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says you can emphasise the different roles of different lines by using heavy and light lines, continuous and dotted lines, or lines in different colours. A figure with many lines becomes hard to read when all of them look alike, so the style tells the eye which lines matter most.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: in a drawing of a roof truss, the beams carrying load are drawn heavy and continuous, the ties are drawn light, and the supporting reactions are drawn dotted.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Redraw a busy sketch with your given facts in one colour and your tentative lines faint.

card.rule: Style your lines so that role shows at a glance.
card.limits: Too many styles can clutter a figure. Our reading: use as few as the roles need.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: In solid geometry, use models and everyday objects
concepts.question: How can you make solid shapes easier to grasp when a flat drawing is hard to read?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For solid geometry, use three-dimensional models where you can, and otherwise drawings that you support with models you make.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To grasp solid figures that flat drawings show poorly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says three-dimensional models are desirable but troublesome to make and expensive to buy, so we are usually satisfied with drawings on paper or blackboard, although it is not easy to make them impressive. A drawing of a solid on a flat surface can mislead the eye, and a physical model removes that difficulty.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: to understand how a cube is cut by a plane through three vertices, you can drag a knife through a block of cheese, or cut cardboard, in addition to studying a drawing.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a box and find the faces, edges and corners that a drawing of it fails to show well.

card.rule: Add models to drawings when solid shapes are hard to see.
card.limits: Models cost time or money. The author accepts drawings as the usual choice and suggests models mainly for beginners.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Give non-geometric problems a geometric picture
concepts.question: Can a figure help with a problem that has nothing to do with geometry?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look for a suitable geometric representation of a non-geometric problem, and use a figure to think with.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To bring the human knack for handling figures to problems of other kinds.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says figures traced on paper are easy to produce, easy to recognise and easy to remember, and plane figures are especially familiar. So if we find a suitable geometrical representation of non-geometric objects, we can use our aptitude for figures on them. Even when your problem is not geometric, you may try to draw a figure.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: to decide the order of five tasks, draw each as a bar on a time line. Overlaps and gaps appear at once, which a list of dates would hide.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a list of numbers you must compare and draw it as bars or points on a line.

card.rule: If the problem is not geometric, try drawing it as a figure anyway.
card.limits: A picture helps only if it represents the problem faithfully. A poor representation can mislead, and the author calls the right one an important step, not the solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Generalization: from one case to a wider set
concepts.question: What does it mean to generalize a problem, and in which directions can you do it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pass from one object to a set that contains it, or from a restricted set to a more comprehensive set.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To see a particular case as one of a family, so that you can use what the family shares.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author defines generalization as passing from the consideration of one object to the consideration of a set containing that object, or passing from a restricted set to a more comprehensive set containing the restricted one. So there are two directions: from a single case to a set, and from a small set to a bigger one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: from the single fact that the angles of one triangle you measured add up to 180 degrees, you pass to the question whether the angles of every triangle do. A move from triangles to polygons is another generalization.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a fact you know about one example and rewrite it as a question about all examples of its kind.

card.rule: Replace one case by the wider set that contains it.
card.limits: A generalization is a question until it is checked. The wider set may not share the property of the single case, so the step is a guess to examine.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Generalizing from a curious sum
concepts.question: How can one curious numerical fact turn into a general question?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a curious fact turns up in one case, ask whether it happens often, among a wider set of similar cases.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To turn a single observation into a question that could lead to a law.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notices that 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 = 100, and that this can be written as the sum of the cubes 1, 2, 3 and 4 equalling 10 squared. He asks naturally whether a sum of successive cubes is often a square. In asking that, he generalizes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sums of the first n cubes for n = 1 to 6 are 1, 9, 36, 100, 225 and 441, which are the squares of 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 and 21. The pattern the observation hinted at appears every time.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: List the sums of the first few odd numbers and see what they have in common.

card.rule: Ask whether a curious fact is common, and test more cases.
card.limits: Several cases do not prove a law; they only make the question worth testing further.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Find the essential property by widening the problem
concepts.question: How can widening a hard-looking problem show which property of the object really matters?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask what property of the object the problem really uses, and state a wider problem that needs only that property.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To strip a problem down to its essential feature, so the solution becomes visible.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author gives a problem: a line and a regular octahedron are given in position; find a plane through the line that bisects the octahedron's volume. Knowing the shape suggests the wider problem: the same, for any solid with a centre of symmetry. The plane must pass through the centre, so the line and the centre fix it. The octahedron has such a centre, so the first problem is solved.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: asked to split a pizza with a straight cut through a given point so that both halves have equal area, you realise only the round, symmetric shape matters, so the cut through the centre works for every circular pizza.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a problem about a regular shape and ask which one property of the shape your solution actually uses.

card.rule: Find the one property the problem uses, and solve for every object with it.
card.limits: The widening works when the extra generality removes details without removing what the solution needs. A wider problem that loses the key property would no longer be solvable.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: The more general problem may be easier
concepts.question: Why can solving a wider problem be easier than solving the special one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a special problem resists you, try the wider problem that contains it; it may be easier.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make a hard problem easier by climbing to a general one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the more general problem may be easier to solve. This sounds paradoxical, but the octahedron example shows why. The main achievement in solving the special problem was to invent the general problem. After that main achievement, only a minor part of the work remains, so the solution of the general problem is a small part of the solution of the special one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the octahedron case the special problem looked hard, yet the wider problem about any solid with a centre of symmetry was much easier, because the details of the octahedron no longer distract.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: For a problem you cannot solve, write the wider problem that contains it and see whether it is easier.

card.rule: Do not fear to climb: the wider problem may be easier.
card.limits: This is not a general law. The wider problem may be harder, or false. The author says it may be easier, not that it always is.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: From numbers to letters
concepts.question: What do you gain by replacing the numbers in a problem with letters?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Replace the given numbers by letters, and solve the problem in letters.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To gain new procedures for solving, and a result that can be checked.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author takes the volume of a square-based frustum with lower side 10 inches, upper side 5 inches and height 6 inches. If we write a, b and h for 10, 5 and 6, we pass from a problem in numbers to a problem in letters, which is a more general problem. This gives access to new procedures.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a garden is 8 m by 5 m and needs fencing, so the perimeter is 26 m. In letters, a garden a by b has perimeter \(2a+2b\); putting a = 8 and b = 5 returns 26.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a calculation you did with numbers and redo it with letters, then substitute your numbers back.

card.rule: Turn given numbers into letters, so one solution covers every case.
card.limits: The letters must stand for the same relations as the numbers did. The wider formula is only as good as the problem it replaces.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Have you seen it before?
concepts.question: Before working from scratch, what should you ask about the problem in front of you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether you have solved this problem before, or met it in a slightly different form.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make use of earlier work instead of repeating it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says it is possible that we have solved the very problem before, or met it in a slightly different form. These are possibilities we should not fail to explore, so we try to remember what happened. The questions to ask are: Have you seen it before? Or have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a programmer faces a program that crashes on an empty list. She asks whether she has met a crash like this before, and recalls last month's bug, which was a missing check for empty input.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Before your next task, spend one minute listing earlier tasks that resemble it.

card.rule: Ask: have I seen this, or something close to it, before?
card.limits: Memory may offer a misleading match. Our reading: a remembered problem has to be checked against the present one before you rely on it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Mobilize what you know, feature by feature
concepts.question: How does the idea of having seen something before reach beyond whole problems to their parts?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look at any striking feature of the problem and ask whether you have met that feature before.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To bring the relevant parts of your dormant knowledge into play.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says the question is often used in a more general meaning. To get the solution, we have to extract relevant elements from our memory and mobilize the pertinent parts of our dormant knowledge. Any feature of the present problem that strikes us as possibly important should be recognised: What is it? Is it familiar to you? Have you seen it before?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: in a word puzzle with the letters QU together, you ask whether you have seen that pair as a feature, and recall that Q is almost always followed by U in English words, which narrows the search.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Pick out the strangest feature of your current problem and write down where you have met anything like it.

card.rule: Ask of each striking feature: have I seen this before?
card.limits: A familiar feature does not guarantee a use. The author says only that it may play a role again.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
concepts.title: A related problem already solved is good news
concepts.question: What should you do when you realise that a problem related to yours has already been solved?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you find a related problem whose solution is known, treat it as an opportunity and ask how it can help.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To profit from work already done instead of starting afresh.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that a problem for which the solution is known, and which is connected with our present problem, is certainly welcome. There is a good chance that such a problem will be useful in solving the present one. The next step is to ask whether we can make use of it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: asked for the area of a regular hexagon, a student recalls how she found the area of an equilateral triangle. The two are related, since a regular hexagon can be cut into six such triangles, so her old solution is worth using.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Name one problem you solved that is related to something you are stuck on now.

card.rule: A related solved problem is a resource: ask how to use it.
card.limits: A related problem need not be useful. Its connection may be loose or its solution may not carry over, so its use must be worked out.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
concepts.title: Recalled problem or invented problem
concepts.question: How does using a recalled solved problem differ from inventing an auxiliary problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Tell which kind of helper you hold: a recalled problem you can solve but not yet use, or an invented one you can use but not yet solve.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To know what remains to be done before the helper pays off.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In both cases we want to solve a problem A and bring in another problem B hoping to profit. The difference lies in our relation to B. With a recalled problem, we know its solution but not yet how to use it. With a newly invented auxiliary problem, we know how to use it but not yet how to solve it. Once the difficulty is overcome, B is used the same way in both cases.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: for a cake that must serve 12, you recall a recipe for 4 that you have baked, so you know the solution but must work out scaling. Alternatively you invent a smaller test cake, which you know how to use but have yet to bake.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you use a helper problem, write which half you lack: the solution or the use.

card.rule: Recalled: solution known, use unknown. Invented: use known, solution unknown.
card.limits: The contrast is a matter of degree in real work. Our reading: often you will know a little of both, so treat the two cases as ends of a range.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
concepts.title: Link the old problem to the new by matching elements
concepts.question: How can you make an old solved problem fit a new one, element by element?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Match each important element of the old problem with a corresponding element in the new one, and introduce it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To carry the old solution across to the new problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that, trying to link the new problem with an old one, we introduce into the new problem elements corresponding to important elements of the old. His example: to find the sphere circumscribed about a tetrahedron, recall the plane problem of the circle circumscribed about a triangle, which used perpendicular bisectors of the sides.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The triangle has three sides and its bisectors are three lines. The tetrahedron has four vertices and six edges, so the analogous elements would be six planes. Counting the sides and edges shows how the correspondence is set up.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write the key element of a method you know, then name its counterpart in the new task.

card.rule: Find the counterpart in the new problem of each key element of the old.
card.limits: Counterparts must really correspond. A pairing that looks neat but does not carry the old argument's logic leads nowhere.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
concepts.title: Introduce an auxiliary element to make the old problem usable
concepts.question: What should you ask when a solved related problem does not fit as it stands?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether to introduce some auxiliary element so that the related problem can be used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To make the old solution fit the new problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author notes that consideration of a formerly solved related problem leads to the introduction of auxiliary elements, and suitable auxiliary elements make it possible to use the related problem to full advantage. When thinking about the possible use of such a problem, we ask: Should you introduce some auxiliary element in order to make its use possible?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: you know how to find the area of a rectangle. To use that for a parallelogram, draw a perpendicular from one vertex to the opposite side and move the cut-off triangle. The added line is the auxiliary element.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Take a method that almost fits a new task and ask what extra step would make it fit.

card.rule: Add the element that lets the old solution apply.
card.limits: Not every added element helps. An auxiliary element is judged by whether it makes the old solution usable, so be ready to drop ones that do not.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Heuristic: the study of discovery and invention
concepts.question: What is heuristic, and what does it study?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read the word heuristic as the study of the methods and rules of discovery and invention.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To know what kind of study the book belongs to, and what it aims to teach.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says heuristic, also called heuretic or ars inveniendi, was the name of a branch of study, not clearly bounded, belonging to logic, philosophy or psychology. It was often outlined, seldom presented in detail, and as good as forgotten today. Its aim is to study the methods and rules of discovery and invention.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a rule for dividing fractions tells you how to carry out a known task. A heuristic remark, such as look for a related problem, helps you find a way when no ready method is known.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Write in one line a problem where you needed a way to find a method, not just a method to carry out.

card.rule: Heuristic studies how to find solutions, not how to check them.
card.limits: The word names a field whose boundaries the author calls unclear. Our reading: he does not claim that heuristic gives a method that always works.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Heuristic reasoning is provisional and plausible
concepts.question: What kind of reasoning is heuristic reasoning, and why do we need it before we have a proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use provisional, plausible reasoning to discover a solution, and expect to replace it with strict proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To find the solution when no proof is yet available.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: As an adjective, heuristic means serving to discover. Heuristic reasoning is reasoning regarded not as final and strict but as provisional and plausible only, and its purpose is to discover the solution of the present problem. Complete certainty comes only when we have the complete solution; before it we must often be satisfied with a more or less plausible guess.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author compares it with scaffolding: we need heuristic reasoning when we construct a strict proof as we need scaffolding when we erect a building.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Label your current best guess as plausible but not yet proved, and write what would make it certain.

card.rule: Heuristic reasoning is the scaffolding, and the proof is the building.
card.limits: Heuristic reasoning gives plausibility, not certainty. It does not replace the final proof, whatever its persuasive force.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Do not mix heuristic reasoning with proof
concepts.question: Where does heuristic reasoning go wrong: in being used, or in how it is labelled?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use heuristic reasoning freely to find ideas, and never mix it up with rigorous proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To keep discovery honest, so that a plausible argument is not mistaken for a proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author says that the fault does not lie in the heuristic reasoning itself. What is bad is to mix up heuristic reasoning with rigorous proof. The fault is therefore in the confusion, which hides from the reader what has been shown and what has only been made plausible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a consultant shows that sales rose after a campaign in three cities, and tells the board that the campaign is proved to work. The data make the claim plausible, but the word proved sells a plausible argument as a rigorous one.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Mark each claim in your latest report as proved or plausible.

card.rule: Say which part is plausible and which is proved.
card.limits: Heuristic reasoning labelled honestly is fine. The author's complaint is only against confusion of the two.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
concepts.title: Show heuristic arguments openly in teaching
concepts.question: How should a textbook treat an argument that is plausible but not a rigorous proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Present heuristic arguments openly, with their advantages and their limits, and not as if they were proofs.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: To prepare learners for the strict proof without misleading them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author argues that teaching could be improved if the nature of heuristic reasoning were better understood, its advantages and limitations openly recognised, and textbooks presented heuristic arguments openly. A heuristic argument offered with taste and frankness may be useful, since it prepares for the rigorous argument. It is likely to be harmful if presented ambiguously.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a physics text derives a formula by a quick plausible argument and says so, adding that a strict derivation follows in a later chapter. The student learns the idea and knows what remains to be shown.

blocks.label: Try it
blocks.text: Next time you explain something plausible, begin with: This is a plausible argument, not a proof.

card.rule: Say openly that an argument is heuristic, and what it leaves unproved.
card.limits: Openness helps only if the heuristic argument is also sound enough to prepare for the proof. A poor or misleading argument is not rescued by an honest label.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
concepts.title: Take an easier success first
concepts.question: When a problem will not yield, what should you do before attacking it again?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the proposed problem resists you, solve some easier related problem first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep your courage and your progress when a direct attack fails.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An easier success gives consolation and builds courage. Devising a suitable auxiliary problem is a way of going around an obstacle instead of battering it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A planner cannot schedule 40 volunteers across a festival weekend. She first schedules just five volunteers across one afternoon and sees which clashes appear.

card.rule: When the proposed problem resists you, solve some easier related problem first.
card.limits: Our reading: the detour helps only if the related problem is truly easier and close enough to the original that something carries over.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
concepts.title: Invent, do not only remember
concepts.question: What is the difference between recalling a related problem and inventing one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you do not remember a suitable related problem, invent one by varying your own problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the problem more accessible when memory offers nothing.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions that follow share one aim, the variation of the problem, reached by generalization, specialization, analogy and other means.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Stuck on counting routes through a 10 by 10 street grid, a courier considers a 2 by 2 grid and counts routes there. She has not recalled a problem; she has made a simpler one.

card.rule: If you do not remember a suitable related problem, invent one by varying your own problem.
card.limits: Our reading: variation helps only when the new problem stays close enough to the old one that its answer informs the original.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Induction and mathematical induction
concepts.question: Why must you keep induction and mathematical induction apart despite the shared name?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the two names apart: induction discovers general laws, mathematical induction proves certain theorems.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid confusing finding a law with proving it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Induction finds general laws by observing and combining particular instances. Mathematical induction proves theorems of a certain kind. The author thinks it unfortunate that the names are linked, since there is very little logical connection, though in practice we often use both together.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Noticing that the sums 1, 9, 36, 100 and 225 of the first five cubes are all squares and guessing a law is induction. Proving that law for every number is a separate job, done by mathematical induction.

card.rule: Keep the two names apart: induction discovers general laws, mathematical induction proves certain theorems.
card.limits: The two work well as a pair, so keep the roles apart even when you use them in sequence.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Tabulate the special cases
concepts.question: When one instance looks remarkable, what should you do to find out whether it is chance?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a curious instance appears, ask the general question and tabulate neighbouring special cases.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find out whether the instance is a chance or a sign of a general law.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author starts from the observation that 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 = 100 = 10 squared, a sum of four cubes that is a square. Like a naturalist, he asks whether it often happens, and then arranges the cases n = 1 to 5 neatly. Each total is a square, which is hard to put down to chance.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The sums of the first n cubes for n = 1 to 5 are 1, 9, 36, 100 and 225, which equal 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15 squared.

card.rule: When a curious instance appears, ask the general question and tabulate neighbouring special cases.
card.limits: A table of cases suggests a law; it does not prove one. The author keeps the claim cautious.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Look for a deeper regularity
concepts.question: After a first conjecture, what can you do to state the law more precisely?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Re-examine the facts that led to the conjecture and look for a deeper regularity to sharpen it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a hazy conjecture into a precise one that can be tested.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The naturalist can add more cases or can reexamine what he has seen. The author takes the second line: the bases 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 of the squares do not grow irregularly. The differences between neighbours are 2, 3, 4 and 5, which is a conspicuous regularity.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Since the differences grow steadily, the bases look related to one another, and a sharper form of the original guess may be hidden there.

card.rule: Re-examine the facts that led to the conjecture and look for a deeper regularity to sharpen it.
card.limits: Our reading: use this only when the cases show a steady regularity; scattered numbers give nothing to sharpen.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: What induction does and where it stops
concepts.question: In mathematics, what has the final say over a result found by induction?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use induction to find regularity, but in mathematics settle a result by rigorous proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use experiment to discover results and proof to establish them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Induction tries to find regularity and coherence behind observations. Its most conspicuous instruments are generalization, specialization and analogy. In the physical sciences nothing outranks observation and induction, but in mathematics there is a higher authority: rigorous proof.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The cube-sum law was reached by tabulating cases and spotting a pattern, which is plausible and provisional. Having found it, the author turns to the task of proving or disproving it.

card.rule: Use induction to find regularity, but in mathematics settle a result by rigorous proof.
card.limits: The author says philosophers disagree widely about induction; he offers a one-sided but undistorted picture.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Sum the first n numbers with a rectangle
concepts.question: How can a rectangle show the value of 1 + 2 + ... + n?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Split a rectangle with sides n and n + 1 into two staircase shapes, each worth 1 + 2 + ... + n.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a simple formula for the sum of the first n whole numbers, to use in the sharper theorem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Take a rectangle with sides n and n + 1 and divide it by a zigzag line into two equal staircase-shaped halves. Each half has area 1 + 2 + ... + n. The rectangle has area n times (n + 1), so each half is that area divided by two.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For n = 4 the rectangle is 4 by 5 with area 20 and each staircase has area 10, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

card.rule: Split a rectangle with sides n and n + 1 into two staircase shapes, each worth 1 + 2 + ... + n.
card.limits: The picture works for each whole number n; it shows the sum, not why cube sums are squares.

media.alt: Two copies of a rectangle side by side. In the first, a zigzag stair-step line splits the rectangle into two equal staircase-shaped halves. In the second, one staircase half is shown as columns whose heights rise one unit at a time, four steps in all.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Test the formula before proving it
concepts.question: If you have no idea how to prove a formula, what can you still do with it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you cannot yet prove a formula, test it on the first case you have not tested.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain confidence in a conjecture at little cost before investing in a proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The formula says that the sum of the first n cubes equals the square of n(n + 1)/2. The first case not yet tested is n = 6. The left side is 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 + 125 + 216 = 441. The right side is 6 times 7 over 2, which is 21, squared, also 441.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A check at n = 6 passed, so the formula survived a case it was not built from.

card.rule: If you cannot yet prove a formula, test it on the first case you have not tested.
card.limits: One more passing case adds confidence but does not prove the formula for every n.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Check the passage from n to n + 1
concepts.question: How can you use one verified identity to carry a formula from each integer to the next?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check that if the formula holds for n it holds for n + 1; with a true start, it holds for every n.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Prove a statement about all whole numbers with a finite check.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Write the formula for n + 1 and subtract the formula for n. What remains is an identity about (n + 1) cubed, and it can be checked directly. If the formula is true for n, adding that identity gives it for n + 1. Since it is true for n = 6, it holds for 7, then 8, and so on.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The identity is that (n + 1) cubed equals the square of (n + 1)(n + 2)/2 minus the square of n(n + 1)/2. Simplifying gives (n + 1) squared times (n + 1), which is (n + 1) cubed.

card.rule: Check that if the formula holds for n it holds for n + 1; with a true start, it holds for every n.
card.limits: The step proves nothing alone: it needs a first true case to start the chain.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: When the passage method is available
concepts.question: Which conditions must an assertion meet before you can prove it by passing from n to n + 1?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the passage from n to n + 1 only when the assertion is precise, depends on an integer n and can be tested at the step.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognise when this proof pattern is available.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The proof above is a pattern for similar cases. The assertion must be given in advance in precise form. It must depend on an integer n. And it must be explicit enough that you can test whether it stays true in passing from n to n + 1.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The claim that the sum of the first n cubes is the square of n(n + 1)/2 meets all three conditions.

card.rule: Use the passage from n to n + 1 only when the assertion is precise, depends on an integer n and can be tested at the step.
card.limits: A hazy assertion, or one that does not depend on an integer, does not fit this pattern as it stands.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: A more precise statement can be easier to prove
concepts.question: Why was the second statement of the cube law easier to prove than the first?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a vague conjecture resists proof, restate it more precisely so that you can test it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Give the proof something explicit to work on.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author found two assertions. The first said the sum of the first n cubes is a square. The second said it is the square of 1 + 2 + ... + n. The second is stronger, since it implies the first, and it is explicit, so the step from n to n + 1 could be tested.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Starting from the hazy first assertion, a proof by passing from n to n + 1 would hardly have been found.

card.rule: If a vague conjecture resists proof, restate it more precisely so that you can test it.
card.limits: The sharper statement must truly imply the original; a statement that merely sounds precise does not help.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: A more ambitious plan may succeed
concepts.question: Why might a more ambitious problem be easier than the one you were given?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When stuck, consider a more general or more ambitious problem; it may be easier to handle.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a route where the modest problem offers none.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The inventor's paradox says the more ambitious plan may have more chances of success. It sounds odd, but moving from one problem to another we often find the new, more ambitious problem easier to handle. The cube-sum law is an example: its stronger form allowed a testable step.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Proving one special total is square was hard to start; proving the law for every n opened a way in.

card.rule: When stuck, consider a more general or more ambitious problem; it may be easier to handle.
card.limits: The claim is hedged: the ambitious plan may succeed, and it does not always.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Ambition needs vision, not pretension
concepts.question: When does a more ambitious plan deserve to be pursued?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Aim higher only when the plan rests on some vision beyond the present facts, not on mere pretension.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid reckless overreach while still using the paradox.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The book qualifies the paradox: the more ambitious plan may have more chances of success provided it is not based on mere pretension but on some vision of the things beyond those immediately present.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our reading: the cube-sum law shows the difference. Its ambition rested on regularities seen in the table. A claim made with no cases behind it would be pretension.

card.rule: Aim higher only when the plan rests on some vision beyond the present facts, not on mere pretension.
card.limits: Our reading: the author gives no formal test of vision. Evidence such as an observed regularity is our guide.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.section: Is It Possible to Satisfy the Condition?
concepts.title: Ask whether the condition can be met
concepts.question: What can you ask about the condition of a problem before working on it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask whether the condition can be satisfied, and whether it is sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Foresee the shape of the result so you know in which direction to go.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is it sufficient to determine the unknown? Or insufficient? Or redundant? Or contradictory? A provisional answer, a guess, is all these questions need. Knowing what to expect shows you in which direction to go.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Find two numbers with sum 10: the condition is insufficient, since many pairs work. Add that their difference is 2: sufficient, giving 6 and 4. Add that the sum is also 12: contradictory.

card.rule: Ask whether the condition can be satisfied, and whether it is sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory.
card.limits: These questions can be answered by a guess; a long search for the answer is not the aim.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.section: Is It Possible to Satisfy the Condition?
concepts.title: Is the problem reasonable?
concepts.question: Why does it help to guess whether a problem has just one solution?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Guess whether the problem has just one solution, since that guess raises your interest and aids your work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Work better because you know what kind of answer to expect.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Problems with a uniquely determined solution are the ones we call reasonable in this sense. Answering the question about uniqueness, even by a plausible guess, raises interest in the problem, and we can work better.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The problem find the positive number whose square is 49 has the single solution 7, so it is reasonable. The problem find two numbers adding to 12 has many.

card.rule: Guess whether the problem has just one solution, since that guess raises your interest and aids your work.
card.limits: Many problems have several solutions and are still worth solving; reasonable here names one kind of problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.section: Is It Possible to Satisfy the Condition?
concepts.title: Do not insist on a hard answer
concepts.question: When should you stop pressing these questions about the condition?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the questions, but do not insist on them when the answer seems difficult or obscure.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Save effort for solving the problem itself.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The trouble you have in getting the answer may outweigh the gain in interest. So the questions about the condition are best asked when the answer is easy and plausible. If it seems difficult or obscure, drop the question and get on with the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Spending an hour to decide whether a puzzle has one solution, when the puzzle itself takes ten minutes, costs more than it gains.

card.rule: Put the questions, but do not insist on them when the answer seems difficult or obscure.
card.limits: Our reading: asking is cheap, so do ask once; the advice concerns how long to persist.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Study the sources of invention
concepts.question: What did Leibnitz consider more interesting than the inventions themselves?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Study how inventions come about, not only the inventions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Learn to invent, which is the aim of the book's heuristic.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Leibnitz, a great mathematician and philosopher, planned to write an Art of Invention but never carried through his plan. Fragments in his works show that he had interesting ideas about the subject and emphasised its importance. He thought the sources of invention more interesting than the inventions themselves.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher shows not only the finished proof but how the idea first appeared. This studies the source of the invention.

card.rule: Study how inventions come about, not only the inventions.
card.limits: Our reading: finished results still matter; the point is that the route to them is also worth study.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: What a lemma is
concepts.question: What does the word lemma mean?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a lemma as an auxiliary theorem, a statement assumed on the way to another.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Read proofs and the book's vocabulary without confusion.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Lemma means auxiliary theorem. The word is of Greek origin.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a paper, Lemma 2 states a small fact that the main theorem later uses; it serves the main theorem and is not the final aim.

card.rule: Read a lemma as an auxiliary theorem, a statement assumed on the way to another.
card.limits: A lemma is auxiliary only relative to the theorem it serves; the same statement can be a main theorem elsewhere. This is our reading.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Assume the helper and go ahead
concepts.question: What can you do when you suspect another theorem would give the one you are proving?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Assume the suspected helper theorem provisionally, postpone its proof and go ahead with the main proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep a proof moving while the helper still waits.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We are trying to prove A. We are led to suspect another theorem B: if B were true we could perhaps prove A with it. We assume B provisionally, postpone its proof, and go ahead with the proof of A. B is then an auxiliary theorem to A.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove that n cubed minus n is divisible by 6 for every whole number, suspect that it is divisible by 2 and by 3. Assume that, go on, and prove it afterwards.

card.rule: Assume the suspected helper theorem provisionally, postpone its proof and go ahead with the main proof.
card.limits: Our reading: until B itself is proved, the proof of A is conditional on it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Keep your aim in sight
concepts.question: What does the old advice to look at the unknown ask of you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep your aim in view: look at the unknown, or at the conclusion, and ask what leads to it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Hold direction while you search for ways and means.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: This is old advice; the Latin saying is respice finem, look at the end. Remember your aim and think of what you want to obtain. For a problem to find, look at the unknown; for a problem to prove, look at the conclusion. Fixing attention on the aim, you then ask what means lead to it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A traveller who must reach a station by noon keeps that goal in view and asks what ways lead to it, instead of thinking about the route she happens to be on.

card.rule: Keep your aim in view: look at the unknown, or at the conclusion, and ask what leads to it.
card.limits: Our reading: the advice sets direction; it does not itself supply the way.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Same unknown is a cheaper search
concepts.question: Why ask for a problem with the same unknown rather than any related problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask for a familiar problem with the same unknown, which narrows the search more than asking for any related problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a useful related problem with less effort.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Do you know a related problem is a general suggestion: related problems may share objects, notions, data or part of the condition. Asking for a problem with the same unknown is special and economical. You need not picture the whole problem, only its unknown, and you consider only problems with that unknown.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a problem that ends with find the length of the line, look at the unknown and recall familiar problems whose unknown is also the length of a line.

card.rule: Ask for a familiar problem with the same unknown, which narrows the search more than asking for any related problem.
card.limits: The special suggestion narrows the search; it does not guarantee a familiar problem exists.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Bring in an auxiliary element
concepts.question: What can you do when a familiar same-unknown problem needs a figure part that is not there?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If a familiar result needs a part your figure lacks, introduce a suitable auxiliary element such as a triangle.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the result of a familiar problem usable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: For a problem ending with find the length of the line, the simplest familiar problems with that unknown concern triangles. To use their results the figure must contain a triangle, so introduce one if there is none. You need not know three parts of the new triangle yet.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The diagonal of a 6 by 8 rectangle is the side of a right triangle with legs 6 and 8, so it has length 10, because 36 + 64 = 100.

card.rule: If a familiar result needs a part your figure lacks, introduce a suitable auxiliary element such as a triangle.
card.limits: The new element must actually relate to the given data, so choose it for that purpose.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Reduce the problem to its unknown
concepts.question: How does the type of unknown suggest a plan of attack?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Write the problem as given-find-the-unknown, and let the kind of unknown suggest your plan.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a plausible first plan quickly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Write the problem schematically: Given something, find the unknown. Four common unknowns suggest plans. A length is the side of some triangle. An angle is an angle of some triangle. The volume of a tetrahedron needs the base area and the altitude. A point to construct is an intersection of two loci, each a circle or a straight line.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find the angle at a corner of a quadrilateral given its sides and one diagonal, split off a triangle that has that angle and use the diagonal.

card.rule: Write the problem as given-find-the-unknown, and let the kind of unknown suggest your plan.
card.limits: Following such a plan may still meet difficulties; it gives an idea to start with.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: When no solved problem has the same unknown
concepts.question: How much can a formerly solved problem with the same unknown matter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check what you know: having a solved problem with the same unknown can make all the difference.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Judge how hard the task will be.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Without a formerly solved problem with the same unknown, the proposed one is much harder to tackle. Archimedes found the area of the surface of a sphere with given radius, for which there was scarcely a simpler problem to use. Given his result, finding the area of a sphere inscribed in a tetrahedron needs only the radius from the six edges.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The inscribed-sphere problem becomes a matter of expressing the radius in terms of the six edges.

card.rule: Check what you know: having a solved problem with the same unknown can make all the difference.
card.limits: The inscribed-sphere problem is not exactly easy even then.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: Look for a similar unknown
concepts.question: What can you do if no solved problem has exactly your unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If none has the same unknown, look for a solved problem with a similar unknown.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Still obtain a guide for the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Archimedes knew no problem with the same unknown but knew several with a similar one. The lateral surfaces of cylinders, cones and frustums of cones were easier to find and well known. We may be certain he considered these simpler similar cases.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find the area of an oval pond when only areas of rectangles and circles are known, the circle is a problem with a similar unknown.

card.rule: If none has the same unknown, look for a solved problem with a similar unknown.
card.limits: Problems with a similar unknown are less closely related than the same unknown, so they are less easy to use.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: For a theorem, look at the conclusion
concepts.question: For a problem to prove, which earlier theorems help most directly?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To prove a theorem, look at its conclusion and recall proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find the starting point of a proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Any theorem proved earlier and related to ours may help, but the most immediate service comes from theorems with the same conclusion. Write the theorem as: if something, then the angles are equal. Focus on the conclusion and look for very simple theorems of this sort.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove that two angles are equal, recall the theorem that corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.

card.rule: To prove a theorem, look at its conclusion and recall proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion.
card.limits: Our reading: a recalled theorem still has to fit your hypothesis before it helps.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
concepts.title: A good start from the unknown
concepts.question: What does recalling problems with the same unknown give you, and when do elementary ones suffice?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recall problems with the same or a similar unknown, and in simple cases the most elementary ones suffice.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Start in the right direction and conceive a plan.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Recalling formerly solved problems with the same or a similar unknown, or proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion, gives a good chance to start in the right direction. In simple cases, the most frequent in less advanced classes, the most elementary ones are usually sufficient.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student asked for the length of a line looks for the simplest familiar triangle problem and uses it.

card.rule: Recall problems with the same or a similar unknown, and in simple cases the most elementary ones suffice.
card.limits: Our reading: harder problems may need more than the simplest recalled problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: What modern heuristic tries to do
concepts.question: What does modern heuristic try to understand, and what practical use does the author hope for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Study problem-solving by describing the mental operations that typically help, so that teaching can use them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Better teaching, above all of mathematics, built on a real understanding of how problems get solved.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author holds that a clearer picture of the typically useful mental operations could exert some good influence on teaching.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The Dictionary's list of questions and suggestions is a list of such operations: each question hints at a mental step that often helps, such as looking at the unknown.

card.rule: Study problem-solving by describing the mental operations that typically help, so that teaching can use them.
card.limits: The aim is understanding and guidance, not a machine for producing answers.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Draw on every source of information
concepts.question: Which sources should a serious study of heuristic use, and which does the author put at the base?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build the study of problem-solving on logic, psychology, the older writers and, above all, unbiased experience.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A study that is general, independent of subject matter, and not blind to any kind of problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: No single source tells the whole story, so none of them should be neglected. Experience of solving and of watching others solve is the foundation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A mathematician who studied only logical form would miss how people actually struggle; one who watched only struggling students would miss what Pappus and Descartes already noticed.

card.rule: Build the study of problem-solving on logic, psychology, the older writers and, above all, unbiased experience.
card.limits: Our reading: a source is useful only as far as it fits what people are seen to do when they solve problems.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Finding the article behind a hint in the list
concepts.question: How do you find the Dictionary article that explains one particular item of the list?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Find the list paragraph that holds the item, take its first sentence, and look up the article with that title.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Quick, exact access to fuller explanation of any hint in the list.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The list has fifteen paragraphs, and the first sentence of each is the title of a Dictionary article. The article behind a hint is therefore the one named by its paragraph's opening words.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Think of a cookbook whose chapters are each named by their opening line: to learn more about a tip inside a chapter, you look up the chapter's opening line, not the tip.

card.rule: Find the list paragraph that holds the item, take its first sentence, and look up the article with that title.
card.limits: This works for items of the list; for a topic that is not in the list, use the Dictionary's own titles.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Aspects of solving, one principal article each
concepts.question: Which aspects of solving does the Dictionary treat in its principal articles, and how do they connect?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: See problem-solving as several aspects: progress, variation of the problem, problems to find or prove, notation and figures.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A map that tells you where each aspect of solving is studied at length.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Solving is a complex process. Working intensively, we roll the problem over and over in the mind, so variation of the problem is essential; decomposing and recombining, definition, generalization, specialization and analogy are ways to vary it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Varying a problem may lead to auxiliary elements or to a more accessible auxiliary problem. Feeling progress or its lack is the topic of the progress and achievement article, which the author says should be read fairly early.

card.rule: See problem-solving as several aspects: progress, variation of the problem, problems to find or prove, notation and figures.
card.limits: Our reading: the aspects overlap, so one move can belong to several of them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Guess, but examine the guess
concepts.question: Why is a plausible argument valuable in solving a problem, and why can it not stand as a proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Guess when you must, then examine the guess before relying on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Discovery of the solution without mistaking a hunch for a result.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Heuristic reasoning is provisional and merely plausible. It points where to look, but an argument of that kind has not shown the guess to be true.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student notices that a pattern holds in the first few cases and suspects it holds in all. The suspicion is a good guess; checking it against further cases and seeking a proof is the examination.

card.rule: Guess when you must, then examine the guess before relying on it.
card.limits: Examining a guess does not need to be a full proof at once, but plausible support must not be reported as proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: What heuristic includes and leaves out
concepts.question: Which problems fall inside heuristic, and which things does this book leave out or deny?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Count practical problems and puzzles as problems for heuristic, and expect no infallible rules of discovery.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A realistic scope: wide in the problems it covers, modest in what it promises.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Heuristic discusses human behaviour in the face of problems, which people have talked about since early times, and the essence of that talk is kept in proverbs. Infallible rules of discovery are beyond serious research.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two entries deal mainly with psychology: one on determination, hope and success, and one on subconscious work. Points that seemed too subtle, too technical or too controversial were kept out of this first short account.

card.rule: Count practical problems and puzzles as problems for heuristic, and expect no infallible rules of discovery.
card.limits: Our reading: leaving out a point is not denying it; the author gives reasons of exposition.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Dialogues as models of mental discourse
concepts.question: How can the teacher-student dialogues help a solver who works alone?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the teacher-student dialogues as a model, and talk through a problem with yourself in the same way.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Guided thinking, even when no teacher is present.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Thinking can fairly be called mental discourse, a conversation of the thinker with himself. The dialogues show the progress of a solution, so a solver who talks to himself can progress along a similar line.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher asks, 'What is the unknown?' A solver working alone asks himself the same question and answers it, taking the part of both teacher and student.

card.rule: Use the teacher-student dialogues as a model, and talk through a problem with yourself in the same way.
card.limits: A dialogue is a model, not a script; follow it with judgment.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Reading the Dictionary by kind of article
concepts.question: Which articles serve methodical questions, teachers, ambitious students, history and technical terms?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pick articles by purpose: methods, teachers, ambitious students, history of the subject, technical terms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reading the parts of the Dictionary that fit your need without wading through all of it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author groups some articles. Methodical ones cover Pappus, working backwards, indirect proof, induction, setting up equations, test by dimension and why proofs. Others speak to teachers or to students more ambitious than average.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Routine problems and diagnosis address teachers. The intelligent problem-solver, the intelligent reader and the future mathematician address ambitious students. History appears under Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano; condition, corollary and lemma explain terms.

card.rule: Pick articles by purpose: methods, teachers, ambitious students, history of the subject, technical terms.
card.limits: The groups are guides to choose from, not walls; a student may read a teacher's article with profit.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: The examples are elementary on purpose
concepts.question: Why does the book use elementary mathematical examples, and what should an expert reader do with them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take the elementary examples as a deliberate restriction, and carry the method to other fields with examples of your own.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A method general enough to work beyond the examples used to show it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Heuristic aims at generality, yet the book quotes almost exclusively elementary mathematics. Such problems offer all the desirable variety and are accessible and interesting to study.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An expert who takes an interest in the study can add examples from his own experience to elucidate the points the elementary examples illustrate.

card.rule: Take the elementary examples as a deliberate restriction, and carry the method to other fields with examples of your own.
card.limits: The restriction limits the examples, not the method; the author admits it is a restriction and hopes it does not impair the study.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: What a good notation does for you
concepts.question: How much easier does a well-chosen, well-known notation make a calculation?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before accepting a clumsy notation, try the work without the good one, and then adopt the one that carries the load.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Appreciating why notation deserves care before using it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A familiar notation lets the mind put its effort into the problem and not into the writing. The author invites you to add a few big numbers while forbidding Arabic numerals: the labour of the task shows how much a good notation does for you.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Try MMMXC + MDXCVI + MDCXLVI + MDCCLXXXI + MDCCCLXXXVII in Roman numerals only. Translated to digits the numbers are 3090, 1596, 1646, 1781 and 1887, and their sum is 10000.

card.rule: Before accepting a clumsy notation, try the work without the good one, and then adopt the one that carries the load.
card.limits: A good notation helps the mind but does not think for you.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Symbols as a language
concepts.question: In what sense are mathematical symbols a language, and what is setting up equations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat mathematical notation as a well-made language, and read setting up an equation as translation into it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Using signs to assist reasoning, in the way words assist speech.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Speaking and thinking are close, so words help the mind; hard thinking can still go on without words, with figures or symbols. Signs in general assist reason. Mathematical notation is concise and precise, with rules that suffer no exception.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 'A number increased by its half is 18' becomes x + x/2 = 18. The words have been translated into the symbolic language, and then x = 12.

card.rule: Treat mathematical notation as a well-made language, and read setting up an equation as translation into it.
card.limits: Notation assists thought but is not the only way to think.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Choosing the notation is a step of the solution
concepts.question: Why spend time on choosing symbols before solving?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose your notation deliberately and early, since the time spent is repaid later.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fewer hesitations and confusions, and a sharper grasp of the problem's elements.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each new problem calls for its own choice of symbols. Choosing carefully forces you to think sharply about which elements of the problem must be named.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Before a mixing problem, decide letters for the amount of each liquid and for the final concentration. A few minutes spent now save the hesitation later.

card.rule: Choose your notation deliberately and early, since the time spent is repaid later.
card.limits: Over-polishing a notation for a trivial problem wastes the time it is meant to save.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: What makes a notation good
concepts.question: Which qualities should a good notation have?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Judge a notation by whether it is unambiguous, pregnant and easy to remember, avoids harmful second meanings and uses helpful ones, and lets the order of signs suggest the order of things.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A checklist for choosing between candidate notations.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each quality guards against a different failure: confusion between objects, a sign that tells you too little (a pregnant notation expresses more, so that more consequences can be drawn from it), a sign you forget, a sign that misleads, or a sign that hides how things are connected.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Writing a, b, c for three lengths that play the same role in a problem shows their likeness; writing a, q, m for them hides it.

card.rule: Judge a notation by whether it is unambiguous, pregnant and easy to remember, avoids harmful second meanings and uses helpful ones, and lets the order of signs suggest the order of things.
