card.limits: No notation has all these qualities in every problem; the later cards show where they pull apart.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: One symbol, one object
concepts.question: What does the rule of unambiguous signs forbid, and what does it allow?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Never let one symbol stand for two objects in the same inquiry; use one sign per object unless you have a reason not to.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping every statement of a solution unmistakable.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A symbol that means two things in one problem makes every formula uncertain. Within a single problem the letter a must name one thing only.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If the width of a field is a, do not also call its angle of slope a. The letter a may be reused freely in the next problem.

card.rule: Never let one symbol stand for two objects in the same inquiry; use one sign per object unless you have a reason not to.
card.limits: The rule is about one inquiry; across problems the same letter may mean something else.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Initials make signs easy to recognise
concepts.question: How can initials help, and when do they fail?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use initials as symbols where you can, so the sign reminds you of the object and the object of the sign.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Signs that are easy to remember and instantly recognised.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A sign that recalls its object saves effort each time it appears. Initials give this for free: r for rate, t for time, V for volume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a problem with a rate, a time, a volume and a radius, r goes to the rate and t to time and V to volume. The radius cannot also be r, so another sign has to be found.

card.rule: Use initials as symbols where you can, so the sign reminds you of the object and the object of the sign.
card.limits: Initials fail when the letter is already taken; other means must then be used to keep signs recognisable.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Letters in order suggest things in order
concepts.question: How can the order of letters in the alphabet reflect how the objects of a problem relate?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose letters near one another in the alphabet for objects that are close in the problem; use early letters for givens and late letters for unknowns.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A notation whose shape reveals the structure of the problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Letters at the start of the alphabet (a, b, c) usually denote given quantities, and letters at the end (x, y, z) denote unknowns or variables. Successive letters stress that several objects play the same role.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the length, width and height of a box whose three edges play the same role, a, b, c shows the likeness. In a proportion a : b = x : y, the letters a, b hint at constants and x, y at variables, and a precedes b as x precedes y.

card.rule: Choose letters near one another in the alphabet for objects that are close in the problem; use early letters for givens and late letters for unknowns.
card.limits: Successive letters can hide differences in role; when the roles differ, other letters may be better.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: One alphabet per category of object
concepts.question: How do different alphabets help keep categories of objects apart?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Draw the letters for one category from one alphabet and for another category from another, pairing corresponding letters for related objects.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A notation in which the kind of an object shows from the kind of letter.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In plane geometry capital Roman letters name points, small Roman letters name lines, and small Greek letters name angles. When two objects of different categories are related in an important way, matching letters of the two alphabets show the relation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a triangle, A, B, C stand for the vertices, a, b, c for the sides, and alpha, beta, gamma for the angles.

card.rule: Draw the letters for one category from one alphabet and for another category from another, pairing corresponding letters for related objects.
card.limits: This is a convention, not a law; depart from it deliberately and only for a reason.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: A pregnant notation says more
concepts.question: What makes one notation more pregnant than another, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Prefer the notation that expresses more, so that consequences can be drawn from the formula without the figure.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reading true statements straight off the symbols.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A notation that expresses more is more pregnant. Writing that triangle ABC is similar to triangle EFG, with vertices matched in the order written, tells A goes to E, B to F and C to G. The older form left the matching to be read off the figure.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From the modern formula we get angle A equal to angle E, and AB : BC = EF : FG. If AB = 6, BC = 9 and EF = 4, then FG = 4 x 9 / 6 = 6.

card.rule: Prefer the notation that expresses more, so that consequences can be drawn from the formula without the figure.
card.limits: A pregnant notation helps only if the reader knows the convention behind it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Second meanings of symbols
concepts.question: When does the history of a symbol help you, and when does it get in your way?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep traditional symbols for their traditional meaning, and use a standing notation to recall procedures while separating the present meaning from the former one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Using the associations of symbols as a help and not a trap.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Words acquire shades of meaning from contexts, and mathematical symbols do too. The letters e, i and pi have firmly rooted meanings: the base of natural logarithms, the square root of minus one, and the ratio of circumference to diameter. Using them otherwise can mislead.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A notation used on former occasions may assist us in recalling a useful procedure, provided the present meaning of the symbol is kept distinct from the former one.

card.rule: Keep traditional symbols for their traditional meaning, and use a standing notation to recall procedures while separating the present meaning from the former one.
card.limits: Reusing a traditional symbol for something else invites confusion even when the context seems clear.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Weighing notations and winning over doubters
concepts.question: How do you choose between two notations, and how do you help a student who dislikes algebra?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Choose between notations with experience and a good reason, and help doubters feel by experience that symbols assist the mind.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A notation chosen on its merits, and students who see the point of learning one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: One reason may favour one notation and another reason the other. Experience and taste decide, as with words, but knowing the advantages and disadvantages helps. A student who finds a new notation arbitrary and a burden on memory is justified unless he sees what it gives him.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher lets the student set up the same word problem first in words and then in symbols, so the student sees for himself how much the symbols shorten the work.

card.rule: Choose between notations with experience and a good reason, and help doubters feel by experience that symbols assist the mind.
card.limits: No argument alone persuades a doubter; the compensation has to be experienced.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Pappus and his Heuristic
concepts.question: Who was Pappus, and what did he say the study of heuristic was for?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Know that Pappus described heuristic as a body of doctrine for people who have studied the Elements and want to learn to solve mathematical problems.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Placing the ideas of analysis and synthesis in their origin and purpose.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Pappus, an important Greek mathematician, lived probably around A.D. 300. In the seventh book of his Collectiones he reports on a branch of study he calls analyomenos, which the author renders as Heuristic. It is useful, he says, for solving mathematical problems and for this alone.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Pappus credits the work to three men: Euclid, the author of the Elements, Apollonius of Perga, and Aristaeus the elder. It teaches the procedures of analysis and synthesis.

card.rule: Know that Pappus described heuristic as a body of doctrine for people who have studied the Elements and want to learn to solve mathematical problems.
card.limits: The quoted passage is the author's free rendering, not a literal translation.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Analysis: assume it done and work backwards
concepts.question: What does analysis ask you to do, and where does it stop?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start from what is required, take it as already done, and ask again and again what could precede it, until you reach something known or admitted.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Finding a starting point for the solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In analysis you assume the thing required is done, found or true. Then you ask from what antecedent it could be derived, then what could be the antecedent of that, and so on, passing from antecedent to antecedent until something already known or admittedly true appears.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Pappus also calls this solution backwards, or regressive reasoning.

card.rule: Start from what is required, take it as already done, and ask again and again what could precede it, until you reach something known or admitted.
card.limits: Analysis stops at a known starting point; it does not by itself carry out the solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Synthesis: retrace the steps forward
concepts.question: How does synthesis relate to analysis, and where does it begin?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start from the last point reached in analysis, derive what preceded it, and retrace the steps until you arrive at what is required.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turning the discovered chain into a finished solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Synthesis reverses the process. You begin with the thing already known or admittedly true at the end of the analysis and derive from it what preceded it there. You go on making derivations, retracing your steps, until you reach what is required.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Pappus calls this synthesis, or constructive solution, or progressive reasoning.

card.rule: Start from the last point reached in analysis, derive what preceded it, and retrace the steps until you arrive at what is required.
card.limits: Synthesis can be carried out only if the analysis reached a usable starting point.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Analysing a problem to prove
concepts.question: How does analysis work on a theorem, and what does the last theorem tell you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To test a theorem A, derive B from A, C from B, and so on to a last theorem L you know about; if L is true A follows, and if L is false A is false.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Deciding a clearly stated theorem whose truth is not yet known.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Starting from A, you do not yet know whether A is true. You derive another theorem B, then C, until you reach a last theorem L about which you have definite knowledge. If L is true, A is also true, provided every derivation can be reversed; then you prove K from L, then each earlier theorem, until you reach A.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If L is false, then A is shown false.

card.rule: To test a theorem A, derive B from A, C from B, and so on to a last theorem L you know about; if L is true A follows, and if L is false A is false.
card.limits: The conclusion that A is true needs each derivation to be convertible, so the steps can be traced back.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Analysing a problem to find
concepts.question: How does analysis work when the task is to find an unknown?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Assume the unknown x exists, link it to a second unknown y, then to a third, until you reach an unknown z you can find, and then work back from z to x.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Finding an unknown when you do not yet know if a solution exists.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Assume there is an x satisfying the condition and derive from it another unknown y that must satisfy a related condition. Link y to still another, and so on, until a last unknown z can be found by a known method. First find z, then the unknown before it, and finally x.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If nothing satisfies the condition on z, the problem concerning x has no solution.

card.rule: Assume the unknown x exists, link it to a second unknown y, then to a third, until you reach an unknown z you can find, and then work back from z to x.
card.limits: The chain from x back to z must also be reversible; otherwise finding z does not give x.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: An algebra example of analysis
concepts.question: How do two substitutions turn a hard exponential equation into a quadratic?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an equation is hard, introduce a new unknown that simplifies it, repeat if needed, and stop when a known method applies; then work back through the substitutions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Solving an equation by repeated reduction.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The equation 8(4^x + 4^-x) - 54(2^x + 2^-x) + 101 = 0 becomes simpler with y = 2^x, since 4^x = y squared. A second substitution z = y + 1/y gives 8z squared - 54z + 85 = 0, a quadratic. Then the synthesis finds z = 5/2 or 17/4.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From z come y = 2, 1/2, 4, 1/4, and from y come x = 1, -1, 2, -2.

card.rule: When an equation is hard, introduce a new unknown that simplifies it, repeat if needed, and stop when a known method applies; then work back through the substitutions.
card.limits: The substitutions need ideas and some luck; analysis does not supply them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: A nonmathematical analysis: crossing the creek
concepts.question: How does the creek story show analysis as thoughts and synthesis as acts?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In any practical problem, plan by analysis in thought, then carry out by synthesis in action, in the reverse order.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing that analysis and synthesis are not special to mathematics.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A primitive man cannot cross a creek because the water has risen. Crossing is his x. He recalls crossing another creek on a fallen tree, so a fallen tree becomes his new unknown y. None is to be found, so he wishes one of the standing trees would fall across, and asks how to tilt one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Walking across is the first desire the analysis starts from and the last act the synthesis ends with. The same objects fill both; the analysis exercises his mind, the synthesis his muscles.

card.rule: In any practical problem, plan by analysis in thought, then carry out by synthesis in action, in the reverse order.
card.limits: The story is the author's illustration of the idea and not a historical record.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Analysis comes first, synthesis after
concepts.question: How do analysis and synthesis fit together as invention and execution?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do the analysis first to invent a plan, then the synthesis to carry it out.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping devising and doing apart so each gets its own attention.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Analysis comes naturally first and synthesis afterwards. Analysis is invention and synthesis is execution. Analysis is devising a plan, and synthesis is carrying through the plan.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the algebra example the invention was the pair of substitutions; the execution was the calculation of z, then y, then x. The order of calculation is opposite to the order of invention.

card.rule: Do the analysis first to invent a plan, then the synthesis to carry it out.
card.limits: The two are not always separate in practice; a solver may switch back and forth.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Why assume the problem is solved?
concepts.question: Why is it not self-deception to assume a problem to find already solved?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Assume the unknown exists and satisfies the condition; the assumption is provisional, harmless, useful and natural.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Examining the condition by picturing the unknown in place.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The assumption is made only to start the analysis and it is provisional. It is harmless: if no such object exists and the analysis leads anywhere, it must lead to a final problem with no solution, which shows the original has none.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: It is useful, since to examine the condition we must picture the relations between x and the data, and we cannot do so without picturing x as existent. It is also natural, as the creek story suggests.

card.rule: Assume the unknown exists and satisfies the condition; the assumption is provisional, harmless, useful and natural.
card.limits: Do not mistake the assumption for a claim that a solution exists; you may find it does not.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Assuming a theorem true to analyse it
concepts.question: What does the advice to assume the theorem true really invite you to do?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Draw consequences from the theorem A as if it were true, even though it is not yet proved.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Starting an analysis of a theorem when no proof is known.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: For a problem to prove, the advice to assume A true is just an invitation to draw consequences from the theorem although it has not been proved. It is a request to explore, not a claim to know.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student asked to show that a statement about triangles holds starts: suppose it is true; then these angles must be equal; then these lines must be parallel. Each consequence is checked against what is known.

card.rule: Draw consequences from the theorem A as if it were true, even though it is not yet proved.
card.limits: People who shrink from drawing consequences of an unproved theorem cannot start an analysis.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Convertible derivations and the missing proviso
concepts.question: Why does the paraphrase add that all derivations must be convertible?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you reason back from the required result, check that each step can be reversed, so that the synthesis really follows.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Making sure that the known end of the analysis really leads back to the required result.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The paraphrase twice states the proviso that all derivations are convertible. Without it, a chain from A to a true L may still say nothing about A, since the steps may not run backwards.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To solve the equation square root of (x + 6) = x, a student squares both sides and gets x squared - x - 6 = 0, so x = 3 or x = -2. Squaring cannot be undone: x = 3 works, while x = -2 gives 2 on the left and -2 on the right.

card.rule: When you reason back from the required result, check that each step can be reversed, so that the synthesis really follows.
card.limits: The proviso is the author's addition; Pappus's text does not state it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Beyond geometry and the textbook tradition
concepts.question: How does the paraphrase differ from Pappus, and why is analysis wrongly confined to geometry textbooks?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not confine analysis and synthesis to geometry; they apply to mathematical problems of every sort and beyond.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Using Pappus's procedures wherever a problem is to be solved.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The paraphrase uses a more definite terminology than the original and introduces symbols A, B, up to L and x, y, up to z, which the original lacks. It says mathematical problems where the original says geometrical ones, to stress that the procedures are not restricted to geometry.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Many elementary geometry textbooks include a few remarks on analysis, synthesis and assuming the problem solved. The tradition goes back to Pappus, though few writers know him directly.

card.rule: Do not confine analysis and synthesis to geometry; they apply to mathematical problems of every sort and beyond.
card.limits: Our reading: the author's complaint is about narrowness, not about the geometry books themselves.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Pedantry and mastery
concepts.question: What separates a pedant from a master in the use of a rule?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Apply a rule with ease and judgment, notice where it fits, and never let its words hide the purpose of the action.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Using rules to serve the purpose, not the other way round.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A pedant applies a rule to the letter, rigidly and unquestioningly, in cases where it fits and in cases where it does not. A master applies it with natural ease and judgment, noticing where it fits.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Some pedants are poor fools who never understood the rule they apply so conscientiously. Others are successful: they understood the rule at the start and chose one that fits in many cases and fails only occasionally.

card.rule: Apply a rule with ease and judgment, notice where it fits, and never let its words hide the purpose of the action.
card.limits: A rule that fits in many cases still fails in some; success so far is no proof that rigid use is mastery.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Using the list without becoming a pedant
concepts.question: How should the questions and suggestions of the list be learned and used?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Learn the list's questions by experience, and ask each only when an attentive look at the problem calls for it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Help for solvers and teachers that does not harden into rigid habit.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions and suggestions can help both problem-solvers and teachers, but they must first be understood and their use learned by trial and error, by failure and success. Their use must never become pedantic.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Ask no question and make no suggestion indiscriminately, following some rigid habit. The next step in a hard problem should come from attentive, open-minded consideration of the problem, and what you say to a student from sympathetic understanding of his difficulties.

card.rule: Learn the list's questions by experience, and ask each only when an attentive look at the problem calls for it.
card.limits: Judgment itself needs the experience of having used the list.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: If you must have a rule, use your own brains first
concepts.question: What single rule does the author offer to a person inclined to be a pedant?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If you must lean on a rule, let it be: use your own brains first.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping your own thinking in charge of every rule you adopt.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The entry closes with advice for those inclined to be pedants who must rely on some rule: Always use your own brains first. The rule puts thinking ahead of any other rule.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Before reaching for a question from the list, look at the problem yourself and see what it asks of you. Then use the list if it helps.

card.rule: If you must lean on a rule, let it be: use your own brains first.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule is a reminder about order, not a ban on using other rules.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Practical and mathematical problems share their motives
concepts.question: How do practical problems differ from mathematical ones, and what do they share?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Solve a practical problem with the same principal motives and procedures as a mathematical one, expecting it to be less sharply defined.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Carrying the habits of mathematical problem-solving over to engineering and everyday tasks.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Practical problems differ from purely mathematical ones in various respects, yet the principal motives and procedures of solving are essentially the same. Practical engineering problems usually involve mathematical problems.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To build a dam, one asks the questions of the list: what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition? The answers are many and loosely bounded, but the questions are the same.

card.rule: Solve a practical problem with the same principal motives and procedures as a mathematical one, expecting it to be less sharply defined.
card.limits: The two kinds of problem are not identical; the differences are real and the next cards describe them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Unknown, data and condition of a dam
concepts.question: What are the unknowns, the conditions and the data in the problem of building a dam?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: List the many unknowns, the many conditions and the many kinds of data of a practical problem before you decide what to do.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing the true size of a practical problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The unknowns include the location, shape and dimensions of the dam and the materials used. The conditions include producing power, supplying water and controlling floods, while disturbing navigation, fish and scenery as little as possible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The data are topographical, geological, meteorological and economic: the terrain, the foundations and leakage, rainfall and floods, and the value of the ground flooded and cost of materials and labour.

card.rule: List the many unknowns, the many conditions and the many kinds of data of a practical problem before you decide what to do.
card.limits: A list is not a solution; the conditions pull against each other and must be balanced.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: The knowledge a practical problem needs
concepts.question: What knowledge does a practical problem draw on, and how sharp is it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take stock of the knowledge you bring to a practical problem, and accept that part of it is empirical and not sharply defined.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Using experience honestly where theory does not reach.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: To solve any problem we need previously acquired knowledge. The ancient Egyptian dam-builder had seen dams, floods and breaks and had heard stories of dams that lasted or failed; he lacked exact concepts of fluid pressure or of strain and stress.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The modern engineer has such concepts, but also relies on knowledge of a rather empirical character: erosion by flowing water, the transport of silt, the plasticity of certain materials.

card.rule: Take stock of the knowledge you bring to a practical problem, and accept that part of it is empirical and not sharply defined.
card.limits: Empirical knowledge is useful, but it is not a theory and can fail where experience has not reached.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: When the concepts are hazy
concepts.question: What should you do when the basic ideas of a practical problem are themselves unclear?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the concepts of a practical problem are hazy, make clarifying them part of the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Not treating vague notions as if they were exact.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In a mathematical problem we start from clear concepts that are fairly well ordered in the mind. In a practical problem we may have to start from hazy ideas, so clarifying the concepts can be an important part of the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Medical science is in a better position to check infectious diseases today than before Pasteur, when the notion of infection itself was hazy.

card.rule: If the concepts of a practical problem are hazy, make clarifying them part of the problem.
card.limits: The question whether you took all essential notions into account is good for all problems, but its use varies with the notions involved.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Using all the data, in a practical sense
concepts.question: How do the questions about using all data and the whole condition change in practical problems?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a practical problem, ask whether you used all the data and conditions that could contribute appreciably, and accept that you must stop collecting somewhere.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Acting before information is complete, without ignoring what matters.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In a well-stated mathematical problem every datum and clause of the condition is essential. A practical problem has a multitude of data and conditions, so you take into account as many as you can and neglect some.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The dam designer weighs public and economic interests but disregards petty claims, and eventually stops collecting geological data although some uncertainty remains. 'If you will sail without danger, you must never put to sea.'

card.rule: In a practical problem, ask whether you used all the data and conditions that could contribute appreciably, and accept that you must stop collecting somewhere.
card.limits: Stopping is a judgment: neglecting a datum that does matter is a real danger.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Do practical problems need more experience?
concepts.question: Is the difference between practical and mathematical problems one of attitude or of knowledge?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In either kind of problem, rely on experience with similar problems, and ask whether you have seen the same problem in a slightly different form.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Not treating practical work as a separate kind of thinking.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: There is a widespread opinion that practical problems need more experience than mathematical ones. The author thinks the difference very likely lies in the nature of the knowledge needed, not in our attitude toward the problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver of either kind of problem relies on experience with similar problems and often asks: have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form? Do you know a related problem?

card.rule: In either kind of problem, rely on experience with similar problems, and ask whether you have seen the same problem in a slightly different form.
card.limits: Our reading: the author states this as likely, not as proved.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Approximation in applied mathematics
concepts.question: Why is it reasonable to accept approximate answers when a practical problem is turned into mathematics?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a practical problem becomes a mathematical one, accept a slight inaccuracy if it buys a real gain in simplicity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Solvable mathematics that still serves the practical aim.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A modern engineer cannot rely on common sense alone for a bold design: he must calculate the resistance of the dam, foreseeing strain and stress with the theory of elasticity. The practical problem thus leads to a mathematical problem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In setting up and solving such a problem we usually content ourselves with approximation. Since some minor data and conditions of the practical problem are neglected, it is reasonable to allow slight inaccuracy, especially when we gain in simplicity what we lose in accuracy.

card.rule: When a practical problem becomes a mathematical one, accept a slight inaccuracy if it buys a real gain in simplicity.
card.limits: Approximation is acceptable only while the neglected parts stay minor.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: The earth as a sphere
concepts.question: How good is the assumption that the earth is a sphere for drawing maps?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Judge an approximation by comparing the size of the error with the gain in simplicity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choosing a simple model that is accurate enough for its use.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Devising a map, we often assume the earth is a sphere. This is only approximate, since the surface is not a mathematically defined surface and the earth is flattened at the poles, but a sphere makes map drawing much easier.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Imagine a ball of the earth's shape with 25 feet across at the equator. The distance between its poles is about one inch less. As 25 feet is 300 inches, the shortfall is about 1 part in 300, roughly 0.33 percent.

card.rule: Judge an approximation by comparing the size of the error with the gain in simplicity.
card.limits: A sphere is good for maps, but not for every purpose; a task needing high precision may demand the real shape.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Problems to find
concepts.question: What is a problem to find, and what kinds of unknown can it have?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recognise a problem to find by its aim: to find a certain object, the unknown, whether the problem is serious or a puzzle.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing what kind of thing you are looking for.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The aim of a problem to find is to find a certain object, the unknown, also called the thing sought or the thing required. The problem may be theoretical or practical, abstract or concrete, serious or a mere puzzle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a mystery story the unknown is a murderer; in a chess problem a move; in a riddle a word; in an elementary algebra problem a number; in a geometric construction a figure.

card.rule: Recognise a problem to find by its aim: to find a certain object, the unknown, whether the problem is serious or a puzzle.
card.limits: Our reading: the kind depends on the aim, not the topic; one subject can give both a problem to find and a problem to prove.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Problems to prove
concepts.question: What is a problem to prove, and why does the author usually leave out disproving?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recognise a problem to prove by its aim: to show conclusively that a clearly stated assertion is true or else false.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing what kind of answer is wanted: a conclusive yes or no with grounds.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The aim of a problem to prove is to show conclusively that a clearly stated assertion is true, or else to show that it is false. We must answer conclusively, either by proving it true or by proving it false.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A judge hears a witness say the defendant stayed at home a certain night. The judge must find whether it is true and give as good grounds as possible: a problem to prove.

card.rule: Recognise a problem to prove by its aim: to show conclusively that a clearly stated assertion is true or else false.
card.limits: A request to prove a theorem leaves disproof unmentioned; the author neglects it only because the chance of disproving Pythagoras is slight.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Principal parts of each kind of problem
concepts.question: What are the principal parts of a problem to find and of a problem to prove?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Name the principal parts exactly: unknown, data and condition for a problem to find; hypothesis and conclusion for a problem to prove.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing what you are given, what you want, and how they are linked.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem to find has an unknown, data and a condition that links the unknown to the data. A problem to prove of the usual kind has a hypothesis and a conclusion, the if-part and the then-part of the theorem.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To construct a triangle with sides a, b, c or one with altitudes a, b, c, the unknown is a triangle and the data the three lengths in both; only the condition differs. In 'If the four sides of a quadrilateral are equal, then the diagonals are perpendicular', the hypothesis is the first part, the conclusion the second.

card.rule: Name the principal parts exactly: unknown, data and condition for a problem to find; hypothesis and conclusion for a problem to prove.
card.limits: Not every theorem splits naturally into hypothesis and conclusion, for example the theorem that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: The list for problems to prove
concepts.question: How do the list's questions about unknown, data and condition change for a problem to prove?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To use the list on a problem to prove, swap unknown for conclusion and data for hypothesis, and keep the rest of the question.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Carrying the same helpful questions over to theorems.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: To solve a problem to find you must know its unknown, data and condition very exactly. For a problem to prove you must know its hypothesis and conclusion just as exactly, and the list's questions have counterparts.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Look at the unknown becomes look at the conclusion, and try to think of a familiar theorem having the same or a similar conclusion. Keep only a part of the condition becomes keep only part of the hypothesis; is the conclusion still valid? Did you use the whole condition becomes did you use the whole hypothesis?

card.rule: To use the list on a problem to prove, swap unknown for conclusion and data for hypothesis, and keep the rest of the question.
card.limits: The correspondence is a guide to adapt the list; some questions need more than a change of words.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
concepts.title: Which kind matters where
concepts.question: Which kind of problem does the book stress, and which matters more at higher levels?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect problems to find to dominate elementary mathematics and problems to prove to dominate advanced mathematics.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Knowing why this book's list is built for one kind and adapted for the other.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Problems to find are more important in elementary mathematics and problems to prove in advanced mathematics. In this book, problems to find are emphasised more than the other kind.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: That is why the list is specially adapted to problems to find. It has to be revised, with some questions changed, in order to apply to problems to prove as well.

card.rule: Expect problems to find to dominate elementary mathematics and problems to prove to dominate advanced mathematics.
card.limits: Our reading: the emphasis is a choice of this book, and does not mean problems to prove are less important in general.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Mobilization: bringing dormant knowledge into play
concepts.question: What has been added to your picture of a problem by the time you solve it, and where did it come from?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pull the relevant items out of what you already know: formerly solved problems, known theorems, definitions.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fill your picture of the problem with material you can actually work with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: By the end of a solution your conception of the problem holds much more than at the start, and what was added came out of your own memory, where it lay dormant.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student must find the area of a regular hexagon. Before any calculation, she recalls how a regular hexagon looks when cut from its centre, and the formula for a triangle. Nothing is solved yet, but the material is on the table.

card.rule: Mobilize first: recall the earlier problems, theorems and definitions that bear on this problem.
card.limits: Recalling is only half the work: isolated facts still have to be combined into an argument that fits the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Organization: fitting recalled facts into one argument
concepts.question: Once facts are recalled, what must the solver do to make them solve this problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Combine what you recalled into one connected argument that is adapted to the problem in hand.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a heap of recalled material into a well adapted whole that reaches the unknown.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A solution needs facts that fit each other and the aim; isolated facts do not by themselves make a solution. Polya calls this adapting and combining activity organization.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A hiker recalls the map, the weather and the bus times. Only when she lays out a route that uses all three, leaving at the hour a bus runs and crossing before the weather turns, has she organized what she mobilized.

card.rule: After recalling, build the argument: connect the materials into a whole adapted to the problem.
card.limits: Organization works only on what has been recalled; with nothing mobilized there is nothing to connect.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Mobilization and organization are one process
concepts.question: Why can recalling and combining never be cleanly separated while someone works at a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat recall and combination as two aspects of the same working, and recall with your aim in view.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid treating the solution as a first step of gathering and a second step of assembling.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Working with concentration, we recall only facts more or less tied to our purpose, and we have nothing to connect but what we have recalled. Each step feeds the other.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A mechanic hunting a noise recalls only the parts that could make that sound, and tries them against each other as he recalls. He does not first list every part he knows and afterwards link them.

card.rule: While working, recall facts connected with your purpose and connect them as you go.
card.limits: Polya says these are only two aspects of one complex process that has still other aspects, so they are not the whole story of progress.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: The conception of the problem changes through variation
concepts.question: How does your view of the problem become fuller, and what makes that possible?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Try various standpoints and view the problem from different sides, restating and varying it to reach a better adapted conception.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Move from the first, rough conception to one better adapted to a solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Enriched with the materials recalled and worked in, the conception at the end is much fuller than at the outset. To get there we must look at the problem from different sides, and hardly any progress is possible without varying it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A driver stuck on how to reach a village first sees it as a point on a road. Rephrasing it as the end of a river valley, then as the place reached from the pass, reveals a route that the first view hid.

card.rule: When your first conception stalls, vary the problem: another standpoint, another side.
card.limits: Variation helps only when it leads to a conception better adapted to the problem; change for its own sake is not progress.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Foreseeing the solution by plausible guesses
concepts.question: How can we know we are nearer the solution before we have a certain answer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat what you foresee, such as a theorem that might apply, as a plausible guess to test, not a certainty.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use provisional insight to steer toward a solution that will be certain and final.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: As work advances we see more of the goal and foresee more clearly what should be done. We foresee it with some plausibility only; certainty comes with the complete solution. Without plausible and provisional considerations, we could never find the certain solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student solving a word problem foresees that the answer is probably a whole number of hours. It is only a plausible guess; she builds the equation and checks it, and the guess becomes certain or is dropped.

card.rule: Use plausible foresight to guide you, then confirm it by complete argument.
card.limits: Plausible foresight can mislead; certainty belongs only to the complete solution.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Judging progress: three signs of advance
concepts.question: When someone asks whether you have made progress, what can you point to?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Name your progress in terms of mobilization and organization, a developing conception, and growing prevision of the final argument.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Answer 'Have you made any progress?' with something specific instead of a feeling.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya sums up progress as advancing mobilization and organization of knowledge, evolution of the conception of the problem, and increasing prevision of the steps that will make up the final argument.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student asked about progress says: I now know which two theorems are relevant, I see the problem as a question about angles, and I expect the last step to use similar triangles. That is progress named in the three ways.

card.rule: Judge progress by what is mobilized and organized, how the conception has changed, and what you now foresee.
card.limits: These are Polya's general account; in a concrete case judging progress remains a matter of judgment, which he admits is easier than stating it in general.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: The bright idea: an abrupt reorganization
concepts.question: What is a bright idea, and how does it differ from steady progress?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recognise a bright idea as an abrupt, momentous change of outlook, a sudden reorganization of how you conceive the problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know what to hope for and how to prepare for it, instead of treating it as luck.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya calls a sudden advance a bright idea, a good idea, a happy thought or a brain-wave. It is an abrupt and momentous change of outlook, a sudden reorganization of the mode of conception, and a just emerging confident prevision of the steps to take.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student failing to place a point suddenly sees the whole figure as one half of a rectangle. Her view of the problem is reorganised at once, and she can foresee the remaining steps.

card.rule: Prepare for the bright idea by working on understanding and planning, and carry it through when it comes.
card.limits: A bright idea is not guaranteed by any rule; the book says the list can only provoke it, not produce it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Reading the list by what each question aims at
concepts.question: Which kinds of question on the list serve which part of progress?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Match the list's questions to their aim: recalling knowledge, organizing it, finding what is missing, varying, or foreseeing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choose the right question for the situation you are actually in.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya groups the questions by situation: those aimed at recalling knowledge, those used when you think the right material is collected and want it better organized, those used when you suspect material is missing, those aimed at varying the problem, and those that try to foresee the nature of the solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A solver who feels the pieces are all there but do not fit asks about using a related problem's result or method. One who feels something is missing asks whether all the data and the whole condition were used.

card.rule: Diagnose your situation first, then pick the question that matches it.
card.limits: Polya says the grouping is a background to the list; the questions are not applied by a rigid rule.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: From concrete cases to a general account of progress
concepts.question: Why does a study of problem solving need a general account of progress when we judge it easily in single cases?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask the progress questions in concrete cases, and then work to state in general what progress and achievement are.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a study of heuristic reasonably complete by clarifying what progress is.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We judge progress and achievement in concrete cases more or less confidently. The step from such cases to a general description is not easy at all, yet a fairly complete study of heuristic has to take it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A coach can say at once whether a swimmer improved this week. Writing down in general terms what improvement in swimming consists of is a different and harder task, and a training manual needs it.

card.rule: Do not stop at feeling you can judge progress; state in general what it consists of.
card.limits: Polya says the step to a general description is not easy at all; his account is an attempt to clarify, not a complete theory.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Testing the list on a puzzle: unknown, data, condition
concepts.question: Do the list's questions work on a word puzzle as they do on mathematics?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Put the list's opening questions to any puzzle: name the unknown, the data and the condition.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Check, in practice, that the list does not depend on the subject-matter.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya says the list's questions are independent of the subject-matter and applicable to all kinds of problems, and tests this on an anagram: rearrange the letters of DRY OXTAIL IN REAR into one word. The unknown is a word; the data are the four given words; the condition is that the word uses exactly those letters and is probably not too unusual an English word.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For a different puzzle, rearrange the letters of 'LISTEN' into another word: the unknown is a word, the data is the word LISTEN, and the condition is that it uses exactly its six letters.

card.rule: On a puzzle, begin as on any problem: what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition?
card.limits: Naming the three parts does not solve the puzzle; it only puts the work on the ground the list expects.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Restating the puzzle: letters, vowels and consonants
concepts.question: How can a restatement of an anagram reveal a feature of the answer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Restate the problem in its equivalent letter form and separate the vowels from the consonants to see a new aspect.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a feature of the answer, such as its number of syllables, that the original wording hid.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya restates the puzzle as: find a word containing, in some arrangement, the letters AAEIIOY and DLNRRRTX. Separating vowels from consonants matters here; alphabetical order does not. There are seven vowels, so the word has seven syllables unless it has diphthongs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To find a word from the letters of 'DRY OXTAIL IN REAR', write the seven vowels in one row and the eight consonants in another; the count of vowels then points to a long word.

card.rule: Restate the puzzle as a set of letters, with vowels apart from consonants, and read off what that shows.
card.limits: A restatement must be equivalent to the original; a feature drawn from it, like seven syllables, holds only unless diphthongs reduce it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Solving a related problem or a part of the puzzle
concepts.question: When the full anagram resists, which smaller tasks bring you closer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If the whole puzzle resists, solve a related problem or part: form shorter words from some letters, guess an ending, or keep part of the condition.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Come nearer to the desired word by building up from words you can find.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya suggests forming words from some of the given letters, then longer and longer ones, since the more letters used the nearer we may come. The desired word is so long that it must have distinct parts: probably it is compound or has a usual ending. We may also keep only part of the condition, such as a long word with an X and a Y and few consonants.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Stuck on an anagram of 'DEMAT ROAS', form words of three or four letters first, then try to extend them, noting an ending such as -ED that may use some letters.

card.rule: Try a related problem or a part, and keep only a part of the condition if needed.
card.limits: These moves do not guarantee the word; Polya warns the list cannot work magic.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: What the list can and cannot do
concepts.question: If the list does not hand us the answer, what use is it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the list to keep the ball rolling when discouraged, not to expect the solution without effort.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep thinking about the problem when you are inclined to drop it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The questions cannot work magic, nor give the solution of all possible puzzles without effort. To find the word, the reader must keep on trying. What the list can do is keep the ball rolling and so keep us thinking.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student stalls on a hard anagram. Asking 'Could you solve a part of the problem?' leads to trying an ending and a shorter word. The list did not solve the puzzle but kept her at work.

card.rule: When about to drop a problem, ask a list question to find a new trial.
card.limits: If no question helps, the list has no further promise: effort on the solver's part is still needed.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Two related procedures, told apart
concepts.question: What does each of reductio ad absurdum and indirect proof do, and why are they confused?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep the two apart: reductio ad absurdum refutes an assumption by drawing an absurdity from it; indirect proof establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know which tool you are using and what it proves.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Reductio ad absurdum shows an assumption false by deriving a manifest absurdity from it. Indirect proof shows an assertion true by showing the opposite assumption false. Polya likens the first to irony, which overstresses an opinion until it looks absurd, and the second to a politician building a candidate by wrecking the opponent.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show that no square number ends in 2, suppose one does and derive a contradiction: the assumption is refuted (reductio). To prove 'this number is even', refute 'it is odd': the claim is established through its opposite (indirect proof).

card.rule: Reductio ad absurdum refutes an assumption by an absurd consequence; indirect proof establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.
card.limits: Polya calls them different but related, and says they often combine; the likenesses to irony and a politician's trick are comparisons, not definitions.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Trying a puzzle and suspecting it cannot be done
concepts.question: What should you do when many trials at a puzzle fail in the same way?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Split the condition into its parts, satisfy one part at a time, and when trials keep failing, suspect impossibility and turn the question into a proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Move from 'find it' to 'prove it cannot be found' when the evidence points that way.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya's puzzle: write numbers that use each of the digits 0 to 9 exactly once and sum to exactly 100. The unknown is a set of numbers, the given is 100, and the condition has two parts. Each part alone is easy to meet; both together resist, and after a few unsuccessful trials we may suspect that 100 cannot be obtained in the way required.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A planner wants a rota covering every shift once and keeping every worker below ten hours. Each aim is easy alone; after many failed rotas she suspects the two cannot hold at once and sets out to show it.

card.rule: Satisfy each part of the condition alone, then, if both together keep failing, ask whether it can be proved impossible.
card.limits: Suspicion from failed trials is not a proof; the puzzle still needs one.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Face the hypothetical situation squarely
concepts.question: How can you examine a situation you suspect cannot exist?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep an open mind and face the situation in which every part of the condition is supposedly satisfied, and examine it closely.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a definitely wrong point in the supposed situation, so that impossibility is shown conclusively.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We suspect the situation cannot arise, and our suspicion has some foundation. Yet nothing is proved until we examine it. Only by facing the hypothetical situation squarely can we perceive a definitely wrong point in it. So imagine a set of numbers whose sum is 100 and in which the ten figures occur just once, and see what follows.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A manager doubts that a project can finish by Friday with the stated staff. Rather than argue, she imagines it finished by Friday and lists what that requires; the list shows an overbooked person.

card.rule: To show a condition cannot be met, assume it is met and look for a definite wrong point.
card.limits: Facing a situation you doubt is uncomfortable; the exposure is brief if a wrong point appears soon. If none appears, nothing is shown.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Deriving the absurdity in the digit puzzle
concepts.question: How does the supposed set of numbers lead to a value that cannot be right?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Name the quantity that matters, set up an equation for it from the supposed situation, and check whether its solution is possible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach a manifest absurdity from the supposition so the supposition can be rejected.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Suppose a set of one- and two-figure numbers uses each of the ten figures just once and sums to 100. The ten figures add to 45. Let t be the sum of the figures standing in the tens place; the units figures then sum to 45 - t. The numbers add to 10t + (45 - t) = 100, so 9t = 55 and t = 55/9, which is not an integer, while a sum of whole figures must be one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Someone claims that a purse holds only 5-cent and 10-cent coins worth exactly 1.13 dollars. In cents the total is 113, but every such coin is a multiple of 5 cents, and 113 is not: the claim fails by an absurd total.

card.rule: From the supposed situation derive an equation; if it has no admissible solution, the situation is impossible.
card.limits: The absurdity must be definite; a merely unlikely value does not refute. Here t must be an integer, and 55/9 is not.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Concluding from the absurdity: the supposition must go
concepts.question: Once an absurd result is derived from a supposition, what has been shown and what has not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When correct reasoning from a supposition ends in a manifest absurdity, reject the supposition, not the reasoning.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a derived absurdity into a conclusion that the original supposition cannot hold.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Starting from the supposition that both parts of the condition hold, correct steps led to a value of t that is not a whole number. How can that be explained? The original supposition must be wrong. Both parts of the condition cannot be satisfied together, and the goal, proving them incompatible, is reached. This is a typical reductio ad absurdum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A clerk assumes a till holds exactly 17 coins worth 1.00 dollar in 5-cent and 10-cent pieces only, works carefully, and finds she would need a fractional coin. Her arithmetic was sound, so the assumption is rejected.

card.rule: If every step is sound and the end is absurd, blame the starting supposition.
card.limits: The conclusion holds only if each step is correct; a slip in the steps would make the blame fall on the slip, not the supposition.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: An open-minded procedure that starts the same either way
concepts.question: Why can you start the same investigation whether you hope to find the unknown or to disprove it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Begin by expressing that all parts of the condition are satisfied, and let the later course show whether a solution or a contradiction appears.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid deciding the answer in advance, because the first steps are the same either way.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Setting up an equation expresses that all parts of the condition hold, without knowing whether that is possible. The same equation for t could have been written with no suspicion at all. So the procedure is open-minded: we may hope to find the unknown or to show the condition cannot be satisfied, and the later course shows which hope is justified.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Planning a trip by writing 'I leave at 9, the bus takes 40 minutes, the meeting is at 9:30' starts the same whether the plan works or not. Only the arithmetic shows it does not.

card.rule: Start by writing down that every part of the condition holds, and see what comes out.
card.limits: Writing it down shows which hope is justified only if you carry the work through; stopping early shows neither.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Setting up the infinitude of primes for indirect proof
concepts.question: How do you turn an unusual problem to prove into a supposition you can examine?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: State the claim to prove, then suppose its contradictory opposite and ask what is definitely wrong with it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a theorem that looks out of reach approachable by examining its opposite.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Primes are the numbers greater than 1 that cannot be resolved into smaller factors; every integer greater than 1 decomposes into them, for example 630 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7. To prove that the series of primes never ends, suppose there is a last prime P and write down all primes 2, 3, 5, ..., P. Then ask what is wrong with that.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To prove there is no largest even number, suppose there is a largest one, N. Then N + 2 is even and larger: the supposition contradicts itself.

card.rule: To prove a claim indirectly, assume its opposite and ask what is definitely wrong with it.
card.limits: The supposition must be a precise contradictory opposite of the claim; a looser opposite proves less.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Euclid's step: build a number the supposed primes cannot divide
concepts.question: Which number built from the supposed list of primes exposes the absurdity?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Under the supposition that 2, 3, ..., P are all the primes, form the product of them plus 1 and see what it is divisible by.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a definitely wrong point in the supposed list.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Let Q = (2 x 3 x 5 x ... x P) + 1. Dividing Q by any of the supposed primes 2, 3, 5, ..., P leaves remainder 1, so none of them divides Q. Yet every integer greater than 1 is either prime or divisible by a prime. That is definitely wrong, so no last prime P can exist.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the primes 2, 3, 5. Then 2 x 3 x 5 + 1 = 31. Dividing 31 by 2, 3 or 5 leaves remainder 1, so a prime outside the list, here 31 itself, is needed.

card.rule: Multiply all the supposed primes, add 1, and note that none of them divides the result.
card.limits: The product plus 1 need not itself be prime; it only needs a prime divisor outside the supposed list.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: How the two procedures combine in Euclid's proof
concepts.question: How can one proof be both indirect proof and reductio ad absurdum?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Spot that the theorem is established by disproving its contradictory opposite, and that the opposite is disproved by deducing an absurdity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Name the structure of a proof so you can follow or reuse it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya calls Euclid's proof a typical indirect proof. The theorem, that the primes never end, is established by disproving its contradictory opposite, that they end somewhere. The opposite is disproved by deducing a manifest absurdity from it, so the proof uses reductio ad absurdum inside it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show a tap is not leaking, suppose it leaks (the opposite). The sink would be wet by now; it is dry. The opposite fails by an absurd consequence, so the claim holds: indirect proof combined with reductio.

card.rule: In an indirect proof, disprove the opposite by deriving an absurdity from it.
card.limits: Not every indirect proof needs an absurdity as such; Polya notes the combination is typical, not obligatory.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: The practical objection: it asks you to hold falsehoods in mind
concepts.question: What is the practical objection to learning from an indirect proof, and what does it assume?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: State the objection fairly: while following the proof we must focus on a false assumption that we then should forget.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understand why some readers dislike these proofs, before judging whether the dislike is fair.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya states a practical form of the objection. Understanding a proof costs effort and we want to keep something true from it. A reductio starts from a false assumption and derives consequences equally false, ending in a manifest falsehood. Listening to it we focus on the false assumption, which we should forget, not on the true theorem, which we should retain.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student reads a long proof that begins 'suppose the bridge could be built with one pillar'. Every line holds a statement about a bridge that cannot exist, and the true conclusion appears only in the last sentence.

card.rule: Put the objection in its strongest form: what we must attend to is false, what we want to keep is true.
card.limits: This is Polya's own statement of the objection; he goes on to qualify it (see the next idea).

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Research tool versus means of exposition
concepts.question: Is the objection fatal to reductio, or does it depend on how the procedure is used?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Distinguish using reductio to discover from using it to explain; value it for discovery and judge a written reductio by whether it is bearable.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep a powerful discovery tool without forcing readers through a painful exposition.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: As a means of exposition, a long reductio is not an unmixed blessing. All its derivations are correct but all its situations impossible; the wording must keep stressing 'hypothetically', 'supposedly', 'allegedly', and the discord of rejecting yet examining the situation may become unbearable. As a tool of discovery, though, it would be foolish to repudiate it: it may present itself naturally and bring a decision when other means seem exhausted.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A mathematician finds a result by supposing it false and tracing the consequences. When writing it up for students, she looks for a form that does not make them live inside the false supposition for pages.

card.rule: Use reductio freely to find results; when writing for others, consider whether a gentler form exists.
card.limits: Polya concedes the exposition problem is real for long reductios, and says it is not a reason to give up the tool.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Look back and ask: can you derive the result differently?
concepts.question: After you have a result by either procedure, what question should you ask next?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After deriving a result by reductio or indirect proof, look back at the solution and ask: can you derive the result differently?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Carry away a true, usable argument rather than only the path of discovery.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya wants us to be familiar with both procedures to make full use of our capacities. When we have derived a result by either, we should not fail to look back at the solution and ask: can you derive the result differently?

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A developer finds a bug by assuming the cache is right and hitting a contradiction. Looking back, she writes the fix as a direct check on the cache version, with no talk of supposition.

card.rule: Once a result is found indirectly, look back for a direct route.
card.limits: The look-back question is a prompt, not a promise; some arguments may not convert easily.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Rearranging the digit reductio into a direct argument
concepts.question: What true statement lies inside the digit reductio, and how does it settle the puzzle without any supposition?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: State the true conditional you found: if the digits are each used once in one- and two-figure numbers, the total is 9(t + 5), so it is a multiple of 9.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace a proof that dwells on an impossible situation with a short direct argument.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The true part of the argument is: if a set of one- and two-figure numbers uses each of the ten figures once, its sum is 10t + (45 - t) = 9(t + 5), a multiple of 9. The puzzle demands 100, and 100 is not divisible by 9. The reductio that led to the discovery has vanished from this presentation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Any set of whole numbers using each digit once has a total that leaves remainder 0 when divided by 9. A total of 110 leaves remainder 2, so 110 is also out of reach.

card.rule: Show that every achievable sum is a multiple of 9, then compare the target.
card.limits: The direct argument shows 100 cannot be reached; it does not show every multiple of 9 can be reached.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
concepts.title: Converting Euclid's indirect proof into a problem to find
concepts.question: How can the claim that primes never end be turned into a construction with no impossible situation?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Reconsider what the original claim means, restate the problem to prove as a problem to find, and reuse the key parts of the old argument.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Obtain a definite procedure instead of an argument about an impossible situation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Saying the series of primes never ends means: given any finite set of primes 2, 3, ..., P, there is always one more. So the problem to prove becomes a problem to find: given the primes 2, ..., P, find a new prime N different from all of them. Take N to be any prime divisor of Q = (2 x 3 x ... x P) + 1, the smallest if you like; if Q is prime, N = Q.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Given the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, Q = 30031 = 59 x 509. Taking the smallest prime divisor gives N = 59, a prime not among the six.
