card.rule: Restate 'prove it never ends' as 'given the primes so far, find a new one', and use a prime divisor of the product plus 1.
card.limits: The converted proof keeps the essential parts of the old argument; it is a new presentation of the same idea, not a different proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: What makes a problem routine
concepts.question: How can you tell that a problem is routine, and what has the teacher already done for the student?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Call a problem routine if it is solved by substituting special data into a formerly solved general problem, or by following a well-worn example step by step with no originality.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognise when the answer to 'Do you know a related problem?' has already been put in the solver's hands.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya's case: solve x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 after the general quadratic equation has been solved in letters, so that the student only substitutes numbers for the letters. It is still routine if half a dozen similar numerical equations were solved just before. The related problem has been supplied, so nothing is left to devise.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After a lesson on converting miles to kilometres by multiplying by 1.609, the homework asks to convert 12 miles. It repeats the worked pattern with new numbers.

card.rule: Judge routine by whether the solution is a substitution into a known general solution or a copy of a conspicuous example.
card.limits: Routineness depends on what was just taught: the same equation set cold, before any model, would not be routine.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Routine problems are fine, but not on their own
concepts.question: Where does Polya stop approving of routine problems in teaching?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use routine problems where practice is needed, but do not give students no other kind.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Leave students room for judgment and inventive faculties.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Routine problems, even many, may be necessary in teaching mathematics, but to make students do no other kind is inexcusable. Teaching mechanical routine and nothing else falls below the level of the cookbook: kitchen recipes leave something to the imagination and judgment of the cook, but mathematical recipes do not.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A coding course sets thirty exercises that each copy a model with new numbers. A better course keeps some of them and adds tasks where the student must choose a method.

card.rule: Mix routine exercises with problems that call for judgment.
card.limits: Polya allows many routine problems; the fault is in making them the only kind.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: The first rules of discovery, and why there are no infallible ones
concepts.question: What do the 'first' and 'second' rules of discovery really tell us about hopes for infallible rules?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not hope for rules that solve every problem; expect no more than useful procedures.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep expectations realistic so that effort is not replaced by a search for magic.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya's jesting rules: the first rule of discovery is to have brains and good luck; the second is to sit tight and wait for a bright idea. They remind us, somewhat rudely, that some aspirations are hopeless. Infallible rules solving every mathematical problem would be more desirable than the philosophers' stone, but they would work magic, and there is no magic.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student asks for a method that will always produce the proof. Polya's reply would be that no such method exists; a good question can only help when the student is stuck.

card.rule: Do not wait for an infallible method; do what is typically useful.
card.limits: The jest is a reminder, not a recommendation to wait: the next idea says what heuristic can offer.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: What a reasonable heuristic can study instead
concepts.question: If it cannot offer unfailing rules, what can a sensible heuristic offer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Study procedures typically useful in solving problems, and collect the questions and suggestions that hint at them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Replace the hope for magic with a neatly ordered collection of typical moves.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A reasonable heuristic cannot aim at unfailing rules, but it may study mental operations, moves and steps that are typically useful. They are hinted by stereotyped questions and suggestions. A collection of such questions, stated generally and neatly ordered, is less desirable than the stone but can be provided; the list we study is one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Instead of a miracle method for chess, a coach collects typical useful moves: ask what the opponent threatens, check checks and captures, look for forcing lines. None is infallible; each is typically useful.

card.rule: Learn the typical useful moves and the questions that call them to mind.
card.limits: The questions are hints, not guarantees; they do not replace the solver's own effort.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Rules of style: have something to say, and say one thing at a time
concepts.question: What two rules of style does Polya give, and how do they apply when you have two things to say?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Have something to say, and take two things to say one after the other.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Write so that the reader can take one point at a time.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya's first rule of style is to have something to say. His second concerns what to do when you have two things to say: take them one after the other. Like the rules of discovery the form is a jest, but the second rule is practical advice for ordering a text.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An email replying to a customer both apologises for a delay and announces a new price list. Split it: send the apology first, the price list afterwards.

card.rule: Have something to say, and say two things one after the other, not both at once.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule does not forbid related points in one text; it forbids saying two things at the same moment.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Rules of teaching: know the subject, and a little more
concepts.question: What do the two rules of teaching ask of a teacher, and how seriously does Polya mean them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Know what you are supposed to teach, and know a little more than that.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be a teacher who can answer the natural next question.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Polya's first rule of teaching is to know what you are supposed to teach; the second is to know a little more. Under 'First things come first' he adds that he does not think all rules of conduct for teachers are useless, otherwise he would not have written a whole book about the conduct of teachers and students.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A teacher who prepares only the exact exercises in the book is stuck when a pupil asks a natural follow-up. One who knows a little more can answer it or say how to look for the answer.

card.rule: Know what you are supposed to teach, and a little more.
card.limits: Polya says the rules are a start: first things come first, and knowing the subject does not by itself give a teacher the right attitude toward problems.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Going into detail: from the whole to each part, then each part's parts
concepts.question: In what order do we go into finer detail when trying to understand a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Understand the problem as a whole, then consider its principal parts each by itself, then the data one by one, then the parts of the condition.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: See the problem distinctly by moving from coarse to fine detail.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Our first duty is to understand the problem. Having done that as a whole we consider its principal parts, the unknown, the data and the condition, each by itself. If no helpful idea has yet occurred, we go further: we consider the various data, each datum by itself. Having understood the condition as a whole, we separate its various parts and consider each part by itself.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A shopper must buy a gift for a friend under 30 euros that is useful and can be posted. She first states the whole task, then separates unknown (the gift), data (the budget), and the parts of the condition: useful, postable, under 30.

card.rule: Go from whole to parts to parts of parts, as far as needed.
card.limits: Going into detail is for when no helpful idea has occurred; a good idea earlier can end the descent.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
concepts.title: Can you write them down? Parts of the condition and equations
concepts.question: Which question follows the separation of the condition, and when does it come up most often?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After separating the parts of the condition, ask: can you write them down?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn the separated parts into explicit statements you can work with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The suggestion has a question attached: separate the various parts of the condition. Can you write them down? Writing each part down makes it a separate item that can be examined, and the full condition is rebuilt by recombining them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 'a rectangle has perimeter 20 and its length is twice its width', write the two parts: 2(l + w) = 20 and l = 2w. Each part is now an item you can use on its own.

card.rule: Write each separated part of the condition down in its own statement.
card.limits: Writing the parts down is possible only if the condition is understood; if a part cannot be written, return to understanding it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Setting up equations is translation
concepts.question: When setting up equations is hard, what two things might be missing?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat setting up equations as translation: first understand the condition stated in words, then express it in the forms of mathematical notation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a condition given in words into equations you can work with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Translating a sentence from English into French needs two things: a thorough grasp of the English sentence and familiarity with the forms of French. Setting up equations needs the same two: a thorough grasp of the condition and familiarity with mathematical forms. The author says our difficulties are difficulties of translation, and credits the comparison to Newton.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a student who can retell a word problem in their own words but cannot write 'a is 3 more than b' as a = b + 3 lacks the second thing. A student who knows the notation but cannot say what is asked lacks the first.

card.rule: Ask which of two things is missing: understanding the condition, or knowing the forms of mathematical expression.
card.limits: The comparison diagnoses difficulties; it does not remove them. Both requirements still have to be met by study and practice.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: When word for word fails, rearrange
concepts.question: What should you do with a part of a condition that will not go straight into symbols?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a condition will not go into symbols part by part, attend less to its words and more to its meaning, and rearrange it before writing formulas.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Express in mathematical symbols a condition whose wording does not match the forms of mathematics.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An English sentence is easy to put into French word for word, but an English idiom cannot be; the translator must look to the whole meaning and may have to rearrange the sentence first. Conditions with parts that cannot be written down at once are the equations' idioms.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: 'the box holds three times as many red as blue marbles' can be written down directly. 'After giving away a fifth of them she had 12 left' is first restated as 'four fifths of her marbles equal 12'.

card.rule: If a part will not translate directly, restate it by its meaning in a form notation can express.
card.limits: Our reading: a condition that translates directly needs no rearranging; the restatement is a means, and wording that already fits notation can be used as it stands.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Understand, separate, ask: can you write it down?
concepts.question: In easy or difficult cases, what three things do you do with a condition before writing formulas?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In every case, understand the condition, separate its various parts, and ask of each part: can you write it down?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Break a condition into pieces each of which can become an equation.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In easy cases the verbal statement splits almost automatically into successive parts that can be put in symbols at once. In difficult cases the right division is less obvious, but the same questions apply, and the author asks us to reread his explanation after studying the examples.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: 'A rectangle has perimeter 30 and its length is 3 more than its width' has two parts, 2(l + w) = 30 and l = w + 3. Each can be written at once; w = 6 and l = 9 satisfy both.

card.rule: Understand the condition, separate its parts, and test each part with 'Can you write it down?'
card.limits: A division can be correct in logic and still unfit for notation: the parts must be ones that can be written, which the symmetric-point example later shows.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Two columns: the statement and its symbols
concepts.question: How can you lay out a page so each part of a condition faces its symbols?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Divide the page by a vertical line: put the verbal statement, split into parts, on the left and opposite each part its algebraic translation on the right.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: See at a glance that every part of the condition has its symbols.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: When the verbal statement splits into successive parts that can each be written down at once, the translation lines up with the original, part by part. Our reading: the layout makes a missing or doubled part easy to see.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Problem: find two quantities whose sum is 78 and whose product is 1296. Left: 'two quantities' faces x, y; 'sum is 78' faces x + y = 78; 'product is 1296' faces xy = 1296. The quantities are 54 and 24.

card.rule: Write the statement in parts on the left and its translation opposite each part on the right.
card.limits: The layout works as it stands only when the parts can be written at once; otherwise the left side must first be rearranged and expanded.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Name unknowns, data and condition first
concepts.question: Before dividing a condition into parts, which three things should you name?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before dividing a condition, name the unknowns, the data and the condition, and then separate the condition into its parts.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be sure what is to be translated before you translate it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author works the prism problem by asking in turn what the unknowns are, what the data are and what the condition is. Only then does he separate the condition, finding that it has two parts, one about the volume and one about the surface area.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a rectangle has area 96 and perimeter 40. Unknowns: length l and width w. Data: 96 and 40. Condition: a rectangle with sides l and w has area 96 and perimeter 40. Two parts: area and perimeter (l = 12, w = 8 fit).

card.rule: Name the unknowns, the data and the condition; then separate the condition.
card.limits: Naming does not by itself make the parts writable; the parts may still have to be restated before they become equations.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Restate each part using the geometry you know
concepts.question: What must you know to write the parts of a geometric condition as equations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the parts cannot be written at once, use what you know of the subject to restate each part in terms of the unknowns, and set that expanded statement on the left of the page.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make a condition about a figure ready for translation into equations.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The prism's volume and surface are not equations yet. The reader must know how to calculate them. With that geometry known, both parts are easily restated in terms of x and y, so the translation becomes feasible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The volume is the area of the base, a square of side x, times the altitude y: x squared times y equals 63. The pair x = 3, y = 7 satisfies it together with the area equation (3 x 3 x 7 = 63).

card.rule: Know the subject's formulas, restate each part with them, then translate.
card.limits: Our reading: the method needs subject knowledge. Without the formulas for volume and surface no amount of care in separating the parts will produce equations.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Choose parts fit for the language you will write in
concepts.question: Why can a correct division of a condition still be useless for setting up equations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Divide the condition into parts that the language of your equations can express, not only into parts that are logically correct.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach a division that you can actually write down.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In the symmetric-point problem the author warns that a decomposition may be logically unobjectionable and nevertheless useless. What is needed is a decomposition into parts which are fit for expression in the language we use, here analytic geometry.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: to find a rectangle with one side 4 whose area equals that of a square of side 6, 'the two shapes cover equal ground' is correct but cannot be written. 'Four times w equals six times six' can.

card.rule: A division is good only if each of its parts can be written in the language you are using.
card.limits: Our reading: the same condition may call for different divisions in different languages; fit is judged against the notation at hand.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Symmetry about a line: two relations
concepts.question: Which two relations between a point and its mirror image can analytic geometry express easily?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To set up the point symmetrical to a given point about a line, go back to the definition of symmetry while keeping an eye on what analytic geometry expresses easily: the joining line is perpendicular to the given line, and its midpoint lies on the given line.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find the unknown point by turning the geometric condition into two equations.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author asks two questions: what is meant by symmetry with respect to a line, and which geometric relations are simple in coordinates. He concentrates on the first and does not forget the second. The result is two parts, each expressible as an equation in the coordinates p and q of the sought point.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Given the line y = 2x and the point (5, 0), the symmetrical point is (-3, 4). The joining line has slope 4 / (-8) = -1/2, perpendicular to slope 2, and the midpoint (1, 2) lies on y = 2x.

card.rule: Express symmetry about a line as perpendicularity of the joining line plus its midpoint lying on the line.
card.limits: Our reading: the slope form of perpendicularity breaks down when the given line is horizontal, because the slope m is then 0; a vertical joining line has to be written another way.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Watch for signs that land is near
concepts.question: When you work hard on a problem, what should you watch for, as sailors watch for signs of land?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: While you work intensely on any problem, watch for signs that you are approaching the solution, as Columbus's crew watched for signs of land.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know whether to press on, change course or turn back.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The crew read birds, floating seaweed and low banks of cloud as favorable signs of nearby land, and were disappointed more than once. On 11 October 1492 the signs multiplied: sandpipers, a green reed, a cane, a worked pole, a branch with berries. Everyone rejoiced, and land was sighted the next day.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author says the same holds when our undertaking is important or unimportant and our problem of any kind. When we work intensely we watch eagerly for signs of progress.

card.rule: Watch eagerly for signs that the solution is near.
card.limits: A sign is an indication, not a guarantee: the crew's birds and seaweed raised hopes that were disappointed more than once.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A datum put to use is a good sign
concepts.question: Why is it encouraging when a new idea brings an unused piece of data into play?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat it as a favorable sign when a candidate step makes use of a datum you had not used before.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Judge a half-formed idea before you invest in it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In a well-constructed chess problem no piece is superfluous, so the right solution uses every piece. A candidate move that brings the idle knight into play agrees with the correct move in this respect: it looks like the correct move, and so might be the correct move.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Mate in two: a white knight far from the black king seems pointless. After trials, a new move brings that knight into play, which gives new hope.

card.rule: A candidate that uses a datum the others ignored resembles the true solution in that respect.
card.limits: The sign is only plausible: a move can use every piece and still fail to give mate.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A partial formula that respects a restriction
concepts.question: Why is it a good sign when a formula under construction fails exactly where the true answer must fail?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Check whether the expression you are building respects a restriction contained in the condition; if it does, take that as a favorable sign.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Judge a half-built formula against the whole condition.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The sum of any two sides of a triangle exceeds the third, so lengths a, b and c cannot be arbitrary: b + c must exceed a. The square root of (b + c - a) becomes imaginary exactly when b + c is smaller than a, when the desired area expression is bound to be illusory. My formula looks like the true formula, and so might be the true one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Task: express a triangle's area in terms of its sides a, b and c. Following the plan, the quantity under a square root turns out to be b + c - a. Cheered by this, the author continues.

card.rule: Take it as a good sign when your expression breaks down in just the circumstances where the true one must.
card.limits: The sign is again only plausible: a formula can respect one restriction and be wrong elsewhere.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A simpler analogous problem is a good sign
concepts.question: Why is it encouraging when an analogous, simpler problem comes to mind by itself?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Take it as a favorable sign when an analogous problem, especially a simpler one, appears of its own accord.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognise real progress when you are stuck.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Analogy is a great guide: a solid-geometry problem often depends on an analogous problem in plane geometry. So an analogous plane theorem that comes to mind might be the lemma needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author, stuck on a solid-geometry proof, rested overnight and next day hit upon an analogous plane-geometry theorem. In a flash he was convinced he had the solution.

card.rule: When an analogous problem comes up unprompted, treat it as a good sign.
card.limits: It is a plausible indication, not a proof; the analogous result must still be shown to fit.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A sign supports only a probable conclusion
concepts.question: What word keeps the conclusion from a sign honest, and why?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Draw conclusions from signs with the word probably: they indicate, but do not prove.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use signs without being fooled by them.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If we are approaching land, we often see birds; now we see birds; therefore, probably, we are approaching land. Without probably the conclusion is an outright fallacy. With it the conclusion is reasonable and natural but not a proof, only a heuristic suggestion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Columbus's crew saw birds many times and were disappointed. Only once did sandpipers come the day before land was found.

card.rule: Conclude from a sign with 'probably', never with 'certainly'.
card.limits: The label 'probably' does not tell how likely the conclusion is; that depends on the case.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Follow signs, but keep your eyes open
concepts.question: How should you treat a sign: trust it, ignore it, or something else?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Follow the signs and trust them, but look for yourself and never renounce your own judgment.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make progress without being fooled by a false sign.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Taking a heuristic conclusion as certain risks being fooled and disappointed. Neglecting heuristic conclusions altogether means no progress at all. The author puts it briefly: follow, but keep your eyes open.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a mechanic hears a rattle and suspects the exhaust. She tries that first, but still checks the other parts when the rattle continues.

card.rule: Use signs as guides, check them, and keep your own judgment.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule asks for judgment, which a rule cannot supply; it guards against two extremes only.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Why these signs are justified
concepts.question: What do the chess, formula and analogy signs share that makes them reasonable signs?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Count progress when you bring one more datum into play, take one more clause of the condition into account, or find a simpler analogous problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know why a feeling of progress is justified.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Solving a problem is essentially finding the connection between the data and the unknown, and in well-stated problems every datum should be connected with it. The whole condition should be used. Analogy is a main source of invention. Each sign matches a step that is useful.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: in a word problem with three conditions, a tentative equation that finally includes the third condition is felt as a step forward.

card.rule: Feel progress where a useful step has succeeded: one more datum, one more clause, or an analogue.
card.limits: Our reading: the datum sign holds for well-stated problems; where a datum is a distractor, using it may be no progress.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Every useful operation has its sign
concepts.question: How can the list of questions in the book also be read as a list of signs?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read the book's list of questions a second time as a list of signs: when an operation it names succeeds, count that as a step forward.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Notice progress that would otherwise pass unnoticed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Understanding the nature of the unknown, disposing the data so you can recall any, visualizing the condition as a whole, separating it into parts, finding a figure or a notation easy to keep, and recalling a related solved problem are all steps forward. Reading such signs needs only common sense and a little experience.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: after drawing a figure you can hold in mind, you feel progress even before any equation exists.

card.rule: When a typical useful operation succeeds, treat it as a sign of progress.
card.limits: The signs are common sense, not occult science; they guide but do not guarantee.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Feelings of pace are signs too
concepts.question: What do we sense about our progress even when we cannot name a distinct sign?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Pay attention to your sense of how fast you are progressing, and treat it like any other sign: useful, but only an indication.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use vague feelings of progress without trusting them blindly.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: When we work intently we feel the pace of progress: elated when it is rapid, depressed when it is slow, without being able to point to a distinct sign. People say it looks good, or that a plan is well-balanced. Behind vague words lies a real feeling that often leads in the right direction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sophisticated worker might say: no, something is still lacking and that spoils the harmony.

card.rule: Notice the pace of progress and the mood of the situation as signs.
card.limits: Such feelings are harder to express than the explicit signs, and need the same watchfulness.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Follow inspiration with a grain of doubt
concepts.question: How should you treat a sudden, strong feeling that you have the answer?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Follow an inspiration, but with a grain of doubt: treat it like any other sign.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain from sudden insight without being misled.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If a guiding feeling is very strong and emerges suddenly, we speak of inspiration. People usually cannot doubt their inspirations and are sometimes fooled by them. The author applies the same advice as for other signs: trust, but keep your eyes open.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a sudden certainty that a proof works should be followed by writing it out to see whether it holds.

card.rule: Follow inspiration, and keep a grain of doubt.
card.limits: Our reading: doubt is advised, not paralysis; the inspiration still guides the search.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Signs tell you whether to go on or turn back
concepts.question: How do signs guide you when you have a plan but are not sure it will work?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start cautiously along your plan and watch for signs: go on with more confidence as they multiply, hesitate when they are rare, and try another road if they stay absent.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spend effort on the right spot and avoid blind alleys.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: With a plan whose first steps are clear but whose later road is not, I start cautiously and keep a lookout. If signs are rare or indistinct I hesitate; if they fail for a long time I may turn back and try another road. If they multiply, hesitation fades and I move on with growing confidence.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The absence of signs may warn us of a blind alley and save time and useless exertion; their presence may make us concentrate effort on the right spot.

card.rule: Let the frequency of signs set how boldly you proceed along a plan.
card.limits: Signs are not certain: absence can mislead you into abandoning a good path, as the next idea shows.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Signs may mislead, yet they are right on average
concepts.question: Signs can mislead in a single case; why should we still follow them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use signs although any single one may mislead, since they guide right in the majority of cases.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stay willing to use signs without being shaken by an occasional failure.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author once abandoned a path for lack of signs; a man who went a little farther on it made an important discovery. Again, one may follow a road cheerfully, encouraged by favorable signs, and run into an unsuspected, insurmountable obstacle. Yet signs guide right in the majority of cases, as a hunter reading traces is right on average.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A hunter may misread the traces of game now and then, but he must be right on average, otherwise he could not make a living.

card.rule: Accept that signs may fail in one case while guiding right on the whole.
card.limits: Our reading: being right on average gives no comfort in the single case that matters; it supports using signs, not trusting any one.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Reading signs takes experience
concepts.question: What does an expert have that lets him read signs better than a beginner?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Build experience of how a situation looks and feels when the solution is near, since reading signs depends on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Become better at telling real signs from false ones.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Some of Columbus's companions knew from experience how the sea looks near the shore, so they could read the signs. The expert knows more signs than the inexperienced and knows them better; this may be his main advantage. The exceptionally talented may add a kind of extraordinary mental sensibility to feel subtle signs.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An expert hunter notices traces of game and appraises even their freshness or staleness where a beginner sees nothing.

card.rule: Practice on many problems until you recognise what nearing a solution looks like.
card.limits: Our reading: experience helps but does not remove the risk that a sign misleads in a given case.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: The heuristic syllogism: if A then B, B holds, so A is more credible
concepts.question: What is the pattern of reasoning behind reading a sign, in its shortest form?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Reason from a sign in the form: if A then B; B is true; therefore A becomes more credible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: State what a sign gives you, without overclaiming.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author rewrites the Columbus argument: if we are approaching land we often see birds; now we see birds; therefore it becomes more credible that we are approaching land. The general pattern is: if A then B, as we know; B turns out true; so A becomes more credible. This is called a heuristic syllogism.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: if the pipe leaks, the bill rises; the bill rose; so a leak is more credible.

card.rule: From if A then B and B true, conclude that A is more credible, not that A is true.
card.limits: The pattern fixes the direction of the change in confidence, not its size; a different reason for B may exist.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Why the conclusion says more credible
concepts.question: Why does the improved wording say more credible rather than probably?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a heuristic conclusion as a change in the level of your confidence, not as a verdict.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: See what signs do for a solver over time.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Columbus and his men conjectured from the start that they would find land westward and gave this some credence, or they would not have started. As they sailed they related every incident to their dominating question, and confidence rose and fell, differently for each man. The wording more credible expresses a reasonable ground for such a change in confidence.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The dramatic tension of the voyage was due to the fluctuations of confidence.

card.rule: Treat a sign as a reason to move your confidence, not as a verdict.
card.limits: Different people may move their confidence by different amounts from the same sign.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Plausible reasoning: not proof, but indispensable
concepts.question: What do an inventor's signs and a scientist's evidence have in common?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Count plausible reasoning as a kind of reasoning in its own right: it gives no certainty, but it is how new knowledge is gained.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understand the place of sign-reading among kinds of evidence.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The inventor's signs, everyday indications, a lawyer's circumstantial evidence, a scientist's inductive evidence and statistical evidence agree on two points. First, none has the certainty of strict demonstration. Second, they are useful in acquiring essentially new knowledge, and indispensable for any knowledge not purely mathematical or logical, any about the physical world. The author calls it plausible reasoning.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author says his subject here is philosophical, though he treats it as practically and informally as possible.

card.rule: Treat heuristic, inductive and circumstantial evidence as plausible reasoning: uncertain but needed.
card.limits: It is not a substitute for demonstration where demonstration is available; the author contrasts the two kinds of reasoning.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Demonstrative and heuristic syllogisms side by side
concepts.question: How does the heuristic syllogism differ from the demonstrative one with the same first premise?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare the two patterns: with if A then B, finding B false makes A false, but finding B true makes A only more credible.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep apart what can be proved and what can only be made plausible.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Both patterns start with if A then B. Their second premises, B false and B true, are exactly opposite but on the same logical level. The conclusions differ: A false is of the same nature as the premises, fully expressed and fully supported; A more credible is vaguer, less sharp and less fully expressed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: if it rained, the street is wet. The street is dry, so it did not rain (demonstrative). The street is wet, so rain is more credible (heuristic).

card.rule: From if A then B, B false gives A false; B true gives only A more credible.
card.limits: The demonstrative pattern is called the modus tollens of the hypothetical syllogism; do not mistake the heuristic one for a proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A heuristic conclusion has direction and magnitude
concepts.question: How can two honest reasoners accept the same premises and still differ about the conclusion?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a heuristic conclusion as a force: the premises fix its direction, but not its strength, which depends on each person's background and reasons.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Expect honest disagreement about how much a sign proves.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The conclusion of the heuristic syllogism pushes us in a direction: A becomes more credible, and for any reasonable person certainly not less credible. It has a strength too: A may become much more credible or just a little. The direction is implied by the premises; the magnitude is not.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: My neighbor and I can honestly disagree how much more credible A becomes, since our temperaments, our backgrounds and our unstated reasons may differ.

card.rule: Agree on direction from the premises; do not expect agreement on the amount.
card.limits: In the demonstrative case no such disagreement is reasonable: if both accept the premises they cannot reasonably disagree about the conclusion.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: The visible and invisible parts of the basis
concepts.question: Why can a heuristic conclusion be overturned while its premises still stand?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Remember that the premises of a heuristic syllogism are only the visible part of its basis; new information can lower the conclusion while both premises stand.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Stay ready to revise a plausible conclusion.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In a demonstrative syllogism the premises are a full basis: if they stand, the conclusion stands. In a heuristic syllogism they are only the visible part. There is an unexpressed, invisible part, such as inarticulate feelings or unstated reasons. New information that leaves both premises intact can lower trust in A.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Tomorrow I may find grounds that do not touch the premises yet make A appear less plausible, or even refute it.

card.rule: Hold heuristic conclusions open to revision, though the premises stand.
card.limits: The invisible part is hard to state; the author says behind any reason clarified there are many others that remain obscure.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Specialization: from a set to a smaller set or one object
concepts.question: What is specialization, and when might it help you?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem about a whole set of objects is hard, consider a smaller set, or just one object, contained in the given set.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get a foothold on a problem, or test a claim, with a case you can handle.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Specialization is passing from the consideration of a given set of objects to that of a smaller set, or of just one object, contained in the given set. The author says it is often useful in the solution of problems.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: facing the claim that the sum of any two odd numbers is even, you try 3 and 5, get 8, and see why the claim might hold.

card.rule: Pass from the whole set to a smaller set or a single member of it.
card.limits: A special case gives hints or refutes; one that complies does not prove the general statement.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Test an unfamiliar claim on a familiar special case
concepts.question: If you cannot recall anything like a claim, what can you do with it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If nothing else occurs to you for an unfamiliar assertion, test it on the best-known special case of the figure.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find out quickly whether an assertion survives, and get a lead.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Take a triangle with inscribed circle radius r, circumscribed circle radius R and longest altitude H, and the assertion that r + R is at most H. We scarcely remember a theorem with a similar conclusion, so we test the best-known special triangle, the equilateral, where r is H/3 and R is 2H/3. The assertion holds there.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Equilateral triangle with side 6: H is about 5.196, r about 1.732, R about 3.464, and r + R equals H.

card.rule: With an unfamiliar assertion, try the best-known special case first.
card.limits: Passing the test shows only that the case complies; the book then goes on to more extended special cases.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Vary the case and look at the extremes
concepts.question: If the first special case complies, what do you test next?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a simple special case complies, vary it, move to a more extended special case, and look at its extreme or limiting cases.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a counterexample or a hint toward a proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The isosceles triangles form a family whose shape changes with the angle at the vertex. The extreme cases are the angle going to 0 degrees and to 180 degrees. At 0 the base vanishes, r is 0 and R is H/2, so the assertion holds. At 180 all heights vanish while R grows without bound, and the assertion fails.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author concludes that the proposed theorem is false and the problem is solved. Very flat isosceles triangles already break it, so the extreme cases can be officially disregarded.

card.rule: Look at the extreme cases of a family, since a rule must hold there too.
card.limits: Our reading: numbers show the failure well before 180 degrees; with legs of 1 and apex angle 120 degrees, r + R is about 1.232 and H about 0.866.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: One counterexample refutes a general statement
concepts.question: How many exceptions does it take to refute a general statement?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To refute a general statement, pick from its set one object that does not comply; one counterexample is enough.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Refute a would-be rule quickly and surely.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The saying that the exception proves the rule is a joke on a certain laxity of logic. Taken seriously, one exception refutes any would-be general statement, and the usual best method to refute it is to exhibit an object that does not comply, called a counterexample.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: the claim that n squared + n + 41 is prime for every n holds for small n but fails at n = 40, giving 1681 = 41 x 41.

card.rule: Specialize to an object that does not comply; one is enough.
card.limits: A counterexample refutes, but failing to find one does not prove a statement.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Prospective exceptions test the rule
concepts.question: Why does a rule that survives its most unusual case earn more trust?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Test a general statement on its extreme or unusual cases, since passing there gives the strongest support.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain strong evidence for a statement that cannot yet be proved.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A statement meant for all mammals must apply to the whale, an unusual mammal. Extreme cases are apt to be overlooked by inventors of generalizations, so there is a good chance of refuting the statement. If it is verified even there, the inductive evidence is strong, just because the prospect of refutation was strong.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author reshapes the saying as: prospective exceptions test the rule.

card.rule: Choose the case most likely to break the rule; if it survives, trust the rule more.
card.limits: Even strong inductive evidence is not proof; it only raises confidence.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Too much variety? Ask for a more special problem
concepts.question: What can you do when a problem could be given in so many ways that you do not see one solution?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a problem feels as if it has too much variety, ask for a more accessible related problem, a more special one, such as an extreme case where one datum vanishes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find an entry into a general problem.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Two ships steer straight courses at constant speeds, and we must find their smallest distance. The initial positions and the two velocities can be chosen in many ways, and the same solution must fit them all. Out of this feeling of too much variety a more special problem emerges: let one ship lie at anchor.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With one ship at rest, the shortest distance from it to the moving ship is the perpendicular to the straight line along which the latter moves.

card.rule: Ask for a more special problem, such as one datum set to a trivial value.
card.limits: The special problem is only a stepping point: solving it does not by itself solve the general problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Use the special result by adding an auxiliary element
concepts.question: How can the result for a ship at rest help when both ships move?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To use the result of a special problem, look for an auxiliary element that reduces the general case to it; here, add to both ships the opposite of one ship's velocity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a hard general case into the solved special one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Rest is a special case of motion, and motion is relative. If the same uniform motion is given to both ships, relative positions and relative distances, including the shortest one, do not change. Add a velocity opposite to the second ship's, of the same amount, to both: the second ship is at rest and the special result applies.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Ship A starts at (0, 0) moving 5 units east per time unit; ship B starts at (10, 6) moving 2 east. Subtract B's velocity: B is at rest, A moves 3 east, and the shortest distance is the perpendicular 6.

card.rule: Add a common motion that brings one ship to rest, and use the special result.
card.limits: The shortest distance in the original motion is the same, but the moment and position of closest approach are described in the new frame; our reading: check that the closest approach lies in the future.

media.alt: Two ships' starting points drawn as dots. The upper one, B, has a short arrow pointing down and to the left towards Q. The lower one, A, has a longer arrow pointing horizontally left towards P. Each arrow shows direction of straight, steady travel.

Ship B's start with a short arrow towards Q and a dashed line dropping from B to a point S on a long slanted line. That line comes from A's start, where a parallelogram of arrows combines A's velocity with a reversed copy of B's velocity. BS is the shortest distance.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: A special problem as a stepping stone
concepts.question: Why can a less ambitious auxiliary problem help solve a more ambitious one?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use the easier special problem as a stepping stone: solve it, then find the extra remark that carries you from it to the original.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Cross from a hard problem to its solution in two steps.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The auxiliary problem was invented in the course of the solution and was much less ambitious than the original. It worked because two remarks were made. First, an advantageous auxiliary problem was invented. Second, an appropriate supplementary remark, on the relativity of motion, was discovered to pass back from the auxiliary problem to the original.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The author compares it to crossing a creek in two steps, with a stone in the middle as a momentary foothold.

card.rule: Solve the special problem, then find the remark that links it back.
card.limits: Without the second remark the special solution stays an isolated result.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Concrete interpretation: a teacher's specialization
concepts.question: How can a teacher make abstract mathematical elements concrete?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Give a concrete interpretation to the abstract elements of a problem, using things in the room.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring mathematics home to students.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A somewhat primitive kind of specialization is useful to the teacher: give concrete meaning to abstract elements. A rectangular parallelepiped can be the classroom. In solid analytic geometry a corner of the room is the origin, the floor and two walls the coordinate planes, and two horizontal edges and one vertical edge the axes.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To explain a surface of revolution, the teacher draws a curve with chalk on the door and opens it slowly.

card.rule: Present abstract mathematics concretely.
card.limits: The author calls these simple tricks; they illustrate and do not replace the abstract argument.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Problems can return clarified after a rest
concepts.question: What often happens to a stuck problem when you leave it for a night or a few days?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you are stuck, leave the problem for a night's rest or a few days: it may come back clarified and nearer to its solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make progress on a problem that conscious effort has not cracked.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author could not recall an author's name one evening, though he remembered everything else about him; the next morning the name came without effort. Problem solvers have the same experience: after a night's rest or a few days' interruption a bright idea appears. The nature of the problem matters little.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A forgotten word, a crossword clue, the start of an annoying letter or a mathematical solution may come this way.

card.rule: A problem returned after a break may be clarified and nearer to its solution.
card.limits: The author says the cause is a theory, not a certainty: who clarified it is hard to say other than oneself working subconsciously.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: There is a limit to forcing conscious effort
concepts.question: When is it better to leave a problem alone for a while?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When forcing conscious reflection has stopped paying, put the problem aside, but first settle some small point so you leave with a sense of achievement.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Get more tomorrow with less effort.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: There is a limit beyond which we should not force conscious reflection; at certain moments it is better to leave the problem alone. Take counsel of your pillow, the old advice goes. An interval of rest may let us obtain more tomorrow with less effort. Before quitting, settle at least some little point, or elucidate some aspect of the question.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If today will not, tomorrow may, says the other old saying.

card.rule: Rest a problem when forcing it stops helping, after settling some small point.
card.limits: Our reading: the advice is for problems already worked hard; it does not tell you to leave a problem you have not tried.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Rest works only after real effort
concepts.question: What must come before a problem can return improved after rest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Work hard on the problem and care about its solution first: only then does a rest tend to bring it back improved.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use rest as part of the work, not as a substitute for it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Only problems whose solution we passionately desire, or for which we have worked with great tension, come back improved. Conscious effort and tension seem necessary to set the subconscious work going. It would be too easy otherwise: we could solve difficult problems just by sleeping and waiting for a bright idea.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Past ages regarded a sudden good idea as a gift of the gods that must be deserved by work or at least by a fervent wish.

card.rule: Strive and care first; rest afterwards.
card.limits: Our reading: effort and desire are described as necessary here, not as a guarantee that the idea will come.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Two meanings of symmetry
concepts.question: What are the two meanings of symmetry the author distinguishes?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep apart the geometric meaning of symmetry (about a plane or a point) and the general, logical meaning (interchangeable parts).

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use the word symmetry precisely.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Symmetry has a more usual, particular, geometric meaning and a less usual, general, logical meaning. In elementary solid geometry there are two kinds: symmetry with respect to a plane and with respect to a point. A statue may be completely symmetrical with respect to a vertical plane so that its two halves appear interchangeable.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The human body appears fairly symmetrical but is not: many interior organs are unsymmetrically placed.

card.rule: Geometric symmetry is about a plane or a point; the general sense is about interchangeable parts.
card.limits: Appearance can mislead: the body seems symmetrical but is not.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Interchangeable parts: cubes and expressions
concepts.question: In what ways can a whole have interchangeable parts, and how do we test for them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To test for symmetry, ask which parts can be exchanged without changing the whole.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognise symmetry in figures and in expressions.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A cube has high symmetry: its faces are interchangeable with each other, and so are its vertices and its edges. The expression yz + zx + xy is symmetric too: any two of x, y, z can be swapped without changing it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Check: swapping x and y turns yz + zx + xy into xz + zy + yx, the same sum.

card.rule: Look for parts that can be swapped without changing the whole.
card.limits: An expression can be unchanged by some swaps and not others: x squared y + y squared z + z squared x is not symmetric (swapping x and y gives a different sum).

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: Treat symmetrical parts symmetrically
concepts.question: If a problem is symmetric, what should you do with its interchangeable parts?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Notice the interchangeable parts of a problem and treat those that play the same role in the same way; do not destroy a natural symmetry.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Save work and keep the solution balanced.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If a problem is symmetric in some ways, we may derive some profit from noticing its interchangeable parts, and it often pays to treat those parts which play the same role in the same fashion. The author advises: try to treat symmetrically what is symmetrical, and do not destroy wantonly any natural symmetry.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: for three equal-role quantities x, y, z in an equation, introduce auxiliary elements for each in the same way instead of favouring x.

card.rule: Treat symmetrically what is symmetrical.
card.limits: Symmetry is a guide, not a command: the next idea gives a case where the parts must be treated one after the other.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
concepts.title: When symmetry must be broken, and symmetry as a check
concepts.question: Is it always possible to treat symmetrical things symmetrically, and what else can symmetry do?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Break a natural symmetry when you must, as with a pair of gloves put on one after the other, and use symmetry to check results.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use symmetry as a guide without being bound by it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We are sometimes compelled to treat unsymmetrically what is symmetrical by nature. A pair of gloves is symmetrical, yet nobody puts on both at the same moment, but one after the other. The author also says symmetry may be useful in checking results.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Our illustration: a result for three symmetric unknowns that favours one of them is suspicious.

card.rule: Treat unsymmetrically only when compelled; test results for the symmetry the problem has.
card.limits: The limits of symmetric treatment come from what the situation compels; our reading: a symmetric problem may still have an asymmetric answer.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Why the vocabulary of problem-solving is shaky
concepts.question: Why does the book warn that terms for solving problems are often ambiguous, and what does it do about it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before you lean on a term for the activity of solving problems, find out which meaning the author gives it, and keep to one meaning in your own use.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Talk and think about how problems are solved without being misled by one word carrying several meanings.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The activity is familiar to everybody and often discussed, but like other mental activities it is hard to describe. No systematic study exists, so there are no true technical terms, and half-technical terms are used in different ways by different authors.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The dictionary entry lists a few new terms the book uses, a few old terms it avoids, and a few old terms it keeps in spite of their ambiguity. A reader who has not yet met these terms in worked examples may find the list confusing.

card.rule: Before you lean on a term for the activity of solving problems, find out which meaning the author gives it, and keep to one meaning in your own use.
card.limits: Our reading: the list is a sample of troublesome terms, not a full glossary. A word with a single agreed meaning needs none of this care.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Analysis, synthesis and the reasoning terms the book avoids
concepts.question: What do analysis and synthesis mean in Pappus's sense, and why does the book avoid both?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you meet analysis, synthesis, progressive or regressive reasoning, check which old sense is meant; in the book, describe the method in plain words instead.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Describe the way of devising a plan that starts from the unknown without using a word that other fields have taken over.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Pappus defined analysis neatly: start from the unknown (or the conclusion) and work backwards toward the data (or the hypothesis). The word has since acquired very different meanings, such as mathematical, chemical and logical analysis, so the book avoids it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Synthesis, which Pappus also defined well, is avoided for the same reasons as its counterpart. Progressive and regressive reasoning were used in the old senses of synthesis and analysis by some authors; the book calls this defensible but avoids them.

card.rule: When you meet analysis, synthesis, progressive or regressive reasoning, check which old sense is meant; in the book, describe the method in plain words instead.
card.limits: Our reading: the book still teaches the backward-working method itself; only the label is avoided.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Condition and hypothesis: a whole and its parts
concepts.question: What trouble arises when the same word names both a whole and each of its parts, and what fix does the book suggest?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When a term names a whole and also each of its parts, call the parts by a separate name such as clause.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep a useful term clear when the whole needs to be split into parts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Condition links the unknown of a problem to find to the data, and hypothesis is an essential part of a theorem of the usual kind. Both are clear and useful in that sense. The difficulty is that each part of a condition is also called a condition, and each part of a hypothesis a hypothesis.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A whole condition may be split into parts, as when a problem is decomposed and recombined, and each part is then also called a condition. The book suggests the technical word clause for such a part.

card.rule: When a term names a whole and also each of its parts, call the parts by a separate name such as clause.
card.limits: Our reading: the book only suggests clause as a remedy; it does not claim that mathematicians use it generally.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Problem to find and problem to prove replace historical terms
concepts.question: Why did the book introduce problem to find and problem to prove in place of the Euclidean terms?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use problem to find and problem to prove for the two kinds of problem; treat proposition, problem and theorem with care, because modern usage has changed them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Name the two kinds of problem clearly, in words not distorted by modern use.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In Latin versions of Greek texts the common name for both kinds is propositio, a problem to find is a problema and a problem to prove is a theorema.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In modern mathematical language the meanings of proposition, problem and theorem have completely changed. The book therefore replaced the historical terms with the new pair.

card.rule: Use problem to find and problem to prove for the two kinds of problem; treat proposition, problem and theorem with care, because modern usage has changed them.
card.limits: Our reading: the card does not say what the modern meanings are; the book states only that they have changed. The principal parts of each kind are defined in a separate entry.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Solution has three meanings
concepts.question: What three things can the word solution name, and how should a careful writer treat them?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: In a mathematical sentence, let solution mean only an object that satisfies the condition of a problem to find, and use other words for the work and its result.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Write sentences about a problem in which no reader mistakes the answer, the work and the finished product.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: In its purely mathematical meaning a solution is any object satisfying the condition of a problem to find. The solutions of an equation are its roots. But the word also means the process or work of solving, and the result of that work.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If one sentence has to speak of the object, the work and its result, calling all three a solution makes the sentence unclear. The mathematical sense, the equation x squared minus 3x plus 2 equals 0 has the solutions 1 and 2, is the clear one.

card.rule: In a mathematical sentence, let solution mean only an object that satisfies the condition of a problem to find, and use other words for the work and its result.
card.limits: Our reading: the book only warns; it does not give replacement words for the other two meanings.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: The test by dimension
concepts.question: How can you check a geometrical or physical formula quickly by looking only at the dimensions of its parts?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Replace every quantity in the formula by its dimension: terms of a sum must share one dimension, a product multiplies dimensions, and a pure number counts as dimension 1.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch an error in a geometrical or physical formula quickly, before any numbers are put in.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A length has dimension cm, an area has cm squared, and a pure number such as pi has dimension 1. A sum is only possible between quantities of one dimension, and that dimension is the sum's own. A product takes the product of the dimensions, and powers follow a similar rule.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Take the area S of the side surface of a frustum of a cone, with radii R and r and height h: \(S=\pi (R+r)\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}\). Replacing quantities by dimensions gives cm squared equals 1 times cm times the square root of cm squared. The sides agree, so the formula passes.

card.rule: Replace every quantity in the formula by its dimension: terms of a sum must share one dimension, a product multiplies dimensions, and a pure number counts as dimension 1.
card.limits: A formula that passes is not thereby proved right; the test can only reveal certain errors.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Where the test can be used
concepts.question: At what points of a piece of work, and on whose formulas, can the dimension test be applied?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Apply the dimension test to any formula you hold, whether it is a final result or an intermediate step, and whether you recalled it or guessed it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Remove doubt about a formula at the moment it is in your hands.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The test needs only the formula and the dimensions of its symbols, so it does not depend on how you got the formula. It can be applied after a whole problem or midway through, to a formula you recollect and to one you merely guess.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: You half-remember that the volume of a cone is either \(\pi r^2 h/3\) or \(\pi r h^2/3\). Both have the dimension cm cubed, so the test cannot choose; it does reject a version such as \(\pi r^2/3\), which comes out in cm squared.

card.rule: Apply the dimension test to any formula you hold, whether it is a final result or an intermediate step, and whether you recalled it or guessed it.
card.limits: Our reading: when two candidates have the same dimension, as in the example, the test cannot decide between them.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Finding a formula's form from dimensions
concepts.question: How can the dimension test do more than check a formula, and find the form a formula must have?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To find how a quantity depends on others, write it as a constant times unknown powers of them and match the powers of each basic unit on both sides.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Foresee the form of a result, such as how a period grows with length, using elementary means only.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: For a simple pendulum, mechanics shows that the period T depends on the wire length l and the gravitational acceleration g alone. Suppose \(T=c\,l^{m}g^{n}\) with c, m, n numbers. The dimension of T is sec, of l is cm, and of g is cm sec to the minus 2.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Then sec equals cm to the power (m+n) times sec to the power (-2n). The powers of cm and of sec must agree on both sides, so \(0=m+n\) and \(1=-2n\). Hence \(n=-\tfrac12\) and \(m=\tfrac12\), and T has the form \(c\sqrt{l/g}\).

card.rule: To find how a quantity depends on others, write it as a constant times unknown powers of them and match the powers of each basic unit on both sides.
card.limits: The argument needs the list of quantities the result depends on; dimensions alone cannot supply it.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: What the test cannot tell you
concepts.question: What can a formula pass the dimension test and still get wrong?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Treat passing the dimension test as necessary but not sufficient: it says nothing of numerical constants or of the range where a formula holds.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use the test for what it can do, without trusting a formula merely because it passed.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A formula that passes the test, like the frustum formula, shows no dimension error, but a pure number such as a factor of one half has dimension 1 and is invisible to it. In the pendulum, the test gives the form of T but not the constant c.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student writes the area of a triangle of base b and height h as \(bh\). It passes, since b times h is cm squared, yet it is twice the true area; the missing one half is a pure number, which the test cannot see.

card.rule: Treat passing the dimension test as necessary but not sufficient: it says nothing of numerical constants or of the range where a formula holds.
card.limits: Passing shows only that one kind of error is absent; constants, signs and ranges of validity still need other checks.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Looking back at a finished solution
concepts.question: What should a future mathematician do once a solution is complete, and what can looking back yield?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: After finishing a problem, look back at the solution and at the course of your work, and ask what it can still teach you.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn each solved problem into knowledge and judgment that stay with you.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The author calls looking back the most important part of the work for a future mathematician. Surveying the course of the work and the final shape of the solution, one finds an unending variety of things to observe, and the questions below show what to look for.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After a long case-by-case solution of a counting puzzle, you ask what the decisive idea was, what hampered you and what helped, whether you can see the result at a glance, and whether you can derive it in a different way.

card.rule: After finishing a problem, look back at the solution and at the course of your work, and ask what it can still teach you.
card.limits: Our reading: the book offers these as things one may do, not as a fixed checklist to be run every time.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Learning by imitation, and finding your own line
concepts.question: How does a future mathematician learn, and what is the first important discovery he should make?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Learn by imitation and practice: find a model to imitate, solve problems in your own line, and so discover your own taste.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find out which kind of mathematical work suits you and become able to do it well.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The future mathematician learns, as everybody does, by imitation and practice. He should look for the right model, watch a stimulating teacher and compete with a capable friend. Above all he should read good authors, not only current textbooks, until he finds one whose ways he is inclined to imitate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student reads several books on number theory and keeps returning to one author's short, clear proofs. She copies how that author sets out an argument, chooses problems of that kind and writes new ones in the same spirit.

card.rule: Learn by imitation and practice: find a model to imitate, solve problems in your own line, and so discover your own taste.
card.limits: Our reading: imitation is a stage toward a personal line, not a goal in itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Using the list of questions with judgment
concepts.question: When should an intelligent problem-solver ask a question from the list, and how does he come to understand it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Ask a question from the list only when careful thought about the problem at hand prompts it, and learn what it is for by seeing it help in your own work.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the questions a working part of your own thinking rather than a script.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: He may follow the explanations and examples and suspect the proper use, but real understanding of a question comes only when he meets, in his own work, the procedure it tries to provoke and sees that it helps.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A climber carries a list of tips. Facing a blank rock face she picks the tip that matches what she sees, because an earlier climb on a similar face showed her when it helps. She does not recite the whole list on every route.
