card.rule: Ask a question from the list only when careful thought about the problem at hand prompts it, and learn what it is for by seeing it help in your own work.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the author's advice about the list; he does not say how many problems are needed before a question is understood.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Concentration and desire
concepts.question: What must a problem-solver bring to a problem beyond understanding it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Understand the problem as fully as you can, then concentrate on it and really want its solution.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Bring enough energy and interest to carry the work through.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The intelligent problem-solver first tries to understand the problem as fully and as clearly as he can. But understanding alone does not suffice. He must also concentrate on the problem and earnestly desire its solution.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student understands a geometry task completely but works on it with half an eye on her phone. She follows each step yet never wants to see the construction finished, so no new idea arrives.

card.rule: Understand the problem as fully as you can, then concentrate on it and really want its solution.
card.limits: Our reading: desire here is about the problem worked on, not general ambition.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: The two wishes of the intelligent reader
concepts.question: What two things does an intelligent reader of a mathematical book want from each step of an argument?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: At every step of a mathematical argument, ask two things: is this step correct, and what is it for?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Follow an argument so that you can see why it goes the way it does, not only that it holds.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The intelligent reader of a mathematical book desires two things. First, to see that the present step of the argument is correct. Second, to see the purpose of the present step. A step that is checked but has no visible purpose leaves the reader without a sense of direction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A proof of a geometry fact adds, without comment, a line parallel to one side of a triangle. The reader checks that the line exists and the next step follows, then asks what the extra line is for and how its use could have been foreseen.

card.rule: At every step of a mathematical argument, ask two things: is this step correct, and what is it for?
card.limits: Our reading: seeing the purpose may come only after later steps; the question is still worth asking at each step.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: A correct derivation is not enough
concepts.question: What more than correctness must an author or teacher give, so that an argument stays accessible?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you write or teach an argument, show what each step is for, as well as that it is correct.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the derivation accessible and instructive, not only correct.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The intelligent teacher and the intelligent author bear the reader's two wishes in mind. To write and speak correctly is necessary but not sufficient. A derivation can be presented correctly in a book or on a blackboard and still be inaccessible and uninstructive if the purpose of the successive steps is incomprehensible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tutor derives the quadratic formula flawlessly by completing the square, but announces each move only after making it. The class verifies every line yet cannot say why the first move was chosen, and no one could have found the derivation alone.

card.rule: When you write or teach an argument, show what each step is for, as well as that it is correct.
card.limits: Our reading: the author states the demand; how much motive to supply in a given proof is a matter of judgment.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Did we use all the data?
concepts.question: How can the question did we use all the data show the reason behind a step of an argument?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you wonder why a step was taken, ask whether it brings in a datum not yet used.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understand the motive of a step so well that you feel you could have found it yourself.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An author or teacher can ask did we use all the data to give a good reason for considering a datum that has not been used so far. The reader or listener can ask the same question to understand why the author turned to a given element.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A proof about a triangle has used its two given sides and nothing about the third angle. The next step brings in that angle. A reader who asks which datum remains unused sees the reason for the step.

card.rule: When you wonder why a step was taken, ask whether it brings in a datum not yet used.
card.limits: Our reading: some steps have other motives; the question explains only the steps that introduce an unused datum.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Varying the problem is how trying again succeeds
concepts.question: Why does try, try again succeed for some and fail for others, and what does the successful one change?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When an attempt fails, do not repeat it unchanged: vary the problem and try another way in.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reach a fuller and better adapted view of the problem than the one you started with.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: An insect tries to escape through a windowpane, repeating the same hopeless attempt, and ignores the open window it came through. A mouse in a trap tries between one pair of bars, then the next, then others; it varies its trials. A man should vary still more intelligently, exploring possibilities with understanding and learning from his errors.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Try, try again is popular advice and good advice, and insect, mouse and man all follow it. Whoever follows it with more success does so because he varies his problem more intelligently.

card.rule: When an attempt fails, do not repeat it unchanged: vary the problem and try another way in.
card.limits: Our reading: the comparison with animals illustrates variation; the book does not claim that people never repeat an attempt usefully.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Why variation helps memory and attention
concepts.question: Why is varying the problem essential, in terms of recalling knowledge and of keeping attention alive?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When stuck, change the problem so that new points enter your mind and a new aspect revives your interest.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recall what you know that is relevant and keep working long enough to use it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We recall by a kind of action by contact, called mental association: what we have in mind now tends to recall what was in contact with it on an earlier occasion. Varying the problem makes it easier to extract the elements we need from memory.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: We also tire if our attention rests on one point, so the object must change. When progress fails, interest fades and we may lose the problem altogether. A new question about it shows a new aspect and brings interest back.

card.rule: When stuck, change the problem so that new points enter your mind and a new aspect revives your interest.
card.limits: Our reading: the book gives these as explanations of why variation works, not as a full theory of memory; it says it has no space to state the theory of association neatly.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Varying the data to learn about the result
concepts.question: What can you learn about the answer by letting one datum grow or shrink to a limiting case?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Vary a datum to an extreme where the figure becomes a familiar one, and note what the unknown must become there.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find properties the final result must have before you have found it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A frustum of a square pyramid has a lower base of side a, an upper base of side b, and height h, with a larger than b. Let b grow until it equals a: the frustum becomes a prism and its volume becomes \(a^2h\). Let b shrink to 0: it becomes a pyramid and the volume becomes \(a^2h/3\).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: So the final formula must give \(a^2h\) when b equals a and \(a^2h/3\) when b equals 0. The problem is meant for a class that already knows the volume formulas for prism and pyramid.

card.rule: Vary a datum to an extreme where the figure becomes a familiar one, and note what the unknown must become there.
card.limits: A limiting case gives conditions a correct formula must meet, not the formula itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Varying the trapezoid: a failed try and a better one
concepts.question: How did varying one side of a trapezoid problem lead to a figure that could be built?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: If varying a datum one way gives a figure you cannot use, vary it the other way, and look for a simple figure you can construct.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Reduce a hard construction to a simpler one whose data you know.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: To construct a trapezoid from its four sides, let a be the lower base and c the upper base, parallel and unequal, with b and d the other sides. First let c shrink to 0: the trapezoid becomes a triangle, a familiar figure, but with only two known sides, a and d, where three are needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Now let c grow until it equals a: the trapezoid becomes a parallelogram. Drawing it adds a triangle with sides b, d and a minus c, and all three are known, so this triangle can be built. Then complete the parallelogram to get the trapezoid.

card.rule: If varying a datum one way gives a figure you cannot use, vary it the other way, and look for a simple figure you can construct.
card.limits: A new figure can be useful only if the data you have fit it; the shrinking case failed for want of a third side.

media.alt: A trapezoid with a long base a along the bottom, a short parallel top c, a left slanted side d and a right slanted side b. A dotted diagonal joins the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner, cutting it into two triangles.

A trapezoid with bottom base a, shorter top c, left side d and right side b. A dotted line extends the top edge to the right and a dashed slanted segment joins its end to the lower-right corner, completing a parallelogram and leaving a small triangle on the right.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Learning by failure and the typical modes of variation
concepts.question: How should you proceed when trial after trial fails, and which kinds of variation usually pay?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep varying, restating and transforming the problem; learn from failed trials and aim for an auxiliary problem that is easier to reach.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: End up with a more accessible problem whose solution helps with the original one.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: We often have to try various modifications, restating and transforming the problem again and again until something useful appears. We may learn by failure: there may be a good idea in an unsuccessful trial, and a more successful trial may come by modifying it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student cannot prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even. Trying 3 + 5 and 7 + 9 shows only a pattern. She restates the problem in the definition of odd numbers and finds a way forward.

card.rule: Keep varying, restating and transforming the problem; learn from failed trials and aim for an auxiliary problem that is easier to reach.
card.limits: Our reading: the book names typical modes but gives no ranking; which one pays depends on the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Using the list of questions: help when stuck, not before
concepts.question: When should the list of questions be used on your own work or with a student, and when should it be left alone?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Leave a solver alone while progress is good; when progress is blocked, bring in a question that may show a new aspect.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Protect independence while preventing the loss of interest when work stalls.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: When the student progresses, he needs no help, and the teacher should ask nothing and let him work alone, which is better for his independence. The same holds when we work alone: when new remarks come spontaneously, asking extraneous questions would hamper progress.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: When progress is blocked and nothing occurs to us, we should think of some general idea or some question from the list that might suit. A coach watching a pupil solve a puzzle steadily says nothing; when the pupil freezes, the coach offers one question.

card.rule: Leave a solver alone while progress is good; when progress is blocked, bring in a question that may show a new aspect.
card.limits: Our reading: the book gives no fixed time after which a question should be offered.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: The three questions about a problem to find
concepts.question: Which three questions direct you to the principal parts of a problem to find?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: At the start, and again whenever needed, ask: what is the unknown, what are the data, and what is the condition linking them?

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Check that you understand the problem and focus your attention on its principal parts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The unknown is what is required, the data are what is given, and the condition is what links the unknown to the data. Each can be asked in several words: what is required, what do you want, what are you supposed to seek? The solution consists essentially in linking the unknown to the data.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a problem asking for the diagonal of a rectangle with sides 6 and 8, the unknown is the length of the diagonal, the data are the sides 6 and 8, and the condition links them: the diagonal joins opposite corners of the rectangle.

card.rule: At the start, and again whenever needed, ask: what is the unknown, what are the data, and what is the condition linking them?
card.limits: Our reading: asking the questions does not solve the problem; it checks understanding and aims attention.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
concepts.title: Adapting the questions: many unknowns, clauses, and problems to prove
concepts.question: How should the questions change when a problem has several unknowns or clauses, or is a problem to prove?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Adapt the questions to the problem: ask about several unknowns, data or clauses, and for a problem to prove ask for the hypothesis and the conclusion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep each part of a complex problem in view, whichever kind of problem it is.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A problem may have many unknowns, or a condition with several parts to consider separately. So the questions can be varied: what are the unknowns, what is the first datum, what are the various parts of the condition, what is the first clause of the condition.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The principal parts of a problem to prove are the hypothesis and the conclusion, so the matching questions are: what is the hypothesis, what is the conclusion? For example, to prove that a triangle with two equal angles has two equal sides, the hypothesis is the two equal angles and the conclusion is the two equal sides.

card.rule: Adapt the questions to the problem: ask about several unknowns, data or clauses, and for a problem to prove ask for the hypothesis and the conclusion.
card.limits: A problem to prove has no unknown in the sense of a problem to find; asking for the unknown there misleads.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: The question behind proofs
concepts.question: Is it better to give no proof, every proof, or some proofs, and then which ones?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Before you decide how much proof to teach or learn, ask which proofs serve a purpose instead of assuming all or none.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choose the amount of proof in a course or a study plan on purpose.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A learner who finds a result evident may see no reason to prove it, so the case for proofs has to be made, not assumed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: As a young student, Newton read Euclid's theorems, saw they were true and skipped the proofs, wondering why anyone should prove things so evident.

card.rule: Before you decide how much proof to teach or learn, ask which proofs serve a purpose instead of assuming all or none.
card.limits: The entry says the story may not be authentic; it uses it only to raise the question of why proofs are learned and taught.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: What a complete proof is
concepts.question: What standard does a complete proof meet, and where can we learn it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Study proofs in plane geometry to learn what a proof with no gaps looks like.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Acquire the idea of rigorous proof.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A strict logician accepts a proof only if it leaves no gap, loophole or uncertainty, and elementary plane geometry is still the best place to meet that standard.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student who has followed a few proofs in geometry knows what no gaps means and can notice a gap in a looser argument.

card.rule: Study proofs in plane geometry to learn what a proof with no gaps looks like.
card.limits: The strict standard is the logician's. The entry itself later allows incomplete proofs for good reasons.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: A proof you can see
concepts.question: How does one extra line prove that a triangle's angles add up to two right angles?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: To prove the angle sum of a triangle, draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and match the angles.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: See a complete proof small enough to hold in the mind.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Alternate angles are equal, so the triangle's other two angles reappear at the vertex, where the three angles together form a straight angle of two right angles.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In triangle ABC, draw a line through A parallel to BC. The angle at B equals the angle on one side of A, and the angle at C equals the angle on the other side. With the angle at A, they fill a straight angle, which is \(180^\circ\).

card.rule: To prove the angle sum of a triangle, draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and match the angles.
card.limits: The proof leans on the fact that alternate angles between parallels are equal; if that fact is doubted, the proof is only as good as it.

media.alt: A triangle ABC with A at the top and BC as the bottom side. A horizontal line through A runs parallel to BC. Matching angle arcs mark the angle at B and the angle at A on the left side, and the angle at C and the angle at A on the right side.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: A standard for evidence
concepts.question: What does a student lose who never understands a geometric proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Learn a few geometric proofs to gain a true standard for judging evidence.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Be able to compare alleged evidence of every sort with genuine evidence.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Proofs are the best and simplest examples of true evidence and strict reasoning; without them a person lacks a measure for the claims aimed at him in modern life.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A shopper who has once followed a real proof can tell when an advertisement says 'proven' but only shows a testimonial.

card.rule: Learn a few geometric proofs to gain a true standard for judging evidence.
card.limits: The entry's claim is about education: it argues that general education should reserve a place for geometric proofs. Our reading: it is an argument for a standard, not a ban on other kinds of evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Proofs hold a system together
concepts.question: Why does one need proofs to understand a subject built like Euclid's geometry?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read a deductive subject as a system in which each proposition is tied to earlier ones by a proof.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understand the essence of a logical system, not a heap of facts.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Euclid placed axioms, definitions and propositions in order so that each rests on what came before, and proofs are the cement between them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a book of geometry, a proposition about triangles is proved from earlier axioms, definitions and propositions; skip the proof and you cannot see where the proposition stands.

card.rule: Read a deductive subject as a system in which each proposition is tied to earlier ones by a proof.
card.limits: Our reading: a subject can have an order of dependence without being as rigid as geometry.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Proofs as a memory aid
concepts.question: If general ideas are not the aim, why might proofs still help a learner?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When only the facts are wanted, attach them to a simple proof or system so they connect.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Retain facts when time is short and logical ideas are not a goal.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Connected facts are more interesting and better retained than isolated ones, and a simple proof connects them naturally and durably.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The figure for the angle-sum proof links two facts: the angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\), and alternate angles between parallels are equal.

card.rule: When only the facts are wanted, attach them to a simple proof or system so they connect.
card.limits: The entry says the system need not be logical for this purpose, only effective for memory; it then calls such a system mnemotechnic.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: The cookbook trap
concepts.question: What goes wrong in a course that keeps procedures and drops every proof?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Do not teach a subject to be understood as a cookbook; give the reasons for the rules, not only the rules.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Teach an applied subject so that students understand and keep it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A cookbook lists ingredients and procedures with no proofs, but a course must be understood and remembered, and unmotivated procedures are not understood while unconnected rules are quickly forgotten.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Engineering students need calculus for applications and lack time, training or interest for long epsilon-proofs, so cutting every proof is tempting; the entry warns this reduces the subject to a cookbook.

card.rule: Do not teach a subject to be understood as a cookbook; give the reasons for the rules, not only the rules.
card.limits: The entry does not ask for every proof in full detail either; it names the opposite temptation as real.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Incomplete proofs, in their place
concepts.question: What are incomplete proofs for, if they cannot replace complete ones?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use an incomplete proof, honestly labelled, to give a result interest, plausibility and coherence when a complete proof is out of reach.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Fix a result in the learner's mind without pretending it is fully proved.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A few easily shown facts can make a hard theorem plausible and connected to what the learner knows, although they never replace a complete proof.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Students unready for the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra know that a first-degree equation has one root and a second-degree one has two. They can also be shown that no equation of degree \(n\) has more than \(n\) different roots.

card.rule: Use an incomplete proof, honestly labelled, to give a result interest, plausibility and coherence when a complete proof is out of reach.
card.limits: The entry says these facts are not a complete proof of the theorem; they only lend interest and plausibility.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: The germ of a proof
concepts.question: Why is the first idea of a proof so often incomplete, and what is it worth?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When you present a proof, start with its germ, the main idea in its simplest form, and add the details afterwards.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Show the learner the central connection before the technical details.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Experience in solving problems shows that the first idea of a proof usually holds the main connection but lacks the details, so the germ is where the insight lives.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To show the angle sum of a triangle, say first: draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. The matching of angles is the detail that follows.

card.rule: When you present a proof, start with its germ, the main idea in its simplest form, and add the details afterwards.
card.limits: A proof that gives only a germ must be marked as incomplete, and presenting one well takes skill and good taste.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Rules against abuse
concepts.question: What keeps incomplete proofs from being abused?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Whenever a proof is incomplete, indicate it as such, somewhere and somehow.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keep the use of incomplete proofs honest.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The entry says advocating incomplete proofs is very dangerous, and a few rules keep possible abuse within bounds.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A textbook that prints the roots argument for the Fundamental Theorem under the heading 'plausibility argument, not a full proof' follows the rule.

card.rule: Whenever a proof is incomplete, indicate it as such, somewhere and somehow.
card.limits: Marking is not enough on its own; the entry adds a second condition on the author.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Which proof for which aim
concepts.question: Given a learner's aim and time, which kind of proof treatment does the entry recommend?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Match the proof treatment to the aim: complete proofs for strict reasoning and system, simple proofs for memory, incomplete proofs where full ones are too heavy, never the bare cookbook.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choose a sensible amount of proof for a given course.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each treatment serves a different end: evidence and reasoning, logical system, memory, or interest and coherence under limits of time and training.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A general course on thinking uses geometric proofs; a vocabulary list uses connecting patterns; a calculus course for engineers uses labelled incomplete proofs.

card.rule: Match the proof treatment to the aim: complete proofs for strict reasoning and system, simple proofs for memory, incomplete proofs where full ones are too heavy, never the bare cookbook.
card.limits: Our reading: this is a summary of the entry's five headings; the entry itself does not give a rule table.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: What proverbs are worth
concepts.question: How far should we trust proverbs about solving problems?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Read proverbs as vivid descriptions of how people solve problems, not as authority.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Borrow common sense about method without treating it as law.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Proverbs keep the comments people made on success and failure in reaching ends, but they form no consistent system and many can be matched by a proverb giving opposite advice.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 'Look before you leap' urges care, while 'If you will sail without danger you must never put to sea' urges boldness; each fits some circumstances.

card.rule: Read proverbs as vivid descriptions of how people solve problems, not as authority.
card.limits: The entry says it would be a pity to disregard proverbs altogether, since they describe heuristic procedures graphically.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Understand the end first
concepts.question: What should you secure before acting on a problem?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Understand the problem and keep its end clearly in mind before you begin to act.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid wandering away from the problem or dropping it.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: If the end is not clear in our minds we may easily stray from the problem and drop it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A team starts building a tool at once, talking and tinkering, without agreeing what the finished tool must do; it keeps changing direction. (Our illustration.)

card.rule: Understand the problem and keep its end clearly in mind before you begin to act.
card.limits: Understanding the problem is the first step only; it does not by itself produce the plan.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Try again, but try differently
concepts.question: When a first attempt fails, what should the next attempt change?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep trying after a failure, but vary the means and keep a second plan in reserve.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Find a plan that works without wasting effort on the same failed approach.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A good idea is a piece of good fortune that we deserve by diligence, but repeating the same trial fails; different means adapted to the circumstances are needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A hiker finds a bridge washed out; she does not keep testing it but turns to the ford upstream she had marked as a reserve.

card.rule: Keep trying after a failure, but vary the means and keep a second plan in reserve.
card.limits: Our reading: switching is worth it only after a fair trial of each means.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Appreciate the small idea
concepts.question: What do experts do with ideas that beginners let slip?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Notice and use the modest ideas that come to mind, and look for opportunities.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn passing thoughts into working plans.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A helpful idea often arrives inconspicuously and we fail to appreciate it; the expert perhaps has no more ideas than a beginner but appreciates and uses what he has better.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A junior engineer mentions in passing that a log shows the same odd gap every night. A senior engineer asks about it, and the gap leads straight to the bug. (Our illustration.)

card.rule: Notice and use the modest ideas that come to mind, and look for opportunities.
card.limits: Our reading: appreciating an idea cannot be forced, but it can be trained by asking of each passing thought what it might do.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Start at the right moment
concepts.question: How do we decide when a plan is ripe to carry out?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Start carrying out the plan when it is ripe, neither rashly nor after endless hesitation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Avoid failure from acting too soon and from never acting.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The proverbs warn both ways, so the right moment must be set by our own judgment.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A cook who starts frying before the oil is hot spoils the dish, and one who waits for perfect oil never serves dinner. (Our illustration.)

card.rule: Start carrying out the plan when it is ripe, neither rashly nor after endless hesitation.
card.limits: No proverb fixes the moment for us; the entry says we must use our judgment.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Carrying out, step by step
concepts.question: How should a plan be carried out once it is made?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Carry out the plan step by step, checking each detail in turn.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make sure the details truly fit the outline of the plan.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A plan usually gives only a general outline, so we must convince ourselves that each detail fits, one after the other.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A planner sketches a trip in outline, then checks each leg of it, one after the other, for times and connections. (Our illustration.)

card.rule: Carry out the plan step by step, checking each detail in turn.
card.limits: Checking each detail takes time; the entry says to proceed by degrees, not all at once.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Looking back is part of the work
concepts.question: Why re-examine a solution that is already complete?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Look back at the completed solution and re-examine it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Catch errors and gain confirmation of the result.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Looking back is an instructive phase of the work: re-examining the solution may reveal an additional confirmation of the result.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: After solving an equation, a student substitutes the answer back into the equation to see that both sides agree. (Our illustration.)

card.rule: Look back at the completed solution and re-examine it.
card.limits: Our reading: a second check that only repeats the first adds little.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Four modern proverbs
concepts.question: What attitudes do the author's own proverbs sum up?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Keep four short reminders: the end suggests the means, ask What, Why, Where, When and How, doubt only what is worth doubting, and look around after a first discovery.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Remember the more systematic attitudes of solving in a compact form.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: They compress more sophisticated attitudes of solving into the compact turn of a proverb.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Faced with a stuck project, a student asks What is wanted, Why is it hard, Where is the obstacle, When does it appear and How could it be removed.

card.rule: Keep four short reminders: the end suggests the means, ask What, Why, Where, When and How, doubt only what is worth doubting, and look around after a first discovery.
card.limits: The entry says imitating the turn of proverbs is not easy, and the four are the author's own, 'synthetic' proverbs.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Working forwards: trial and error
concepts.question: What happens when we attack the water puzzle by starting from the data and trying things?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Recognise forward trial and error from the data as the usual first attack, and do not count on it.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Know why a direct, trying-things approach to a puzzle may not get you to the answer.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Starting from the empty containers and filling and emptying at will can succeed, but only by accident after many trials.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To bring up exactly 6 quarts with a 4-quart and a 9-quart pail, most people fill the big pail and empty as much as possible into the small one. That leaves 5 quarts, not 6.

card.rule: Recognise forward trial and error from the data as the usual first attack, and do not count on it.
card.limits: Our reading: forward play is not useless, since it can show amounts you can measure, like the 5 quarts.

media.alt: Two empty upright containers with open tops and flat bottoms, drawn side by side. The tall one on the left is labelled 9 and the short one on the right is labelled 4, showing their heights and capacities.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Look at the data; find something nearer
concepts.question: If you cannot reach the unknown, what can you try to reach instead?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Picture exactly what you are given, and if the unknown is out of reach, aim for a related quantity you can reach.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Gain a foothold when the target is out of sight.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A clear picture of the given tools shows what they can and cannot do, and a nearby result may lead on to the one wanted.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The two pails are pictured as cylinders with equal bases and heights in ratio 9 to 4. Filling the big one and pouring into the small gives 5 quarts, a related amount, though not the 6 required.

card.rule: Picture exactly what you are given, and if the unknown is out of reach, aim for a related quantity you can reach.
card.limits: The related result is a foothold, not an answer; the entry does not claim the 5 quarts solves the puzzle.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Assume the goal is already reached
concepts.question: What picture do you start from when you work backwards?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Picture the goal as already reached, as clearly as you can, and start your thinking from that picture.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn the question 'how do I get there?' into a question about what must come just before.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Pappus advises starting from what is required and assuming what is sought as already found; the final situation is then a concrete starting point.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the six-quart puzzle, imagine the large pail holding exactly 6 quarts and the small pail empty, and begin from there.

card.rule: Picture the goal as already reached, as clearly as you can, and start your thinking from that picture.
card.limits: The picture is only the start; it gives no sequence of operations until you ask what could have come before.

media.alt: The goal situation: the tall pail on the left is filled with hatching up to a mark labelled 6, a little below its rim, and the short pail on the right beside it is empty.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Asking for the antecedent, again and again
concepts.question: How do you get from a pictured goal to a sequence of operations?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: From the goal, ask from what foregoing situation it could be obtained, and repeat for each answer until you reach something you can do.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Discover a usable sequence of operations.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Each answer is a situation one move nearer the start, and the chain ends when it connects with something already known.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To have 6 quarts in the big pail, fill it to 9 and pour out 3. That needs 1 quart in the small pail. Getting 1 quart is easy: fill the big pail and pour 4 away twice, because \(9-4-4=1\).

card.rule: From the goal, ask from what foregoing situation it could be obtained, and repeat for each answer until you reach something you can do.
card.limits: Our reading: the chain may branch, and not every antecedent leads to something known.

media.alt: The tall pail is drawn full to its top, hatched all over and labelled 9, while the short pail beside it holds only a thin hatched layer of water at its bottom, labelled 1.
The tall pail is drawn completely empty. The short pail beside it holds a thin hatched layer of water at its bottom, labelled 1. Only the one quart in the small pail matters.
The tall pail holds only a thin hatched layer at its bottom, labelled 1, and the short pail beside it is empty. One quart sits in the big pail and nothing in the small.
The tall pail is full and hatched up to a mark labelled 9. Dashed level lines mark the water heights 5 and 1 inside it, so the level falls in two equal drops. The short pail beside it is empty.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Retrace the steps
concepts.question: Once the backward chain is found, how do you actually produce the result?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When the backward chain reaches something you can do, perform the operations in the reverse order of discovery.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Turn a discovered chain into a working solution.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The sequence is discovered in retrogressive order, so what remains is to reverse the process and start from the point reached last in the analysis.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Fill the big pail and pour 4 away twice, leaving 1 quart. Pour it into the small pail, refill the big pail, and pour from it into the small pail until full. The big pail then holds 6 quarts.

card.rule: When the backward chain reaches something you can do, perform the operations in the reverse order of discovery.
card.limits: Our reading: the reverse order works only if each backward step is one you can actually perform going forward.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Common sense, stated in general terms
concepts.question: Who can use working backwards, and what did the Greeks add to it?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Use working backwards as a common-sense procedure within everyone's reach, for any kind of problem.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Make the method usable in mathematical and nonmathematical problems alike.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: Anybody can solve a concrete problem this way by concentrating on the final position and asking from what foregoing position it could be reached.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A child planning a surprise asks what must be ready just before the guest arrives, then what must come before that.

card.rule: Use working backwards as a common-sense procedure within everyone's reach, for any kind of problem.
card.limits: The tradition crediting Plato may not be quite reliable.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Why turning round is hard
concepts.question: Why do able people find it hard to move away from the goal?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Expect resistance to turning away from the goal, and present working backwards carefully.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Help learners overcome the pull of the direct path.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The mind must proceed in an order exactly the reverse of the performance, which feels unnatural.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A student asked to plan a lesson from the final exam backwards hesitates, because it means not heading straight toward the goal.

card.rule: Expect resistance to turning away from the goal, and present working backwards carefully.
card.limits: The entry says it does not take a genius to solve a concrete problem this way.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: The dog, the hen and the fence
concepts.question: What does the fence experiment show about animals that turn round and those that do not?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: When food is in plain view but a fence blocks the direct path, turn away from it and go around the end.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Compare animal problem solving with human working backwards.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: A dog may first strike a posture to spring at the food, then turn about and dash around the end of the fence; a hen run back and forth against the fence.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A fence forms three sides of a rectangle and leaves the fourth side open. A dog stands at the fence, food lies on the other side. The dog reaches it in a smooth curve; the hen may not reach it at all.

card.rule: When food is in plain view but a fence blocks the direct path, turn away from it and go around the end.
card.limits: Animal behaviour differs by species and by the distance between animal and food.

media.alt: Three sides of a rectangular fence drawn with dots: top, left and right, with the bottom side open. Inside the fence is a dog D; outside, beyond the closed top side, is food F directly above the dog.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: People as dogs and hens
concepts.question: How do the dog's and hen's behaviours resemble ours in solving problems?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Compare your own way of solving with the dog's and the hen's: muddling through or turning round with insight.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognise which style of solving you are using.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: The hen's trying again and again until a lucky accident resembles people who muddle through, while turning round needs a different habit of mind.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In the water puzzle we first worked forwards, like the dog that barked and scratched, and only afterwards turned round.

card.rule: Compare your own way of solving with the dog's and the hen's: muddling through or turning round with insight.
card.limits: The entry says we should not even blame the hen; her difficulty is like ours.

concepts.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
concepts.title: Don't build a theory on one experiment
concepts.question: How much weight can one sketchy experiment bear?

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Notice analogies from one sketchy experiment, but treat them as hypotheses to be rechecked and revalued.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Use the experiment's suggestions without overclaiming.

blocks.label: Why it works
blocks.text: One simple experiment, only sketchily reported, cannot support a big theory, but noticing obvious analogies does no harm if we are prepared to recheck them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: From the hen and dog we may suspect that muddlers resemble hens, and then look for more evidence before believing it.

card.rule: Notice analogies from one sketchy experiment, but treat them as hypotheses to be rechecked and revalued.
card.limits: The entry offers the analogies as plausible, not proved.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One design: phases, list, classroom and Dictionary
concepts.question: How do the four phases, the list, the classroom method and the Dictionary fit together as one design?

paragraphs: The book is one design seen from several sides. The list of questions is its core. Its questions are grouped under the four phases (understand, plan, carry out, look back), and behind the wording each one points to a mental operation typically useful in solving problems, listed in the order in which the operations most likely occur.

Part I shows the list in a classroom, where a teacher moves from general questions to specific ones. Part II turns those moves into a talk the solver holds with himself. The Dictionary explains the list: each of its fifteen paragraphs has an article named by its opening words, and twelve principal articles treat aspects such as progress, variation, problems to find and to prove, notation and figures.

Our reading: the parts differ in how you use them. Watch the method at work in Part I and the dialogue, carry the list in your head, and visit the Dictionary, which is arranged alphabetically, with a question from your own problem. Part IV offers problems with hints and solutions for practice.
card.example: A solver stuck on a rota puzzle sees that she is in the second phase and asks the list's question about a related problem. Wanting more, she finds the list paragraph that holds it, takes its opening sentence and reads the Dictionary article with that title.
card.rule: Use the list in the order of the four phases, and consult the Dictionary article behind a question when your own problem raises it.
card.limits: The book calls its list a first list that could be improved, and its questions are no magic. The Dictionary is not arranged by phase, so the paragraph titles of the list are the way in.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Locate the trouble, then choose the question
concepts.question: Which phase is the solver stuck in, and which question of the list aims at that phase?

paragraphs: The four phases give the first coordinate for choosing a question. The book finds a typical trouble in each: incomplete understanding of the problem; rushing in without a plan, or waiting clumsily for an idea; carelessness in carrying out the plan; and failure to check the result at all. Each trouble has questions of the list aimed at it.

Our reading: so the list works as a lookup. Cannot say what is asked: unknown, data, condition. Understood, but no idea: related problem, same unknown, then variation. Idea in hand, steps shaky: check each step. Answer in hand: check the result and argument, derive it differently, use it elsewhere. Diagnose first, then press the questions that aim at the fault.
Timing matters too. While a solver is progressing, extra questions would only hamper the work. When progress is blocked and nothing occurs to him, a question that may show a new aspect is welcome.
card.example: A trainee's invoice template gives a total that looks odd. He can say what the total should be, so understanding is not his trouble. He has an answer but has not examined it, so the fourth phase was skipped, and Can you check the result? is the question aimed at him.
card.rule: Name the phase where the trouble lies and ask the question of the list that aims at it, but only when progress is blocked.
card.limits: Our reading: the phases overlap and a solver moves back and forth, so a diagnosis is a first guess. The book gives its faults as typical behaviour, and says a careful diagnosis gives some chance of a cure, not a certainty.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: No plan yet: recall first, then vary
concepts.question: No plan comes: in what order do the book's suggestions run, and what makes each give way to the next?

paragraphs: Begin the search with the cheapest move: Do you know a related problem? Many problems are somewhat related, so narrow the search. Look at the unknown and recall a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown. If you recall one, exploit the luck: could you use its result, its method, or an auxiliary element that makes it usable?

If no recalled problem helps, change the problem instead of waiting. Restate it, go back to definitions, or solve first a related problem that is more accessible, more general, more special or analogous. Keep part of the condition, derive something from the data, or change the unknown or the data. These moves often end in an auxiliary problem.

After wandering among related problems, come back with: Did you use all the data? Did you use the whole condition? Our reading: the order runs from the cheapest move to the costliest. The book says its questions cannot work magic, so a failed move is a signal to vary, not to repeat.
card.example: A planner must seat 40 guests with rival pairs kept apart. She names the unknown, a seating plan, and recalls a rota problem with a similar unknown, but it ignores the rivals. She drops that part of the condition, solves the easy part, then asks whether she used every rival pair.
card.rule: Recall a problem with the same or a similar unknown first; if none helps, vary the problem; after wandering, check that all the data and the whole condition are used.
card.limits: Our reading: the order is a guide, and no question is guaranteed. Variation can carry you so far from the original that you lose it, and the last question is the way back.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: When the plan stalls halfway
concepts.question: A plan has stalled partway: should I repeat it, change something, or rest, and what tells me?

paragraphs: A plan is an idea, not a guarantee. When an attempt along it fails, the book gives old advice with a twist: try again, but do not repeat the same attempt unchanged. Restate the problem, go back to the definition, specialise or generalise, or solve a smaller related problem and keep the little success. A failed trial may hold a good idea, and a modified trial may do better.

Signs tell you how boldly to go on. If an expected sign appears, such as a datum put to use or a simpler analogue turning up, go on with more confidence. If signs are rare, hesitate. If they stay absent for long, turn back and try another road. Signs support only a probable conclusion, and any one of them may mislead.
When forcing conscious effort has stopped paying, put the problem aside for a night or a few days after real work on it; it may return clarified. Our reading: change first, rest after real effort.
card.example: A developer's bug fix fails twice. She does not retry the same patch. She restates the failure as a smaller test, which she can fix, and sees a sign: the fixed small case now fails in the same way as the big one. Encouraged, she follows that road.
card.rule: When a plan stalls, vary the problem or the road instead of repeating the attempt, weigh the signs you meet, and rest only after real effort.
card.limits: Signs are probable, not certain: their absence can make you drop a good road. Rest works only after real work on the problem and does not replace it.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Find or prove: choose the form of the question
concepts.question: Is the task to find an object or to prove an assertion, and how does that change the questions I ask?

paragraphs: Decide the kind of problem by its aim. A problem to find asks for an object, the unknown. A problem to prove asks you to show conclusively that a clearly stated assertion is true, or else false. The kind decides the principal parts you must know exactly: unknown, data and condition for the first; hypothesis and conclusion for the second.

The list is built for problems to find, and it carries over to proofs by swapping the parts. Look at the unknown becomes look at the conclusion and recall a theorem with the same or a similar conclusion. Keep part of the condition becomes keep part of the hypothesis. Did you use all the data? becomes Did you use the whole hypothesis?
Our reading: much of the list needs no change. Restating the problem, drawing a figure, going back to definitions, using analogy or specialisation and working backwards apply to both kinds.
card.example: Find the cheapest of three delivery plans: the unknown is a plan, the data are the prices, the condition is delivery by Friday. Show that no plan beats 40 pounds: the hypothesis is the plans allowed, the conclusion is that every cost is at least 40. Same facts, two kinds of task.
card.rule: Name the kind first, then ask the matching questions: about unknown, data and condition, or about conclusion and hypothesis.
card.limits: The matching is a guide, not an exact table. Some theorems do not split naturally into hypothesis and conclusion, and the book's example is the theorem that there are infinitely many primes.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Starting from the goal: working backwards
concepts.question: When should I start from the goal and work backwards, and how does that differ from recalling a problem with the same unknown?

paragraphs: Working backwards is the method Pappus called analysis. Assume the goal is reached, ask from what situation immediately before it could be obtained, and ask the same of that, until you reach something you can do or know. Synthesis retraces the steps forwards. The book gives analysis to devising the plan and synthesis to carrying it out, so doing runs opposite to discovering.

Our reading: working backwards and Look at the unknown both begin at the goal, but they use different things. Looking at the unknown needs a solved problem you can recall. Working backwards needs no recalled problem; it builds a chain of antecedents from the goal. When neither helps, the book says the data side must often be tried too.

Starting forward from the data by trial and error is the usual first attack, but it tends to succeed only by accident. The book says that starting from the unknown is usually preferable, and a goal pictured as reached is a concrete place to begin.
card.example: A host wants dinner served at 7. The roast must leave the oven at 6:30, so it must go in at 4:30; the oven must be hot by 4:15; the shopping must be done before that. Cooking then runs in the opposite order: shop, heat, roast, serve.
card.rule: When no related problem comes, picture the goal as reached, ask what must come immediately before it, repeat until you reach something you can do, then carry the steps out in reverse order.
card.limits: Our reading: a backward step must be reversible, or the forward retracing may not follow. The chain can branch, and some problems yield more easily to a recalled problem or to the data.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Specialise, generalise, use analogy, or add an auxiliary problem
concepts.question: Which way of varying the problem fits what blocks me, and what must an auxiliary problem give me?

paragraphs: When recall fails, the book names the typical ways of varying a problem: going back to the definition, decomposing and recombining, generalisation, specialisation and analogy. Variation may lead to auxiliary elements, or to a more accessible auxiliary problem. All of them aim at a nearer contact with what you already know.

Our reading, drawn from the book's cases: choose by what blocks you. Too much variety to cover at once: specialise, for example by setting one datum to a trivial value. An unfamiliar setting with a simpler cousin: use analogy, such as a plane problem for a solid one. A special case with no foothold: try a wider problem. A recalled result that nearly fits: add the missing element.

Before investing in an auxiliary problem, ask which of its result or its method you expect to use, and remember its time is taken from the original. The book names no infallible way to find a good one; look at the unknown and vary the problem.
card.example: A teacher cannot see why the angles of a hexagon add to 720 degrees. She specialises to a triangle and a quadrilateral, notices that each extra side adds 180 degrees, and then states the pattern for n sides. Specialising gave a foothold, and widening to n gave the rule.
card.rule: Choose the variation by what blocks you, and before solving an auxiliary problem say whether you expect to use its result, its method or both.
card.limits: Our reading: the book gives these moves as typical, not ranked. Each change costs time taken from the original, and the book says no sure recipe exists for finding an auxiliary problem.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: From plan to checked result
concepts.question: How strict must I be while planning and while carrying out, and how do I test the finished result?

paragraphs: The phases ask for different standards of evidence. While devising a plan you may use guesses, analogies and plausible reasoning, which the book likens to scaffolding. While carrying out the plan you accept only steps you can see clearly or prove, and in a long solution you check the great steps before the small ones.

A finished result is still open to tests. For a formula in letters, ask whether all the data appear, whether it respects the problem's symmetry, whether it matches the analogous simpler problem, and whether it behaves correctly when a measure shrinks to zero, grows, or the units change. Then test the argument: recheck its touchy points, vary the order, derive the result another way, or seek a short argument.
Our reading: match the check to what you hold. A passed test raises confidence without proving, so choose tests of different kinds, and keep the heavy re-derivation for difficult and important cases.
card.example: A student claims a trapezoid with parallel sides a and b and height h has area (a + b)h/2. Setting b = a gives a rectangle of area ah, and setting b = 0 gives a triangle of area ah/2. Both agree with known cases, so confidence rises, though the tests do not replace the derivation.
card.rule: Be free while planning and strict while carrying out, then test the finished result and its argument by several different checks.
card.limits: A passed test raises confidence but does not prove the result. The test by dimension, for example, cannot see pure numbers such as one half. Choose checks in proportion to difficulty and importance.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What looking back adds
concepts.question: What does the fourth phase give that the first three cannot, and how does it feed the next problem?

paragraphs: Looking back is more than checking. Once the solution is complete and correct, it can add four things: confidence (check the result and argument, derive the result another way), economy (simplify, see it at a glance, find a shorter proof by studying the result), connection (use the result or method for another problem), and new problems (vary the solved problem by generalisation, specialisation, analogy or recombination).

Our reading: it also closes a loop. The planning phase hunts for a related problem solved before, and looking back is where such problems are stocked, with their results and methods. The book adds that no problem is completely exhausted, and that the habit builds well-ordered knowledge ready to use.
card.example: A team fixes a slow report query. They ask whether the fix really works, whether it could be simpler, whether the method fits other reports, and what related queries it suggests. Their notes become the related problem they recall for the next slow query.
card.rule: After every solution, check it, simplify it, connect it to other problems and note the method and result for next time.
card.limits: Looking back starts from a complete, correct solution, and its rewards are possibilities, not promises. Our reading: the lasting value is the habit; a single review may find nothing new.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What the teacher and the student should aim at
concepts.question: What two aims should a teacher keep, and what should a student become able to do with the questions?

paragraphs: The teacher has two aims with each question: to help the student solve the problem at hand, and to develop his ability to solve later problems alone. The aims are linked, since each success adds a little to the ability. To serve both, help in measure and naturally: begin with a general question and come down to specific ones only until one gets a response.

The student's aim is to make a few questions his own: to put the right question to himself at the right moment and carry out the matching mental operation vigorously. The book says solving problems is a practical skill learned by imitation and practice, like swimming. The student must also understand the problem and want its solution.

Both aims are served by mastery, not pedantry: use the questions with judgment, and notice where they fit. Our reading: the list, the dialogue, the examples and the Dictionary are all means to that single end.
card.example: A senior developer helps a junior with a failing deployment. She asks what the junior wants to happen, then whether a similar deployment worked before, and only then points to the config file. The junior leaves with a fix and with questions he can ask himself next time.
card.rule: Help so that the solver does the thinking, and practise until the questions are your own habit, used with judgment.
card.limits: Our reading: the book gives no number of problems after which a question becomes habit. It warns a teacher to proceed with caution, prepare examples and watch how the class takes the method.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A girl of ten works half an hour on a small puzzle and solves it alone. What does Polya think this may do for her?
options: It gives her nothing lasting, since only great problems bring any sense of discovery
It teaches her the puzzle's answer, which is its only gain, as feelings play no part
It may give her the tension and triumph of discovery and start a taste for mental work
It makes her dislike mental work, because struggling alone discourages young learners
optionExplain: It sounds modest, but Polya says even a modest problem holds a grain of discovery.
Learning the answer is a gain, but Polya stresses the experience of discovery itself.
A real taste of discovery can come from a puzzle that is hers to solve.
Struggle is discouraging when the problem is too hard; here the effort ends in success.
questions.explain: A good guess is fair here. The card next shows what Polya says even a modest problem can bring.
questions.rule: Solve problems that challenge your curiosity by your own means, and let the pleasure of finding the answer win you a taste for mental work.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Polya says there is a grain of ____ in the solution of any problem.
questions.explain: Even a modest problem holds a small grain of discovery when you solve it by your own means.
questions.rule: Every problem solved by your own means holds a grain of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Which pupil has the experience Polya describes?
options: Dev, who struggles with a modest puzzle until his own idea cracks it
Mia, who copies the worked answer from the back of the book into her notes
Tom, who is led through each step by a friend and nods at every one
Lena, who reads a finished solution and sees that it appears to be correct
optionExplain: Right: Dev solves it by his own means, so the problem brings him tension and triumph.
Copying an answer hands over the result without the discovery.
Following a friend's steps makes the friend the discoverer, not Tom.
Seeing that a solution appears correct is not the same as finding it.
questions.explain: The experience comes from solving by your own means; being given the result does not bring it.
questions.rule: Your own solving brings the triumph.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Sort each study habit: does it give a taste of discovery, or not?

items.t: Trying your own ideas on a puzzle until one works
Working a modest problem that challenges your curiosity
Solving a crossword clue on your own
Copying the last line from a classmate's page
Learning a method only to forget it after the exam
Following someone else's solution without trying anything

questions.explain: Discovery needs your own effort on a problem that challenges you. Copying, cramming to forget and passive following leave out the effort that brings the triumph.
questions.rule: Effort of your own is the source of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: True or false: According to Polya, a problem must be a great one before solving it can bring any experience of discovery.
questions.explain: He says a great discovery solves a great problem, but a modest problem, if it challenges curiosity and is solved by your own means, still holds a grain of discovery.
questions.rule: Modest problems count too.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A parent doubts that a child's first puzzle triumph will matter later. What does Polya's preface suggest?
options: It matters only for children with natural talent, since others cannot taste discovery
It fades by adulthood, because tastes for mental work are formed only by examinations
It matters little, because curiosity is fixed at birth and no experience changes it
Such experiences at a young age may leave a lasting mark on mind and character
optionExplain: Polya holds that everyone must discover their talents and tastes by trying, so talent is not a precondition.
Polya never ties the taste to examinations; he ties it to the experience of discovery.
Polya says early experiences can create a taste, so he does not treat curiosity as fixed.
Right: Polya says such experiences at a susceptible age may create a taste for mental work and leave an imprint for a lifetime.
questions.explain: The preface adds a point about timing: a triumph of discovery in youth may shape character for life.
questions.rule: Early discovery can leave a lifelong mark.
questions.teaches: Polya adds that a triumph of discovery at a susceptible age may create a taste for mental work and leave a mark on mind and character that lasts a lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A teacher has a full term for fractions. Which plan does Polya's preface favour?
options: Fill the term with drills in routine operations so that every skill is firm
Set problems the class has the knowledge to tackle, and help with stimulating questions
Give the hardest problems she knows, so that only keen students stay interested
Present each solution complete and ask students to copy it carefully
optionExplain: Drill feels safe, but Polya says it kills interest and hampers intellectual development.
Right: this plan keeps students' curiosity alive and leaves the solving to them.
Hard problems feel stimulating, but problems must be proportionate to students' knowledge.
Copying a complete solution leaves the students with nothing to discover.
questions.explain: The next card gives Polya's advice for the teacher.
questions.rule: Set problems proportionate to your students' knowledge and help with stimulating questions rather than filling the time with routine drill.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A teacher should challenge curiosity by setting students problems ____ to their knowledge.
questions.explain: Problems that fit the students' knowledge can be solved with effort and so challenge curiosity.
questions.rule: Fit the problem to the students' knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A class stalls on a puzzle. Which reaction follows Polya's advice?
options: Write the full solution on the board so that time is not wasted
Move on to routine drill, since the puzzle has already lost the class
Tell them to look up the answer and copy it down neatly
Ask a stimulating question that nudges them toward finding the next step themselves
optionExplain: Writing the solution out ends the students' own work.
Drill is the thing Polya warns kills interest.
Copying an answer gives no discovery at all.
Right: a question helps them solve the problem without solving it for them.
questions.explain: Help comes as stimulating questions that leave the discovery to the students.
questions.rule: Help with questions, not answers.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Sort each teacher's choice by Polya's preface: does it build interest and thinking, or kill it?

items.t: Setting a problem matched to what the class already knows
Answering a stall with a stimulating question
Letting students find the solution by their own means
Filling the allotted time with drill in routine operations
Treating routine operations as the whole of the subject
Setting only problems far beyond what students know

questions.explain: The first three choices challenge curiosity. Drill kills interest by Polya's words. Problems far beyond the class are not matched to its knowledge; that last point is our reading.
questions.rule: Matched problems and good questions build interest.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: If a teacher fills all the allotted time with routine drill, what does Polya expect?
options: Students' interest dies and their intellectual development is hampered
Students gain a firm base that later makes independent thinking easy
Students enjoy the safety of routine and ask for harder problems
Nothing changes, since drill and problem solving build the same skill
optionExplain: Right: Polya says drilling kills interest and hampers development, and counts it as a misused opportunity.
A base is useful, but Polya does not say drill leads to independent thinking.
Routine may feel safe, but Polya says it kills interest, so students do not ask for more.
Polya separates drill from the challenge of problems that give independent thinking.
questions.explain: Polya names two costs of drill and calls it a misuse of the teacher's opportunity.
questions.rule: Drill alone costs interest and growth.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A tutor's pupils love puzzles but cannot start a new one alone. In Polya's terms, which gift is still missing?
options: The taste for mental work, which they have not yet acquired at all
Credit for the course, which only the teacher can award them
Some means of independent thinking, since the pupils already have a taste for it
Routine drill, which the tutor has not yet given them
optionExplain: Loving puzzles is already a taste for mental work.
Credit is not one of the gifts Polya names.
Right: loving puzzles shows a taste for mental work, but not yet the means to think alone.
Polya treats drill as harmful, not as a gift.
questions.explain: Polya names two gifts, a taste and some means, so one can be present without the other.
questions.rule: A taste and the means are two different gifts.
questions.teaches: Polya says a teacher who challenges curiosity and helps with questions may give students two things: a taste for independent thinking and some means of it.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A student checks a textbook solution step by step and finds it correct. Which question might still bother a curious student?
options: How could anyone have thought of such a solution in the first place?
Whether the answer at the back of the book has a misprint in it
Whether the solution would earn full credit in the next examination
Whether the steps could have been set out on fewer lines
optionExplain: Right: checking shows the solution is correct but not how it was found.
A misprint check is about the book, not about how solutions arise.
Credit concerns marks, not the origin of the solution.
Length is a matter of style, not of how the idea was found.
questions.explain: A correct solution can still leave the question of origin open. The next card shows how Polya treated it.
questions.rule: Ask not only whether a solution is correct but how it could have been invented, and how you could invent such things yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: As a student Polya asked how he could invent or ____ such things by himself.
questions.explain: His question was about the power to find solutions and facts himself, not only to follow them.
questions.rule: Ask how to find such things yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A teacher solves a puzzle on the board and the class agrees it is right. Which follow-up question is Polya's kind?
options: Can the last line be copied down before the bell rings?
How did she come to think of that first step?
Does the result agree with the answer at the back?
Will this type of puzzle appear on the test?
optionExplain: Copying is about notes, not about how the idea arose.
Right: it asks how the solution was invented, not only whether it works.
Agreeing with the back of the book is a check on correctness.
A question about the test is about marks.
questions.explain: Polya's question looks behind the solution to the thinking that produced it.
questions.rule: Ask how the step was found.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Sort each question: does it check that a solution works, or ask how it was invented?

items.t: Does each step follow from the one before?
Is the final number correct?
Does the arithmetic agree when I recheck it?
What led the solver to try this idea?
