How could I find a solution like this myself?
What motives and procedures lay behind the solution?

questions.explain: The first three questions test a finished solution. The others look at how the solution came to be, which is Polya's concern.
questions.rule: Checking and inventing are different questions.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: True or false: According to Polya's preface, seeing that a solution is correct also shows how a person could discover such a solution.
questions.explain: Polya's student question arose exactly because a solution can appear to work while still not showing how it was invented.
questions.rule: Correct does not mean explained.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Polya notes that newspapers give space to crosswords and other riddles. What does he take this to show?
options: Crossword solvers are mostly mathematicians who need regular practice
Riddles are popular only because newspapers can print them cheaply
Behind the wish to solve problems with no material gain may lie a deeper curiosity about the ways of solution
Problems with no practical use matter little, so books on method suit few readers
optionExplain: Polya makes no claim about who solves crosswords.
Polya treats the space given to riddles as a sign of interest, not of cost.
Right: Polya reads this as a sign of a wider interest in the ways and means, the motives and procedures, of solution.
He says the opposite: the interest may be more widespread than one would assume.
questions.explain: Polya extends his audience beyond teachers and students of mathematics.
questions.rule: Interest in how problems are solved is wide.
questions.teaches: Polya thinks interest in the ways and means of solution may be more widespread than assumed, so the book is meant to interest anybody concerned with invention and discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A teacher says mathematics is only a tidy chain of deductions. What might Polya add?
options: The chain is wrong, since deduction plays no part in mathematics
Only mathematicians of the past ever invented anything new in it
It also has a face where it is made by experiment and guesswork
Tidy deduction is for school, and real mathematics uses none of it
optionExplain: Polya keeps the rigorous science of Euclid as a real face.
Polya says nothing so narrow about invention.
Right: Polya says the deductive picture is one face, and mathematics in the making is another.
Polya does not say real mathematics drops deduction.
questions.explain: The next card names the two faces.
questions.rule: Look at mathematics both as a finished deductive system and as an experimental science in the making.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Match each name to its description.
pairs: The study of methods of solving problems
questions.explain: The first two are the two faces; heuristic is the name some writers give to studying how problems are solved.
questions.rule: Two faces, and the study that shows the second.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Which item shows mathematics in the making?
options: A page of trial guesses, tests and corrections made while hunting for a pattern
A finished proof set out in numbered, logical steps
A list of definitions and theorems in textbook order
A table of results printed at the back of a book
optionExplain: Right: guessing and testing while a result is still being found is mathematics in the making.
A polished proof is the first face.
A textbook list is the deductive picture.
A table of results has no sign of how they were found.
questions.explain: The second face shows the process of finding, not only the finished product.
questions.rule: Making shows guesses and tests.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: Sort each item by the face of mathematics it shows.

items.t: A proof set out as a systematic chain of deductions
A theorem stated with its proof in textbook order
A rigorous derivation from agreed starting points
Trying small cases to see what might be true
Guessing a result from examples before proving it
A false start dropped in favour of a better idea

questions.explain: Systematic proof is the Euclidean face. Trying cases, guessing and dropping false starts are the work of mathematics being invented.
questions.rule: Euclid's face is finished; the other is in the making.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: True or false: Polya says the experimental face of mathematics replaces its Euclidean face.
questions.explain: He says mathematics is the rigorous science of Euclid but also something else, so the faces sit side by side.
questions.rule: Both faces are real.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the First Printing
questions.q: A student sees only polished proofs in class. What does Polya say is new about showing her mathematics in the making?
options: The experimental face itself is new, since older mathematicians used only deduction
Both faces are as old as mathematics, but showing the second to students, teachers and the public in this manner is new
Nothing is new, since textbooks have long taught how results are invented
Only the word heuristic is new, and the manner of presenting is as old as Euclid
optionExplain: Polya says both aspects are as old as mathematics itself.
Right: the second aspect is as old as mathematics, but presenting it in this manner has not been done before.
He says it has never before been presented in quite this manner.
He claims the manner of presentation, not just the word, is new.
questions.explain: Polya separates the age of the experimental face from the novelty of presenting it.
questions.rule: The face is old; presenting it is new.
questions.teaches: Both aspects of mathematics are as old as the science itself; what is new is presenting mathematics while it is being invented to the student, the teacher and the general public.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
questions.q: A book's seventh-printing preface announces the author's new work. What does that most likely tell a reader?
options: That the new work continues the line of thought begun in this book
That this book has been withdrawn in favour of the new work
That the earlier chapters were wrong and are now corrected
That the new work is on a subject unrelated to this book
optionExplain: Right: a later preface usually points forward to related work.
Withdrawal is not what a printing preface signals.
Correction would be stated as correction.
An unrelated work would not be mentioned in this preface.
questions.explain: A preface points a reader onward; the next card shows what Polya's does.
questions.rule: Read later prefaces to see how an author's later work continues the book.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
questions.q: Polya's later work is titled Mathematics and ____ Reasoning.
questions.explain: The title names plausible reasoning, which Polya's later volumes treat in the line of thinking begun in this book.
questions.rule: The later work is Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
questions.q: A cookbook's fifth-printing preface says the author has finished the promised volume on baking, carrying on the earlier approach. What follows?
options: The first cookbook is now out of date and should not be used
The author has changed to an unrelated method in the new volume
An earlier promise has been kept, and the new volume continues the same line of thinking
The promise was dropped and the baking volume replaces it
optionExplain: The preface says continues, not replaces.
The preface says the approach is carried on.
Right: this mirrors Polya's seventh preface.
The promise was fulfilled, not dropped.
questions.explain: Later prefaces tell you whether earlier promises were kept.
questions.rule: Prefaces track promises and sequels.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
questions.q: True or false: The seventh-printing preface says the promise made in the first preface has been kept in full.
questions.explain: The preface says Polya has succeeded in fulfilling the promise at least in part.
questions.rule: The promise was kept in part.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.section: From the Preface to the Seventh Printing
questions.q: A library lists Induction and Analogy in Mathematics and Patterns of Plausible Inference. How should a reader of this book place them?
options: As two earlier editions of this book under new titles
As the two volumes of Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning, which continue the line begun here
As translations of this book into other languages
As unrelated books by authors with similar names
optionExplain: Earlier editions would not continue the line of thought; they would be the same book.
Right: the preface says these two volumes make up the later work.
The preface does not call them translations.
They are by the same author and continue the same line.
questions.explain: The preface names the two volumes that make up the later work.
questions.rule: The sequel has two volumes.
questions.teaches: The later work consists of two volumes, Induction and Analogy in Mathematics and Patterns of Plausible Inference, which together make up Mathematics and Plausible Reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A school's future teachers learn to dislike a subject. What may happen when they teach it?
options: They will teach it better, since they know what pupils find dull
Their dislike has no effect, because pupils judge subjects for themselves
They will drop the subject from the curriculum
They may pass the dislike on to the next generation of pupils
optionExplain: Knowing what is dull does not lead to teaching it well in the preface's account.
The preface says the dislike is handed on.
The study speaks of teaching, not of dropping the subject.
Right: this is the cycle the preface describes.
questions.explain: The next card gives the study that Polya quotes and his hope.
questions.rule: Do not treat mathematics only as a necessary avenue to jobs; it may be fun and a vista of mental activity at the highest level.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: The study Polya quotes called mathematics the ____ popular subject in the curriculum.
questions.explain: The quoted study gives mathematics the dubious honour of being the least popular subject.
questions.rule: The study named mathematics the least popular subject.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A tutor dreads her algebra lessons and hurries through them. Which idea from the preface does this fit?
options: Mathematics is a necessary avenue to engineering jobs and nothing more
A teacher who has learned to detest a subject risks teaching pupils to detest it
Solving problems by one's own means brings the triumph of discovery
Mathematics has two faces, the Euclidean one and the one in the making
optionExplain: That claim concerns the usefulness of mathematics, not teaching.
Right: this is the cycle in the study Polya quotes.
This is from the first preface and is about discovery, not detest.
That claim concerns the nature of mathematics.
questions.explain: The cycle runs from teacher to pupil to future teacher.
questions.rule: Dislike spreads from teacher to pupil.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Polya denies that mathematics is a necessary avenue to engineering jobs and scientific knowledge.
questions.explain: He grants it is a necessary avenue and adds that it may also be fun and open a vista of mental activity.
questions.rule: Usefulness and fun go together.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A reader owns the first printing and sees the second edition. According to its preface, what has been added?
options: A new first part giving the Educational Testing Service study in full
A complete rewrite of the dictionary of heuristic
A new fourth part, Problems, Hints, Solutions, and a few minor improvements
A translation of the whole book into several languages
optionExplain: The study is only quoted in the preface.
The preface mentions only minor improvements elsewhere.
Right: the preface names one new part and a few small changes.
The preface does not mention translation.
questions.explain: The preface lists the second edition's additions.
questions.rule: The second edition adds Part IV.
questions.teaches: The second edition adds, besides a few minor improvements, a new fourth part titled Problems, Hints, Solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: You have a school problem to solve. Which order of work seems best?
options: Carry out the first calculation you think of, then look for a plan
Understand it, find a plan, carry the plan out, then examine the result
Plan first, then understand the problem, then check the plan
Look back first, then understand it, then carry out a calculation
optionExplain: Calculation first is tempting but a plan should come before it.
Right: this is the order the list sets out.
A plan needs an understood problem first.
Looking back needs a solution to look at.
questions.explain: The next card gives the four phases of the list.
questions.rule: Work in four phases: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, look back.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Put the four phases of the list in order.
items: Understanding the problem
Devising a plan
Carrying out the plan
Looking back
questions.explain: The list is headed First, Second, Third and Fourth in this order.
questions.rule: Understand, plan, carry out, look back.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Mia has finished a calculation and now tests her answer a second way. Which phase is she in?
options: Looking back, where she examines the solution obtained
Carrying out the plan, where she performs the steps
Devising a plan, where she seeks a connection
Understanding the problem, where she names its parts
optionExplain: Right: testing a finished answer belongs to the fourth phase.
The calculation is already done.
A plan was already made.
The problem was understood at the start.
questions.explain: Each phase has its own job; checking a finished solution is the last.
questions.rule: Checking the result is looking back.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Match each phase to a question that belongs to it.
pairs: Do you know a related problem?
questions.explain: Each phase asks its own questions: name the parts, find a connection, check the steps, check the result.
questions.rule: Each phase has its own questions.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Sam works a problem. Which of his moves break the order of the list? Select all that apply.
options: He starts calculating before he can say what is unknown
He reads the problem, then looks for a related problem
He stops as soon as he has a number, with no checking
He examines the result after carrying out the plan
optionExplain: Wrong: calculating comes after understanding and planning.
Fine: the second phase asks about related problems.
Wrong: the fourth phase, looking back, is skipped.
Fine: examining the result is the last phase.
questions.explain: He breaks the order by calculating before understanding and by skipping the last phase.
questions.rule: No phase is skipped.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A teacher addresses the list's questions to a student, using them properly. What may happen, according to the introduction?
options: They replace the student's thinking so he need not try
They help only the teacher, as a record for marking
Nothing, since the list is meant only for the solver himself
They may help the student solve his own problem
optionExplain: The list asks questions; it does not think for the student.
The introduction says the questions help the student.
The introduction says the same questions help either the solver or the student.
Right: the introduction says addressing the questions to a student may help him solve his problem.
questions.explain: The same questions work whether you ask yourself or a student.
questions.rule: Ask yourself or the student.
questions.teaches: Addressed properly to yourself the questions may help you solve your problem, and addressed to a student they may help him solve his.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Pens cost 40p each and you have 3 pounds. You want to know how many pens you can buy. What must you find?
options: The price of one pen
The 3 pounds you have
The number of pens
The change from the pens
optionExplain: The price is given in the problem.
The 3 pounds is given.
Right: the number of pens is what the question asks for.
Change is not asked for.
questions.explain: A good guess is fair. The card next names what the list calls the thing to find.
questions.rule: Before planning, name the unknown, the data and the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: The first question of the list's first phase asks: What is the ____?
questions.explain: Naming the unknown is the first step in understanding the problem.
questions.rule: Name the unknown first.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A ticket office sells adult tickets at 5 pounds and child tickets at 3 pounds. Four adults and some children paid 29 pounds in all. Which are the data?
options: The 5 pounds, the 3 pounds, the four adults and the 29 pounds total
The number of children, the 5 pounds and the 3 pounds
Only the 29 pounds total, because it is the final figure
The number of children and the 29 pounds total
optionExplain: Right: these are given. The unknown is the number of children.
The number of children is what you must find.
The prices and the number of adults are also given.
The number of children is not given; it is the unknown.
questions.explain: Data are what you are given; the unknown is what you must find.
questions.rule: Data are given, the unknown is asked.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A baker has 3 trays of 12 rolls and sells 20. How many remain? Sort each item.

items.t: 3 trays
12 rolls on each tray
20 rolls sold
The number of rolls remaining

questions.explain: The trays, the rolls per tray and the number sold are given. The number remaining is what you must find.
questions.rule: Given is data; asked is unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A problem says two numbers add to 10 and each is larger than 6. What does the list's question about the condition reveal?
options: The condition is redundant, since one statement can be dropped
The condition is insufficient, since more data are needed to fix the numbers
The condition is fine, since many pairs of numbers satisfy it
The condition is contradictory, since no pair of numbers satisfies it
optionExplain: Dropping a statement would not make the other satisfiable.
More data cannot help when no pair satisfies the condition.
No pair of numbers satisfies it.
Right: two numbers each larger than 6 would add to more than 12, so no pair adds to 10.
questions.explain: The list asks whether the condition can be satisfied at all, and whether it is sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory.
questions.rule: Ask if the condition can be satisfied.
questions.teaches: The list asks whether it is possible to satisfy the condition and whether the condition is sufficient to determine the unknown, or insufficient, redundant or contradictory.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A gardener wants to fence a rectangular plot of known area. Which suggestion from the list's first phase helps?
options: Look for a related problem solved before
Draw a figure and introduce suitable notation for the unknown length
Check the final answer by solving it a second way
Carry out the first calculation that comes to mind
optionExplain: That belongs to the second phase, devising a plan.
Right: the first phase also asks you to draw a figure and introduce suitable notation.
That belongs to the fourth phase, looking back.
That belongs to the third phase, carrying out the plan.
questions.explain: The first phase suggests a figure, notation and separating the parts of the condition.
questions.rule: Draw it and name it.
questions.teaches: The first phase also suggests drawing a figure, introducing suitable notation, and separating the parts of the condition so that you can write them down.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: You are stuck on a school problem. Which first move is the most promising?
options: Start again from the statement of the problem with a new pen colour
Ask whether you have met a similar problem and could use it
Wait for a flash of inspiration before writing anything
Pick the biggest numbers and combine them in any way
optionExplain: A fresh start with a new pen changes nothing in the thinking.
Right: the list asks for a connection to something you already know.
Waiting does not use what you know.
Combining numbers without a plan leaves out the unknown.
questions.explain: A good guess is fair. The next card gives the list's advice.
questions.rule: Look for a connection to a related problem you have solved, starting from the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: To find a familiar problem, the list says: look at the ____, and think of a familiar problem with a similar one.
questions.explain: The list suggests starting from the unknown.
questions.rule: Start from the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: You must find the area of an L-shaped floor. Which step follows the list?
options: Recall how the area of a rectangle was found and see if that method fits the parts
Measure the floor again, since the problem cannot be solved otherwise
Guess a number and hope to correct it later
Check the final answer before computing anything
optionExplain: Right: a familiar problem with the same kind of unknown suggests a method.
Measuring again does not connect data and unknown.
Guessing has no plan behind it.
There is no answer yet to check.
questions.explain: Use a familiar problem with a similar unknown.
questions.rule: Use a familiar problem.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Sort each question by the list's phase it belongs to.

items.t: What are the data?
Is the condition sufficient to determine the unknown?
What is the unknown?
Have you seen it before?
Do you know a related problem?
Could you restate the problem?

questions.explain: Phase one asks what the problem contains. Phase two asks what connects it to what you know.
questions.rule: Phase one names; phase two connects.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: No familiar problem comes to mind. What does the list suggest next?
options: Repeat the first phase until a familiar problem appears
Choose the most general problem you can imagine, and nothing else
Drop the unknown and look only at the data
Try first a related problem, such as a more accessible, more general, more special or analogous one
optionExplain: Repeating names does not produce a connection.
The list names several kinds of related problem, not only the most general.
The unknown is the starting point of the search.
Right: the list names several kinds of related problem to try first.
questions.explain: If you cannot solve the problem, solve a related one first.
questions.rule: Try a related problem first.
questions.teaches: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, the list says to try first some related problem: a more accessible, more general, more special or analogous one, or a part of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A fair planner has a plan using the prices of juice and cake, but did not use the number of guests, which was given. What does the list suggest?
options: Accept the plan, since extra data are noise
Delete the number of guests from the problem
Ask whether all the data and the whole condition were used
Look back only after finishing the arithmetic
optionExplain: The list asks you to question unused data.
Deleting data changes the problem.
Right: the list asks whether you used all the data and the whole condition.
The check on data belongs to the plan phase.
questions.explain: An unused given is a prompt to question the plan.
questions.rule: Use all the data.
questions.teaches: At the end of the plan phase the list asks whether you used all the data, the whole condition and all the essential notions involved in the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A pupil gets 42 as an answer and hands in her work at once. What is she most likely missing?
options: A check of the result and the argument
A longer calculation, since short answers are doubtful
A new unknown, since the old one is already solved
A different teacher to mark the answer
optionExplain: Right: examining the result is the last phase of the list.
Length is no test of a result.
A new unknown is a different problem.
Marking is not checking.
questions.explain: A good guess is fair. The card next shows the last two phases of the list.
questions.rule: Check each step while you work, then examine the result and the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Carrying out your plan of the solution, ____ each step.
questions.explain: The list asks you to check each step as you carry out the plan.
questions.rule: Check each step.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Ben has finished solving a mixture problem. Which action belongs to looking back?
options: Naming the unknown, the data and the condition
Checking the result and the argument once more
Recalling a related problem from last term
Performing the first line of the calculation
optionExplain: That belongs to phase one.
Right: examining the solution obtained is the fourth phase.
That belongs to phase two.
That belongs to phase three.
questions.explain: Looking back follows the work, not precedes it.
questions.rule: After the work, check the result.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Sort each action by the phase it belongs to.

items.t: Checking that each step is correct as you write it
Asking whether you can prove a step is correct
Performing the calculation the plan calls for
Checking the result once the solution is complete
Examining the argument as a whole
Asking whether the result could help with another problem

questions.explain: Step checks belong to the work. Examining the finished result and argument belongs to looking back.
questions.rule: Steps in the work, whole in looking back.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: True or false: In the list, checking each step during the work removes the need for looking back.
questions.explain: Looking back is a separate fourth phase that examines the result and the argument after the work is done.
questions.rule: Looking back is still due.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A pupil has solved a puzzle and asks what else the list invites. Which question belongs to looking back?
options: What is the unknown?
Could you use the result or the method for some other problem?
Have you seen the same problem before?
Can you carry out the first step now?
optionExplain: That is a phase-one question.
Right: using the result or method elsewhere is part of looking back.
That is a phase-two question.
That is a phase-three question.
questions.explain: Looking back also asks you to derive the result differently or see it at a glance.
questions.rule: Look back for new uses.
questions.teaches: Looking back also asks whether you can derive the result differently, see it at a glance, and use the result or the method for some other problem.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: A new reader opens a short dictionary attached to a guide. How should she probably use it?
options: Read it quickly from A to Z in one sitting
Skip it, since a dictionary adds nothing to a guide
Look up articles when a point comes up in her own work
Memorise the titles of its articles in order
optionExplain: Speed reading skips the subtle points.
A dictionary can add background to the guide.
Right: a reference works best when a real question sends you to it.
Titles alone teach little.
questions.explain: A good guess is fair. The next card gives the book's four parts.
questions.rule: Read Part I, the dialogue and the problems as written, and consult the Dictionary when a point arises in your own work.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Match each part of the book to its description.
pairs: The list in practice, with examples
Part II, How to Solve It
A short dialogue between a teacher and a student
Part III, Short Dictionary of Heuristic
Problems, each followed by a hint and a solution
questions.explain: Each part has a different form: practice with examples, a dialogue, a dictionary and a set of problems.
questions.rule: Four parts, four forms.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: While solving, Ana wonders how the book uses the term heuristic. Where should she look?
options: Part II, the dialogue, which defines every term
Part IV, in the hint after each problem
Part I, in sections 18 to 20 only
The Dictionary, in its article with that title
optionExplain: The dialogue is not a glossary.
Hints are for problems, not for terms.
Sections 18 to 20 give more examples.
Right: the introduction says the term is explained in an article with that title.
questions.explain: Look terms up in the Dictionary.
questions.rule: The Dictionary explains terms.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: True or false: The Dictionary is meant to be read quickly from start to finish.
questions.explain: The introduction says it should not be read too quickly, because the text is condensed and subtle.
questions.rule: Do not rush the Dictionary.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: In Part I, where would a reader find the explanation of the list's main divisions and a first practical example?
options: Sections 6 to 17
Sections 1 to 5
Sections 18 to 20
Part II only
optionExplain: Right: sections 6 to 17 explain the main divisions and the first example.
Sections 1 to 5 discuss the purpose of the list.
Sections 18 to 20 add more examples.
Part II is a dialogue.
questions.explain: Part I has twenty sections in three groups.
questions.rule: Sections 1 to 5, 6 to 17, 18 to 20.
questions.teaches: Part I has twenty sections: sections 1 to 5 discuss the purpose of the list, sections 6 to 17 explain its main divisions and a first example, and sections 18 to 20 add more examples.

questions.unitTitle: Prefaces, the List and the Introduction
questions.q: Reading the Dictionary, whose point of view does the author mostly take?
options: A university examiner marking solutions
A person who is neither teacher nor student but anxious to solve a problem
A high school teacher only
A student only
optionExplain: The introduction does not name an examiner.
Right: the introduction says this is the point of view most of the time, especially in the third part.
The teacher's view predominates in the first part, not the third.
The student's view alone is not what the introduction names.
questions.explain: The student may be anyone studying mathematics and the teacher anyone interested in teaching it.
questions.rule: Mostly the problem solver's view.
questions.teaches: The student may be anyone studying mathematics and the teacher anyone interested in its teaching; the teacher's view predominates in the first part, but mostly, especially in the third part, the view is of a person anxious to solve a problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A pupil has stared at a problem for ten minutes without writing anything. What is the best thing for the teacher to do?
options: Work the whole problem on the board so the pupil sees how it goes
Leave the pupil entirely alone, since struggling alone teaches most
Ask a question or point to a step that the pupil could have thought of himself
Give the final answer and ask the pupil to find the method afterwards
optionExplain: It ends the stuck feeling, but leaves the pupil nothing to do.
It protects independence, but a pupil left with no help may make no progress at all.
Right: this keeps the pupil working while moving him on.
It saves time, but the pupil's own work is mostly taken away.
questions.explain: Good help sits between doing nothing and doing everything. The card next shows how the author describes it.
questions.rule: Help, but leave the work to the student.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: According to the author, the teacher should help so that the student keeps a reasonable share of the ____.
questions.explain: Help is measured by what it leaves: the student must still do a reasonable share of the work.
questions.rule: Leave the student a reasonable share of the work.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Tom is stuck finding the width of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and has an area of 40 square cm. Which reply fits the author?
options: What are you asked to find, and how are length, width and area connected?
Divide 40 by 8 and you will have the width, so write that down now
Keep trying by yourself, because I cannot say anything that would help
Here is a finished worked solution for you to copy into your book
optionExplain: Right: it is a natural question that Tom could have thought of, and it leaves the work to him.
This gives the step away, so nothing is left for Tom to find.
This leaves Tom with no help, and he may make no progress at all.
Copying a finished solution takes away the whole of the student's share.
questions.explain: The first reply points the way without doing the work. The others either do too much or too little.
questions.hint: Which reply could have occurred to Tom himself?
questions.rule: Offer a question the student could have asked himself.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Sort each teacher action: does it follow the author's advice on helping, or break it?

items.t: Asks the pupil what he is supposed to find
Does the whole problem on the board while the pupil watches
Says nothing and leaves the pupil alone for the whole lesson
Thinks about what the pupil is probably thinking, then asks a question he could have thought of
Points to a step lightly, so the pupil feels he found it himself
Hands over the finished answer to speed things up

questions.explain: Good help starts from the student's own state of mind and leaves him the work. Doing it all, or nothing at all, are the two ways to break the advice.
questions.rule: Neither too much nor too little.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: True or false: if a teacher steps in with the next step each time the pupil hesitates, more and more of the work is left to the pupil.
questions.explain: The author warns that if the teacher helps too much, nothing is left to the student. Each step handed over is a step the pupil no longer does.
questions.rule: Too much help leaves nothing for the student.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A student can do very little by himself. According to the author, what should the teacher still try to leave him?
options: A short summary of the solution to study later
At least some illusion of independent work
A shorter problem with the answer already filled in
Nothing: weak students need the teacher to carry the problem
optionExplain: A summary may help later, but the author is talking about the work of the moment.
Right: help is given discreetly and unobtrusively so that the student still feels he is working on his own.
An easier problem with its answer given again removes his share of the work.
The author does not say weak students should be carried; he asks for at least some independent work.
questions.explain: Even when the student can do little, the help should be discreet so that some feeling of independent work is kept.
questions.rule: Help discreetly so the student keeps some independent work.
questions.teaches: When a student can do little, the teacher should help discreetly and unobtrusively so that he keeps at least some illusion of independent work.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A parent has five minutes before dinner. A child is stuck on a sharing problem. Which approach fits the author?
options: Give the answer, since time is short and answers are what counts
Say the child must learn the hard way and walk off to the kitchen
Let the child copy the answer from the back of the book
Take a moment to see the child's case and ask one question the child could ask
optionExplain: It is quick, but it removes the child's share of the work.
Leaving the child with no help may mean no progress at all.
Copying the answer leaves nothing of the child's own work.
Right: the author says helping needs time, practice, devotion and sound principles, and a short question can still carry them.
questions.explain: Helping well is a task that demands time, practice and devotion. A single natural question is one way to fit it into a short moment.
questions.rule: Natural help takes understanding the student's case, not a lot of time.
questions.teaches: The author says that helping students is not quite easy: it demands time, practice, devotion and sound principles.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A pupil is stuck finding how many 40-seat buses are needed for 130 people. Which nudge directs attention to the right place?
options: Try harder and read the problem again out loud
What do you want to find?
Do you remember your times tables?
Why did you take this school subject?
optionExplain: Rereading may help, but it does not point attention anywhere in particular.
Right: it focuses the pupil on what the problem asks for.
The tables may matter later, but this does not direct attention to the problem's structure.
This is unrelated to the problem and may only discourage.
questions.explain: A good nudge points to a specific part of the problem. The card next shows how the author uses such questions.
questions.rule: Aim the question at part of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Different wordings such as What do you want to find? all aim to focus the student's attention on the ____.
questions.explain: What is required?, What do you want to find? and What are you supposed to seek? are variations of What is the unknown?
questions.rule: Reword freely: the aim stays the same.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: In the bus problem (130 people, 40 seats per bus), which is another way of asking What is the unknown?
options: What number are you supposed to seek?
What numbers are you given in the problem?
Could you check your arithmetic again?
Is there a simpler problem with smaller numbers?
optionExplain: Right: it points at the number to be found, the same attention as What is the unknown?
This points at the data, which is a different question of the list.
Checking arithmetic comes later and does not point at the unknown.
This is a different suggestion about another problem, not a rewording.
questions.explain: Rewording keeps the target: the unknown, here the number of buses.
questions.rule: A rewording keeps the same target.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Sort each question or suggestion: does it aim at the unknown, or is it another question of the list?

items.t: What are you supposed to seek?
What are the data?
Look at the unknown!
What is the condition?
What is required?
What do you want to find?

questions.explain: Four are variations that focus attention on the unknown. What are the data? and What is the condition? are separate questions of the list that point elsewhere.
questions.rule: Same aim, different words; different aim, different question.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, changing the wording of a question changes the mental operation it provokes.
questions.explain: The author varies the words of a question, and also replaces a question by a suggestion, while the effect, focusing attention on the unknown, stays the same.
questions.rule: The operation matters, not the wording.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A reader who sees the action behind each suggestion finds the list names indirectly what, and in which order?
options: Topics of mathematics, in the order a school course teaches them
Problems from easy to hard, so that each exercise prepares the next
Mental operations typically useful for solving problems, in the order they are most likely to occur
Rules that guarantee a solution, in the order the author tested them
optionExplain: The list is not a table of contents of the subject; it is about how to think about problems.
The list is not a ranking of problems; it concerns the solver's operations.
Right: the list indirectly enumerates useful mental operations, in the order they are most likely to occur.
The author calls them typically helpful, not guaranteed, and does not describe testing them in this section.
questions.explain: Behind each question or suggestion stands an action, and the list arranges these actions roughly in the order a solver is likely to need them.
questions.rule: Read the list as a sequence of useful actions.
questions.teaches: Behind the questions and suggestions the list enumerates, indirectly, mental operations typically useful for solving problems, listed in the order in which they are most likely to occur.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Sam works alone on a puzzle with no teacher present. According to the author, what can he do with the teacher's list?
options: Nothing, since the list only works as a dialogue with a teacher
Use it only after a teacher has approved each question for him
Use it as a problem-solver, since it is equally useful to someone working by himself
Use it only for school subjects, not for puzzles
optionExplain: It was gathered for discussing problems with students, but the author says it is no less useful alone.
The list needs no approval; the author recommends it to the solver working alone.
Right: the author says the list is equally useful to the problem-solver who works by himself.
The author applies the list to all sorts of problems, including puzzles.
questions.explain: The questions can be put to oneself, so the list serves a solver with no teacher.
questions.rule: Put the questions to yourself.
questions.teaches: The list is equally useful to the problem-solver who works by himself, not only to a teacher.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Which best describes the list's question about the unknown?
options: Simple and natural, yet usable on problems of every subject
A trick for geometry that only experts use
A rule that works on puzzles but not on serious problems
A deep question that needs advanced training to understand
optionExplain: Right: it is general in scope but plain in sense.
It is not tied to geometry or to experts.
The author says it applies to serious problems and mere puzzles alike.
The author says the questions are natural and simple, not technical.
questions.explain: The questions are plain and broad. The card next explains why the author says so.
questions.rule: Plain in sense, broad in use.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: The questions of the list are general, but except for that they are natural, simple, obvious and proceed from plain ____.
questions.explain: The author calls them plain common sense stated in general terms.
questions.rule: General words for plain common sense.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: Which of these problems could the list's question about the unknown help with, according to the author? Select all that apply.
options: Finding the width of a rectangle from its area and length
Working out how to split a restaurant bill among friends
Solving a riddle about the ages of two cousins
Proving that the sum of two even numbers is even
optionExplain: It is a problem to find, so the question applies.
A practical, non-mathematical problem is no obstacle; subject does not matter.
A puzzle is still a problem to find with an unknown.
Wrong: this is a problem to prove, and some questions of the list apply only to problems to find.
questions.explain: The restriction is the kind of problem, not the subject. Problems to prove need different questions.
questions.rule: Subject matter is no limit; kind of problem is.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A student says: Look at the unknown is too obvious to be useful. Which reply fits the author?
options: Agreed: advice that obvious adds nothing, so the list can be skipped altogether
It looks obvious, but works only on the one kind of problem it was written for
It is obvious by design: it states in general words what a serious solver does anyway
It is obvious only to the teacher, and a student would never think of it alone
optionExplain: It sounds fair, but the author says the questions are obvious and still on the right track, since they state in general terms what a person with common sense does.
It is wrongly narrow: the author stresses that the questions suit all subject matter.
Right: the list expresses in general terms the conduct that comes naturally to a serious solver.
The author says the questions are natural enough to have occurred to the student himself.
questions.explain: The question is plain common sense in general terms. That it is obvious is why it comes naturally, not a defect.
questions.rule: Obvious does not mean useless.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: True or false: the list's question about the unknown can be applied unchanged to a problem to prove.
questions.explain: Certain questions of the list apply to problems to find only, not to problems to prove, which need different questions.
questions.rule: Problems to prove need different questions.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.q: A classmate solves problems well but cannot say how. What does the list try to do for such a person's way of working?
options: Replace it, since a method that cannot be stated is probably wrong
Put it into general words, which the person usually does not do and perhaps cannot
Prove it correct, so the classmate may keep using it
Hide it, so the method stays as private as it was
optionExplain: The author thinks such behaviour is right, only unspoken.
Right: the person who behaves the right way usually does not care to put it in words, perhaps cannot; the list tries to.
Proof is not the aim; the list expresses conduct in words.
The list is about stating, not hiding.
questions.explain: Good conduct is often unspoken. The list states it in general terms so that others can use it too.
questions.rule: The list states in words what good solvers do by habit.
questions.teaches: A person who behaves the right way usually does not put his behaviour into clear words and perhaps cannot; the list tries to do so.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: How is a person most likely to become good at solving problems?
options: By memorising a list of rules until they can be recited
By watching others solve problems and then practising solving them
By waiting for flashes of insight, which cannot be trained
By reading about the subject without trying problems
optionExplain: Recitation gives words but not the skill.
Right: the author compares it to learning to swim, by imitation and practice.
Insight may come, but the author says the skill can be developed.
Reading is not practice; the skill needs doing.
questions.explain: Skills grow by doing. The card next gives the author's comparison.
questions.rule: Skills grow by imitation and practice.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: We acquire any practical skill by imitation and ____.
questions.explain: The author says solving problems is a practical skill, acquired by imitation and practice.
questions.rule: Imitate, then practise.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: Which plan helps a student make the list's question about the unknown their own, as the author would see it?
options: Memorise the question from a printed list and be tested on it
Hear it once in a lecture, then expect it to be remembered
See it asked by the teacher on many problems, then try asking it on their own
Wait until a problem is hard and then hope that the question comes up
optionExplain: This gives words without the action behind them.
One hearing gives no practice, and practice is how the skill is built.
Right: repeated use lets the student notice the question and ask it himself.
Waiting gives no imitation and no practice.
questions.explain: A question that proves helpful again and again is noticed, and asking it repeatedly leads to success and to real assimilation.
questions.rule: See it often, then use it often.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: A pupil solves a problem after the teacher's question. How are the two aims of the teacher connected, according to the author?
options: Solving the problem at hand adds a little to the student's ability to solve problems
They are unrelated: the first helps now and the second helps only later
The second aim is met only if the student fails at the problem first
Only the first aim matters, since ability cannot be developed
optionExplain: Right: the author says the two aims are closely connected because success adds a little to ability.
The author says they are closely connected, not separate.
Failing is not required; success itself adds to the ability.
The author takes development of ability as a real second aim.
questions.explain: A success on the present problem is also a small step toward the second aim.
questions.rule: Each success builds the skill a little.
questions.teaches: The two aims are closely connected: if the student succeeds in solving the problem at hand, he adds a little to his ability to solve problems.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: Mia's teacher asks about the unknown in five different problems, and it helps each time. What does the author expect?
options: She will find the question tiresome and ignore it in future
She will rely on the teacher to ask it every time
She will remember the words but not the use of the question
She will notice it and ask it herself in a similar situation
optionExplain: Nothing in the author's account says repetition breeds tiredness.
The aim is the opposite: that the student puts the question to himself.
Success in using it is how the student discovers the right use.
Right: a repeatedly helpful question will scarcely fail to be noticed, and the student will be induced to ask it by himself.
questions.explain: Repetition of a helpful general question leads the student to ask it himself, and success shows him how to use it.
questions.rule: Repeated helpful questions get noticed.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: Sort each teacher habit: does it fit the author's way of building the skill, or not?

items.t: Puts the list's questions to students whenever it is natural to do so
Hands out the list to be memorised, with no practice on problems
Gives students plenty of opportunity to imitate and practise
Tries to instil some interest for problems in the students
Solves problems silently at the board so as not to confuse anyone
Asks the same question after every line, natural or not

questions.explain: The author wants natural, repeated use, with interest and opportunity for imitation and practice. Silent solutions, rote lists and forced questions do not fit.
questions.rule: Interest, imitation and practice, in natural use.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Purpose
questions.section: Teacher and student. Imitation and practice
questions.q: A club leader solves a puzzle in front of children. What does the author advise beyond reaching the answer?
options: Work in silence, so that the answer comes out clean and quick
Say the answer first and then explain the working in full afterwards
Dramatize her ideas a little and put to herself the questions she uses to help them
Skip the thinking and only show the final tidy written working
optionExplain: Silence hides the questions the children need to imitate.
Starting from the answer hides how it was found.
Right: she puts to herself the same questions, so the children can imitate and, in time, discover their use.
Tidy working shows no thinking to imitate.
questions.explain: Showing the questions in use gives the children something to imitate. Learning to use them is worth more than any one fact.
questions.rule: Solve aloud and show the questions.
questions.teaches: When the teacher solves a problem before the class, he should dramatize his ideas a little; the student then acquires something more important than the knowledge of any particular mathematical fact.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil is asked how many 50 cm tiles cover a 3 m by 2 m floor. Which description fits good work from start to finish?
options: Pick a likely operation straight away, do the arithmetic, then write down whatever number results
Do the arithmetic first, then work out what the numbers were supposed to mean
See what is asked, think how the sizes link, do the arithmetic, then review the answer
Guess a number, then adjust it until a teacher says the answer is right
optionExplain: A common habit, but it skips both the understanding and the review.
It reverses the order: the meaning of the numbers has to come first.
Right: this is understanding, planning, carrying out and looking back, the order the card names.
It leaves the solver's own reasoning out of the work altogether.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next names the four phases and why each has a place.
questions.rule: Know what the work consists of before you start it.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Put the four phases of solving a problem in the order the author gives them.
items: Understand the problem
Devise a plan
Carry out the plan
Look back at the solution
questions.explain: The author lists understanding first, then planning, then carrying out, and finally looking back to review and discuss the completed solution.
questions.rule: Understand, plan, carry out, look back.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Priya has found that 24 sweets shared among 6 children is 4 each, and now asks if the result seems sensible. Which phase is she in?
options: Looking back, because she reviews a finished solution
Understanding, because she is rereading what was asked
Devising a plan, because she is picking a method
Carrying out the plan, because she is still computing
optionExplain: Right: reviewing a completed solution is the fourth phase.
Understanding comes first, before any solution exists to review.
A method has already been chosen and used; the answer 4 is in hand.
The computing is done; she is now checking what came out.
questions.explain: The fourth phase is the review of a completed solution.
questions.rule: Reviewing a finished answer is phase four.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author says our view of a problem is likely to be complete when we begin and stays the same until the solution.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: our conception is rather incomplete at the start, and our outlook is different after progress and again near the solution.
questions.rule: Expect your view of the problem to change as you work.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which reason does the author give for distinguishing four phases?
options: They fix a single route that every solver must follow in order without ever leaving it
They separate problems into four kinds that need four kinds of teacher
They show that only the third phase involves real mathematical work
They let the questions and suggestions of his list be grouped conveniently
optionExplain: The author expects us to change our point of view repeatedly, so no route is fixed.
The phases are stages of work on one problem, not kinds of problem.
He says the plan is the main achievement; carrying out mainly needs patience.
Right: the author says he distinguishes the phases in order to group the questions conveniently.
questions.explain: The phases are an organising device for the questions, not a rigid route.
questions.rule: The phases organise the questions.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A cook must scale a stew for 12 instead of 4. In which phase would she see how the quantity wanted is linked to the quantities given?
options: The first, because understanding the problem means finding the answer at once
The second, devising a plan, where the connections are worked out
The third, because the links appear only while computing
The fourth, because links are found when tasting the result
optionExplain: Understanding is seeing what is required, not yet the route to it.
Right: the second phase is about seeing how the various items connect, how the unknown links to the data.
By the third phase the connection should already be seen, so the details can be filled in.
Looking back may reveal more links, but the first plan is made earlier.
questions.explain: In the second phase we see how the items are connected and how the unknown is linked to the data, in order to get the idea of a solution.
questions.rule: Phase two links the unknown to the data.
questions.teaches: The second phase is where we see how the unknown is linked to the data in order to obtain the idea of the solution.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil reads a word problem and at once starts adding every number in it. What is the main risk?
options: The arithmetic will be slower than if she had stopped to make a plan first
Effort goes into details of a problem not yet understood
The teacher will mark the working as untidy
Addition is a weaker operation than multiplication
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue; the effort may be aimed at the wrong thing.
Right: working before understanding is where the author sees the worst outcome.
Tidiness is not the concern in the author's warning.
The operation is not the point; the missing understanding is.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next explains what each phase protects.
questions.rule: Understanding comes before computing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: According to the author, the worst may happen if the student starts computations without having ____ the problem.
questions.explain: The author calls it the worst case when computations or constructions are begun with no understanding of the problem.
questions.rule: Understand what is asked before you compute.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Lena finishes a ticket-price problem, writes the result and closes her book without rereading it. What does the author say she may lose?
options: Her right to claim the answer, since unreviewed answers do not count
The ability to compute, since computing needs a review to be learned
Nothing at all, since a correct answer needs no further attention
Some of the best effects of the work that reviewing would give
optionExplain: The author does not say an unreviewed answer is invalid.
Computing skill is not what the review mainly builds.
He says the review adds value even when the answer is already correct.
Right: failing to reexamine and reconsider the finished solution can cost some of the best effects.
questions.explain: Looking back consolidates knowledge and builds problem-solving ability.
questions.rule: Do not close the book on a solution without a look back.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author calls it undesirable when a student has a lucky bright idea and blurts out the solution.
questions.explain: He calls such lucky ideas most desirable. What he warns against is leaving out phases without having a good idea.
questions.rule: A good idea may replace the phases; its absence may not.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sort each habit: does it leave out a phase without a good idea, or follow the author's advice?

items.t: Begins calculating before saying what is asked
Carries out detailed work with no sort of plan
Closes the book as soon as an answer appears
Checks every step while carrying out the plan
Restates the problem before planning
Rechecks the result and tries to use it elsewhere

questions.explain: The first three skip understanding, planning or looking back. The last three keep a phase alive.
questions.rule: Each phase protects something; skipping one needs a good idea to excuse it.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil budgeting a trip fills pages with careful sums before spotting how costs link to the money available. According to the author, how useful is that detail?
options: Generally useless without the main connection or a sort of plan
Useful, because careful sums always lead to a plan if there are enough of them
Useful, because detail work replaces the need to understand
Harmful only when the sums contain arithmetic mistakes
optionExplain: Right: carrying out details without having seen the main connection is generally useless.
A plan has to be conceived; it does not arrive from sums alone.
Understanding cannot be replaced by detailed work.
The sums are wasted even when they are correct, if no plan guides them.
questions.explain: Detail work needs a plan; the details only matter once the main connection is seen.
questions.rule: Without the main connection, details are generally useless.
questions.teaches: It is generally useless to carry out details without having seen the main connection, or having made a sort of plan.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil works hard on a problem she has not understood. What is the best description of her effort?
options: Admirable, since effort alone will make understanding follow in time
Neutral, since the question will become clear after working
Foolish, since it answers a question that is not yet understood
Efficient, since a sum done early saves time later
optionExplain: Effort helps only if aimed at the right question.
Understanding is a precondition, not a by-product.
Right: the author calls it foolish to answer a question you do not understand.
The time saved is lost if the work answers the wrong question.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Understand first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The student should understand the problem, and he should also ____ its solution.
questions.explain: The author asks for desire as well as understanding: it is sad to work for an end you do not desire.
questions.rule: Understanding and desire both matter.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A class loses interest in a problem set that is much too hard. According to the author, where might the fault lie?
options: Wholly in the pupils, who ought to want to solve every problem they are given
In the teacher's voice, which is the only cause of boredom
Nowhere, because interest has no connection with solving
In the choice of problem, which should be not too hard and not too easy
optionExplain: The author says it is not always the student's fault.
Presentation matters, but the choice of problem matters too.
He treats interest as important to the work.
Right: the problem should be well chosen, natural and interesting, neither too difficult nor too easy.
questions.explain: A badly chosen problem can cause lack of interest.
questions.rule: Choose problems that are not too hard and not too easy.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a student's lack of interest can be due to a badly chosen problem.
questions.explain: He says that lack of understanding or interest is not always the student's fault; the problem should be well chosen.
questions.rule: Interest depends on the problem as well as the pupil.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil says she understands a problem but sees no reason to solve it. Which statement fits the author?
options: She is ready to start, because understanding is the only requirement for solving
Understanding alone is not enough; the desire for the solution matters too
She is wrong, because understanding cannot exist without desire
She should hide her feeling, since interest is a private matter
optionExplain: He adds desire to understanding as a second requirement.
Right: the author wants the student to desire the solution as well as understand it.
He treats them as two things; a person can have one without the other.
He wants the teacher to help create interest, not hide the lack.
questions.explain: Understanding and desire are two requirements.
questions.rule: Aim for both understanding and desire.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In a club, the leader sets a puzzle and pupils shrug. Which move fits the author's advice?
options: Insist they start computing so interest can arise from effort
Give a harder puzzle, since difficulty always raises interest
Present the puzzle in a natural, interesting way, with time for it
Blame the pupils for lacking motivation and move on to the next problem
optionExplain: Working without understanding or desire is the sad case he describes.
The problem should be not too difficult and not too easy.
Right: the author asks for time for a natural and interesting presentation.
He says lack of interest is not always the pupil's fault.
questions.explain: Interest can be encouraged by the choice and presentation of the problem.
questions.rule: A teacher can help create interest.
questions.teaches: Some time should be allowed for a natural and interesting presentation of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A shop sells pens at 40 pence each. A pupil must say what a pack of 6 costs. What is the unknown here?
options: The cost of a pack of 6 pens
The price of one pen, 40 pence
The number of pens in the pack, 6
The shop where the pens are sold
optionExplain: Right: the unknown is what we are asked to find, the cost of the pack.
That price is given, so it is a datum, not what is sought.
The 6 is also given in the problem.
The shop is only the setting.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next defines the three principal parts.
questions.rule: The unknown is what is sought.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The principal parts of a problem are the unknown, the data and the ____.
questions.explain: The author names the unknown, the data and the condition as the principal parts a student should point out.
questions.rule: Name unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sofia must find the width of a rectangular garden 12 m long when its area is 60 square metres. Which line states the data?
options: The width of the garden, which must be found
The idea that area equals length times width, alone
The length 12 m and the area 60 square metres
The word garden and the metres used
optionExplain: The width is the unknown.
The link between length, width and area is the condition, not the data.
Right: the length and the area are what is given.
The setting and unit are not the principal parts.
questions.explain: The data are the given quantities.
questions.rule: Data are what you are given.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Match each part of the garden problem (length 12 m, area 60 square metres, width wanted) to its name.
pairs: The length 12 m and the area 60 square metres
Length times width gives the area
questions.explain: The width is what is sought, the two numbers are given, and the relation between width, length and area links them.
questions.rule: Unknown sought, data given, condition links them.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: For the garden above, a pupil says the condition is 60. What is wrong with that?
options: 60 is a datum; the condition is the link between length, width and area
Nothing is wrong; the condition is whichever number in the problem is largest
60 is the unknown, since it is the final number we see
The condition is the pupil's choice of unit, metres
optionExplain: Right: the condition links the unknown to the data; 60 is a given quantity.
The condition is a relation, not a size.
The area is given, so it is not the unknown.
Units may appear in a statement, but they are not the condition.
questions.explain: The condition connects the unknown with the data.
questions.rule: The condition is the link, not a number.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil can repeat a train problem only by reading it word for word. What does the author suggest about her understanding?
options: Reading it word for word is the best available sign of understanding
Understanding can only be judged after the final answer has been found
Fluency is unimportant when the unknown can be guessed
She should state it fluently and point out its principal parts
optionExplain: Reciting is different from stating it fluently and pointing out the parts.
The check comes at the start, before a plan.
Fluent statement and the three parts are the author's check.
Right: the teacher checks by asking for a fluent restatement and the principal parts.
questions.explain: A fluent restatement plus naming the principal parts is the teacher's check.
questions.rule: State it fluently and name the parts.
questions.teaches: The teacher checks understanding of the verbal statement by asking the student to repeat it; he should be able to state it fluently.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil must find how far up a wall a 5 m ladder reaches when its foot is 3 m from the wall. What helps before computing?
options: Writing down the answer from memory of a similar problem
A sketch with the unknown and the given lengths marked on it
Rereading the numbers aloud over and over until one of them stands out
Starting with the largest number and adding the rest
optionExplain: Recall may help later, but it does not show the structure of this problem.
Right: a figure with unknown and data marked helps study the principal parts.
Repetition alone does not show how the parts are connected.
The size of a number says nothing about its role.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next explains what the figure and letters do.
questions.rule: Sketch the problem before computing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: If there is a figure connected with the problem, the student should ____ a figure and point out on it the unknown and the data.
questions.explain: The author asks the student to draw the figure and point out the unknown and the data on it.
questions.rule: Draw the figure and mark the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Three friends, Ann, Ben and Cy, have ages that must be found from clues. Which notation follows the author's advice?
options: Use the same letter x for every age so that nothing is mixed up
Use a different letter for each age, such as a, b and c
Use no letters at all until the final answer has been found
Use letters picked at random so that they cannot bias the thinking
optionExplain: One letter for three different quantities loses the difference between them.
Right: separate letters let each object be named and considered.
Names help when they are needed; waiting until the end gives no help.
Suitable signs are chosen with attention to the objects, not at random.
questions.explain: Choose signs that match the objects they stand for.
questions.rule: Suitable notation names each object.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, choosing signs carefully obliges the student to consider the objects the signs will name.
questions.explain: This is his reason for devoting attention to the choice of signs.
questions.rule: Choosing a name makes you think about the thing named.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A problem asks which weekday follows 100 days from a Monday and there is no figure to draw. What follows from the advice?
options: The advice stops entirely, since figures and names go together in every problem
A figure must still be invented so that the advice can be applied
The problem should be thrown out as unsuited to the four phases
No figure is needed, but names may still be introduced if they are necessary
optionExplain: The two parts of the advice are separate conditions.
The advice says a figure is drawn if there is one connected with the problem.
The phases suit any problem; only the tools differ.
Right: the advice speaks of a figure connected with the problem and of names where necessary.
questions.explain: Our reading: the advice to draw applies only where a figure is connected with the problem.
questions.rule: Draw when there is something to draw.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil must find the brace across a rectangular shelf unit with length, width and height given. Which labelling matches the book's dialogue?
options: x for the unknown brace, and a, b, c for the three given measures
One letter for the brace and one letter for all three given measures
x for the length, with every other quantity left without a letter
A different letter for every pencil mark in the sketch
optionExplain: Right: the book's dialogue lets x stand for the unknown and a, b, c for length, width and height.
The three measures differ, so one letter would hide that.
The unknown is the quantity to be sought and deserves a letter.
Letters go on the objects of the problem, not on every mark.
questions.explain: The book's classroom dialogue uses x for the unknown and a, b, c for length, width and height of the box.
questions.rule: One letter for the unknown, one for each datum.
questions.teaches: In the book's example the unknown is called x and the length, width and height are called a, b and c.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Before solving, a teacher asks whether the condition can be satisfied. Which reply is fair at this early stage?
options: A complete proof that a solution exists, written out in full
A refusal to answer until the whole solution is finished
A first guess such as: I think so, but I am not sure yet
A statement that the question should only be asked after the plan
optionExplain: A proof is more than the early stage calls for.
Waiting for the finished solution defeats the purpose of the question.
Right: a provisional answer is all that is asked.
The question belongs to the first phase, not to the planning.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next says what kind of answer the question wants.
questions.rule: A provisional answer is enough.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: At the preparatory stage we do not expect a definitive answer to this question, only a ____ answer, a guess.
questions.explain: The author says that a provisional answer, a guess, is all that is expected.
questions.rule: Early answers are provisional.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Marco is asked for three whole numbers adding to 10, each larger than 4. Which first response follows the advice?
options: Certainly yes: the problem would not have been set to the class otherwise
I will not answer until I have tried every possible triple
The question is not allowed until the plan has been made
Probably not: three numbers above 4 would add up to at least 15
optionExplain: A problem being set does not show that its condition can be met.
A full search is far more than a provisional guess.
The question belongs to the early stage of understanding.
Right: a quick provisional answer with a reason, held open for later checking.
