questions.explain: Three whole numbers larger than 4 are each at least 5, and 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, more than 10.
questions.rule: Give a quick guess with its reason.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author expects a definitive answer to this question in the preparatory stage.
questions.explain: He says that we should expect only a provisional answer, a guess, at this stage.
questions.rule: Do not demand certainty yet.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In which phase does the author place the question whether the condition can be satisfied?
options: Devising a plan, once related problems have been found
Understanding the problem, in the preparatory stage
Carrying out the plan, as each step is checked
Looking back, when the result is compared with the problem
optionExplain: Planning comes later and uses what understanding revealed.
Right: it is useful in the preparatory stage of understanding.
Checking steps is a different question.
Looking back reviews the finished solution.
questions.explain: The question is part of understanding the problem.
questions.rule: It belongs to understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil's first quick reading of a problem is a time to become familiar with it. What names that stage in the author's Part II?
options: Working for better understanding, the second of two stages within understanding
Devising a plan, which comes after understanding
Getting acquainted, the first of two stages within understanding
Looking back, which comes after the solution
optionExplain: The second stage follows once the first acquaintance has been made.
Planning is a separate phase after understanding.
Right: Part II divides understanding into getting acquainted and working for better understanding.
Looking back needs a finished solution first.
questions.explain: In Part II understanding is subdivided into two stages, getting acquainted and working for better understanding.
questions.rule: Understanding has two stages in Part II.
questions.teaches: Part II divides understanding the problem into two stages: getting acquainted and working for better understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A teacher wants pupils to care about finding the diagonal of a box with known length, width and height. What helps most?
options: Point to the classroom as a box whose diagonal they can estimate
Hand them a long list of box problems to copy out and then memorise
Tell them the formula before they meet the problem
Ask them to prove a theorem about every box
optionExplain: Right: making the problem concrete makes it interesting.
Copying does not create understanding or interest.
Giving the formula takes away the work of the problem.
A theorem about all boxes is further from their experience.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next shows the author's way.
questions.rule: Make the problem concrete.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the example the teacher makes the problem interesting by making it ____, using the classroom as the box.
questions.explain: The classroom is a box whose dimensions can be measured or estimated.
questions.rule: Concrete problems are easier to care about.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A class must find the straight distance across the hall floor from one corner to the opposite corner. Which first question follows the dialogue?
options: Could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras?
Is the answer a whole number of metres?
What is the unknown, and what are the data?
How many tiles does the hall floor have altogether?
optionExplain: That names the method before the pupils understand the problem.
The size of the answer is a question for later.
Right: the dialogue begins with the unknown, the data and the condition.
Tiles are a different problem.
questions.explain: Opening questions ask about the principal parts.
questions.rule: Start with unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the box problem only length and width were given, with no height. What answer would the question about whether the condition is sufficient get?
options: No: without the height the box is not fixed, so no diagonal is determined
Yes: the diagonal depends only on length and width
Yes: any measure that is missing can be found later by luck or by guessing
No: a diagonal can only be found for a cube
optionExplain: Right: the box must be determined for the diagonal to be determined.
A taller box has a longer diagonal, so height matters.
Luck is not a method, and the data would still be incomplete.
The problem concerns any box whose three sizes are given.
questions.explain: In the book the pupils answer yes because a, b and c fix the box, and the box fixes its diagonal.
questions.rule: Check that the data fix the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author's box discussion goes well even with pupils who have not met the theorem of Pythagoras.
questions.explain: He says the pupils must be familiar with that theorem and some of its plane applications for the problem to be discussed profitably.
questions.rule: Check that pupils have the background the problem uses.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Pupils have little formal solid geometry. What may the teacher rely on, according to the author?
options: Their ability to prove every fact about solid figures
Their having already solved this very problem
Nothing at all, since solid geometry must be taught before anything else
Their unsophisticated familiarity with spatial relations
optionExplain: Proof is not what the discussion needs from them.
If they had solved it, no discussion would be needed.
He says little systematic knowledge of solids is enough.
Right: the author says the teacher may rely on this ordinary familiarity.
questions.explain: The author says the pupils may have very little systematic knowledge of solid geometry; ordinary familiarity with space is enough.
questions.rule: Everyday familiarity with space is enough here.
questions.teaches: The pupils may have very little systematic knowledge of solid geometry, since the teacher can rely on their unsophisticated familiarity with spatial relations.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: What does it mean to have a plan for a problem?
options: To have the final answer written down before starting
To know in outline which calculations or constructions give the unknown
To have the whole problem copied out neatly in a clean notebook
To have checked each number in the statement for possible mistakes first
optionExplain: Having the answer is the end of the work, not a plan for reaching it.
Right: this is the author's description of a plan.
Copying the statement is not a plan.
Checking numbers is part of understanding, not a plan.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's description.
questions.rule: A plan is a route to the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the solution of a problem, the main achievement is to conceive the idea of a ____.
questions.explain: The author calls the idea of a plan the main achievement in the solution of a problem.
questions.rule: The plan is the main achievement.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Mia must cost the paint for two walls 4 m wide and 2.5 m high at 3 pounds per square metre. Which statement shows she has a plan?
options: She notes that numbers such as 4, 2.5 and 3 are given
Find one wall's area, double it, then multiply by the price
She says the answer will be a fairly large number of pounds sterling
She writes the price of the paint at the top of the page
optionExplain: Listing the data is understanding, not planning.
Right: the steps lead from the data to the unknown. Two walls give 20 square metres, which at 3 pounds is 60 pounds.
A guess about size does not say how to find the number.
Writing a datum down does not give a route.
questions.explain: A plan names the steps that lead from the data to the unknown.
questions.rule: A plan names the steps to the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author says the idea of a plan may occur suddenly, in a flash, after trials that seemed unsuccessful.
questions.explain: He says the idea may emerge gradually, or may occur suddenly as a bright idea after hesitation.
questions.rule: Plans can come slowly or suddenly.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A teacher's questions have been well understood and seriously considered, but a pupil still has no idea. What does the author say?
options: The pupil has failed and the problem should be dropped
The questions work magic, so the pupil must have been pretending all along
The teacher should give the plan away so that the work can go on
They often help, but not always; the solver must explore other approaches
optionExplain: The author suggests exploring and varying the problem instead.
He says the questions cannot work magic at all.
The best the teacher can do is unobtrusive help toward the idea.
Right: the questions cannot work magic, and the solver must look for other approaches.
questions.explain: The questions very often help but cannot help always.
questions.rule: If the questions fail, look for other points of contact.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A new coach tells a team member struggling with a puzzle. What does the author advise a teacher to remember about the student's position?
options: His own earlier difficulties and successes in solving problems
That students never need any help at all to reach their own good ideas
That a formula can always be given in place of a plan
That teaching is easier than solving
optionExplain: Right: the author says the teacher should think of his own experience of difficulties and successes.
The author advises unobtrusive help, not none.
A formula does not replace the pupil's own plan.
The author does not say teaching is easier than solving.
questions.explain: To see the student's position, the teacher should recall his own difficulties and successes in solving problems.
questions.rule: Remember your own struggles.
questions.teaches: To see the student's position, the teacher should think of his own experience, of his difficulties and successes in solving problems.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil is stuck on a problem. Which first move is most helpful?
options: Wait quietly until an idea arrives by itself, without doing anything
Copy the numbers into a new layout
Ask whether she has met a related problem before
Ask for the final answer so as to work backwards
optionExplain: Ideas need material to work on; waiting alone supplies none.
Layout does not bring any knowledge to bear.
Right: past knowledge is the material of a good idea.
Working backwards from a given answer misses the pupil's own idea.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's question.
questions.rule: Ask what you already know.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The work of finding a plan often starts with the question: Do you know a ____ problem?
questions.explain: The author says it is often appropriate to start with this question.
questions.rule: Do you know a related problem?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Kai must find the change from 20 pounds after buying 3 items. Which recollection follows the advice?
options: A story from his last holiday, about a very long train journey to the coast
The number of pages in his school notebook
A rule for spelling the word change
An earlier problem where he took several prices away from a sum of money
optionExplain: A story with no shared structure does not help.
The page count has no link to the problem.
Spelling is unrelated to the task.
Right: it shares the structure of the present problem.
questions.explain: A useful memory shares something essential with the problem.
questions.rule: Recall problems that share structure.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, a solver with no knowledge of a subject can still have a good idea about it.
questions.explain: He says it is hard to have a good idea with little knowledge and impossible with none.
questions.rule: Good ideas need knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which statements agree with the author's view of remembering and ideas? Select all that apply.
options: Remembering alone does not make a good idea
A good idea cannot occur without recalling some pertinent facts
Past solved problems can serve as material
Good ideas appear without any past experience
optionExplain: Right: he says mere remembering is not enough.
Right: pertinent facts must be recalled.
Right: formerly solved problems are part of the material.
Wrong: good ideas are based on past experience and acquired knowledge.
questions.explain: Remembering is needed but does not by itself produce the idea.
questions.rule: Knowledge is the material, not the house.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A student preparing to solve many kinds of problems asks what to collect as material. What does the author name?
options: Only the final answers to as many problems as possible
Solved problems and proved theorems he has already mastered
Only formulas, since they alone can be applied to new problems
Nothing, since materials appear during the solving
optionExplain: Answers alone do not give the methods used.
Right: the author names solved problems and proved theorems.
Formulas are only some of the material.
Material has to be gathered first.
questions.explain: The materials are relevant items of formerly acquired mathematical knowledge, such as formerly solved problems or proved theorems.
questions.rule: Solved problems and proved theorems are the material.
questions.teaches: The materials for solving a mathematical problem are relevant items of formerly acquired knowledge, such as formerly solved problems and proved theorems.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Many remembered problems share something with the one in hand. Which feature best picks out the useful ones?
options: They were set in the same lesson and the same week as this present one
They use the largest numbers in the book
The unknown, the thing to be found, is the same or similar
They were easy and quickly solved
optionExplain: A shared lesson is a weak link between the problems.
Size of numbers does not decide usefulness.
Right: the unknown is an essential common point.
Ease does not make a problem relevant.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's suggestion.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The author's suggestion for choosing a useful related problem: Look at the ____!
questions.explain: The suggestion is Look at the unknown, and think of a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Lily must find how many days a 12 kg bag of rice lasts at a fixed use per day. Which earlier problem is the best start?
options: One whose unknown was also a length of time
One that used the number 12 in its data
One set in a kitchen with the same sort of story as this one
One that she solved faster than any other
optionExplain: Right: a similar unknown makes the earlier problem promising.
A shared number is a coincidence, not a common essential point.
A shared setting is not what links the structure of problems.
Speed of solving says nothing about relevance.
questions.explain: Choose problems by their unknown, not by their numbers or setting.
questions.rule: Match the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The unknown of the present problem is the length of a fence. Sort earlier problems: promising by the unknown, or related only loosely.

items.t: A problem asking for the length of a path
A problem asking for the length of one side of a triangle
A problem with the same story but asking for a number of sheep
A problem with the same numbers but asking for a price
A problem from the same lesson asking for an angle
A problem asking for the length of a rope

questions.explain: Problems with a similar unknown, here a length, are promising. Shared story, numbers or lesson are loose links.
questions.rule: Sort by the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: if the unknown is the same, the earlier problem will certainly solve the present one without change.
questions.explain: A matching problem is a promising start; it must still be used, and may need some added element.
questions.rule: A lucky memory must be exploited.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has recalled a related problem solved before. What should he ask next, according to the author?
options: Why was the earlier problem so much easier than the present one?
Which of the two problems has the larger numbers?
Could you use it, and what would make its use possible?
Who set the earlier problem and in which year?
optionExplain: Comparing difficulty does not use the problem.
Number size does not help.
Right: we deserve our luck by exploiting it, perhaps with an auxiliary element.
Who set it is irrelevant.
questions.explain: After recalling a related problem the author asks whether you could use it.
questions.rule: Recalled problems are for use.
questions.teaches: Once a related problem has been recalled, the next question is whether it can be used, perhaps after introducing some auxiliary element.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil recalls nothing related and is stuck. Which move could still make progress?
options: Restate the problem, or solve an easier related problem first
Repeat the same attempt more slowly and more carefully until it works
Give up because no related problem exists
Pick a new problem with a different unknown
optionExplain: Right: varying the problem opens a new point of contact.
The same method will give the same stall.
A problem can be transformed to find related material.
A different problem is no longer the task.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's list.
questions.rule: Vary the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: The author's suggestion is to solve first a related problem, which may become an auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: Solve a related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sam cannot place as many 30 cm square tiles as possible on a 2 m by 1.2 m worktop. Which move varies the problem usefully?
options: Add up all the numbers in the statement
Wait for the tiles to be delivered before thinking about the worktop
Decide that tiles cannot be placed on worktops
First try a smaller worktop, 60 cm by 60 cm, and see what happens
optionExplain: Adding unrelated numbers does not vary the problem in a helpful way.
Waiting does not change the problem at all.
This abandons the problem rather than varying it.
Right: an easier special case is a way to vary the problem. (The real worktop takes 6 tiles by 4 whole tiles, which is 24.)
questions.explain: A special, easier case is a related problem to solve first.
questions.rule: Try an easier version first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author lists dropping a part of the condition as one of the ways to vary a problem.
questions.explain: He names generalization, specialization, use of analogy and dropping a part of the condition.
questions.rule: Dropping part of the condition is a means of variation.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which moves vary a problem in the author's sense? Select all that apply.
options: Restate the problem in other words
Drop a part of the condition
Use an analogous problem
Repeat the same failed method more slowly
Wait for the answer from a neighbour
optionExplain: Right: restating is the author's question 'Could you restate the problem?'
Right: dropping a part of the condition is on the list.
Right: analogy is another means.
Wrong: this repeats rather than changes the problem.
Wrong: this does not change the problem.
questions.explain: Variation transforms the problem; repetition does not.
questions.rule: Vary means change, not repeat.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A gardener cannot plan a path around a pond of odd shape. Which move fits the author's advice?
options: Insist that only the true pond will do and keep waiting for an idea
Solve first a related problem, such as a simple rectangular pond
Plant flowers at random and see what happens
Ask the neighbour to plan it with no further thought
optionExplain: Waiting does not change the problem.
Right: an auxiliary problem may bring the contact that is missing.
Random work is not a plan.
The solver's own ideas are the aim.
questions.explain: Variation of the problem may lead to some appropriate auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: A simpler related case can open the way.
questions.teaches: Variation of the problem may lead to an appropriate auxiliary problem, a related problem solved first to help with the proposed one.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: After many experiments with helper problems, a solver fears she has drifted from the task. Which question could help?
options: Is my helper problem more interesting than the original problem?
Have I used all the data and the whole condition?
Which helper problem has the largest numbers?
Can I finish the helper problem without any help?
optionExplain: Interest does not decide whether she is still solving the original task.
Right: this question leads back to the original problem.
Size of numbers is not the point.
Finishing the helper does not show it serves the original.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's question.
questions.rule: Return to the whole original problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The author asks: did you use all the ____, and did you use the whole condition?
questions.explain: These two questions bring a solver back to the original problem.
questions.rule: Use all the data and the whole condition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A taxi costs 3 pounds plus 2 per km, and a 5-pound tip is added. For a 6 km ride Lena answers 15 pounds. Which remark follows the advice?
options: Her answer is right because 15 is a round number
The tip is not data and may be dropped
The 6 km has not been used, and so 3 + 2 pounds is the whole cost of the ride
The 5-pound tip has not been used; with it the cost is 20 pounds
optionExplain: Roundness does not show that every datum was used.
A tip stated in the problem is part of the data.
The 6 km was used in 2 times 6.
Right: 3 + 2 times 6 gives 15, and the unused tip makes 20.
questions.explain: Check that every datum has a place in the solution.
questions.rule: An unused datum signals that something is missing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A box has length 8, width 6 and height 5, and its diagonal is wanted. Sort each plan: uses all the data, or leaves some out.

items.t: Combine 8, 6 and 5 in one expression
Use only 8 and 6, since two measures are enough
Take the face with sides 8 and 6, then bring in the 5
Add the largest two measures and ignore the third
Use only the biggest measure, 8
Work with all three measures one after another

questions.explain: A plan for a problem with three given measures should place each measure somewhere. Dropping the 5 leaves part of the data unused.
questions.rule: Every datum should appear in the plan.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has found a formula for a result. Where else, apart from wandering among helper problems, can the question about using all the data be asked?
options: When checking a result: do all the data appear in the formula?
Never; it applies only while wandering among helper problems and not later
Only before the problem has been understood
Only after the teacher has marked the work
optionExplain: Right: the author asks it again when checking a result.
The question has a second use, in looking back.
Before understanding the data are not yet known.
The check belongs to the solver, not the marker.
questions.explain: In looking back the author asks, of a formula, whether all the data appear in it.
questions.rule: The same question checks a result.
questions.teaches: The question about using all the data is asked again when checking a result: do all the data appear in the formula?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A teacher asks the class whether they know a related problem. There is only silence. What should the teacher do next?
options: Give the complete solution at once, to save time
Move on to the next problem, since nobody knows
Repeat it in a modified form, then ask more specific questions
Repeat the identical sentence louder and louder until someone answers
optionExplain: That takes the whole discovery away from the pupils.
The silence is a signal to help, not to move on.
Right: the author wants the teacher to be ready to meet silence with modified, more specific questions.
The same words will meet the same silence.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next shows the author's way.
questions.rule: Meet silence with a modified, more specific question.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Put the teacher's questions in the order of the box example, from general to explicit.
items: Do you know a related problem?
Do you know a problem having the same unknown?
Did you ever solve a problem whose unknown was a length?
Have you any triangle in your figure?
questions.explain: The teacher moves from the general question to the same unknown, then to a similar unknown, and finally to the triangle in the figure.
questions.rule: Go from general to specific.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A club leader asks whether anyone knows a problem related to a timetable puzzle. Nobody answers. Which next question follows the author's pattern?
options: Why did nobody take the trouble to prepare for this timetable puzzle?
Do you know the answer, as the leader does?
Which of you has the best timetable app?
Have you solved a problem whose unknown was a length of time?
optionExplain: Blame does not help the pupils to an idea.
The leader's answer would give the secret away.
A tool is not the same as a related problem.
Right: it moves from the general question to a more specific one about the unknown.
questions.explain: Narrow toward the unknown when a general question fails.
questions.rule: Narrow down to the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: in the example, each hint gives the pupils a little more help than the one before.
questions.explain: The teacher goes from the general question to the same unknown, then a similar unknown, then a triangle in the figure, each time more explicit.
questions.rule: Hints grow more explicit step by step.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Even a fairly explicit hint, such as asking whether there is a triangle in the figure, has not moved the class. What does the author say?
options: The hint was too explicit and has spoiled the problem for the class
The teacher should have more and more explicit hints ready
The class is unfit for the problem and should stop
The teacher should now write the plan on the board
optionExplain: He sees the hint as fairly explicit but possibly still not enough.
Right: the author says that a whole gamut of more explicit hints should be prepared.
He does not recommend giving up the problem.
Writing the plan removes the pupils' share of the work.
questions.explain: More explicit hints can follow, one after another.
questions.rule: Have several grades of hint ready.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A tutor's hints about a related problem and then about a problem with the same unknown both meet silence. What does the author's pattern suggest for the third hint?
options: A more explicit hint, such as asking about a problem with a similar unknown
The second hint repeated once more, slowly
The full solution, since two hints have failed
A change of subject to something the class already knows
optionExplain: Right: each hint gives a little more, from same unknown to similar unknown and finally to the triangle in the figure.
Identical words are likely to meet the same silence.
The full solution removes the pupils' share of the discovery.
Changing the subject abandons the problem the class has not yet been helped with.
questions.explain: The teacher must be prepared to repeat with some modification the questions which the students do not answer.
questions.rule: Modify the question, do not just repeat it.
questions.teaches: The hints grow from the same unknown to a similar unknown, and the teacher keeps a whole gamut of more explicit hints ready.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has drawn an extra triangle in the figure. Is she ready to compute?
options: Not yet; she should check the unknown is in it and its other parts findable
Yes; drawing a triangle always completes a plan, so computing can begin at once
Yes; computing will show what is needed
No; she must start again with a different figure
optionExplain: Right: the teacher checks that pupils see far enough ahead.
A good idea is not yet a plan.
Computing without seeing ahead risks wasted detail.
Nothing in the figure needs to be abandoned.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next shows the check.
questions.rule: See ahead before computing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Before encouraging pupils to go into actual calculations, the teacher should convince himself that they see sufficiently far ____.
questions.explain: The author wants the teacher to be sure the pupils see the way before they compute.
questions.rule: See ahead before calculating.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil splits a ribbon needed for a box into a top piece and a side piece. Which teacher question follows the author's check?
options: Is the ribbon the colour you wanted?
Can you give the final length now, without working?
Does it contain the unknown, and are the other pieces known or findable?
Would the whole box have been better without any ribbon on it at all, in your view?
optionExplain: Colour is not part of the plan.
Asking for the final answer skips the check.
Right: it asks whether the unknown is in the plan and whether the rest can be found.
It leaves the problem.
questions.explain: Check the unknown and the other parts.
questions.rule: Ask: have you the unknown, and are the rest known?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: in the box example, the plan is complete once the pupils see that the other leg is the hypotenuse of a second right triangle.
questions.explain: That step shows the whole chain, and the teacher then says he sees that they have a plan.
questions.rule: A chain of steps from data to unknown is a plan.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The pupils have a triangle containing the unknown, but one leg is not given. What does the author's dialogue ask?
options: Whether both legs are known, which leads to the second triangle
Whether the triangle is drawn neatly
Whether the unknown is bigger than the data
Whether the box in the classroom has a window in one of its walls
optionExplain: Right: the teacher asks whether both legs are known.
Neatness does not matter here.
Comparing sizes does not link the parts.
The classroom is only the setting.
questions.explain: Asking whether the other parts are known shows what is missing.
questions.rule: Ask whether the other parts are known.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil planning a trip budget finds a total that needs an intermediate cost, found from a smaller sum. What does this show?
options: The plan has failed and must be dropped
Intermediate sums are not allowed in a plan, which must go in one step
The final answer is already known
A plan can be a chain, one quantity found from a smaller problem
optionExplain: A chain is a normal form of plan.
Nothing forbids an intermediate quantity.
The final answer still has to be found.
Right: in the book the other leg comes from a second right triangle, so one problem creates another smaller one.
questions.explain: In the book's plan one unknown is found by solving a smaller problem of the same kind.
questions.rule: A plan may be a chain.
questions.teaches: A plan can be a chain: the missing leg of one right triangle is itself the hypotenuse of another, so a smaller problem of the same kind is solved on the way.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which quality does carrying out a ready plan chiefly demand?
options: Good luck, as in finding the plan
Patience in working through the details
A brilliant new idea at every step
Speed, since the plan has done the thinking
optionExplain: Luck is more needed when devising the plan.
Right: the author says that carrying out the plan mainly takes patience.
New ideas are needed to find the plan, not to carry it out.
Speed without examining the details risks hidden errors.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Carrying out takes patience.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: To carry out the plan is much easier than to devise it; what we need is mainly ____.
questions.explain: The author contrasts the luck and knowledge needed for a plan with the patience needed to carry it out.
questions.rule: Patience.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Jo has a plan for a long budget sum but skips one detail because the outline looks right. What may happen?
options: Nothing, since the outline of the plan guarantees that its details fit
An error may remain hidden in the detail she did not examine
The plan will change itself to fit
The skipped detail will check itself later
optionExplain: The outline does not prove that its details fit.
Right: the author wants no obscure corner in which an error could be hidden.
Plans do not adjust themselves.
Details are checked only by someone who looks.
questions.explain: Details must be examined until nothing is obscure.
questions.rule: No obscure corner.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: having a plan means the details of the solution no longer need to be examined.
questions.explain: The plan is only an outline; the details have to be examined one after another.
questions.rule: A plan is an outline, not the finished work.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sort each habit of a pupil carrying out a plan to cost a party: patient, or skipping details.

items.t: Goes through each line of the bill and writes the sub-total
Skips a line because the outline looks right
Works through the details one after another
Leaves an unclear item to be sorted out later
Stops only when no item remains unclear
Trusts the total without adding the lines

questions.explain: Patience means examining the details one after another until nothing is obscure. Skipping or postponing an unclear item leaves a corner where an error can hide.
questions.rule: No obscure corner may remain.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A tutor hands a learner a finished plan for a project and walks away. What risk does the author's view point to?
options: The learner may forget it, since it came from outside on authority
The plan will be carried out so quickly that the learner cannot follow it
The learner will be unable to be patient
The tutor's plan can never be correct
optionExplain: Right: this is the main danger in carrying out the plan.
The author's worry is forgetting, not speed.
Patience is not what is lacking in his view.
The plan may be correct; the problem is how it was received.
questions.explain: A plan conceived with satisfaction after working for it is not easily lost; one received on authority is.
questions.rule: Let learners work for the plan.
questions.teaches: The main danger in carrying out the plan is that the student forgets it, which easily happens when he received it from outside on the teacher's authority.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: How should a student make sure that a step in her reasoning is correct?
options: Accept it if the teacher does not object
Accept it if it leads to the answer she expects
Check until she is honestly convinced, by direct insight or by proof
Accept it once she has copied it carefully and neatly into her notebook
optionExplain: The teacher's silence is not her conviction.
A step reaching the expected answer may still be wrong.
Right: honest conviction by insight or by formal proof.
Copying does not test correctness.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's two ways.
questions.rule: Be honestly convinced.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The main point is that the student should be ____ convinced of the correctness of each step.
questions.explain: The author wants a conviction that is honest, not borrowed.
questions.rule: Honest conviction.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Match each way of checking a step to its name in the author's text.
pairs: Concentrating until the point is so clear there is no doubt
Deriving the point according to formal rules
Accepting it because the teacher said so
questions.explain: Insight and formal proof are the two ways the author names. Taking the teacher's word is neither.
questions.rule: Seeing or proving, never borrowing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil sees that 3 rows of 7 chairs make 21 chairs. Which step gives her a formal proof of that?
options: Decide that 21 looks about right for chairs
Ask a friend whether 21 is a likely total
Notice that 21 is a bigger number than 7 and a smaller one than 30
Write 7 + 7 + 7 and add the three rows to get 21
optionExplain: A feeling of plausibility is not a derivation.
Another opinion is not her own conviction.
Comparing sizes does not derive the total.
Right: deriving the total by rules of addition is a formal route to the same conviction.
questions.explain: Formal proof derives the point by rules; insight sees it directly.
questions.rule: Derive it by rule to prove it.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author asks the student to check each step while carrying out the plan.
questions.explain: He says many mistakes can be avoided if the student checks each step.
questions.rule: Check as you go.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil says: I trust this step because the teacher wrote it on the board. What is missing?
options: A longer explanation by the teacher
Her own conviction, by insight into the step or by proof
A faster way to copy the board
Nothing, since teachers cannot be wrong about what they write
optionExplain: The point is the pupil's own conviction, not more explanation.
Right: the student should be honestly convinced of each step herself.
Copying does not test correctness.
The author asks for personal conviction.
questions.explain: Convince yourself, do not just accept.
questions.rule: Authority is not a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A tutor wants a pupil to notice the difference between seeing and proving. Which pair of questions fits the author?
options: Is the step long? Is it short?
Did you copy the step carefully? Did you tidy it up afterwards?
Can you see the step is correct? Can you also prove it?
Is the step famous? Is it new?
optionExplain: Length does not decide correctness.
Copying and tidying do not test the step.
Right: the teacher may emphasise the difference with these two questions.
Fame and novelty are not tests.
questions.explain: The teacher may ask the two questions to bring out the difference between seeing and proving.
questions.rule: Ask both: can you see it, can you prove it?
questions.teaches: The teacher may emphasise the difference between seeing and proving by asking both: can you see that the step is correct, and can you also prove it?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Two relations are known: x squared equals y squared plus c squared, and y squared equals a squared plus b squared. How is y removed?
options: Put the second relation into the first
Divide the first relation by the second
Add a, b, c and take the answer as x
Remove y from both relations and keep c only
optionExplain: Right: substituting gives x squared equals a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
Division would not remove y.
The result involves squares and a root, not a plain sum.
Dropping y loses the link to a and b.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next works it out.
questions.rule: Eliminate the auxiliary unknown by substitution.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the plan, the auxiliary unknown y is the diagonal of the ____ of the box whose sides are a and b.
questions.explain: The face diagonal is the other leg of the big right triangle.
questions.rule: The face diagonal is the auxiliary unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A box has edges 3, 4 and 12. Following the plan, what is the length of the box diagonal?
options: 19, found by adding 3, 4 and 12
169, found by forgetting to take the final square root
13, since the face diagonal is 5 and 25 + 144 = 169
5, found by using only the first two edges
optionExplain: The diagonal is not the sum of the edges.
169 is the square of the diagonal.
Right: 9 + 16 + 144 = 169 and the square root is 13.
5 is only the face diagonal.
questions.explain: Square each edge, add, then take the root.
questions.rule: Add the squares, then take the root.
questions.hint: Find the face diagonal first, then use it with the third edge.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil gets x squared equals y squared plus c squared and y squared equals a squared plus b squared, then writes x = a + b + c. Where is the slip?
options: The squares and root were dropped; x squared is a sum of squares
Nothing; the sum of the three edges is the diagonal
The first relation is wrong; the diagonal is c squared
y should have been added to c without taking any squares at all
optionExplain: Right: the result is the square root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared.
The sum of the edges is longer than the diagonal.
The first relation is a right-triangle relation, written correctly.
The relation needs squares.
questions.explain: Elimination keeps the squares until the final root.
questions.rule: Keep the squares until the end.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil says yes when asked whether the triangle with sides x, y, c is a right triangle. Should the teacher press for a proof of that?
options: Yes, since a step is not valid until it has been proved to a beginner
Yes, since the proof is the main point of the problem
Not at all, since checking steps is never useful
Better not, unless the class has had a good start in solid geometry
optionExplain: The author weighs the pupils' preparation before pressing.
The proof is not the aim of the example.
He does want each step checked, but with judgment.
Right: the author warns that an incidental question may become the main difficulty.
questions.explain: The author says the teacher should rather suppress this question unless the class has a good initiation in solid geometry.
questions.rule: Choose questions the class can answer.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: y is removed by putting y squared equals a squared plus b squared into x squared equals y squared plus c squared.
questions.explain: Substituting leaves x squared equal to a squared plus b squared plus c squared, with no y left.
questions.rule: Substitute to eliminate.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil is working through the details of a plan correctly. What does the author say a teacher should do?
options: Interrupt at each step to ask for a formal proof of that step
Not interrupt, except to remind the pupil to check each step
Take over and finish the calculation
Walk away and stop checking the work
optionExplain: Pressing proofs can hurt the class's progress.
Right: no reason to interrupt if details are correct, except for the reminder.
Taking over removes the pupil's work.
The reminder to check each step still helps.
questions.explain: The teacher has no reason to interrupt if the student carries out the details correctly, except to warn him to check each step.
questions.rule: Do not interrupt good work.
questions.teaches: The teacher has no reason to interrupt a student who carries out the details correctly, except possibly to warn him to check each step.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has written out a correct answer neatly. What would the author most like her to do next?
options: Close the book and look around for something else to do
Reconsider the result and the path that led to it
Copy the answer a second time more neatly
Ask the teacher to mark it at once
optionExplain: That is just what fairly good students do, and they miss a phase.
Right: looking back consolidates knowledge and builds the ability to solve problems.
Neatness adds little to understanding.
Marking is not the pupil's own review.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next explains why this phase pays.
questions.rule: Look back before moving on.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: The author holds that no problem whatever is completely ____.
questions.explain: There remains always something to do, and our understanding can always be improved.
questions.rule: No problem is exhausted.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Dev has finished a paint-mixing problem correctly. Which act is a real look back?
options: Putting the pencil away because the answer is right
Rewriting the same working with larger handwriting
Waiting for the teacher to say well done and then moving on to the next one
Asking if a shorter path existed and where the method applies
optionExplain: Stopping because the answer is right is the habit the author criticises.
Larger handwriting does not reconsider anything.
Praise from the teacher is not a review.
Right: this reexamines the result and the path to it.
questions.explain: Reconsider the path as well as the result.
questions.rule: Look at the path, not just the result.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, only students who got a wrong answer have reason to look back.
questions.explain: He says that by looking back even at a completed solution, students can consolidate their knowledge and develop their ability to solve problems.
questions.rule: Look back after correct answers too.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: What does the author say about a solution the student has checked step by step?
options: Good reasons to believe it, but errors are possible, so checks help
It is now certain, so nothing more can be done
It is worthless unless the teacher has also checked every single line of it
It has been checked, so the problem is exhausted
optionExplain: Right: the author calls verifications desirable even after checking each step.
He says errors are always possible, especially in long arguments.
He does not make the teacher's check the test.
He says no problem is completely exhausted.
questions.explain: Checking each step gives good reasons, not certainty.
questions.rule: Good reasons are not certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A strong student says: I am good at this, so I need not look back. What does the author's remark about good students suggest?
options: Strong students gain nothing from looking back
Looking back is only for slow students
Even fairly good students lose a phase by shutting the book at once
Only the teacher should look back at the solutions the pupils hand in
optionExplain: He says the opposite.
He does not restrict the phase to slow students.
Right: the author says that even fairly good students miss this phase.
The student must do the review herself.
questions.explain: The author says even fairly good students, once the argument is neatly written, shut their books and miss an important and instructive phase.
questions.rule: Ability does not excuse skipping the look back.
questions.teaches: Even fairly good students tend to shut their books once the solution is written, and so miss an important and instructive phase of the work.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil finds that 5 boxes of 12 pencils hold 60 pencils. What is the best way to build confidence in the result?
options: Repeat the same multiplication exactly as before
Ask a friend what she remembers of a similar sum
Decide the result must be right because it happens to be a round number
Get the result a second way, such as taking half of ten boxes
optionExplain: The same slip would be repeated.
A vague memory is not a check.
Roundness does not show correctness.
Right: a different derivation gives an independent reason.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next lists the author's checks.
questions.rule: Derive it differently.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: One of the author's questions: Can you derive the result ____?
questions.explain: A second, different derivation adds conviction to the first.
questions.rule: Derive the result differently.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil gets 60 for 5 boxes of 12 pencils. Which of these is a different derivation?
options: Multiply 12 by 5 again in exactly the same way as before
Ten boxes would hold 120, and half of that is 60
Add up 12 once and call it 60
Round 12 to 10 and give 50
optionExplain: Repeating the same way is not a different derivation.
Right: this is a different route to the same result, and 10 times 12 is 120.
That does not reach 60 in any way.
Rounding gives an estimate that is not equal to 60.
questions.explain: Check by another route.
questions.rule: A second route is a check.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: since the student checked each step, the author says no further verification is needed.
questions.explain: He says that errors are always possible, especially if the argument is long, so verifications are desirable.
questions.rule: Further checks are desirable.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Two arguments reach the same result: one short and intuitive, one long and heavy. Which does the author prefer?
options: The long one, since its length shows how much effort was spent on it
Neither, since a result needs no argument
The short and intuitive one, which can be seen at a glance
Both equally, since only the result matters
optionExplain: Length does not make an argument better.
He wants an argument, and a check of it.
Right: he asks whether the result can be seen at a glance.
He prefers the argument that is quick to grasp.
questions.explain: A short intuitive argument is preferred to a long, heavy one.
questions.rule: Prefer a short argument you can see.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil gets the same answer by two quite different methods. How does the author compare this to ordinary experience?
options: Like perceiving an object through two senses, seeing and touching it
Like hearing an answer repeated twice by one person
Like trusting a single quick glance at a large crowd of people passing by
Like guessing the same number twice by chance
optionExplain: Right: we prefer conviction by two different proofs just as we prefer perception by two senses.
Repeating the same thing is not independent.
A single glance is the weaker case.
Chance agreement is not a check.
questions.explain: The author compares two different proofs with perceiving something through two different senses.
questions.rule: Two different routes are better than one.
questions.teaches: The author compares conviction by two different proofs with perception through two senses: to be sure of an object we like to see it and touch it.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has solved a problem. Which question links it to other problems?
options: Is this the longest and the hardest problem in the whole book?
Who first thought up this type of problem?
Can the result or the method be used for some other problem?
How many marks was this problem worth?
optionExplain: Length does not show connections.
History does not show connections between problems.
Right: using the result or method elsewhere shows the connections.
Marks do not either.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next shows the author's question.
questions.rule: Ask where else it can be used.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Can you use the result, or the ____, for some other problem?
questions.explain: The author asks about the result and about the method.
questions.rule: Result or method.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Lena found that a 60-litre tank takes 12 minutes to fill at 5 litres a minute. Which new problem uses her method?
options: How long to empty a 90-litre pool at 15 litres a minute: 6 minutes?
Check once more that 60 divided by 5 is 12, using exactly the same working
Fill the tank at a slower rate and wait
Ask what a litre weighs in a different country
optionExplain: Right: 90 divided by 15 gives 6, so the method of dividing volume by rate carries over.
That checks the old result; it does not apply the method elsewhere.
Waiting is not a new problem.
The weight of a litre is unrelated to the method.
questions.explain: Apply the method to a new setting.
questions.rule: Carry the method to a new case.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: According to the author, when are pupils most likely to find looking back really interesting?
options: Before any effort has been made, since looking back is then easy
When they did not understand the problem
Only when marks are given for it
After an honest effort, when they feel they have done well
optionExplain: Interest comes from effort already made.
Without effort the connections do not matter.
The author does not tie it to marks.
Right: then they are eager to see what else the effort could accomplish.
questions.explain: The pupils find it interesting if they have made an honest effort.
questions.rule: Effort first, then the look back is interesting.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author counts it among the teacher's first duties to avoid giving the impression that problems are unconnected with each other.
questions.explain: He calls it one of the first and foremost duties of the teacher.
questions.rule: Show that problems are connected.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A class cannot think of any use for what they solved. What does the author suggest the teacher do?
options: Say that no further use exists and move on
Encourage them to imagine cases where they could reuse the method or result
Set a further test on the same problem in order to force some interest in it
Give them the next problem and hope links appear
optionExplain: That would cut off the look back.
Right: with a little encouragement and an example or two, pupils find applications.
Testing does not create connections.
Hoping does not bring the links.
questions.explain: The teacher should encourage the students to imagine cases in which they could use the procedure again or apply the result.
questions.rule: Encourage pupils to imagine uses.
questions.teaches: The teacher should encourage the students to imagine cases in which they could utilize the procedure again or apply the result obtained.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A result is written in letters for a box with length a, width b and height c. Length, width and height play the same role in the problem. Which test could expose a flaw?
options: Check that the formula is printed in a large and readable font
Swap two letters and see whether the formula stays unchanged
Check that the answer is a whole number
Check that the letters are in alphabetical order
optionExplain: Print size has no link to correctness.
Right: if the problem is symmetric, the formula should be too.
A correct result need not be a whole number.
Order of the letters does not decide correctness.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next lists the tests.
questions.rule: Symmetric problems need symmetric formulas.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Length, width and height play the same role, so the expression for the diagonal should be ____ in a, b and c.
questions.explain: Swapping a, b and c should leave the expression unchanged.
questions.rule: Symmetric problem, symmetric formula.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil claims the perimeter of a rectangle with sides p and q is 2p + q. The problem treats p and q equally. What does the symmetry test show?
options: The formula is right, since it uses both of the letters p and q
The test does not apply to rectangles
The formula is right if p is bigger than q
The formula changes if p and q are swapped, so it has a flaw
optionExplain: Using both letters is not enough; the roles must match.
A rectangle is symmetric in its sides.
Size order does not rescue the formula.
Right: 2p + q becomes 2q + p when the sides are swapped, but the perimeter is the same.
questions.explain: A symmetric problem needs a symmetric result.
questions.rule: Swap the letters.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: swapping a and b in the expression with the square root of a squared plus b squared plus c squared leaves its value unchanged.
questions.explain: The sum of squares does not depend on which of a and b comes first.
questions.rule: The box formula is symmetric.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil proposes the root of a squared plus b squared plus c for the box diagonal. With a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, swapping a and c changes the value. Why does this show a flaw?
options: The problem treats the edges alike, so the value should not change
Any formula should change when letters are swapped
The swap is not allowed in algebra
The value shows only an arithmetic slip, not a flaw in the formula itself
optionExplain: Right: the swap gives the root of 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 instead of the root of 1 + 4 + 3 = 8.
A symmetric problem needs a symmetric result.
Swapping is permitted as a test.
The inconsistency comes from the form, not an arithmetic slip.
questions.explain: A non-symmetric formula for a symmetric problem must be wrong.
questions.rule: Unequal treatment of equal edges is a flaw.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: After several similar problems, what general habits does the author hope a pupil forms from such tests?
options: Memorising each formula together with its page number
Avoiding all problems that have letters in them
Using all data, varying the data, symmetry and analogy
Asking the teacher to name the right test each time one is needed
optionExplain: Tests are meant to build habits, not memory of pages.
Letters give the advantage in testing.
Right: the author names these four general ideas.
The pupil should learn to ask the questions himself.
questions.explain: The author expects an intelligent pupil to see the underlying general ideas: use of all relevant data, variation of the data, symmetry, analogy.
questions.rule: Four habits: all data, variation, symmetry, analogy.
questions.teaches: After experience with similar problems, a pupil may see the general ideas behind the tests: use of all relevant data, variation of the data, symmetry and analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: If the height of a box shrinks to zero, what should the box diagonal become?
options: Zero, since a flat box has no diagonal
The length alone, since the width must disappear along with the height
Infinity, since a flat box is unstable
The diagonal of the flat rectangle formed by the length and width
optionExplain: The rectangle still has a diagonal.
Only the height is shrinking.
Nothing in the box suggests infinity.
Right: the box becomes a rectangle and its diagonal that of the rectangle.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next lists these tests.
questions.rule: A vanishing measure should give the plane result.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: If all three measures of the box are doubled, the diagonal should be ____ as well.
questions.explain: The whole box is enlarged in the same proportion, so its diagonal is too.
questions.rule: Scale all measures, scale the diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A box has edges 3, 4 and 12 and diagonal 13. All edges are doubled. What is the new diagonal?
options: 169, which is the square of the old diagonal of 13 itself
26, since doubling every edge doubles the diagonal
52, doubled twice
13, unchanged because the shape is the same
optionExplain: 169 is the square of 13.
Right: the edges become 6, 8 and 24 and the root of 36 + 64 + 576 = 676 is 26.
52 doubles twice.
The shape is the same but the size is not.
questions.explain: Scale all measures, scale the diagonal.
questions.rule: Double the edges, double the diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: if the height c increases while a and b stay the same, the expression for the diagonal should increase.
questions.explain: A taller box has a longer diagonal, and the square root of a sum with bigger c grows.
questions.rule: A taller box has a longer diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A formula passes every test in the section. What does the author say this gives?
options: A complete proof that makes the derivation unnecessary
Nothing, since tests can never be passed
More confidence, as a sort of experimental evidence
Proof for that particular box only, and not for any other box
optionExplain: He treats tests as support, not proof.
He expects a correct formula to pass.
Right: the author says the confidence comes from a sort of experimental evidence.
The tests concern the formula in letters, which covers any box.
questions.explain: The student is more convinced because the formula passes so many tests.
questions.rule: Tests add confidence, not proof.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In a recipe, doubling all quantities should double the total weight, and giving quantities in kilograms rather than grams should leave a correct formula correct. How does the author relate these two tests?
options: They are essentially equivalent; this is the test by dimension
They are unrelated; one concerns size while the other concerns taste
The first is valid and the second is invalid
They are equivalent only for rectangles
optionExplain: Right: the author calls the last two questions essentially equivalent and refers to test by dimension.
Both test how the formula responds to a change of scale or unit.
Both are valid tests.
The equivalence is general.
questions.explain: The author says the scaling and change-of-units questions are essentially equivalent.
questions.rule: Scale and units are the same kind of test.
questions.teaches: The questions on multiplying all measures by the same factor and on changing the unit of measurement are essentially equivalent; the author refers to this as test by dimension.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A long argument has been written out. How much rechecking does the author usually think is enough?
options: Rechecking every single step of the argument in all cases
No rechecking after the first time through
Picking out the touchy points for rechecking
Rechecking only the final line
optionExplain: That is needed only in difficult and important cases.
Errors are possible, so some rechecking is desirable.
Right: step-by-step rechecking is for difficult and important cases.
The touchy points may lie anywhere in the argument.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Recheck the touchy points.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Usually it is enough to pick out ____ points of the argument for rechecking.
questions.explain: The author says touchy points are enough in usual cases.
questions.rule: Recheck touchy points.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A box has edges 6, 8 and 24. What is the distance from its centre to one corner?
options: 13, which is half the diagonal of 26
26, the full diagonal
5, half the diagonal of the 6 by 8 face
19, half the sum of the edges
optionExplain: Right: the root of 36 + 64 + 576 = 676 is 26, and half of that is 13.
The centre is only halfway along the diagonal.
The face diagonal is 10, so half of it is 5; the centre is not at that distance from a corner.
The sum of the edges is not involved.
questions.explain: The centre-to-corner distance is half the diagonal.
questions.rule: Half the diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A top of a building is 21 yards long and 16 wide, a pole 8 yards high stands at its centre, and a cable runs from 2 yards below its tip to a corner. What is its length?
options: 27.1 yards, from the full length, width and 6
24.5 yards, from the sum of the half edges
10.5 yards, from the half length alone
14.5 yards, from edges 10.5, 8 and 6
optionExplain: The full length and width would reach the opposite corner of a bigger box.
The sum of edges is longer than the diagonal.
One half edge is only one of the edges.
questions.explain: Use half the length and half the width as the horizontal edges.
questions.rule: The cable is the diagonal of a smaller box.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the distance from the centre of a box to a corner is the full diagonal.
questions.explain: The centre lies halfway along the diagonal, so the distance is half of it.
questions.rule: Centre to corner is half the diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Students offer the cafeteria in place of the classroom. What does the author say a teacher may then do?
options: Praise it as the best possible use
Pose a slightly different problem, such as centre-to-corner distance
Close the discussion at once
Ask for a full proof of the formula before the class goes any further
optionExplain: He calls such a suggestion dull.
Right: the teacher may put a slightly different problem himself.
The discussion can continue with a better problem.
The proof is a different matter.
questions.explain: If students do not volunteer more imaginative remarks, the teacher may put a slightly different problem.
questions.rule: Offer a slightly different problem.
questions.teaches: Using the same classroom for the cafeteria is a dull application; if pupils offer nothing better, the teacher may put a slightly different problem, such as the distance from the centre of the box to a corner.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Pupils cannot link a problem about a solid with anything they know. Which move might help?
options: Insist that they work much harder on the solid problem itself
Think of a simpler analogous problem about a flat figure
Give them the answer for the solid
Pick a problem with a larger solid
optionExplain: More effort alone gives no new contact.
Right: an analogue in the plane can provide a point of contact.
The answer would remove the discovery.
A larger solid is harder, not simpler.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the second approach.
questions.rule: Look for an analogue.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the second approach the contact with the idea of the solution is provided by ____, not by the unknown.
questions.explain: The first approach used a problem with a similar unknown; the second uses an analogous problem.
questions.rule: Analogy is another way in.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Pupils cannot find how many unit cubes fill a 3 by 4 by 5 block. Which analogous flat problem helps?
options: How many cubes would make up a block that is much bigger than this?
How heavy is each cube in the block?
How many faces does a cube have?
How many unit squares fill a 3 by 4 grid, which is 12?
optionExplain: A bigger block is no easier.
Weight is not the question.
Faces are a different matter.
Right: the flat case suggests layers, and the block holds 12 times 5 equal layers, which is 60 cubes.
questions.explain: A flat version of the problem can show the idea.
questions.rule: Find the flat analogue.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: in the second approach even very slow pupils are obliged to contribute at least a small part of the idea.
questions.explain: They have to supply the word that completes the question about the plane figure.
questions.rule: Slow pupils too can contribute.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: How do the two approaches to the box problem compare?
options: Same idea; contact by the unknown in one, by analogy in the other
They give two different ideas, of which one is correct and one is wrong
They differ because the first needs no knowledge at all
They are the same approach under two names
optionExplain: Right: the author says the idea is essentially the same but the approach differs.
Both reach the same kind of idea.
Both draw on the pupils' knowledge.
The route into the idea differs.
questions.explain: The two approaches differ in how the contact is made.
questions.rule: Same idea, different way in.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A teacher planning a lesson on a solid knows the class is slow. What does the author advise about the analogous flat problem?
options: Skip it and give the formula directly
Introduce it only after the answer is found
Discuss it with the class beforehand, to prepare them
Avoid it altogether, since slow classes cannot make any use of analogy
optionExplain: The formula would remove the discovery.
Introducing it afterwards loses its purpose.
Right: if the students are slow, the analogous problem should be discussed first.
The author recommends analogy for slow pupils.
questions.explain: The teacher should not take up the solid problem without having discussed the analogous plane problem first, in order to prepare slow students.
questions.rule: Prepare slow classes with the analogue.
questions.teaches: If the students are slow, the teacher should discuss the analogous plane problem before taking up the solid problem, in order to prepare them.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A teacher wants to help a stuck pupil but leave her most of the work. Which approach fits?
options: Start with the most specific hint and keep it brief
Give the full plan to save time for practice
Wait silently, never asking a question
Start general and become specific only when needed
optionExplain: A specific hint at the start leaves less for the pupil.
A given plan is not the pupil's own.
Silence is not help.
Right: a gradual descent gives the pupil the largest share of the work.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's method.
questions.rule: Start general.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Begin with a general question or suggestion and, if necessary, come down gradually to more ____ and concrete ones.
questions.explain: The aim is to reach a question that elicits a response.
questions.rule: General first, specific if needed.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Order a tutor's questions about a savings puzzle from the most general to the most specific.
items: What is the unknown?
Do you know a related problem?
Do you know a problem with the same unknown?
Could a total-cost problem be used here?
questions.explain: Each question narrows the help a little further.
questions.rule: Narrow step by step.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: if the general question already brings a good response, the teacher need not go on to a more specific one.
questions.explain: The author says to come down to more specific questions only if necessary.
questions.rule: Stop at the first question that works.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sort each teacher move: in line with the author's method, or against it.

items.t: Opens with a question that fits many problems
Moves to a narrower hint only after silence
Opens with a hint that fits only this problem
Tells the pupil the first step at once
Returns to a general question when helping to use an idea
Asks only questions that suit just this one problem

questions.explain: The method starts general, narrows only when needed, and restarts general when the pupil must exploit the idea.
questions.rule: General first, narrow only if needed.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil has an idea but cannot work it out. What does the author suggest the teacher do?
options: Take over and finish the work himself
Start again from a general question of the list, descending if necessary
Switch to an entirely different problem
Give the pupil a rigid, fixed list of steps to follow in the same order each time
optionExplain: Taking over removes the pupil's share.
Right: the same method applies when helping the pupil exploit the idea.
Changing problem drops the idea.
The author disfavours rigid, mechanical procedure.
questions.explain: To help the student exploit his idea, start again from a general question or suggestion and return to a more special one if necessary.
questions.rule: The same ladder helps with using an idea.
questions.teaches: To help the student exploit his idea the teacher starts again, if possible, from a general question of the list and goes back to a more special one only if necessary.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A tutor wants a list of helpful questions for pupils. Which features should the list have?
options: Long and specific, with a separate hint for each type of problem
Secret, so that pupils cannot imitate it
Short and general enough to be repeated in many problems
Fixed, so that no tutor may vary it
optionExplain: A long, specific list cannot be used often and naturally.
The point is that pupils assimilate the questions.
Right: this lets the questions be repeated until they become a habit.
The author prefers elasticity.
