questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Keep the list short and general.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Match each quality of the suggestions to the author's reason for it.
pairs: So that they can be unobtrusive
So that they help develop ability and not just a special technique
So that they can be repeated often and become a habit
So that the student has as great a share of the work as possible
questions.explain: Each quality serves one end of the method.
questions.rule: Each quality has its reason.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which tutor's list suits the author's advice best?
options: Three short questions that fit any problem, such as the unknown
Forty hints, one for each type of exercise
One trick to remember for each exam question
A different and carefully chosen set of questions for every single pupil
optionExplain: Right: short, general and repeatable.
Too many hints cannot be repeated until they are a habit.
A trick for each question teaches a special technique.
Variety for each pupil loses the repetition.
questions.explain: A short general list can be repeated until it is assimilated.
questions.rule: Short and general beats long and special.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, any rigid, mechanical, pedantical procedure in these matters is necessarily bad.
questions.explain: He calls any rigid, mechanical, pedantical procedure necessarily bad in these matters and asks that his method admit elasticity and variation.
questions.rule: Be elastic.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A reader plans to try the method in class tomorrow without preparing. What does the author advise instead?
options: Go ahead at once tomorrow, since the method needs no preparation at all
Use the method only with the best class
Proceed with caution, preparing the examples and starting with trials
Use the method on every problem from the first day
optionExplain: He asks the teacher to prepare the examples and various approaches.
He does not limit it to a best class.
Right: the author advises caution and preparation.
He suggests starting with a few trials.
questions.explain: The reader should study the examples, prepare carefully and start with a few trials.
questions.rule: Try it with care.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: How should the teacher's questions be applied, according to the author?
options: So that the questions could have occurred to the student himself
So that the student cannot tell which of the teacher's tricks they are
So that they surprise the student with a clever turn
So that they follow a single rigid sequence
optionExplain: Right: they should seem natural enough to be the student's own.
A mystery source makes the help look like a trick.
Surprise is not the aim.
Rigid sequences are not wanted.
questions.explain: The method can and should be applied so that the questions asked by the teacher could have occurred to the student himself.
questions.rule: Questions the student could ask himself.
questions.teaches: The method should be applied so that the questions asked by the teacher could have occurred to the student himself.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A pupil is stuck on a geometry problem. Which hint teaches more?
options: Could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras?
Use the formula the teacher wrote yesterday
Multiply the two largest numbers
Do you know a related problem?
optionExplain: It names the method and gives the secret away.
It also names the method.
It is a direct instruction with no explanation.
Right: it is general and leaves the pupil to find the connection.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next gives the author's objections.
questions.rule: General questions teach more.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: If the suggestion is understood, the question gives the whole ____ away, and very little remains for the student to do.
questions.explain: That is one of the author's objections to the Pythagoras question.
questions.rule: Do not give the secret away.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Sort each hint: good by the author's standard, or bad.

items.t: Do you know a related problem?
Look at the unknown
Did you use all the data?
Could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras?
Why not simply add the two lengths and halve them?
Use the same trick as in problem seven

questions.explain: The good hints are general questions that apply to problems of all sorts. The bad ones name the method for this problem.
questions.rule: Prefer questions that fit many problems.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: Which are among the author's objections to the Pythagoras question? Select all that apply.
options: It gives the whole secret away if understood
It is too special to teach anything for future problems
It is so general that no student can follow it
It fails to help where help is most needed
optionExplain: Right: very little remains for the student to do.
Right: nothing is learned for future problems.
Wrong: the hint is special, not general.
Right: a student far from the solution may not see the point.
questions.explain: The hint is both too special and too helpful in the wrong place.
questions.rule: Special hints give away and teach nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: True or false: the author says the same objections can be raised against the procedures of sections 10 and 15.
questions.explain: He says none of these objections can be raised against those procedures, which begin with general questions.
questions.rule: The general questions avoid the objections.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: A coach gives a clever trick, and a player cannot see how the coach came to think of it. Which objection of the author does this match?
options: The question is too general to be useful
It appears as an unnatural surprise, a rabbit out of a hat
The question comes too late to matter
The question is exactly what the student needs, so there is no objection
optionExplain: The trick is special, not general.
Right: the student cannot see how he himself could find such a question.
Lateness is not the objection.
The student cannot use it as his own.
questions.explain: Even if he understands the suggestion, the student can scarcely see how the teacher came to put it. It appears as an unnatural surprise, a rabbit pulled out of a hat.
questions.rule: Help the student see where a question came from.
questions.teaches: Even when understood, such a hint appears as an unnatural surprise, a rabbit out of a hat, because the student cannot see how the teacher thought of it or how he himself could find such a question.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Asked to draw a circle through three given points, what is a good first step?
options: Draw circles at random and keep the one that looks closest to all three points
Look for a formula for the biggest circle that fits on the page
Say what is to be found, what is given and what has to hold
Measure the distances between the points and wait for a pattern to appear
optionExplain: Trial and error may work, but with no clear target you cannot tell when to stop.
A formula may exist, but you have not yet said what the problem asks for.
Right: the circle is to be found, the points are given and the circle must pass through them.
Measuring collects numbers, but without a target you do not know which numbers matter.
questions.explain: A good first step is to say what is wanted, what is given and what must hold. The card next shows this three-part naming.
questions.rule: Start by saying what is asked, what is given and what must hold.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In a problem to find something, the thing you must find is called the ____.
questions.explain: The unknown is what you are asked to find. What you are given are the data, and the condition links the two.
questions.rule: Unknown = what to find; data = what is given; condition = what must hold.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Find a rectangle with perimeter 24 cm whose length is twice its width. Which split into parts is right?
options: Unknown: the perimeter; data: the length and the width; condition: the rectangle is closed
Unknown: the ratio of 2 to 1; data: nothing is given; condition: the area is as large as possible
Unknown: the number 24; data: the rectangle itself; condition: all four sides are equal in length
Unknown: the length and width; data: the 24 cm perimeter; condition: length is twice the width
optionExplain: The perimeter is given, not asked for, and a closed shape is not the condition of this problem.
The ratio is part of the condition and the perimeter is given; nothing here asks for the largest area.
24 is a given number, not the target, and the sides of a rectangle need not all be equal.
Right: the sides are to be found, 24 cm is given, and length twice width is the condition (the sides turn out to be 4 cm and 8 cm).
questions.explain: The sides are wanted, so they are the unknown. The perimeter is given, and twice-as-long is the link between the sides. With width 4 and length 8 the perimeter is 24.
questions.rule: Each part has its own role: target, material, link.
questions.hint: Which part tells you what the answer will look like?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Sort each statement about the problem: inscribe a square in a given triangle, two corners on the base.

items.t: The unknown is a square
The data are a triangle
The condition puts two corners on the base
The unknown is the triangle
The data are the four corners of the square
The condition puts all four corners on the base

questions.explain: The square is to be found, the triangle is given, and the corners must sit two on the base and one on each other side. The other statements swap the roles or change the condition.
questions.rule: Check each part against the statement, not against what you expect.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In the book's dialogue, what does the teacher ask right after the three parts have been named?
options: Whether it is possible to satisfy the condition
Whether the data are enough to draw the triangle
Which theorem the student plans to use
Whether the student has met a problem like this before
optionExplain: Right: the teacher asks if it is possible to satisfy the condition.
The triangle is simply given, so there is no question about drawing it.
A plan comes later; the dialogue first checks that the target can be reached.
Remembering earlier problems matters later, but it is not what the dialogue asks here.
questions.explain: After the three parts, the book's teacher asks whether it is possible to satisfy the condition. That checks that the problem asks for something that can exist.
questions.rule: After naming the parts, ask whether the condition can be satisfied.
questions.teaches: After the unknown, data and condition are named, the teacher asks whether it is possible to satisfy the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Maya names the unknown, data and condition of a baking task but is unsure it can be done. What does the book's dialogue suggest?
options: She named the parts wrongly, since a correct naming settles whether the task can be done
Naming the parts is a start; being unsure afterwards is normal and calls for more work
She should drop the condition altogether, so that the task becomes possible to complete
She should stop, because a task that still feels uncertain must have no solution at all
optionExplain: Correct naming does not decide solvability; the book's student named them well and was still unsure.
Right: the student in the book names the parts correctly and still says he is not sure.
Dropping the whole condition changes the problem instead of solving it.
Feeling unsure says nothing about whether a solution exists.
questions.explain: In the book the student names the parts and still replies 'I think so. I am not so sure.' Uncertainty after naming is normal and is the cue for further steps.
questions.rule: Naming the parts does not settle whether the problem is easy or solvable.
questions.teaches: Naming the unknown, data and condition correctly can still leave you unsure that the condition can be satisfied; in the book the student is in just that position.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A puzzle in your homework looks too hard as it is written. Which response would the book's teacher encourage?
options: Change the question to a different problem and forget this one
Read the statement again and again until the solution appears
Ask for the answer and copy it, then explain it later
Solve first some related problem that is easier to handle
optionExplain: A different problem does not help with this one; a related problem is chosen to bear on it.
Rereading is worth doing, but it adds nothing once you have understood the statement.
Copying leaves you with no method for the next problem.
Right: a related problem is the teacher's suggestion for a problem you cannot solve directly.
questions.explain: The teacher suggests turning to a related problem when the given one is hard. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When stuck, solve a related problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: The teacher advises a related problem: a problem connected to the original that you can handle.
questions.rule: Related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: You must price tiles for an L-shaped bathroom floor and do not see how to start. Which move follows the advice?
options: Guess a total price and then correct it against the receipt once the work is done
Wait until a builder quotes a price for the L shape and then compare it
First find the cost for a plain rectangular floor, a related and easier problem
Tile only the shortest corner of the floor and ignore the rest of the room
optionExplain: A guess gives no method, and a receipt is not available yet.
Waiting hands the problem to someone else instead of working on it.
Right: a plain rectangle is related and easy, and the method may carry over to the L shape.
This throws away most of the floor, so it answers a different question.
questions.explain: The rectangle is a related problem: same kind of question, simpler shape. Solving it first gives a method to adapt.
questions.rule: Pick a related problem that is simpler but of the same kind.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A student says: 'I think it can be done, but I am not sure.' Which replies fit the book's teacher? Select all that apply.
options: Say that it certainly can be done, so there is no reason to hesitate
Note that the problem does not seem too easy for him
Tell him to wait until he is sure before doing anything
Suggest that he solve a related problem first
optionExplain: The teacher does not push confidence; the student's doubt is honest and is used.
Right: the teacher remarks that the student does not seem to find the problem too easy.
Waiting until he is sure would stop all progress; the doubt is a reason to try a related problem.
Right: this is the teacher's proposal.
questions.explain: The teacher takes the doubt seriously, says that the problem is not too easy for him, and proposes a related problem.
questions.rule: Doubt is a cue for a related problem, not for waiting.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Before proposing a related problem, what does the teacher say to a student who is unsure the square can be drawn?
options: He praises the student for being certain that the square can be drawn
He says the student does not seem to find the problem too easy
He gives the first step of the construction and asks for the next
He reads the statement of the problem again, more slowly, to the student
optionExplain: The student did not claim certainty.
Right: he puts the difficulty into words and then turns to a related problem.
The teacher gives no step; he proposes a way of finding one.
Nothing in the dialogue suggests that the statement was misunderstood.
questions.explain: The teacher names the difficulty aloud ('You do not seem to find the problem too easy') and only then proposes a related problem.
questions.rule: Name the difficulty, then change the problem.
questions.teaches: The teacher puts the student's hesitation into words, saying that he does not seem to find the problem too easy, before proposing a related problem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A scheduler cannot meet four requirements for a meeting time. Which related problem follows the teacher's suggestion in the book?
options: Find a time that meets only some of the requirements
Find a time that meets none of the four requirements at all
Choose a day at random and tell everyone that they must attend
Remove the meeting from the calendar until a time appears
optionExplain: Right: in the book the related problem satisfies only a part of the condition.
Meeting none of them gives no help in seeing how to meet all four.
A random day ignores the requirements instead of studying them.
Removing the meeting abandons the problem.
questions.explain: The teacher's related problem in the book is to satisfy only a part of the condition. For the scheduler, that means meeting some requirements first.
questions.rule: A related problem can keep part of the condition.
questions.teaches: In the book, the related problem the teacher proposes is to satisfy only a part of the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Putting all four corners of a square on the sides of a triangle looks hard. What could you try first?
options: Put the whole triangle inside the square instead of the other way round
Give up on squares and draw a rectangle that touches all the sides
Draw a square with fewer than four corners on the sides of the triangle
Wait until a ruler suggests the right size for the square to be drawn
optionExplain: That swaps the roles of the shapes and changes the problem.
A rectangle is a different unknown, so the problem is no longer the same one.
Right: satisfying fewer corners is a part of the condition and is easier.
A ruler does not suggest anything until you have something drawn.
questions.explain: Satisfying only some of the corners is easier and keeps the same unknown. The card next names this move.
questions.rule: Satisfy part of the condition first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: To simplify a condition, keep one piece of it and drop the rest. The teacher's name for that piece is a ____ of the condition.
questions.explain: The teacher asks for a part of the condition: a piece that is concerned with less than the whole.
questions.rule: Part of the condition first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A class trip must cost under 12 pounds, take under 2 hours to reach and include a museum. None is found. Which move follows the rule?
options: Drop all three requirements and choose any trip that takes your fancy
Raise the cost limit to 100 pounds and the other limits to any size
Keep adding more requirements until one trip stands out from the others
Keep two requirements, find trips meeting them, then check the third
optionExplain: Dropping everything leaves no problem to solve.
Changing every limit replaces the condition instead of using a part of it.
More requirements make the condition harder, not easier.
Right: two requirements are a part of the condition, easier to meet, and the third can be checked afterwards.
questions.explain: Keeping two of the three requirements is a part of the condition. Trips that meet it can then be checked against the dropped one.
questions.rule: Keep some requirements, check the rest afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The task: put a square so that all four of its corners are on the sides of a triangle. Sort each idea.
groups: Keeps a part of the condition

items.t: Put only two corners of the square on the sides
Put three corners on the sides and leave the fourth free
Put only the two lower corners on the base
Replace the triangle by a circle
Draw a rectangle instead of a square
Make the triangle larger until a square fits easily

questions.explain: A part of the condition still asks for corners of the same square on the same triangle. Changing the shape of the triangle or the square changes the given or the unknown.
questions.rule: A part of the condition keeps the unknown and the data.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In the book's dialogue, how many corners of the square does the student say can easily be put on the triangle's outline?
options: Two, or even three
Four, since a square is easy to draw once the triangle is given
Only one, since one corner is the most she can place with care
Two, but never three, since the third corner fixes the square
optionExplain: Right: two corners are easy, even three.
Four is the original, harder condition; it is the whole condition, not a part.
One corner is easy, but the student goes further and says two or even three.
The student does not rule out three; with three corners on the outline the square is still not determined.
questions.explain: The student says it is easy to draw a square with two corners on the outline, even with three. A part of the condition can therefore be met quite far.
questions.rule: A part can be nearly the whole condition.
questions.teaches: The student finds it easy to draw a square with two corners on the outline of the triangle, or even three.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A baker's loaf must be gluten-free, under 200 calories a slice and ready in an hour. By the teacher's question, which part is kept first?
options: The part that looks hardest, to get it out of the way first
A part she can satisfy easily, so that she can build from it
A part chosen at random, since every part is as good as another
All three at once, since the parts cannot really be separated
optionExplain: Starting with the hardest part defeats the purpose of simplifying.
Right: the teacher asks what part of the condition is easy to satisfy.
Parts differ in difficulty, and the teacher asks for the easy one.
The whole point is that the condition can be split.
questions.explain: The teacher's question is 'What part of the condition is easy to satisfy?' So the baker keeps an easy part first.
questions.rule: Choose the part that is easy to satisfy.
questions.teaches: The teacher guides the choice of the part with the question: what part of the condition is easy to satisfy?

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Only three corners of a square must lie on a triangle's outline. How many such squares can be drawn?
options: Exactly one square, since three corners fix its size and place
Exactly three squares, one for each corner left free
None, since three corners cannot lie on the outline together
Many different squares, small ones and large ones
optionExplain: That would be true only if the three corners fixed the square, which they do not.
There is no reason for exactly three.
Squares with three corners on the outline are easy to draw, so there are some.
Right: the square can be drawn small or large, so it is not fixed.
questions.explain: Fewer conditions leave more freedom, so many squares fit. The card next calls this 'not determined'.
questions.rule: Fewer conditions leave more squares.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: a square with only three corners on the triangle's outline is completely determined.
questions.explain: Three corners on the outline do not fix the square; it can still vary, as its fourth corner shows.
questions.rule: A partial condition leaves the unknown free.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 20 cm and nothing else is known. Which rectangles fit? Select all that apply.
options: 4 cm by 6 cm
3 cm by 7 cm
5 cm by 5 cm
6 cm by 6 cm
optionExplain: Right: 2 times (4 + 6) = 20.
Right: 2 times (3 + 7) = 20.
Right: a square is a rectangle, and 2 times (5 + 5) = 20.
Its perimeter is 24 cm, not 20.
questions.explain: Length plus width must be 10 cm. Three of these pairs add to 10, so the rectangle is not determined by the perimeter alone.
questions.rule: Count what the kept condition still allows.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: a square with only two corners on the triangle's base, and nothing else required, can be drawn small or large.
questions.explain: Our reading, from the same idea: two corners on the base leave the size of the square free, so it can be small or large, which is the variation the teacher asks the student to draw.
questions.rule: Ask each time what remains free.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The student says the square is not determined by the part he kept. How does the teacher respond?
options: He says the answer is wrong and asks for the whole condition
He ends the lesson and gives the solution
He approves it and then asks how the square can vary
He asks the student to drop a second part of the condition
optionExplain: The student's answer is correct, not wrong.
The teacher gives no solution; he keeps asking.
Right: he says 'Good!' and goes on to ask how the square can vary.
Dropping a further part would leave the square even less determined.
questions.explain: Finding the unknown undetermined is not a failure: the teacher says 'Good!' and asks how it can vary.
questions.rule: An undetermined unknown is a lead: ask how it can vary.
questions.teaches: When the student says the square is not determined, the teacher approves and asks how it can vary.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A pupil draws rectangles with three corners fixed on given lines and the fourth free. What would the book's method have her watch?
options: Only the three fixed corners and the lines they lie on
The free fourth corner and how it can vary
The colour and thickness of the pencil she uses
Only the first rectangle she drew, ignoring the rest
optionExplain: The fixed corners are already settled; watching them shows nothing about what can vary.
Right: in the book the teacher draws attention to the one corner not yet where it should be.
The pencil has no bearing on the shape.
One example shows nothing about variation.
questions.explain: In the book the teacher focuses the student on the fourth corner, the one that is not yet where it should be, and on how it can vary.
questions.rule: Watch the one part that is still free.
questions.teaches: The teacher turns attention to the single corner of the square that is not yet where it should be, and asks how that corner can vary.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Several squares with three corners on a triangle's outline are drawn, and each fourth corner is marked. The marks might form:
options: A path or pattern that can be described
A single point, since all squares are alike
A scatter with no pattern at all
A circle around the triangle
optionExplain: Right: marked corners of varying figures often fall on a describable path, called a locus.
The squares differ in size, so their corners do not coincide.
Some scatter is possible, but the method hopes for a pattern, so draw enough cases to see one.
Nothing in the problem points to a circle.
questions.explain: A good guess is that the marks follow a pattern. The card next calls the set of positions a locus.
questions.rule: Look for the path of the free point.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The set of positions that the free corner takes as the square varies is called its ____.
questions.explain: The locus of a point is the set of positions it can take while the figure varies.
questions.rule: Locus = set of positions of the free point.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Tom draws six squares with three corners on a triangle and marks each fourth corner. What should he do next?
options: Average the six marks to get one point to stand for them all
Erase the squares because they all fail the full condition of four corners
Look at the marks and ask what path they seem to lie on
Draw a seventh square without looking at the marks of the others
optionExplain: Averaging loses the pattern the marks show.
The squares are not failures; they are the experiment.
Right: the pattern of the marks is the thing to name.
Ignoring the marks wastes what the drawings show.
questions.explain: The marks are the data of the experiment; the question is where they seem to lie.
questions.rule: Study the marks after drawing the cases.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Put the steps of the book's approach in order.
items: Keep three corners on the outline and drop the fourth
Ask how the square can vary
Draw more squares, small and large
Ask what the locus of the fourth corner seems to be
questions.explain: First keep part of the condition, then ask how the unknown can vary, then draw cases, and then ask where the free corner goes.
questions.rule: Part of the condition, how it varies, cases, locus.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In the book, which guess about the locus of the fourth corner would solve the key difficulty?
options: That it is a single point
That it is a circle
That it is the base of the triangle
That it is a straight line
optionExplain: The corners of different squares do not coincide.
No circle appears in the passage.
The base holds two of the corners already, not the fourth.
Right: if the student guesses it is a straight line, he has got it.
questions.explain: The book says that if the student can guess that the locus of the fourth corner is a straight line, he has the key to the solution.
questions.rule: A good guess of the locus can be the key.
questions.teaches: If the student guesses that the locus of the fourth corner is a straight line, he has got the key to the solution.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A tutor wants a pupil to find the path of a point herself. By the book's example, which tutor move fits?
options: Ask her to draw more cases and say what the path seems to be
Give her a formula for the path and ask her to check it by hand
Tell her the path right away to save time for the lesson
Tell her to stop drawing and trust what she remembers of the topic
optionExplain: Right: the teacher in the book asks for more drawings and a guess.
A formula skips the experiment.
Telling removes the discovery that the teacher in the book works to bring about.
Memory is no substitute for the drawn cases.
questions.explain: The teacher in the book brings the student very near to the idea without stating it, by asking for more cases and a guess.
questions.rule: Lead by questions; let the pupil see the pattern.
questions.teaches: The teacher brings the student very near to the idea of the solution without stating it; the guess is left to the student.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: You are asked to prove: if two whole numbers are both even, their sum is even. What do you write first?
options: The sum of two particular numbers, such as 4 and 6
What is given and what has to be shown
A long list of even numbers
The word even, defined several ways
optionExplain: One example shows the claim for 4 and 6 only; a proof must cover all pairs.
Right: the two parts, hypothesis and conclusion, come first.
A list can suggest the claim but does not state the parts.
Defining even may be needed later, but it comes after the parts are stated.
questions.explain: First say what may be assumed and what must be reached. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Hypothesis and conclusion first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In a problem to prove, the statement that must be established is the ____.
questions.explain: The conclusion is what has to be shown. What you may use is the hypothesis.
questions.rule: Hypothesis = given; conclusion = to show.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Prove: if a triangle has two equal sides, then it has two equal angles. Which pair of parts is right?
options: Hypothesis: two angles of the triangle are equal; conclusion: two of its sides are equal
Hypothesis: the triangle is drawn large on the page; conclusion: its sides are all equal
Hypothesis: the triangle has been drawn; conclusion: the triangle has then been named
Hypothesis: a triangle has two equal sides; conclusion: it has two equal angles
optionExplain: This swaps the two parts.
Size is not in the statement.
Drawing and naming are tools, not the statement.
Right: the 'if' part is the hypothesis and the 'then' part is the conclusion.
questions.explain: The 'if' clause is the hypothesis and the 'then' clause is the conclusion.
questions.rule: If-part = hypothesis; then-part = conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Sort each statement about the two-angle theorem: part of the hypothesis, or the conclusion?

items.t: The two angles lie in different planes
Each side of one angle is parallel to the matching side of the other
The matching sides point in the same direction
The two angles are equal
Angle BAC equals angle B'A'C'

questions.explain: Everything about planes, parallel sides and directions is given. Only the equality of the angles is to be shown.
questions.rule: Sort given facts from the claim to be shown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: What does the book say about its list of questions when the problem is one to prove?
options: Only the question about the unknown is kept, and the rest dropped
The list cannot be used for problems to prove at all
Questions of the list have counterparts for problems to prove
The list is replaced by a new set of questions with nothing in common
optionExplain: Even the unknown has a counterpart, the conclusion.
The text treats the list as usable, with counterparts.
Right: the questions that correspond to the earlier ones are used for problems to prove.
The counterparts correspond to the earlier questions; they are not unrelated.
questions.explain: Problems to prove correspond to problems to find, so the list has counterpart questions; 'What is the hypothesis?' and 'What is the conclusion?' stand where the data and unknown stood.
questions.rule: The same list works, with counterpart questions.
questions.teaches: The questions and suggestions of the list have counterparts for problems to prove, in the way problems to prove correspond to problems to find.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Before setting the two-angle proof, what does the book say about the students?
options: They must already have studied calculus and differentiation rules
They should know plane geometry and a few facts of solid geometry
They need no earlier geometry, because the theorem is stated in words
They must know Euclid's whole work by heart before they begin
optionExplain: Calculus appears in the rate problem, not here.
Right: the book names plane geometry and a few facts of solid geometry.
The theorem needs some background before it can be proved.
Only the facts that prepare this theorem are needed, not the whole work.
questions.explain: The book says the problem may be given to students who know plane geometry and the few facts of solid geometry that lead to this theorem.
questions.rule: Check what students know before setting a proof.
questions.teaches: The problem suits students who know plane geometry and the few facts of solid geometry that prepare the theorem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: You must prove two lengths equal. What would help most as a first thought?
options: A theorem you know that ends by saying two lengths are equal
A large picture drawn with as many colours as the pen box allows
The longest proof you can remember, whatever its subject
The hypothesis of a theorem about something unrelated to the goal
optionExplain: Right: a familiar theorem with a similar conclusion shows what you need to establish.
Colours can make a figure clearer but do not connect to what you know.
Length of proof does not make it relevant.
An unrelated hypothesis has no connection with your goal.
questions.explain: A result you already know and which ends as your goal ends is a natural help. The card next says how to look for it.
questions.rule: Match the conclusion with a known theorem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Look at the conclusion and try to think of a familiar ____ having the same or a similar conclusion.
questions.explain: The teacher asks the student to think of a familiar theorem whose conclusion resembles the one to be proved.
questions.rule: Match the conclusion to a known theorem.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: To show two shelves are the same length, Ana recalls: two rods each equal to a third rod are equal to each other. What should she look for?
options: A rule with the word shelf somewhere in its name or its wording
A shelf that is longer than both of the two shelves to be compared
A third object, such as a rail, equal in length to each shelf
Nothing, because the recalled rule cannot be used in this problem
optionExplain: The name of the object is irrelevant to whether a rule fits.
A longer shelf says nothing about the two being equal.
Right: the recalled rule works if she can find a third thing equal to each shelf.
The rule may fit; Ana has to see what it needs.
questions.explain: The recalled rule says what its use requires: a third thing equal to each. Ana now has something definite to look for.
questions.rule: A known theorem shows what you need to find.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: a recalled theorem is useless as soon as you do not yet see how to apply it.
questions.explain: In the book the student thinks he can use the theorem but does not yet see how, and the teacher goes on with a further step. Not seeing how yet is a stage, not an end.
questions.rule: Not seeing how yet is not the same as not fitting.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The student thinks the theorem can be used but does not see how. What does the teacher ask next?
options: Whether to give up the theorem and look for a different one
Whether the theorem has a different name in older books
Whether the student has the hypothesis stated correctly
Whether some auxiliary element should be introduced
optionExplain: The teacher keeps the theorem.
The name of the theorem is not at issue.
The hypothesis was already stated correctly.
Right: the next question is about introducing an auxiliary element.
questions.explain: When the student cannot yet see how to use the theorem, the teacher asks whether an auxiliary element should be introduced.
questions.rule: If a theorem does not fit, ask whether something should be added.
questions.teaches: When the student cannot yet see how to use the recalled theorem, the teacher asks whether to introduce an auxiliary element to make its use possible.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A student picks a familiar theorem and the teacher remarks that he could have chosen a worse one. What does this show?
options: Several familiar theorems may be tried; some fit better
Only one theorem can ever be chosen for a given problem
The choice made no difference to how the problem goes
The student should now go back and pick the worst one
optionExplain: Right: the teacher implies that other choices were possible, some of them worse.
The remark itself shows that there were other choices.
If it made no difference the remark would be empty.
No one is asked to pick the worst.
questions.explain: The remark means that the student's choice was a good one among several possible choices, some of which would have been worse.
questions.rule: More than one theorem may be tried; some fit better.
questions.teaches: The student's choice of theorem is not the only possible one; the teacher notes that he could have chosen a worse one.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A theorem you want to use is about triangles, but your figure shows none. What could you do?
options: Change the theorem so that it fits the figure better
Add lines so that triangles appear in the figure
Drop part of the hypothesis to make room for triangles
Decide that the problem cannot be solved at all
optionExplain: Changing a proved theorem makes it unproved.
Right: adding what the theorem needs is the idea of an auxiliary element.
Dropping part of the hypothesis usually removes what you need to know.
Having no triangles yet is a gap to fill, not a proof of impossibility.
questions.explain: You can add the missing objects to the figure. The card next names this an auxiliary element.
questions.rule: Add what the theorem needs to your figure.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Should you introduce some ____ element in order to make the use of the theorem possible?
questions.explain: An auxiliary element is something added to the figure that was not in the problem, so that a theorem can be used.
questions.rule: Auxiliary element = added to make a theorem usable.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Mia wants to use the rule that a rectangle's area is length times width on an L-shaped garden. Which auxiliary element helps most?
options: A guess at the total area, written on the plan
A fence around the garden painted in a bright colour
A second garden of the same L shape beside the first
A line that splits the L into two rectangles
optionExplain: A guess does not make the rule applicable.
Colour does not change the shape.
A second garden is no easier to measure.
Right: two rectangles are shapes to which the rule applies.
questions.explain: The rule is about rectangles, so Mia adds a line that makes rectangles appear. That is the same move as joining B to C.
questions.rule: Add the missing shape, then use the known rule.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: After the student joins B to C and B' to C', which statements fit the book? Select all that apply.
options: Two triangles ABC and A'B'C' now appear in the figure
He gives up on the triangles after drawing them
He chooses the points so that AB = A'B' and AC = A'C'
If the triangles are congruent, the angle conclusion follows immediately
optionExplain: Right: the added lines make two triangles.
He keeps the triangles: they are what the congruence theorem needs.
Right: choosing equal lengths is how he sets up the congruence.
Right: corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal, so the conclusion follows at once.
questions.explain: The added lines produce triangles, he sets AB = A'B' and AC = A'C', and congruence would give the equal angles. He does not give them up.
questions.rule: Auxiliary elements serve the theorem you recalled.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: After the new aim of proving the triangles congruent, which theorem does the student recall, and what does it make his new aim?
options: Triangles with equal angles are congruent; prove the angles equal
Parallel lines are equal; prove AB = A'B'
Three equal sides make triangles congruent; prove BC = B'C'
Triangles with equal areas are congruent; prove the areas equal
optionExplain: That would assume the angle equality that is to be proved.
The student does not recall a rule about parallel lines here; AB = A'B' is already known, not the new aim.
Right: with AB = A'B' and AC = A'C' already, the missing pair is BC = B'C'.
Equal areas do not give congruence.
questions.explain: The student again looks at the new conclusion, recalls the three-sides theorem, and sees that only BC = B'C' is missing.
questions.rule: A new aim can start the same search again.
questions.teaches: The same search is repeated for the new aim: the student recalls that triangles with three pairs of equal sides are congruent, which makes proving BC = B'C' the next aim.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Lena recalls a rule that ends as her goal ends, but its starting conditions cannot be found in her figure. By the book's dialogue, what next?
options: Conclude that the recalled rule must be wrong, and discard it for good
Ask whether an auxiliary element would link the rule to the figure
Replace the goal by an easier goal that the rule does fit
Wait for the figure to change so that the rule fits
optionExplain: The rule is a proved theorem; it may simply not fit yet.
Right: this is the teacher's sequence of questions in the book.
Changing the goal abandons the problem.
A figure does not change unless you change it.
questions.explain: In the book the student recalls a theorem that does not fit. The teacher asks about auxiliary elements and then asks whether the whole hypothesis has been used.
questions.rule: A theorem that does not fit calls for an added element or a fuller use of the hypothesis.
questions.teaches: A recalled theorem may fail to fit, as the student's theorem about equal lines did, and then the teacher turns attention to auxiliary elements and to the hypothesis.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A proof stalls. Which question might uncover a missing step?
options: Have I used everything the hypothesis says?
Is the figure large enough?
Can I write the same line again more neatly?
Is the conclusion too long?
optionExplain: Right: an unused part of the hypothesis may be the missing link.
Size does not matter to the logic.
Neatness does not add a fact.
Length of the conclusion has no bearing on the steps.
questions.explain: Checking the whole hypothesis is a good way to find a missing step. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Use the whole hypothesis.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Did you use the ____ hypothesis?
questions.explain: The teacher asks whether the whole hypothesis has been used, not just the part the student first picked out.
questions.rule: Use the whole hypothesis.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Ravi knows a rod is parallel to a wall and also exactly 2 m long. He has used only the parallel fact. What does the rule suggest?
options: Look for a new wall that the rod can be tried against
Ignore the length because it is only a number, not a fact
Check what else the hypothesis says, such as the rod's length
Decide the problem has no solution because the first idea failed
optionExplain: Another wall is not in the problem.
A given length is part of the hypothesis and should not be dropped.
Right: the rod's length is part of the hypothesis and may be the missing link.
Unused information is a reason to look further, not to stop.
questions.explain: The rule asks whether the whole hypothesis was used. The length is given, so it may be what is needed.
questions.rule: List what the hypothesis says, and check each fact.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: two segments that are parallel, equal and point the same way, joined end to end, form a parallelogram.
questions.explain: Opposite sides that are parallel and equal give a parallelogram. This is the familiar configuration the student recognises.
questions.rule: Parallel and equal sides suggest a parallelogram.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Where does the student get AB = A'B', which he uses to see the parallelogram?
options: From the hypothesis, which states the lengths
From measuring the figure with a ruler
From the theorem about congruent triangles
From the construction he made earlier
optionExplain: The hypothesis gives parallel and same direction, not equal lengths.
Measuring would not prove anything.
The congruence theorem is what he wants to use, not a source of the equality.
Right: he chose the points so that AB = A'B'.
questions.explain: The equality comes from the student's own earlier construction, in which he chose B, C, B', C' so that AB = A'B' and AC = A'C'.
questions.rule: Your own constructions count as things you know.
questions.teaches: Facts that came from your own construction, such as AB = A'B' chosen earlier, count along with the hypothesis as things you can use.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A pupil sees that sums of consecutive odd numbers from 1 give 1, 4, 9 and says: 'They seem to be squares; I hope I can prove it.' What does this show?
options: He can guess a result and tell a guess from a proof
He treats his guess as if it were already proved true
He has no real interest in finding a proof of it
He should avoid guessing at all when facing a proof
optionExplain: Right: this is the quality the book praises in the student's remark.
He says he hopes to prove it, which shows he treats it as a guess.
He wants to prove it.
The book praises the ability to guess.
questions.explain: The book's teacher says the student can guess a mathematical result and distinguish clearly between proof and guess, knowing that guesses can be more or less plausible.
questions.rule: A guess may be plausible, but only a proof settles it.
questions.teaches: A good problem solver can guess a result and still keep guess and proof apart, knowing that guesses can be more or less plausible.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A word problem gives several numbers and asks for a rate. When would the book's teacher put the numbers in?
options: Before looking at any connection between the quantities
At the end, after the unknown is expressed in letters
Only after a test on a different problem
Never, because numbers are not allowed
optionExplain: Early numbers can hide connections.
Right: letters first, numbers last.
A test on another problem is not part of the method.
Numbers are used at the end.
questions.explain: Letters first keeps the connections visible. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: Letters first, numbers at the end.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: the teacher substitutes the given numbers before looking for any connection between the quantities.
questions.explain: He suggests disregarding the numerical values for now, working with the letters and substituting the numbers only at the end.
questions.rule: Numbers last.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Water fills a box-shaped tank with an l by w base at r cubic metres per minute. Working with letters, which expression gives the rate at which the depth rises?
options: r times l times w
l times w divided by r
r divided by the sum l plus w
r divided by (l times w)
optionExplain: This multiplies the inflow by the base area, which makes the depth rise faster for a bigger base.
This inverts the correct expression.
The base area is l times w, not l plus w.
Right: volume added per minute r spread over the base area l times w.
questions.explain: In one minute r cubic metres spread over a base of area l times w, raising the depth by r divided by (l times w).
questions.rule: Find the expression in letters first.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The rate of rise is r divided by (l times w). With l = 2 m, w = 3 m and r = 0.3 cubic metres per minute, the depth rises ____ metres per minute.
questions.explain: The base area is 6 square metres, and 0.3 divided by 6 is 0.05. With r = 0.6 the rate would be 0.10, since doubling r doubles the rate.
questions.rule: Once the expression is in letters, any numbers drop in at the end.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In the cone problem, why does the teacher have the student disregard y = 1 ft for now?
options: Because feet cannot be used in a formula
Because 1 ft is too small to measure
Because y is the depth, which changes with time
Because the unknown does not depend on the depth at all
optionExplain: Units are not the issue.
The size of the number is not the issue.
Right: y has to be imagined as changing, so it is a variable.
The unknown is the rate at which the depth changes.
questions.explain: The depth y increases with time, so the student must treat it as a changing quantity and not as the single value 1 ft.
questions.rule: Keep a changing quantity as a letter.
questions.teaches: The given depth y = 1 ft is the depth at one moment; since y changes as time goes by, it must stay a letter until the end.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A worksheet ends: 'Finally, find the number when the length is 5 m.' What does this wording suggest?
options: Replace the length by 5 at the start to save effort
Work with letters first and put in 5 at the end
Letters are not allowed on this worksheet
Only the final number is worth checking
optionExplain: Early substitution hides how the answer depends on the length.
Right: like the book's rate problem, the statement asks for the number only finally.
The worksheet does not forbid letters.
Checking only the last step wastes the general result.
questions.explain: In the book the statement asks for the numerical value 'finally', and the teacher takes that as a suggestion to work with letters first.
questions.rule: Read the statement for a hint about the order of work.
questions.teaches: In the book it is the statement itself that suggests the order, since it asks for the numerical value only finally.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: You are asked how fast the water is rising in a tank. What is a useful first move?
options: Say it in other words, such as how fast the depth increases
Fix the depth at a single value and then ignore how time passes
Measure the tank at once, before saying what is asked
Skip the wording and guess a number to start from
optionExplain: Right: restating it brings you nearer to something you can write.
Fixing the depth hides the change that is being asked about.
Measuring is useful later but does not clarify the unknown.
A guess gives no method.
questions.explain: Restating the unknown in plainer terms is the first step. The card next shows where it ends.
questions.rule: Restate the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Restating the unknown again and again leads back to a ____.
questions.explain: The teacher keeps asking 'What is that?' until the student reaches the definition of the rate of change.
questions.rule: Restate until you reach a definition.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Restate how fast a candle is getting shorter in the book's way. Where does the chain end?
options: At the height of the candle at the moment it was lit
At the product of the height h and the time t
At dh/dt, the rate of change of the height h
At the total burning time t of the whole candle
optionExplain: A starting value is a number, not a rate.
Multiplying h and t does not give a rate.
Right: the rate of change of a quantity with time is its derivative.
Total time is not the rate at which the height changes.
questions.explain: The rate at which the candle shortens is the rate of change of its height h, a function of time t, written dh/dt.
questions.rule: A rate of change of a function is its derivative.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Sort each phrase against the unknown 'the rate at which the water surface is rising'.

items.t: The rate at which the depth of the water increases
The rate of change of the depth
dy/dt, where y is the depth and t the time
The volume of the water in the vessel
The rate at which water flows in
The radius of the base

questions.explain: The first three say the same thing in different words. The volume, the inflow rate and the radius are other quantities of the problem.
questions.rule: A restatement must keep the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: The data r is the rate at which water flows into the vessel. How does the teacher write it?
options: r is the depth y of the water at the moment considered
r = dy/dt, which is the same as the unknown rate
r is the rate of change of the radius of the cone's surface
r = dV/dt, with V the volume of the water at time t
optionExplain: The depth is the quantity y, not r.
dy/dt is the unknown, not the data.
The radius is not the quantity whose change is r.
Right: r is the rate of change of the volume of the water.
questions.explain: The teacher treats the data r in the same way: r is the rate of change of the volume, written dV/dt.
questions.rule: Data that are rates can be restated too.
questions.teaches: The data r is also a rate, and the teacher restates it as the rate of change of the volume V of the water at time t, written dV/dt.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A pupil writes dr/dt for how fast a balloon's radius grows but does not say what r stands for. What would the book's teacher ask?
options: What is r, and at which moment is it the radius?
Why not use the letter x instead of the letter r?
What colour is the balloon before it is blown up?
How many balloons are there in the room altogether?
optionExplain: Right: like 'What is V?', he asks what the symbol means, here the radius at time t.
The letter is not the issue; the meaning is.
Colour is not part of the problem.
The number of balloons is not part of the problem.
questions.explain: In the book the teacher asks 'What is V?' and the student answers: the volume of the water at the time t. Every symbol needs a stated meaning.
questions.rule: Say what each symbol stands for.
questions.teaches: After writing a symbol, the teacher asks what it is, and the student must say what it stands for and at what moment.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Water is poured into a funnel. You want the volume in terms of the depth but see no direct link. What might help?
options: Wait until the funnel is completely full and then measure the water
Look for a simpler link, such as depth and surface width
Choose any number for the volume and work from that
Ignore the depth and use only the size of the funnel
optionExplain: Waiting changes nothing about the relation.
Right: simpler connections can serve as stepping stones.
A chosen number is not a relation.
The depth is the quantity you are linking to, so it cannot be ignored.
questions.explain: Look for simpler links between related quantities. The card next shows how they chain.
questions.rule: Chain simpler connections.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: the depth of the water and its volume are independent of each other.
questions.explain: When the depth increases the volume must increase too, so the two quantities are connected.
questions.rule: Dependent quantities are linked by a relation.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A conical funnel (point down) has top radius a = 6 cm and height b = 12 cm. The water is 4 cm deep. With x = ay/b and V = (1/3)πx²y, what is V?
options: About 268.1 cubic cm
About 50.3 cubic cm
About 150.8 cubic cm
About 16.8 cubic cm
optionExplain: This uses x = by/a = 8 cm, the ratio upside down.
This leaves out the factor one third.
This uses the full top radius 6 cm instead of the radius 2 cm at the water's surface.
Right: x = 2 cm, so V = (1/3)π(4)(4) = 16π/3, about 16.8.
questions.explain: By similar triangles x = 6 times 4 divided by 12 = 2 cm. Then V = (1/3)π times 2 squared times 4 = 16π/3, about 16.8 cubic cm.
questions.rule: Use the surface radius, not the top radius.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: With a and b fixed, V = πa²y³ divided by 3b². If the depth y doubles, V is multiplied by ____.
questions.explain: Because y appears cubed, doubling y multiplies the volume by 2 cubed = 8.
questions.rule: Check how the relation depends on each variable.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: How does the teacher lead the student to see that the depth and the volume are connected?
options: By handing the student the formula for the volume
By measuring a real vessel and noting readings
By asking if y and V are independent of each other
By differentiating at once, before any link has been found
optionExplain: The formula is found by the student.
No real vessel is measured.
Right: the question about independence exposes the connection.
Differentiating comes later.
questions.explain: Asking whether two quantities are independent of each other makes the student see the dependence, which is then written as a relation.
questions.rule: Ask whether two quantities are independent.
questions.teaches: Asking whether two quantities are independent of each other is a way to expose a connection that can then be written down.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A pupil finds that a trip's cost depends on its length, then that its length depends on the number of stops. What does the teacher's example advise?
options: Stop here, since only the first link she found can count
Use the new link too, as it may lead to what she wants
Drop the first link as soon as the second one is found
Wait until a third link appears before using any of them
optionExplain: Each new link can help.
Right: the teacher says one more connection is not to be missed, since it can help.
The first link is still useful, and the chain needs both.
One more link is already available to use.
questions.explain: The teacher says: one more connection, you see; I would not miss profiting from it. Each new link extends the chain.
questions.rule: Use every connection that leads toward the goal.
questions.teaches: Each new connection should be used: the teacher says not to miss profiting from one more connection.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: You have a relation giving V in terms of y, but need the rate at which y changes with time. What is a natural next move?
options: Differentiate it with respect to time
Replace y by the number 1 at once and carry on
Draw a larger vessel and measure it again
Choose V to equal y so that they cancel
optionExplain: Right: differentiating links the rates.
Putting in a number removes the change you want.
A larger vessel gives the same relation.
V and y are different quantities.
questions.explain: To get a relation between rates, differentiate. The card next shows the result.
questions.rule: Differentiate to get rates.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: Having a relation between V and y, the student ____ it to link the rates of change.
questions.explain: Differentiating the relation with respect to time turns it into a relation between dV/dt and dy/dt.
questions.rule: Differentiate the relation to link rates.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A cone vessel (point down) has a = 3 ft and b = 6 ft. Water enters at r = 1.5 cu ft per minute. Using dV/dt = (πa²y²/b²)(dy/dt), how fast does the depth rise at y = 2 ft?
options: About 0.95 ft per minute
About 0.08 ft per minute
About 0.48 ft per minute
About 2.09 ft per minute
optionExplain: This takes y to the first power instead of squared.
This uses b instead of b squared.
Right: dy/dt = r b² divided by (π a² y²) = 54 divided by 36π = 1.5/π, about 0.48.
This turns the expression upside down.
questions.explain: Solving for dy/dt gives r b² divided by (π a² y²) = 1.5 times 36 divided by (π times 9 times 4) = 1.5/π, about 0.48 ft per minute.
questions.rule: Solve for the unknown rate, then put the numbers in.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: True or false: with r, a and b fixed, dy/dt = r b² divided by (π a² y²) gets smaller as the depth y grows.
questions.explain: A bigger y makes the denominator bigger, so dy/dt falls. The same inflow spreads over a wider surface as the depth grows.
questions.rule: Read what the formula says about each variable.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: With V expressed in terms of y, the teacher says the student should not forget his goal. What is the goal?
options: To find V for y = 1
To find the angle of the cone
To find the radius x
To find the unknown dy/dt
optionExplain: V is a stepping stone, not the goal.
No angle is asked for.
The radius x is only a helper quantity.
Right: the unknown is dy/dt, the rate of change of the depth.
questions.explain: After the connection between V and y is found, the teacher reminds the student that the unknown is dy/dt, which is what the next step must reach.
questions.rule: Check the unknown before the next step.
questions.teaches: The teacher calls the relation a stepping stone but reminds the student of his goal by asking what the unknown is.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: A cylindrical vessel of base radius a is filled at rate r, so V = πa²y. Using the same method, how does the rate of rise depend on the depth?
options: It does not depend on y: dy/dt = r divided by πa²
It increases as y increases, because the surface widens
It decreases as y squared increases, as in the cone
It depends on y cubed, as the cone's volume does
optionExplain: Right: dV/dt = πa² times dy/dt, and y does not appear in the factor.
This would need y in the numerator.
That is the cone's behaviour, not the cylinder's.
Cubes appeared in the cone's volume, not here.
questions.explain: Differentiating V = πa²y gives dV/dt = πa² times dy/dt, so the rate of rise is r divided by πa² at every depth. In the cone the factor of dy/dt is πa²y²/b², which contains y.
questions.rule: The shape of the vessel decides how the rate depends on depth.
questions.teaches: In the cone the factor multiplying dy/dt is πa²y²/b², which contains y, so the rate of rise there depends on the depth.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A friend hands you a word problem about a ladder against a wall. What is a sound first move?
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The author begins with the statement and a view of the whole; the card next shows why.
options: Start calculating at once with the first numbers you see in the text.
Picture the whole situation and what is asked, leaving details for later.
Recall the nearest formula you know and put the given numbers into it.
Split the text into sentences and solve each sentence on its own first.
optionExplain: Numbers feel productive, but computing before you grasp the question often solves the wrong thing.
Right: the author starts from the statement and pictures the problem as a whole, without concern for details at first.
A formula may fit, but choosing one before understanding the problem is premature.
Sentences are not separate problems; the parts only make sense in relation to the whole.
questions.rule: See the whole first, then relate the principal parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Complete: in the first pass, visualize the problem as a ____ and do not concern yourself with details yet.
questions.explain: The author asks you to see the problem as a whole, as clearly and vividly as you can, before details.
questions.rule: First the whole, then the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: You must find a meeting date and room for a group, within a budget. Which action follows the second pass?
questions.explain: The second pass isolates the principal parts and relates them to each other and to the whole.
options: Book the cheapest room first, then see which dates remain open for the group.
Reread the first line slowly while picturing the whole event once more.
List the unknown, the data and the conditions, and relate them to each other.
Copy last year's arrangements and adjust them wherever they happen to fail there.
optionExplain: This commits to a detail before the parts have been related to each other.
This repeats the first pass; the second pass moves on to the principal parts.
Right: the principal parts of a problem to find are the unknown, the data and the conditions, considered one by one and in combination.
Past arrangements may help later, but the second pass prepares details first.
questions.rule: See the whole first, then relate the principal parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it follows the dialogue's advice for the first two phases.
questions.explain: The advice is: see the whole, wait until the statement is clear, then relate the principal parts to each other and to the whole. Calculating early, starting the second pass on a hazy statement, or listing parts without relating them breaks that.
questions.rule: Do not skip the whole, and do not list parts without relating them.

items.t: Pictures the whole problem before looking at any detail
Names the data, the condition and the unknown, then asks how each relates to the rest
Starts working numbers from the second sentence before reading the question
Isolates the hypothesis and conclusion of a proof problem and relates them
Begins the second pass while the statement is still hazy, planning to reread it later
Lists the details one by one but never compares them with each other or with the whole

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Now the task is to prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even. According to the author, which are its principal parts?
questions.explain: Which parts you isolate depends on the kind of problem: to prove or to find.
options: The unknown, the data and the conditions.
The hypothesis and the conclusion.
The plan, the steps and the check.
The statement, the picture and the answer.
optionExplain: These are the principal parts of a problem to find, and this is a problem to prove.
Right: for a problem to prove, the author names the hypothesis and the conclusion as the principal parts.
These are phases of work, not parts of the problem itself.
These are not parts the author names; the statement is the starting point.
questions.rule: See the whole first, then relate the principal parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A technician must trace why a monthly report shows wrong totals. Before checking any formula she studies the whole report's purpose. What else can this do, according to the author?
questions.explain: Looking at the whole is about understanding, and the author adds that it can also awaken relevant memories.
questions.teaches: Giving full attention to the problem may also stimulate memory and prepare the recollection of relevant points.
options: It can stimulate her memory and prepare recalling relevant points.
It can replace the later step of examining the report's parts in turn.
It can show her the solution at a glance in most such cases.
It can guarantee she will not need any further ideas for the repair.
optionExplain: Right: the author says close attention to the problem may also stimulate memory and prepare the recollection of relevant points.
The author describes a second pass on the parts afterwards; the first does not replace it.
The author promises understanding, not an instant solution.
Nothing in the dialogue promises that no more ideas are needed; the later phases exist for them.
questions.rule: See the whole first, then relate the principal parts.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: You are stuck on a problem and nothing comes to mind. Which approach seems most promising?
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next sets out the author's two moves.
options: Wait quietly until a flash of insight arrives by itself in its own time.
Reread the same wording again, with the same emphasis, until it opens up.
Look at the problem from several sides and link it to what you know.
Look up the final answer first and then work backwards from it to the start.
optionExplain: Insight may come, but waiting adds no new view of the problem.
Repeating one reading rarely changes what you see; the author wants different emphases.
Right: the author advises considering the problem from various sides and seeking contacts with formerly acquired knowledge.
The dialogue does not recommend this; it is about finding the idea yourself.
questions.rule: Vary your view, connect to what you know, and follow each idea as far as it goes.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Complete: consider your problem from various sides and seek contacts with your formerly acquired ____.
questions.explain: The author names two moves: look at the problem from various sides, and seek contact with what you have already learned.
questions.rule: Vary the view; connect to what you know.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A volunteer's rota keeps clashing. Which step follows the author's advice to seek contacts with formerly acquired knowledge?
questions.explain: Seeking contacts means asking what helped before and whether it recurs here.
options: Recall a past scheduling clash that was solved and test its fix here.
Write the rota again from scratch without ever looking at the old one.
Ask each volunteer to swap shifts until nobody is left complaining.
Treat the clash as unsolvable until a new scheduling tool is bought.
optionExplain: Right: the author asks you to think of what helped in similar situations in the past and to recognise something familiar.
Starting over discards what the old rota can tell you and does not use past knowledge.
Swapping at random does not draw on any earlier solved problem.
Giving up does not seek any contact with earlier knowledge.
questions.rule: Vary your view, connect to what you know, and follow each idea as far as it goes.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Put the author's steps for handling an incomplete idea in order.
questions.explain: You consider the idea first; if it looks advantageous, consider it longer; if it looks reliable, find how far it leads; then, because the situation has changed, reconsider it from various sides and seek contacts again.
questions.rule: Consider, consider longer, see how far it leads, then look again.
items: Consider the incomplete idea
If it looks advantageous, consider it longer
If it looks reliable, find out how far it leads you
Reconsider the changed situation from various sides and seek contacts again

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, every helpful idea will carry you straight to the solution.
questions.explain: False. The author says ideas are more or less complete, you may be led astray by some of them, and several may be needed.
questions.rule: Ideas vary in completeness; some mislead.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Sort each action by the move it belongs to.
questions.explain: Emphasizing parts, examining details in new ways, and combining them differently change the view. Recalling similar past help and recognising something familiar connect to earlier knowledge.
questions.rule: Vary the view, or connect to what you know.

items.t: Emphasize a different part of the problem
Recall what helped in a similar situation before
Combine the same details in a new way
Try to recognise something familiar in what you examine
Examine the same detail again in a different way
Think of an earlier problem with the same kind of unknown

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A writer spends an hour restructuring a muddled essay and finds no breakthrough, but now sees it as three separate arguments. What does the author say about this?
questions.explain: A clearer, better-balanced view of the problem is progress even without a breakthrough.
questions.teaches: Even when no appreciable new idea arrives, be grateful if your conception of the problem becomes more complete, coherent or better balanced.
options: It was wasted time, since only a decisive idea ever counts as real progress.
It is worth being grateful for, as her view of the problem became more coherent.
It shows the writer should have started from the conclusion in the first place.
It proves the earlier muddled version was correct after all, once reread.
optionExplain: The author says to be grateful for lesser and hazy ideas too, so a decisive idea is not the only progress.
Right: the author says to be grateful if the conception of the problem becomes more complete, coherent, homogeneous or better balanced, even without a new idea.
The dialogue says nothing about where to start in this case.
Nothing links a clearer view to the earlier version being correct.
questions.rule: Vary your view, connect to what you know, and follow each idea as far as it goes.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: You have a plan for a long calculation. How would you make sure the finished solution is right?
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next gives the author's approach.
options: Check the plan's main stages first, then the details inside each.
Check the last line only, since any error will show up there.
Recompute every line from the end back to the start, one by one.
Trust each step that looks familiar and check only the strange ones.
optionExplain: Right: the author says to check the great steps first, then the smaller ones.
A correct last line can come from compensating errors; the author wants each step justified.
This is thorough but the author recommends a structured order, not a mechanical reversal.
Familiar steps can also be wrong; each step needs a reason or insight.
questions.rule: Justify every step, and check great steps before small ones.
