questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Complete: in a complex problem, check the ____ steps first and get down to the smaller ones afterwards.
questions.explain: The author distinguishes great steps from small ones and checks the great ones first.
questions.rule: Great steps first, small steps afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A tenant is reviewing a ten-page rental contract she has summarised in four main points. How should she check her summary, following the author?
questions.explain: Structure the checking: great steps first, then small.
options: Reread every clause once, in page order, hoping to catch any errors.
Ask a friend whether the summary sounds right to them, and stop there.
Check only the one point that worries her most and trust the rest.
Check each of the four points against the contract, then its clauses.
optionExplain: Page order is thorough but ignores the structure of main and minor steps.
A friend's impression is not a reason or an insight into each step.
Skipping parts leaves steps that are not correct beyond doubt.
Right: the great steps (the four points) come first, then the smaller steps inside them.
questions.rule: Justify every step, and check great steps before small ones.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it follows the author's advice for carrying out a plan.
questions.explain: The author wants a secure grasp before detailed work, each step justified by reasoning or insight, and great steps checked before small ones.
questions.rule: Secure grasp, justified steps, great before small.

items.t: Writes out details while only guessing at the main connection
Convinces herself of each step by formal reasoning, insight, or both
Accepts a step because it looks plausible, without a reason
Carries through the operations recognised earlier as feasible
Checks the smallest steps first and leaves the big stages unchecked
Checks the main stages of a long solution before the details inside them

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: If you carry out the plan as the author describes, what does the author say you gain?
questions.explain: Carrying out the plan aims at certainty step by step; improving comes later.
options: A new and better solution than the one you originally found yourself.
Well-ordered knowledge that is ready for use on other problems later.
A presentation of the solution with every step correct beyond doubt.
A shorter solution that you can take in at a single glance at once.
optionExplain: That is the gain the author gives for looking back, not for carrying out the plan.
This is a gain the author ties to the habit of looking back.
Right: this is the stated gain of carrying out the plan.
Seeing the whole at a glance is also an aim of looking back.
questions.rule: Justify every step, and check great steps before small ones.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A cook has the idea of scaling a recipe by weight. When does the author say it is time to start writing out every step in detail?
questions.explain: Detailed work starts from a secure grasp of the main connection.
questions.teaches: Start carrying out the plan when you feel sure of your grasp of the main connection and confident you can supply the missing minor details.
options: Once she has the first rough hint of an idea and a little time.
Once she has the first rough hint of an idea.
After she has tried every other approach she can think of.
As soon as she has restated the problem in her own words.
optionExplain: Right: the author says to start when you are sure of the main connection and confident of supplying the missing minor details.
A rough hint belongs to the hunting phase; carrying out needs a firmer grasp.
Nothing in the dialogue requires exhausting other approaches.
Restating the problem belongs to the understanding phase.
questions.rule: Justify every step, and check great steps before small ones.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: You have finished solving a problem and the answer is right. What is the most useful next move?
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next explains the author's looking back.
options: Start the next problem right away while you are still warmed up and keen.
Put the work away and avoid touching an answer that is already correct.
Check the answer again and again until you feel more sure of its truth.
Examine the solution for simpler ways and for uses of its method.
optionExplain: Moving on loses what this solution could still teach.
Leaving it alone gives up possible improvements.
The solution is already correct in each detail at this point.
Right: the author advises simplifying and shortening the solution and examining the method and result for other problems.
questions.rule: Review a finished solution to improve it and reuse its method.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Complete: scrutinize the method that led you to the solution, try to see its ____, and make use of it for other problems.
questions.explain: The author asks you to see the point of the method and reuse it.
questions.rule: Seek the point of the method and reuse it.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A scheduler has a working shift plan for her team. Which action follows the author's looking back?
questions.explain: Looking back improves a finished solution and extracts its lessons.
options: Print the plan and file it away as final without any further changes made.
Rebuild the plan from scratch with a different tool of some other kind.
Try to shorten longer parts of the plan and see the whole at a glance.
Check once more that every single shift in every week is fully covered.
optionExplain: Filing it leaves the plan unexamined.
Starting over is not what the author describes; he asks to improve this solution.
Right: the author suggests simplifying details, shortening longer parts and seeing the whole at a glance.
Coverage was settled when the solution was complete and correct.
questions.rule: Review a finished solution to improve it and reuse its method.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: Sort each reaction to a finished, correct solution by whether it follows the author's advice.
questions.explain: The author asks you to survey the solution, improve it, and scrutinize the method and result for other problems. Skipping the review, starting it too early, or treating the solution as untouchable breaks that.
questions.rule: Review the finished solution; do not treat it as closed.

items.t: Rereads the answer, then moves on to the next task
Tries to see the whole solution at a glance
Asks what the method could do for other problems
Starts the review before the solution is complete and correct
Looks at the result for use in other problems
Treats a working solution as too settled to modify

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, looking back is certain to produce a new and better solution.
questions.explain: False. The author says you may find a better solution or new facts, so these are possible but not guaranteed.
questions.rule: Looking back may pay off; it is not certain to.

questions.unitTitle: Part II: How to Solve It, a dialogue
questions.q: A team finishes a software migration that went well and a manager asks why they should review it. What reason does the author's advice give?
questions.explain: The habit of looking back is what builds knowledge and skill over time.
questions.teaches: Getting into the habit of surveying and scrutinizing solutions builds well-ordered, ready-to-use knowledge and develops your ability to solve problems.
options: It builds well-ordered, ready-to-use knowledge and develops their ability.
It lets them prove that the migration was in fact perfect in every way.
It replaces any need to plan the next project in advance of starting it.
It guarantees that their next project will go well for the whole team.
optionExplain: Right: the author says the habit of surveying and scrutinizing solutions gives such knowledge and develops ability.
The review looks for improvements and facts; it is not a way to prove perfection.
Nothing in the dialogue says it replaces planning.
The author promises possibilities and growth, not guarantees.
questions.rule: Review a finished solution to improve it and reuse its method.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A dentist says a tooth is like a house: both have a foundation and a frame. What does the book call agreement in relations among parts?
options: Analogy
Equivalence
Identity
Induction
optionExplain: Right: analogy is sameness of relations among the parts of two systems.
Equivalence is a term for problems that have the same solutions, which comes later in the dictionary.
Identity feels strongest, but two analogous systems are not the same objects at all.
Induction is a kind of conclusion drawn from cases, not the name for matching relations.
questions.explain: Analogy is agreement in the relations among parts. The next card shows how to put such a relation into words.
questions.rule: Analogy is sameness of relations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Similar objects agree in some respect; analogous objects agree in certain ____ of their parts.
questions.explain: The book separates plain similarity from analogy: analogy is a matching pattern of relations between parts.
questions.rule: Analogy matches relations, not surfaces.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A cook compares a recipe card to a building plan. Which statement names a relation that holds in both?
options: Both are printed on paper
Each step depends on earlier steps being finished first
Both contain numbers and abbreviations in a tidy layout
Both are kept in a drawer or a file
optionExplain: Paper is a shared property of the objects, not a relation among their parts.
Right: this is a relation among parts (steps or stages) that holds in both systems.
Numbers are a shared feature, but not a pattern linking part to part.
Where the objects are stored says nothing about how their parts relate.
questions.explain: A relation links parts to one another, such as depending on or being parallel to. Shared surface features do not make an analogy in the book's sense.
questions.rule: Look for how parts relate, not how things look.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each remark: does it describe an analogy in the book's sense, or only a shared feature?

items.t: Each room of a flat opens onto one hallway, as each file in a folder sits under one folder
A lion and a tabby cat are both furry
Two teams both wear red
Each section of a report supports one chapter, as each branch grows from one limb
Both a violin and a ruler are made of wood
In both systems every part is paired with exactly one opposite part

questions.explain: A relation links parts to each other. Colour, material or fur are properties of the objects themselves.
questions.rule: Analogy needs a pattern of relations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book gives rectangle sides and box faces a common name. Why does that help state the analogy?
options: It proves the two figures have the same area, which settles the analogy
It turns the rectangle into a box
One sentence about bounding elements then covers both systems
It removes the need to check the relation holds
optionExplain: Area is not at issue; the name is about wording the relation.
A name does not change a figure; it only lets us speak of both at once.
Right: the shared name lets a single statement describe both systems.
The relation still has to be true of each system; the name only compresses the description.
questions.explain: Agreeing on one term for both kinds of part lets one sentence state the common relation, and that is what makes the analogy usable.
questions.rule: A shared term lets one sentence state the shared relation.
questions.teaches: The book calls this community of relations the analogy of the two systems: the analogy consists in the relations they share.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: A shared name proves that two systems are analogous, even before checking how their parts relate.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book builds the name after checking the relation in both systems. A name alone could hide a mismatch, so the check comes first.
questions.rule: Check the relation, then name it.
questions.teaches: The book coins a common term only after showing the same relation in each system, which keeps the name honest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: Only exact mathematical analogies are worth using when solving a problem.
questions.explain: The book says all sorts of analogy may help, from vague to precise. The card next sets out why.
questions.rule: Do not neglect any sort of analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: According to the book, we should not ____ any sort of analogy when looking for a solution.
questions.explain: Analogies of all kinds can play a part in discovery.
questions.rule: Keep all sorts of analogy in play.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You are stuck on a seating plan for 30 guests. A friend says it is like sorting laundry by colour, a loose likeness. What fits the book?
options: Ignore it, because a likeness this vague cannot help
Treat it as proof the plan is solved
Wait until an exact mathematical match appears
Try the likeness as a lead and see whether it helps
optionExplain: Vagueness feels disqualifying, but the book says vague analogies may still help.
A loose likeness suggests a path; it does not settle anything.
Waiting for precision throws away leads the book says we should not neglect.
Right: the book says even incomplete analogies can play a role in discovery.
questions.explain: A loose analogy can still give an idea to try. Whether it works is decided by trying it, not by how neat it sounds.
questions.rule: Try a rough analogy; do not trust it blindly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student uses a vague analogy and finds it fails. What does the book's attitude suggest she does next?
options: Conclude analogy is useless in problem solving
Drop that analogy and look for others, since any sort may help
Switch only to analogies that are mathematically exact
Insist the analogy must be right and force the problem to fit it
optionExplain: One failure feels decisive, but the book says analogy pervades thinking and all sorts may help.
Right: failure of one analogy does not close the door on others.
Restricting to exact analogies ignores the book's advice to neglect no sort.
Forcing a poor fit confuses a clue with a proof.
questions.explain: A failed lead is dropped; the habit of looking for analogies stays. Our reading: the cost of trying a rough analogy is small compared with the possible gain.
questions.rule: Do not dismiss a rough analogy; use it as a lead, and know how rough it is.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: According to the book, where does analogy appear? Select all that apply.
options: Everyday speech
Trivial conclusions
Artistic ways of expression
Only in geometry
The highest scientific achievements
optionExplain: Right: the book names everyday speech.
Right: even trivial conclusions rest on analogy.
Right: art uses analogy too.
Geometry gives the book's examples, but it does not limit analogy to geometry.
Right: analogy reaches the highest scientific work.
questions.explain: The book says analogy pervades all our thinking, from daily speech to great science. It is not confined to one subject.
questions.teaches: Analogy can reach the level of mathematical precision, so it covers a range from vague to exact.
questions.rule: Do not dismiss a rough analogy; use it as a lead, and know how rough it is.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A manager compares onboarding a new hire to teaching a child to ride a bike. What is the best use of this comparison, on the book's view?
options: A lead to examine: which relations really match?
A rule that must be followed to the letter
A proof the training plan is sound
Worthless, since the two cases differ in many ways
optionExplain: Right: a rough analogy is a source of ideas to test.
Following it to the letter treats a likeness as a law.
A likeness cannot prove a plan sound.
Differences exist in every analogy; the book would still keep the lead open.
questions.explain: Our reading: treat a rough analogy as a prompt to ask which relations match and where they break. The book says vague analogies may still help find a solution.
questions.teaches: Analogies are often vague, ambiguous or incompletely clarified; clarifying them is part of using them.
questions.rule: Do not dismiss a rough analogy; use it as a lead, and know how rough it is.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You must plan a seating chart for 200 wedding guests and cannot see where to start. Which first move might the book support?
options: Ask for a bigger venue to remove the problem
Seat everyone at random and fix problems later
Wait until the guest list is final before doing any planning
Plan a similar chart for 8 guests and see what it teaches
optionExplain: A bigger venue changes the situation instead of understanding the problem.
Random seating feels fast, but it ignores structure the simpler case would reveal.
Waiting avoids the difficulty rather than reducing it.
Right: a smaller problem of the same shape is a simpler analogue.
questions.explain: Working a smaller version with the same pattern is the kind of step the card describes. The card next states it as a rule.
questions.rule: Try a simpler problem of the same kind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's example, the simpler problem for the centre of gravity of a tetrahedron concerns a ____.
questions.explain: The triangle in the plane is the simpler analogous problem to the tetrahedron in space.
questions.rule: The triangle stands in for the tetrahedron.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book earlier used a rectangle to help with a box. Which pairing follows the same move?
options: Find the volume of a box before the area of a rectangle
Find the colour of the box before its size, so that the box is easier to see
Find the length of a diagonal of a rectangle before a diagonal of a box
Find the diagonal of a box before any smaller case
optionExplain: This goes from a simple figure to a harder one's quantity, not from the hard problem to a simpler one.
Colour has no relation to the structure of the question.
Right: the rectangle is a simpler analogous problem to the box.
This keeps the hard problem and adds nothing simpler.
questions.explain: The simpler case shares the pattern (a diagonal across a figure with right angles) but has one dimension fewer.
questions.rule: Drop a dimension, a case or a constraint but keep the pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each choice: is it a simpler analogous problem for a 12-person tournament schedule, or not?

items.t: Schedule a tournament with 4 people
Schedule a tournament with 6 people
Choose a trophy colour
Schedule 12 people, but ignore the venue limits
Schedule a similar tournament with 3 teams
Count how many chairs the hall has

questions.explain: A good simpler problem keeps the pattern (every pair must meet) and shrinks the size. Choosing a colour or counting chairs belongs to other questions.
questions.hint: Does it keep the same pattern with fewer demands?
questions.rule: Replace a hard problem by an analogous easier one, and connect the two on purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book says two questions may be easier to answer than one, provided they are intelligently connected.
questions.explain: The extra question helps because its answer is fed back into the original. If the two are unconnected, nothing is gained.
questions.rule: Connect the two problems on purpose.
questions.teaches: The two problems must be intelligently connected; an easier problem with no link to the original adds work without help.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A programmer must fix a bug in a 5,000-line program. She tries to reproduce it in a 20-line program. When does this pay off?
options: When the small program has the same structure that causes the bug
Whenever the small program is shorter than the large one, whatever it does
Whenever the small program runs without any errors at all
Only when the original program has fewer than 6,000 lines
optionExplain: Right: the shortcut works only if the small case is truly analogous.
Being shorter makes it simpler, but not necessarily analogous.
Running without errors says nothing about whether it shares the cause.
The line count of the original is not the issue; the shared structure is.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's tetrahedron-triangle pair shares a pattern (parts, symmetry, balance). Without a shared pattern, a smaller problem is just a different problem.
questions.teaches: The book calls us lucky when a simpler analogous problem is found, so finding one is not guaranteed.
questions.rule: Replace a hard problem by an analogous easier one, and connect the two on purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: When you move to a simpler analogous problem, you should keep working on both problems at once.
questions.explain: The book puts the original aside for the moment and concentrates on the simpler problem. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Finish the simple problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the triangle solution, the midpoints of all the strips lie on a line joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, called a ____.
questions.explain: Each strip's balance point is its midpoint, and these lie on one median of the triangle.
questions.rule: Strip midpoints lie on a median.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Put the steps of the triangle solution in order.
items: State a plausible principle about centres of gravity in a plane
Cut the triangle into thin strips parallel to one side
Note that each strip's midpoint lies on one median
Conclude the centre lies on that median
Repeat for the other sides: the centre is where the three medians meet
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before: the principle licenses the use of strip midpoints, which fixes a line, then three lines fix a point.
questions.rule: Principle, strips, midpoints, one median, then three medians.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student says: the triangle strips are parallel to AB, so the centre lies on side AB itself. What went wrong?
options: Strips parallel to a side cannot be used in a triangle
The centre of gravity must be a vertex, since vertices carry all the weight of a triangle
Medians cannot contain the centre of any figure
Strip midpoints lie on the median from the opposite vertex, not on side AB
optionExplain: The book uses exactly such strips, so this denies the method.
A vertex is a corner, not a balance point of an even triangle.
The book shows the centre lies on every median.
Right: the strips' midpoints line up on the median from the vertex opposite AB.
questions.explain: The line of midpoints runs from the opposite vertex to the midpoint of AB. It meets AB only at its middle, not along it.
questions.rule: Midpoints of strips parallel to a side lie on the median to that side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How many medians must the centre of gravity of a triangle lie on, according to the same argument repeated for each side?
options: One
Three
Two only
Six
optionExplain: One median is what a single set of strips gives, but the argument works for every side.
Right: one median per side, and the centre lies on all of them.
Two lines already fix the point, but the argument gives a third for every side.
Six is the number of median planes in the tetrahedron, not medians of the triangle.
questions.explain: Because the same argument works for each of the three sides, the centre lies on three medians. They therefore have a common point.
questions.rule: One median per side; all pass through the centre.
questions.teaches: Since the centre lies on all three medians, the three medians must meet in a single point, which is exactly the centre.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A planner tests an event schedule on a 1-day mini version, with the full plan set aside. Which choice mirrors the book?
options: Alter the big plan every time the mini plan changes at all
Skip the mini plan if it needs one assumption
Finish the mini schedule completely before returning to the big plan
Judge the mini plan by how it looks, not by whether it works out
optionExplain: Constant switching splits attention, which the book avoids.
The book's own triangle solution leans on a plausible principle, so a stated assumption is allowed.
Right: the book completes the simple problem first and only then uses it.
A mini plan is only useful once it is worked through.
questions.explain: Our reading: a solved simpler case is useful because it is complete enough to copy or quote. A half-solved one gives neither a method nor a result.
questions.teaches: Having solved the analogue, the book adds that it is desirable to verify the key fact by pure geometry, independent of the mechanical assumption.
questions.rule: Work the simple problem to the end, naming the principle you lean on.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You have solved a problem about a flat floor plan, and now face the same kind of problem for a two-storey house. What first?
options: Start from nothing, since a house is a different thing
Choose a third problem unrelated to either of the first two
Look at your flat solution for steps you can repeat on two storeys
Assume the answers are identical
optionExplain: Starting over wastes the solved case.
A third problem does not help either one.
Right: reuse of the earlier steps is the point of a model.
Assuming identical answers confuses a model with a copy.
questions.explain: Following the earlier route is the move the card next describes.
questions.rule: Use a solved analogue as a model.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the tetrahedron solution, the thin strips are taken parallel to an ____ of the solid.
questions.explain: In the triangle the strips were parallel to a side; in the tetrahedron the matching part is an edge.
questions.rule: Side becomes edge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Match each part of the triangle solution to its counterpart in the tetrahedron solution.
pairs: Median from C to the midpoint M of AB
Median plane through M, C and D
questions.explain: Each triangle ingredient has a matching tetrahedron ingredient, so the solution can be copied with small changes. The triangle has three sides and so three medians; the tetrahedron has six edges and so six median planes.
questions.rule: Translate each part, then count.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Following the model, how many median planes does the argument give for a tetrahedron?
options: Six, one for each edge
Four, one for each face
Three, one for each side
Twelve, one for each pair of edges
optionExplain: Right: a tetrahedron has 6 edges, and each edge gives one median plane.
Four is the number of faces and vertices, but the argument runs on edges.
Three belongs to the triangle, which has three sides.
Pairs of edges would be 15, not 12, and the argument does not pair edges.
questions.explain: Six median planes pass through the centre: the model's counting rule is one per edge, and a tetrahedron has six edges.
questions.rule: One median plane per edge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: In the tetrahedron solution, the strips are cut so that each is parallel to the edge AB, and each strip's balance point is its midpoint.
questions.explain: That is the direct counterpart of the triangle strips, and it makes the midpoints lie in one plane.
questions.rule: Midpoints lie in the median plane.
questions.teaches: The tetrahedron has six such median planes, one per edge, and each holds the centre, so they meet in one point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tutor solved a seating puzzle for a table of 3 by a method she can repeat. She now faces a table of 5. What mirrors the book's advice?
options: Throw away the 3-person method, since the table is bigger
Repeat the method's steps, adjusting the counts to the larger table
Use the 3-person answer unchanged, since the method is the same
Assume the 5-person answer equals the 3-person one, since the steps repeat
optionExplain: Dropping a working method is the opposite of the book's advice.
Right: copy the steps and adjust the counts, as three medians became six median planes.
Unchanged reuse breaks when the size changes: the triangle's three medians became six planes.
The shape of the method carries over, not the numbers.
questions.explain: Our reading: the method carries over by translation, as sides became edges. The numbers change: 3 medians became 6 median planes.
questions.teaches: A method translated from the simpler case may change its counts: three medians became six median planes.
questions.rule: Translate the model solution step by step: sides become edges, medians become median planes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You know that the three medians of any triangle meet in one point. Where might that help in a solid with triangular faces?
options: To show the solid has three faces
Nowhere at all, since solids are not triangles
Only if you reprove the fact first
On a triangular face, to locate the point where its medians meet
optionExplain: The number of faces has no connection to the medians.
A solid contains triangles; the fact applies inside them.
The result may be used as it stands, without reproof.
Right: the fact is about triangles, so it applies on a triangular face.
questions.explain: A result can be used inside a bigger problem when a matching piece appears. The card next shows the book's use.
questions.rule: A result applies wherever its case reappears.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Using the result of the simpler problem means we do not care how that result had been ____.
questions.explain: Only the finished fact matters here; its proof is not copied.
questions.rule: Result: take it, do not copy the route.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A box has edges 1, 2 and 2. You know the diagonal of a rectangle with sides a and b has length equal to the square root of a squared plus b squared. How can you use the result?
options: Add the three edges to get 5
Take the largest edge as the diagonal, 2
Multiply the edges to get 4, which is the volume and not a length of a diagonal
Find the base rectangle diagonal, then combine it with the height to get 3
optionExplain: Adding edges ignores the right angles that make the diagonal shorter than the sum.
The diagonal is longer than any edge.
Multiplying gives a volume, not a length.
Right: the base diagonal is the square root of 5, and the box diagonal is the square root of 5 plus 4, which is 3.
questions.explain: Rectangle 1 by 2 has diagonal root 5. With height 2 the box diagonal squared is 5 + 4 = 9, so it is 3. Check: 1 + 4 + 4 = 9.
questions.rule: Feed the analogue's result into the next level.
questions.hint: Square the base diagonal, then add the square of the height.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: A result about triangles can be applied to a figure that contains no triangle, without adding anything.
questions.explain: The result needs its figure. When the triangle is missing, an auxiliary element may bring it in, as the next section shows.
questions.rule: Check the result's figure is actually in your problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A baker knows that doubling a bread recipe doubles the flour. She now plans a cake in three layers, each like her tested single layer. Which use of the result fits?
options: Retest every ingredient from scratch
Ignore the tested layer, because a cake differs from a bread
Treat each layer like the tested layer and combine the results
Assume that three layers need three times the oven time, because quantities scale
optionExplain: Retesting throws away the known result.
The layers are the same kind of part, so the tested one applies.
Right: the tested layer is a result that applies to each layer.
Oven time is a separate question and does not scale just because quantities do.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same reasoning combines per-part results into a whole. The book's tetrahedron uses the triangle result on a face and then ties the planes together.
questions.teaches: Results from the simpler problem can be combined through several vertices: the book applies the triangle result at D, then A, B and C.
questions.rule: Look in the analogue's results for a fact that fits a part of your problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student copies the steps of a solved flat problem to a solid one. Is that using the method or the result?
questions.explain: Method means following the route; result means taking the endpoint. The card next separates the two clearly.
questions.rule: Method: route. Result: endpoint.
options: The method, since the route is repeated
The result, since the final answer is the thing being reused
Both, since steps and answer are copied
Neither, since the shapes differ
optionExplain: Right: repeating the route is using the method.
The answer is not reused here; only the steps are.
Only steps are copied in this case.
Different shapes do not stop a route from being copied.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Using the simpler problem's method means imitating its solution one ____ at a time, rather than copying only its conclusion.
questions.explain: The first use imitates the analogue step by step. The second takes its conclusion only.
questions.rule: Method copies the route point by point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student keeps notes on a solved square-grid puzzle. Sort her uses for a new cubic-grid puzzle.

items.t: Applies the same row-by-row counting steps in each layer
Starts from the known count for one square layer
Cuts the cube into layers just as she cut the square into rows
Quotes the finished total for one layer from her notes instead of recounting it

questions.explain: Counting steps that she repeats are method; a layer total she picks up as a fact is result.
questions.hint: Is she repeating steps or taking a conclusion?
questions.rule: Decide which of method and result the original needs, and rework the model if neither fits.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student can neither imitate the analogue's steps nor use its result directly. What does the book suggest next?
options: Give up on analogy altogether, because the analogue did not fit directly
Reconsider and modify the analogue's solution until a form extends to the original
Replace the original problem with the analogue
Assume the analogue is wrong
optionExplain: Giving up forgets that the analogue's solution can be reshaped.
Right: vary the solution through various forms until one can be extended.
Replacing the problem changes the task.
The analogue may be perfectly right yet not directly usable.
questions.explain: The book says it may be worthwhile to vary and modify the solution, trying various forms until one extends to the original problem.
questions.rule: If it does not fit, vary the model.
questions.hint: The book's advice is to reshape the borrowed solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: the book promises that the method of a simpler analogue can be copied step by step into the harder problem without any change.
questions.explain: The book warns that complications may arise in harder cases, so the analogue's solution may have to be varied before it extends.
questions.rule: Both can be used in one solution.
questions.teaches: The book warns that complications may arise in harder cases.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tutor reuses her solved fractions lesson in a decimals lesson by copying the order of examples and quoting one finished table. Which describes this?
options: Only the method, since the order of examples is copied
Both: she copies the method and uses a result
Only result
Neither, since the topics differ
optionExplain: The table adds a result.
Right: copying the order of steps is method; quoting the table is result.
The order of examples adds a method.
Topics may differ and the analogy can still supply both.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same split applies outside geometry. Steps repeated are method; a finished item quoted is result.
questions.teaches: A solution can use both the method and the result of the analogue, as the centre-of-gravity solution did.
questions.rule: Decide which of method and result the original needs, and rework the model if neither fits.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: An engineer proves a bridge formula using an assumption from physics, and the assumption seems likely. What would make the result more solid?
options: Trusting the formula because the assumption seems likely enough
Repeating the same argument twice
A separate confirmation that does not use that assumption
Dropping the formula and starting again
optionExplain: Likely is not the same as shown.
Repeating the same path repeats the same dependence.
Right: an independent route removes the dependence on the assumption.
The formula may be right; it simply needs an independent check.
questions.explain: The card next states why the book asks for a pure-geometry check after a mechanical argument.
questions.rule: Confirm trusted facts independently.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book wants the meeting of the medians verified by pure ____, independently of mechanical assumptions.
questions.explain: The mechanical argument suggests the medians meet; geometry alone should confirm it.
questions.rule: Verify by pure geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A solver shows by a physical balancing argument that two lines cross at the centre. What does the book suggest she do?
options: Accept the physical argument as final
Ignore the lines and measure the figure
Add a second physical argument that uses the same principle again
Show by geometry alone that the lines really meet at one point
optionExplain: Accepting it leaves the claim resting on an assumption from another field.
Measuring a drawing is not a proof of the claim.
A second argument with the same principle shares the same weakness.
Right: the geometric claim should stand on geometric grounds.
questions.explain: The book's wording: it is desirable to verify, independent of any mechanical assumption, that the three medians meet.
questions.rule: Finish with a check that stands alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: A second proof that uses the same assumption counts as an independent check.
questions.explain: Independence means the second route does not use the assumption in question. Our reading: otherwise a flaw in the assumption spoils both.
questions.rule: Independent means not sharing the assumption.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: For the tetrahedron, the book verifies by geometry that the six median planes meet in a point. Which simpler result does it rely on?
options: That the three medians of a triangle meet in one point
That all median planes are parallel
That every tetrahedron has all its edges equal
That the centre of gravity is a vertex of the solid
optionExplain: Right: the verification reuses the triangle result.
Parallel planes would not meet in a point.
Tetrahedra here are not assumed regular.
A vertex is not a balance point in this problem.
questions.explain: The geometric check uses the earlier triangle result. So the independent check itself rests on the simpler analogue.
questions.teaches: The geometric check for the six median planes uses the triangle's result, so the analogue serves both the discovery and the verification.
questions.rule: List the facts your solution took on trust, and prove each by a route that does not use that trust.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A writer supports a claim with an anecdote she half trusts. To follow the book's attitude, what should she add?
options: Another anecdote of the same sort from a second source
A separate line of support that does not rely on the anecdote
A shorter claim that needs less support
A confident tone
optionExplain: A second anecdote shares the same weakness.
Right: an independent source of support.
Shortening changes the claim, not its basis.
Tone does not support a claim.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book asks for independence at the point where a solution rests on an assumption, and the same demand carries to other fields.
questions.teaches: The book calls the geometric check desirable, which makes it a completion of the solution and not a repeat of it.
questions.rule: List the facts your solution took on trust, and prove each by a route that does not use that trust.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A triangle's balance point is also the balance point of its three corner weights. What might you suspect about a solid with four corners?
options: Its balance point may be the balance point of its four corner weights
Its balance point must be at one of the corners of the solid
Nothing can be suspected without proof
Its balance point equals the triangle's
optionExplain: Right: the similar case suggests a plausible guess for the new case.
Nothing in the case points to a corner.
The book encourages plausible guesses, which proof can later confirm.
The solid is a different figure, so the same point is not implied.
questions.explain: The book calls the step an inference by analogy. The card next explains how to weigh it.
questions.rule: Analogy suggests what to expect.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A conjecture drawn from a similar case is called an inference by ____.
questions.explain: Inference by analogy is a conclusion that two things alike in many respects are alike in one more.
questions.rule: Alike in many respects, maybe alike in one more.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tested crash-test result holds for 3 car models of one design. A fourth model follows the same design. What attitude fits the book?
options: Treat it as certain, since three models agree
Ignore it, since the models differ in name and appearance
Expect the same result, but treat it as plausible and check it
Expect the opposite result
optionExplain: Certainty overstates what analogy gives.
Ignoring it is described as even more foolish than treating it as certain.
Right: plausible, not certain, and worth testing.
Nothing supports the opposite.
questions.explain: The book says it would be foolish to regard such plausibility as certainty and even more foolish to disregard it.
questions.rule: Neither trust blindly nor disregard.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: A forecast made by analogy is a proved result.
questions.explain: It is a conjecture that experience or stricter reasoning may confirm or reject.
questions.rule: Forecast, then test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: According to the book, which kind of conclusion appears to be the most common and possibly the most essential?
options: Reading from a table
Proof from first axioms alone
Exact calculation
Inference by analogy
optionExplain: Tables record facts, they do not infer.
Proof is rarer in daily thinking.
Calculation needs prior results.
Right: the book calls inference by analogy the most common kind of conclusion.
questions.explain: The chemist testing drugs on animals to foresee the effect on humans draws conclusions by analogy. So the method reaches from science to ordinary life.
questions.teaches: Experimenting on animals to foresee a drug's effect on humans is an inference by analogy, which the book gives as an example from science.
questions.rule: Guess by analogy, label the guess as a guess, and test it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A city copies a bike-lane scheme that worked in three similar towns. Which statement follows the book's view?
options: The result is guaranteed
The three towns are irrelevant, since the city's streets are different from theirs
The scheme fails if one detail differs
The result is plausible, and it is worth watching for differences while testing
optionExplain: Guaranteed overstates analogy.
Three similar cases are real support.
One difference does not decide the matter.
Right: plausible forecast, with testing.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same attitude carries from geometry to policy: use the similar cases to forecast, then test.
questions.teaches: Experience and stricter reasoning decide whether an inference by analogy stands, so the forecast is only the start of the work.
questions.rule: Guess by analogy, label the guess as a guess, and test it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which supports a forecast better: five vague resemblances, or three cases laid out in a clear series?
options: Five vague resemblances, since five outnumbers three
Three cases in a clear series
They support it equally
Neither supports anything
optionExplain: Number appeals, but vague likeness is weak.
Right: quality outweighs quantity.
Both are not equal; the book ranks the clear ones higher.
Both give some support; the book simply ranks them.
questions.explain: The card next states the book's ranking of evidence for analogy.
questions.rule: Quality beats quantity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In weighing analogies, the book says ____ is still more important than quantity.
questions.explain: Clear-cut analogies and systematic arrangements count more than a pile of cases.
questions.rule: Quality over quantity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which evidence best supports the claim that a new tablet will sell well?
options: Six unrelated gadgets that sold well
One snack that sold well, because snacks sell in any shop and anywhere
Three earlier tablets of the same line, each with one more feature and rising sales
A friend's feeling that it looks good
optionExplain: Six cases look strong, but they are unrelated.
One unrelated case is weakest.
Right: related cases, in order.
A feeling is not a case.
questions.explain: A systematic series where each step adds a feature resembles the book's segment-triangle-tetrahedron series.
questions.rule: Prefer clear, ordered cases to many loose ones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each piece of evidence: does it add weight by the book's standard, or little?

items.t: A clear-cut parallel case
A vague similarity
Cases arranged in a systematic series
A random collection of cases
Another clear-cut parallel case
A resemblance noticed only after the conclusion was chosen

questions.explain: The book prefers clear cases and systematic arrangement. Our reading: a resemblance spotted only after choosing the answer is the kind of vague likeness that adds little.
questions.hint: Ask whether the case is clear and in order.
questions.rule: Prefer clear, ordered cases to many loose ones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book strengthens the tetrahedron conjecture by adding which analogous case?
options: A homogeneous rod, a straight segment of uniform density
A sphere of uniform density
A cube of uniform density, as the next solid after the tetrahedron
An empty box
optionExplain: Right: the rod completes the series segment, triangle, tetrahedron.
A sphere has no corners to compare.
A cube is not the next simplest step of the series.
An empty box has no centre of gravity to find.
questions.explain: The rod is a one-dimensional figure; the triangle is two-dimensional; the tetrahedron is three-dimensional. Together they form a clear series.
questions.teaches: The segment, the triangle and the tetrahedron are the simplest bounded figures of one, two and three dimensions, which is what makes them a systematic series.
questions.rule: Prefer clear, ordered cases to many loose ones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student argues a new diet works, citing 40 social media posts. Another cites two controlled tests of the same diet. By the book's weights, which carries more?
options: The 40 posts
They carry the same
The two controlled tests
Neither can carry any weight
optionExplain: Number tempts, but the posts are a random collection.
They do not weigh the same by the book's standard.
Right: clear, systematic cases outweigh a random pile.
Some weight remains for the tests.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's ranking of systematic over random instances carries outside mathematics.
questions.teaches: The book says a conclusion from many parallel cases is stronger than from fewer, so numbers do count once quality is equal.
questions.rule: Prefer clear, ordered cases to many loose ones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How many vertices, edges and faces does a tetrahedron have, in that order?
options: 4, 6 and 6
4, 4 and 6, with edges and faces swapped
3, 6 and 4
4, 6 and 4
optionExplain: A tetrahedron has 4 faces, not 6.
This swaps edges and faces.
A triangle has 3 vertices, not the tetrahedron.
Right: 4 vertices, 6 edges, 4 faces.
questions.explain: These counts are the last row of the book's table. The card next shows the whole table.
questions.rule: Tetrahedron: 4, 6, 4.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The table of counts for the segment, triangle and tetrahedron is a section of ____'s triangle.
questions.explain: The numbers 2, 1; 3, 3, 1; 4, 6, 4, 1 are rows from Pascal's triangle.
questions.rule: The rows are binomial coefficients.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Counting the interior as one more element, what is the next row for the figure with five corners that comes after the tetrahedron in the series?
optionExplain: Right: the next row of Pascal's triangle after 4, 6, 4, 1 gives 5, 10, 10, 5, 1.
Equal entries do not follow the pattern.
Adding to 8 breaks the binomial pattern.
This row belongs to a figure with six corners.
questions.explain: The binomial coefficients C(5,1) to C(5,5) = 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. The reading: this extends the book's table by its pattern.
questions.rule: Next row: add neighbouring entries of the row above.
questions.hint: Each entry is the sum of the two above it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The numbers in the table suggest a regularity that links the segment, triangle and tetrahedron.
questions.explain: The book says a remarkable regularity can be recognised in these numbers.
questions.rule: A table can expose regularity.
questions.teaches: Recognising these numbers as a section of Pascal's triangle needs only a little familiarity with the powers of a binomial.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A reader says: the tetrahedron row has 4 vertices, 6 edges and 6 faces, so it matches the cube's row. What is wrong?
options: Tetrahedra have no faces
A tetrahedron has 4 faces, and the cube row differs
Counting must exclude vertices
Edges equal vertices in a tetrahedron, so the rows match
optionExplain: A tetrahedron has 4 triangular faces.
Right: the tetrahedron has 4 faces; the cube has 6.
Vertices are counted in the table's first column.
Edges are 6 and vertices 4; they are not equal.
questions.explain: The row is 4, 6, 4 (then 1 for the interior). The cube's row is 8, 12, 6, 1.
questions.rule: Tabulate the parts by dimension for each case and compare the rows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A city planner studies a street, a square and a cube-shaped hall. What parallel to the book's step helps?
options: Choose the largest case and ignore all the others
List parts by dimension for each case and compare the rows
Replace counts with colour notes
Compare only the first case and then stop there
optionExplain: One case gives no pattern.
Right: a table of parts per dimension is the book's step.
Colour is not a structural count.
One case gives nothing to compare.
questions.explain: Our reading: tabulating parts by dimension suits any series of figures. The book does this for three figures.
questions.teaches: The book's table has one row per figure and one column per dimension of bounding element, from zero-dimensional endpoints up to the interior.
questions.rule: Tabulate the parts by dimension for each case and compare the rows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Ratios 1 to 1, then 2 to 1, appear for a rod and a triangle. What would you guess for the next figure in the series?
options: 4 to 1, skipping a step
1 to 3
2 to 2
3 to 1
optionExplain: Skipping a step breaks the regularity.
Reversing the pattern has no support.
2 to 2 is the same as 1 to 1.
Right: the pattern 1, 2, 3 suggests 3 to 1.
questions.explain: The pattern is the point of the card that follows.
questions.rule: Continue the pattern, then test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The Latin saying quoted in the book, simplex sigillum veri, means simplicity is the seal of ____.
questions.explain: The book uses it to express that harmonious simple order guides discoverers.
questions.rule: Simplicity is the seal of truth.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tetrahedron has vertices (0,0,0), (4,0,0), (0,4,0) and (0,0,4). The average of the vertices is (1,1,1). At what ratio does it divide the path from (0,0,0) to the average of the other three vertices?
options: 3 to 1
1 to 1, the ratio of a rod
2 to 1
4 to 1
optionExplain: Right: the other three average to (4/3,4/3,4/3), and (1,1,1) is three quarters of the way, so 3 to 1.
1 to 1 would be halfway.
2 to 1 is the triangle's ratio.
4 to 1 would be four fifths of the way.
questions.explain: Computed: (1,1,1) is 3/4 of the way to (4/3,4/3,4/3); the parts are 3 and 1. This matches the conjecture.
questions.rule: Test the extension on one example.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book treats the beauty of a regularity as a proof that the next case follows it.
questions.explain: The book says it appears extremely unlikely that the regularity would be spoiled, which is a reason to suspect it, not a proof.
questions.rule: Simplicity guides; it does not prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book suggests the pattern may extend to n dimensions. What kind of inference is this?
options: A deduction from axioms, as in a geometry text
A guess with no basis
An inference by induction, based on analogy
A direct measurement
optionExplain: The pattern is not derived from axioms.
The guess rests on cases n = 1, 2, 3.
Right: the book says induction is naturally based on analogy.
Dimension n is not measured.
questions.explain: Cases n = 1, 2, 3 all agree, so the book finds it unlikely that the pattern ceases for larger n. Our reading: the next cases to check would be n = 4.
questions.teaches: Induction is naturally based on analogy: the book's extension to n dimensions is an inference by induction.
questions.rule: Extend the numbers of the series by their regularity, and test the extension.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Three years of a charity's sales rise by 10%, 20%, 30%. A volunteer says the fourth will be 40%. How should she treat that?
options: As a plausible continuation that still needs checking
As meaningless, because a pattern of three cases proves nothing
As proof the pattern is a law
As a certain result
optionExplain: Right: plausible, to be checked.
The pattern is some evidence.
Three cases do not prove a law.
Certainty is unwarranted.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's attitude is to follow a neat pattern and also to test it.
questions.teaches: The book's extension to n dimensions is itself an inference that may or may not be confirmed, so the pattern is a guide, not a guarantee.
questions.rule: Extend the numbers of the series by their regularity, and test the extension.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Two sets of objects are paired so that each object has exactly one partner and a relation between objects is kept. The book calls this
questions.explain: The card next defines the exact forms of analogy.
questions.rule: Three exact forms of analogy.
options: Sagacity
Induction
Convertible reduction
Isomorphism
optionExplain: Sagacity is the quality behind a bright idea.
Induction is a kind of inference.
Convertible reduction is about problems.
Right: a one-one match that preserves relations is isomorphism.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A one-one correspondence between two systems that preserves certain relations is called ____.
questions.explain: That is the book's name for the very precise sort of analogy with a one-one match.
questions.rule: One-one match, relations kept: isomorphism.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Each member of a club of 6 is paired with one distinct seat in a row of 6 so that who sits next to whom is preserved. What kind of correspondence is this?
options: A one-many correspondence
A one-one correspondence preserving relations
No correspondence
A correspondence that quietly loses the relations
optionExplain: Each member maps to a single seat, so it is one-one.
Right: each member has exactly one seat and the neighbour relation is kept, so it is isomorphism.
Each member does have exactly one seat here, so a correspondence exists; the question is only its kind.
The neighbour relation is preserved by assumption.
questions.explain: A one-one match that keeps relations is the book's isomorphism.
questions.rule: Check the type of correspondence between the systems and name it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each case: is the correspondence one-one or one-many?

items.t: Each person in a class has one seat number, and no two share a number
Many dates fall on the same weekday
Every house on a street has one house number
Many students share one grade level

questions.explain: A one-one match gives each object a single partner. When many objects share one partner, the match is one-many. Our reading: the examples are ours, since the book gives none outside mathematics.
questions.rule: Check the type of correspondence between the systems and name it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book says the two forms of correspondence are very precise sorts of analogy. Which advanced branch does it mention for merohedral isomorphism?
options: Number Theory, since it deals with integers
Probability
Theory of Groups
Topology
optionExplain: Number theory deals with integers, but the book does not name it for this isomorphism.
Probability is not the branch the book names for this isomorphism.
Right: the book names the Theory of Groups.
Topology is a plausible neighbour of structure-preserving maps, but the book names the Theory of Groups.
questions.explain: The book says merohedral isomorphism is important in advanced mathematical study, especially in the Theory of Groups.
questions.teaches: Merohedral isomorphism is also called homomorphism, though the book suggests homoiomorphism would be a better term.
questions.rule: Check the type of correspondence between the systems and name it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A map of a subway keeps which stations connect to which, but not distances. In the book's terms, what has the map kept?
options: The relations among the stations, as in a precise analogy
The distances between the stations along each line
The colours of the trains
Nothing of the real network, since a map is only a picture
optionExplain: Right: the connection relation is preserved.
A map of this kind drops distances, so they are not what it kept.
The colours of the trains are a surface feature, not a relation among the stations.
A map that keeps which stations connect has kept the relation of connection, which is the point of the analogy.
questions.explain: Our reading: a diagram that keeps relations while dropping other features is an analogy of the exact kind the book describes.
questions.teaches: Exact analogy is defined by the relations kept: what is dropped does not matter if the relations stay the same.
questions.rule: Check the type of correspondence between the systems and name it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student draws an extra line in a geometry figure, hoping it will reveal an angle. What would the book call that line?
options: A theorem
A false construction
An auxiliary line
A given
optionExplain: A theorem is a statement to be proved, not a line.
The line may help, so nothing marks it as false.
Right: an auxiliary line is a kind of auxiliary element.
Givens come with the problem; this line was added.
questions.explain: The card next defines the term.
questions.rule: An element added in the hope of helping is auxiliary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: An element that we introduce in the hope that it will further the solution is called an ____ element.
questions.explain: Auxiliary elements are additions made to help.
questions.rule: Added to help: auxiliary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Match each addition to its kind of auxiliary element.
pairs: A new line drawn in a figure
A new letter standing for a hidden quantity
A statement we prove first to help the main proof
questions.explain: The book names lines, unknowns and theorems as kinds of auxiliary element.
questions.rule: Lines, unknowns, theorems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each item: is it an auxiliary element, or part of the original problem as given?

items.t: A line you draw from a vertex to the opposite side
The length of the base stated in the question
A letter y you introduce for x squared
The angle given in the question
A lemma you decide to prove first
The perimeter given in the question

questions.explain: Anything we bring in ourselves, hoping it helps, is auxiliary. The data stated by the problem is not.
questions.hint: Who brought it in: the problem or the solver?
questions.rule: Add elements on purpose, and say what each one is for.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: According to the book, how does our conception of a problem at the end of the work compare with the start?
options: It cannot be compared
It is exactly the same
It contains less, since we drop details as we go
It contains much more than it did at the start
optionExplain: It can be compared, and the book does.
The same conception would mean nothing was added.
Details are added, not dropped, in this passage.
Right: new elements are added as work progresses.
questions.explain: The book points out that, as work progresses, new elements join the original ones.
questions.teaches: The book cites progress and achievement here: the growth of our conception of a problem is part of how work advances.
questions.rule: Add elements on purpose, and say what each one is for.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student in a spreadsheet adds a helper column that splits a long date into year, month and day to solve a sorting problem. In the book's terms, the helper column is closest to
options: A part of the original data in the spreadsheet
An auxiliary element introduced to help
A final answer
A mistake
optionExplain: The data was the date; the column is new.
Right: it is added in the hope of helping.
It is a tool, not the answer.
Nothing suggests it is a mistake.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's definition is about purpose, so it carries over to helper columns and variables.
questions.teaches: The book counts an element as auxiliary by its purpose, not its shape: a line, an unknown or a whole theorem can each be auxiliary.
questions.rule: Add elements on purpose, and say what each one is for.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You remember a solved problem about triangles, but your figure shows only a circle and two chords. What should you consider?
options: Giving up the solved problem and starting over
Erasing the circle so that the figure is simpler
Adding lines so that a triangle appears
Waiting for a hint
optionExplain: Giving up discards the solved problem, which is exactly the clue that suggests what to add.
Erasing the circle removes information the problem gave and does not bring a triangle into the figure.
Right: add auxiliary lines so the known result applies.
Waiting for a hint adds nothing; the book's reasons point to something the solver can do now.
questions.explain: The card next states this as one of two good reasons.
questions.rule: Add what a recollected problem needs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Explaining the definition of a circle should include drawing its centre and its ____.
questions.explain: Without drawing, a definition cannot be used concretely.
questions.rule: Draw the elements named in the definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A problem says a quadrilateral has equal diagonals. To use the definition of a diagonal, what might you do?
options: Write the word diagonal beside the figure and leave it there
Ignore the diagonals
Colour the sides
Draw both diagonals in the figure
optionExplain: A written label is words only.
Ignoring them loses the data.
Colour does not use the definition.
Right: put the elements named in the definition into the figure.
questions.explain: Making the defined elements visible lets you reason with them.
questions.rule: Go back to definitions and draw the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which situations call for an auxiliary element, by the book's two main reasons? Select all that apply.
options: You recall a solved problem about a shape that is not in your figure
You are applying the definition of a circle to your figure
You feel nervous about the problem
You want to decorate the figure
You have already used every element in your figure
optionExplain: Right: add the missing shape.
Right: put the defined parts in.
Nervousness is not a reason to add anything.
Decoration does not serve the solution.
If every element is used, no reason has been given.
questions.explain: The two reasons are to use a known related problem and to apply a definition concretely. The others give no reason about the problem itself.
questions.hint: Which options connect to the problem?
questions.rule: Ask whether adding an element makes a known result or a definition usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book says the best reasons to introduce auxiliary elements are two. Is that all?
options: No; we may also add elements to make the problem fuller or more suggestive
Yes, there is no third reason
No; we may add any element at random, whenever we feel like it
Yes, but only for geometry problems
optionExplain: Right: the book mentions further reasons.
The book says they are not the only ones.
Random addition is warned against.
The reasons are not limited to geometry.
questions.explain: Beyond the two best reasons, elements may make the problem fuller, more suggestive or more familiar.
questions.teaches: Elements may be added to make a problem fuller, more suggestive or more familiar, even before we know explicitly how they will be used.
questions.rule: Ask whether adding an element makes a known result or a definition usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tenant disputes a late fee. The lease says a payment is late if it arrives after the due date. To use that definition, what is the equivalent of drawing the elements?
options: Quote the lease aloud
Write out the due date and the arrival date and compare them
Wait for the landlord to explain
Argue that the fee is unfair and refuse to pay it
optionExplain: Quoting alone stays at words.
Right: put the parts of the definition on the table.
Waiting hands the work to someone else.
Fairness is a different question.
questions.explain: Our reading: a definition becomes usable when its parts are laid out, as the circle's centre and radius are drawn.
questions.teaches: Stating a definition without drawing anything is, in the book's words, mere lip-service: it cannot be used concretely.
questions.rule: Ask whether adding an element makes a known result or a definition usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: Any extra line drawn into a figure is as good as another, so long as it is drawn.
questions.explain: The book asks for some reason, however slight. The card next explains what counts.
questions.rule: Have a reason.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book says we should not introduce auxiliary elements ____.
questions.explain: Even a vague reason is better than none.
questions.rule: No wanton additions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which addition to a figure of a triangle follows the book's advice?
options: Fifteen random lines, in case one helps
A line chosen by rolling a die
A midpoint, added because it makes the figure more familiar and symmetric
A line drawn because the pencil happened to be nearby
optionExplain: Random lines have no reason.
A die gives no reason related to the problem.
Right: there is some reason, even if vague.
Convenience of the pencil is not a reason connected to the solution.
questions.explain: The book allows a hunch-based reason such as making the figure more familiar. It excludes additions with no reason at all.
questions.rule: A vague reason beats no reason.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each justification: is it a reason the book would accept, or not?

items.t: It makes the figure more suggestive
Because I had space on the page
It brings in a known related problem
Because I wanted to add something
It makes the problem more familiar
Because the page looked empty

questions.explain: A reason ties the addition to the problem. Space, urge and appearance do not.
questions.rule: Before adding, say why: what does it connect to or make visible?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which situation shows an element added with only a feeling that it is a bright idea?
options: A solver adds a point by accident
A solver adds a point after proving it is needed
A solver adds a point by copying a textbook figure exactly, without asking why
A solver adds a point because the problem seems more natural with it, without yet knowing how to use it
optionExplain: An accidental point has no reason behind it at all, while the situation asked about has the feeling of a bright idea.
Proof of need is stronger than the case here.
Copying a figure is a reason of another sort.
Right: the book allows additions that make the problem fuller before the use is clear.
questions.explain: The book allows elements added to make the problem fuller, more suggestive or more familiar even before we see how to use them.
questions.teaches: The book accepts a bright idea of conceiving the problem with certain elements added as a reason, even before explicit use is known.
questions.rule: Before adding, say why: what does it connect to or make visible?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student adds a lot of formatting to a messy table of data before analysing it, hoping a pattern will pop out. When is that in the book's spirit?
options: When it is added at random
When the formatting is chosen to make patterns easier to see, like sorting by one column
When it makes the table longer, since longer tables show more of the data
When it changes the data
optionExplain: Random formatting has no reason.
Right: the addition has a purpose connected to the problem.
A longer table is not easier to read, and the book wants an addition with a reason.
Changing the data goes beyond adding.
questions.explain: Our reading: a purpose such as making a pattern visible is a reason in the book's sense.
questions.teaches: The book's test for an added element is that there should be some reason for it, not that the element must succeed.
questions.rule: Before adding, say why: what does it connect to or make visible?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A task gives a base, a height and a perimeter for a shape. Your sketch shows only the base and height. What is the book's likely advice?
options: Find a way to show the perimeter in the sketch
Delete the perimeter from the task to simplify it
Estimate the perimeter later
Redraw the base
optionExplain: Right: the unused datum must be brought in.
Deleting data changes the problem.
Postponing leaves the sketch incomplete.
The base is already there.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's example of this step.
questions.rule: Use every datum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's construction problem, the datum missing from the first figure is the given ____ of the triangle.
questions.explain: The angle and altitude are placed easily; the perimeter is not.
questions.rule: Find the missing datum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A problem gives a radius, an angle and a chord length. Your diagram shows the radius and the angle. What next?
options: Assume the chord length is unnecessary, since two data are enough
Ignore the angle
Ask where the chord length appears, and add it to the diagram
Redefine the radius
optionExplain: The book asks whether all the data is used.
The angle is already used.
Right: apply the question about unused data.
The radius is already placed.
questions.explain: A missing datum is a prompt for an auxiliary element.
questions.rule: Ask: have I used all the data?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book says that once a datum is missing from the figure, we know exactly how to place it.
questions.explain: It says we must introduce the perimeter, but how to do so takes experiments; the book tries clumsy placements first.
questions.rule: Missing data tells what to place, not how.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's first attempts to introduce the perimeter, why do the figures appear clumsy?
options: They are too small to show the lengths that were given
They omit the angle
They use the wrong colour
They lack symmetry between the two unknown sides
optionExplain: Size is not the book's complaint.
The angle is included in the figures; the clumsiness lies elsewhere.
Colour is not mentioned.
Right: the placements treat the two sides differently.
questions.explain: The two unknown sides b and c play the same role, so a good placement should treat them alike. The next idea develops this.
questions.teaches: The two unknown sides are interchangeable in the problem, so placing the perimeter in a way that favours one of them spoils the natural symmetry.
questions.rule: Count the data; put the missing item into the figure by an auxiliary element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A cook's task: make dinner for 6 using the given budget, the oven time and the guest allergy list. The plan ignores the allergy list. What is the equivalent step?
options: Treat the allergies as optional, since the budget is the main limit
Revise the plan to include the allergy list
Add more guests
Drop the budget so that the plan is easier
optionExplain: Optional treatment ignores a datum.
Right: bring the unused datum in.
Guests are not data to change.
Dropping the budget loses another datum.
questions.explain: Our reading: checking that every datum is used applies to plans as well as figures.
questions.teaches: The question Did you use all the data? is a standard question in the book's list; here it points to a gap in the figure.
questions.rule: Count the data; put the missing item into the figure by an auxiliary element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Two sisters share a task equally. A plan gives one sister extra duties without reason. What does it lack?
options: Symmetry between the two
Efficiency, since extra duties finish the task sooner
Simplicity, since the plan has more steps than it needs
Clear deadlines, since no date was set for the task
optionExplain: Right: the roles are the same, so the plan should treat them alike.
Efficiency is a fair worry, but the plan fails in treating two equal roles unequally.
The number of steps is not what is wrong; the unequal treatment is.
Deadlines are not the issue here; the two sisters' roles are the same and the plan should treat them alike.
questions.explain: The card next applies the same idea to two sides of a triangle.
questions.rule: Interchangeable parts, balanced treatment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's problem, the sides b and c play the same role, so the problem is ____ with respect to b and c.
questions.explain: Swapping b and c leaves the problem unchanged.
questions.rule: b and c are interchangeable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: To show the perimeter p, the book extends side a by b on one side and by c on the other. What is the length of the whole segment?
