options: b + c only, leaving out the middle side
b + a + c, which equals p
a only
2a
optionExplain: Without a it would be missing the middle part.
Right: the segment has length b + a + c = p.
a alone is just the side.
2a has no link to the perimeter.
questions.explain: Adding the two extensions to side a gives the segment whose length equals the perimeter.
questions.rule: Extend by the two interchangeable lengths.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each placement of the perimeter: does it treat b and c alike, or not?

items.t: Add b on one side of a and c on the other
Add the whole of b and c on the right of a
Add b + c as one piece above a
Add c on the left and b on the right of a

questions.explain: A balanced placement uses the two lengths symmetrically about side a. Piling both on one side treats the sides unequally.
questions.hint: Would swapping b and c change the figure?
questions.rule: Ask which parts are interchangeable and keep your addition balanced between them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book's first figures place the length p so that b and c get different treatment. What does the book say about that?
options: It spoils the natural symmetry of the problem
It is required by the givens of the problem, so it cannot be avoided
It gives the shortest proof of the result
It makes the figure easier
optionExplain: Right: lack of symmetry explains why the figures appear unsatisfactory.
The givens do not require it.
Nothing suggests a shorter proof.
It makes the figure look worse, not easier.
questions.explain: The book diagnoses the clumsiness as a lack of symmetry.
questions.teaches: When we try to make clear to ourselves why a figure looks unsatisfactory, we may find the cause is lost symmetry, and that points to the better placement.
questions.rule: Ask which parts are interchangeable and keep your addition balanced between them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Two departments split a bonus equally. A draft puts the whole bonus in one department's budget line. How does the book's habit help?
options: Keep one line only, to save space on the page
Remove the bonus
It suggests splitting the entry between both lines alike
Double the bonus
optionExplain: Saving space ignores the symmetry.
Removing the bonus drops the datum.
Right: treat the interchangeable parts alike.
Doubling changes the data.
questions.explain: Our reading: matching the structure of a record to the symmetry of the problem is the same instinct.
questions.teaches: The book finds a placement unsatisfactory when it spoils the natural symmetry of the problem with respect to the interchangeable unknowns.
questions.rule: Ask which parts are interchangeable and keep your addition balanced between them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A figure has two points on a line at distance equal to the lengths of sides b and c from a vertex. Which familiar shape might you look for?
options: A regular hexagon
A circle
A trapezium with two parallel sides
An isosceles triangle
optionExplain: A hexagon needs six equal sides.
No circle is implied by equal lengths alone here.
A trapezium needs parallel sides.
Right: equal lengths from a point make isosceles triangles.
questions.explain: The card next shows why isosceles triangles help in the book's example.
questions.rule: Look for familiar shapes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's figure, each of the lines AD and AE is the base of an ____ triangle.
questions.explain: That is the familiar shape that the added lines create.
questions.rule: AD and AE are bases of isosceles triangles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The given angle at A is 60 degrees. By the book's relation, what is angle DAE?
options: 120 degrees
60 degrees, the same as the given angle itself
90 degrees
150 degrees
optionExplain: Right: the relation gives 90 + 60/2 = 120 degrees.
60 is the given angle itself, not DAE.
90 forgets the half of the given angle.
150 comes from adding the full angle to 90.
questions.explain: The relation is DAE = 90 + (given angle)/2 = 90 + 30 = 120 degrees.
questions.rule: DAE = 90 + half the given angle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: By the book's relation, if the given angle grows, angle DAE grows too.
questions.explain: DAE equals 90 degrees plus half the given angle, so any increase in the given angle raises DAE by half as much.
questions.rule: Add the elements that bring in familiar shapes, then see what angles or lengths they reveal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: After finding that angle DAE is known, what does the book do?
options: It gives up the construction
It tries to construct triangle DAE, an auxiliary problem easier than the original
It measures the figure with a ruler and reads off the answer
It changes the givens
optionExplain: The book proceeds, it does not give up.
Right: the construction of triangle DAE becomes the auxiliary problem.
Measurement is not a construction.
The givens stay as they are; the book builds an auxiliary triangle from them and does not change them.
questions.explain: With angle DAE known, the altitude from A and the length ED are given, so the triangle DAE can be built.
questions.teaches: The auxiliary problem is to construct triangle DAE, which the book calls much easier than the original problem.
questions.rule: Add the elements that bring in familiar shapes, then see what angles or lengths they reveal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A landscaper must lay a path between two points around a pond. She adds a straight line across to form a right triangle on the pond edge. Which feature matches the book's habit?
options: She adds a random curve
She removes the pond
She doubles the path length
She adds a simple, familiar shape that exposes a usable relation
optionExplain: A random curve has no known relation.
Removing the pond changes the problem.
Doubling the length is not a shape.
Right: a familiar shape makes a relation visible.
questions.explain: Our reading: a right triangle brings in the Pythagorean relation, as the isosceles triangles brought in their angle relation.
questions.teaches: Isosceles triangles are particularly simple and familiar, and the book says it is not unreasonable to introduce them for that reason.
questions.rule: Add the elements that bring in familiar shapes, then see what angles or lengths they reveal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A tutor shows a clever trick that solves a problem but does not say why anyone would think of it. How might a keen student feel?
options: Eager to repeat it blindly
Fully satisfied, since the answer turns out right
Disappointed, as if the trick came out of nowhere
Indifferent to the method
optionExplain: Repeating blindly teaches little.
Correctness alone does not satisfy those who want the motive.
Right: the book says such students feel cheated.
Keen students care about the method.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's view.
questions.rule: Show the motive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book says an intelligent student wants to know the motive and the ____ of the various steps.
questions.explain: Verifying a step is not enough; understanding why it is taken matters.
questions.rule: Motive and purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which presentation follows the book's advice about an auxiliary line?
options: Draw this line, and the result follows
We need a triangle to use a known result, so we add this line to create one
Note that experts always add this line, so it needs no explanation
Skip the explanation to save time for the next problem
optionExplain: This shows the step without reason.
Right: it gives the reason for the step.
This appeals to authority and gives no motive.
The book says it may be worth the time.
questions.explain: A short remark about purpose turns a trick into something a student can reuse.
questions.rule: Say why the line is drawn.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, an intelligent reader is fully satisfied once every step has been checked as correct.
questions.explain: The book says such readers also want to know the motive and purpose of the steps.
questions.rule: Give the reason for each conspicuous step in a solution you present.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How does the book say the motive of a step can be made comprehensible?
options: By suitable remarks or by carefully chosen questions and suggestions
By removing the step
By adding more steps without any comment on them
By leaving it to the reader
optionExplain: Right: remarks or questions that guide the reader.
Removing the step is not offered.
More steps do not give motive.
The book wants teachers to do the work.
questions.explain: The book points to the example in section 3 for remarks, and to sections 10, 18, 19 and 20 for questions.
questions.teaches: The book says making steps comprehensible takes a lot of time and effort, but may be worth while.
questions.rule: Give the reason for each conspicuous step in a solution you present.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A software team lead reviews code with a surprising helper function but no comment. Which review note follows the book's spirit?
options: Delete the function, since an unexplained helper is a risk
Say nothing, since the code runs and passes its tests
Add a note explaining why the helper is needed
Rewrite the whole module in a different style
optionExplain: Deleting may remove a step the code needs; the book asks that its motive be explained.
Running is not the same as understanding.
Right: explain the motive.
Rewriting everything goes beyond what is needed, which is to make the purpose of the step clear.
questions.explain: Our reading: the demand to give motive applies to any conspicuous step, in code as in proofs.
questions.teaches: The book says a tricky step that appears abruptly and solves the problem leaves intelligent readers feeling cheated, because its motive stays hidden.
questions.rule: Give the reason for each conspicuous step in a solution you present.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A fly keeps bumping against a closed window and ignores the open one next to it. What does the book say a person should do in such a case?
options: Stop trying altogether
Push harder at the same spot
Wait for the window to open by itself
Go around the obstacle, for instance by posing a helping problem
optionExplain: The book encourages another approach.
Repeating the same attempt is the insect's way.
Waiting leaves the person doing nothing, while the book wants a way around the obstacle.
Right: a person should be able to go around an obstacle that cannot be overcome directly.
questions.explain: The card next states how the book frames this in terms of auxiliary problems.
questions.rule: Go around the obstacle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The original problem is the end we wish to attain; the auxiliary problem is a ____ by which we try to attain it.
questions.explain: End and means: the auxiliary problem serves the original.
questions.rule: Original: end. Auxiliary: means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A hiker cannot cross a flooded path. Which action is an auxiliary problem in the book's sense?
options: Crossing the stream at the widest point, in one try
Waiting for a bridge
Finding where the stream is narrowest, as a step towards crossing
Crossing at the same place after a longer run-up
optionExplain: Crossing is the original aim.
Waiting is not posing a problem.
Right: finding the narrow place is posed for the sake of crossing.
A harder try at the same crossing is still the original aim, not a helping problem.
questions.explain: The narrow place is sought not for its own sake but as a means to the crossing.
questions.rule: Auxiliary problems serve the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each: is this problem the end or an auxiliary problem for it?

items.t: Find the total cost of a trip
Find the cost of one day of the trip, to scale up
Plan a three-course dinner
Plan just the dessert first, to learn how long it takes
Solve a quadratic equation we were asked about
Solve a simpler equation that leads back to it

questions.explain: A problem is auxiliary when it is considered because it may help another, and the other is the aim.
questions.hint: Which would you drop if the other were solved another way?
questions.rule: Make the means into a clearly stated problem of its own, keeping the original as the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: What does the book say human superiority consists in here?
options: Repeating the same attempt many times
Working faster than any insect could, however many tries it takes
Never meeting obstacles
Going around an obstacle that cannot be overcome directly, by devising a suitable auxiliary problem
optionExplain: Repetition is the insect's pattern.
Speed is not what the book claims; it is the ability to go around an obstacle.
Obstacles are expected; the superiority lies in how a person deals with one.
Right: the book says this is what a person should be able to do.
questions.explain: Devising a suitable auxiliary problem when the original appears insoluble is called an important operation of the mind.
questions.teaches: To conceive distinctly as an end what is means to another end is, the book says, a refined achievement of the intelligence.
questions.rule: Make the means into a clearly stated problem of its own, keeping the original as the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A manager cannot decide on a new office layout. She first surveys how many people are in the office on each day. In the book's terms, the survey is
options: The original problem
An auxiliary problem posed to help with the layout
An obstacle standing in the way of the layout decision
A final answer
optionExplain: The original is the layout decision.
Right: it is considered for the sake of the layout.
It is a step, not an obstacle.
It is a step, not the answer.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same end-and-means relation holds outside mathematics.
questions.teaches: The book says it is an important task to learn, or to teach, how to handle auxiliary problems intelligently.
questions.rule: Make the means into a clearly stated problem of its own, keeping the original as the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The equation x to the fourth minus 5 x squared plus 4 equals zero has no x cubed or x term. What helps?
options: Treat x squared as one unknown, since x to the fourth is its square
Take the fourth root of both sides term by term to remove the powers
Divide every term by x to lower each power by one
Guess a value such as x equals 10 and adjust it until the left side is zero
optionExplain: Right: with y = x squared the equation becomes a quadratic in y.
A fourth root cannot be taken term by term of a sum.
Dividing by x leaves x cubed and 4/x; it does not remove the trouble with the fourth power.
Guessing has no basis here when a structural move is available.
questions.explain: The card next shows this substitution in the book's example.
questions.rule: Look for a repeated pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the equation x to the fourth minus 13 x squared plus 36 equals 0, the book sets y equal to x to the power ____.
questions.explain: Since x to the fourth is the square of x squared, y = x squared reduces the degree.
questions.rule: Set y = x squared.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Solve x to the fourth minus 5 x squared plus 4 equals 0 with y equal to x squared. Which values of x result?
options: 1 and 4, the values of y
2 and -2 only
optionExplain: Right: y = 1 or 4, so x = ±1 or ±2.
1 and 4 are the values of y, not of x.
This forgets y = 1: from x squared = 1 the roots x = 1 and -1 also belong.
These are not roots of the original equation: x = 4 gives 256 - 80 + 4 = 180, not 0.
questions.explain: The quadratic y squared minus 5y plus 4 equals 0 factors as (y - 1)(y - 4), so y = 1 or 4. Then x squared = 1 or 4, so x = 1, -1, 2 or -2.
questions.rule: Go back from y to x, taking both roots.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: After finding y = 4 or 9 in the book's example, the answer to the original equation is x = 4 or 9.
questions.explain: The auxiliary unknown y stands for x squared, so we must return to x: x = 2, -2, 3 or -3.
questions.rule: Return to the original unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book calls y in this example an auxiliary unknown. Why is the new problem an auxiliary problem?
options: It has the same unknown
It is a means for solving the original equation
It is harder than the original
It is a different equation altogether, with unrelated roots
optionExplain: The unknown differs: y, not x, so this is not the reason.
Right: it is solved in order to solve the original equation.
It is easier than the original, not harder, so this cannot be why it is auxiliary.
It is tied to the original through y = x squared, so its roots are not unrelated.
questions.explain: The new problem is considered because we intend to use it as a means of solving our original problem.
questions.teaches: The book calls the auxiliary problem a means for solving the original one: it is considered because we intend to use it, not for its own sake.
questions.rule: Name the repeating part by a new letter, solve for it, then go back for the original unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Solve 2 to the power 2t minus 6 times 2 to the power t plus 8 equals 0. With y = 2 to the power t, which t values result?
options: t = 2 and t = 4, which are the values of 2 to the t
t = 3 only
t = 0 and t = 1
t = 1 and t = 2
optionExplain: Those are the values of y.
This loses one root: 2 to the t = 2 gives t = 1 as well as t = 2 from 2 to the t = 4.
This slips from y to t incorrectly.
Right: y squared minus 6y plus 8 equals 0 gives y = 2 or 4, so 2 to the t equals 2 or 4, which gives t = 1 or 2.
questions.explain: We solved y squared minus 6y plus 8 = 0 to get y = 2 or 4, then took 2 to the t equal to each. Our reading: the repeated part need not be a power of x.
questions.teaches: The repeated part can be any expression that appears in a simple way, such as 2 to the t: the idea is not tied to powers of x.
questions.rule: Name the repeating part by a new letter, solve for it, then go back for the original unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student solves a rectangle-diagonal problem to help with a box-diagonal problem. What could the rectangle problem give back?
questions.explain: The card next explains the kinds of profit.
questions.rule: Result: answer. Method: route.
options: Nothing, since it is a different problem
Only its result
Its result, its method, or both
Only its colour scheme
optionExplain: Different problems can still help.
Results are one possible gain.
Right: the book says we may use the result, the method or both.
Colour is not part of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the equation example, the book uses the ____ of the auxiliary problem to find all the values of x.
questions.explain: The values of y obtained give x squared, then x.
questions.rule: Result of the auxiliary problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: To estimate the diagonal of a room 3 m by 4 m by 12 m, a student first finds the floor diagonal. What is the floor diagonal and the room diagonal?
options: 5 m and 12 m
7 m and 19 m
5 m and 13 m
12 m and 13 m
optionExplain: 12 m is the height, not the diagonal.
Adding edges gives larger numbers than the diagonals.
Right: the floor diagonal is 5, and the room diagonal is the square root of 25 + 144 = 13.
The floor diagonal is 5, not 12.
questions.explain: Floor: sqrt(9+16)=5. Room: sqrt(25+144)=13. The floor diagonal (result) feeds into the room diagonal.
questions.rule: The auxiliary result becomes a side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: In the book's box-diagonal example, only the result of the plane auxiliary problem can be used, not its method.
questions.explain: The book says that in this example we can use both the method and the result.
questions.rule: Before investing in an auxiliary problem, ask which of its method and result you expect to use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Why is it reasonable to choose an analogous but simpler auxiliary problem?
options: Because it removes the original problem
Because it needs no thought and can be solved by anyone at once
Because it is always equivalent
It may let us familiarise ourselves with methods, operations or tools we use afterwards
optionExplain: The original problem remains the aim; the auxiliary problem only helps towards it.
A simpler problem still needs thought; the book hopes it will be instructive, not trivial.
Analogous does not mean equivalent.
Right: it is instructive.
questions.explain: The book says it is reasonable to introduce an auxiliary problem of this kind in the hope that it will be instructive.
questions.teaches: Using an easier problem as practice for methods and tools is a legitimate profit even before its result is known to fit.
questions.rule: Before investing in an auxiliary problem, ask which of its method and result you expect to use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A coach has a team practise a simpler drill before a complex play. Which profit from the drill fits the book's 'method'?
options: The drill replaces the play, so the play is never run
Players learn moves they will reuse in the complex play
The play is cancelled
The drill's score counts toward the result of the complex play
optionExplain: The play is still needed.
Right: methods learned carry over.
Cancelling is not a profit.
Scores are not the point.
questions.explain: Our reading: practice transfers methods; sometimes an outcome transfers too, as the floor diagonal does.
questions.teaches: In the book's equation example the auxiliary problem pays through its result, while in the box example it pays through both its method and its result.
questions.rule: Before investing in an auxiliary problem, ask which of its method and result you expect to use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: Working on an auxiliary problem costs nothing, since the original problem is untouched meanwhile.
questions.explain: The time and effort spent are taken from the original. The card next lists the costs and reasons.
questions.rule: Detours cost time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: If the investigation of the auxiliary problem fails, the time and effort we devoted to it may be ____.
questions.explain: That is the book's statement of the risk.
questions.rule: The risk is lost time and effort.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student has 30 minutes left. Which auxiliary problem is the wiser choice by the book's reasons?
options: A special case that looks accessible and instructive
A harder generalisation with no clear route to a solution
A problem chosen only because it is new
A random puzzle nearby
optionExplain: Right: accessible and instructive.
A harder problem with no route is risky.
Novelty alone is the weakest ground.
A random puzzle gives no link.
questions.explain: With little time, choose accessibility and instruction over novelty.
questions.rule: Prefer accessible and instructive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which reasons for choosing an auxiliary problem does the book give? Select all that apply.
options: It looks more accessible than the original
It looks instructive
It has some aesthetic appeal
It is guaranteed to succeed
It is the first problem that comes to mind
optionExplain: Right: accessibility is a reason.
Right: instruction is a reason.
Right: aesthetic appeal is a reason.
No guarantee exists; the book speaks of risk.
The first idea is not named as a reason.
questions.explain: The book lists accessibility, instruction and aesthetic appeal, and mentions novelty when approaches are exhausted. It never promises success.
questions.rule: Pick an auxiliary problem that looks accessible or instructive, and keep an eye on the cost.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: When may an auxiliary problem be chosen only because it is new?
options: When the original is easy
Never
When time is plentiful and we are fresh and have not yet tried the original
When all approaches to the original seem exhausted and we are tired of it
optionExplain: Easy problems do not call for detours.
The book allows it in this case.
The book ties novelty to being tired.
Right: the book names this case.
questions.explain: Novelty offers unexplored possibilities when other approaches have run dry.
questions.teaches: Sometimes the only advantage of the auxiliary problem is that it is new and offers unexplored possibilities.
questions.rule: Pick an auxiliary problem that looks accessible or instructive, and keep an eye on the cost.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A founder stalled on a pricing model starts a side analysis of competitor websites, only because it is different. By the book's reasons this is
options: A guaranteed gain that repays the time spent
Allowed as a weak reason, with the risk of lost time
Forbidden, because novelty is never a reason to pick a problem
A proof of the model
optionExplain: The book promises no gain from a problem chosen only for novelty, so this overstates it.
Right: novelty is allowed but weak.
The book does allow novelty.
An analysis is not a proof.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's reasons rank accessibility and instruction above mere novelty.
questions.teaches: The book says we should exercise judgment in choosing an auxiliary problem, because the effort given to it is taken away from the original problem.
questions.rule: Pick an auxiliary problem that looks accessible or instructive, and keep an eye on the cost.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book gives a sure method for finding a suitable auxiliary problem.
questions.explain: It says there is no infallible method. The card next gives the helpful questions it does offer.
questions.rule: No infallible method exists.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Two helpful suggestions for finding auxiliary problems are to look at the ____ and to vary the problem.
questions.explain: The book names Look at the unknown and Variation of the problem.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown; vary the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student cannot find the area of an irregular garden. Which move follows the book?
options: Wait for inspiration to arrive, and then draw the figure
Pick a plausible area and test whether it fits the garden
Ask what the unknown is, and what is known about finding areas of simpler shapes
Skip it until a measuring tape is available
optionExplain: Waiting leaves the unknown untouched, whereas the book's suggestion is to look at it now.
A guess is not a method; it does not use what is known about similar unknowns.
Right: look at the unknown.
Skipping avoids the question, while the book's move is to look at the unknown now.
questions.explain: Looking at the unknown connects the problem to earlier ones with the same kind of unknown.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown and vary the problem to generate candidate auxiliary problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, the questions it suggests for finding auxiliary problems are frequently helpful but do not guarantee success.
questions.explain: The book says there is no infallible method, yet some questions and suggestions are frequently helpful.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown and vary the problem to generate candidate auxiliary problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: What does the book say the discovery of the solution often depends on?
options: Finding a suitable auxiliary problem
Remembering the formulas of the chapter exactly
Luck alone, with no help from method
Setting aside the original problem for good
optionExplain: Right: the book says the discovery of the solution often depends on discovering a suitable auxiliary problem.
Formulas may be useful, but the book does not say the discovery depends on remembering them.
The book does not say luck alone decides; it says the discovery often depends on finding a suitable auxiliary problem.
The original problem stays the aim; the auxiliary problem serves it and does not replace it.
questions.explain: That explains why the book treats finding auxiliary problems as a skill worth learning.
questions.teaches: Varying the problem is one of the ways the book names for being led to useful auxiliary problems.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown and vary the problem to generate candidate auxiliary problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A teacher stuck on a timetable clash asks what exactly is unknown, then tries the same clash with fewer classes. Which two suggestions did she use?
options: Work backwards, and then guess at the answer
Ask a friend, and wait
Look at the unknown, and vary the problem
Use a formula, and stop
optionExplain: Working backwards is another heuristic, not named here.
Asking a friend is not named.
Right: these are the two named in the book.
A formula is not one of the two suggestions named in the book.
questions.explain: Our reading: the two suggestions carry over to scheduling.
questions.teaches: The book names Look at the unknown as a question that frequently helps in finding a suitable auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown and vary the problem to generate candidate auxiliary problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Problem P can be solved if and only if problem Q can be solved, and each solution gives the other. What is the relation of P and Q?
options: Q is harder than P
They are identical sentences
They are unrelated
They are equivalent
optionExplain: Neither is harder by this relation alone.
Equivalent problems need not be identical in wording.
They are related: each can be solved through the other, so they are not unrelated.
Right: the solution of each involves the solution of the other.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's definition.
questions.rule: Equivalent: each solves the other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The passage from the original problem to an auxiliary problem whose solution gives the original is called a convertible or ____ reduction.
questions.explain: Both names are used in the book.
questions.rule: Convertible, bilateral or equivalent reduction.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which pair is equivalent in the book's sense?
options: In any equilateral triangle each angle is 60 degrees; in any equiangular triangle each angle is 60 degrees
Find x with x squared 4; find x with x cubed 8
Prove a statement about all triangles; prove it for one single triangle only
Solve a puzzle; delete the puzzle
optionExplain: Right: each follows from the other.
The solutions differ: 2 and -2 versus 2 only.
Proving it for one triangle is narrower.
Deleting is not equivalent.
questions.explain: The first pair is the book's example. Our check: x squared = 4 has x = 2 or -2, but x cubed = 8 has only x = 2 in the reals, so the pair is not equivalent.
questions.rule: Same solutions, mutually derivable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book says the two triangle theorems about equal sides and equal angles are identical, not only equivalent.
questions.explain: They contain different notions, one about sides and one about angles, though each follows from the other.
questions.rule: Equivalent is weaker than identical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Why can we foresee that theorem B is easier than A?
options: B is shorter to write
B is concerned only with angles, so it is more homogeneous
B has fewer words
B was proved earlier
optionExplain: Length is not the reason.
Right: A mixes angles and sides.
Word count is not the reason.
The book does not mention an earlier proof.
questions.explain: Homogeneity makes the statement easier to handle.
questions.teaches: We may judge, from the outset and before proving, that one equivalent problem is easier than another, because of homogeneity.
questions.rule: When possible, replace the problem by an equivalent one that looks simpler.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Two tax forms ask for the same figure in different words, and each form's figure can be computed from the other. In the book's language the forms are
options: Equivalent, not identical
Identical
Unrelated, since the wording differs
Both wrong
optionExplain: Right: different forms, same content.
The two forms are worded differently, so they are not identical, even though their content matches.
The wording differs but each figure can be computed from the other, so they are connected.
Nothing in the setting makes either form wrong; they are equivalent.
questions.explain: Our reading: the example extends the idea of equivalent but not identical.
questions.teaches: Equivalent problems may be different statements built on different notions, because each only has to follow from the other.
questions.rule: When possible, replace the problem by an equivalent one that looks simpler.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Problem A is equivalent to B, B to C, and C to D, whose solution is obvious. What follows for A?
options: A is harder than D
Nothing, because a chain of three links is too long to trust
A is equivalent to D, so A is solved through D
A has no solution
optionExplain: Equivalence does not rank difficulty.
Length of the chain does not matter if each link is equivalent.
Right: equivalence passes along the chain.
D's solution is obvious, so A's solution follows along the chain; A does have a solution.
questions.explain: The card next states the book's chain argument.
questions.rule: Equivalence carries along a chain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In a chain of equivalent problems, the last problem L is one whose solution is known or ____.
questions.explain: The chain ends at a problem we can solve at once.
questions.rule: The chain ends at an easy problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Put these forms of the book's equation chain in order, from the original to the answer.
items: x to the fourth minus 13 x squared plus 36 equals 0
The square of (2 x squared minus 13) equals 25
2 x squared minus 13 equals plus or minus 5
x squared equals (13 plus or minus 5) over 2
x equals 3, -3, 2 or -2
questions.explain: Each form follows from and leads back to the one before. The numbers check: (13 + 5)/2 = 9 and (13 - 5)/2 = 4.
questions.rule: Each step is small and reversible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Solve (x - 3) squared equals 16 by a chain. Which sequence of equivalent conditions is correct?
options: x - 3 = 4, so x = 7 and nothing else
x - 3 = 4 or x - 3 = -4, so x = 7 or x = -1
x - 3 = 16, so x = 19, as the square is removed
x = 4 or x = -4
optionExplain: Keeping only the positive root loses -1.
Right: taking both roots keeps the chain equivalent.
x - 3 = 16 is not equivalent.
The shift of 3 is dropped.
questions.explain: Both 7 and -1 satisfy it: (7-3)^2 = 16 and (-1-3)^2 = 16.
questions.rule: Make each link a small, clearly purposeful step, and keep every link equivalent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How does the book's equation chain differ from the chain described by Pappus?
options: It uses only inequalities
It uses a different unknown at every step of the chain, as Pappus does
It has no last problem
All problems in the chain have the same unknown and differ only in the condition
optionExplain: No inequality is involved.
That describes Pappus's problems to find.
The chain ends at x equal to 3, -3, 2, -2.
Right: the unknown stays x.
questions.explain: The book notes the Pappus description is restricted to chains of problems to find with different unknowns; here the unknown is constant.
questions.teaches: Chains of equivalent problems need not change the unknown; they may change only the form of the condition imposed on it.
questions.rule: Make each link a small, clearly purposeful step, and keep every link equivalent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A bookkeeper rewrites a total as a sum of simpler subtotals, each rewriting giving the same total. What matches the chain idea?
options: Each rewriting loses a little, so the final form is smaller than the total
Each rewriting is equivalent, so the last form gives the original total
The last form is a new total
No rewriting can be trusted
optionExplain: Losing value breaks equivalence.
Right: if every step preserves the value, the final form stands for the original.
A new total would not be the same.
Trust is warranted when each step is checked.
questions.explain: Our reading: the chain argument is about preserving the thing sought through every link.
questions.teaches: Equivalent conditions are satisfied by the same objects, so passing along a chain of them keeps exactly the same solutions.
questions.rule: Make each link a small, clearly purposeful step, and keep every link equivalent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: You turn an equation into a new one with more solutions than the original. What risk does this carry?
options: Nothing changes
You lose solutions that the original equation had
Some solutions of the new equation may not solve the original
The original has no solutions left
optionExplain: Widening changes the solution set.
Losing solutions comes from narrowing.
Right: wider conditions admit adventitious solutions.
Solutions of the original may still exist.
questions.explain: The card next states both dangers.
questions.rule: Wider adds false solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: If we pass from a proposed condition to a narrower one, we ____ solutions.
questions.explain: A narrower condition drops some solutions.
questions.rule: Narrower loses solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: From x squared equals 3 x, a student divides by x and gets x equals 3. What happened?
options: The condition was widened, so a false root crept in
The equation had no solution at all after the division
The step was equivalent
The condition was narrowed, and the solution x = 0 was lost
optionExplain: Widening would add solutions.
The equation still has solutions: 3 is one, and x = 0 is the one the division lost.
Equivalent steps keep all solutions; 0 was dropped.
Right: dividing by x assumes x is not zero.
questions.explain: x = 0 satisfies x squared = 3x, as 0 = 0, so dividing by x lost it.
questions.rule: Dividing by an unknown can lose a solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Squaring both sides of the square root of (x + 2) equals x gives x + 2 = x squared with roots 2 and -1. Which is a true solution?
options: Only x = 2
Both
Only x = -1
Neither
optionExplain: Right: for x = 2 the root of 4 is 2, but for x = -1 the root of 1 is 1, not -1.
The check eliminates -1.
-1 gives root 1 which is not -1.
x = 2 works, since the root of 4 is 2, so neither cannot be right.
questions.explain: Squaring widened the condition: -1 satisfies the squared equation but not the original, because the root of 1 is 1, not -1.
questions.rule: After widening, check the candidates.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each step: is the reduction equivalent, narrowing or widening?
groups: Keeps all solutions and adds none

items.t: Add 5 to both sides of an equation
Divide both sides by the unknown
Square both sides of an equation
Subtract 7 from both sides
Multiply both sides by a nonzero number
Replace an equation by only one of its two cases

questions.explain: Adding or subtracting a number and multiplying by a nonzero number can be undone, so they keep the solution set. The others can lose or add solutions. Our reading: the examples go beyond the book's two.
questions.hint: Can the step be undone exactly?
questions.rule: After each transformation, ask: Is it equivalent to the original condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A manager narrows a customer survey to people who answered the first question, then widens it by adding new regions. What danger does the book's warning suggest?
options: None, since the result is larger than before
Losing track of what the data originally described
The survey is complete, because it now covers more regions and answers
The sample is certainly accurate
optionExplain: Larger does not mean faithful.
Right: narrowing and then widening may lose track of the original.
Completeness is not assured.
Accuracy is not assured.
questions.explain: The book warns that passing to a narrower condition and then again to a wider one may lose track of the original problem completely. Our reading: the same holds for data selection.
questions.teaches: The book says narrowing and then widening in succession can lose track of the original problem completely, even if some solutions remain.
questions.rule: After each transformation, ask: Is it equivalent to the original condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Problem A, if solved, would also solve B fully. But solving B would not solve A. Which is more ambitious?
options: Both equally
B
A
Neither
optionExplain: They are not equal: solving A solves B, but solving B does not solve A.
B gives less, since its solution does not contain A's.
Right: solving A also solves B, so A achieves more and is the more ambitious.
One of them exceeds the other.
questions.explain: The card next defines the pair.
questions.rule: Solving the more ambitious gives the less.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: If a step goes from the original to a more or a less ambitious problem, the book calls it a ____ reduction.
questions.explain: Unilateral means one-sided: the problems are not equivalent.
questions.rule: Unilateral: one-sided.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which pair has A more ambitious than B?
options: A: colour the chart. B: cost the chart
A: find total sales for January. B: find total sales for every month of the year
A: sales this week. B: sales this week
A: find the total sales for every month. B: find the total sales for January
optionExplain: Colouring and costing a chart are different tasks, so neither includes the other.
The roles are reversed here.
The two are identical, so neither is more ambitious.
Right: the all-months problem would give January.
questions.explain: Solving for every month includes January; solving January alone gives no other month.
questions.rule: Decide which problem would give the other, and note that this lopsided link is the price.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a unilateral reduction is more risky than a convertible reduction.
questions.explain: Both kinds of unilateral reduction are, in some way, more risky than a bilateral or convertible one.
questions.rule: Decide which problem would give the other, and note that this lopsided link is the price.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How does the book describe the effect of solving the less ambitious problem B for A?
options: We would obtain, possibly, some information about A, but not the full solution
We would obtain nothing at all about A from the solution of B
We would obtain the full solution of A
We would obtain the solution of a third problem
optionExplain: Right: B gives some information about A at most.
The book says possibly some information.
That is true of A, not B.
No third problem is mentioned.
questions.explain: If we could solve B, we would not know how to derive the full solution of A from it.
questions.teaches: Solving the more ambitious A achieves more than solving B, because the full solution of B follows from that of A and not the reverse.
questions.rule: Decide which problem would give the other, and note that this lopsided link is the price.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A caterer plans for 50 guests (A) instead of the 10 she is hosting (B). A plan for 50 can be trimmed to 10. Which is more ambitious?
options: The 10-guest plan
The 50-guest plan
They are equivalent
Neither
optionExplain: The smaller does not include the larger.
Right: the larger plan includes the smaller.
Plans for different sizes are not equivalent.
One plan includes the other: the plan for 50 can be trimmed to 10, so it is the more ambitious.
questions.explain: Our reading: a plan that can be scaled down is more ambitious than one that cannot be scaled up.
questions.teaches: Solving the less ambitious problem may still give some information about the more ambitious one, though not its full solution.
questions.rule: Decide which problem would give the other, and note that this lopsided link is the price.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A box problem with sides a, b, c includes the flat case when c is zero. Which problem is less ambitious?
options: Both are equal
The box problem, since it has the extra height
The flat rectangle problem
Neither
optionExplain: They are not equal in scope.
The box problem includes the flat one.
Right: the flat case is contained in the box case.
One is contained in the other.
questions.explain: The card next explains the book's use of this relation.
questions.rule: Special case: less ambitious.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the book's example, setting c equal to ____ turns the box into a rectangle.
questions.explain: With no height, the box becomes flat.
questions.rule: c = 0 gives the flat case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Using the flat diagonal sqrt(a squared + b squared) and a supplementary remark about a right triangle with height c, what is the box diagonal for a=2, b=3, c=6?
options: sqrt(65)
sqrt(13)
optionExplain: 11 adds the three edges 2, 3 and 6, but the diagonal is a root of a sum of squares.
sqrt(65) adds 13 and 52, a slip.
sqrt(13) forgets the height.
Right: the flat diagonal squared is 13, plus 36 gives 49, whose root is 7.
questions.explain: 4 + 9 + 36 = 49, and the root is 7.
questions.rule: Add the square of the height to the flat diagonal squared.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: Solving the flat rectangle case is enough by itself; no supplementary remark is needed to get the box case.
questions.explain: The book says the solution of the less ambitious problem is combined with an appropriate supplementary remark.
questions.rule: Pick a special case, solve it, then ask what extra step reaches the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: What does the book say about the chance that the less ambitious auxiliary problem will serve?
options: With some luck it may serve as a stepping stone
It always serves
It never serves
It serves only for boxes and similar solid figures
optionExplain: Right: the book says that with some luck the less ambitious problem may serve as a stepping stone.
The book hedges with 'some luck', so 'always' overstates it.
It does serve in the example.
The use is not restricted to boxes.
questions.explain: The book points to Specialization for further examples.
questions.teaches: The book points to its article on Specialization for other examples of a reduction to a less ambitious problem.
questions.rule: Pick a special case, solve it, then ask what extra step reaches the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: To plan a school timetable for 20 classes, a deputy first plans for 2 classes, then adds the extra rooms and teachers one by one. Which part is the supplementary remark?
options: The 2-class plan itself
The final timetable that the deputy hands to the school
The extra step that adapts the small plan for more rooms and teachers
Nothing
optionExplain: The 2-class plan is the stepping stone.
The final timetable is the goal.
Right: it carries the small result to the big problem.
Something must bridge them.
questions.explain: Our reading: the bridging step is the supplementary remark.
questions.teaches: The book shows the flat problem inside the box problem by putting the height c equal to 0, which gives a rectangle with length a and width b.
questions.rule: Pick a special case, solve it, then ask what extra step reaches the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: If a problem is more ambitious than the original, it is certain to be harder to solve.
questions.explain: The book calls it the inventor's paradox that a more ambitious problem may be more accessible. The card next explains.
questions.rule: More ambitious need not mean harder.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: The book calls the fact that a more ambitious problem may be more accessible the ____ paradox.
questions.explain: That is the name the book gives.
questions.rule: The inventor's paradox.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which move is a reduction to a more ambitious problem?
options: Checking the statement by drawing
Proving the statement for n = 1 only, as a special case
Dropping the statement
Proving a statement for every n instead of for n = 5
optionExplain: Drawing does not change ambition.
n = 1 is a special case, which is less ambitious.
Dropping is not a reduction.
Right: the statement for every n includes the case n = 5.
questions.explain: Solving the general case gives n = 5, so it is more ambitious.
questions.rule: Try generalising the problem when the special case offers no foothold.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Sort each problem: is it more ambitious or less ambitious than proving a fact for n = 5?
questions.explain: A problem is more ambitious if solving it would also give the n = 5 case. The cases n = 1 and n = 2 are special cases that do not give n = 5.

items.t: Prove the fact for every n
Prove the fact for n = 1
Prove the fact for all n from 1 to 10
Prove the fact for n = 2

questions.rule: Try generalising the problem when the special case offers no foothold.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which articles does the book point to for examples of reduction to a more ambitious problem?
options: Generalization, and Induction and Mathematical Induction
Pappus, and Bolzano
Notation, and Symmetry, which treat other matters
Diagnosis, and Decomposing, which treat other topics
optionExplain: Right: those two articles.
Those are unrelated entries.
Those are other articles.
Those are not named here.
questions.explain: The book mentions Generalization 2 and the first two problems in Induction and Mathematical Induction.
questions.teaches: The book names Generalization and Induction and Mathematical Induction as the places where reduction to a more ambitious problem succeeds.
questions.rule: Try generalising the problem when the special case offers no foothold.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A teacher cannot find a rule for a pattern in 5 examples. A colleague suggests finding the rule for any number of examples at once. In the book's terms, this is
options: A convertible reduction, since the two problems are equivalent
A reduction to a more ambitious problem, which may be more accessible
A non-reduction
A reduction to a less ambitious problem, since it narrows the case
optionExplain: The two problems are not equivalent: the rule for any number would give the rule for five, but not the reverse.
Right: a rule for any number includes the rule for five examples, so the new problem is more ambitious yet may be more accessible.
It is a reduction: the colleague replaces one problem by another to help solve the first.
It enlarges the problem.
questions.explain: Our reading: wanting the rule for any number can reveal the structure that five examples hide.
questions.teaches: The book cites the reduction of the first to the second problem in its article on induction as an example of passing to a more ambitious problem.
questions.rule: Try generalising the problem when the special case offers no foothold.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Which phrase best describes Bernard Bolzano in the book?
options: A logician and mathematician who wrote on heuristic
A Greek geometer who lived before Pappus
An astronomer of Aristotle's time
A physician who wrote on health
optionExplain: Right: logician and mathematician, 1781 to 1848.
Pappus is the Greek mathematician mentioned elsewhere.
Aristotle's contemporary appears in another entry.
No medical role is mentioned.
questions.explain: The card next gives his claims.
questions.rule: Bolzano: logician, wrote on heuristic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Bolzano devoted an extensive part of his Wissenschaftslehre to the subject of ____.
questions.explain: It is in volume 3, the book notes.
questions.rule: Heuristic is his subject here.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A trainer says: I do not claim these tips are new; I want to put into words what good nurses already do. Whose attitude does this echo?
options: Aristotle's
Bolzano's
Pappus's
The insect's
optionExplain: Aristotle defined sagacity.
Right: he states the rules followed by able people, without claiming novelty.
Pappus described chains of problems.
The insect repeats attempts.
questions.explain: Bolzano promises nothing quite new but wants to state in clear words what able men follow, often unconsciously.
questions.rule: State clearly what experts do.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: Bolzano claims that the procedures of investigation he presents were unknown before him.
questions.explain: He says he does not think he presents any procedure not perceived long ago by all men of talent.
questions.rule: Aim to make existing good practice explicit and usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How does Bolzano describe his hope for what he presents?
options: That it will be complete and cover every procedure of investigation
That it will replace all earlier methods
That the little presented may please some people and have some application afterwards
That it will be the last word
optionExplain: He says he is free from the illusion of full success.
He claims no replacement.
Right: his hope is modest.
He does not claim finality.
questions.explain: The book quotes him saying he is free from the illusion that he will fully succeed.
questions.teaches: Bolzano writes that he is free from the illusion that he will fully succeed even in stating clearly the rules that able people follow.
questions.rule: Aim to make existing good practice explicit and usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A software team writes a guide of habits their best engineers follow without noticing. Which claim is in Bolzano's spirit?
options: These habits are brand new
This guide is complete
Engineers never used these habits before the guide was written
We are not inventing these habits; we are stating them in plain words so others can use them
optionExplain: Bolzano disclaims novelty, so a claim that the habits are brand new does not fit his spirit.
Completeness is disclaimed.
Able people already follow them.
Right: no novelty is promised.
questions.explain: Our reading: the modest aim of stating existing practice carries over to any craft.
questions.teaches: Bolzano gave his extensive treatment of heuristic in volume 3 of his Wissenschaftslehre.
questions.rule: Aim to make existing good practice explicit and usable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: What does the book say the coming of a bright idea feels like?
options: A slow accumulation of facts, one by one
A sudden advance toward the solution
A rule applied step by step
A random guess
optionExplain: Slow accumulation is the opposite of sudden.
Right: it is a sudden advance.
A rule applied step by step is not sudden.
A guess hits the essential connection, which is more than random.
questions.explain: The card next quotes the definition the book borrows from Aristotle.
questions.rule: A bright idea is sudden.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Aristotle defines sagacity as a hitting by guess upon the essential ____ in an inappreciable time.
questions.explain: The essential connection is what the guess hits.
questions.rule: Sagacity hits the essential connection.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A mechanic hears an odd noise and at once guesses that a loose belt links the noise to the engine speed. Which part of Aristotle's description does this show?
options: Slow measurement
Long calculation
Hitting by guess upon the essential connection in an inappreciable time
Copying a manual
optionExplain: The guess is quick, not a slow measurement.
The guess is quick, not a long calculation.
Right: quick insight into a connection.
Copying a manual is not the quick grasp of a connection that Aristotle describes.
questions.explain: The guess is fast and aims at the connection between noise and cause.
questions.rule: Look for the essential connection, and judge how bright an idea is by how much it explains.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: True or false: The book calls Aristotle's example of the rich man a very bright idea.
questions.explain: It calls the example not bad but rather trivial, and the idea not very bright.
questions.rule: Brightness depends on how deep the connection is.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Why does the book say the rich-man example is not very bright?
options: Not much sagacity is needed to guess things of that sort
The man was not rich
The guess was wrong, so no sagacity was needed
Aristotle did not mean it as an example of sagacity
optionExplain: Right: it is a trivial guess.
The man's wealth is not the issue.
The book does not say it was wrong.
Aristotle did offer the rich-man example, so this does not explain the book's remark.
questions.explain: Triviality, not error, lowers the brightness.
questions.teaches: The book also refers to Progress and Achievement, section 6, for the same notion of a sudden advance.
questions.rule: Look for the essential connection, and judge how bright an idea is by how much it explains.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A student sees at once that two different-looking word problems share the same hidden equation. Compared with the book's examples, this is
options: A trivial guess about rich men
No insight at all, since the two problems look different on the page
A rule
A modest bright idea: a quick grasp of a connection between problems
optionExplain: The link is mathematical, not a social guess.
Seeing a hidden link is insight.
A flash of insight is not a rule that can be applied by following steps.
Right: a quick hit on a connection.
questions.explain: Our reading: the size of the idea depends on how hard the connection was to see.
questions.teaches: The book rates Aristotle's first example, the rich man, as not very bright, and the second, the moon, as quite impressive.
questions.rule: Look for the essential connection, and judge how bright an idea is by how much it explains.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Why would a person in Aristotle's time watch the sun, stars and moon closely?
options: For entertainment only, as a pastime of the evening
To know the time and to plan travel by night
To copy the heavens into written tables
To set the dates of religious festivals
optionExplain: Entertainment is not the book's reason.
Right: no wristwatches or street lights.
Written tables are not the book's reason; its point is how well acquainted an ancient person was with the sky.
The book does not give festival dates as the reason; the sky served the practical needs of ordinary life.
questions.explain: The book uses this to show how well acquainted an ancient person was with the sky. The card next gives the full setting.
questions.rule: Recover the setting.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Before the leap, the ancient observer saw the full moon as a flat ____.
questions.explain: He thought of sun and moon as flat discs.
questions.rule: Flat disc, then a ball.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: Put the steps of the moon discovery in order.
items: Observe the moon's changing shapes and positions
Notice that its bright side is always toward the sun
Compare the phases with a ball lit from one side
Conceive sun and moon as round bodies, one giving light and one receiving it
Conclude that the moon shines by the sun's light
questions.explain: The book follows this path from observation to the leap of imagination.
questions.rule: Observe, notice, compare, rearrange, conclude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A reader says the moon idea is trivial because every child knows it. What does the book's approach reply?
options: Agree with the reader, since modern people know the idea already
Say it was never made
Say it is false
Judge it in its setting: for someone who saw discs, it was a leap of imagination
optionExplain: Hindsight hides the effort.
The book credits the idea.
The book does not call the idea false; the idea is correct and the question is how to judge it.
Right: the book asks us to make an effort of imagination.
questions.explain: The book says the example is quite impressive if we imagine it in its proper setting.
questions.rule: When judging a discovery, recover what was known then and how the pieces were rearranged.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: How does the book say the observer rearranged his conceptions?
options: He did it instantly, in an inappreciable time, by a sudden leap of the imagination
Slowly over many years, by repeated careful observation
By a long calculation from the moon's period
By asking a teacher to explain it step by step
optionExplain: Right: the rearrangement was sudden, a leap of the imagination in an inappreciable time.
The book stresses that the rearrangement was instant, not the result of years of observation.
No calculation is mentioned; the change was a leap of the imagination.
Aristotle is the source of the description, and no teacher's step-by-step help is mentioned.
questions.explain: He understood the essential connection and rearranged his former conceptions.
questions.teaches: He conceived the sun and the moon as round bodies, one giving and the other receiving the light, which turns the phases into aspects of a lit ball.
questions.rule: When judging a discovery, recover what was known then and how the pieces were rearranged.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: A manager finally sees that late deliveries and angry calls come from the same cause, a missing step in packing. Which feature matches the moon example?
options: A slow survey
A lucky coin toss
Two observations suddenly join into one explanation
An order from above
optionExplain: A survey is slow and systematic, while the moon example is a sudden joining of facts.
A lucky toss gives no explanation, whereas the moon example links facts into one explanation.
Right: a connection that rearranges what was known.
An order from above supplies no insight; the moon example is the solver's own connection.
questions.explain: Our reading: the moon story shows facts rearranged in an instant into a single explanation.
questions.teaches: The book counts it a respectable achievement in itself to have found out that the bright side of the moon is always toward the sun.
questions.rule: When judging a discovery, recover what was known then and how the pieces were rearranged.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A pupil works out that a school bus travels at 4,000 km/h. What is the best next move?
options: Accept it, because every step of the working was written out neatly
Change the units so that the number looks smaller and less odd
Doubt the figure and recheck, because no bus goes that fast
Ask a classmate whether 4,000 is a common answer for this kind of problem
optionExplain: Neat working does not make a number believable.
Changing units changes the look of the number, not its plausibility.
Right: a speed far outside what buses do signals a mistake somewhere.
A classmate's answer is not an observation of the world.
questions.explain: A commonsense estimate of what a bus can do rejects the figure at once. The card next shows the book's version of this check.
questions.rule: Compare a numerical result with observed numbers or with a commonsense estimate before you trust it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Numerical results can be tested by comparing them with observed numbers or with a commonsense ____ of observable numbers.
questions.explain: The book names two comparisons: with observed numbers, or with a commonsense estimate of them.
questions.rule: Compare the answer with the world.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A cook scales a recipe from 4 people to 40 and gets 3 tablespoons of salt for the pot. Which response follows this check?
options: Estimate what a pot for 40 people normally needs and compare it with the 3 tablespoons
Trust the 3 tablespoons because the scaling sum was done twice with the same result
Trust it because salt is cheap and a small error costs very little in the end
Question whether the original recipe for 4 people was written correctly before going on
optionExplain: Right: an estimate from outside the calculation is the comparison the book describes.
Repeating the same sum does not compare the answer with anything observable.
The cost of an error is not the test; plausibility is.
Doubting the recipe is a different job from checking the result.
questions.explain: The check needs a figure from outside the calculation, such as what a large pot usually takes.
questions.rule: Use an outside estimate, not the same arithmetic again.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each reported result: would a commonsense check catch it, or could it pass unnoticed?

items.t: A person's age found to be 212 years
A room whose height is found to be 0.3 metres
A parcel's weight found to be 40 tonnes
A person's age found to be 37 when the true age is 39
A room height of 2.9 metres when it is really 2.6
A parcel weight of 4.5 kg when it is really 5.4 kg

questions.explain: Wild results clash with what we know of the world. Small slips stay inside the believable range, so this check cannot catch them.
questions.rule: Estimates catch wild answers, not small slips.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the author, what does a student's calm acceptance of an absurd answer most likely show?
options: A weak grasp of arithmetic that calls for much more drill in long division
Deliberate carelessness in order to finish sooner
A habit of trusting the answer key at the back of the book
Indifference toward artificial problems, rather than stupidity
optionExplain: On the author's reading the gap is in attention to meaning, not arithmetic skill.
The book does not say the student is being deliberately careless.
The book does not mention answer keys.
Right: the book reads such neglect as indifference toward artificial problems.
questions.explain: Artificial problems touch no real facts, so students feel no pull to compare. Our reading: making a problem feel real would invite the check.
questions.rule: A problem that feels real invites the check.
questions.teaches: The author reads failure to check as indifference toward artificial problems, not as stupidity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A budget sheet shows a family spending 480 percent of its income on food. What does this card suggest?
options: Accept it, because a spreadsheet formula cannot be wrong
Treat it as a sign of an error and trace it, because spending that size cannot match the family's real situation
Delete the figure and keep the rest of the sheet as it is
Wait until the end of the month and see whether the figure corrects itself once the rest of the receipts are entered by hand
optionExplain: Formulas are written by people and can hold errors.
Right: a number that cannot match the real situation is a prompt to trace the mistake.
Deleting hides the clue instead of using it.
Waiting does not test anything.
questions.explain: The same comparison with what could be observed works outside mathematics. The book says a good answer to the check questions strengthens trust in the solution.
questions.rule: An impossible number is a lead, not a result.
questions.teaches: A good answer to the check questions strengthens our trust in the solution and adds to the solidity of our knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A friend claims a formula gives the area of any trapezoid. How could you test it quickly?
options: Try a case you already know, such as a rectangle, and see whether the formula agrees
Compare how long it is with other area formulas you know, since a longer formula is usually more careful
Try it on the largest trapezoid you can picture
Check that every letter in it appears at least twice
optionExplain: Right: a rectangle is a trapezoid with a known area.
The length of a formula says nothing about its truth.
Size alone does not give a known answer.
Repeated letters are not a test.
questions.explain: A known case is the quickest test. The card next shows the book's version.
questions.rule: Test a result in letters by specialization: give the letters values for which you know the answer and see whether the formula agrees.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: in the frustum example, setting the upper side equal to the lower side turns the solid into a prism.
questions.explain: When b equals a, both ends are equal squares, so the solid is a prism of volume \(a^2h\).
questions.rule: Equal ends make a prism.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student offers \(\frac{a^2+ab-b^2}{3}h\) for the frustum volume. Which special case exposes the error?
options: Setting h equal to 0 gives a volume of zero, which cannot be right
Setting a equal to 1 shows that the formula has three terms in it
Setting b equal to 0 gives \(a^2h/3\), which is a pyramid, so the formula must be wrong for that case
Setting b equal to a gives \(a^2h/3\), but a prism of that size has volume \(a^2h\)
optionExplain: A solid of zero height does have zero volume, so that result is correct.
Having three terms is not a fault in itself.
With b = 0 the formula does give the pyramid volume, so that case passes.
Right: with b = a the three terms give \(a^2+a^2-a^2=a^2\), so the formula returns one third of the prism volume.
questions.explain: Putting b = a gives \(a^2h/3\), where the known answer is \(a^2h\). One failed special case is enough.
questions.rule: One failed special case is enough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which uses of special cases follow the book's test? Select all that apply.
options: Replace every letter by 1 and accept the formula if the result is a whole number
Set b = 0 and compare with the known volume of a pyramid
Accept the formula after it passes one special case, with no further tests
Set b = a and compare with the known volume of a prism
optionExplain: A whole number is not a comparison with a known answer.
Right: the pyramid volume is known.
Passing one case raises trust but does not prove the formula.
Right: the prism volume is known.
questions.explain: A useful special case is one whose answer you know. Passing makes the formula more credible, not certain.
questions.rule: Use special cases whose answers you know.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In the frustum example, why does setting the upper side b to 0 make the solid a pyramid?
options: The upper face doubles in size, so the solid grows into a prism
The upper face shrinks to a single point, which is the apex of a whole pyramid
The height falls to zero, so the solid is flattened onto its base and has no volume left
The lower base vanishes, so only the sloping faces are left
optionExplain: That describes b = a, not b = 0.
Right: a side of length 0 turns the upper square into a point, the apex.
Height is a different letter, and flattening would give volume zero.
The lower side is a; b is the upper side.
questions.explain: A frustum is a pyramid with its top cut off, so shrinking the cut face to nothing restores the whole pyramid.
questions.rule: Zero top side means a full pyramid.
questions.teaches: With the upper side equal to 0 the frustum becomes a full pyramid, for which the formula gives \(a^2h/3\).

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A formula for the area of a ring between circles of radii R and r is proposed as \(\pi(R^2+r^2)\). Which special case tests it?
options: Setting r equal to 0: the formula gives \(\pi R^2\), the area of a full disc, so the formula is now proved correct
Setting R equal to 1: the formula then has fewer letters, so it is simpler
Setting r equal to R: the ring has no width, so its area should be 0, but the formula gives \(2\pi R^2\)
Setting r larger than R: the ring turns inside out, so the formula must be wrong
optionExplain: The r = 0 case passes, but passing does not prove it and the other case fails.
Fewer letters is not a test of truth.
Right: the circles coincide, yet the formula returns a positive area.
With r larger than R the ring is not defined in this way, so no known answer exists.
questions.explain: The correct area is \(\pi(R^2-r^2)\). The method works for any letter formula with a limiting case whose answer is known.
questions.rule: Test limiting cases.
questions.teaches: Specialization works on any letter formula: choose a limiting case such as zero width or zero size.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Someone writes the area of a rectangle with sides x and y as \(x+y^2\). What is wrong, before you compute anything?
options: The formula has two different letters, and an area needs a single letter squared to be a real area
The formula is missing a factor of one half
Areas can only be written with a square on every letter
An area is a square of a length, but x + y squared adds a length to a square of a length
optionExplain: Two letters are fine; area is x times y.
A half belongs to triangles, and this is a different slip.
Areas need not have a square on every letter; x times y is correct.
Right: you cannot add a length to an area.
questions.explain: Terms that are added must have the same dimension. The card next shows the book's version.
questions.rule: Check that the expression has the dimension the quantity should have: a cube of a length for a volume, a square for an area.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The frustum volume expression has as its dimension the ____ of a length.
questions.explain: Volume is a length multiplied by itself three times, a cube of a length.
questions.rule: Volume is a cube of a length.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student gives the volume of a cone with base radius r and height h as \(\frac{\pi r h}{3}\). What does the dimension test say?
options: It passes: the expression contains pi, and a factor of pi is enough to make any formula a volume
It fails: the expression is a length squared, but a volume must be a length cubed
It passes: the factor three in the denominator fixes the dimension
It is undecided: the test needs a numerical value for r first
optionExplain: Pi is a pure number with no dimension.
Right: r times h is a length squared, one factor short of a volume.
A numerical factor carries no dimension, so it cannot repair this.
The test works on the symbols alone, without any numerical value.
questions.explain: Counting lengths: \(\pi r h\) has two, but a volume needs three. The right formula is \(\pi r^2 h/3\).
questions.rule: Count the lengths in each term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: if a volume formula passes the dimension test, its numerical factors must also be right.
questions.explain: Numbers carry no dimension, so a wrong factor such as 2 for 3 passes the test unnoticed. Our reading.
questions.rule: Dimension cannot check pure numbers.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: An expression adds a term that is a length squared to a term that is a length cubed. What does the dimension test conclude?
options: The expression is right, because the larger power dominates
The expression is right, because the sum is still a volume
