The expression is wrong, because only terms of the same dimension can be added
It cannot be decided without knowing the units in which the two terms were originally measured
optionExplain: Size of power does not rescue a mixed sum.
A sum of an area and a volume is neither.
Right: terms with different dimensions cannot be added.
Units are irrelevant to the mismatch in dimension.
questions.explain: Our reading: the frustum terms all have the same dimension, a square of a length, before h multiplies them. That is why they can be added.
questions.rule: Added terms share a dimension.
questions.teaches: Terms added inside a formula must share one dimension, which is why the frustum terms a squared, ab and b squared can be added.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The time for a trip is proposed as \(t = d v\), distance times speed. Which check catches this?
options: The dimension test: distance times speed is not a time, whereas distance divided by speed is
The dimension test: the formula has only two letters, and so it is too short to give a time at all
Specialization: setting v to 1 makes the formula equal d, which is fine
Neither test: a formula for time cannot be checked with letters
optionExplain: Right: length times length per time is not a time, so the formula fails.
Two letters are fine; correctness depends on the combination.
Setting v = 1 gives a number, but it does not catch a dimension fault.
Letter formulas can be checked by the tests in this card.
questions.explain: The same test works for any physical formula, not only geometry. Our reading: that is why the book speaks of dimension in general.
questions.rule: Check units of every formula.
questions.teaches: The dimension test applies beyond geometry, to any formula whose quantities have a dimension, such as time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A formula says the time to fill a tank is the tank volume times the pump rate. What is the fault, before any numbers?
options: The formula uses two quantities, but filling needs three
A faster pump should shorten the time, but the formula makes the time longer
The formula has no square or cube in it, so it cannot be a real formula for a filling time
A bigger tank should take less time, but the formula says more
optionExplain: Two quantities are enough to state a time.
Right: raising the pump rate raises the formula's time, which is the wrong direction.
Powers are not needed for correctness.
A bigger tank should take longer, so the formula is right on that.
questions.explain: The direction of change tests the formula. The card next shows the book's version.
questions.rule: Vary the data in your head: if a quantity grows, check that the result grows or shrinks as the situation demands.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: in the frustum volume, increasing the height h increases the value of the expression.
questions.explain: The expression is a positive amount times h, so a taller frustum has a larger volume.
questions.rule: Taller means more volume.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A formula for the diagonal of a box with edges l, b and h is \(\sqrt{l^2+b^2-h^2}\). What does a variation of the data show?
options: Increasing l makes the diagonal larger, so the formula is wrong
Increasing b changes nothing, so the formula is wrong
Doubling every edge gives a diagonal of zero, so the formula must be wrong when the box grows
Increasing h makes the diagonal smaller, but a taller box has a longer diagonal
optionExplain: Larger l giving a larger diagonal is the correct direction.
Increasing b does raise the value under the root here.
Doubling every edge doubles this diagonal as well, so it does not give zero.
Right: a taller box should have a longer diagonal, yet the formula shrinks.
questions.explain: The minus sign makes h work against the diagonal. The correct formula has a plus sign.
questions.rule: Check each datum's direction.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each situation: is there a clear expected direction for the variation test, or not?

items.t: Volume of a cube as its edge grows
Distance covered at a fixed speed as time grows
Area of a circle as its radius grows
Earnings from a product as its price rises
Comfort of a room as its temperature rises
Skill of a player as practice time grows beyond need

questions.explain: The test needs a direction the situation itself dictates. Where a quantity can rise or fall with a datum, there is nothing to compare with.
questions.rule: Know the expected direction first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A formula passes the variation test. What follows?
options: The formula is proved correct for all values of the letters, since it moves the right way for each of them
The formula must also pass the dimension test
The result moves in the expected direction, but the formula can still be wrong in other ways
The formula gives the exact size of every change
optionExplain: Direction alone does not prove a formula.
Passing one test does not imply the other.
Right: the test checks direction only.
Direction says nothing about the size of change.
questions.explain: Our reading: each test catches different slips, which is why the book offers several for the same formula.
questions.rule: Use more than one test.
questions.teaches: The book offers several tests for one result, specialization, dimension and variation of the data, each catching different slips.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A bakery formula says the number of loaves from a batch is dough weight divided by loaf weight. How does the variation test judge it?
options: It fails: more dough should give fewer loaves
It fails: heavier loaves should give more loaves, since heavier loaves are worth more to a baker
It passes: more dough gives more loaves, and heavier loaves give fewer
It cannot be judged without knowing a price
optionExplain: More dough gives more loaves.
Heavier loaves use up the dough sooner, giving fewer.
Right: both directions match what happens in a kitchen.
Price plays no part in the test.
questions.explain: Each datum is varied one at a time, and its direction compared with the situation.
questions.rule: Vary one datum at a time.
questions.teaches: Vary the data one at a time and compare each direction with what the situation demands.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have a long calculation with a final number you cannot easily judge. What helps most?
options: Wait for the final number and then redo every step in order
Test the intermediate results on the way, so a slip shows up near where it was made
Round every intermediate number to keep the working short
Give the working to someone else and accept their final number as the check on your own
optionExplain: Redoing everything in the same order repeats the same slip.
Right: tests on intermediate results locate a fault early.
Rounding adds new errors.
A second person's number is not a test of yours.
questions.explain: Tests can be applied along the way. The card next shows the book's advice.
questions.rule: Apply the tests to intermediate results as well as the final one, and turn a problem in numbers into a problem in letters so that the tests become possible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The book says it may pay to generalize a problem in numbers into a problem in ____.
questions.explain: Letters make several tests possible that a single number does not.
questions.rule: Put numbers into letters to open the tests.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You find the diagonal of a 3 by 4 by 12 box as 13 through a face diagonal of 5. Which check of the intermediate result fits?
options: Check that 5 is more than 12, since a diagonal exceeds every edge
Check that 13 equals 3 + 4 + 12 divided by 2
Check only the final answer, since the book says intermediate numbers are not meant to be tested at all
Check that 3, 4 and 5 fit the right triangle relation, since the face diagonal is a hypotenuse
optionExplain: The face diagonal is 5, which is less than the edge 12.
The book says tests can be applied to intermediate results.
Right: \(3^2+4^2=25=5^2\), so the face diagonal passes.
questions.explain: The face diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, and 9 + 16 = 25.
questions.rule: Each step has its own test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, a problem in letters allows more and more interesting tests than a problem in numbers.
questions.explain: The book says problems in letters are susceptible of more, and more interesting, tests than problems in numbers.
questions.rule: Letters bring in more tests.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The book says the tests are worth preparing for. Which entry does it point to for the idea of varying a problem to make such tests possible?
options: The entry on corollaries, which collects useful consequences
The entry on conditions, which counts equations against unknowns and so decides which problems are well posed
The entry on variation of the problem, which suggests generalizing a problem in numbers
The entry on carrying out, which sets the Euclidean order
optionExplain: A corollary is a theorem found by examining another.
The condition entry deals with parts of a problem, not tests.
Right: the book refers the reader to variation of the problem for this.
Carrying out concerns working out the details of a plan.
questions.explain: The tests are so useful that the book suggests preparing for them in advance by choosing how a problem is posed.
questions.rule: Prepare for tests when you pose the problem.
questions.teaches: The book suggests preparing for the tests by varying the problem, in particular by generalizing a problem in numbers into one in letters.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A trader works out profit from 120 items sold at 5 each with 3 costing each. Which change would make the profit formula testable?
options: Write n for items, p for price and c for cost, so profit is \(n(p-c)\) and special cases can be tried
Round the numbers to 100, 5 and 3 so that the sum is easier and the answer comes out as a round figure
Keep the numbers and avoid any formula
Replace the price by the cost so the answer is positive
optionExplain: Right: with letters, n = 0 gives zero profit and p = c gives zero profit, both easy to check.
Rounding changes the problem, not its testability.
Without a formula only a comparison with the world is left.
Swapping price and cost changes the meaning.
questions.explain: With the letter form, special cases such as n = 0 or p = c have known answers. Our reading: the same step works outside geometry.
questions.rule: A letter formula can be tested; a bare number mostly cannot.
questions.teaches: Putting a business calculation into letters opens special-case tests such as zero items or price equal to cost.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You finish a long argument and want to be sure of it. What is the better way to check it again?
options: Read it again slowly in the same order, so that nothing at all is skipped on the way
Skim it quickly because you wrote it and know it well
Copy it out neatly and trust the tidy version
Go through it again with the steps in a different order or grouping
optionExplain: The same order may repeat the same slip.
Skimming skips the very steps that might hide a slip.
Copying is not checking.
Right: a changed order gives the mind a new path through the same steps.
questions.explain: The book gives two reasons to avoid plain repetition. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: When you check an argument step by step, avoid plain repetition; at least change the order of the steps or their grouping.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Where we stumbled once, there we are likely to stumble ____ if the circumstances are the same.
questions.explain: This is the book's second reason for avoiding mere repetition.
questions.rule: Same circumstances, same stumble.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A programmer reviews a test script top to bottom twice and finds nothing. Which next review follows the book's advice?
options: Review it a third time top to bottom with more care
Review it again from the last step to the first, or group the steps by purpose
Run it once and assume it is correct if it passes
Ask the original author to read it aloud in the same order, so that no step is missed this time
optionExplain: A third identical pass repeats the same circumstances.
Right: a different order or grouping is the variation the book names.
A pass shows one result, not a check of the argument.
The same order repeats the same path.
questions.explain: The aim is to meet the steps in new circumstances so an old blind spot is not repeated.
questions.rule: Reorder or regroup the steps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each way of re-checking: does it follow the book's advice, or is it mere repetition?

items.t: Check the steps in reverse order
Group the steps by purpose and check each group
Start from the middle and work outward
Reread the same steps in the same order, more slowly
Read the working aloud in the same order
Go through it a third time exactly as before

questions.explain: Any change of order or grouping adds variation. Doing the same thing again, however slowly, keeps the circumstances the same.
questions.rule: Change the path, not the speed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What reasons does the book give against mere repetition when checking an argument step by step?
options: It is boring, uninstructive and a strain on the attention, and a past stumble is likely to recur
It is slow, expensive and likely to introduce new errors into an argument that was already correct
It is rude to the author, whose argument is already proved
It shows distrust of the teacher and discourages students
optionExplain: Right: these are the reasons the book lists.
Slowness and cost are not the reasons given.
Politeness is not mentioned.
Trust in the teacher is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The book names two reasons: repetition is boring, uninstructive and a strain, and we are likely to stumble again where we stumbled before.
questions.rule: Repetition tires without teaching.
questions.teaches: The book gives two reasons against mere repetition: it is boring, uninstructive and a strain on attention, and we stumble again in the same circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: An editor re-reads a contract she has already read twice and wants a different path through it. Which fits the advice?
options: Read it a third time in page order, but in a quieter room
Read only the first and last pages, since the opening and the closing terms of a contract matter most
Ask a colleague to confirm that the contract looks fine
Read the clauses by topic, such as all payment terms together, instead of page order
optionExplain: A quieter room does not change the path.
Skipping most clauses is not a check of the argument.
Asking whether it looks fine gives no new path.
Right: grouping by topic changes the grouping of steps.
questions.explain: Our reading: grouping and ordering work for any chain of reasoning, not only proofs.
questions.rule: Regroup by topic.
questions.teaches: Regrouping an argument by topic is one way to vary the grouping of its steps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You must check a long proof written by a friend. Where do you start?
options: At the first line, and then every line in order without exception
At the point that looks weakest, where a slip is most likely
At the last line, since the conclusion matters most
At the line your friend is most proud of
optionExplain: Order alone does not locate a fault.
Right: the weakest point repays attention soonest.
The last line depends on all earlier ones.
Pride is not evidence of strength.
questions.explain: The book prefers a targeted start. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Pick out the weakest point of the argument and examine it first; the question Did you use all the data? helps you find such points.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A question useful in finding points of the argument worth examining is: Did you use all the ____?
questions.explain: If a datum was never used, the argument may be missing something.
questions.rule: Ask: did you use all the data?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A solver found a rectangle's area using its length only, though the problem also gave its width. What follows from the book's advice?
options: Delete the width because the answer is already found and nothing more can be learned from it
Recompute the length, since it must have been wrong
Look first at the unused width, since the argument may have a gap there
Conclude that the answer is certainly correct
optionExplain: Dropping the datum ignores the hint.
Nothing suggests the length was wrong.
Right: an unused datum marks a point worth examining first.
An unused datum does not prove correctness.
questions.explain: The unused width points to the part of the argument that may be missing.
questions.rule: Unused data point to weak spots.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: if a datum was left unused, the solution must be wrong.
questions.explain: Our reading: an unused datum is a prompt to look, but a problem can contain a redundant datum, so it does not prove an error.
questions.rule: A hint, not a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Why does the book recommend starting with the weakest point?
options: It proves the rest of the argument without further work, since a sound start makes the end sound
It is required by the rules of formal logic
It is the only way to find mistakes at all
It requires less exertion and is more interesting than going over everything evenly
optionExplain: Examining one point does not prove the others.
The book does not appeal to formal logic here.
Other methods also find mistakes.
Right: the book gives less exertion and more interest as the reasons.
questions.explain: The advantage is practical: effort goes where it is likely to pay.
questions.rule: Spend effort where it pays.
questions.teaches: The book gives less exertion and more interest as its reasons for examining the weakest point first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A tester must audit a monthly report with 40 figures. Three figures depend on a manual copy. How should the audit begin?
options: With the first figure and then each in order, giving every figure the same amount of time and care
With the three hand-copied figures, since they are the likely weak points
With the largest figure, since big numbers matter most
With the figures that were checked last month
optionExplain: Equal time ignores where slips are likely.
Right: hand copying is where slips are likely.
Size is not likelihood of error.
Figures already checked are the least likely to need it.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's advice carries over to audits and reviews, where one looks first at the point most likely to fail.
questions.rule: Start where slips are likely.
questions.teaches: Outside mathematics the weakest point is often where a manual step or an unchecked source enters.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What do you think best describes where a person's mathematical knowledge comes from?
options: From formal proofs alone, since anything else is only guesswork and cannot be called knowledge
From memorising rules, with proofs added later
From proofs together with a wide base of tests and experience
From a teacher's authority, which needs no testing
optionExplain: The author states that knowledge is not based on formal proofs alone.
Memorising does not appear as the source in the entry.
Right: that is the author's view, as the card shows.
Authority is not the source the author names.
questions.explain: The pretest is a fair guess. The card next gives the author's claim.
questions.rule: Treat each successful test of a result as widening the experimental base on which your knowledge stands.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, your knowledge of mathematics is based on formal proofs alone.
questions.explain: He says it is certain that anyone's knowledge in mathematics is not based on formal proofs alone.
questions.rule: Not proofs alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student confirms a formula on five numerical cases and on a dimension check. According to the author, what does this do?
options: It broadens the experimental basis of what the student knows about the result
It replaces the need for any later understanding
It is worthless unless the formula is also proved formally, because tests only suggest and do not settle
It proves the formula for every case
optionExplain: Right: each successfully tested result broadens the base.
The author does not say tests replace understanding.
He treats tests as valuable, not worthless without proof.
Tests do not prove the formula for every case.
questions.explain: The author says the experimental basis is broadened by each problem whose result is successfully tested.
questions.rule: Each successful test widens the base.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each source of support: formal proof, or tested experience?

items.t: A chain of steps from the hypothesis to the conclusion
A derivation set out in the order of Euclid
A rigid argument checked step by step
A careful measurement in a laboratory
A result confirmed again and again in daily life
A formula checked on several numerical cases

questions.explain: Proof moves by steps from premises; tests compare a result with experience. The author says knowledge rests on both.
questions.rule: Proof and tested experience both count.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: How does the author treat the question whether mathematics can rest on formal proofs alone?
options: As settled by Euclid, who is said to have proved everything formally in the Elements, leaving no experimental basis
As unimportant, so he gives no view on it
As a question he answers at length with experiments
As a philosophical question he does not debate, while stating that no one's knowledge rests on proofs alone
optionExplain: The entry does not claim this.
He gives a view, though briefly.
He does not describe any experiment on this.
Right: he declines to debate but gives his view.
questions.explain: He sets the question aside as philosophical, but adds that if solid knowledge exists at all it has a broad experimental basis.
questions.rule: Declines to debate, still states a view.
questions.teaches: The author sets the philosophical question aside but asserts that any solid knowledge has a broad experimental basis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A nurse trusts a dosage rule partly because it has worked safely in many patients. Which reading matches the author's idea?
options: Her trust rests on more than a derivation: past successful use widens the base for it
Her trust is misplaced unless the rule is formally proved
Her trust is a social habit that has nothing to do with knowledge, since habits are copied from others
Her trust should disappear after one failure of a sort
optionExplain: Right: tested success is part of what supports solid knowledge.
The author denies that proof alone supports knowledge.
The author counts tested experience as part of knowledge.
The entry does not say one failure removes trust; it speaks of broadening.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author's point about experience generalises beyond mathematics to everyday knowledge, as the entry itself says.
questions.rule: Success in use supports knowledge.
questions.teaches: The author places mathematical knowledge alongside everyday knowledge, which is also continually tested and strengthened by experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: You solved a problem by a long calculation and the answer looks right. What would the author advise?
options: Stop, because a correct answer needs no second derivation and a second one would only waste time
Redo the same calculation to see that it repeats
Ask whether the result can be derived differently, since a second route adds conviction
Throw the answer away and start again from scratch
optionExplain: The author says one may still be interested in finding another solution.
Repeating the same route is the plain repetition he warns against.
Right: a second derivation strengthens conviction.
A satisfactory answer does not need to be discarded.
questions.explain: The card next shows his reason.
questions.rule: Even after a satisfactory solution, try to derive the result differently and, if the first route was long, look for a clearer one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: The author says two proofs are better than one: it is safe riding at two ____.
questions.explain: He quotes the proverb about riding at two anchors.
questions.rule: Two proofs beat one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A student proves a triangle result by algebra and wants more assurance. Which follows the entry?
options: Check the algebra again in the same order
Accept the algebra because it is rigorous
Look for a geometric or intuitive derivation of the same result
Copy a proof from a textbook without reading it, since a proof from a book is bound to be sound
optionExplain: This repeats the first route.
Rigour does not forbid a second look.
Right: a different derivation is the entry's aim.
A copied proof adds no insight.
questions.explain: The entry compares two derivations to seeing an object and then touching it.
questions.rule: Use a second route.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: True or false: the author compares finding a second proof to touching an object after having seen it.
questions.explain: He says that having found a proof we wish to find another, as we wish to touch an object after having seen it.
questions.rule: See, then touch.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: What does the author suspect when a final solution is long and involved?
options: That the long solution must contain an error somewhere that a second reading would reveal
That the problem has no solution at all
That the result should be thrown out
That a clearer and less roundabout solution may exist
optionExplain: Length does not show an error.
A solution has been found.
The result may be fine; a shorter route is sought.
Right: that suspicion is what prompts the question.
questions.explain: He says we naturally suspect a clearer solution and asks: can you derive the result differently, can you see it at a glance?
questions.rule: A long route invites a shorter one.
questions.teaches: The author says that a long and involved solution naturally makes us suspect a clearer, less roundabout one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A data analyst gets a growth figure from a long spreadsheet chain. Which step follows the author's idea?
options: Estimate the same growth figure by a quick independent route and compare
Re-run the same chain of formulas in the same order to confirm that the number comes out again
Hide the working and share only the figure
Trust the figure because it came from software
optionExplain: Right: an independent second route gives a second kind of evidence.
The same chain gives the same path.
Hiding the working removes a check.
Software output can contain slips.
questions.explain: Our reading: the idea of two independent derivations carries over to any calculation.
questions.rule: Cross-check by an independent route.
questions.teaches: Outside proofs, a quick independent estimate of the same figure plays the role of a second derivation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A formula is a product of two factors, and you want to understand it. What is a sound first move?
options: Expand the product into as many separate terms as possible before looking at any of them
Check only that the units are consistent
Ask what each factor means on its own in the problem
Ignore the factors and test numbers at random
optionExplain: Expanding often hides the meaning of the parts.
Units help but do not give meaning.
Right: giving each factor a meaning is the first step towards seeing the whole.
Random numbers do not tell you what a factor means.
questions.explain: Looking at the parts one by one is the book's route. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: To see a result intuitively, look for the geometric meaning of each part of it in turn.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: In the frustum formula, the square root \(\sqrt{(R-r)^2+h^2}\) is the length of the ____ height.
questions.explain: It is the non-parallel side of the trapezoid that, turned about its axis, generates the frustum.
questions.rule: The root is the slant height.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: With R = 4, r = 1 and h = 4, what is the slant height of the cone frustum?
options: 5, since the root of 9 plus 16 is 5
3, since R minus r is 3
8, since 4 plus 4 is 8
\(\sqrt{17}\), since 4 squared plus 1 squared is 17
optionExplain: 3 is the difference of radii, one leg of the right triangle.
Adding R and h is not the formula for the slant height.
This uses R and r instead of their difference and the height.
questions.explain: The slant height is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs R minus r and h.
questions.rule: Slant height from R minus r and h.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: What does \(\pi(R+r)\) stand for in the frustum formula?
options: The difference of the two base areas, since a factor with pi and two radii looks like an area
The sum of the two slant heights
The volume of the mid-section
The arithmetic mean of the perimeters of the two bases
optionExplain: Areas would involve squares of radii.
There is only one slant height.
A mid-section is a plane figure with a perimeter, not a volume.
Right: the mean of \(2\pi R\) and \(2\pi r\) is \(\pi(R+r)\).
questions.explain: The perimeters are \(2\pi R\) and \(2\pi r\); their mean is \(\pi(R+r)\), which is also the perimeter of the mid-section.
questions.rule: Look for a mean and a mid-value.
questions.teaches: The factor pi times (R plus r) is both the mean of the two base perimeters and the perimeter of the mid-section.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: True or false: with R = 4 and r = 1, the perimeter of the mid-section of the frustum is \(5\pi\).
questions.explain: The mid-section has radius (4 + 1) / 2 = 2.5, so its perimeter is \(2\pi\times2.5=5\pi\), equal to \(\pi(R+r)\).
questions.rule: Mid-section radius is the mean radius.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A cylinder's side area is written \(2\pi r h\). Which reading of its parts follows the book's method?
options: \(2\pi r\) is the area of the base and h is the volume
\(2\pi r\) is the circumference of the base and h the height, so the side unrolls to a rectangle of those sides
\(2\pi\) is the height and r h is the circumference
Nothing can be read from the parts, since the formula is already known and a known formula needs no reading of its pieces
optionExplain: The base area is \(\pi r^2\).
Right: each part has a geometric meaning, and together they give a rectangle.
Pi times two is a number, not a height.
Knowing a formula does not prevent giving its parts meaning.
questions.explain: Our reading: this is the same move, applied to a case where the whole becomes a familiar figure.
questions.rule: Read each part, then the whole.
questions.teaches: Giving each part a meaning can show the whole as a familiar figure, here an unrolled rectangle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: You have read each piece of a formula and know its meaning. What next step does the book suggest?
options: Read the whole formula in a different light and compare it with something familiar
Drop the formula and begin a new problem, since the pieces are now understood and the formula is spent
Memorise the formula for the exam
Expand every term to hide the pieces
optionExplain: Right: put the pieces together as a new statement.
The aim is to use what you saw.
Memorising gives no insight.
Expanding hides the meaning.
questions.explain: The card next shows how the book does it.
questions.rule: Put the interpreted parts together and restate the whole result in words, then compare it with a familiar statement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: The frustum result reads: area equals perimeter of the mid-section times ____ height.
questions.explain: Slant height is the sloping side, the root in the formula.
questions.rule: Area = mid-section perimeter times slant height.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A trapezoid has parallel sides 6 and 10 and altitude 4. What is its area by the middle-line rule?
options: 64, since the sum of the parallel sides, 16, times the altitude 4 is 64
40, since 10 times 4 is 40
24, since 6 times 4 is 24
32, since the middle-line is 8 and 8 times 4 is 32
optionExplain: This forgets the division by two in the middle-line.
This uses only the longer side.
This uses only the shorter side.
Right: the middle-line is the mean of the parallel sides, 8, so 8 x 4 = 32.
questions.explain: The rule is area equals middle-line times altitude, with the middle-line the mean of the parallel sides.
questions.rule: Area = middle-line times altitude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: Match each part of the frustum statement to its partner in the trapezoid rule.
questions.explain: The frustum statement and the trapezoid rule have the same form: a mid-way quantity times the length across.
questions.rule: Mid-quantity times length across.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: What does the author say we feel after seeing the likeness between the two statements?
options: That the long calculation was a waste and must now be removed from the account of the result
That the result is false and needs a different formula
That we are very near a short and direct proof of the result found by a long calculation
That the likeness proves the frustum formula already
optionExplain: The calculation found the result, so it was not wasted.
Nothing suggests the result is false.
Right: the author says we feel very near a short proof.
The likeness suggests, but does not prove.
questions.explain: He says that seeing the analogy, we see the result almost at a glance and feel near a short proof.
questions.rule: An analogy suggests a proof.
questions.teaches: The author says the likeness makes us feel very near a short and direct proof of a result found by a long calculation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A team lead sees that a project's cost is the mid-point of the staff cost range times duration. What parallel does the method suggest?
options: Throw away the staff range because it is not exact and use a single figure for the whole project
Replace the duration with the cost
Treat the likeness as proof
Compare it with a familiar rule of average times length and look for a direct argument
optionExplain: Discarding data does not help.
Swapping the quantities changes the meaning.
A likeness suggests a proof; it does not prove.
Right: restating and comparing is the step of the method.
questions.explain: Our reading: the move is general: restate a result as a sentence and test it against a rule you trust.
questions.rule: Restate, compare, then prove.
questions.teaches: After interpreting the parts, restate the whole as a sentence and compare it with a rule you already trust.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: You dislike the long proof you found. What is a promising way to look for a better one?
options: Forget the result and prove something else
Study the result itself for new ways to read its parts
Rewrite the same proof in a smaller handwriting, so that it looks shorter on the page
Ask the teacher for the answer and stop
optionExplain: Changing the problem is not the same as improving the proof.
Right: reading the result differently may suggest a new proof.
Smaller writing does not change the proof.
Asking stops the search.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's process.
questions.rule: When you are not satisfied with a derivation, study the result: find a new reading of one part, then of another, until the whole looks different.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: Put the steps of the process in the order the book describes.
items: Notice a new reading of one small part of the result
Find a new reading of another part
Consider the whole result in a different light
Let the new view suggest a new proof
questions.explain: The entry builds from a small part, to other parts, to the whole, to a new proof.
questions.rule: Part, parts, whole, proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A student has the sum formula \(n(n+1)/2\) for 1 to n. Which move follows the book's method?
options: Cancel the 2 and try again with n(n+1) alone, since a factor of two only complicates the sum
Test only n = 1
Read the parts: n is the count and (n + 1) / 2 is the average of the first and last term
Replace n by a letter m
optionExplain: Cancelling does not interpret anything.
A single test is not a new reading.
Right: each part gets a meaning, and count times average is a neat reading of the whole.
Renaming a letter changes nothing.
questions.explain: Count times the average of first and last term is a new way to see the sum, which suggests the pairing proof.
questions.rule: Count times average.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: True or false: the book says this method works as easily for a beginner as for an experienced mathematician.
questions.explain: The book says it is more likely to happen to an experienced mathematician on an advanced problem than to a beginner on an elementary one.
questions.rule: Experience helps this search.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: How does the book describe the way the search proceeds?
options: By small steps: a new reading of one part, then of another, accumulating until the whole is recast
By a single flash of insight that needs no preparation and cannot be helped by studying parts of the result
By repeating the old proof until it is short
By a rule that can be applied without thought
optionExplain: Right: small advantages accumulate.
The entry stresses small, accumulating readings.
Repetition is the thing he warns against.
The process is described as luck and experience, not a rule.
questions.explain: The book says we may succeed first in a new reading of a small part, then of another, and so recast the whole.
questions.rule: Accumulate small readings.
questions.teaches: The search for a new proof proceeds by accumulating small advantages, each a new reading of a small part of the result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A chef adapts a long recipe and wants a simpler method. Which step follows the book's pattern?
options: Repeat the long recipe until it feels short, since practice makes any method seem quicker to follow
Study the finished dish part by part to see what each step really contributes
Drop the dish and cook another
Ask what other cooks think of it
optionExplain: Repetition does not shorten.
Right: study the result to find indications of a shorter route.
Changing the dish drops the problem.
Opinions do not reveal what each step contributes.
questions.explain: Our reading: studying the result for hints of a shorter route is useful outside mathematics.
questions.rule: Look in the result for the short route.
questions.teaches: The result itself can hold indications of a shorter route, in cooking as in proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A beginner hands in a very long solution to a simple problem. What should a good teacher do?
options: Mark it wrong because it is long
Ignore it, since a correct solution needs no comment and the student has already got the answer right
Give the answer without any explanation
Show a shorter solution and how to find signs of it in the result itself
optionExplain: A long solution is not wrong for being long; the teacher's job is to show the shorter way as well.
The author wants the shorter way shown, at least once or twice.
An answer without explanation teaches nothing.
Right: the author asks the teacher to show both.
questions.explain: The card next shows his advice.
questions.rule: Teach students at least once or twice how to solve a problem more shortly and how to find, in the result itself, signs of a shorter solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: The teacher should show students, at least once or ____, how to solve the problem more shortly.
questions.explain: The book says at least once or twice.
questions.rule: Show the short way once or twice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A class finds a long way to solve an area problem. According to the entry, what should the teacher also show?
options: How to find, in the result itself, indications of a shorter solution
That the long way is always best
How to write the long way more neatly
That shorter ways never exist for beginners, since beginners can only follow the longer way to a result
optionExplain: Right: the entry asks for both a shorter solution and how it was found.
The author does not say that.
Neatness is not the point.
He says it can happen even in elementary classes.
questions.explain: Seeing how the short route was found in the result is the lasting lesson.
questions.rule: Show how, not only what.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: True or false: the author says the experienced mathematician is more exposed than the beginner to the danger of mobilizing too much knowledge.
questions.explain: He says the mathematician with a great deal of knowledge is more exposed to this danger, though better placed to appreciate a small reinterpretation.
questions.rule: Knowledge cuts both ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: What advantage does the author give the experienced mathematician over the beginner?
options: Being less exposed to unnecessary complexity, since greater knowledge protects against framing a needlessly involved argument
Needing no check of the result
Being better placed to appreciate the reinterpretation of a small part and accumulate such advantages
Being able to skip the plan
optionExplain: The author says the expert is more exposed to complexity.
Checking is still needed.
Right: he can recast the whole by accumulating small gains.
Nothing says planning is skipped.
questions.explain: The compensation for the danger is a better eye for small reinterpretations.
questions.rule: Expertise has a cost and a gain.
questions.teaches: The author says the experienced mathematician is better placed to appreciate the reinterpretation of a small part and to recast the whole result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Can You Derive the Result Differently?
questions.q: A senior engineer designs a very complex system for a simple task, while a junior's design is plain. Which reading fits the author's observation?
options: The junior is right, because beginners keep to simple methods and so avoid complexity in their designs
The senior may have mobilised too much knowledge, which a review of the result could simplify
Complexity proves the senior's design is better
Seniors should stop reviewing designs
optionExplain: The author does not say beginners are always right.
Right: the observation covers more than mathematics, if our reading holds.
Complexity is not a proof of quality.
Nothing here suggests that.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author's point about too much knowledge applies by analogy to design.
questions.rule: Review for needless complexity.
questions.teaches: By analogy, expert designs can also be more involved than needed, and reviewing the result may simplify them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You solve a problem on your own after a long struggle. What does the author advise you to do next?
options: Put the problem behind you and rest on the success, since one solved problem is reward enough for the effort
Check that no one else has solved it already
Try the same problem again by the same method
Ask whether the result or the method can serve for some other problem
optionExplain: The author says not to fail to inquire whether there is more behind it.
Priority of discovery is not his concern.
Repeating the same problem gains nothing new.
Right: the advice is to exploit the success.
questions.explain: The card next gives his reason.
questions.rule: After solving a problem, ask whether the result or the method can be used for some other problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The author puts the advice in three words: Exploit your ____.
questions.explain: The phrase names the habit of making further use of a solved problem.
questions.rule: Exploit your success.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have found how to split a restaurant bill fairly among five people. Which follow-up fits the advice?
options: Ask whether the same method fits splitting a shared taxi fare or a group gift
Stop, since the bill is split and the problem is over, so there is nothing further to learn from it
Check the bill again in the same way
Look up who invented bill splitting
optionExplain: Right: the method may serve for other problems.
The advice is to look beyond the solved problem.
Rechecking is a different step.
History does not exploit the method.
questions.explain: Using the same method on similar problems tests whether it was a trick or a tool.
questions.rule: Try the method elsewhere.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each follow-up: does it reuse the method, or only repeat the result?

items.t: Use the same construction idea on a different figure
Apply the same trick to a new equation
Carry the same argument over to a similar theorem
Quote the old answer for the same problem
Copy the old numbers into a new table
Recheck the old answer once more

questions.explain: To exploit a success is to ask whether the method serves another problem; quoting the old answer does not.
questions.rule: Reuse the method on a new problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the author say about even a modest solution that you found by your own means?
options: It is a discovery nevertheless, though a less momentous one if the problem is not difficult
It is not a real discovery unless the problem is new to everyone who has ever worked on it before
It is a discovery only if you also prove it formally
It is not worth any further thought
optionExplain: Right: the author counts it as a discovery, however modest.
He counts discovery by your own means.
He does not tie discovery to formal proof here.
He asks you to look for more.
questions.explain: Because every solution found alone is a discovery, there is reason to look for what lies behind it.
questions.rule: Your own discovery counts.
questions.teaches: The author counts any solution found by your own means as a discovery, however modest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A programmer fixes one bug by adding a missing check. How does the advice apply?
options: Close the ticket and move on at once
Remove the check to see if it was needed
Add the check to every function in the program, whether or not that function can ever need it
Look for other places in the code where the same check might be missing
optionExplain: The advice is to look around.
Removing the fix undoes the success.
Adding it everywhere without looking is not selective use.
Right: the method may fit other places, and bugs tend to cluster.
questions.explain: Our reading: the advice carries over to any craft: use what you have learned on neighbouring cases.
questions.rule: Check the neighbours.
questions.teaches: In other crafts, exploiting a success means checking neighbouring cases for the same flaw or the same trick.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You solved a problem about the diagonal of a box. Which activity produces new problems from it?
options: Solving the same problem again
Making the problem more general, more special, or turning it into an analogue
Reading about the history of boxes
Changing the numbers to larger ones and nothing else, since a new set of data makes a new problem
optionExplain: Repeating gives no new problem.
Right: these are means of varying a problem.
History does not vary the problem.
Changing only the numbers varies the data but little else.
questions.explain: The card next lists the book's means.
questions.rule: From a solved problem, derive others by generalization, specialization, analogy, and decomposing and recombining.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Match each means of varying a problem to its description.
pairs: Replace the data by a wider class
Move to a similar problem in another setting
Split into parts and join them differently
questions.explain: These are the four means the book names for deriving new problems.
questions.rule: Four means of varying a problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: From 'find the diagonal of a rectangle with sides a and b', which new problem is obtained by analogy?
options: Find the diagonal of a box with edges a, b and c
Find the diagonal of a square with side 5
Find the diagonal of a rectangle with sides 4 and 3
Find the diagonal of the same rectangle by another name
optionExplain: Right: moving from a plane figure to a similar solid figure is an analogy.
A square is a special case, so specialization.
This is a special case with numbers, again specialization.
This is the same problem restated.
questions.explain: Analogy moves to a similar problem in a different setting; the box is the solid counterpart of the rectangle.
questions.rule: Analogy: a similar problem elsewhere.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the author says the process of deriving new problems is unlimited in theory.
questions.explain: Because each new problem can be varied again, the process has no theoretical end; in practice we seldom carry it far.
questions.rule: Unlimited in theory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the author, why do we seldom carry the process far in practice?
options: The means of variation are too few to continue
Each variation returns exactly the original problem
Teachers forbid it because remote problems are thought to be too hard for classes
The problems obtained become apt to be inaccessible
optionExplain: The book lists several means and says the process is unlimited.
Variation yields different problems.
The book gives no such rule.
Right: the problems reached tend to be inaccessible.
questions.explain: A new problem several steps from the original is often too remote to solve with what we have.
questions.rule: Remote problems become inaccessible.
questions.teaches: The reason we seldom carry the derivation far is that problems obtained after several steps tend to be inaccessible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher makes up practice problems about train speeds by changing the setting to boats. Which means is this?
options: Specialization, since one case is picked
Analogy, since a similar problem is posed in another setting
Generalization, since the data class widens
Decomposing, since the problem is split into parts that are then solved one at a time
optionExplain: Specialization narrows to one case.
Right: the structure stays and the setting changes.
Generalization widens the data class, but here only the setting changes and nothing is widened.
Decomposing splits a problem into parts, but here the problem is kept whole and only the setting changes.
questions.explain: The same relation between distance, speed and time carries over to boats, which is an analogy.
questions.rule: Same structure, new setting.
questions.teaches: Changing only the setting while keeping the structure of the problem is a derivation by analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You create new problems from one you solved. Which kind is the likeliest to be both easy and dull?
options: A problem in a completely different field
A problem with no known solution
A problem that is scarcely different from the one you solved
A problem three steps removed from the original, where each step changed the data a little
optionExplain: A new field is unlikely to be easy.
An open problem is neither easy nor assured.
Right: close variants are easy and tend to be uninteresting.
Remote problems tend to be inaccessible.
questions.explain: The author makes this contrast. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: When deriving new problems, aim for ones that are both interesting and accessible; expect that this takes experience, taste and good luck.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: To find a new problem that is both interesting and accessible we need experience, taste, and good ____.
questions.explain: The book adds luck to experience and taste.
questions.rule: Experience, taste and luck.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each variation by the author's trade-off: easy but dull, or interesting but hard to reach.

items.t: Ask the same question with one number changed
Ask for the same quantity in a figure that is nearly identical
Ask the same question with the data renamed
Ask for the same quantity in a space of many dimensions
Ask for the quantity on the surface of a sphere
Ask a question that nobody has settled

questions.explain: Variants that follow at once from the solution are easy and dull. Those that change a great deal tend to be inaccessible.
questions.rule: Near is easy and dull; far is hard.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the author, what two things should we not fail to do after solving a good problem?
options: Look for the author of the problem and thank them
Look for proof that this is the last problem of its kind, since a find may exhaust its cluster
Look up the answer to check it
Look around for more good problems, since they grow in clusters
optionExplain: Authorship is not discussed.
The text says there are probably more near.
The answer is already found.
Right: good problems grow in clusters.
questions.explain: The author compares good problems with certain mushrooms.
questions.rule: Look around after a find.
questions.teaches: The author compares good problems with mushrooms of certain kinds: they grow in clusters, so one find suggests more nearby.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which situation is a case of the trade-off the author names?
options: A new problem is hard because the solver has no experience with problems of that kind and cannot recall one
A new problem is easy because it follows at once from the old solution, but it is uninteresting
A new problem is interesting because it is old
A new problem is easy because the data are small
optionExplain: Lack of experience is not the trade-off.
Right: that is the first half of the trade-off.
Age is not the trade-off; the author contrasts easy-but-dull with interesting-but-inaccessible.
Small data is not what the author names.
questions.explain: The author contrasts easy-but-dull with interesting-but-inaccessible.
questions.rule: Easy and dull versus interesting and hard.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A coach designs drills by modifying one exercise. Which drill follows the author's balance?
options: One identical to the last, so that no player fails and every player feels that the work has been done
One so advanced no one can try it
One close enough for the team to manage yet adding a new element they find engaging
One chosen at random each day
optionExplain: Identical drills are easy and dull.
Too advanced is inaccessible.
Right: accessible and interesting together.
Random choice ignores both.
questions.explain: Our reading: the balance between reach and interest applies to any craft of making exercises.
questions.rule: Near enough to reach, new enough to engage.
questions.teaches: In making exercises, the balance is a drill near enough to reach and different enough to interest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You found one remarkable problem in a book. What does a mushroom hunter's habit suggest you do?
options: Look around nearby, since more are likely close
Move to another book at once
Stay with the one and stop looking
Look only at the first page of each chapter, since good problems are usually placed there
optionExplain: Right: finds come in clusters.
Leaving ignores the likely neighbours.
Stopping gives up the harvest.
First pages are arbitrary.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's comparison.
questions.rule: Having found a good problem, look around for more nearby; good problems grow in clusters like certain mushrooms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The author compares good problems with certain kinds of ____, which grow in clusters.
questions.explain: He says good problems and certain mushrooms grow in clusters.
questions.rule: Find one, look around.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: after solving one good problem, the author advises looking around for more because there is a good chance some are quite near.
questions.explain: That is his advice, and the comparison with mushrooms supports it.
questions.rule: Good chance of more nearby.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student finds one rich question and decides there will be no others like it. Which reading of the author fits?
options: The student correctly judged that rich questions are rare and that one find is all a book offers
The student overlooked that good problems grow in clusters
The student should now find the author of the question
The student should check the question for mistakes
optionExplain: The author says the opposite.
Right: the cluster comparison says more are likely near.
Authorship is not in the entry.
Nothing in the entry asks for this.
questions.explain: Looking for neighbours is the way to use a find.
questions.rule: Do not stop at one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What do the neighbours listed in the box example have in common?
options: Each needs a different branch of mathematics, so the neighbours have little in common beyond the subject
Each is harder than the original
Each has nothing to do with the original
Each adds a new notion to the original problem and falls back on it once the notion is removed
optionExplain: They are scarcely different from the original.
They are easy, because they reduce to the original.
They are close to the original.
Right: the added notions are circumscribed sphere, pyramid and coordinates, and removing them gives back the original.
questions.explain: The cluster is held together by the original solution.
questions.rule: Neighbours share a root problem.
questions.teaches: The neighbours of the box problem each add a new notion, such as a circumscribed sphere, which is easily removed to fall back upon the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A researcher finds one fruitful experiment design. How does the cluster idea apply?
options: Consider close variations of the design that may be fruitful too
Wait for another group to extend the design
Treat the design as the only one possible
Retire the design
optionExplain: Right: nearby variations are good candidates.
Waiting gives up the harvest.
Nothing makes it the only one.
Retiring discards a find.
questions.explain: Our reading: the comparison with mushrooms invites an outward search from any good find.
questions.rule: Search near a find.
questions.teaches: In research, a fruitful design suggests nearby variations as likely fruitful too.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You know how to find a box's diagonal. A new problem asks for the radius of the sphere that passes through all eight corners. How hard is it?
options: Very hard, because spheres need a new theory of curved surfaces that the box problem does not supply
Impossible without calculus
Not hard, because the sphere's diameter is the diagonal you can already find
Easy only if the box is a cube
optionExplain: The solved diagonal does most of the work.
No calculus is needed: the sphere's diameter is the diagonal already found.
Right: the sphere's diameter equals the box diagonal.
The box need not be a cube.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's reasoning.
questions.rule: To make an easy new problem from a solved one, add some new notion that is easily eliminated, then fall back on the original problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: With a box of edges 3, 4 and 12, the diagonal is ____.
questions.explain: The root of 9 + 16 + 144 is 13.
questions.rule: Diagonal of a 3 by 4 by 12 box is 13.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: For that box, what is the radius of the sphere through all eight corners?
options: 13, the whole diagonal
3.25, a quarter of the diagonal
6.5, which is half the diagonal of 13
6, the mean of the edges 3, 4 and 12 less one
optionExplain: 13 is the diameter, not the radius.
A quarter of the diagonal has no basis; the diagonal is a diameter, so the radius is half of it.
Right: the diagonal is a diameter, so the radius is 6.5.
This invents a rule for the radius.
questions.explain: The sphere around the box has the box diagonal as a diameter, so the radius is half of 13.
questions.rule: Radius is half the diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which new problems come from the box-diagonal problem by adding a notion that can be removed? Select all that apply.
options: Find the diagonal of a cube with a given edge
Find the radius of the sphere around a box with given edges
Find the height of a box from its diagonal, length and breadth
Find the distance between two points given by rectangular coordinates
optionExplain: Coordinates are a new notion that is easily removed.
Right: the sphere is added and its diameter is the diagonal.
Sphere is a new notion that is easily removed.
Right: the coordinates are added and the points are corners of a box.
questions.explain: Adding a notion keeps the old unknown and brings in a new idea such as a sphere or coordinates.
questions.rule: Add a notion, then strip it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Why does the book say the distance problem is not only an easy problem but an important one?
options: Because it is more difficult than the original
Because it needs no solution of the box
Because it was posed by Euclid
Because rectangular coordinates are important
optionExplain: It is easy, since it reduces to the original.
It uses the box solution.
Euclid is not mentioned here.
Right: the notion added is an important one.
questions.explain: The interest of such a problem comes from the interest of the notion added.
questions.rule: The notion added sets the interest.
questions.teaches: The interest of a derived problem comes from the notion added; coordinates are important, so the distance problem is too.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher knows how to convert litres to millilitres and asks for the number of millilitres in a bottle filled from three jugs. Which statement fits the pattern?
options: The added notion, three jugs, is easily removed, leaving the conversion already known
The new problem is hard because three jugs are more than one, and the old conversion no longer applies
The new problem has no relation to the old
The new problem is an analogy
optionExplain: Right: add and remove a notion, and fall back on the known method.
Three jugs only add a sum.
They share the conversion.
Analogy would change the setting.
questions.explain: Our reading: the pattern works wherever a new feature can be stripped off to reveal the old problem.
questions.rule: Add, strip, fall back.
questions.teaches: The add-and-remove pattern works in everyday problems when the added feature can be stripped off to reveal the known one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You know how to find a box's diagonal from its three edges. What can you now find with the same knowledge?
options: Only boxes whose three edges are equal, because the relation holds for no other kind of box
Nothing, because the method is one-way
A missing edge, if the diagonal and the other two edges are given
Only the volume of the box
optionExplain: The method does not need equal edges.
A relation can be read either way.
Right: the relation among four quantities works in any direction.
The volume is a different quantity.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's pattern.
questions.rule: To get an easy new problem from a solved one, regard the original unknown as given and one of the original data as the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The solution of the box problem establishes a relation among four quantities: the three dimensions and the ____.
questions.explain: If any three of the four are given, the fourth can be calculated.
questions.rule: Four quantities, one relation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A box has length 2, breadth 3 and diagonal 7. What is its height?
options: 6, since 49 less 4 less 9 is 36
2, since 7 less 2 less 3 is 2
\(\sqrt{58}\), since 4 plus 9 plus 49 is 62 less 4
8.5, since 7 plus 2 less 3 is 6 plus 2.5
optionExplain: This subtracts without squaring.
This adds the squares, which is the wrong direction.
This invents an arithmetic rule.
questions.explain: Squares add to the square of the diagonal, so the missing square is 49 - 4 - 9 = 36.
questions.rule: Square, subtract, then root.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: with the diagonal and two edges known, the box height is found by the same relation as the diagonal from three edges.
questions.explain: The relation is the same in both problems; only the roles of the quantities change.
questions.rule: Same relation, roles exchanged.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: How does the book describe the pattern of interchanging roles compared with adding a new notion?
options: It is the same pattern with different names, since both derive a new problem from the old one
It is a pattern for problems to prove only
It never leads to a solvable problem
It is very different from the pattern followed when new notions are added
optionExplain: The book says very different.
The pattern is for problems to find.
The new problems are solvable.
Right: the two patterns are different.
questions.explain: Adding a notion keeps the original unknown; interchanging replaces it.
questions.rule: Two patterns, not one.
questions.teaches: Interchanging the roles of unknown and datum is, in the author's words, very different from the pattern of adding a new notion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You know how to find the total cost from a price and a count. Which new problem uses the interchange pattern?
options: Find the total cost with a bigger count, keeping the price and changing only the number of items
Find the price when the total cost and the count are given
Find the cost of a different item
Find the count by guessing
optionExplain: This keeps the same unknown.
Right: the old unknown, the cost, is now given, and the price is unknown.
This changes the item, not the roles.
Guessing is not the pattern.
questions.explain: The same relation, cost equals price times count, is read for the price. Our reading: this is how division undoes multiplication.
questions.rule: Read the same relation another way.
questions.teaches: Interchanging roles turns a total-cost problem into a price problem using the same relation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You know the diagonal of any box from its three edges. Which new problem is solved at once with that knowledge?
options: The diagonal of a cube with given edge
The diagonal of a box when the edges are not perpendicular
The diagonal of a regular octahedron with given edge
The distance between two cities on the globe
optionExplain: Right: a cube is a box with equal edges.
Non-perpendicular edges change the problem.
An octahedron is another solid.
A globe distance is a curved case.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the book's examples.
questions.rule: Derive problems from a solved one by generalization, specialization and analogy, and expect only the specialization to be solvable at once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The diagonal of a cube with edge e is e times the square root of ____.
questions.explain: Putting equal edges in the box formula gives \(\sqrt{e^2+e^2+e^2}=e\sqrt3\).
questions.rule: Cube diagonal: e root three.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What is the diagonal of a cube with edge 2, to two decimals?
options: 2.83, since 2 times the root of 2 is about 2.828
4.00, since 2 plus 2 is 4
6.00, since the cube has three edges of length 2 and 2 times 3 is 6, which is the full space diagonal
3.46, since 2 times the root of 3 is about 3.464
optionExplain: This is a face diagonal, not the space diagonal.
Adding two edges is not the formula.
Multiplying by 3 skips the root.
Right: \(\sqrt{4+4+4}=\sqrt{12}\approx3.46\).
questions.explain: The space diagonal uses all three edges under the root, giving root 12.
questions.rule: Cube diagonal: edge root three.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each derived problem: solved at once from the box-diagonal solution, or not?

items.t: Diagonal of a cube with given edge
Diagonal of a box that is a square on its base and given height
Diagonal of a regular octahedron with given edge
Distance between two places given by latitude and longitude on the Earth
Diagonal of a parallelepiped given three edges and three angles
Radius of the sphere around a regular tetrahedron

questions.explain: A cube and a square-based box are special boxes. The others change the figure or the data in ways the box solution does not cover.
questions.rule: Only the special case is covered.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the book, which derived problem about the Earth is an analogy of the box-diagonal problem?
options: Find the diagonal of a cube whose edge is known, which follows from the box-diagonal solution at once
Find the spherical distance between two points given by latitude and longitude
Find the height of a box
Find the radius of the sphere around a box
optionExplain: This is a specialization of the box problem, not an analogy.
Right: it is listed among the analogies.
This is an interchange of unknown and datum, a different means of variation.
This adds a notion, the sphere, which is another means of variation, not an analogy.
questions.explain: The book lists it with the octahedron and the tetrahedron as analogies.
questions.rule: Analogy: similar, not covered.
questions.teaches: The book lists the spherical distance of two points given by latitude and longitude on the Earth as an analogy of the box-diagonal problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You know how to compute the area of any rectangle. Which derived problem is solved at once?
options: The area of a regular hexagon with given side
The area of a rectangle on a curved surface
The area of a square with given side
The area of a rectangle in four dimensions
optionExplain: A hexagon is a different figure.
Curved surfaces change the problem.
Right: a square is a special rectangle.
Four dimensions change the problem.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book's pattern holds beyond its example: a special case is covered by a solution of the general problem.
questions.rule: Special cases are free.
questions.teaches: A special case is covered at once by the solution of the general problem; a general or analogous problem is not.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A cube and a sphere share a center, and the sphere slowly grows. Which radius would be interesting to find?
