options: The radius at which the sphere weighs most, since a bigger sphere of the same material is heavier
The radius at which the cube changes color
The radius of the smallest possible sphere
The radius at which the sphere first touches the faces of the cube
optionExplain: Weight depends on the material, not on the geometry of the cube and sphere.
Colour is irrelevant to the geometry of the two solids.
There is no smallest sphere with a meaning here, since the radius can shrink toward zero.
Right: touching the faces is a critical moment.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's three moments.
questions.rule: Derive new problems by letting a fixed element vary, and ask which values of the varying quantity are critical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Put the three critical moments of the growing sphere in order.
items: The sphere touches the faces of the cube
The sphere touches the edges
The sphere passes through the vertices
questions.explain: As the radius increases, it reaches the faces first, then the edges, then the vertices.
questions.rule: Faces, edges, vertices.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The cube has edge 2. What is the radius of the sphere when it passes through the vertices?
options: 1, half the edge
\(\sqrt3\), half the space diagonal of \(2\sqrt3\)
\(\sqrt2\), half the diagonal of a face, which is where the sphere meets the middle of each edge
2, the whole edge
optionExplain: 1 is the radius at which it touches the faces.
Right: the vertices lie at distance half the diagonal from the center.
\(\sqrt2\) is the radius touching the edges.
2 is the whole edge, which has no meaning as the radius through the vertices.
questions.explain: Radii for edge 2: 1 at the faces, \(\sqrt2\approx1.414\) at the edges, \(\sqrt3\approx1.732\) at the vertices.
questions.rule: Faces, edges, vertices: 1, root 2, root 3.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: for any cube, the radius at which the sphere touches the edges is larger than at the faces and smaller than at the vertices.
questions.explain: For edge a the radii are a/2, a root 2 / 2 and a root 3 / 2, increasing in that order.
questions.rule: Faces < edges < vertices.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The growing-sphere problem is a special case of which earlier problem in the entry?
options: Finding the radius of a sphere circumscribed about a cube with given edge
Finding the diagonal of a cube with given edge, by specialization
Finding the distance between two points from their coordinates
Finding the height of a box from its diagonal and two edges
optionExplain: Right: the book calls it a special case of the circumscribed-sphere problem, and then lets the radius vary.
That problem is the cube's diagonal, a different special case of the box problem.
That problem adds coordinates and has no sphere in it.
That problem swaps unknown and datum and has no sphere in it.
questions.explain: The fixed circumscribed sphere becomes a family of spheres when its radius is allowed to vary.
questions.rule: Let a fixed element vary.
questions.teaches: The growing-sphere problem is a special case of finding the radius of a sphere circumscribed about a cube with given edge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A baker raises the oven temperature slowly. Which question follows the pattern of the growing sphere?
options: At what temperatures does something change, such as the crust browning or the center setting?
Which oven is the cheapest to buy and run, given that baking temperature is the only thing that varies?
Which flour is the whitest?
How long is the recipe?
optionExplain: Right: critical values of a varying quantity.
Price does not follow from variation.
Whiteness is not an event of the variation.
Length of the recipe is unrelated.
questions.explain: Our reading: any smoothly changing quantity has critical moments worth asking about.
questions.rule: Ask about the critical moments.
questions.teaches: Any smoothly changing quantity has critical moments, and asking about them makes a new problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher has shown how to solve one problem. What helps the student's experience most?
options: Giving the same problem again with new numbers
Asking the student to invent a new problem from it
Moving straight to a different topic
Showing a longer solution of the same problem
optionExplain: New numbers keep the problem the same.
Right: inventing a problem is part of complete experience.
Moving on skips the opportunity.
A longer solution adds nothing new.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Give students the chance to invent problems from one solved: the teacher may show how and leave part of the invention to them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student's mathematical experience is incomplete, says the author, if he has not once solved a problem invented by ____.
questions.explain: The author says a problem invented by himself.
questions.rule: Invent your own.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher wants to follow the book after a class solved a rectangle-area problem. What should she say?
options: Remember this solution for tomorrow, since a method that is learned today will serve in the next lesson
Here are all the problems I invented earlier
Ignore the topic and begin the next lesson
What other problem could we make from this one, and which one would interest you?
optionExplain: Remembering is not inventing.
Her own inventions do not give them the experience.
Moving on loses the chance.
Right: she leaves part of the invention to the students.
questions.explain: She shows a derivation and asks what would they try to calculate.
questions.rule: Ask what they would try to calculate.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the author says the teacher may show the derivation of new problems and may also leave part of the invention to the students.
questions.explain: He says both: the teacher may show the derivation, and may leave part of the invention to the students.
questions.rule: Show, then hand over.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What effect does the author expect from showing the derivation of new problems from one solved?
options: It reduces the need to practice
It makes the original problem easier
It provokes the curiosity of the students
It makes tests unnecessary
optionExplain: Nothing says practice is reduced.
The original is not changed.
Right: that is the stated effect.
Tests are not mentioned.
questions.explain: Curiosity is what drives students to invent.
questions.rule: Show, and curiosity follows.
questions.teaches: The author says showing the derivation of new problems from one solved provokes the curiosity of the students.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A music teacher has taught a scale. Which follow-up matches the author's advice?
options: Ask the student to play the scale ten more times
Ask the student to read the history of scales, since knowing where a scale came from helps in playing it
Ask the student to make up a short tune from the notes learned
Play a tune for them without comment
optionExplain: Repetition is not invention.
History is not invention.
Right: invention from what was learned.
Listening is not inventing.
questions.explain: Our reading: inventing something from what you have mastered rounds out experience in any subject.
questions.rule: Make something of your own.
questions.teaches: Outside mathematics, making up something from what was learned rounds out experience in the same way.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have a plausible guess that helped you see how a proof might go. What should the written proof contain?
options: The guess, because it led you to the idea and the written proof should show how the idea was found
Only steps that you can show are strictly correct, without leaning on the guess
The guess, repeated as often as it helped
Whatever feels convincing at the time of writing
optionExplain: The guess was a means of finding the idea.
Right: strict arguments carry the final proof.
Repeating a guess does not make it a proof.
Feeling convinced is not conclusive.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's picture.
questions.rule: Use provisional and plausible reasoning freely while devising the plan, but accept only conclusive, strict arguments when carrying it out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The author compares provisional arguments to the ____ used to support a bridge during construction.
questions.explain: When the bridge is advanced, the scaffolding is taken off.
questions.rule: Take off the scaffolding.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student's proof says 'the pattern held for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, so it holds for all n'. Which verdict fits the book?
options: A strict proof, since four cases is plenty for a pattern that has held every time it was tried
A valid hint that needs no further step
A proof, provided the cases were checked twice
Scaffolding left in the bridge: a plausible argument stands in for a strict one
optionExplain: Four cases do not cover all n.
A hint belongs to devising, not the final proof.
Checking the cases twice does not extend them.
Right: cases suggest a pattern but do not prove it.
questions.explain: In devising the plan the guess is welcome; in carrying out, a step must be conclusive.
questions.rule: Cases suggest, proofs settle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each activity: does it belong to devising the plan, or to carrying it out?

items.t: Try a few special cases to guess a pattern
Argue by plausible analogy to find an idea
Use a heuristic hunch to pick an auxiliary problem
Check that each step follows strictly from the last
Reject any step that rests only on a plausible guess
Write each step so it is conclusive

questions.explain: Plausible and heuristic reasoning belong to devising. Strict checking belongs to carrying out.
questions.rule: Heuristic to plan; strict to carry out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the author say about how freely we may use heuristic reasoning while devising the plan?
options: The more painstakingly we check steps when carrying out, the more freely we may use it when devising
We may not use it at all, since it is unreliable
We may use it only after the proof is written
We may use it only if we also write a strict proof first and show that the plan is already correct
optionExplain: Right: careful checking later buys freedom earlier.
The book says we should not be too afraid of it.
The use comes before, not after.
A strict proof is the later step.
questions.explain: The two stages support each other: strict checking later pays for freedom earlier.
questions.rule: Strict later, free earlier.
questions.teaches: The more painstakingly we check our steps when carrying out the plan, the more freely we may use heuristic reasoning when devising it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A software team prototypes a feature with quick hacks and then ships it. Which reading matches the book's picture?
options: The hacks are the final structure and need no change, since they showed that the feature works as hoped
Prototyping should be forbidden
The hacks are scaffolding and should be replaced by sound code before release
Release requires no review
optionExplain: Hacks are not meant to stay.
The book welcomes provisional work in devising.
Right: scaffolding supports the build but should not stay.
Strict checking applies to the final.
questions.explain: Our reading: the metaphor applies to any build that starts with provisional supports.
questions.rule: Remove the scaffolding before release.
questions.teaches: Provisional work is welcome while building, provided it is replaced before the result is relied on.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have a plan for a proof and begin writing it out. How should you proceed?
options: Examine each step as you reach it, asking whether it is correct
Write all the steps first and check the last line only, since a correct last line shows the rest are correct
Trust the plan and skip the checks
Check the first step and assume the rest follow
optionExplain: Right: each step is checked as it arises.
The last line depends on all the earlier ones.
A plan does not guarantee its steps.
One step does not stand for the rest.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's question.
questions.rule: Carrying out your plan, check each step by asking: can you see clearly that the step is correct?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The question to ask of each step is: can you see ____ that the step is correct?
questions.explain: The book's question is whether you can see clearly that the step is correct.
questions.rule: Can you see clearly that the step is correct?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In a long derivation, you are unsure whether line 6 follows from line 5. What should you do?
options: Go on, since later lines may confirm it
Delete line 6 and guess the next
Ask the reader to check it
Stop and examine that step before going on
optionExplain: Later lines depend on it.
Deleting avoids the question.
The check is your job as the author.
Right: each step must be examined when it is met.
questions.explain: A step that is not clearly correct cannot support those after it.
questions.rule: Check as you go.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the book says the checks during carrying out may be done after the whole solution is written.
questions.explain: The advice is to check each step while carrying out the plan.
questions.rule: Check during, not after.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the author offer as the two senses in which a step may be seen to be correct?
options: By a teacher's word or by a textbook
By intuitive insight or by formal rules
By speed or by length
By memory or by luck
optionExplain: Authority is not the book's test.
Right: checking may rely on intuition or on formal rules.
Speed and length are not tests.
Memory and luck are not tests.
questions.explain: He says checking our step, we may rely on intuitive insight or on formal rules.
questions.rule: Check by seeing or by proving.
questions.teaches: In checking a step we may rely on intuitive insight or on formal rules, and it is useful to try both.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: An accountant reconciles a ledger line by line. Which habit matches the book's advice?
options: Confirming each entry as it is reached before moving to the next
Totalling at the end and hoping the total matches, since a matching total shows that every entry is right
Checking only the largest entries
Letting a colleague check the first page only
optionExplain: Right: a step-by-step check.
A total at the end may hide offsetting errors.
The small entries are steps too.
One page is not the whole.
questions.explain: Our reading: step-by-step checking applies to any chain of reasoning or records.
questions.rule: Check as you reach.
questions.teaches: In bookkeeping, checking every entry as it is reached plays the part of checking each step of a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A long proof has a few major steps and many small calculations. Where should you begin your check?
options: With the smallest calculation, since it is quickest and a quick check builds confidence for the rest
With whichever step was written last
With a random step, to avoid bias
With the major steps, since a break there makes small checks pointless
optionExplain: Small checks first may be wasted.
Last-written is not special.
Randomness ignores the structure.
Right: the main line first.
questions.explain: The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Work out the details in proper order: do not check minor details before the major steps are sound, and expect the orders of inventing, working out and writing down to differ.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: It is not reasonable to check minor ____ before we have good reasons to believe the major steps are sound.
questions.explain: A break in the main line makes secondary checks useless.
questions.rule: Major steps before minor details.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You suspect your main argument has a gap and also have a tangled arithmetic detail. Which do you tackle first?
options: The arithmetic detail, since it is concrete
The suspected gap in the main line
Both together, at random
Neither until someone asks
optionExplain: The concrete arithmetic may be wasted effort if the main line has a gap.
Right: if the main line breaks, details are useless.
Mixing both at random wastes effort; the main line should be settled first.
Waiting until someone asks leaves the suspected gap unexamined.
questions.explain: The detail only matters if the main line holds.
questions.rule: Fix the main line first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which are orders the book distinguishes for the details of an argument? Select all that apply.
options: The order in which we write them in a final exposition
The alphabetical order of their names
The order in which we work them out
The order in which we invented them
The order of their length
optionExplain: Right: the final exposition may differ again.
No order of this kind appears in the entry; names do not decide how details are checked.
Right: the order of working out.
Right: the order of invention.
No order of this kind appears in the entry; length does not decide how details are checked.
questions.explain: The book says the order of working out may be very different from the order of invention, and the final exposition may differ again.
questions.rule: Three orders may differ.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What example does the book give of a rigid systematic order of presenting the details?
options: A modern textbook of algebra
A dictionary of mathematical terms
Euclid's Elements
A newspaper account of a discovery
optionExplain: No modern algebra textbook is named in the entry as the example of rigid order.
The book itself is a dictionary but does not use it as the example.
Right: it was often imitated and often criticized.
No newspaper is named; the example is Euclid's Elements.
questions.explain: The entry presents the Elements as a rigid, systematic order.
questions.rule: Euclid sets the rigid order.
questions.teaches: Euclid's Elements present the details of the argument in a rigid systematic order which has often been imitated and often criticized.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A builder plans a house. Which order matches the book's principle?
options: Choose paint colors first, then check the foundation, since colors are what the owner will see and judge
Check every small fitting before the plan
Order all materials in alphabetical order
Make sure the foundation and frame are sound before checking the paint colors
optionExplain: If the foundation fails, colors do not matter.
Small fittings come after the structure.
Alphabetical order has no merit here.
Right: the main structure first.
questions.explain: Our reading: the principle is general: secure the load-bearing parts before polishing details.
questions.rule: Load-bearing first.
questions.teaches: Secure the load-bearing parts of any plan before polishing its details.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In which direction should a proof written in Euclid's way run?
options: From the conclusion back to the hypothesis, since a proof should begin with what is wanted at the end
From what is given toward what is to be found or proved
From the middle outward
From the hardest step to the easiest
optionExplain: That is the order of analysis, not Euclid's exposition.
Right: from the data to the unknown, or from the hypothesis to the conclusion.
The method has a fixed direction.
Difficulty is not the order.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's description.
questions.rule: In the Euclidean way every argument runs from the data toward the unknown, or from the hypothesis toward the conclusion, and each new element or assertion is examined once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Arrange the stages of a Euclidean argument for a problem to find.
items: Start from the data
Derive each new element from the data or earlier elements
Examine each new element when first met
Reach the unknown as the last element examined
questions.explain: The argument runs from the data to the unknown, with each new element examined once.
questions.rule: Data first, unknown last.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In a Euclidean proof of a theorem, which statement is examined last?
options: The hypothesis
The longest step
The conclusion
The first lemma
optionExplain: The hypothesis is the starting point, so it comes first.
The order depends on the chain of assertions, not on the length of a step.
Right: the very last assertion to be examined is the conclusion.
A lemma comes early in the chain, so it is examined before the conclusion.
questions.explain: If each assertion is correct, including the last, the whole argument is correct.
questions.rule: Conclusion last.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: in the Euclidean way, each step must be examined more than once as the argument proceeds.
questions.explain: Each new element or assertion is examined when it is first encountered, so only once.
questions.rule: Each step is examined once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Why does the book say we need not look behind us or ahead in the Euclidean way?
options: Each step depends only on what has already been correctly established
Because the steps are independent of one another, so each can be taken in any order without loss
Because the unknown is already known
Because the steps are checked by someone else
optionExplain: Right: each step rests on correct earlier steps.
The steps depend on earlier ones.
The unknown is derived at the end.
The checking is the solver's own.
questions.explain: We may concentrate all our attention on the present step.
questions.rule: One step at a time.
questions.teaches: In the Euclidean way we may concentrate all attention on the present step, without looking behind or ahead.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A cook follows a recipe where each step uses only what earlier steps made. How is this like the Euclidean way?
options: The final dish is checked first
Each step can be checked on its own against what came before
The order of steps does not matter
Each step needs the next one to be understood, so the cook must read the whole recipe backwards first
optionExplain: In the Euclidean way the final assertion is examined last, not first.
Right: each step depends only on earlier ones.
The order matters, since each step uses only what earlier steps made.
The Euclidean order needs no look ahead.
questions.explain: Our reading: any chain where each link relies only on earlier links can be checked in order.
questions.rule: Forward chains check easily.
questions.teaches: Any chain in which each link relies only on earlier links can be checked one link at a time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have a long, complicated argument and want to check it in detail. What does the author recommend?
options: Keep it in your head, since you found it
Explain it to a friend in the order you discovered it
Write only the conclusion
Write the whole argument out in the Euclidean way
optionExplain: Memory does not examine each point.
The order of discovery hides some detail.
The conclusion alone is not a check.
Right: for detailed checking nothing is better.
questions.explain: The card next gives his two verdicts.
questions.rule: Use the Euclidean way to examine an argument in detail, especially your own; do not rely on it alone to convey an argument to someone who has not heard of it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The Euclidean exposition is excellent to show each particular point but not so good to show the main ____ of the argument.
questions.explain: He says it is not so good to show the main line of the argument.
questions.rule: Good at points, poor at the main line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher wants to explain a new theorem to a class who have not met it before. Which presentation does the entry caution against using alone?
options: A pure Euclidean proof from hypothesis to conclusion
A short sketch of the main idea first
A discussion in which students guide the discovery
A proof in which the details follow the idea
optionExplain: Right: it is not recommended without reservation for conveying an argument.
The sketch is recommended.
Guided discovery is recommended.
This is the sketch-then-details manner the book favours.
questions.explain: The Euclidean order shows steps but hides purpose and source.
questions.rule: Do not rely on Euclid to explain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each purpose: does the Euclidean exposition suit it, or not?

items.t: Checking your own long and complicated argument in detail
Examining each particular point of a proof
Confirming that the last step, the unknown or conclusion, follows
Showing a stranger the source of the argument
Making the main line of the argument understandable
Showing the purpose and connection of the whole

questions.explain: The order is excellent for checking each point and poor for showing source, purpose and connection.
questions.rule: Check with Euclid; explain otherwise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the author, why does the intelligent reader of a Euclidean proof have difficulty with the whole?
options: The proofs are too long for a reader to keep in mind, so the reader loses the thread of the whole argument
The steps are not correct
The exposition often proceeds in an order opposite to the natural order of invention
The reader is not intelligent enough
optionExplain: Length is not given as the reason.
The steps are correct; that is its strength.
Right: the order reverses the order of invention.
The reader is described as intelligent.
questions.explain: He adds that Euclid's exposition follows the order of synthesis, as in the entry on Pappus.
questions.rule: Synthesis reverses invention.
questions.teaches: Euclid's exposition follows rigidly the order of synthesis, which the book discusses under Pappus.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A manual lists every setting in strict dependency order but does not say what the device is for. How is it like Euclid?
options: It teaches the main idea best, since the strict order makes the purpose of the device plain to a beginner
It is useless for reference
It shows each point well but hides the purpose of the whole
It is the best presentation for a beginner
optionExplain: Strict order shows each point well but does not convey the main idea or purpose to a beginner.
The manual is useful as a reference, so useless overstates it.
Right: points clear, purpose hidden.
A beginner needs to know the purpose, which this manual leaves out.
questions.explain: Our reading: strict order is a virtue for reference and a fault for teaching.
questions.rule: Order alone does not explain.
questions.teaches: A strict order that shows each point clearly may still hide the purpose of the whole, in manuals as in proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A teacher is planning how to present a new proof. Which presentation do you think is best?
options: The strict details only, so the class cannot go wrong and no step is left to the students' guesswork
A sketch of the main idea first, with the details in strict order afterwards
The main idea only, with no details
The conclusion first, with no reasoning
optionExplain: Strict details alone hide the main idea.
Right: the author finds this manner desirable.
Without details the argument is unchecked.
A bare conclusion proves nothing.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's advice.
questions.rule: Encourage students to examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner, without enforcing it rigidly; present intuitive sketches before details.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the author says students should examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner, though nothing of this kind should be too rigidly enforced.
questions.explain: He finds it highly desirable but warns against rigid enforcement.
questions.rule: Euclid for self-checks, not as a rule.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: After students have found the key idea of a proof with the teacher's guidance, what is the Euclidean presentation useful for?
options: Replacing the discussion with a finished proof, so that class time is not spent on false starts
Hiding the main idea
Making the proof shorter
Setting out the details in order after the discovery
optionExplain: It follows the discussion; it does not replace it.
It should not hide the main idea.
It does not shorten the proof.
Right: it may be very useful afterwards.
questions.explain: The order of discovery comes first, and the strict order consolidates it.
questions.rule: Discover first, then set out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each teaching practice: does the author find it desirable, or less so?

items.t: Students examine their own arguments in the Euclidean manner
A sketch of the main idea first, details after
Euclidean order after students found the idea themselves
Many proofs presented in pure Euclidean form
Rigidly enforcing the Euclidean manner on students
Details only, with no hint of the main idea

questions.explain: The author favors Euclid for self-checking and after discovery, and a sketch before details; he does not favor pure Euclid presentations or rigid enforcement.
questions.rule: Sketch first; Euclid to check.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the author suggest a textbook might do about the order of exposition?
options: Present the details first and the sketch of the main idea last, so that the reader is not misled early
Omit the details altogether
Present an intuitive sketch of the main idea first and the details in the Euclidean order afterwards
Omit the main idea altogether
optionExplain: The order is the reverse.
The details are part of it.
Right: some textbooks adopt this manner, and he finds it desirable.
The main idea is part of it.
questions.explain: The sketch gives the source and purpose; the details give the checkable steps.
questions.rule: Sketch, then details.
questions.teaches: Some textbooks adopt the manner of giving an intuitive sketch of the main idea first and the details in the Euclidean order afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A trainer teaching a new process to staff gives the goal and outline first, then the steps. How does this compare with the author's view?
options: It matches: a sketch of the main idea before the exact details
It contradicts it, because details should come first so that staff can follow every step before the outline
It is irrelevant to teaching
It makes checking impossible
optionExplain: Right: the same order of sketch and details.
The author puts the sketch of the main idea first and the exact details after.
The entry concerns how to present material to learners, so it bears on teaching directly.
Checking can follow the sketch, so the order does not make it impossible.
questions.explain: Our reading: the sketch-then-details order works in any instruction.
questions.rule: Outline before steps.
questions.teaches: Giving the goal and outline before the exact steps follows the same sketch-then-details order in any training.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You believe a statement is true because you can picture it. What would the author advise?
options: Stop, since a clear picture is proof enough
Stop, since a picture is worthless
Ask someone else to picture it
Try also to prove it formally
optionExplain: The author values both ways of perceiving; a picture alone is not proof enough.
The author does not dismiss intuition; he treats seeing as one of two ways of perceiving.
Another person's picture is no more a proof than your own.
Right: seeing and proving are two ways of perceiving the truth.
questions.explain: The card next shows his comparison.
questions.rule: Wishing to satisfy yourself that a proposition is true, try to see it intuitively and to give a formal proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The author compares intuitive insight and formal proof to perceiving a material object through two different ____.
questions.explain: He names sight and touch.
questions.rule: Two senses, two ways to truth.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have proved a theorem by a long formal chain but cannot see why it is true. What next step does the author suggest?
options: Be content, since a complete proof is all that a conscientious mathematician needs in order to be satisfied
Try to see intuitively what you have proved formally
Drop the theorem
Repeat the proof in the same order
optionExplain: The author calls the reverse exercise invigorating.
Right: the exercise works in both directions.
Dropping it does not help.
Repetition is mere repetition.
questions.explain: The entry says trying to prove formally what is seen, and to see intuitively what is proved, is an invigorating exercise.
questions.rule: Both directions are worth a try.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the author compares the mathematician's wish to see and to prove a proposition with a shopper who wishes to see and touch a fabric.
questions.explain: He says the conscientious mathematician acts like the lady who is a conscientious shopper, who wants to see and to touch the fabric.
questions.rule: See and prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the author say about the classroom and this exercise?
options: It is forbidden by the syllabus
It is too easy to bother with
It is only for advanced students
There is not always enough time for it
optionExplain: The text does not say the exercise is forbidden; it points to a lack of time.
The author does not call it too easy; he calls it invigorating.
He does not restrict the exercise to advanced students.
Right: he notes the lack of time.
questions.explain: He points to the example discussed in sections 12 and 14 as typical of this limit.
questions.rule: Time limits the exercise.
questions.teaches: The author admits that in the classroom there is not always enough time to try to prove what is seen and to see what is proved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A doctor trusts a treatment because trials support it and because the mechanism makes sense. How does this resemble the author's view?
options: Only the trials count, since the evidence of experiment is the one kind that a doctor can rely upon
Two independent ways of perceiving the same truth strengthen conviction
Only the mechanism counts
Neither counts without a third opinion
optionExplain: Counting only the trials ignores the mechanism, while the author values two different ways of perceiving a truth.
Right: the author values two different ways of perceiving.
Counting only the mechanism ignores the trials, while the author values two ways of perceiving.
Nothing in the entry requires a third opinion; two independent ways already strengthen conviction.
questions.explain: Our reading: the two-senses image fits evidence of different kinds anywhere.
questions.rule: Two kinds of evidence beat one.
questions.teaches: Two independent kinds of evidence for one claim give more conviction than either alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which is easier to see at a glance: three random lines in a plane, or five random planes in space?
options: The planes, since space is richer than a plane and so offers more for the eye to take in at once
Both are equally easy
The lines; five planes in space are very hard to picture
Neither can be pictured
optionExplain: The richness does not make it easier.
The book contrasts the two.
Right: the plane case can be seen at once.
Three lines in a plane can be pictured at once, so they are not impossible to see.
questions.explain: The card next gives the numbers.
questions.rule: In checking a step, sometimes intuition is ahead and sometimes formal reasoning is; do the exercise both ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Three straight lines taken at random divide the plane into ____ parts.
questions.explain: Look at the finite triangle included by the three lines, plus six open regions.
questions.rule: Three lines: 7 parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: According to the book, how many parts do five random planes divide space into?
optionExplain: Guesses like this are what intuition produces.
32 is a power of two, a tempting guess.
25 is five squared, a tempting guess.
Right: it can be rigidly proved that the number is 26.
questions.explain: The count is 1 + 5 + 10 + 10 = 26, though no one sees it directly.
questions.rule: Five planes: 26 parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each case: is intuition ahead of formal proof, or formal reasoning ahead of intuition?

items.t: Two lines parallel to a third are parallel to each other
Anyone who understands the terms sees this at once
Euclid's long preparation for the same fact
Five random planes cut space into 26 parts
A count no one can see, yet rigidly proved
A proof that is not even long or difficult

questions.explain: Parallel lines are seen at once but proved with long preparation. The plane count is proved easily but cannot be pictured.
questions.rule: Each way can lead.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the book say about the proof that five planes make 26 parts?
options: It is long and difficult
It can be rigidly proved and is not even long or difficult
It cannot be proved, since a count of parts in space is beyond what formal reasoning can reach
It is proved only by experiment
optionExplain: The book says the opposite.
Right: the proof is not long or difficult.
The book says it is proved.
The book says rigid proof.
questions.explain: Intuition fails here but formal reasoning succeeds easily.
questions.rule: Formal reasoning can outrun intuition.
questions.teaches: The proof that five random planes divide space into 26 parts is rigid and not even long or difficult, though intuition cannot reach it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student finds a calculation shows a result, but cannot picture why. Which approach follows the book?
options: Reject the result since it cannot be pictured
Stop thinking about it, since a result that cannot be pictured is not worth any further effort
Accept the proof as a step, and try also to build an intuitive picture afterwards
Rely only on the picture
optionExplain: Failure to picture is not a refutation here.
The book urges more thought.
Right: do the exercise both ways.
Picture alone is not enough.
questions.explain: Our reading: the example of 26 parts shows a result can be correct beyond intuition.
questions.rule: Do not reject what you cannot picture.
questions.teaches: A result that cannot be pictured can still be correct, as the 26 parts show, so a failure of intuition is not a refutation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A problem asks for a rectangle with perimeter 20 and one side 6. Which part states that the perimeter is 20 and a side is 6?
options: The condition and data together tell what the rectangle must satisfy
The unknown, since it describes the rectangle that the perimeter and side are meant to pin down
The unknown is the number 20
The condition is the number 6 alone
optionExplain: Right: the unknown is the rectangle, and the rest says what it must meet.
The unknown is what we look for, here the rectangle.
20 is a datum, not the unknown.
A number alone is a datum.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's three parts.
questions.rule: In a problem to find, name the unknown, the data and the condition separately; the condition is a principal part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The condition is a principal part of a problem to ____.
questions.explain: The entry says the condition is a principal part of a problem to find.
questions.rule: Condition belongs to problems to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Find two numbers whose sum is 12 and whose difference is 2. Which is the condition?
options: The two numbers that we are asked to find, since they are what the problem is about
The sum is 12 and the difference is 2, linking the two numbers
The numbers 12 and 2
The word 'find'
optionExplain: The two numbers are the unknown.
Right: the condition is what links unknown and data.
12 and 2 are the data, not the condition that links them to the unknown.
The word 'find' names the task, not a part.
questions.explain: The unknown is the pair of numbers; the data are 12 and 2; the condition relates them.
questions.rule: Condition links unknown to data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each item from the problem of finding a number whose double plus 3 is 17 by its part.

items.t: The number we look for
The number 3
The number 17
Twice the number plus 3 equals 17
The number must satisfy a relation to 3 and 17
The relation that ties the number to the data

questions.explain: The unknown and data are the objects; the condition is the requirement that links them.
questions.rule: Objects versus the requirement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In which kind of problem does the entry say the condition is a principal part?
options: A problem to prove
Both equally
A problem with no unknown
A problem to find
optionExplain: A problem to prove has a hypothesis and a conclusion.
The entry names only the problem to find.
A problem to find has an unknown.
Right: it is named so in the entry.
questions.explain: For problems to prove the principal parts are hypothesis and conclusion, as the entry on decomposing says.
questions.rule: Find: three parts. Prove: two.
questions.teaches: For a problem to prove the principal parts are the hypothesis and the conclusion rather than unknown, data and condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A job ad asks for 'a baker with five years of experience who can start in May'. Which part plays the part of the condition?
options: The requirements of experience and start date that the person must meet
The baker who is being sought, since the ad is written entirely about that one person
The number five
The month May
optionExplain: Right: the requirements restrict who counts.
The baker is the unknown.
Five years is a datum of the search, a quantity the baker must match.
May is a datum, a given date; the requirement that links it to the baker is the condition.
questions.explain: Our reading: any search with requirements has an unknown, data and a condition.
questions.rule: Unknown, data, condition everywhere.
questions.teaches: Any search with requirements has an unknown to find, data to use and a condition that ties them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A problem asks for a number that is both greater than 10 and less than 5. What is wrong with it?
options: The condition has too many solutions
The condition is correct but the number is hard to find, so the fault lies with the solver
No number satisfies the condition, so the problem has no solution
The problem lacks a question
optionExplain: Nothing satisfies it, so there are none.
The number does not exist.
Right: the parts oppose each other.
It does ask for a number.
questions.explain: The card next names the idea.
questions.rule: Call a condition redundant if it has superfluous parts, contradictory if its parts oppose one another so that nothing satisfies it, and insufficient if it does not fix the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A condition is called ____ if its parts are mutually opposed and inconsistent, so that no object satisfies it.
questions.explain: That is the book's definition.
questions.rule: Contradictory: no object satisfies it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The problem of finding x with x + 2 = 7 and 2x + 4 = 14 has a condition that is:
options: Contradictory, since two equations oppose
Insufficient, since x has too few conditions to be fixed by the two equations given
Redundant, since the second part says the same as the first
Neither, since both equations are needed
optionExplain: The two agree, not oppose.
One equation already fixes x.
Right: doubling the first gives the second, so the second adds nothing.
The second is superfluous.
questions.explain: Both equations give x = 5, and the second adds nothing the first lacks.
questions.rule: Superfluous parts: redundant.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Match each condition on a number x to its label.
pairs: x is more than 5 and x is less than 3
x is 4 and x is 2 plus 2
questions.explain: Opposed parts leave no solution, a repeated part is superfluous, and a loose condition leaves many numbers.
questions.rule: Contradictory, redundant, insufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the book call a condition whose parts are mutually opposed?
options: Redundant
Insufficient
Principal
Contradictory
optionExplain: Redundant means superfluous parts.
Insufficient means not determining.
Principal is about main parts.
Right: the definition is in the entry.
questions.explain: The entry adds a cross-reference from the word contradictory back to condition.
questions.rule: See Condition for contradictory.
questions.teaches: The dictionary lists the word contradictory with a cross-reference back to the entry on condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A contract says delivery must be by Monday and also after Wednesday. How would you classify its condition?
options: Contradictory, since no delivery date can satisfy both
Redundant, since the two dates are close together and one of them could be left out
Insufficient, since no date is named
Complete, since both are stated
optionExplain: Right: no date meets both parts.
The parts oppose, not repeat.
Dates are named; they conflict.
Stating both makes the contradiction.
questions.explain: Our reading: the three labels apply to any set of requirements.
questions.rule: Test requirements for conflict.
questions.teaches: The labels redundant, contradictory and insufficient apply to any set of requirements, not only equations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Three equations are given for two unknowns. What can you say before solving?
options: It is certainly insufficient
It certainly has exactly one solution, since any system of equations has a single answer
The condition is either redundant or contradictory
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: Insufficient needs fewer equations.
One solution is not certain.
Right: with more equations than unknowns, one is superfluous or they conflict.
Counting says something.
questions.explain: The card next gives the whole rule.
questions.rule: When a condition is a set of linear equations, compare their number with the number of unknowns: more is redundant or contradictory, fewer is insufficient, equal is usually sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: If a condition has fewer equations than unknowns, it is ____ to determine the unknowns.
questions.explain: The book says it is insufficient.
questions.rule: Fewer equations: insufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each system by what the equation count suggests, before solving.

items.t: Two equations in two unknowns
Three equations in three unknowns
One equation in one unknown
One equation in two unknowns
Two equations in four unknowns
Three equations in five unknowns

questions.explain: With fewer equations than unknowns the condition is insufficient; with equal numbers it is usually sufficient, though the book allows exceptions.
questions.rule: Fewer equations: insufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The system x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 5 has as many equations as unknowns. What is its status?
options: Sufficient, since the numbers match
Insufficient, since the equations repeat and so leave many pairs that satisfy them both
Redundant, since each adds nothing
Contradictory, since doubling the first gives 2x + 2y = 4, not 5
optionExplain: Equal numbers are only usually sufficient.
Repeating without conflict would be insufficient; here they conflict.
The second adds a conflict, not nothing.
Right: the equal count does not guarantee sufficiency.
questions.explain: The first doubled says 4, the second says 5, so no pair satisfies both.
questions.rule: Equal count can still fail.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The system x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4 has two equations and two unknowns. What is its status?
options: Contradictory: the equations oppose each other, so that no pair of numbers can satisfy both of them
Insufficient: the second repeats the first, so many pairs satisfy both
Sufficient: the unknowns are fixed
Redundant and contradictory together
optionExplain: The equations agree rather than oppose each other: the second is twice the first.
Right: the equal count hides a repeated equation.
The pairs are not fixed.
The equations do not conflict, so the system is not contradictory.
questions.explain: Both equations say x + y = 2. In effect there is only one equation.
questions.rule: Repeats count once.
questions.teaches: With equal numbers the condition can still be insufficient when one equation merely repeats another.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A puzzle gives two clues for three unknown ages. How would you describe the condition before solving?
options: Insufficient: fewer clues than unknowns cannot fix all ages
Contradictory: the ages cannot conflict, since each clue is true of someone, and so no clash can arise
Redundant: the clues repeat
Sufficient: two clues are enough
optionExplain: Right: two clues, three unknowns.
Nothing in two clues about ages shows a conflict; the trouble is too few clues.
Nothing shows repetition.
Fewer clues than unknowns leave freedom.
questions.explain: Our reading: the counting idea applies to any set of independent clues, not only equations.
questions.rule: Count clues against unknowns.
questions.teaches: Counting clues against unknowns tells you early whether a puzzle can have a single answer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have proved a theorem and notice another one follows almost at once. What is the second called?
options: A hypothesis
A condition
A definition
A corollary
optionExplain: A hypothesis is what is assumed.
A condition belongs to a problem to find.
A definition states a meaning.
Right: that is the name for it.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's definition.
questions.rule: After finding a theorem, examine it for further theorems that come easily out of it; those are corollaries.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The word corollary is of ____ origin.
questions.explain: The entry says the word is of Latin origin.
questions.rule: Corollary: Latin, a tip.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The word 'corollary' comes from Latin. A more literal translation, according to the book, would be:
options: Reward or prize
Gratuity or tip
Proof or demonstration
Beginning or source
optionExplain: A reward suggests payment for work, but the book's literal sense is a small gift on top.
Right: the book gives gratuity or tip as the more literal sense, a small gift on top of a theorem.
A proof is a different thing from a corollary, which follows from a theorem already found.
Beginning or source is not the book's translation; a corollary follows from a theorem.
questions.explain: A corollary comes as a gratuity, a small gift on top of a theorem.
questions.rule: A corollary is a tip.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the book describes a corollary as a theorem that requires a long separate proof.
questions.explain: It is a theorem we find easily in examining another one.
questions.rule: Easy to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: When does the book say a corollary is found?
options: Before any theorem is known
Only after many other theorems
In examining another theorem found
By a new method unrelated to the theorem
optionExplain: It depends on a theorem already found.
One theorem already found is enough for a corollary, so many are not needed.
Right: the entry says in examining another theorem found.
It depends on the first theorem.
questions.explain: The theorem has been found, so the idea is fresh.
questions.rule: Look right after the theorem.
questions.teaches: A corollary is found in examining another theorem found, so the time to look for one is straight after.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A physicist derives a law for a pendulum and then notices that it also gives the period of a clock easily. How would the book name that second finding?
options: A condition of the first law, which any result found afterwards would be required to meet
A hypothesis of the second
A definition
A corollary of the first, found easily from it
optionExplain: A condition is a part of a problem.
A hypothesis is assumed.
A definition gives a meaning.
Right: it comes easily from the first.
questions.explain: Our reading: the notion extends beyond mathematics to any result that follows easily from another.
questions.rule: Easy follow-ons are corollaries.
questions.teaches: Outside mathematics, a result that follows easily from one obtained plays the part of a corollary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You face a problem with data and an unknown but no obvious link. Where may you begin?
options: Only from the data, in the order given
From the unknown or from the data, whichever suggests something
Only from the unknown, never from the data, since the answer is the only thing that is not yet known
Only from the answer in the back of the book
optionExplain: The unknown is also a start.
Right: the bridge can be started from either side.
The data are also a start.
The answer is not available in a real problem.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's picture.
questions.rule: Picture the unsolved problem as a gap between the data and the unknown, and start building the bridge from either side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: We can start constructing our bridge from either side, from the unknown or from the ____.
questions.explain: The book names the unknown and the data as the two sides.
questions.rule: Two sides: unknown and data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You are asked to find the height of a tree from its shadow. Which start works from the unknown?
options: List everything you know about the shadow's length
List everything you know about the shadow's length and the angle of the sun, and begin there
Recall a familiar problem with a similar unknown, such as finding a height by similar triangles
Ask what time it is
optionExplain: That begins from the data.
That solves a different problem.
Right: looking at the unknown to recall a similar one.
The time of day is a datum of the problem; it does not start from the unknown.
questions.explain: Looking at the unknown asks what other problems have this kind of unknown.
questions.rule: Unknown: recall a problem like it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Sort each question by the side it starts from.

items.t: Do I know a problem with the same kind of unknown?
What have I solved that asks for a quantity like this?
What familiar problem has a similar unknown?
Could you derive something useful from the data?
What can be calculated from the given numbers alone?
What does the first datum tell me by itself?

questions.explain: The first three look at the unknown; the last three look at the data.
questions.rule: Unknown side or data side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: How does the book picture the unsolved problem?
options: As open space between the data and the unknown, a gap to be bridged
As a maze with one exit, in which the solver must try each path in turn until the way out is found
As a ladder with two ends
As a lock without a key
optionExplain: Right: a gap across which a bridge is built.
The maze is not the book's picture; it pictures a gap between data and unknown with a bridge to build.
A ladder with two ends is not the book's picture; the book speaks of a bridge across a gap.
A lock without a key is not the book's picture; the book pictures a gap to be bridged.
questions.explain: The bridge can start from either bank.
questions.rule: The problem is a gap.
questions.teaches: The book pictures an unsolved problem as open space between the data and the unknown, a gap across which a bridge has to be constructed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A manager must get a project from where it stands to a finished product. Which pair of starts matches the two banks?
options: Plan only backwards from the finished product, never forward, since the goal is the only fixed thing
Plan backwards from the finished product, or forward from the resources at hand
Wait for the gap to close
Ask others to build the bridge
optionExplain: The data side is also a start.
Right: from the unknown side or from the data side.
Waiting for the gap to close builds nothing; the solver has to build the bridge.
The bridge is built by the solver, not by others, in the book's picture.
questions.explain: Our reading: planning forwards and backwards correspond to starting from the data and from the unknown.
questions.rule: Build from both banks.
questions.teaches: Planning forward from the resources and backward from the goal correspond to the two banks of the bridge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Which start does the author say is usually preferable?
options: From the data
From a random point
From the conclusion of another problem
From the unknown
optionExplain: The data start is the alternative.
No random start is advised.
The book does not claim that starting from another problem's conclusion is usually preferable.
Right: it appears usually preferable.
questions.explain: The card next gives his full view.
questions.rule: Starting the reasoning from the unknown is usually preferable; yet starting from the data has chances of success and must often be tried.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Starting the reasoning from the ____ is usually preferable.
questions.explain: The author gives this as a tendency.
questions.rule: Unknown first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You tried to recall a problem like yours and found none. What does the entry suggest?
options: Try the other side and ask what you can derive from the data
Give up
Repeat the same search for an hour
Pick any formula and apply it
optionExplain: Right: the alternative start must often be tried.
The entry offers another start.
Repeating the search is not a new start.
Random formulas do not follow.
questions.explain: When one bank fails, build from the other.
questions.rule: If one start stalls, try the other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book says starting from the data has no chance of success.
questions.explain: It says the alternative start also has chances of success and must often be tried.
questions.rule: Data start has chances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Which two later entries does the book cite as supporting the preference for the unknown?
options: Analogy and Generalization
Condition and Corollary
Pappus and Working backwards
Carrying out and Check
optionExplain: Analogy and Generalization are other entries, but the text does not cite them for this preference.
Condition and Corollary are not the entries the text refers to for starting from the unknown.
Right: the text refers to these.
Carrying out and Check concern later phases, not the choice to start from the unknown.
questions.explain: The preference is tied to reasoning backwards from the unknown.
questions.rule: Unknown first is working backwards.
questions.teaches: The book supports the preference for starting from the unknown by referring to the entries on Pappus and on Working backwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A detective can reason from the crime to the suspect, or from the known facts about the suspects. How does the advice apply?
options: Reason only from the facts about the suspects, since the crime itself tells the detective nothing yet
Reason only from the crime
Start from what is to be found, but be ready to reason from the facts as well
Wait for a confession
optionExplain: The unknown start is also useful.
The data start is also useful.
Right: both starts are used.
Waiting is not reasoning.
questions.explain: Our reading: the advice is flexible.
questions.rule: Keep both starts.
questions.teaches: Reasoning from what is sought is usually preferable, but facts at hand supply the second start.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A problem gives three points and asks for a line through the first that is the same distance from the other two. What is the unknown?
options: The point A
A straight line
The distance
The two other points
optionExplain: A is given as the point the line passes through, so it is a datum, not the unknown.
Right: the thing to be found is a line.
The equal distance is part of the condition the line must satisfy, not the thing to be found.
B and C are given points, so they are data.
questions.explain: The card next follows the book's questions.
questions.rule: Begin by asking what the data, the unknown and the condition are, and draw a figure that shows them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: In the example, the data are three ____ given in position.
questions.explain: The three points A, B and C are given in position.
questions.rule: Data: three points.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: What does the condition of the example say?
options: The line joins B and C, and so is fixed by two of the three given points in the problem
The line is as long as AB
The line passes through B only
The line passes through A and between B and C, at the same distance from each
optionExplain: That is a different line.
Length is not mentioned.
B is a given point, not on the line.
Right: that is the required relation.
questions.explain: The condition ties the unknown line to the data.
questions.rule: Condition: through A, between, equidistant.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: What does the figure that exhibits the required relations contain, according to the book?
options: The right angles involved in the definition of distance from a point to a line
Only the three points as they were given, with nothing yet drawn to show the line that is wanted
A circle through A, B and C
A triangle with equal sides
optionExplain: Right: perpendiculars from B and C to the line.
That is the figure of the data alone.
No circle is drawn; the figure shows the line through A and perpendiculars from B and C.
No triangle with equal sides is drawn; the figure shows the perpendicular distances.
questions.explain: The distance of a point from a line is measured along a perpendicular.
questions.rule: Distance is along a perpendicular.
questions.teaches: The figure for the equidistance condition shows perpendiculars from B and C to the unknown line, because distance is measured at right angles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book says the first figure shows only the data, and a second adds the unknown and the required relations.
questions.explain: Fig. 13 exhibits the data; Fig. 14 assembles unknown and data with the required relations.
questions.rule: Data figure, then relation figure.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A town planner must place a road through point A so that two villages B and C are the same distance from it. Which first step follows the book?
options: Build the road first and measure afterwards, since the surveyor's figures are easy to correct once built
Ask the villagers where they want it
Mark A, B and C and say what is unknown and what the road must satisfy
Choose the longest road
optionExplain: Building first and measuring afterwards reverses the order; the book names unknown, data and condition and draws a figure before anything is built.
The villagers' wishes are opinions; the first step is to set out unknown, data and condition.
Right: name unknown, data and condition, and draw.
The longest road is not asked for; the condition is equal distances from B and C.
questions.explain: Our reading: naming the parts and drawing the figure applies to any location problem.
questions.rule: Name, then draw.
questions.teaches: Drawing the points and naming unknown, data and condition applies to any location problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You drew the figure and the unknown still hangs loose from the data. What next?
options: Look for an auxiliary line or other addition that ties the unknown to the data
Redraw the same figure at a larger scale, since a bigger picture makes the missing link easier to see
Remove the unknown from the figure, so that only the given data remain to be studied
Search for a formula that already contains the unknown, and put the figure aside
optionExplain: Right: the figure still needs some auxiliary line, some addition.
A larger copy has the same missing connection.
The unknown is what the figure must be tied to; removing it cuts the link entirely.
A formula may help later, but the figure's job is to show how the unknown connects to the data, so setting it aside skips that step.
questions.explain: The card next describes the book's remedy.
questions.rule: If the figure is still too empty and the unknown is not connected to the data, look for an auxiliary line or other addition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: The figure is still too empty, and needs some auxiliary ____.
questions.explain: The text says the figure needs some auxiliary line, some addition.
questions.rule: Auxiliary line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A student cannot connect the unknown to the data in a figure. According to the entry, what is the best question to refloat him?
options: Have you read the problem aloud?
Is the figure large enough?
Do you remember the formula for the area?
Could you derive something useful from the data?
optionExplain: Rereading may help at the start, but a stranded student has already understood the problem; the book names a question aimed at the data.
The size of the figure is not what is missing; the figure lacks a connection between the unknown and the data.
A formula may be needed later, but the book's best question points at the data first.
Right: the book calls this the best question to refloat the student.
questions.explain: The book says the best question to refloat a stranded student is that one.
questions.rule: Ask: what useful from the data?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book calls the figure too empty because the unknown line is still unsatisfactorily connected with the data.
questions.explain: That is the book's reason for saying the figure needs some auxiliary line, some addition.
questions.rule: Empty means disconnected.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Why does the book say a fairly good student can get stranded here?
options: The right auxiliary line is not obvious and there are various things to try
Students dislike geometry and tend to give up as soon as the figure fails to show the answer at once
The problem has no solution, so any figure will leave a student stranded
The figure is drawn wrongly, so it must be redrawn before anything else is tried
optionExplain: Right: the book says there are various things to try, so a good question is needed to choose among them.
The book says nothing about dislike; it says a fairly good student can get stranded.
The problem has a solution, found in a flash once the two figures are superposed.
The figure is correct but still too empty.
questions.explain: There are various things to try, so a student can get stranded; the book's best question, could you derive something useful from the data?, points at what to use next.
questions.rule: Open choices strand students.
questions.teaches: A fairly good student can get stranded when the figure needs an auxiliary line and there are various things to try.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A programmer's diagram shows a bug but does not connect to its cause. What parallel step follows?
options: Redraw the diagram in color so that the symptom and the data stand out from one another on the page
Delete the symptom from the diagram, so that only the cause remains to be found
Wait for another report of the bug before adding anything to the diagram
Add a trace or log line to connect the symptom to the data
optionExplain: Color changes how the diagram looks but adds no link between symptom and cause.
The symptom is the unknown here; removing it removes what you want to explain.
Waiting leaves the diagram as disconnected as before.
Right: an auxiliary element supplies the missing link.
questions.explain: Our reading: an auxiliary element is any addition that ties the unknown to the data.
questions.rule: Add what connects.
questions.teaches: In debugging, an added trace or log plays the part of an auxiliary line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A figure has three points, but only one has been used. What would you do with the other two?
options: Erase them
Join them by a straight line
Ignore them
Move them closer
optionExplain: Erasing discards the data.
Right: with two points, the natural thing is the joining line.
Ignoring them leaves them unused.
The points are given in position.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's remark.
questions.rule: Ask what you have not yet used among the data, and derive something from it; with two points alone, join them by a straight line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: What can you do with two points alone? Join them by a ____ line.
questions.explain: The book answers: join them by a straight line.
questions.rule: Two points: join.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book says we have not yet used the points B and C sufficiently, so we derive something from them.
questions.explain: That is the reason it gives for drawing the line BC.
questions.rule: Use unused data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: Which question led the student to join B and C?
options: What is the unknown?
What is the condition?
What can you do with two points alone?
Where does the line end?
optionExplain: That question is asked at the start of the problem, before the student joins B and C.
That question is also asked at the start; joining B and C comes from a question about the data.
Right: a question about the data.
Where the line ends is not what the book asks; the guide is a question about what can be done with the data.
questions.explain: The book asks it as a guide.
questions.rule: Ask what can be done with the datum.
