questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: In the book's example, what are the data once the three points are named?
options: The three points A, B and C, nothing else
The three points and the line that is to be found
The three points and their distances from the line
The three points and the right angles of the figure
optionExplain: Right: the book says the data are the three points exhibited in the first figure, nothing else.
The line is the unknown, not a datum.
The distances belong to the condition, not the data.
The right angles come from the definition of distance and appear in the figure of the relations.
questions.explain: Because the data are only the three points, any further element has to be derived from them.
questions.rule: Derive new elements from the data.
questions.teaches: The data of the example are the three points, nothing else, so any further element has to be derived from them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A planner has the positions of two warehouses but has not used them. A natural first use is:
options: Ignore them for now, since two warehouses with no stated link are not yet part of the problem
Join them with a route to see the line between them
Close them
Count the staff of each warehouse
optionExplain: Ignoring the two warehouses leaves given data unused, which the book advises against.
Right: use the data to form a connecting element.
Closing a warehouse says nothing about using the positions given.
The staff of each warehouse is not among the data the problem gave.
questions.explain: Our reading: a connecting element between two given items is a general first move.
questions.rule: Connect the unused data.
questions.teaches: Connecting two given items is a general first use of unused data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You have two figures of the same problem. What does superposing them offer?
options: A smaller combined figure, since two pictures laid together take up less room than the two apart
A guarantee that the answer is right, because every line in the picture has been checked
A chance to see how the parts meet, so the solution may appear in a flash
A way to avoid thinking, since the picture does the reasoning for the solver
optionExplain: Size is not the aim of the step.
No guarantee is made; the book says may.
Right: the book says the solution may appear in a flash.
The step asks for seeing and thinking.
questions.explain: The card next describes the step.
questions.rule: Put the figure of the data and the figure of the required relations together and study what the combination shows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book says that when the two figures are superposed, the solution may appear in a flash.
questions.explain: The text says that if the figures are superposed the solution may appear in a flash.
questions.rule: Superpose and look.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: B and C lie on opposite sides of a line and at equal distances from it. Where does the line meet BC?
options: At the midpoint of BC
At B, since the line is drawn from B
At a point twice as far from C as from B
Nowhere, since B and C lie on opposite sides
optionExplain: Right: the congruent triangles give equal segments, so the meeting point is the midpoint.
B is at a positive distance from the line, so it is not on it.
Equal distances give equal segments, not a two-to-one split.
Points on opposite sides are exactly the ones a line between them separates, so it must cross BC.
questions.explain: Our reading: the two right triangles have equal perpendiculars and equal vertical angles, so they are congruent and the meeting point bisects BC.
questions.rule: Equal distances: the midpoint.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: B = (1, 0), C = (5, 2) and A = (0, 4). Through which point of BC does the line from A, equidistant from B and C, pass?
options: (2, 1), the midpoint of B and the origin
(3, 1), the midpoint of BC
(3, 2), the point above the midpoint of BC
(6, 2), the point where C is reflected in B
optionExplain: This is not the midpoint of BC; it halves the wrong segment.
Right: the midpoint is (3, 1), and the line x + y = 4 is at distance 3 over root 2 from both B and C.
The y-value 2 is C's, so the point is not halfway.
This is a reflection, not a midpoint.
questions.explain: Our reading: the line through A and (3, 1) has slope -1, so it is x + y = 4. B gives |1 - 4| / root 2 and C gives |7 - 4| / root 2, both 3 over root 2.
questions.rule: Check by distances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: In the superposed figure, the two right triangles are ____ to each other.
questions.explain: Congruent triangles give equal segments, and that is what settles the position of the line.
questions.rule: Look for congruent triangles.
questions.teaches: In the superposed figure there are two right triangles, and the book says they are congruent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: An electrician lays a plan of wiring over a plan of pipes. Where does the book's example suggest looking first?
options: At new points where lines of the two plans meet, since the book calls the new point of intersection all-important
Nothing new, since each sketch already shows everything about its own part of the room
At the longest line, since it carries the most
At the title block, since it names the building
optionExplain: Right: in the example a new point of intersection is the key.
Alignment is not the point of the step.
Length is not what the example singles out.
The title block holds no relation between the plans.
questions.explain: Our reading: where lines from two figures cross, a link between them is likely to be found.
questions.rule: Look at new meeting points.
questions.teaches: The book calls the new point of intersection in the superposed figure all-important, so look first where lines of the two figures meet.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: You are stuck and every attempt returns the same wall. A good suggestion is:
options: Repeat the attempts more quickly, since speed is what breaks through a wall that has stopped you
Change the data at random
Restate the problem in other words, and return to the definitions
Leave the problem forever
optionExplain: Repetition keeps the wall.
Random change is not guided.
Right: restating and definitions open new views.
The book gives better steps.
questions.explain: The card next gives the entry's suggestions.
questions.rule: When stuck, ask whether you could restate the problem, even differently, and go back to the definitions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: The book asks the stuck solver: could you ____ the problem, and could you do so still differently.
questions.explain: The entry uses these words.
questions.rule: Restate the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A problem asks for a point 'equidistant' from two others. Which step goes back to definitions?
options: Look up the area of a circle, since a figure with equal distances is likely to be a circle
Count the letters in the word 'equidistant'
Write what distance means, as a length measured along a perpendicular
Choose a bigger figure to work on
optionExplain: Equal distances do not imply a circle, and the area of a circle is not a definition of the term.
Counting letters says nothing about what the term means.
Right: the definition brings in the right angles.
A bigger figure is no step towards the meaning of the term.
questions.explain: The definition of a term can introduce new elements.
questions.rule: Unfold the definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: True or false: the book says that asking whether you could restate the problem aims at suitable variation of the problem.
questions.explain: The text says these questions aim at suitable variation of the problem.
questions.rule: Restate to vary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: What does the entry send the reader to next after the suggestion to go back to definitions?
options: The entry on Corollary
The entry on Condition
The entry on Carrying out
The entry on Definition
optionExplain: Corollary is another entry; the book refers the reader to Definition at this point.
Condition is another entry; the reference here is to Definition.
Carrying out is a later phase and is not the referenced entry.
Right: the entry ends with See DEFINITION.
questions.explain: The reference points to the entry on definition.
questions.rule: See Definition.
questions.teaches: The entry ends by sending the reader to the entry on Definition for the suggestion to go back to definitions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: A support agent cannot make sense of a vague complaint. Which step follows the entry?
options: Ask the customer to restate it in other words, and fix the meaning of the key terms
Repeat the same question louder and more slowly until the customer's meaning is made plain to you
Close the ticket
Guess a cause
optionExplain: Right: restate and fix the terms.
Repeating the same question louder does not clarify the complaint; restating and fixing terms does.
Closing the ticket avoids the problem and makes no attempt to understand it.
A guessed cause is not guided by the meaning of the complaint's terms.
questions.explain: Our reading: restating and defining terms apply well beyond mathematics.
questions.rule: Restate, define.
questions.teaches: Asking for a restatement and fixing the meaning of key terms is a general way to unstick a vague problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You study a puzzling letter. After reading it once, you still do not grasp it. What process does the book recommend?
options: Read it aloud until it makes sense, since the sound of the words will bring out the meaning
Ignore the details and keep the first impression
Look at its details one by one, then put them together afresh
Count the words and stop
optionExplain: Repetition may not change the view.
A first impression is not definite enough.
Right: decompose, then recombine.
Counting is not understanding.
questions.explain: The card next names the two operations.
questions.rule: Examine an object or a problem by looking at its details one after another, then recombine the parts into a whole you see differently.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Put the stages of the book's description in order.
items: Form an impression of the whole
Focus on one detail
Concentrate on another detail and on combinations
See the whole again, now differently
questions.explain: The impression of the whole comes first; attention goes to details and combinations; the whole is seen anew.
questions.rule: Whole, parts, combinations, whole again.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A manager reads a long contract once and still feels unsure about it. Which approach follows the book?
options: Take the clauses one at a time, then consider how they combine
Re-read the first page until it is memorised, since the opening clauses frame everything that follows
Accept the contract on trust
Ask for the contract to be shortened
optionExplain: Right: decompose and recombine.
Memorising one page is not recombining.
Trust skips examination.
Shortening is outside the operation.
questions.explain: Details first one by one, then combinations, give a new view of the whole.
questions.rule: Parts, then the whole anew.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: after decomposing and recombining, the book says you see the object as a whole in exactly the same way as before.
questions.explain: You consider the object as a whole again, but you see it differently.
questions.rule: The second view is new.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which examples of objects does the book use for these operations?
options: A clock and a river
A song and a letter of thanks, which are the objects the book takes as its two leading examples
A tree and a mountain
A house you intend to rent and an important but cryptic telegram
optionExplain: A clock and a river are not the book's examples of objects to decompose and recombine.
A song and a letter of thanks are not the book's two leading examples.
A tree and a mountain are not the book's examples.
Right: house and telegram are the book's examples.
questions.explain: The book adds any problem you intend to solve.
questions.rule: Houses, telegrams, problems.
questions.teaches: The book illustrates decomposing and recombining with a house to rent and a cryptic telegram, as well as problems to solve.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A coach watches a match and then replays the key moments one by one before judging the team as a whole. Which description fits?
options: Memorising the score and the names of the scorers, which are the details that a coach should retain
Decomposing the match into details, then recombining them into a new view
Skipping the details
Waiting for the next match
optionExplain: The score is one detail.
Right: the same two operations.
The details are the point.
Waiting is not the process.
questions.explain: Our reading: the two operations apply to any object of study.
questions.rule: Parts, then whole.
questions.teaches: The two operations apply to any object of study, including a match, a contract and a text.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You open a long, hard problem. What should you do first?
options: Understand it as a whole
List every tiny detail
Start with the arithmetic
Look for the answer at the back
optionExplain: Right: whole first, then details.
Too many tiny details burden the mind before the whole is understood.
Arithmetic is a detail that comes after the whole has been grasped.
Looking up the answer teaches nothing about the problem itself.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's reason.
questions.rule: First understand the problem as a whole; then decompose gradually, and not further than you need.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Too many or too minute particulars are a ____ on the mind.
questions.explain: The book says they prevent you from seeing the main point.
questions.rule: Detail can be a burden.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student starts calculating with the first number she sees, without reading the whole problem. Which verdict fits the book?
options: A good habit: details are the safest start
A good habit: it saves time, since the numbers are the part of the problem that eventually matters
No verdict is possible
A bad habit: she began with details before understanding the whole
optionExplain: The book recommends the whole first, so details are not the safest start.
Starting with the first number wastes time when it turns out not to matter.
The book gives a verdict: starting with details before understanding the whole is foolish.
Right: the book calls it foolish.
questions.explain: Having understood the whole, she could judge which details matter.
questions.rule: Whole before details.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each habit: does it follow the book's advice, or go against it?

items.t: Understand the aim and main point first
Decompose gradually and stop when enough
Judge next details after examining one or two essential points
Dive into the smallest details at once
Decompose as far as possible in every case
Skip understanding the problem as a whole

questions.explain: The book's order is whole first, then gradual decomposition, no further than needed.
questions.rule: Whole, gradual, no further than needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Why can we not decide in advance which details to examine?
options: Details are all equally important, so every one must be examined before any can be set aside
We cannot say beforehand which will turn out necessary and which will not
Details cannot be examined
The teacher decides
optionExplain: The book does not claim that all details are equally important.
Right: that is the difficulty.
Details can be examined; the difficulty is knowing in advance which ones matter.
The book does not say the teacher decides which details to examine.
questions.explain: That is why we decompose gradually and judge as we go.
questions.rule: Judge as you go.
questions.teaches: The difficulty is that we cannot say beforehand which details will turn out necessary and which will not.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A new employee reads every page of a hundred-page manual before doing any task. What does the book suggest?
options: Read nothing before starting, since a manual is for looking things up and the work will show what matters
Read only the last page
Get the main point of the whole first, then go deeper where it matters
Read aloud to colleagues
optionExplain: Reading nothing at all ignores the whole; the book wants the main point first, then details where they matter.
The last page is just another detail, not a view of the whole.
Right: the book advises grasping the whole first and going into details only where they matter.
Reading aloud to colleagues does not help the employee to grasp the whole.
questions.explain: Our reading: whole-first applies to learning any large body of detail.
questions.rule: Main point, then depth.
questions.teaches: Getting the main point of a large body of detail first guides where to read deeper.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You have understood a problem to find as a whole and want to go into detail. Where do you start?
options: With the smallest word in the text, since a small piece is the easiest place to make a first move
With the last datum
With the answer you expect
With its principal parts: unknown, data and condition
optionExplain: The smallest word is not a part.
Order of data is arbitrary.
An expected answer biases the search.
Right: those are the principal parts.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's three questions.
questions.rule: To go into detail, begin with the questions: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The principal parts of a problem to find are the unknown, the data and the ____.
questions.explain: The book names the three together.
questions.rule: Unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Fairly often, after the principal parts, what does the book advise?
options: Combine the data into one quantity, since a single number is easier to examine than several separate ones
Examine each datum by itself and separate the various parts of the condition
Drop the data
Add new data
optionExplain: Combining the data is recombining, which comes in a later step.
Right: take each datum alone and split the condition.
Dropping the data loses information the problem needs.
Adding new data is another step and not what the book advises after the principal parts.
questions.explain: Separate parts can be examined one at a time.
questions.rule: One datum at a time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: for a difficult problem the book allows decomposition to go back to the definition of a term and examine the new elements it introduces.
questions.explain: It says it may be necessary to go back to the definition of a certain term and examine the elements introduced.
questions.rule: Definitions can add new elements.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The book says the condition's various parts may be treated how?
options: Separated and each examined by itself
Merged into a single sentence
Dropped altogether
Checked by someone else
optionExplain: Right: separate the parts of the condition.
Merging the parts into one sentence is the reverse of separating them.
Dropping the parts altogether discards information.
The solver does the examination; the book does not hand it to someone else.
questions.explain: The next ideas use separation of the condition.
questions.rule: Split the condition.
questions.teaches: The book advises separating the various parts of the condition and examining each part by itself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A tenant has a dispute with a landlord. Which opening follows the book's pattern?
options: Argue loudly for the outcome you want, since the strength of the case sets what the rule must be
State what is wanted, what facts are given, and what rule must hold
List all past quarrels
Ask for a new landlord
optionExplain: Loud argument is not an analysis of what is wanted and what is given.
Right: unknown, data, condition.
Listing past quarrels buries the case in details before the whole is clear.
Asking for a new landlord skips the analysis of unknown, data and condition.
questions.explain: Our reading: naming what is sought, what is given and what rule binds them organises any dispute.
questions.rule: Sought, given, rule.
questions.teaches: Naming what is sought, what is given and what rule binds them organises a dispute much as it does a problem to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You want a new problem from an old one. Which of these is NOT one of the book's three cases?
options: Keep the unknown, change the rest
Keep the data, change the rest
Change both the unknown and the data
Keep everything and change nothing
optionExplain: This is the first of the book's three cases: the unknown is kept and the rest changes.
This is the second case: the data are kept and the rest changes.
This is the third case: both the unknown and the data change.
Right: that gives no new problem.
questions.explain: The card next lists the three.
questions.rule: Build a new problem from a proposed one by keeping the unknown and changing the rest, keeping the data and changing the rest, or changing both unknown and data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Match each recombination to what it keeps.
questions.explain: In case three both unknown and data change.
questions.rule: Keep unknown, keep data, change both.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You change an old problem 'find the area of a field with sides 5 and 8' to 'find the perimeter of a field with sides 5 and 8'. Which case is it?
options: Case 2: the data are kept and the unknown is changed
Case 1: the unknown is kept, since an area and a perimeter are both measures of the same field
Case 3: both are changed
None of the three
optionExplain: Right: same data, new unknown.
The unknown changed from area to perimeter, so the unknown is not kept.
The data 5 and 8 are the same in both problems, so not both changed.
It fits case two, the data kept and the unknown changed.
questions.explain: The data 5 and 8 stay; the unknown moves from area to perimeter.
questions.rule: Same data, new unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the book gives a fourth case beyond the three, in which the condition alone is changed.
questions.explain: It gives three cases and remarks in brackets that (1) and (2) overlap, since the form of the condition alone may be changed.
questions.rule: Three cases, with an overlap.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Why does the book put a bracketed remark after the three cases?
options: To say the list is wrong
To add a fourth case
To note that cases (1) and (2) overlap
To praise Euclid
optionExplain: The remark does not say the list is wrong; it comments on cases that fall in between.
The remark adds no fourth case; it notes that the list does not exhaust the possibilities.
Right: both unknown and data can be kept.
Euclid is not mentioned in the remark.
questions.explain: The remark says it would take too much space to discuss such cases.
questions.rule: The cases overlap.
questions.teaches: The classification has an overlap: one may keep both unknown and data and change only the form of the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A recipe for 4 portions of soup is changed to a recipe for 4 portions of stew from the same ingredients. Which case?
options: Case 1: same unknown
Case 2: same data, new unknown
Case 3: both changed
No case applies, since a recipe is not a problem and the classification covers only mathematics
optionExplain: The unknown changed from soup to stew, so this is not case one.
Right: the ingredients stay.
The ingredients are the same, so the data did not change and this is not case three.
A recipe task has a goal and resources like a problem, so the classification applies; it fits case two.
questions.explain: Our reading: the classification applies to any task with a goal, resources and requirements.
questions.rule: Goal, resources, requirements.
questions.teaches: The three-way classification applies to any task with a goal, resources and requirements.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You want a helpful related problem with the same unknown. Which is the better choice?
options: One with entirely new data and a new condition, since the more it differs the more it can teach
One chosen only because it looks interesting, whether or not it resembles the proposed problem
One that keeps some of the data and part of the condition, changing as little as feasible
One that keeps the data but states the opposite condition, so that the two can be compared
optionExplain: Too much change loses the relation to the proposed problem, so it has a poorer chance of helping.
A problem chosen without regard to the proposed one is not related to it and has no better chance than any other.
Right: the closer the relation, the better the chance of being useful, so change as little as feasible.
Stating the opposite condition changes the problem more than keeping part of it would, and relates it less closely.
questions.explain: The card next explains.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown and try to recall a solved problem with the same or a similar unknown; if none, invent one by thinking of other data that determine the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Look at the ____! The book then asks you to recall a familiar problem with the same or a similar one.
questions.explain: That is the book's suggestion.
questions.rule: Look at the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You need the area of an odd-shaped plot. Which step keeps the unknown?
options: Recall how the areas of simpler shapes such as triangles were found
Work out the cost of fencing the plot, since a landowner usually wants that figure
Find a solved problem about the plot's perimeter, since perimeter and area both measure the plot
Work out how much grass seed the plot needs, since seed is sold by the area
optionExplain: Right: the unknown, an area, is shared with problems already solved for simpler shapes.
The unknown there is a cost, not an area, so the recalled problem would have a different unknown.
A perimeter is a length, not an area, so the unknown has changed.
The unknown there is an amount of seed, so a recalled seed problem has a different unknown.
questions.explain: The recalled problem shares the unknown.
questions.rule: Same unknown, simpler problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Sort each change: is it the book's good method, or something else?

items.t: Keep the unknown and keep only part of the condition
Drop the other part of the condition
Introduce no new clause or datum
Add a new clause to the condition
Introduce a new datum
Replace the unknown

questions.explain: The good method omits without adding: the unknown stays, one part of the condition goes, and nothing new comes in.
questions.rule: Omit, do not add.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: If we cannot recollect a problem with the same unknown, what does the book suggest?
options: Try to invent one by asking for other data appropriate to determine the unknown
Wait for a similar problem to be suggested by a teacher or a book
Keep the condition whole and add a further datum to narrow the unknown
Choose a problem with a different unknown, since the first unknown is too hard
optionExplain: Right: the book asks, could you think of other data appropriate to determine the unknown?
Waiting adds nothing; the book gives a step to try: ask for other data that determine the unknown.
The book's good method omits something without adding anything, so adding a datum goes against it.
The suggestion keeps the unknown; it does not switch to a different one.
questions.explain: The question is: could you think of other data appropriate to determine the unknown?
questions.rule: Invent by changing the data.
questions.teaches: If no similar problem is recalled, ask: could you think of other data appropriate to determine the unknown?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A chef wants a sauce for fish and recalls a sauce for chicken that has a similar role. Which move is this?
options: Changing both the goal and the ingredients, since fish and chicken are different foods and need new work
Dropping the goal of a sauce and serving the fish plain
Breaking the fish into its parts and treating each part separately
Keeping the unknown, a sauce, and recalling a familiar one for a similar dish
optionExplain: The goal, a sauce for a dish, is unchanged and so is the kind of unknown; only the dish differs.
The unknown, a sauce, is dropped rather than kept.
Splitting the fish decomposes the data, which is a different move from recalling a problem with a similar unknown.
Right: the unknown (a sauce) is kept and a solved problem with a similar unknown is recalled.
questions.explain: Our reading: recalling a solved problem with a similar target is the first move.
questions.rule: Recall a similar target.
questions.teaches: Recalling a solved task with a similar target is the first move when you keep the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You cannot reach the unknown directly from the data. What might help?
options: Choose the hardest unknown you can find, since the hardest case contains the easier ones
Find something else, easier to reach, that helps you on toward the unknown
Forget the data
Guess the answer
optionExplain: A harder unknown does not bring you nearer; the book suggests something easier to reach.
Right: a stepping stone.
The data are the starting point, so forgetting them leaves nothing to build on.
Guessing the answer is not a way of reaching the unknown from the data.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's image.
questions.rule: Keeping the data, look for a new unknown that is both more accessible than the original and useful for finding it; settle for less if need be.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In short, the new unknown should be a sort of ____ stone.
questions.explain: The book compares it with a stone in the middle of a creek.
questions.rule: Stepping stone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: For the diagonal of a box with edges 3, 4 and 12, which new unknown is a good stepping stone?
options: The diagonal of the face with sides 3 and 4, which is 5
The volume of the box, which is found from the same three edges and leads directly to the diagonal
The surface area of the box, which uses all three edges
The volume of the box divided by its longest edge
optionExplain: Right: it is easy and then the box diagonal follows from 5 and 12.
The volume does not lead to the diagonal; it is a different quantity, found from the same edges.
The surface area is a different quantity from the diagonal and is no stepping stone to it.
A volume divided by an edge is the area of a face, which does not lead to the diagonal.
questions.explain: The face diagonal is 5; then the box diagonal is the root of 25 plus 144, which is 13.
questions.rule: Face diagonal first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the book wants a new unknown that is both more accessible than the original and useful for finding it.
questions.explain: It wants accessible and useful, but says in practice we must often content ourselves with less.
questions.rule: Accessible and useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: If our problem is to construct a circle, what two parts does it have?
options: Its circumference and its area
Its center and its radius
Its diameter and its area
Its tangent and its secant
optionExplain: Circumference and area follow from the radius; they are not the two parts of the construction.
Right: the center and the radius.
Diameter and area are not the two parts the book names; it names the center and the radius.
A tangent and a secant are not parts of the circle's construction in the text.
questions.explain: One part may be more accessible, so we ask: could you solve a part of the problem?
questions.rule: A part can be the new unknown.
questions.teaches: Constructing a circle has two parts, the center and the radius, and one may be more accessible as a new unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A manager must find the cost of a project and first estimates the cost of its largest task. Which idea is that?
options: A condition: a requirement that the total must meet, which the manager lists before any estimate
A corollary
A stepping stone: an easier unknown that helps on toward the main one
A contradiction
optionExplain: A condition is a requirement the total must meet, not an easier unknown that leads to the total.
A corollary follows from a theorem; it is not a partial target for a cost.
Right: the largest task cost helps the total.
Nothing in the manager's estimate conflicts; the largest task's cost helps towards the total.
questions.explain: Our reading: breaking a target into an easier partial target is the same move.
questions.rule: Estimate the big part first.
questions.teaches: Estimating a large part of a total first is a stepping stone toward the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Which kind of change to a problem departs most from the original course?
options: Keeping the unknown and changing the data
Keeping the data and changing the unknown
Changing the form of the condition only
Changing both the unknown and the data
optionExplain: Keeping the unknown and changing only the data leaves the target as it was, so it departs less.
Keeping the data and changing the unknown leaves the starting facts as they were, so it departs less.
Changing only the form of the condition restates the same problem and departs least.
Right: when both the unknown and the data change, little of the original remains.
questions.explain: The card next explains.
questions.rule: Change both the unknown and the data when milder changes have failed, so that the new unknown and the new data are nearer to each other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Could you change the unknown, or the data, or both if ____, so that the new unknown and the new data are nearer to each other?
questions.explain: The book phrases it as a question with this word.
questions.rule: Both if necessary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the book recommends changing both the unknown and the data as the first thing to try.
questions.explain: It is a last resort, accepted if milder changes have failed.
questions.rule: Last resort.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What danger does the book name in changing both?
options: The new problem may turn out easier than the original, which defeats the purpose
The original problem may be lost from sight altogether
The new data may turn out to contradict the old unknown
The old solution may no longer be checkable against anything
optionExplain: An easier problem is the aim of the change, not its danger; the danger the book names is drifting away from the original.
Right: the book says we dislike such a deviation because we sense the danger of losing the original problem.
The book does not warn of contradiction; its worry is drifting from the original problem.
The book does not mention checking; it says the original problem itself may be lost.
questions.explain: That is why we dislike it.
questions.rule: Risk: losing the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What pattern does the book name as an interesting way of changing both?
options: Doubling every datum so that the unknown doubles too
Dropping the condition and keeping only the data
Interchanging the unknown with one of the data
Replacing the unknown by a new one with no link to the old
optionExplain: The book names no such doubling; it would change the data but not the roles of unknown and data.
Dropping the condition leaves no problem to solve.
Right: the unknown and one datum swap roles, as in the entry on using the result.
The book wants the new unknown nearer to the new data, not cut loose from the old problem.
questions.explain: The book refers to the entry on using the result, section 3.
questions.rule: Swap unknown and a datum.
questions.teaches: An interesting way of changing both the unknown and the data is to interchange the unknown with one of the data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A student, stuck after milder changes, replaces both the goal and the givens of a problem by new ones that sit closer together. What does the book say?
options: It is acceptable as a last resort, but she risks losing the original problem
It is the best first move, since the new pair is closer together
It is barred, because the unknown has to stay the same
It is pointless, because a changed problem cannot help with the original
optionExplain: Right: the book accepts it when milder changes fail and it promises success, while warning of the danger of losing the original.
The book calls it a last resort because of that danger, not a first move.
The book does not bar it; it names it as a possible change when milder ones fail.
The aim is a problem nearer to something solvable, so it can help.
questions.explain: Our reading: keep a way back to the original problem.
questions.rule: Keep a way back.
questions.teaches: Polya prefers to change as little as feasible, only one or two data and a small part of the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A condition has two parts, and together they fix the unknown. What does keeping only one part do?
options: It fixes the unknown more exactly, since each part kept adds a detail that narrows down the answer
It leaves the unknown less determined, so many objects may satisfy it
It makes the problem false
It has no effect
optionExplain: Keeping only one part fixes the unknown less, not more, because the dropped part no longer limits it.
Right: weaker condition, freer unknown.
A weaker condition does not make the problem false; it makes the unknown freer.
Dropping a part does have an effect: it leaves the unknown less determined.
questions.explain: The card next shows the book's use of this.
questions.rule: Separate the parts of the condition, keep only one, drop the other, and ask how the unknown can then vary; the answer is a locus or a set of objects.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Keep only a part of the condition, ____ the other part.
questions.explain: The book states the pattern in these words.
questions.rule: Keep a part, drop the other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In the triangle example, where can the apex lie if only the altitude h is required?
options: On the circle with center B, since the points at a given distance from B form such a circle
On the line BC
At a single point
On a line parallel to BC at distance h from it
optionExplain: Not the locus for this part.
The line BC has altitude 0.
Many points satisfy this part.
Right: all such points form the locus.
questions.explain: The book says all points of a parallel to the line BC at distance h satisfy part (I).
questions.rule: Altitude gives a parallel.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: True or false: the locus of points satisfying the angle part of the triangle condition is a circular arc whose end-points are B and C.
questions.explain: The book says the locus of the points satisfying part (II) is a certain circular arc whose end-points are B and C.
questions.rule: Angle gives an arc.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What general pattern does the book draw for problems of geometric construction?
options: Use a ruler before any other tool, since measurement settles most figures
Draw a larger figure so that the details are easier to see
Reduce the problem to the construction of a point, and construct the point as an intersection of two loci
Construct the unknown from memory of a similar figure, then adjust until the condition is met
optionExplain: The book's pattern concerns the condition, not the tool used to draw.
A larger figure is not the pattern; the pattern keeps one part of the condition to get a locus.
Right: reduce to a point and intersect two loci.
Adjusting a remembered figure is trial and error, while the pattern keeps part of the condition to build a locus.
questions.explain: The book adds that the pattern keep only a part of the condition works for problems to find of any kind.
questions.rule: Point as intersection of two loci.
questions.teaches: In geometric construction the pattern is to reduce the problem to a point and construct it as the intersection of two loci.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You must find a meeting spot that is within 10 minutes of the station and also within 5 minutes of the office. Which step follows the pattern?
options: Pick a spot at random and then walk to the station and the office to see how long each walk takes
Ignore the office
Describe all spots near the station, then all spots near the office, and take the overlap
Wait for the others
optionExplain: A random spot does not use the two requirements to narrow the search.
Ignoring the office drops a requirement without using it to narrow the search.
Right: each part gives a set; the overlap solves it.
Waiting for the others is no step towards the spot.
questions.explain: Our reading: the same pattern solves any problem with two requirements.
questions.rule: Overlap of two sets.
questions.teaches: With two requirements, describe the set meeting each one and take their overlap.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A crossword clue reads 'forward and backward part of a machine (5 letters)'. What is the unknown?
options: A machine
A word
A direction
A part of speech
optionExplain: A machine part is mentioned in the clue but it is not what we are asked to find.
Right: the thing sought is a word.
Forward and backward are part of the clue's description, not the thing sought.
The clue does not ask for a part of speech; it asks for a word.
questions.explain: The card next follows the book's reasoning.
questions.rule: In a puzzle, ask what is unknown and what the condition is, split the condition into parts, and run through the objects that fit one part to see which fit the other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In the clue, the unknown is a ____.
questions.explain: The book asks: what is the unknown? A word.
questions.rule: The unknown is a word.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: The clue has two parts. Which pair is correct?
options: Length and shading of the answer, since the clue gives a number of letters and some squares may be shaded
Sound and rhyme of the answer, since a clue about direction may be a sound pun
Origin and date of the word, since the clue refers to a machine part
Meaning (a short word for a machine part) and spelling (five letters that read backward as another machine part)
optionExplain: Shading is not in the clue; the book takes meaning and spelling as the two parts.
Sound and rhyme are not in the clue, which asks for meaning and spelling.
Origin and date are not in the clue; the parts are meaning and spelling.
Right: part (I) is meaning, part (II) is spelling.
questions.explain: The unknown must be a short word meaning a machine part and a 5-letter word reading as one backward.
questions.rule: Meaning and spelling.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Put the steps of the book's crossword method in order.
items: Ask what the unknown is and what the condition is
Notice the condition is too loose to fix one word
Separate the parts of the condition
List words fitting the meaning, and test each for the spelling
questions.explain: The book names the unknown, finds the condition insufficient, splits it into meaning and spelling, then runs through candidates.
questions.rule: Split the condition, then test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What did the book suspect that led to part (II)?
options: That the clue was misprinted and a letter is missing
That the answer had six letters, since the clue seemed to count more squares than the grid showed
That forward and backward reading might both be meant
That the answer was the name of a person
optionExplain: A misprint is not what the book suspects; it takes the two readings as intended.
The clue gives five letters, so a six-letter answer does not fit.
Right: the ambiguity was intentional.
The clue asks for a machine part, so a person is not what the book suspects.
questions.explain: The condition is ambiguously expressed on purpose.
questions.rule: Suspect a double reading.
questions.teaches: The clue is ambiguously expressed on purpose: if nothing is a forward and a backward part of a machine, the reading may be forward and backward spelling.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You need a password that has eight characters and is also a word spelled backwards. Which first step follows the pattern?
options: Split the requirements and list words that fit one, then test the other
Choose any eight characters you like and then test whether the result happens to read as a word
Skip the second requirement
Ask someone else
optionExplain: Right: separate parts, test candidates.
Choosing any eight characters ignores the two parts of the requirement.
Skipping the second requirement drops half of the condition.
Asking someone else is no step of the pattern, which separates the parts and tests candidates.
questions.explain: Our reading: listing candidates for one requirement then testing the other is general.
questions.rule: List, then test.
questions.teaches: Listing candidates for one requirement and testing each against the other is a general way to use a split condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What are the principal parts of a problem to prove?
options: The unknown and the data, as in a problem to find, with the same three questions asked of them
The condition and the figure
The proof and the example
The hypothesis and the conclusion
optionExplain: The unknown and the data are the principal parts of a problem to find, not of a problem to prove.
The condition and the figure are not the principal parts of a problem to prove.
The proof and the example are not the principal parts; the parts are hypothesis and conclusion.
Right: that is the book's answer.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's three recombinations.
questions.rule: In a problem to prove, take the hypothesis and the conclusion as the principal parts, separate the parts of the hypothesis, and recombine in three ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In a problem to prove, we ask for the hypothesis and for the ____.
questions.explain: The book asks these two questions.
questions.rule: Hypothesis and conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: You want to prove a theorem. Which first change keeps the conclusion?
options: Change the conclusion into its opposite, since proving the opposite false is the same as proving the claim
Recall a theorem with the same or a similar conclusion
Drop the theorem
Add a new conclusion
optionExplain: Changing the conclusion into its opposite changes the problem and does not keep the conclusion.
Right: look at the conclusion.
Dropping the theorem loses the problem instead of relating it to another.
Adding a new conclusion adds to the problem and does not keep the old conclusion.
questions.explain: This is the proof analogue of looking at the unknown.
questions.rule: Look at the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: Match each way of recombining a theorem to its question.
pairs: Keep the conclusion, change the hypothesis
Could you think of another hypothesis?
Keep the hypothesis, change the conclusion
Could you derive something useful from the hypothesis?
Keep a part of the hypothesis
questions.explain: Each way of recombining has its own question, parallel to the ones for problems to find.
questions.rule: Three recombinations, three questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: What does the book advise when we keep only a part of the hypothesis?
options: Add a clause
Drop the conclusion
Prove the converse
Ask whether the conclusion is still valid
optionExplain: Adding a clause strengthens the hypothesis; the book advises keeping only a part of it.
Dropping the conclusion removes what is to be proved.
Proving the converse is a different theorem, not the question asked of the part-hypothesis.
Right: is the conclusion still valid?
questions.explain: Dropping a part of the hypothesis is the analogue of dropping part of the condition.
questions.rule: Does it still hold?
questions.teaches: Keeping only part of the hypothesis, the question is whether the conclusion is still valid.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: A lawyer wants to prove a claim and first asks if a weaker set of facts already gives the same conclusion. Which move is it?
options: Changing both
Keeping the conclusion and dropping part of the hypothesis
Keeping the hypothesis only, and changing the conclusion until it follows from the facts given
Changing the conclusion
optionExplain: Changing both would change the conclusion too, but the lawyer keeps the conclusion.
Right: weaker premises, same conclusion.
Changing the conclusion until it fits the facts alters the claim, whereas the lawyer keeps the claim.
Changing the conclusion alters the claim; the lawyer keeps it and weakens the facts.
questions.explain: Our reading: arguments in law have the same two parts as theorems.
questions.rule: Try weaker premises.
questions.teaches: In argument as in geometry, ask whether a weaker set of premises already gives the same conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A text says: a circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point in a plane. What must you know to learn from it?
options: How to draw circles accurately with a compass, since the picture carries the meaning
The meaning of the other words it uses, such as point, distance and plane
The history of how the word circle entered the language, since meaning follows origin
A theorem already proved about circles, since the definition is built on theorems
optionExplain: Drawing may help later, but the definition itself states meaning in words.
Right: a definition explains the new term in words you are expected to know already.
History is interesting, but the definition does not depend on it.
A theorem comes after the term is defined, not before.
questions.explain: A definition works by stating the new meaning in terms already understood. The card next shows this.
questions.rule: Read a definition as a statement of a term's meaning in other terms that you are expected to know well.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A definition states the meaning of a term in other terms that are supposed to be well ____.
questions.explain: The words used in the definition are supposed to be familiar to the reader.
questions.rule: A definition rests on well-known terms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A manual defines a quorum as the minimum number of members who must be present for a vote to count. Which word is the manual explaining?
options: Members, because the manual says who may take part in a vote
Vote, because it is the last key word in the sentence and sounds technical
Present, because it carries the main condition that makes a vote count
Quorum, because the others are assumed to be understood
optionExplain: Members is part of the explaining words, so it is assumed.
Position in the sentence does not decide what is defined.
Present is one of the explaining words, so it is assumed known.
Right: the defined term is the new one; members, vote and the rest are expected to be known.
questions.explain: The term being defined is the one the sentence introduces; the rest carry the meaning.
questions.rule: Find the new term first; the rest is the explanation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student says: I must know focus and directrix before I can read the definition of a parabola. What is wrong with that?
options: Those two terms are introduced by the definition, so they need not be known beforehand
Nothing is wrong with it, since every word in a definition must be known beforehand
Those two words are primitive terms, so they are not defined anywhere in the text
Only the word parabola needs to be known in advance, since the others come with it
optionExplain: Right: parabola, focus and directrix are the terms being defined; the reader is not expected to know them yet.
If every word had to be known first, nothing could be defined.
Focus and directrix are defined in the book's text, not primitive.
The word parabola is the one being defined, so it is not assumed.
questions.explain: The book states that the reader is not supposed to know the three defined terms.
questions.rule: Separate the terms being defined from the terms assumed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If a reader does not know the meaning of plane, the definition of a parabola cannot give that reader a full meaning.
questions.explain: Our reading: the definition uses plane among its well-known terms, so a reader without it lacks part of the foundation.
questions.rule: Missing background words weaken a definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A lease defines a break clause as the right to end the lease early by giving notice. A tenant has not met the word notice. What happens?
options: The tenant learns what notice means from the same sentence that defines the clause
The definition still works, since a lease is a legal text and legal words are exact
The definition gives the tenant little, since a word it relies on is unfamiliar
The tenant need only know the word clause, since the other words explain themselves
optionExplain: The sentence uses notice, it does not define it.
A legal setting does not make background words unnecessary.
Right: the definition leans on notice; without it the new term stays unclear.
Clause is the term being defined, so knowing it is not the point.
questions.explain: The book states that the reader is supposed to know point, straight line, plane, distance, fixed and locus, but not parabola, focus or directrix.
questions.teaches: In the book's parabola definition, the reader is supposed to know point, straight line, plane, distance, fixed and locus, but not parabola, focus or directrix.
questions.rule: Read a definition as a statement of a term's meaning in other terms that you are expected to know well.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A geometry text does not formally define point but formally defines circle. What is the likely reason?
options: Point is too easy to need any definition, while circle is hard enough to need one
Circle was discovered later than point, so only later notions get formal definitions
Point has no meaning that anyone could state, so no text can say anything about it
Point is a starting term, and circle can be stated using point and distance
optionExplain: Ease is not the reason; the starting terms are accepted as primitive.
Discovery order does not decide how terms are defined.
The point is not meaningless; it is just not defined formally.
Right: something must be accepted first, and circle can then be built from it.
questions.explain: Terms are split into starting ones and built ones. The card next shows the split.
questions.rule: Take a few starting terms as primitive and undefined, and define every other term from primitive or earlier defined terms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Sort each term as primitive (not formally defined) or derived (formally defined).

items.t: point
straight line
plane
circle
parabola
bisector of an angle

questions.explain: The book names point, straight line and plane as primitive and the other three as formally defined.
questions.rule: Few starting terms, many derived ones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A chess rulebook treats square and piece as understood, then defines capture as removing an opposing piece by moving onto its square. What is capture?
options: A primitive term, since players already know what a capture is from experience
A derived term, defined from terms taken as understood
A derived term, but one that needs no definition since players already know it
Neither of the two, since a rule of a game is not a term of a mathematical kind
optionExplain: Being familiar does not make a term primitive; here it is defined.
Right: capture is explained through square and piece, which are accepted as the starting terms.
A derived term is exactly the kind that is formally defined.
A defined word in a rulebook is a term like any other.
questions.explain: A term stated through simpler accepted terms is derived.
questions.rule: Defined from simpler terms means derived.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Suppose a focal chord is defined using parabola and focus, which were defined earlier. What may its definition use, by the book's scheme?
options: Only primitive terms, not other defined terms
Only formerly defined derived terms, not primitive ones
Primitive terms and formerly defined derived terms
Any term at all, including ones defined later
optionExplain: Only primitive is too strict; earlier defined terms are allowed.
Primitive terms are allowed too; the line is not excluded.
Right: the book says derived terms are stated in primitive terms and in formerly defined derived terms.
Terms defined later would make the chain circular.
questions.explain: The order of definition matters: a derived term may rest on what came before.
questions.rule: Build only on what is already available.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: A derived term must be defined using primitive terms only and not other defined terms.
questions.explain: The book allows primitive terms and formerly defined derived terms together.
questions.rule: Earlier defined terms may be used.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher draws a dot on the board and says, roughly, this is what we mean by a point. Does this break the rule that point is not formally defined?
options: No, because illustrations are allowed and welcome in teaching, though they are not formal definitions
Yes, since any attempt to explain a primitive term in class breaks the rule
Yes, since drawings and spoken examples count as formal definitions of a term
No, since a point is a derived term after all and can be defined from other terms
optionExplain: Right: the book allows illustrations, and even calls them very desirable in teaching.
The rule is about formal definition, not about every explanation.
A drawing is an illustration, not a formal definition.
Point is primitive in this scheme, not derived.
questions.explain: The book adds that Euclid's definitions of point, line and plane are scarcely formal, rather intuitive illustrations.
questions.teaches: The book says Euclid's so-called definitions of point, line and plane are scarcely formal and are rather intuitive illustrations, which are allowed and desirable in teaching.
questions.rule: Take a few starting terms as primitive and undefined, and define every other term from primitive or earlier defined terms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A rule says: a safe lane is the set of points equally far from two fixed walls. Which part decides if a given point is in the lane?
options: The word lane, because it names the thing that the sentence is describing
The two fixed walls, because they are the only fixed items named in the sentence
The property of being equally far from both walls
The word set, because it tells you that the points are gathered into a group
optionExplain: The name labels the set but gives no test for a point.
The walls supply the reference but the test is equal distance.
Right: the defining property is the test a point must pass.
Set tells you the kind of object, not the test.
questions.explain: A definition has a name, a test and a setting. The card next shows them in the parabola.
questions.rule: Take a definition apart into the thing defined, the property that defines it and the setting it assumes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A parabola is the locus of points at equal distance from a fixed point and a fixed ____.
questions.explain: The second reference is a fixed straight line, called the directrix.
questions.rule: Equal distance from the focus and the directrix.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: In a plane, a point X is 3 cm from the focus F and 4 cm from the directrix d. Does X lie on the parabola?
options: No, because its two distances are not equal
Yes, because it is close to both of them
Yes, because it is inside the plane
Only if it also lies on the directrix itself
optionExplain: Right: the test is equal distance, and 3 is not 4.
Closeness is not the test; equality is.
Being in the plane is a requirement of the setting, not the test.
Lying on the directrix is not what the definition asks for.
questions.explain: A point is on the parabola exactly when its two distances match.
questions.rule: Equal distance is the test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If the focus is moved to another place off the directrix, the same definition still describes a parabola, a different one.
questions.explain: Our reading: the definition names a fixed point and a fixed line, so moving the focus gives another parabola of the same kind.
questions.rule: The definition fixes the test, not a particular focus.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student writes: a parabola is the set of points at equal distance from a fixed point. What is missing?
options: A fixed circle around the fixed point, to show how far away the points may be
A requirement that the points lie in space, not in a single flat plane
A stated radius for the distance, so that the points can be measured from it
A second reference: the distances must be equal from a fixed point and a fixed line
optionExplain: No circle appears in the definition.
The book places all the elements in one fixed plane, not in space.
Distances are compared, not measured against a set radius.
Right: the definition compares the distance to a point with the distance to a line.
questions.explain: Both references, point and line, are part of the test.
questions.rule: Do not drop a part of the definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A map-maker defines a border strip as the points equally far from a fixed town and a fixed river on one flat map. Which condition mirrors the parabola's?
options: The town must be larger than the river
The town must not lie on the river
The river must be straight and short
The strip must be wider than the town
optionExplain: Size is not part of the definition.
Right: the book states that the focus is not on the directrix.
Straightness is part, but shortness is not stated.
Width is not mentioned in the definition.
questions.explain: The book adds that all elements lie in a fixed plane and that the focus is not on the directrix.
questions.teaches: The book adds the condition that the focus is not on the directrix.
questions.rule: Take a definition apart into the thing defined, the property that defines it and the setting it assumes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A dictionary and a geometry text both define circle. Which definition can be wrong if everyday speakers use the word differently?
options: The geometry text's, because a mathematical definition must match what people say
The dictionary's, because it reports how the word is currently used
Both of them, because every definition must follow the way speakers use a word
Neither of them, because a definition is a statement and cannot be wrong at all
optionExplain: The geometry definition creates its own meaning.
Right: a dictionary tries to match current meaning, so it can be corrected by usage.
Only the dictionary is tied to usage.
A dictionary entry can be wrong about usage.
questions.explain: The two kinds of definition answer to different things. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Take a technical definition as creating the meaning, and do not test it against ordinary speech.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each writer or feature with what the book says about it.
pairs: Accepts the current meaning and states it neatly
Lets the definition create the meaning of a technical term
questions.explain: The forms look alike, but the spirit differs.
questions.rule: Same form, different spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A spec defines active user as someone who logged in during the last 30 days. A manager objects: in ordinary speech active means daily. What follows?
options: The spec must be changed to match ordinary speech, so that readers are not confused
The spec is wrong until a dictionary entry agrees with its stated definition
The manager's reading wins, since it is the more common sense of the phrase
Inside the spec, the stated definition sets the meaning, whatever ordinary speech says
optionExplain: Matching speech is the dictionary's job, not the spec's.
A dictionary does not decide a technical definition.
Frequency of use does not override a stated definition.
Right: like a mathematical definition, it creates its meaning for the document.
questions.explain: A technical definition governs within its own text.
questions.rule: The definition creates the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Everyday speakers start using the word circle for ovals too. What happens to the geometric definition of circle?
options: Nothing; it creates its own meaning, though a dictionary entry would be updated
It must widen to include ovals, because the definition has to follow what speakers mean
It becomes wrong until it is revised, because meaning is fixed by common use
It matches the dictionary entry automatically, because the two are the same kind
optionExplain: Right: the mathematical definition is not governed by usage.
Mathematics does not follow usage.
It was not tied to usage, so it cannot become wrong that way.
There is no such automatic link.
questions.explain: Only the dictionary follows the drift of speech.
questions.rule: Usage moves dictionaries, not technical definitions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Sort each task by the spirit it belongs to.

items.t: Report how most speakers use the word today
Fix the meaning of a new term for use in proofs
Revise an entry when usage drifts
Ignore what the word means in ordinary talk
Accept the current meaning and state it neatly
Let the definition create the meaning

questions.explain: The dictionary follows usage; the mathematician sets meaning.
questions.rule: Follow usage or set meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A contract defines business day as Monday to Saturday. The other side says that is not what the phrase means in talk. Which reading fits the book's idea?
options: Ordinary meaning counts for nothing at all in any kind of text, so the clause stands alone
Ordinary meaning overrides the contract definition whenever the two sides disagree
The contract definition governs the contract, though ordinary meaning still matters a little
The phrase has no meaning in the contract until a dictionary has been checked first
optionExplain: The book says little, not nothing.
The definition is stated to settle the meaning.
Right: the definition creates the meaning, but the book says ordinary meaning matters little, not zero.
Defined meaning does not wait for a dictionary.
questions.explain: The book says ordinary meaning matters little to the mathematician, and that he is not primarily concerned with it.
questions.teaches: The book says the mathematician is not primarily concerned with ordinary meaning and that it matters little to him, not that it matters not at all.
questions.rule: Take a technical definition as creating the meaning, and do not test it against ordinary speech.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A problem concerns the median of a triangle, a term you half remember. What is a good first move?
options: Guess a value for the median and test whether it works for the problem
Skip the term and work on the part of the problem that is easier to follow
Draw a very large triangle and measure the median directly with a ruler
State what a median is by definition, in words you know
optionExplain: Guessing ignores what the term says.
The term is probably essential, so skipping it loses content.
Measuring replaces reasoning with a single case.
Right: the definition lays out the facts behind the word.
questions.explain: Going from a word to its meaning is the move. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Replace each technical term by the facts its definition states, and work with those.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Going back to ____ means replacing a technical term by the facts it stands for.
questions.explain: The book calls this procedure going back to definitions.
questions.rule: Substitute the defining facts for the term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: You must show that a circle's diameter is its longest chord. Which move is going back to definitions?
options: Look up a theorem about chords in another book and apply it to the circle at once
Write that every point on the circle is the same distance from the centre, and that a chord joins two such points
Try one circle of radius 5, draw some chords and measure which one is longest
Name the circle C and the chord AB and then move on to the next step of the proof
optionExplain: A theorem is a different resource from the definition.
Right: this unpacks circle and chord into their meaning.
One measured case does not unpack the terms.
A label adds no content.
questions.explain: Unpack the terms into what they say.
questions.rule: Use what the term means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which of these is an instance of going back to definitions?
options: Drawing a clear figure of the triangle and marking the sides on it
Solving a simpler version of the same triangle problem first
Restating isosceles as two sides are equal
Working backwards from the unknown to the data that would give it
optionExplain: A figure is another heuristic.
A simpler version is another heuristic.
Right: it replaces the term by its defining fact.
Working backwards is another heuristic.
questions.explain: Only substitution of a term by its definition counts.
questions.rule: Definition in, term out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If you cannot state the definition of a term in the problem, going back to definitions is not available to you.
questions.explain: Our reading: the move rests on the definition, so without it you must find or recall it, or use known facts about the notion.
questions.rule: You need the definition to go back to it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A policy says the vendor must be solvent. An analyst replaces solvent by assets exceed debts and asks for the balance sheet. What does this change?
options: The term is gone, but new elements and relations enter the problem
Nothing changes, since the new wording states exactly the same single idea
The problem has become easier only because a definition was used
The analyst has dropped the requirement that the vendor must be solvent
optionExplain: Right: assets and debts are new elements, and a relation links them.
The wording is now different and the conception changes.
Easier is not guaranteed; the change just reframes it.
The requirement is kept, just stated through facts.
questions.explain: The book says that going back to a definition removes the term but introduces new elements and relations, and some restatement of the problem results.
questions.teaches: Going back to a definition removes the term but introduces new elements and relations, so some restatement, or variation, of the problem is bound to result.
questions.rule: Replace each technical term by the facts its definition states, and work with those.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student writes out the definition of a technical term from memory and does nothing more. What has happened to the term in the problem?
options: It is gone, since the student now knows its meaning from memory
It is gone, since the meaning has now been written down on the page
It is still there; the definition has not yet been used
It has been replaced by a theorem that the student recalled
optionExplain: Knowing the meaning does not remove the term.
Writing the meaning down does not apply it.
Right: knowing the definition is not the same as using it.
No theorem has been used.
