questions.explain: The term leaves only when its meaning is used. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Introduce suitable elements, state the relations the definition gives them, and rewrite the problem without the term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Put the steps for eliminating a technical term in order.
items: Start from the statement that contains the technical term
Introduce suitable elements into the figure
Use the definition to state relations between those elements
Check that the relations express the whole meaning
Restate the problem without the term
questions.explain: The book describes this procedure: start, introduce elements, relate them by the definition, and restate.
questions.rule: Elements, then relations, then restatement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Problem: find a point on line c that lies on the circle with centre O and radius 5. Which step eliminates circle?
options: Name the point P and state that P is 5 units from O
Draw the circle freehand and mark the point P on it by eye
Recall that a circle has area pi times r squared and use that
Call the circle K and keep K in the statement of the problem
optionExplain: Right: P and its distance to O are the new elements and relation.
A drawing does not express the relation.
Area is a fact about circles but does not unpack the term.
Renaming keeps the term.
questions.explain: The distance relation is the content of the word circle here.
questions.rule: Replace the term with the relation it names.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If no new elements are added to the figure, the equal-distance relation of the parabola cannot be stated.
questions.explain: Equality of PF and PQ needs the segments PF and PQ to exist in the figure; relations hold between elements.
questions.rule: Elements come first, then relations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which restatement of the parabola problem has the term parabola eliminated?
options: Find P on c lying on the parabola with focus F and directrix d
Find the intersection of the line c with the given parabola
Find P on c, remembering that a parabola is a locus of points
Find P on c with PF equal to PQ, where PQ is the perpendicular from P to d
optionExplain: That restatement keeps parabola.
It keeps parabola and just points to the intersection.
It mentions parabola again.
Right: only the first has no trace of parabola.
questions.explain: A restatement is free of the term only if the term is absent.
questions.rule: The term must not remain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A manual says a fair die is one where each face is equally likely. An engineer writes only: the die is a cube. Has fair been eliminated?
options: Yes, since a cube has six equal faces and equal faces mean equal chance
No, because the stated relations do not express the whole meaning of fair
Yes, since a cube is a known shape and shape settles the matter
No, since the term fair cannot be eliminated from any statement
optionExplain: Equal faces in shape do not give equal chance.
Right: equal chance for each face is not captured by shape alone.
Shape is a different notion.
The term can be eliminated if the full meaning is stated.
questions.explain: The book says that if the relations express the meaning completely, the definition has been used and the term eliminated.
questions.teaches: If the relations you state express the meaning of the term completely, then you have used the definition and eliminated the term.
questions.rule: Introduce suitable elements, state the relations the definition gives them, and rewrite the problem without the term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A problem mentions a locus and a directrix that you barely know. What attitude fits a beginner?
options: Leave the terms where they are and hope the answer appears by itself
Try to get rid of the unfamiliar terms by their definitions
Wait for more terms to turn up that make the first ones clearer
Memorise the terms carefully without ever putting them to use
optionExplain: Ignoring the terms leaves the content hidden.
Right: if you know little, the terms are embarrassing and you want to be rid of them.
More terms would not help.
Memorising is not using.
questions.explain: A beginner removes terms rather than leaning on them. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Name the unknown, data and condition, go back to the definition, draw the figure, and state the problem plainly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Put the dialogue's steps in order.
items: Name the unknown, the data and the condition
Recall the definition of the parabola
State what follows for the point P
Draw a figure with the lines PF and PQ
Restate: find P on c with PF equal to PQ
questions.explain: The dialogue moves from naming the parts, through the definition and a figure, to a plain restatement.
questions.rule: Parts, definition, figure, restatement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Recall: the perpendicular bisector of AB is the set of points equally far from A and B. Restate: on line c, find a point of this bisector.
options: On c, find a point P on a line through the midpoint of AB
On c, find a point P that minimises PA plus PB
On c, find P and then bisect AB
On c, find a point P with PA equal to PB
optionExplain: A line through the midpoint is not the defining relation.
Minimising a sum is a different condition.
Bisecting AB does not use the definition.
Right: equal distances replace the term.
questions.explain: The definition becomes the restated condition.
questions.rule: Turn the term into its equal-distance relation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If the line c is replaced by another line c prime, the restatement keeps the same form, with c prime in place of c.
questions.explain: The defining relation does not depend on which line is given, only the line changes.
questions.rule: The method stays; the data change.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student restates the problem as: find P on c that lies on the parabola with focus F and directrix d. The teacher says it is not deflated. Why?
options: The technical term parabola is still in the statement
The statement has no unknown in it, so nothing is left to find
The student forgot to name the line c in the new statement
The statement mentions a point P at all, which the teacher does not allow
optionExplain: Right: the restatement must be free of the technical terms.
The unknown P is named.
The line c is named.
Naming P is needed.
questions.explain: The book calls success a restatement with the technical terms gone.
questions.rule: Do not keep the term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Two analysts get a task with the term amortization schedule. One has used schedules for years; the other recently met the term. How do their approaches differ, by the book's reasoning?
options: Both must start from the definition only, since a definition is the sole safe start
Both should avoid the term entirely, since terms only confuse a problem
The expert reaches for known facts; the novice replaces the term by its definition
The novice has the advantage, since a fresh mind finds terms easy to ignore
optionExplain: The expert has more to use than the definition.
Avoiding the term loses content.
Right: how you approach depends on how much you know about the notion.
Knowing little is not an advantage here.
questions.explain: The book says that if we know much about the parabola we use that knowledge, and if we know little we want to get rid of the terms.
questions.teaches: If you know much about the notion you try to use that knowledge; if you know little, you want to get rid of the technical terms.
questions.rule: Name the unknown, data and condition, go back to the definition, draw the figure, and state the problem plainly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: You must prove something about a derived notion but know only its name and a rough picture. What is missing?
options: Nothing is missing; a name and a rough picture are enough to argue from
Only a bigger and more careful picture of the notion drawn on the page
A new axiom for the notion, added next to the existing ones
At least its definition, and better some theorems about it
optionExplain: A name and a vague shape cannot support an argument.
A bigger picture is still only a picture.
Axioms deal only with primitive terms.
Right: the book says to know at least the definition, but it is better to know some theorems too.
questions.explain: An argument about a derived notion needs real knowledge of it. The card next shows what.
questions.rule: Use either the definition of the notion or a theorem about it; if you know only the definition, use that.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: An argument about a derived notion must use its definition or ____ about it.
questions.explain: Axioms mention only primitive terms, so a derived notion enters through its definition or theorems.
questions.rule: Definition or theorem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student knows only the definition of a prime number and nothing else about primes. What does the book's reasoning imply?
options: The student should wait until some theorems are learned before starting
The student has no choice but to use the definition
The student may use the axioms in place of the definition instead
The student can skip the notion altogether and work around it
optionExplain: Waiting is not required; the definition is usable.
Right: if you know just the definition, you are obliged to use it.
Axioms do not mention derived notions.
A needed notion cannot be skipped.
questions.explain: With only the definition, going back to it is the way forward.
questions.rule: No other option means use the definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Another student knows many theorems about primes and has much experience with them. How does the situation change?
options: The definition can no longer be used, since theorems replace it for good
Theorems are guaranteed to solve the problem once they are known
There is a chance of finding a suitable theorem to use
The student no longer needs the notion in order to solve the problem
optionExplain: The definition is still usable.
Nothing guarantees success.
Right: more knowledge of the notion widens the options.
The notion is still involved.
questions.explain: Knowledge of theorems gives you more than the definition.
questions.rule: More knowledge, more options.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: In a geometry problem about the parabola, the axioms alone can supply the facts you need.
questions.explain: The axioms deal with primitive terms only; the parabola needs its definition or theorems.
questions.rule: Derived notions need definitions or theorems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A junior engineer must debug code that uses a library function whose documentation only defines it formally. A colleague knows many of its known behaviours. Who has an edge?
options: The colleague, since known facts may offer a ready tool beyond the bare definition
The junior, since a formal definition is enough to debug any code
Neither of them, since a definition and known behaviours are the same thing
The junior, since known behaviours can mislead where a definition cannot
optionExplain: Right: more known facts give more to use.
A definition suffices only if nothing else is known.
Facts about the notion are not the same as its definition.
Known facts help, they do not mislead by default.
questions.explain: The book says that to solve such a problem you must know at least the definition, but it is better to know some theorems too.
questions.teaches: To solve a problem about a derived notion you must know at least its definition, but it is better to know some theorems as well.
questions.rule: Use either the definition of the notion or a theorem about it; if you know only the definition, use that.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: To find the surface area of a sphere, which definition would you want?
options: The oldest one, since age gives authority
The shortest one, since short is simple
Whichever suggests a method for the area
The first one you meet in a textbook
optionExplain: Age does not decide usefulness.
Brevity does not decide usefulness.
Right: the definition should fit the case.
Order in a book does not decide usefulness.
questions.explain: Fit to the problem decides the choice. The card next shows an example.
questions.rule: List the definitions you know and choose the one that fits the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each item with its description.
pairs: Points at a given distance from a given point
Surface described by a circle revolving about a diameter
questions.explain: The book gives two definitions and says Archimedes chose the second.
questions.rule: Two definitions, one fitted the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A hospital defines readmission either as any return within 30 days or as a return for the same condition within 30 days. Studying one condition, which should it go back to?
options: The one that counts returns for that condition
The one with fewer words, since a short definition is easier to apply
The broader one, since more cases count and the study is then more complete
Whichever definition the first report on the topic happened to use
optionExplain: Right: the definition is chosen to fit the case.
Length is not the criterion.
Broader does not fit a single condition.
Habit is not the criterion.
questions.explain: Choose the definition that fits.
questions.rule: Fit decides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Suppose Archimedes had used the locus definition of the sphere. What would that have suggested?
options: A direct formula for the area, read off from the equal distances
A way to avoid circles entirely and so avoid any approximating step
An exact method with cones, as in the revolving-circle approach
No simple approximation of the surface
optionExplain: No formula follows from it.
Circles still arise.
The cone approximation came from the other definition.
Right: the book says no simple approximation is suggested.
questions.explain: The revolution definition lends itself to approximation; the locus definition does not.
questions.teaches: If the sphere is conceived as the locus of points equally distant from the centre, no simple approximation to its surface is suggested.
questions.rule: List the definitions you know and choose the one that fits the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student says: the two definitions of the sphere describe different solids, so only one can be correct. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; only one definition of a notion is ever valid at a time
Both describe the same sphere; many definitions can be correct
The second one is a theorem about the sphere and not a definition
The first one holds only in a plane and so cannot describe a sphere
optionExplain: Several can hold at once.
Right: the book notes that other definitions are known and many more are possible.
Both are given as definitions.
The first is stated for points in space.
questions.explain: Different definitions of one notion can all be right.
questions.rule: One notion, many definitions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: Choosing among definitions is only possible when you know more than one.
questions.explain: Our reading: with a single known definition there is nothing to choose between.
questions.rule: You need alternatives to choose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A designer estimates paint for a dome by stacking truncated cones, a rotating-polygon approach. Which idea of Archimedes does this echo?
options: Approximating a surface by cubes placed inside it, one layer at a time
Approximating a surface by two cones and several frustums from a rotating polygon
Finding the surface from points at equal distance from a centre
Splitting a curved surface into a mesh of small flat triangles
optionExplain: No cubes appear in the book's account.
Right: Archimedes inscribed a polygon in the circle, revolved it, and got cones and frustums.
That is the locus definition and gives no approximation.
Triangles are not mentioned.
questions.explain: The book says the revolved polygon forms a convex surface of two cones and several frustums, which approximates the sphere.
questions.teaches: Archimedes inscribed a regular polygon with an even number of sides in the circle; revolving it gives two cones and several frustums that approximate the sphere.
questions.rule: List the definitions you know and choose the one that fits the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A colleague presents a proof about convex sets but does not use what convexity means. What should you conclude?
options: The proof is sound, since the topic of convex sets is named at the start
The proof is sound if it is long enough and careful about its steps
The proof is wrong only if its final conclusion turns out to be false
The proof cannot be trusted, since it does not use the notion
optionExplain: Naming the topic is not using it.
Length does not supply the missing step.
A true conclusion does not make an unsupported proof good.
Right: without using the notion, the argument gives no reason to believe the claim.
questions.explain: An argument must use what it is about. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Wait for the moment the argument uses the notion's meaning or a theorem about it; if that moment does not come, distrust it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: While listening, wait for the moment the speaker uses the notion's ____ or a theorem about it.
questions.explain: The book says to wait for the moment someone uses the definition or a theorem.
questions.rule: Listen for use of the definition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A proposal says its zero-downtime design improves resilience, yet does not state what zero-downtime means or use it. By the book's check, what is it?
options: Unconvincing, since the notion is not used
Convincing, since the term zero-downtime appears in the title of the proposal
Convincing, since resilience is a good aim and the design aims at it
Neutral, since the proposal makes no definite claim that could be checked
optionExplain: Right: the moment of using the notion does not come.
Being in the title is not using it.
Good aims do not supply an argument.
A claim is made, so it is not neutral.
questions.explain: No use of the notion means no good argument.
questions.rule: Use of the notion is the test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: An argument that begins with a correct statement of the notion but does not use it later passes the book's check.
questions.explain: The book says that if the solver fails to use the idea in the argument, you cannot know he had any idea at all.
questions.rule: Stating is not using.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A reviewer says: the author wrote the word sphere fifty times, so the argument is substantial. What is wrong?
options: Fifty uses is too few to count as substantial, a hundred would be enough
Sphere is a word that cannot be used in an argument about area
Repeating the word is not using its meaning
Substance comes from the title of a work and not from its steps
optionExplain: Count does not matter.
The word can be used; it just was not.
Right: use means relying on its definition or a theorem.
Substance is in the argument, not the title.
questions.explain: Using a notion is more than naming it.
questions.rule: Look for use, not mention.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A reviewer reads a claim that a fair contract is one both sides would sign freely. She mentally replaces fair contract by that definition inside the argument to test it. Whose rule is this?
options: Descartes's: notice rules that emerge from your own inventing
Hadamard's: avoid defined terms in an argument so that nothing can be misread
Archimedes's: use a revolving polygon to approximate a surface
Pascal's: substitute the defining facts for the defined terms
optionExplain: Descartes described rules arising from practice.
Hadamard stressed the use of definitions in devising arguments.
Archimedes's polygon is about the sphere.
Right: Pascal stated this rule for examining the validity of an argument.
questions.explain: The book says Pascal stated the rule for examining the validity of arguments, and Hadamard stressed the idea in devising an argument.
questions.teaches: Pascal stated the rule of substituting the defining facts for the defined terms to test an argument, and Hadamard stressed that going back to definitions is also important in devising one.
questions.rule: Wait for the moment the argument uses the notion's meaning or a theorem about it; if that moment does not come, distrust it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A seller calls a product revolutionary, certified and premium. What does the book's attitude suggest you ask?
options: Which word sounds the most impressive?
What facts do these words stand for?
How many such words are used?
Who says the words most often?
optionExplain: Sound and impact are not what matters.
Right: the power of a word lies in the facts behind it.
Counting words does not reveal meaning.
Repetition does not supply facts.
questions.explain: The question is about facts behind words. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Look behind a word to the ideas and facts it stands for, not to its sound.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each person with what they look for behind technical terms.
questions.explain: The book pairs each with a way of getting past the words.
questions.rule: Each seeks content behind the term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A memo says the new process is agile. Which question follows the book's tendency?
options: Is agile a modern-sounding word that other firms also use in memos?
Do other teams use the word agile in the same way as ours?
What do we do differently, in terms others can observe?
Can the word agile be made shorter or replaced by a stronger one?
optionExplain: Modernity of sound is not the test.
Common use does not give meaning.
Right: it turns the word into facts.
Length is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Ask what the word stands for in practice.
questions.rule: Facts before words.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: The book advises thinking without words, signs or symbols.
questions.explain: The book says we can hardly use our minds without them; it asks only that we look behind them.
questions.rule: Use words, but look through them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student says: since words have power, repeating a key term loudly strengthens my proof. What is the error?
options: The power comes from the ideas and facts, not from the sound
Words have no power at all, so repeating a term can do nothing
Loudness only helps in speech and has no effect in a written proof
Key terms should not be repeated in a proof, however loudly or often
optionExplain: Right: the power does not reside in the sound.
Words do have power, as the book says.
Sound is not the source of power at all.
Repeating is not forbidden; it just does not add proof.
questions.explain: The power of a word lies in the ideas and facts behind it.
questions.rule: Not the sound.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A village believes that naming a storm will calm it. How does the book regard such belief about words?
options: It should be shared, since words are powerful
It is silly and cannot be understood
It can be understood, but it should not be shared
It is correct for primitive peoples only
optionExplain: The book does not endorse it.
The book allows that it can be understood.
Right: the book says we may understand it but should not share it.
It does not call it correct for anyone.
questions.explain: The book says primitive peoples believe words and symbols have magic power; we may understand such belief but should not share it.
questions.teaches: The book notes that primitive peoples believe words and symbols have magic power; we may understand this belief, but we should not share it.
questions.rule: Look behind a word to the ideas and facts it stands for, not to its sound.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Descartes planned a universal method for solving problems. Which of his works holds more material on solving problems?
options: The unfinished Rules for the Direction of the Mind
His better known Discourse on Method, since fame goes with richer content
Both hold exactly the same amount, since they treat one subject
Neither mentions problem solving, since both deal with philosophy only
optionExplain: Right: the unfinished fragments contain more, and more interesting, material.
It is the better known, but it holds less on this subject.
The amounts are not the same.
Both treat the subject.
questions.explain: The less famous work is the richer one here. The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: Notice the rules you actually use when you invent a solution, and collect them as a method.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Descartes planned to give a ____ method to solve problems, but left his Rules unfinished.
questions.explain: The book says he planned a universal method.
questions.rule: Universal method, unfinished.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A chess coach notices that, as a teenager, she kept winning with a few habits she had not named. Which remark of Descartes does this parallel?
options: He planned a universal method and finished it before he died
He read all earlier authors carefully before he tried to invent anything
He wrote the Discourse after the Rules and so reversed the usual order
He noticed by degrees that, inventing alone, he was using certain rules
optionExplain: He did not finish it.
He tried inventing without reading the author.
That is a fact about order of writing, not a parallel.
Right: both noticed rules inside their own successful practice.
questions.explain: Method can be read out of practice.
questions.rule: Name the rules you already follow.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: The Rules for the Direction of the Mind were published by Descartes himself before his death.
questions.explain: The fragments were found in his manuscripts and printed after his death.
questions.rule: Found in manuscripts, printed afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student says: the Rules are an abandoned fragment, so they contain little on problem solving. What is wrong?
options: The Rules were in fact finished and complete, so they are not a fragment
The fragments contain more, and more interesting, material on solving problems than the better known work
The fragments cover only geometry and say nothing general about method
The Discourse contains nothing at all about problems and their solution
optionExplain: The book says they were left unfinished.
Right: being unfinished does not make them thin on this subject.
No such limit to geometry is stated.
The Discourse is the better known work; the unfinished Rules are the richer source on solving problems.
questions.explain: The unfinished work is richer on problem solving than the Discourse.
questions.rule: Do not judge content by finish.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A chef's well known cookbook sits beside his unfinished notebook, edited after his death, which has more on technique. Which of Descartes's two works is the cookbook like?
options: The Rules, which were written first and were widely read in his lifetime
The Discourse, which was very likely written after the Rules
The Rules, which were printed before his death and are therefore well known
The Discourse, which was left unfinished and printed after his death
optionExplain: The Rules are the notebook-like work.
Right: the better known Discourse was very likely written after the Rules.
The Rules were printed after his death.
The unfinished work is the Rules.
questions.explain: The book says the Discourse was very likely written after the Rules.
questions.teaches: The book says the Discourse on Method was very likely written after the Rules, even though the Rules contain more on problem solving.
questions.rule: Notice the rules you actually use when you invent a solution, and collect them as a method.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which statement best describes the role of emotions in solving a hard problem?
options: They matter little, since problems are purely intellectual
They matter only for beginners
They matter only when the solution is near
They matter, because will power is needed to keep going
optionExplain: The book calls that view a mistake.
Experts need will power for serious problems.
They matter when stuck too.
Right: determination and emotions play an important role.
questions.explain: Problem solving involves the will as well as the mind. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Expect serious problems to need will power, and expect your determination to rise and fall with hope and disappointment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: The book calls solving problems a purely intellectual affair.
questions.explain: The book says it would be a mistake to think so; determination and emotions play an important role.
questions.rule: Emotions and will matter.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Elena's program ran smoothly all morning; then an unexplained crash blocks her chosen approach. What does the book lead you to expect?
options: Her determination wavers, which is a usual response to a blocked way
Her determination rises, since a new challenge appears when a way is blocked
Her determination is unaffected, since will does not depend on outcomes
She has lost the ability to solve the problem, since the crash proves it
optionExplain: Right: when a way followed with confidence is blocked, determination wavers.
Elation comes when a forecast comes true, not when blocked.
Determination fluctuates with outlook.
A dip says nothing about ability.
questions.explain: A blocked way lowers determination.
questions.rule: Setbacks lower will; plan for it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Elena's forecast about the cause of the crash proves right. By the book, she is now ____.
questions.explain: The book says we are elated when our forecast comes true, and determination rises with it.
questions.rule: Mood follows outlook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student says: my determination dropped when I got stuck, so I lack willpower. What does the book suggest?
options: The student is right, and determination should not drop in a good solver
The student should stop at once, since the dip shows the work is hopeless
A drop with disappointment is the normal pattern, not proof of lack of will
Being stuck means the problem is unsolvable and further effort is wasted
optionExplain: The book describes dips as usual.
Stopping does not follow.
Right: determination fluctuates with hope and disappointment.
Being stuck does not mean unsolvable.
questions.explain: Our reading: the book treats the fluctuation as ordinary.
questions.rule: Dips are normal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A job seeker's routine task at work needs only a little sustained effort, while her research problem is serious. How do their needs compare, by the book?
options: Both need equal will power, because the effort is the same in every problem
The routine task needs the most will, since it is dull and repeated
Neither task needs any will power, since skill alone decides the outcome
The routine task may need only lukewarm determination; the serious problem needs far more
optionExplain: The book separates routine from serious.
Routine does not demand the most.
Will is needed for the serious problem.
Right: lukewarm determination may be enough for a routine classroom problem.
questions.explain: The book says lukewarm determination and sleepy consent may be enough for a routine classroom problem.
questions.teaches: Lukewarm determination and sleepy consent to do a little something may be enough for a routine problem in the classroom.
questions.rule: Expect serious problems to need will power, and expect your determination to rise and fall with hope and disappointment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A researcher finds a problem dull and expects little from it. What does the book advise a scientist about taking it up?
options: Take it up and give it full effort, since effort alone makes problems interesting
Do not take it up unless it has some interest
Take it up only if it is easy, since easy problems succeed
Take it up out of duty alone, whatever its interest or promise
optionExplain: Full effort is for great promise.
Right: you do not take up a problem unless it has some interest.
Ease is not the criterion.
Duty alone is the stance the book says does not suit the scientist.
questions.explain: Effort follows interest and promise. The card next shows the scale.
questions.rule: Take up a problem if it has some interest, work seriously if it is instructive, and give your whole self when the promise is great.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Order the levels of effort from least to most as promise grows.
items: Take up a problem because it has some interest
Settle down to serious work because it seems instructive
Throw in your whole personality because the promise is great
questions.explain: The book describes effort rising with interest, instruction and promise.
questions.rule: Interest, instruction, promise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Dan has three side projects: one mildly interesting, one that seems instructive, one that promises a breakthrough. How should he spread his effort?
options: His whole self on all three, since a scientist should hold nothing back
The same moderate effort on all three, so that none is neglected
Some effort, serious work, and his whole self respectively
His whole self on the dullest one, because it needs the most help
optionExplain: That ignores the difference in promise.
That ignores the difference in promise.
Right: determination is apportioned to outlook.
Fairness is not the criterion.
questions.explain: Apportion effort to outlook.
questions.rule: Effort follows promise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: The promise of Dan's breakthrough project collapses after a month. What does the book's rule suggest?
options: Lower the effort to match the new outlook
Keep the whole self in it regardless, since a plan once made is kept
Switch to the dullest project at full effort so the work is not wasted
Stop all work on every project at once until a new promise appears
optionExplain: Right: effort is apportioned to outlook.
That ignores the changed promise.
Effort should follow promise, not dullness.
Stopping everything is not implied.
questions.explain: Our reading: re-judge the outlook as you learn more.
questions.rule: Effort tracks outlook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a scientist should throw his whole personality into every problem.
questions.explain: The book says to apportion determination to outlook; whole-personality effort is for great promise.
questions.rule: Not every problem deserves everything.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A volunteer tells a discouraged teammate: you can undertake without hope and persevere without success. What attitude does the book say this expresses, and does it suit the scientist?
options: A scientist's attitude, which the book endorses as the right one to take
An attitude suited to routine problems only, where little is at stake
An inflexible will, honour and duty; it would not do for the scientist
A mark of lukewarm determination, which the book warns against
optionExplain: The book says it would not do for the scientist.
It is not about routine problems.
Right: the book says this suits a nobleman with a noble cause, not the scientist.
It is the opposite of lukewarm.
questions.explain: The book attributes this saying to an inflexible will, or honour and duty, or a nobleman with a noble cause.
questions.teaches: The saying You can undertake without hope and persevere without success belongs to an inflexible will, honour and duty, or a nobleman with a noble cause; the book says it would not do for the scientist.
questions.rule: Take up a problem if it has some interest, work seriously if it is instructive, and give your whole self when the promise is great.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: You are stuck on a hard proof. Which move does the book recommend?
options: Try to solve first some related problem
Wait for inspiration to arrive before trying anything further
Repeat the same attempt again, with more force and more care
Drop the problem as too hard and take up an easier one for good
optionExplain: Right: if you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some related problem.
Waiting does not give a foothold.
Repeating a blocked way does not help.
Dropping it ignores the advice.
questions.explain: A related problem is the suggested step. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: Do not despise little successes; if the proposed problem resists, solve a related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: The book says to try some related problem first.
questions.rule: A related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A learner cannot play a hard passage of a piece. Which choice follows the book's advice?
options: Replay the hard passage ten more times at full speed
Skip the piece entirely and choose a different piece
Wait until she feels more inspired before touching it again
Practise a simpler, related passage she can play, then return
optionExplain: That repeats the blocked approach.
That gives up the goal.
Waiting does not build a success.
Right: a related problem solved first gives a success and a foothold.
questions.explain: Little successes help.
questions.rule: A related success first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: Refusing to count little successes as worthwhile tends to leave determination without support.
questions.explain: Our reading: because determination follows success and hope, ignoring small successes takes away what sustains it.
questions.rule: Small successes sustain will.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student solves an easier related problem and declares the original solved. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since solving a related problem counts as solving the original
The related problem was a step; the proposed problem remains
The student should have skipped the related problem and stuck to the original
Easier problems cannot help with a hard one and should be avoided
optionExplain: The goal is the proposed problem.
Right: little successes are for progress, not substitutes.
The book recommends the related problem.
The book says to seek little successes.
questions.explain: Our reading: do not confuse a step with the goal.
questions.rule: A step is not the goal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A marathon runner sets a distant target but also small checkpoints. What does the book say about holding to your purpose?
options: Make it as hard as possible, to prove how strong your will is
Stick to it, but do not make it unnecessarily difficult for yourself
Change the purpose at the first setback, since purposes should be flexible
Avoid any purpose that is hard, since hardness wastes effort
optionExplain: The book warns against unnecessary difficulty.
Right: if your purpose is set, you stick to it without making it unnecessarily difficult.
A set purpose is kept.
Hard problems are fine; unnecessary difficulty is not.
questions.explain: The book says that if your purpose is set, you stick to it, but you do not make it unnecessarily difficult for yourself.
questions.teaches: If your purpose is set you stick to it, but you do not make it unnecessarily difficult for yourself.
questions.rule: Do not despise little successes; if the proposed problem resists, solve a related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student keeps making silly errors on a problem. What does the book say is the usual trouble?
options: Poor memory of formulas, which makes every step of the work slip
Lack of intelligence, which no teacher can fully repair
Too little practice with arithmetic and routine procedures
No desire to solve it, or even to understand it properly
optionExplain: Memory is not the diagnosis given.
The book names missing desire, not low intelligence, as the usual trouble behind careless errors.
Practice is not the diagnosis given.
Right: without desire the problem has not been understood.
questions.explain: Desire comes before understanding. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Before helping with the work, stir the student's curiosity and give some desire to solve the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher should first stir up the student's ____, giving some desire to solve the problem.
questions.explain: The book says to stir up curiosity.
questions.rule: Curiosity first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A new employee keeps misreading tickets. By the book's reasoning, what should the manager try first?
options: Find what would make the tickets matter to the employee
Send the employee a full list of past errors, to show how many there are
Add extra drill on the same tickets until they are routine
Reassign the employee to other work that needs less attention
optionExplain: Right: stir the wish to solve before anything else.
Listing errors does not create desire.
Drill does not address missing desire.
That avoids the cause.
questions.explain: Desire first.
questions.rule: Interest before instruction.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If a tutor responds to blunders only with more drill, the missing desire is still unaddressed.
questions.explain: Our reading: drill does not give the student a reason to want to understand.
questions.rule: Drill is not desire.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher decides that a student making silly blunders lacks ability. What does the book offer instead?
options: The book agrees that ability is the cause and nothing else is needed
The book says blunders have no cause that a teacher could find
Missing desire to understand the problem is the usual trouble
The book blames the choice of textbook for most of the blunders
optionExplain: The book names desire.
Blunders do have a cause.
Right: the cause named is lack of desire.
The textbook is not named.
questions.explain: Almost always, the trouble is desire.
questions.rule: Check desire first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A remote tutor has recently joined a student's call. Besides stirring interest, what does the book say the tutor should allow?
options: An immediate quiz, to test what the student has understood so far
A speed target, to raise the sense of urgency from the first minute
A full lecture before any work, so the student has the whole picture
Some time for the student to make up his mind and settle down to the task
optionExplain: No such step is named.
Pressure is not recommended.
A lecture is not named.
Right: the book says to allow time to make up his mind and settle down.
questions.explain: The book says the teacher should also allow time to the student to make up his mind and settle down to his task.
questions.teaches: The teacher should also allow the student some time to make up his mind and settle down to the task.
questions.rule: Before helping with the work, stir the student's curiosity and give some desire to solve the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which problem set best serves the long-run aim of teaching problem solving?
options: Only problems the student can solve at once, so that confidence stays high
Problems that are not too easy, so the student meets some struggle
Only problems far beyond the student, so that effort is at its greatest
Only problems copied from the textbook, so that the practice is standard
optionExplain: No struggle means no practice.
Right: problems not too easy build perseverance.
The book says not too easy, not impossible.
Source is not the point.
questions.explain: Some struggle is needed. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Give students problems that are not too easy, so they practise the struggle for a solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which of these does the book list as lessons of solving problems that are not too easy? Select all that apply.
options: Memorise every formula by heart
Avoid every difficult problem
Persevere through unsuccess
Appreciate small advances
Wait for the essential idea
optionExplain: Memorising is not the lesson.
Avoiding difficulty is the opposite.
Right: perseverance is listed.
Right: small advances count.
Right: patience for the essential idea.
questions.explain: The book lists perseverance, appreciation of small advances, waiting for the idea and concentration when it comes.
questions.rule: Learn to persist.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A language teacher gives only exercises that learners finish in a minute. What does the book's view suggest she add?
options: Some exercises that resist for a while, so learners practise persisting
More of the same easy exercises, so that fluency becomes automatic
Exercises with no answer at all, so that learners must invent one
Exercises given only in the final week, so that they do not disturb the term
optionExplain: Right: not-too-easy problems teach persistence.
More ease adds no struggle.
Impossible tasks teach nothing.
Timing is not the point.
questions.explain: Add some struggle.
questions.rule: Some struggle is needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: A class that only ever sees problems solved at once teaches learners the emotions of the struggle for a solution.
questions.explain: Without struggle there is little chance to become familiar with those emotions.
questions.rule: No struggle, no practice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher says: my pupils get everything right at once, so their problem-solving education is complete. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since getting everything right at once is the best result
They should have been given fewer problems so that none go wrong
They have not met the struggle that educates the will
They need only more speed, since the content is already mastered
optionExplain: Right answers do not show persistence training.
Fewer problems would give less practice.
Right: quick success skips the training in persistence.
Speed is not the aim.
questions.explain: Our reading: easy success hides the lesson.
questions.rule: Struggle trains the will.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A coding bootcamp lets students avoid every hard exercise. What does the book say about a student who does not get to know the emotions of the struggle?
options: The education failed in its most vital point
The education is complete
The education failed only in speed
The education succeeded in its most vital point
optionExplain: Right: the book says it failed in the most vital point.
Not so, according to the book.
Speed is not the point named.
It is the opposite.
questions.explain: The book says that if the student had no opportunity to become familiar with the varying emotions of the struggle, his education failed in the most vital point.
questions.teaches: If a student does not have the chance to become familiar with the varying emotions of the struggle for the solution, his mathematical education failed in its most vital point.
questions.rule: Give students problems that are not too easy, so they practise the struggle for a solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A report card says C plus. What does a teacher who wants to improve the work need in addition?
options: A higher grade, since a grade is the only measure a school keeps
A longer test, so that the grade rests on more answers
A ranking against the class, so the student sees where they stand
A closer description of its good and bad points
optionExplain: A higher grade says nothing about causes.
A longer test gives more grades, but the grade still does not say what is good or bad in the work.
A rank only compares students; a diagnosis describes the good and bad points of one piece of work.
Right: a diagnosis is a closer characterization.
questions.explain: Grades are blunt. The card next explains diagnosis.
questions.rule: Describe a student's work by its good and bad points, not by a grade alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each item with the book's description.
pairs: A closer characterization of good and bad points
Needs a diagnosis, as a physician does
questions.explain: The book uses the medical comparison to explain diagnosis.
questions.rule: Grade is crude; diagnosis is closer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A coach scores a presentation 6 out of 10. Which comment is a diagnosis?
options: Needs to try harder next time, since effort decides the result
Clear structure and slides, but a rushed ending and unchecked numbers
Better than average, but not the best in the group
Good effort overall, and a pleasant manner in delivery
optionExplain: It names no points.
Right: it names good and bad points.
It ranks without detail.
It is general praise.
questions.explain: A diagnosis names the particulars.
questions.rule: Name good and bad points.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: A grade is useless to a teacher, according to the book.
questions.explain: The book says a grade characterizes the work, though crudely.
questions.rule: Crude, not useless.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher writes the word weak on a paper and calls it a diagnosis. What is wrong?
options: It is a diagnosis, since a short word is enough to characterize the work
It gives no closer characterization of what is good or bad
It should be a number, not a word, to be a proper diagnosis
It should list every error, however small, to count as a diagnosis
optionExplain: Brevity is not the point.
Right: a one-word verdict is as crude as a grade.
A number is no better.
Every error is not required.
questions.explain: Diagnosis is closer.
questions.rule: Say what is good and bad.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A code review team wants to improve junior work. By the book, in which respect do they characterize it?
options: By the number of lines written in each piece of work
By how fast the junior types and finishes each task
By how often the junior is praised by teammates in reviews
By how the junior behaves in each of the four phases of solving a problem
optionExplain: Size is not the criterion.
Typing speed is not the criterion.
Praise is not the criterion.
Right: the book characterizes problem-solving efficiency through the four phases.
questions.explain: The book says it is particularly concerned with the student's efficiency in solving problems and uses the distinction of the four phases.
questions.teaches: The book characterizes a student's efficiency in solving problems by their behavior in the four phases of the solution.
questions.rule: Describe a student's work by its good and bad points, not by a grade alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which fault is the opposite of rushing into calculations with no plan?
options: Waiting clumsily for an idea, doing nothing to hasten it
Planning too carefully before doing any work at all
Checking every step of the work again and again
Understanding the problem fully before starting anything
optionExplain: Right: rushing and clumsy waiting are the book's two opposite planning faults.
The book does not call careful planning a fault here.
Checking is a later phase.
That is not a fault.
questions.explain: There are two opposite faults. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Look for incomplete understanding, and for the two opposite planning faults: rushing without a plan or waiting clumsily for an idea.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each fault with the book's description.
pairs: Calculations and constructions without a plan or general idea
Cannot do anything that would hasten the idea
questions.explain: The book links each fault to its behavior.
questions.rule: Each fault has its sign.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Sort each behavior by the planning fault it shows.

items.t: Starts computing before reading the question twice
Stares at the page hoping inspiration arrives
Draws random constructions in the hope one works
Takes no step that could bring an idea closer

questions.explain: Rushing means acting without a plan; clumsy waiting means no action to bring an idea.
questions.rule: Act without plan or wait without action.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: The two planning faults named by the book are the same fault described in two ways.
questions.explain: They are opposite faults: one acts without a plan, the other cannot act to bring an idea.
questions.rule: Opposites, not synonyms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher tells a student who rushes into calculation to wait for the idea to come. What is wrong with this advice?
options: Nothing is wrong, since waiting for an idea works for every student
Rushing is not a fault at all, so no advice is needed
Waiting is the opposite fault; the student needs a plan before acting
The student should rush even more quickly through the calculation
optionExplain: Waiting is itself the other fault.
The book names rushing as a fault.
Right: the cure for rushing is a plan, not clumsy waiting.
More speed is not a cure.
questions.explain: The cure for one fault should not produce the other.
questions.rule: Match advice to the fault.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which is, according to the book, perhaps the most widespread deficiency in solving problems?
options: Carelessness in carrying out the plan, step after step of the work
Waiting for a plan to arrive without doing anything to hasten it
Failing to check the result once an answer has been reached
Incomplete understanding of the problem owing to lack of concentration
optionExplain: That is the most frequent in carrying out, not overall.
That is a planning fault but not named as most widespread.
That is frequent but not named as most widespread.
Right: the book calls incomplete understanding perhaps the most widespread.
questions.explain: The book says incomplete understanding of the problem, owing to lack of concentration, is perhaps the most widespread deficiency.
questions.teaches: The book calls incomplete understanding of the problem, owing to lack of concentration, perhaps the most widespread deficiency in solving problems.
questions.rule: Look for incomplete understanding, and for the two opposite planning faults: rushing without a plan or waiting clumsily for an idea.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student computes that a house is 400 metres tall and moves on. Which fault does this show?
options: Waiting for an idea
Failing to check the result
Misunderstanding the problem
Rushing into calculation
optionExplain: Waiting is a planning fault.
Right: the result was not checked.
Understanding is not the issue shown.
Rushing is a planning fault.
questions.explain: Checking the result is a phase of its own. The card next names the faults.
questions.rule: Watch for carelessness in carrying out the plan and for failure to check the result at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: In carrying out the plan, the most frequent fault is ____.
questions.explain: The book says the most frequent fault is carelessness, a lack of patience in checking each step.
questions.rule: Carelessness.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A technician sends out a bill of two cents for a month of service without a second look. What does the book call this?
options: Lack of any plan, since the technician began at once
Incomplete understanding of the problem at the start of the work
Failure to check the result, even though it is most unlikely
Waiting for the idea, since the bill was sent without thought
optionExplain: A plan is not the issue.
Understanding is not the issue.
Right: the answer was accepted without checking.
Waiting is not the issue.
questions.explain: Check the result.
questions.rule: Check the answer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Sort each behavior by the phase in which the fault arises.

items.t: Skips checking one step out of impatience
Does not check the final answer at all
Throws down the pencil, glad to have an answer
Is not shocked by a wildly unlikely result
Copies a number wrongly and does not recheck
Lacks patience in checking each step

questions.explain: Carelessness belongs to carrying out; the missing check belongs to looking back.
questions.rule: Fault belongs to its phase.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: A student who checks each step carefully is thereby guaranteed to catch an unlikely final result.
questions.explain: Our reading: step checks and a check of the final result are different habits, and the book names both faults separately.
questions.rule: Both checks matter.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student gets an answer, throws down the pencil, and is happy. What else does the book say about such students?
options: They are not shocked by the most unlikely results
They check twice before they hand anything in
They do not reach an answer, since checking takes all their time
They cannot understand the problem even when it is explained
optionExplain: Right: the book says they are not shocked by the most unlikely results.
The behavior shows the opposite.
They do reach an answer.
The problem here is checking, not understanding.
questions.explain: The book says that such a student is glad to get an answer, throws down his pencil, and is not shocked by the most unlikely results.
questions.teaches: Students who fail to check are glad to get an answer, throw down the pencil, and are not shocked by the most unlikely results.
questions.rule: Watch for carelessness in carrying out the plan and for failure to check the result at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher knows a student does not check results. What does the book say may help?
options: Giving a bigger penalty for each error, so the habit is dropped
Moving to a harder topic, so the old habit has no place
Insisting on the questions of the list that suit the fault
Ignoring the fault until it fades with time and maturity
optionExplain: Penalties do not aim at the fault.
A harder topic skips the cause.
Right: a careful diagnosis allows targeted questions.
Ignoring leaves the fault.
questions.explain: Diagnosis comes first, then the questions. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Diagnose the fault first, then insist on the questions of the list that aim at it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: The teacher should diagnose the fault before choosing which questions to insist on.
questions.explain: The book says a careful diagnosis of a fault gives some chance to cure it by insisting on certain questions.
questions.rule: Diagnose, then ask.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Match each fault with a question of the list that fits it. This pairing is our reading.
pairs: What is the unknown? What are the data?
Do you know a related problem?
questions.explain: Our reading: each question aims at a phase where the fault occurs.
questions.rule: Target the phase.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student's real fault is not understanding the problem, but the teacher insists only on checking the result. What is likely?
options: Little benefit, since the question does not aim at the fault
Large benefit, since checking the result helps with every kind of fault
The student now understands the problem, since the check forces it
The fault becomes the teacher's, since the wrong question was asked
optionExplain: Right: our reading is that a question must match the fault.
Checking is aimed at a different phase.
Understanding does not follow.
The fault stays the student's.
questions.explain: Match question to fault.
questions.rule: Diagnosis before treatment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A teacher answers every fault with the same question, whatever phase it belongs to. What does the book's approach say is wrong?
options: A sure cure within a week, as long as the prompts are repeated
No chance at all, since faults are fixed traits of the learner
A cure only if the fault is minor and the learner is young
The questions should be chosen to suit the diagnosed fault
optionExplain: A single question cannot aim at faults in different phases.
Grades are the crude measure that diagnosis improves on.
Nothing in the text asks for a reversal of roles.
Right: the book ties the cure to a careful diagnosis of the fault, then to certain questions of the list.
questions.explain: Diagnosis tells you which question to insist on.
questions.rule: Match the question to the fault.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A driving instructor has diagnosed a learner's fault and begins targeted prompts. What does the book promise about the result?
options: A sure cure within a week
Some chance of a cure, not a certainty
No chance at all
A cure only if the fault is minor
optionExplain: The book does not promise this.
Right: the book says the teacher has some chance to cure it.
The book says there is some chance.
The book does not limit it to minor faults.
questions.explain: The book says that, having made a careful diagnosis, the teacher has some chance to cure the fault by insisting on certain questions.
questions.teaches: The book says a teacher who has made a careful diagnosis has some chance to cure the fault by insisting on certain questions of the list.
questions.rule: Diagnose the fault first, then insist on the questions of the list that aim at it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: You solved a word problem using two of its three numbers. What is the most useful next question?
options: Is my answer a whole number?
Did I use all the data?
Is the problem too long?
Did I finish quickly?
optionExplain: A whole number is not the test.
Right: an unused number suggests something is missing.
Length is irrelevant.
Speed is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Ask what was left out. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask whether you used all the data and the whole condition; an unused item points to a missing element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Complete the pair of checks: did you use all the data, and did you use the whole ____?
questions.explain: The book pairs the data with the condition.
questions.rule: Data and condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A taxi problem gives 8 km at 2 per km, a base fee of 3, and 5 minutes waiting at 1 per minute. A solver gets 19. What does the question reveal?
options: The base fee was not used, so the answer should be higher by 3
The answer is already complete, since the main charge was used
The kilometres were counted twice, so the answer should be lower
The waiting charge was not used, so the answer is probably 24
optionExplain: The base fee is in 19.
19 omits waiting.
There is no double counting.
Right: 3 plus 16 plus 5 is 24.
questions.explain: An unused datum is a clue.
questions.rule: Find the unused datum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If every datum was used, the solution is certainly correct.
questions.explain: Using all the data does not guarantee correctness; it checks completeness of the conception.
questions.rule: Complete is not correct.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A solver finds that datum c was unused and drops it as irrelevant. What does the book suggest instead?
options: Try to bring c into play, since it may be the missing element
Agree that unused data are harmless and carry on with the rest
Stop the search for a solution, since the data do not fit
Replace c with a different number, so that it fits the method
optionExplain: Right: a missing element gives a definite line of inquiry.
Unused may mean missing.
Stopping does not follow.
Changing data changes the problem.
questions.explain: The book says that knowing an element is missing, we try to bring it into play.
questions.rule: An unused datum is a lead.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A reviewer asks whether a proof of a theorem accounted for every condition. For problems to prove, which question matches Did you use all the data?
options: Did you use the conclusion twice in the course of the proof?
Did you draw a figure with all the parts of the theorem on it?
Did you use the whole hypothesis?
Did you name the unknown and write it at the top of the page?
optionExplain: The conclusion is what is to be shown.
A figure is a different step.
Right: the corresponding question for proofs is about the hypothesis.
Naming the unknown is a different step.
questions.explain: The book states the matching question for problems to prove: Did you use the whole hypothesis?
questions.teaches: For problems to prove, the matching question is: Did you use the whole hypothesis?
questions.rule: Ask whether you used all the data and the whole condition; an unused item points to a missing element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student has found the diagonal of one face of a box and is stuck. Which question might move him?
options: Is the box a cube?
Can you draw a bigger box?
How long is the box?
Did you use all the data?
optionExplain: Not required by the problem.
A bigger box changes the problem.
A single length is not the aim.
Right: the face diagonal leaves out an edge.
questions.explain: The question exposes the missing edge. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: When your expression lacks one of the data, build a figure that brings the missing datum in.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: The expression for the face diagonal does not contain the third datum ____.
questions.explain: The face diagonal uses only a and b.
questions.rule: The third edge is missing.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which right triangle brings the missing edge c into play?
options: One whose legs are a and b, with c as the hypotenuse of the triangle
One whose legs are the face diagonal and c, with the box diagonal as hypotenuse
One whose legs are c and a, with b as the hypotenuse of the triangle
One whose three sides are a, b and c, with no hypotenuse at all
optionExplain: That ignores the face diagonal.
Right: the book calls this the decisive right triangle.
That ignores the face diagonal.
A triangle has three sides, not three legs.
questions.explain: The book describes the decisive right triangle as having legs the face diagonal and c, and hypotenuse the desired diagonal.
questions.teaches: The decisive right triangle has legs equal to the face diagonal and the edge c, and its hypotenuse is the desired diagonal of the box.
questions.rule: When your expression lacks one of the data, build a figure that brings the missing datum in.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A box has edges 2, 3 and 6. Using that triangle, how long is the box diagonal?
options: About 9.6, adding 6 to the face diagonal
11, adding all three edges
About 3.6, the face diagonal alone
optionExplain: That adds the lengths instead of squares.
That adds all edges.
Right: face diagonal squared is 13, and 13 plus 36 is 49, so the diagonal is 7.
That is only the face diagonal.
questions.explain: Add the squares and take the root.
questions.rule: Pythagoras twice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If the edge c shrinks to zero, the box diagonal equals the face diagonal.
questions.explain: With c equal to zero the triangle collapses and the hypotenuse equals the face diagonal.
questions.rule: Zero c leaves the face diagonal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A student wiring a rectangular room finds the diagonal of the floor and stops. The teacher only asks whether she used all the data. What does the book say about this hint?
options: The student can scarcely fail to notice that the height is missing
The student must ask many more questions before the missing edge is seen
The hint is too weak to help, since it names no edge
The hint gives away the whole solution, so the student learns nothing
optionExplain: Right: the book says the student can scarcely fail to observe it.
One question is enough here.
The book says it works.
It points, it does not solve.
questions.explain: The book says the student can scarcely fail to observe that the expression does not contain the third datum.
questions.teaches: Once the question is asked, the student can scarcely fail to observe that the face-diagonal expression does not contain the third datum.
questions.rule: When your expression lacks one of the data, build a figure that brings the missing datum in.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A theorem has three conditions, and if any is dropped it becomes false. A proof does not mention the second. What follows?
options: The proof is fine if the conclusion is true
The proof is fine if the other two are used
The proof must be wrong
The theorem is false
optionExplain: A true conclusion does not repair the proof.
Using two of three leaves a gap.
Right: an essential condition went unused.
The theorem is fine; the proof is not.
questions.explain: Each essential part must be used. The card next explains.
questions.rule: If every part of a hypothesis is essential, ask where the proof uses each part; any part left unused means the proof is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: If the proof neglects to use any part of the hypothesis, the proof must be ____.
questions.explain: The book says the proof must be wrong.
questions.rule: Unused essential part, wrong proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A grant rule has three conditions, all needed. A reviewer approves a case citing only two. By the book's checking logic, what is the approval?
options: Flawed, since the third condition is not accounted for
Sound, since two of three conditions are a majority of the conditions
Sound, since the case is strong on the two conditions that were cited
Unknown, since the conditions of a rule cannot be checked one by one
optionExplain: Right: all three are essential.
Majority is not the rule.
Strength does not replace a condition.
Conditions can be checked one by one.
questions.explain: Ask where each condition is used.
questions.rule: Each essential condition must appear.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: If one of the hypothesis parts is redundant, a proof that does not use it is necessarily wrong.
questions.explain: The check rests on every part being essential; a redundant part may go unused.
questions.rule: Redundant parts break the check.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A checker says: the proof uses the first and third parts; two of three is plenty. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since two parts out of three are plenty to carry a proof
The first part should be skipped instead, since it is the weakest
The checker should ignore the third part and keep only the first
If the second part is essential, a proof that skips it is wrong
optionExplain: Two of three is not enough if all are essential.
No part may be skipped.
The third is also required.
Right: every essential part must be used.
questions.explain: Ask where each part is used.
questions.rule: Check each part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A reviewer checks a long, heavy specification document. Why does the book value asking where each part of the hypothesis is used?
options: It makes long arguments shorter, since fewer steps then need to be read
It is effective, instructive, and almost necessary for understanding a long argument
It replaces reading the argument, since the questions cover every step
It proves the argument is true, since every part is then accounted for
optionExplain: It does not shorten.
Right: this is how the book describes it.
It does not replace reading.
It checks, not proves truth.
questions.explain: The book says this sort of checking is effective, instructive and almost necessary for thorough understanding if the argument is long and heavy.
questions.teaches: This sort of checking is effective, instructive, and almost necessary for thorough understanding if the argument is long and heavy.
questions.rule: If every part of a hypothesis is essential, ask where the proof uses each part; any part left unused means the proof is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A solution uses every number in a problem but does not use what a key term means. Is the conception complete?
options: Yes, since every number in the problem was used in the solution
No, since an essential notion has not been taken into account
Yes, since terms are only labels and carry no content of their own
No, since more numbers are needed before the conception is complete
optionExplain: Numbers are not everything.
Right: meaning is part of completeness.
Terms carry meaning.
The data are enough; the notion is missing.
questions.explain: Completeness covers notions as well. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Also ask whether you have taken into account all the essential notions in the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
