questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Have you taken into account all essential ____ involved in the problem?
questions.explain: The book asks about essential notions.
questions.rule: Essential notions count.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A dispute turns on the term reasonable notice. An analysis counts days from the data but does not say what reasonable notice means. What is missing?
options: More data about the number of days that have passed
A shorter analysis that leaves out the term altogether
A different dispute that turns on a different term
The meaning of the essential notion
optionExplain: More days will not supply meaning.
Length is not the issue.
The dispute is as given.
Right: the term itself has not been used.
questions.explain: Use the meaning.
questions.rule: Notions need meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: An incidental term that does not matter to the problem has to be defined for the conception to be complete.
questions.explain: The test concerns essential notions only.
questions.rule: Only essential.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A solver says: I used all the data, so my conception is complete. What is missing from that claim?
options: The essential notions may still be unused
Nothing is missing, since using all the data completes the conception
The solver should have used fewer data, so that the notions come through
Data are not part of a conception, which is made of notions alone
optionExplain: Right: completeness includes notions.
Data are not all.
Fewer data is not the advice.
Data are part.
questions.explain: Check notions too.
questions.rule: Data are not enough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Which two questions does the book add to check how you used an essential notion?
options: Did you name it in a title? Did you draw a figure of it?
Did you prove it correct? Did you try to disprove it as well?
Did you use its meaning or definition? Did you use known theorems about it?
Did you shorten its statement? Did you extend it to more cases?
optionExplain: Naming and drawing are not asked.
Proving is not asked.
Right: both are asked in the book.
Shortening is not asked.
questions.explain: The book asks: How did you use this notion? Did you use its meaning, its definition? Did you use essential facts, known theorems about it?
questions.teaches: To check how you used an essential notion, ask whether you used its meaning or definition and whether you used essential facts or known theorems about it.
questions.rule: Also ask whether you have taken into account all the essential notions in the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A real budgeting question lists many numbers. Must every number be used in the answer?
options: Yes, since every datum in a problem is essential to its answer
Yes, since the question is written down and so must be complete
No, since data do not matter once the main idea is found
Not necessarily, since real problems may include irrelevant or missing data
optionExplain: That holds for perfectly stated problems.
Writing does not make it so.
Data do matter when the problem is well posed.
Right: practical problems are rarely perfectly stated.
questions.explain: The rule has limits. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask use everything only of perfectly stated, reasonable problems; if in doubt, ask whether the condition can be satisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A perfectly stated problem to find has all necessary data and not a single ____ datum.
questions.explain: The book says not a single superfluous datum.
questions.rule: No superfluous datum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A textbook problem gives a train's speed, a distance, and the driver's age. What does the book say about the question Did you use all the data?
options: It must be asked unmodified, since the age is part of the data given
It cannot be asked unmodified, since the problem seems not perfectly stated
It applies only to the age, since the other data are used already
It is meaningless for trains, since trains are not mathematical objects
optionExplain: That holds only for perfectly stated problems.
Right: a superfluous datum signals that the problem is not perfectly stated.
The age is the superfluous one.
Trains are fine.
questions.explain: Check whether the problem is perfect.
questions.rule: Perfect statement first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: A problem asks for a triangle with sides 1, 2 and 5. What should you ask?
options: Did you use all the data in the statement of the triangle problem?
Did you draw a figure of the triangle with its three sides marked?
Is it possible to satisfy the condition?
Did you name the unknown and write down the data of the problem?
optionExplain: The condition cannot be met, so all data cannot be used.
A figure will not help.
Right: 1 plus 2 is less than 5, so no such triangle exists.
Naming does not help.
questions.explain: Check the condition first.
questions.rule: Is it possible?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: True or false: Because a problem comes from a traditional textbook, you can fully rely on it being perfectly stated.
questions.explain: The book says not to rely too much on this and to ask whether the condition can be satisfied when in doubt.
questions.rule: Do not over-trust the textbook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Definition to Did You Use All the Data?
questions.section: Did You Use All the Data?
questions.q: Chess problems are supposed to be perfectly stated. What does the book say a good one has?
options: Only one solution and no superfluous piece
Many solutions and several extra pieces on the board
No solution at all, which is why it is hard to solve
A different solution each time it is set, to keep players alert
optionExplain: Right: this is how the book describes a good chess problem.
That would not be perfect.
A problem needs a solution.
Solutions do not change.
questions.explain: The book says good chess problems are supposed to have but one solution and no superfluous piece, and that practical problems are usually far from perfectly stated.
questions.teaches: Good chess problems are supposed to have only one solution and no superfluous piece, whereas practical problems are usually far from perfectly stated.
questions.rule: Ask use everything only of perfectly stated, reasonable problems; if in doubt, ask whether the condition can be satisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You get a strong hunch about why a problem has stuck. What is the best next move?
options: Act on it as if it were settled, since it feels so strong
Drop it, because a hunch without proof is worthless
Test it, expecting it to be partly right and partly wrong
Wait until someone else confirms it before you think about it
optionExplain: A strong feeling is not evidence; settled belief ends the checking.
Unproven does not mean useless; many hunches hold part of the truth.
Right: a hunch is a starting point to be checked.
Waiting wastes the chance to test it yourself.
questions.explain: A hunch is neither proof nor rubbish; it deserves a test. The card next shows the author's reason.
questions.rule: A guess earns a test: not belief, and not dismissal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: It is foolish to accept a vivid guess as a proven ____, and foolish to disregard it altogether.
questions.explain: The author warns against both mistakes: treating the guess as proven truth, and waving it away.
questions.rule: Neither believe nor bin a vivid guess.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A coach guesses that a swimmer's slow times come from poor turns, after watching many races closely. What does the author's advice suggest?
options: Film the turns and compare them with the best swimmers before changing anything
Rebuild her whole training plan around turns at once, since the guess came from careful watching
Ignore the idea, since nobody has proved turns matter
Ask the swimmer to choose any other cause she likes instead
optionExplain: Right: the guess follows careful study, so it is worth a test.
That treats the guess as proven.
That disregards a guess formed after close attention.
Swapping guesses without testing the first one tests nothing.
questions.explain: The guess comes from attentive observation, so it earns an examination, not action on faith and not dismissal.
questions.rule: A guess earns a test: not belief, and not dismissal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: According to the author, which guesses deserve to be taken seriously?
options: Every guess without exception, because no idea is truly bad and all deserve the same attention as any other
Only guesses that have already been proved
The first guess that comes to mind, whatever the situation
Those that occur after we have attentively considered and understood a problem that interests us
optionExplain: The author does say no idea is bad unless we are uncritical, but he picks out one kind to take seriously.
A proven guess is no longer a guess; the point is to examine unproven ones.
Speed is not the mark; understanding of the problem is.
Right: understanding and genuine interest are the conditions.
questions.explain: The author singles out guesses that follow real understanding of a problem in which we are genuinely interested.
questions.rule: A guess earns a test: not belief, and not dismissal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: a hurried guess about a problem you have not tried to understand deserves the same attention as one made after careful study.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author's reasons apply to guesses that follow understanding and interest, and a hurried guess lacks that basis.
questions.rule: The value of a guess depends on the understanding behind it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: One nurse treats every strong hunch as settled fact; another dismisses every hunch as unproven. In the author's terms, who makes which mistake?
options: The first resembles pedantic people, and the second resembles primitive people
The first resembles primitive people who accept vivid guesses as proven; the second resembles pedantic people who disregard them
Both resemble primitive people, since neither tests the hunch
Neither makes a mistake, since hunches should be left to experts
optionExplain: The labels are reversed: pedantic people disregard guesses.
Right: the author gives exactly these two labels.
The second nurse does not accept anything as proven; she dismisses it.
The author calls both attitudes foolish.
questions.explain: The author names primitive people as accepting vivid guesses as proven truth and pedantic people as disregarding them altogether.
questions.rule: Name the two opposite mistakes, and avoid both.
questions.teaches: The author ties accepting a vivid guess as proven to primitive people and disregarding it altogether to pedantic people.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: having a guess that turns out wrong is worse than having no guess at all.
questions.explain: A wrong guess that is examined can lead on to a better one; having none gives nothing to examine. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: A wrong guess that you examine beats having no guess at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: According to the author, no idea is really bad unless we are ____.
questions.explain: The author places the badness in the uncritical attitude, not in the idea itself.
questions.rule: The fault lies in being uncritical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: An engineer's first theory about a cracked beam proves wrong after a load test. How should she regard the theory?
options: As a mistake that should be hidden in the report
As useful, since testing it ruled out a cause and pointed to a better theory
As evidence that she should not form theories early
As a waste of the testing time that was spent on it, since the theory turned out wrong anyway
optionExplain: Hiding it throws away what the test taught.
Right: a wrong guess that is tested can lead to a better one.
The author says having no idea is what is really bad.
The test produced information that the next theory can use.
questions.explain: A wrong guess is useful when examined, because it leads toward a better one.
questions.rule: A wrong guess that you examine beats having no guess at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which of these does the author count as really bad? Select all that apply.
options: Having no idea at all
A guess that turns out to be wrong
Holding an idea without examining it critically
A guess that is dropped after a fair test refutes it
optionExplain: Right: the author calls this really bad.
Wrong guesses can still lead to better ones.
Right: the author says no idea is bad unless we are uncritical.
Dropping a refuted guess is what critical examination is for.
questions.explain: The author locates the badness in uncritical holding of an idea and in having no idea, not in wrong guesses as such.
questions.rule: Bad: no idea, or an idea held uncritically.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: One student guesses at a puzzle, tests it and fails. Another will not guess for fear of error. By the author, who is better placed?
options: The first, who now has a failed guess to learn from and may find a better one
The second, who has avoided error entirely by never committing to any guess at all
Neither, because a failed guess is the same as none
The second, since an idea untested cannot mislead
optionExplain: Right: the failed test gives information; the second has nothing to examine.
The author counts having no idea at all as the really bad case.
A tested guess leaves behind something to build on.
Untested is not the safe choice; the author prefers a critical, active mind.
questions.explain: The first student has something to examine and build on; the second has no idea at all, which the author counts as really bad.
questions.rule: A wrong guess that you examine beats having no guess at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A scientist's hypothesis is wrong but contains a fragment of the truth. By the author's view of guesses, what chance remains?
options: None, since a wrong hypothesis has to be discarded whole
It must be kept unchanged until it is proved
Examined appropriately, it may still help to extract the whole truth
A second scientist should adopt it as proven, since it already holds part of the truth
optionExplain: The author says such guesses usually contain a fragment of the truth.
Keeping it unexamined is the uncritical attitude he warns about.
Right: the author sees a chance to extract the whole truth by appropriate examination.
A guess is not proven by being shared.
questions.explain: The author says guesses seldom show the whole truth, yet there is a chance to extract it if we examine such a guess appropriately.
questions.rule: Examine the guess to extract what is true in it.
questions.teaches: Although a guess seldom shows the whole truth, there is a chance to extract the whole truth by examining it appropriately.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Your suspicion about a colleague's motive grows stronger every day. What is the greatest danger?
options: You may be proved wrong at the end
You stop noticing signs that point the other way
You will have to confront the colleague sooner
Having a suspicion at all marks you out as a poor judge
optionExplain: Being wrong is not the danger; a fair test would reveal it.
Right: a growing suspicion filters what you see.
Confronting may be fine; the problem is acting on an unexamined belief.
Suspicions are natural; the fault is leaving them unexamined.
questions.explain: A suspicion that is never questioned filters the evidence. The card next tells the author's story of this.
questions.rule: A suspicion is allowed; refusing to examine it is the fault.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Mr. Jones's real mistake was not forming the suspicion but becoming ____ to the signs pointing in the opposite direction.
questions.explain: The author says we cannot blame Jones for the suspicion; the fault was his blindness to the opposite signs.
questions.rule: The suspicion is not the fault; the blindness is.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A manager suspects a new hire leaked a file, since the hire was the last to open it. What follows the author's advice?
options: Treat the hire coldly until the suspicion fades by itself
Drop the matter, because suspecting anyone is unfair
Ask colleagues who also dislike the hire what they think, and treat their agreement as confirmation
List who else had access, and check the access log for signs that point away from the hire
optionExplain: The suspicion is left unexamined, so it can only harden.
The author does not blame the suspicion; he asks for examination.
Gathering agreement for the suspicion looks only one way.
Right: it looks for opposite signs before the suspicion hardens.
questions.explain: The cure is to look for signs against the suspicion as well as for it, before it becomes fixed.
questions.rule: A suspicion is allowed; refusing to examine it is the fault.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Sort each behaviour: does it repeat Mr. Jones's fault, or avoid it?

items.t: Reads every later event as more proof of the original suspicion
Writes down two facts that contradict the suspicion
Refuses to discuss the matter because the mind is made up
Asks a neutral person which signs point the other way
Acts on the suspicion before checking one detail
Holds the suspicion lightly and tests it when time allows

questions.explain: Jones's fault was letting the suspicion grow without examination; each behaviour on the left keeps it from being tested.
questions.rule: Keep a suspicion open to evidence both ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What was the practical cost to Mr. Jones of his unexamined suspicion, in the author's story?
options: He nearly turned the director into a real enemy by behaving stupidly
He lost his post when the director found out
He lost the raise that his colleagues received, which then made him suspect the director
He lost the trust of his colleagues in the office
optionExplain: Right: his behaviour almost made the imagined enmity real.
The story does not say he lost his job.
The raise was already missed before the suspicion formed.
The author names only the near-enmity with the director.
questions.explain: The author notes that Jones behaved so stupidly that he almost succeeded in making a real enemy of Director Brown.
questions.rule: An unexamined suspicion can do real damage.
questions.teaches: Acting on an unexamined suspicion can nearly create the very enmity that was only imagined.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A busy parent has time to examine only a few of her many convictions about a child's school. By the author's concession, what remains sensible?
options: Examine none, since busy people cannot be asked to doubt anything and should keep what they believe
Examine all of them, whatever the time it takes
Examine the few that matter most, and do not let any suspicion grow ineradicable
Choose the most comfortable convictions and keep those firm
optionExplain: The author concedes the limit, yet still says do not do as Jones does.
The author grants that only a few can be examined.
Right: the author grants the time limit but keeps the warning.
That protects the convictions least in need of protection.
questions.explain: The author concedes that a busy man has little time and can examine only a few convictions; he still asks that no suspicion grow ineradicable without examination.
questions.rule: Time is short, but keep each suspicion open to examination.
questions.teaches: The author concedes that busy people can examine only a few convictions, yet asks that no suspicion grow ineradicable unexamined.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: For a fixed length of fence, you suspect a square yard holds most space. What best shows courage with your guess?
options: Keep the idea in mind and see whether it feels right later
Say that squares are probably good, but you cannot be sure
Build the square yard first and see whether it seems big enough compared with other yards
Write: of all rectangles with this fence length, the square has the greatest area
optionExplain: An unstated guess cannot be tested.
This hedges so much that nothing is claimed.
Building proves nothing about all possible yards.
Right: a definite statement can be proved or disproved.
questions.explain: Stating the guess as a clear claim is what makes testing possible. The card next shows the author's term for it.
questions.rule: Say the guess as a definite claim, and then you have something to prove or disprove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: After stating the guess, the problem to find becomes a problem to ____.
questions.explain: A stated guess is a claim; the work becomes to prove or disprove it.
questions.rule: A stated guess turns finding into proving.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A baker suspects that the oven's left side bakes hotter. Which statement turns this into a problem to prove?
options: Ovens are sometimes uneven, in a way that matters
Loaves on the left shelf finish browning before loaves on the right shelf when baked together
Find out which side of the oven is best
The left side is the better one for baking bread, so it should always be preferred for loaves
optionExplain: This is too vague to prove or disprove.
Right: it is definite and can be shown true or false.
This is still a problem to find, not a claim.
This calls the left side better without saying how to check it.
questions.explain: A definite claim can be proved or disproved; a general remark or a question cannot.
questions.rule: Say the guess as a definite claim, and then you have something to prove or disprove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which of these is a problem to find, and which a problem to prove? Pick the pair that is correctly labelled.
options: Find the largest field for 100 m of fence (prove); show the square field is the largest (find)
Both are problems to find, since both mention fields
Find the largest field for 100 m of fence (find); show the square field is the largest (prove)
Both are problems to prove, since both involve fences
optionExplain: The labels are swapped.
The second already states a claim.
Right: the first asks for an unknown, the second states a theorem to establish.
The first asks for an unknown to be found.
questions.explain: A problem to find asks for an unknown; a problem to prove states a claim and asks if it holds.
questions.rule: Say the guess as a definite claim, and then you have something to prove or disprove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: once the guess is written as a definite statement, the author regards the problem as solved.
questions.explain: The author says that, after formulating the guess, we have to prove or disprove it; stating it is the start of the work.
questions.rule: Stating is a start, not a finish.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: An analyst states her guess as a definite claim, but knows no similar claim ever settled. By the author, what should she expect?
options: A tougher task, because no solved similar problem is there to guide her
An easier task, since a definite claim is already half proved once it has been written down
No task at all, since stating the claim settles the matter
An impossible task, so she should drop the claim
optionExplain: Right: the author says the task may be pretty tough without a similar solved problem.
Stating a claim does not prove any part of it.
A stated guess still has to be proved or disproved.
The author calls it tough, not impossible, and suggests a related problem.
questions.explain: The author says that if we know no similar problem solved before, our task may be pretty tough, and he then turns to a related problem.
questions.rule: A stated claim still needs work, and the work is harder without a solved model.
questions.teaches: If we know no similar problem that has been solved, the task of proving the stated guess may be pretty tough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You cannot prove that a method works for every kind of case. Which is the best next move?
options: Announce that the method works, since you could not find a failure
Give up on the method, since the full proof is out of reach
Try to prove it for a narrower group of cases, which is easier
Rewrite the claim so that it says nothing definite
optionExplain: Not finding failures is not a proof.
A part may still be provable and useful.
Right: a part or weaker version is easier and builds toward the whole.
A claim with no content cannot be disproved but also teaches nothing.
questions.explain: A more accessible part is a stepping stone. The card next shows the author's own use of it.
questions.rule: When the whole claim is out of reach, prove a weaker part of it first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: If the square is best among all quadrilaterals, it must also be best among ____.
questions.explain: The author notes that the square would be privileged among rectangles too, giving a weaker, more accessible theorem.
questions.rule: Special cases of a claim are easier to test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You suspect that a tax rule is fair for all households. Which weaker claim is a sensible first test?
options: The rule is fair for households with the same size and the same income
The rule is fair for households that like it
The rule is fair for all households, or at least for nearly all of them, which is the full claim again
The rule is probably fair, because it was fairly designed
optionExplain: Right: it keeps the idea but narrows the cases, so it is easier.
That narrows by opinion and does not reduce the difficulty of the claim.
That is hardly easier than the original claim.
A statement of hope is not a weaker theorem.
questions.explain: A weaker version holds the same idea over a smaller range, so it is nearer to proof.
questions.rule: When the whole claim is out of reach, prove a weaker part of it first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: proving the claim for rectangles alone would prove that the square has the greatest area among all quadrilaterals.
questions.explain: The rectangle theorem is weaker; the author says we have not solved the problem yet, though progress has been made.
questions.rule: A part is not the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which question from the author's list prompts the move to a weaker part of the problem?
options: Can you check the result?
What is the unknown?
Have you seen it before?
Could you solve a part of the problem?
optionExplain: That question comes after a result has been reached.
That question helps to understand the problem, not to cut it down.
That asks for memory of an earlier problem, not a smaller one.
Right: the author asks it directly before turning to rectangles.
questions.explain: The author asks Could you solve a part of the problem? before settling on the rectangle theorem.
questions.rule: Ask: could you solve a part of the problem?
questions.teaches: The author prompts the move to a weaker part with the question: Could you solve a part of the problem?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student cannot prove a recipe scales to any batch size, so she tests doubling and halving only. What has she gained?
options: A full proof, since doubling and halving cover every size
A weaker, easier result that suggests how the general claim may be approached
Nothing, because a result that is not general is worthless and cannot count as progress at all
A disproof of the general claim, since it was not tested at all sizes
optionExplain: Two sizes are not every size.
Right: a part of the problem is solved, but not the whole.
The author counts a part as progress.
A partial test cannot disprove a claim that fits the cases tested.
questions.explain: The author says that facing obvious guesses squarely brought progress although the problem was not yet solved; a tested part is progress, not the whole proof.
questions.rule: A proved part is progress, and the original problem stays open.
questions.teaches: The author notes that we can make some progress just by facing our rather obvious guesses squarely, even before the problem is solved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A rectangle has sides 3 and 7. A square has the same perimeter. Which has the larger area?
options: The rectangle, with area 21 against 16
Neither; both areas are 21 because the perimeters match
The rectangle, with area 21 against 20
The square, with area 25 against 21
optionExplain: Sixteen comes from a side of 4; the square's side is 5.
Equal perimeter does not mean equal area.
Twenty is the perimeter, not the square's area.
Right: the square has side 5, so its area is 25.
questions.explain: Perimeter 20 gives the square side 5 and area 25, against 3 times 7, which is 21. The card next shows why this always happens.
questions.rule: The square beats the rectangle unless the rectangle is already a square.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Put the steps of the book's algebra in order.
items: Write the rectangle's area as ab and perimeter as 2a+2b
Find the side of the square with that perimeter: (a+b)/2
State the claim that its area, ((a+b)/2) squared, exceeds ab
Multiply out to get a squared + 2ab + b squared > 4ab
Rearrange to (a-b) squared > 0 and check it
questions.explain: Each step follows from the one before: name the sizes, build the square, state the claim, expand, then reduce to something checkable.
questions.rule: Name, build, state, expand, reduce.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A rectangle has sides 12 and 8. What are its area and that of the square with the same perimeter?
options: 96 and 96
optionExplain: This takes the square's side as 12, the longer side, instead of 10.
Right: the perimeter is 40, so the square has side 10 and area 100.
This takes the square's side as 20, half the perimeter, instead of a quarter.
This assumes that equal perimeters give equal areas.
questions.explain: The square's side is a quarter of the perimeter, 40 divided by 4, which is 10; 10 times 10 is 100, and 12 times 8 is 96. The gap is 4, matching (12-8) squared over 4.
questions.rule: Square side = perimeter divided by 4.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: for a rectangle with equal sides, such as 5 and 5, the strict inequality (a-b) squared > 0 still holds.
questions.explain: With a = b the expression (a-b) squared is 0, so the strict inequality fails; the two areas are equal, both 25.
questions.rule: Equality occurs exactly when a = b.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student argues: the claim reduces to (a-b) squared > 0, so every rectangle is beaten by its square. Which correction is needed?
options: The claim should compare perimeters, not areas
The square's side should be a+b, not (a+b)/2
A square rectangle (a = b) is not beaten; it ties with its square
The reduction is wrong; the claim needs a cubic expression, because areas involve three factors
optionExplain: Both shapes share one perimeter, so areas are what differ.
A side of a+b would give a perimeter twice too large.
Right: the reduced inequality holds only when a differs from b.
The reduction to a squared difference is valid.
questions.explain: The reduced form is greater than zero unless a equals b, and then the rectangle already is a square.
questions.rule: Check the edge case where the sides are equal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: To show a squared + b squared is at least 2ab for any a and b, which route follows the book's pattern?
options: Rewrite it as a squared - 2ab + b squared being at least 0, that is (a-b) squared at least 0, which holds
Try a = 3 and b = 7, and conclude from that one pair that it holds for all numbers a and b, since it checks out
Assume it is true and derive 0 = 0, then stop
Compare it with the perimeter of a rectangle
optionExplain: Right: each rewrite is an equivalent form, so the truth of the last carries back to the first.
One pair of numbers tests the claim; it does not prove it.
Deriving something true from the claim does not run backward unless each step reverses.
Perimeter has no role in this inequality.
questions.explain: The book's route turns the claim into equivalent forms until one is plainly true. Because each form is equivalent, the final truth proves the first.
questions.rule: Rewrite by equivalent steps until the form is obviously true.
questions.teaches: Each rewrite must give an equivalent form, so that the truth of the last, simplest inequality carries back to the original claim.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A crossword clue means begin again and the answer has six letters. You suspect it starts with RE. What should you do first?
options: Fill RE into the grid in ink and move on
Ignore the guess, since a clue needs a full proof before any letter can be written in the grid
Write RE and four blanks, and check the R against a crossing word
Count the vowels in the alphabet before trying anything
optionExplain: That treats the guess as settled without any check.
A tentative guess is worth testing; it does not need a proof.
Right: spell out the pattern, then test it against other evidence.
That does not use the clue or the grid.
questions.explain: Writing the guess as a pattern shows what it implies and where it can be checked. The card next shows the author's two guesses.
questions.rule: Spell out what the guess means, then test it against something else.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's example, the first guess was that the word starts with ____ because the clue stresses repetition.
questions.explain: The clue's again suggests repetition, so the author guesses the word starts with RE.
questions.rule: Turn a hint into a concrete pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A clue says: level, whichever way you read it. The answer has five letters and starts with T. Which pattern follows the author's method?
options: T at both ends, and the second letter equal to the fourth
T at both ends, and the second letter equal to the third
T at the start only, with four free letters, because the clue says nothing about the ending
T in the middle and every other letter free
optionExplain: Right: reading the same both ways pairs the letters from the two ends.
The third letter pairs with itself; the second pairs with the fourth.
That ignores what the clue's hint implies.
The clue says nothing that puts T in the middle.
questions.explain: A word that reads the same both ways has its letters in mirror pairs: first and last, second and fourth, with the middle one free.
questions.rule: Spell out what the guess means, then test it against something else.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: if the crossing word cannot start with R, the guess that the word starts with RE is supported.
questions.explain: A crossing word that cannot take R is a reason against the guess, so the guess is in doubt.
questions.rule: A check can count against the guess.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's crossword, when does he come back to the original word after checking the R in the crossing word?
options: Only when the R is proved correct beyond doubt
Only after every other word in the grid is solved and all the crossing letters are known
Only when the crossing word has been rejected
When the R is verified, or at least no reason against it is found
optionExplain: The author also allows returning when no reason against it appears.
He returns after the one check; he does not wait for the whole grid.
A rejected crossing word would count against the guess, not for it.
Right: failing to find a reason against it is enough to come back.
questions.explain: The author says that if we succeed in verifying the R, or at least find no reason against it, we come back to the original word.
questions.rule: A guess survives a check if nothing speaks against it.
questions.teaches: We go back to the original word if the check verifies the guess, or at least finds no reason against it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A mechanic suspects a dead battery and asks what that would imply for the dashboard lights. By the author's method, what is she doing?
options: Treating the guess as proved because it explains one sign
Spelling out a consequence of the guess so that she can check it against another sign
Replacing the guess with a second guess about the starter, then testing nothing about the first one
Waiting for the engine to start by itself again
optionExplain: Explaining one sign does not prove the guess.
Right: dim or dead lights would support the guess, bright lights would count against it.
She is testing the first guess, not replacing it.
Waiting tests nothing.
questions.explain: The author writes down what the guess would look like (the RE pattern) and checks it; the mechanic does the same with the lights. The author calls his second guess, reading both ways, less obvious, yet still worth facing.
questions.rule: Face even a less obvious guess by writing out what it implies.
questions.teaches: The author calls the second guess, that the word reads both ways, a less obvious guess, and still faces it by writing out what it means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You must compare six measurements of a shape one after another. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Picture the shape in your mind and go through the numbers
Sketch the shape and mark every measurement on it
Memorise the six measurements in order and work from them
Wait until you meet a similar problem before starting
optionExplain: You can hold only a few details in imagination at once.
Right: on paper all the details are present together.
Memory is exactly what the sketch spares you.
Waiting does not help with this one.
questions.explain: A sketch keeps all details in sight. The card next gives the author's reason.
questions.rule: Put many details on paper so that none depends on memory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A detail pictured in our imagination may be forgotten, but a detail traced on ____ remains.
questions.explain: The author contrasts a figure in the mind, whose details can fade, with one on paper, which stays.
questions.rule: What is on paper stays.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student examines a triangle, an inscribed circle, and three tangent points, one detail at a time. What should she do?
options: Imagine it, since drawing is for beginners
Draw only the triangle and keep the rest in her head
Skip the figure, because the algebra will carry the proof and the figure only repeats it
Draw the figure, since many details have to be examined in turn
optionExplain: The author ties drawing to the number of details, not to skill.
Details left in the head can be forgotten.
The figure helps to see the connections the algebra needs.
Right: this is the author's condition for drawing rather than imagining.
questions.explain: With many details to examine in turn, the figure on paper holds them all together.
questions.rule: Put many details on paper so that none depends on memory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: the author holds that a figure should be drawn on paper in every problem, even when a single detail is in question.
questions.explain: The author says that on certain occasions it may be desirable to imagine the figure without drawing it. Drawing becomes desirable when various details are examined one after the other.
questions.rule: Draw when details are many.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Besides holding all details together, what else does a figure on paper do for the solver, according to the author?
options: It reminds us of our previous remarks and saves the trouble of recollecting them
It proves the points we have noticed
It removes the need to reread the problem, since everything about it is now drawn
It shows the answer once all details are marked
optionExplain: Right: coming back to a traced detail brings back earlier thoughts.
A figure is a help, not proof.
Nothing in the text says that.
A figure organises details; it does not give the answer.
questions.explain: The author says a traced detail, when we come back to it, reminds us of previous remarks and saves recollection effort.
questions.rule: A figure also serves as a record of your earlier thinking.
questions.teaches: A detail traced on paper reminds us on our return of our previous remarks, and saves the trouble of recollecting them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A project manager has twelve tasks with dependencies. By the author's two reasons for figures, what does a diagram help with here?
options: Nothing, because figures belong only to geometry
Only the arithmetic, not the structure of the tasks
It helps with a problem that is not geometric, by showing all the links at once
It replaces the task list, which can then be discarded once the diagram has been drawn
optionExplain: The author says figures help with problems that have nothing geometric at the outset.
Seeing structure is the main gain.
Right: figures help in all sorts of problems, not only geometric ones.
Nothing in the text suggests a figure replaces the facts.
questions.explain: The author gives two good reasons to consider figures: geometric problems need them, and they are an important help for all sorts of problems with nothing geometric at the outset.
questions.rule: Figures help beyond geometry too.
questions.teaches: The author names two reasons to use figures: they are the object of geometric problems, and an important help in problems that are not geometric.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A construction problem gives you a base, an angle and a height. How should you begin?
options: Calculate the answer first by any method available, then draw it at the end as a record
Draw only the given base and wait for inspiration
Look for a formula before drawing anything
Draw a figure that includes the unknown triangle together with the base, angle and height
optionExplain: The figure is a means to find the answer.
The unknown and the other data belong in the figure.
A formula may help later; the author starts with the figure.
Right: put unknown and data together as the condition says.
questions.explain: The figure includes the unknown along with the data. The card next says how to use it.
questions.rule: Put unknown and data in one figure, study the parts, then see the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Put the author's steps for a construction problem in order.
items: Draw a figure with the unknown and the data as the condition prescribes
Consider each datum and each part of the condition separately
Reunite the parts and see the condition as a whole
questions.explain: The author separates the parts to understand each, then recombines them to see the whole condition.
questions.rule: Assemble, separate, recombine.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A problem gives two sides and the angle between them, and asks for the triangle. What does the first figure contain?
options: Only the third side, since it is the unknown
A triangle with the two given sides, the given angle between them, and the unknown third side
Two separate segments with no angle between them
A circle with the sides as radii
optionExplain: The data must be in the figure as well.
Right: unknown and data arranged as the condition prescribes.
The condition fixes the angle between them.
Nothing in the condition mentions a circle.
questions.explain: The figure shows the unknown and every datum in the relation the condition requires.
questions.rule: Put unknown and data in one figure, study the parts, then see the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which describes the purpose of looking at each datum separately and then together?
options: To check which datum is wrong
To shorten the problem by dropping the least useful datum before trying to see the whole
To understand each element, then to see the connections the problem requires
To replace the figure with a list of numbers
optionExplain: The data are given as correct.
The author keeps all parts and recombines them.
Right: separate study first, then the whole condition.
The figure stays; it holds the parts together.
questions.explain: Parts first, then whole: the figure holds the parts so that they can be recombined.
questions.rule: Put unknown and data in one figure, study the parts, then see the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: drawing the figure of a construction problem shows that a solution exists.
questions.explain: Before the problem is solved, it stays doubtful whether the figure can be drawn at all; the figure is a way to examine the problem.
questions.rule: The figure examines; it does not guarantee.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A carpenter must fit a shelf into an alcove given its width, depth and a sloping ceiling. What follows the author's method?
options: Sketch the alcove with the shelf in place, look at each measurement alone, then at all of them together
Order the wood first, since the sketch can wait until the shelf has actually been built
Measure the width only, because the others follow from it
Sketch only the shelf and leave the alcove blank
optionExplain: Right: the same assemble, separate, recombine method.
The sketch helps decide what to order.
Each datum and part of the condition is considered.
Unknown and data belong together in the figure.
questions.explain: The author's method for construction applies to this fitting problem: one figure, parts first, then the whole. He adds that the reunited view tries to see simultaneously the various connections required.
questions.rule: Study the parts, then see the connections together.
questions.teaches: Having separated the parts, we reunite them and try to see simultaneously the various connections that the problem requires.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: To find a point equally far from three towns, you sketch the towns and a point O supposed to be that far. Is this legitimate?
options: No, because it assumes the answer that you are trying to find, which is circular reasoning
Yes, and it proves that such a point exists
Yes, as a supposition to examine, provided you do not treat O as certain to exist
No, because a figure must show only what is already known
optionExplain: It assumes only a possibility, not a result.
A sketch proves nothing.
Right: it is a possibility examined without commitment.
The unknown is part of the figure.
questions.explain: A hypothetical figure supposes the condition met without committing to it. The card next gives the author's analogy.
questions.rule: Suppose the condition satisfied, draw it, and keep the supposition open.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author warns against confusing mere ____ with certainty when drawing the hypothetical figure.
questions.explain: The figure shows a possible object satisfying the condition; it does not show that such an object exists.
questions.rule: Possibility is not certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: To find a circle that touches two crossing lines and passes through a given point, which first step follows the author?
options: Sketch the lines and point, and draw a circle supposed to touch both and pass through the point
Wait until a circle is found by other means before drawing any figure, so as not to assume it
Draw only the lines and the point, with no circle
Argue that no circle can exist before drawing one
optionExplain: Right: a hypothetical figure with the condition supposed satisfied.
Then the figure could never help to find it.
The unknown should appear in the figure.
That decides the question without examining it.
questions.explain: The author's advice is to draw the unknown in place, as if the condition were satisfied, and examine what follows.
questions.rule: Suppose the condition satisfied, draw it, and keep the supposition open.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which situation matches the judge's attitude in the author's comparison?
options: A teacher treats the student as guilty and looks only for proof
A teacher ignores the possibility of copying to avoid unfairness
A teacher asks the student to confess before looking at the work
A teacher asks what the data would imply if a student had copied, while staying open to the opposite
optionExplain: That is commitment, not examination.
A judge must still consider the hypothesis.
That presumes the result.
Right: considering a hypothesis without committing to it.
questions.explain: A judge considers the hypothesis of guilt in questioning the defendant but postpones judgment until the examination yields a result.
questions.rule: Suppose the condition satisfied, draw it, and keep the supposition open.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author connects the hypothetical figure with an ancient recommendation. Whom does he attribute it to?
options: Descartes, who first proposed it for algebra as a rule for finding unknown quantities in equations
The Greek geometers, in a short phrase of Pappus: assume what is required to be done as already done
Euclid, in the opening of his book of proofs
Leibnitz, as part of his system of heuristic
optionExplain: Descartes appears in the entry on heuristic, not here.
Right: he traces the method back to the Greeks and to Pappus.
The text names Pappus.
The text names Pappus here.
questions.explain: The author says the method of starting with a sketch that supposes the condition satisfied goes back to the Greek geometers and is hinted at by Pappus.
questions.rule: The method is old: assume the thing done.
questions.teaches: The method of drawing a hypothetical figure goes back to Greek geometers, hinted at by Pappus: assume what is required to be done as already done.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A planner wants a delivery schedule that meets every customer's deadline. In the author's general form, what is a first step?
options: Collect more deadlines until a solution appears from the data by itself without being supposed
Examine the hypothetical situation in which every deadline is supposed to be met
Declare the schedule impossible without drawing anything
Fix the first delivery and ignore the others for now
optionExplain: More data alone does not examine the supposed situation.
Right: the recommendation extends to all problems to find.
That settles the question without examination.
The hypothetical situation supposes the whole condition satisfied.
questions.explain: The author states the general form: examine the hypothetical situation in which the condition of the problem is supposed to be fully satisfied, for all problems to find.
questions.rule: For any problem to find, examine the situation where the condition is met.
questions.teaches: The recommendation is not limited to geometric constructions: it extends to all problems to find, as examining the situation in which the condition is fully satisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: once the hypothetical figure is drawn, the problem is known to have a solution.
questions.explain: The figure only supposes the condition satisfied; whether it can be satisfied is settled only by the definitive solution.
questions.rule: The figure supposes; the solution decides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You sketch a triangle by hand for a proof. The angle that should be arbitrary looks like a right angle. What is the safest view?
options: Treat it as right-angled, since the drawing shows so and the figure is part of the problem
Redraw it with instruments until it is exact
Abandon the figure, since it cannot be trusted
Do not rely on how it looks; base the argument on what the problem states
optionExplain: The look of a drawing is not a given of the problem.
Exactness does not remove the risk of a suggestive shape.
A figure remains a useful help.
Right: the logical connections are the basis.
questions.explain: The drawing helps, but conclusions rest on the stated conditions. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Draw quickly and carefully by hand, and base the argument on logic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author says the figure is a help, but by no means the basis of our conclusions; the logical ____ constitute the real basis.
questions.explain: The real basis of a conclusion is the logical connections, not the look of the picture.
questions.rule: Logic is the base; the figure is a help.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student is short of time. Which figure follows the author's advice for a reasoning exercise?
options: A neat free-hand sketch, with straight lines straight and circles round
A scrawl, since only the logic matters
An exact instrument drawing of every case
No figure at all, because figures can mislead and logic is the only safe basis for a proof
optionExplain: Right: careful free-hand is usually good enough and much quicker.
The figure should not look absurd.
That costs time that reasoning does not require.
The author keeps figures and guards against their dangers.
questions.explain: Care without instruments is the author's balance for reasoning.
questions.rule: Draw quickly and carefully by hand, and base the argument on logic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: when an inaccurate figure suggests a false conclusion, the author advises protecting yourself by varying the figure.
questions.explain: The author calls the danger not great and says we protect ourselves especially by varying the figure, and by resting on the logical connections.
questions.rule: Vary the figure to test what it suggests.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Who, according to the author, should construct many figures as exactly as possible?
options: The advanced mathematician, as proof of a theorem
Everyone, in every problem, without exception, because exact figures are always the best basis
The beginner, to acquire a good experimental basis
Nobody, because exactness has no value
optionExplain: Exact figures may suggest theorems; they are not proofs.
He says free-hand figures usually suffice for reasoning.
Right: exact figures give beginners experience, and may suggest theorems to advanced readers.
He gives exact figures a role, like exact measurement in physics.
questions.explain: The author says the beginner should construct many figures as exactly as he can to gain an experimental basis; exact figures may suggest theorems even to the advanced.
questions.rule: Exactness trains the eye; reasoning needs only careful figures.
questions.teaches: Beginners should construct many figures as exactly as they can, to gain an experimental basis, and exact figures may also suggest theorems to the advanced.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A coder sketches a data-flow diagram by hand to reason about a bug. The diagram's boxes are uneven. What is the right attitude?
options: Redraw it with a tool before reasoning, since the boxes are uneven and could confuse the reader
Distrust the diagram altogether and read only the code
Treat the drawn layout as evidence of how the code runs
Use it for reasoning, but rely on the actual connections in the code
optionExplain: Neatness is not what carries the reasoning.
The diagram still helps to organise the reasoning.
A layout is a picture, not a fact about the program.
Right: the connections, not the drawing, are the basis.
questions.explain: The author's view carries over: a quick careful sketch helps, but it is the logical connections that settle the matter. He adds that certain paradoxes exploit a figure's intentional inaccuracy.
questions.rule: Trust the connections, not the drawing.
questions.teaches: Some well-known paradoxes exploit cleverly the intentional inaccuracy of a figure, which shows that the figure is not the basis of conclusions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You must draw two angles so that one is three times the other. Which start is easier?
options: Choose the big angle freely, then find the small one by trisecting
Choose the small angle freely, then make the big one three times as large
Draw both at random and measure the ratio afterwards
Draw them equal and adjust later by eye until the larger looks about three times the smaller
optionExplain: Trisecting an arbitrary angle is the hard direction.
Right: multiplying is easy to construct.
The relation must hold by construction.
Adjusting later does not help to get the ratio exact.
questions.explain: Starting from the part that makes the other easy to build is the point. The card next gives the author's example.
questions.rule: Start with the part that makes the rest easy to construct.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's example, you start from a fairly small angle beta and construct alpha, which equals ____ times beta.
questions.explain: The required relation is alpha equals three times beta; beta is chosen first.
questions.rule: Choose the free part first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A poster needs a logo exactly three times as wide as the slogan, which is set at 12 cm. How wide is the logo?
options: 4 cm
15 cm
36 cm
24 cm
optionExplain: This divides by 3 instead of multiplying.
This adds 3 to 12 instead of multiplying.
Right: build the relation from the part you fix first, 3 times 12.
This multiplies by 2; the relation is three times.
questions.explain: Fixing the slogan at 12 cm and multiplying by 3 gives 36 cm, with the relation true by construction.
questions.rule: Fix the free part, then build the related part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: building the figure in a different order from the problem's wording invalidates the figure.
questions.explain: The order of construction is unimportant; what matters is that the elements finally stand in the required relations.
questions.rule: Only the final relations matter.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: When the figure is finished, which of these must hold?
options: The elements stand in the relations that the problem requires
The elements were drawn in exactly the order in which the problem lists them one after another
The first element drawn is the unknown
The figure was drawn with instruments rather than free-hand
optionExplain: Right: the required relations are what counts.
The author says the order is unimportant.
Nothing requires the unknown to come first.
Nothing requires instruments.
questions.explain: The author separates what matters, the relations among the elements, from what does not, the order of construction.
questions.rule: Relations matter; order does not.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A pupil draws angles with alpha equal to three times beta, using only ruler and compasses, starting from an arbitrary alpha. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; any starting point works equally well with any tools
Alpha must be drawn last, whatever the tools
She cannot construct beta from an arbitrary alpha with those tools; she should start from beta
Beta must be a right angle for the relation to hold, because three right angles fill a circle
optionExplain: The convenient order matters when the tools limit what can be built.
No rule fixes alpha as last; the tools decide the convenient order.
Right: tripling is easy to construct; trisecting is not.
Beta only needs to be a fairly small, otherwise arbitrary angle.
questions.explain: The author notes that, starting from an arbitrary alpha, one cannot construct beta with ruler and compasses, so one chooses beta first.
questions.rule: Pick the order your tools can follow.
questions.teaches: Starting from an arbitrary alpha, you cannot construct beta with ruler and compasses, so beta is chosen first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You need a triangle to stand for a general triangle in a proof. Which sketch is the best choice?
options: One with three well-separated angles, none of them a right angle
An equilateral triangle, since it is the most symmetric
A right-angled triangle, since it is easiest to measure
An isosceles triangle, since it is easiest to draw and its equal sides make it look typical
optionExplain: Right: no accidental equality or right angle.
Symmetry adds relations the problem does not require.
A right angle is a special property.
Equal sides are a special property.
questions.explain: A general triangle must not suggest special properties. The card next shows the author's candidate.
questions.rule: Draw the general triangle as neither right-angled nor isosceles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: For a general triangle the author suggests angles 45, 60 and ____ degrees.
questions.explain: These three angles sum to 180 degrees and are far from equal and from a right angle.
questions.rule: Pick a triangle that is neither isosceles nor right-angled.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which triangle's angles are the best choice to stand for a general triangle?
options: 40, 70 and 70 degrees
30, 60 and 90 degrees
50, 60 and 70 degrees
45, 60 and 75 degrees
optionExplain: Two equal angles make it isosceles.
It has a right angle.
It is fine, but its smallest gap is 10 degrees, so it is closer to a special shape.
Right: all gaps between angles, and from a right angle, are 15 degrees.
questions.explain: The 45, 60, 75 triangle keeps the smallest gap at 15 degrees, the most remote from the special shapes.
questions.rule: Maximise the smallest gap.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: if a figure shows two lines of equal length without the problem requiring it, the reader may wrongly use their equality.
questions.explain: A figure's apparent relations tempt us to use them; that is why the author asks to avoid unrequired ones.
questions.rule: Apparent relations tempt.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What is the property of the 45, 60, 75 triangle that the author mentions?
options: It is the only triangle with whole-number angles
It is, in a precise sense, the most remote from both the isosceles and the right-angled shape
It is the easiest triangle to construct with ruler and compasses, so it is preferred for that reason
It has equal area to any isosceles triangle
optionExplain: Many triangles have whole-number angles.
Right: its smallest gap from those shapes is as large as it can be.
The text does not claim this.
No such claim appears in the text.
questions.explain: The author says that, in a precise sense, this is the triangle most remote from both the isosceles and the right-angled shape.
questions.rule: Most remote from the special shapes.
questions.teaches: The 45, 60, 75 degree triangle is, in a precise sense, the most remote from both the isosceles and the right-angled shape.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student claims an acute triangle whose three gaps (90 minus the largest angle, then the neighbouring differences) all exceed 15 degrees. What follows?
options: Possible, with angles 80, 60 and 40 degrees
Impossible: three times the first gap plus twice the second plus the third always equals 90
Possible, but only if two angles are equal
Impossible, because the angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, so no further identity is needed to see it
optionExplain: Its gaps are 10, 20 and 20, so the first is not above 15.
Right: if every gap exceeded 15, that weighted sum would exceed 90.
Equal angles give a gap of zero.
The sum is the reason behind the identity, but the identity is what rules the claim out.
questions.explain: With gaps x = 90 - largest angle, y and z for the next differences, 3x + 2y + z equals 270 minus the angle sum, which is 90. If x, y, z were all above 15, 3x + 2y + z would exceed 6 times 15, which is 90.
questions.rule: The three gaps cannot all exceed 15 degrees.
questions.teaches: For angles below 90 degrees, 3(90 - a) + 2(a - b) + (b - c) always equals 90, so at least one gap is 15 degrees or less unless the angles are exactly 75, 60 and 45.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A figure has many lines, and you cannot tell the given ones from the ones you added. What is a good remedy?
options: Draw all lines the same so that none is favoured
Erase the lines you added, since they clutter the figure
Number every line and ignore its appearance, so that each can be named in the written argument
Draw them in different styles, such as heavy, light or dotted
optionExplain: Uniform lines hide the roles.
Added lines may be needed; they just need distinguishing.
Numbers are slower to read than style.
Right: style shows roles.
questions.explain: Different styles give different roles different looks. The card next lists the author's means.
questions.rule: Style your lines so that role shows at a glance.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author suggests heavy and light lines, continuous and ____ lines, or lines in different colours.
questions.explain: Dotted lines, along with weight and colour, are the author's means of marking roles.
questions.rule: Weight, pattern and colour mark roles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student draws a triangle with a median and a possible helper line. How should the figure look?
options: The triangle in heavy lines, the median in medium lines, the helper in a light dotted line
All three in the same heavy pen so that nothing is missed and every line looks equally firm
The helper in the heaviest line because it is new
Only the triangle, with no further lines until sure
optionExplain: Right: more certain parts heavier, tentative parts lighter.
Same weight hides the difference in role.
A tentative line should not dominate.
Tentative lines may be drawn lightly.
questions.explain: Style should rank the lines by role and by certainty.
questions.rule: Style your lines so that role shows at a glance.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: if all the lines in a busy figure share one style, the roles of the lines are easier to read.
questions.explain: A uniform style gives the eye no cue, so the roles become harder to read.
questions.rule: Same style hides roles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: When you are not yet decided whether to use a line as an auxiliary line, how does the author suggest drawing it?
options: In the heaviest pen, to test it
In red, to mark it as new
Very lightly
Not at all, until it is certain to be useful
optionExplain: A heavy line suggests a decision already made.
The author assigns red to the given elements.
Right: a light line can stay or be ignored without cluttering the figure.
He allows drawing it, lightly, before deciding.
questions.explain: The author says you draw a line very lightly if you are not yet quite decided to use it as an auxiliary line.
questions.rule: Draw tentative lines lightly.
questions.teaches: A line that you are not yet decided to use as an auxiliary line is drawn very lightly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A teacher draws an electric circuit for a class. By the author's suggestion, how might she colour the elements?
options: All elements in one colour to keep the diagram neat, since colour adds nothing to the reasoning
The unknown element in the lightest shade so that it does not distract
Each element in a different random colour
The given elements in one colour, such as red, and important parts in other colours
optionExplain: A single colour gives no role cues.
The unknown is the target, not a distraction.
Colours should follow roles, not chance.
Right: the author uses red for the given elements and other colours for key parts.
questions.explain: The author says you may draw the given elements with a red pencil and use other colours to emphasise important parts, such as a pair of similar triangles.
questions.rule: Colour by role: given elements one way, key parts another.
questions.teaches: The author draws the given elements in red, and uses other colours to emphasise important parts, such as a pair of similar triangles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A beginner cannot visualise a solid from a flat drawing. What is the most helpful extra?
options: A longer written description of the drawing
A simple model of the solid, even a home-made one
A drawing with more shading and no other change
A rule that solids may not be studied until later
optionExplain: Words are further from the solid than the drawing.
Right: a model shows what the drawing cannot.
Shading helps only a little.
Delay does not make the shape clearer.
questions.explain: Models make solids concrete. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Add models to drawings when solid shapes are hard to see.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author says three-dimensional models are desirable but ____ to make and expensive to buy.
questions.explain: Cost and effort are why drawings remain the usual choice.
questions.rule: Models are good but costly; drawings are the usual choice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A class has no budget for ready-made models and must learn about a pyramid. What follows the author?
options: Skip solids altogether until models can be bought
Rely on a single drawing and assume it is enough, since good pupils can imagine the solid
Use drawings, and let pupils make simple cardboard models
Buy one expensive model and ban other methods
optionExplain: The author accepts drawings as the usual choice.
He suggests supplementing drawings.
Right: usually drawings, with self-made models for beginners.
Expense is why he accepts drawings.
questions.explain: Drawings are usually what we have; some experimentation with self-made cardboard models is very desirable for beginners.
questions.rule: Add models to drawings when solid shapes are hard to see.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: the author regards drawings as unnecessary once a model is available.
questions.explain: He accepts drawings as usual and recommends models as a supplement, especially for beginners.
questions.rule: Models supplement drawings.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Match each everyday object with the solid the author says it can represent.
pairs: A box, a tile or the classroom
Frustum of a right circular cone
questions.explain: The author notes that taking objects of our everyday surroundings as representations of geometric notions is helpful.
questions.rule: Look around for real objects that show the solid.
questions.teaches: Everyday objects can represent solids: a box, a tile or the classroom a rectangular parallelepiped, a pencil a circular cylinder, a lampshade a frustum of a right circular cone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A chemistry teacher wants first-year pupils to grasp the shape of a molecule. By the author's advice for solids, what is best?
options: Let them build simple models themselves, then compare with drawings
Show only a textbook drawing and ask them to imagine the molecule, since models are costly
Wait until the school buys professional models
Replace drawings with models entirely
optionExplain: Right: self-made models are very desirable for beginners.
Imagining a solid from a flat drawing is the difficulty.
Self-made ones are already helpful.
Drawings keep their usual role.
questions.explain: The author says some experimentation with self-made cardboard models is very desirable for beginners.
questions.rule: Let beginners build simple models.
questions.teaches: Some experimentation with self-made cardboard models is very desirable for beginners.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You must schedule five tasks that overlap in time. Which approach uses the strength of figures?
options: Write the tasks as a long paragraph
Memorise all start and end times
Draw each task as a bar on a time line and look at the overlaps
Ask someone else to arrange them, since a person who knows the people can judge best
optionExplain: Prose hides overlaps.
Memory is the weakness figures help.
Right: a geometric representation of the schedule.
That does not use the problem's own structure.
questions.explain: A figure turns a schedule into something the eye can read. The card next gives the author's reason.
questions.rule: If the problem is not geometric, try drawing it as a figure anyway.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Figures traced on paper are easy to produce, easy to recognise, and easy to ____.
questions.explain: Ease of production, recognition and memory is why the author values figures.
questions.rule: Figures are easy to make, see and keep.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Ann is taller than Ben, Ben is taller than Cy, and Cy is taller than Di. Which representation helps you answer who is shortest?
options: Put the four names along a vertical line, tallest at the top
Draw four equal circles with names inside
List the names in alphabetical order, so that each can be found quickly in the list
Draw a triangle with Ann at the top corner only
optionExplain: Right: height becomes position on a line.
Equal circles do not show the order.
Alphabetical order is unrelated to height.
A triangle has three corners; there are four people.
questions.explain: Turning the relation into position along a line makes the answer visible: Di is lowest.
questions.rule: If the problem is not geometric, try drawing it as a figure anyway.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: the author draws figures of non-geometric problems because our aptitude for figures may make them easier to see.
questions.explain: The author argues from our aptitude: plane figures are especially familiar, so a suitable geometric representation lets us use that aptitude.
questions.rule: Use the human knack for figures.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In which fields does the author say geometric representations, graphs and diagrams are used?
options: Only in mathematics and physics
Only in the natural sciences, not in the social ones
Only in teaching, not in research
Physics, chemistry and the natural sciences, economics, and even psychology
optionExplain: He names many more.
He names economics and psychology.
He speaks of their use in all sciences.
Right: the author lists these.
