questions.explain: The author says geometrical representations, graphs and diagrams of all sorts are used in all sciences, naming economics and psychology among them.
questions.rule: Graphs and diagrams are standard tools across the sciences.
questions.teaches: Geometrical representations, graphs and diagrams are used in all sciences, including physics, chemistry, the natural sciences, economics and even psychology.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A manager cannot see why a team's output stalls. She plots weekly tasks finished against weeks. By the author's view, what has she done?
options: Solved the problem, since the plot shows the cause
Found a geometric representation of a non-geometric problem, which may be an important step
Misused geometry, which belongs only to shapes
Added nothing, because the numbers already say the same thing as the plot does
optionExplain: The author calls it an important step toward a solution.
Right: the plot is a figure for the problem.
He extends figures to non-geometric problems.
The picture shows patterns that numbers hide.
questions.explain: The author says that to find a lucid geometric representation for a non-geometric problem could be an important step toward the solution.
questions.rule: A good picture is a step, not the end.
questions.teaches: Finding a lucid geometric representation of your non-geometric problem could be an important step toward the solution, though not the solution itself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You solve a problem for the number 12 and wonder what happens for any whole number. What are you doing?
options: Specializing: passing from a wide set to one particular object that belongs to it
Generalizing: passing from one object to a wider set that contains it
Checking the result by substituting the number back
Decomposing the problem into smaller parts
optionExplain: That is the reverse direction.
Right: from 12 to all whole numbers.
Substituting verifies; it does not widen.
Nothing is being split.
questions.explain: Moving from one object to a set containing it is generalization. The card next gives the author's definition.
questions.rule: Replace one case by the wider set that contains it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Generalization is passing from the consideration of one object to the consideration of a ____ containing that object.
questions.explain: A set containing the object is the wider setting to which we pass.
questions.rule: From one object to a set containing it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Sort each move: is it a generalization, or not?

items.t: From one rectangle to all rectangles
From triangles to all polygons
From all polygons to one chosen square
From a single recipe to a whole class of recipes
From a class of cars to one named model
From the case n = 3 to every whole number n

questions.explain: Generalization moves to a set that contains the original object or set; moving to one member does the reverse.
questions.rule: Wider set in, generalization.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: a statement that holds for a single object must also hold for the wider set that contains it.
questions.explain: A wider set may contain objects that do not share the property; generalization raises a question, not a certainty.
questions.rule: A generalization is a question to check.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What, according to the author, has come of lucky generalizations in science?
options: Only results in pure mathematics, never in physics
Only results that were already proved by other methods
No results, because generalizing is only a guess and no discovery can come from a guess
Many results in mathematics, physics and the natural sciences were found by lucky generalizations
optionExplain: He names physics and the natural sciences too.
He says results were found this way.
A guess can still lead to discoveries.
Right: the author says so.
questions.explain: The author states that many results were found by lucky generalizations in mathematics, physics and the natural sciences.
questions.rule: Lucky generalizations have produced real discoveries.
questions.teaches: Many results in mathematics, physics and the natural sciences were found by lucky generalizations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A cook has perfected one soup and asks what makes any soup balanced. Which move is a generalization in the author's sense?
options: Passing from this one soup to the set of all soups, and looking for what they share
Adding more salt to this soup until it tastes right
Checking that this soup is cooked through and seasoned the way the family likes it
Copying this soup's recipe exactly for a party
optionExplain: Right: from one object to a set containing it.
That adjusts the single soup.
That checks the single soup.
That repeats the one case.
questions.explain: The generalization asks about the set of all soups, not about the one in the pot. The author adds that generalization may be useful in the solution of problems.
questions.rule: Widen the question to see what the cases share.
questions.teaches: Generalization may be useful in the solution of problems, as well as in the discovery of general laws.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You notice that 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, which is 3 squared. What is a sensible next question?
options: Is 9 a special number for some other reason, such as being the square of three?
Is 1 + 3 + 5 harder to compute than 1 + 3?
Does the sum of the first few odd numbers often come to a square?
Should 3 squared be replaced by 3 times 3?
optionExplain: That keeps attention on the single case.
That is unrelated to the pattern.
Right: it widens the single observation into a question.
That is a change of notation, not a question.
questions.explain: A curious fact invites the question whether it recurs. The card next shows the author's example.
questions.rule: Ask whether a curious fact is common, and test more cases.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author notes that 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 equals ____.
questions.explain: The sum of the first four cubes is 100, which is 10 squared.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What is the sum of the first five cubes, 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 + 125, and is it a square?
options: 225, which is not a square
215, which is not a square
250, which is 5 times 50
225, which is 15 squared
optionExplain: 225 equals 15 squared.
This miscalculates 100 + 125.
This adds 125 twice and is not a square.
questions.explain: Adding 125 to 100 gives 225, and 15 times 15 is 225, so the pattern holds again.
questions.rule: Test the generalization on the next case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: since the first six sums of cubes are all squares, the author regards the law as proved.
questions.explain: Cases suggest the law; they do not prove it.
questions.rule: Cases suggest; they do not prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's wider question, what replaces the four cubes 1, 2, 3 and 4?
options: The first four cubes, but with different bases chosen from the whole numbers
The successive cubes up to any n: the sum of 1, 2, 3 and so on up to n cubed
The sum of squares up to n
The product of the first four cubes
optionExplain: The base list stays successive; the number of terms becomes general.
Right: the sum of successive cubes with n terms.
The question is about cubes, not squares.
The question concerns a sum.
questions.explain: The author writes the sum 1 cubed + 2 cubed + 3 cubed + ... + n cubed and asks whether it is often a square.
questions.rule: Replace the particular count by n.
questions.teaches: The wider question concerns the sum of successive cubes 1, 2, 3, up to any number n, and asks whether it is often a square.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A baker notices that 3 loaves out of 12 sell by noon every Friday and wonders about every day. Which question generalizes her observation?
options: Why did Friday's twelve loaves taste so good?
Should she bake exactly twelve loaves on Friday and fewer on the other days of the week?
Do about a quarter of the loaves sell by noon on most days?
How many loaves are in a dozen?
optionExplain: That keeps to the single day.
That is a decision, not a generalization.
Right: it widens one Friday to a set of days.
That is unrelated to the pattern.
questions.explain: The generalization asks whether the pattern of one case recurs in a wider set. The author calls his own such step a lucky one.
questions.rule: Ask whether it recurs.
questions.teaches: The author calls the step from the one observation about cubes to the general question a lucky generalization, since it leads to a remarkable general law.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: One plane through a given line must cut a cube-shaped cake into equal volumes. What helps most?
options: Notice that the cube is symmetric about its centre, and use only that fact
Compute the cube's volume to the last decimal
Try random planes through the line until one looks as if it cuts the cake evenly
Ask for a different, simpler cake
optionExplain: Right: the essential property is the centre of symmetry.
The volume is not what fixes the plane.
Random trials ignore the structure.
The problem is to be solved as given.
questions.explain: The symmetric shape does the work. The card next shows the author's version of this.
questions.rule: Find the one property the problem uses, and solve for every object with it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's wider problem, the plane passes through the ____ of symmetry of the solid.
questions.explain: The plane passes through the given line and the centre of symmetry, which fixes it.
questions.rule: Line plus centre fixes the plane.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A line is given in space and a solid with a centre of symmetry. Which description fixes the bisecting plane?
options: Any plane at right angles to the given line
The plane that touches the solid at one point and is parallel to the given line
The plane containing the given line and the centre of symmetry
The plane through the line and the solid's heaviest corner
optionExplain: Such planes need not pass through the centre.
A touching plane misses the solid's interior.
Right: it bisects the volume by symmetry.
A solid with a centre has no preferred heaviest corner.
questions.explain: Symmetry about the centre means that any plane through it halves the volume; adding the line fixes which plane.
questions.rule: Find the one property the problem uses, and solve for every object with it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: the author's solution of the octahedron problem depends on the octahedron having eight triangular faces.
questions.explain: The solution uses only the centre of symmetry, which the author calls the essential property; the number of faces plays no part.
questions.rule: Use only the essential property.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: In the author's account, what is the main achievement in solving the octahedron problem?
options: Inventing the wider problem, which shows the role of the centre of symmetry
Computing the volume of the octahedron exactly, so the plane can be placed to halve it
Proving that planes can bisect volumes at all
Finding a line that crosses the octahedron
optionExplain: Right: the wider problem is the main achievement.
The volume is not computed.
That is not the achievement he names.
The line is given.
questions.explain: The author says our main achievement in solving the first problem was to invent the second problem and so recognise the role of the centre of symmetry.
questions.rule: The invention of the wider problem is the main work.
questions.teaches: The main achievement in solving the first problem was to invent the second, wider problem, which reveals the role of the centre of symmetry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A straight path through a given gate must halve a regular hexagonal park. Which idea carries over from the octahedron?
options: A regular hexagon has no property useful for halving, so the area must be measured instead
Only a path parallel to a side halves the area
The park's area must be computed first
Use the park's centre of symmetry: the path through the gate and the centre halves it
optionExplain: It has a centre of symmetry.
Any straight line through the centre halves it.
The area is not needed for the bisection.
Right: the same essential property solves this special case.
questions.explain: The wider problem needs only the centre of symmetry, and a hexagon has one. As the author says of the octahedron, the original problem is then also solved.
questions.rule: A solution of the wider problem solves each special case with the key property.
questions.teaches: Because the octahedron has a centre of symmetry, the solution of the wider problem also solves the original problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: a problem can sometimes become easier when you make it more general.
questions.explain: It sounds odd, yet the author shows a case where the more general problem is easier. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Do not fear to climb: the wider problem may be easier.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: The author says the more general problem may be ____ than the special one.
questions.explain: In the octahedron example, the general problem was easier.
questions.rule: Wider can be easier.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You cannot solve a question about one particular 7-sided polygon. What may help, in the author's spirit?
options: Add more detail about that particular polygon, so that nothing of its structure is overlooked
Pose the question for all polygons, or for polygons with the property you suspect matters
Wait until the polygon changes shape
Repeat the calculation with greater care
optionExplain: More detail buries the key property.
Right: the wider question may show the key property.
The polygon does not change.
Care does not change the view of the problem.
questions.explain: Stepping up to a wider question can show what the problem really uses.
questions.rule: Do not fear to climb: the wider problem may be easier.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: once the general problem is invented, the author says only a minor part of the special problem's work remains.
questions.explain: The author says the main achievement was to invent the general problem, and that after it only a minor part of the work remains.
questions.rule: After the invention, little remains.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which claim goes beyond what the author says?
options: The main achievement was inventing the general problem, as the octahedron example shows
A more general problem is always easier than the special one
The general problem can look paradoxically simple
Little work remains once the general problem is invented
optionExplain: The author says this about the octahedron example.
Right: the author says it may be easier, not that it always is.
He says the claim sounds paradoxical.
He says only a minor part remains.
questions.explain: The author says the more general problem may be easier. Claiming that it is always easier would go beyond his words.
questions.rule: May be easier, not always easier.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A teacher widens a failing lesson-plan question to any class. What does the author call the idea that a wider problem may be easier?
options: The auxiliary problem
Induction
Decomposing and recombining
The inventor's paradox
optionExplain: That is an easier or related problem used as a means; it is a different entry.
That is the finding of general laws from instances; it is a different idea.
That splits a problem into parts; it is a different idea.
Right: he points the reader to this entry for the idea.
questions.explain: The author ends his passage with See Inventor's Paradox. The teacher's move, widening the question, is a case of the idea.
questions.rule: This is the inventor's paradox.
questions.teaches: The author names the idea that a more general problem may be easier the inventor's paradox.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A pool is 10 m long, 5 m wide and 2 m deep, so its volume is 100 cubic metres. Which move generalizes the problem?
options: Call the sides l, w and d, and find the volume in terms of them
Fill the pool and measure the water
Check that 10 times 5 times 2 equals 100 again
Choose a smaller pool to work out first
optionExplain: Right: numbers become letters.
That tests one pool.
That repeats the numerical case.
That specializes instead of generalizing.
questions.explain: Replacing the data by letters widens the problem to all such pools. The card next gives the author's example.
questions.rule: Turn given numbers into letters, so one solution covers every case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Replacing the numbers 10, 5 and 6 by a, b and c turns a problem in numbers into a more general problem written with ____.
questions.explain: The book calls this a more general problem in letters.
questions.rule: Numbers to letters is a generalization.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A garden 8 m by 5 m has perimeter 26 m. Which formula gives 26 for sides a = 8, b = 5?
optionExplain: This gives 13, half the perimeter.
This gives 40, the area.
Right: 2 times 8 plus 2 times 5 is 26.
This gives 18; one side is counted once.
questions.explain: The perimeter counts each side twice: 16 plus 10 is 26, and the letter formula 2a + 2b returns that value.
questions.rule: Substitute the numbers back to test the letter formula.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: if a formula in letters is correct, substituting the original numbers into it gives the original answer.
questions.explain: The letter formula covers every case, so it must cover the original numbers.
questions.rule: The general result must contain the special one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student says a rectangle with sides a and b has perimeter ab. For 8 and 5 it is 26. What does the test show?
options: The formula is right, since 40 is a natural number
The test is wrong, since letters cannot be tested
The formula is right for areas, so it must be right here
The formula gives 40, not 26, so it is wrong
optionExplain: Being a number does not make it the right one.
Letters can be tested by substitution.
A correct area formula says nothing about perimeter.
Right: checking a letter formula against a known case exposes errors.
questions.explain: The formula ab gives 40, the area. The known perimeter is 26, so the formula fails the check.
questions.rule: Test a general formula on a case you know.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A shop owner works out a 20 percent mark-up on a 50 pound item. What does passing to letters allow, by the author?
options: To stop checking, because a formula in letters is always right once it has been derived
To vary the price and rate and check the result in various ways
To keep exactly one price and one rate in mind
To avoid arithmetic entirely
optionExplain: A formula still needs checking.
Right: with letters you can vary the data and check.
Letters free you from one price and rate.
Arithmetic is still done when values are substituted.
questions.explain: The author says that passing from numbers to letters gives access to new procedures: we can vary the data, and doing so we may check our results in various ways.
questions.rule: Letters let you vary the data and check.
questions.teaches: With letters we can vary the data, and by doing so we may check our results in various ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You face a puzzle that looks tricky. What is the most economical first question?
options: How long will I need to solve this from scratch?
Is this puzzle fair to people like me?
Have I seen this puzzle, or one like it, before?
Who made up this puzzle, and why?
optionExplain: That plans the effort without looking for help.
Fairness does not help to solve it.
Right: it may save the whole effort.
The maker is not relevant to the solution.
questions.explain: Earlier experience is the cheapest source of help. The card next gives the author's question.
questions.rule: Ask: have I seen this, or something close to it, before?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Have you seen the same problem in a slightly ____ form?
questions.explain: A problem may come back with small changes; the author asks the reader to recall it anyway.
questions.rule: Look for the same problem in other dress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A tutor must find two numbers with sum 20 and product 96. She once solved the same with product 99. What follows the author?
options: Use the earlier solution as a model, adjusting for the changed product
Ignore it, since the product differs, and so the old solution cannot be of any help
Reuse the old answer 9 and 11 unchanged
Wait to meet the exact earlier problem
optionExplain: Right: the problem seen in a slightly different form.
The author asks to explore such similarity.
The products 99 and 96 differ; the numbers differ.
A slightly different form is enough.
questions.explain: A problem seen in a slightly different form is a source of method. The new numbers need working out: 8 and 12 give sum 20 and product 96.
questions.rule: Adjust the old method to the new data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: if you cannot recall having seen the problem before, asking the question has been a waste of time.
questions.explain: Even a negative answer may start the mobilization of useful knowledge.
questions.rule: Even a no helps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What does the author say about asking the question when the answer turns out negative?
options: The question loses its value and should be dropped
The question proves the problem is entirely new
Such questions may still start the mobilization of useful knowledge
The question should then be replaced by a guess, since memory has failed to help here
optionExplain: The author says the opposite.
A negative answer shows only that you do not recall it.
Right: asking brings relevant knowledge to mind.
He does not link the two.
questions.explain: The author says that, even if the answer is negative, such questions may start the mobilization of useful knowledge.
questions.rule: Ask even when you expect no.
questions.teaches: Even if the answer is negative, asking whether you have seen the problem may start the mobilization of useful knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A nurse meets an unusual symptom. By the author's three possibilities, what can she recall?
options: Recall a case she has handled, one she has heard about, or a very similar one
Only a case she has handled herself, since heard-of cases cannot count as experience
Only a case identical in every detail
None, since unusual symptoms are new by definition
optionExplain: Right: solved, heard of, or very similar.
The author includes cases heard of.
A very similar case counts.
She may still recall something related.
questions.explain: The author lists three possibilities: we have solved the same problem, we have heard of it, or we had a very similar problem.
questions.rule: Solved, heard of, or very similar.
questions.teaches: The author lists three possibilities: we have solved the same problem before, we have heard of it, or we had a very similar problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A problem contains an odd expression you cannot place. What is a good habit?
options: Skip the odd expression and work on the rest, since it is probably only decoration
Replace the expression with one you like better
Wait for a hint from someone else
Ask what it is, whether it is familiar, and where you have seen it
optionExplain: The odd feature may hold the key.
That changes the problem.
Waiting does not use what you already know.
Right: features recognised may lead to relevant knowledge.
questions.explain: Recognising a striking feature calls up knowledge. The card next gives the author's questions.
questions.rule: Ask of each striking feature: have I seen this before?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: To obtain a solution, we have to mobilize the pertinent parts of our ____ knowledge.
questions.explain: The author speaks of dormant knowledge, which questions about the problem can awaken.
questions.rule: Wake the knowledge that sleeps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A geometry problem mentions a tangent to a circle. What follows the author's advice?
options: Treat the tangent as decoration and ignore it
Ask what you know of tangents, and where you have used one before
Wait until the tangent shows its use by itself as the work proceeds along the circle
Look only for a problem with the same numbers
optionExplain: A feature that strikes you may be important.
Right: this feature may play a role again.
Waiting does not mobilize knowledge.
The question concerns features, not only numbers.
questions.explain: Any feature that played a role elsewhere may play one again; asking about it brings up what you know.
questions.rule: Ask of each striking feature: have I seen this before?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: recognising a familiar feature of the problem guarantees that it will help to solve it.
questions.explain: The author says only that a feature which played a role elsewhere may play a role again; there is no guarantee.
questions.rule: A familiar feature may help; it need not.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Why, according to the author, should we recognise a feature that strikes us as possibly important?
options: Because every feature of a problem is important, and so all of them must be recognised in turn
Because a feature that played a role in another problem may play a role again
Because recognising a feature solves the problem
Because unfamiliar features are always misleading
optionExplain: He says only those that strike us as possibly important.
Right: that is his reason.
Recognition only brings knowledge to hand.
He does not say so.
questions.explain: The author says that any feature of the present problem that played a role in the solution of some other problem may play again a role.
questions.rule: A feature that worked once may work again.
questions.teaches: Any feature of the present problem that played a role in some other problem's solution may play a role again.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A mechanic hears a rattle at 40 mph and not at 30. By the author's idea, what should she do?
options: Ignore it, since only whole faults matter
Replace the wheels, since they turn at that speed
Drive faster until the rattle vanishes
Ask whether she has met that feature, a rattle depending on speed, before and what caused it
optionExplain: The author applies the question to features.
That jumps to a repair without recalling anything.
That tests nothing and is unsafe.
Right: she examines a striking feature.
questions.explain: She treats the speed-dependent rattle as a feature to recognise, as the author advises for any feature that strikes us. She cannot know beforehand whether the memory will be relevant, yet the possibility should be explored.
questions.rule: Check features against past experience.
questions.teaches: We cannot know in advance which parts of our knowledge may be relevant, but there are possibilities we should not fail to explore.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Halfway through a problem you recall a related problem you solved last year. What is the best response?
options: Welcome it, and ask how its solution could help with the present problem
Ignore it, because last year's problem was different in its details and cannot help now
Copy last year's answer as the present answer
Abandon the present problem as already solved
optionExplain: Right: a related solved problem is a resource.
A related problem is exactly what to explore.
Related is not the same; the answer must be earned.
It is not the same problem.
questions.explain: A related, solved problem gives a good chance of help, but its use must be found. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: A related solved problem is a resource: ask how to use it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A problem whose solution is known and which is connected with ours is certainly ____.
questions.explain: The author calls such a problem good news.
questions.rule: A related solved problem is welcome.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: You must find the area of a parallelogram. You recall how to find the area of a rectangle. What follows?
options: Ignore it, since a parallelogram is not a rectangle and the area rule cannot be adapted
Use the rectangle's area formula unchanged
Treat the rectangle as a related solved problem and look for a way to use it
Wait until you meet an identical problem
optionExplain: The difference is what you must bridge.
That would ignore the slant.
Right: the connection is promising.
A related one is already available.
questions.explain: The rectangle is a related solved problem, and the next question is how to use it.
questions.rule: Ask how the related solution can be used.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: True or false: once you know a related problem has a known solution, you already know how to use it for the present problem.
questions.explain: The author says we know the solution of the related problem but do not know yet how to use it; the next question is how.
questions.rule: Knowing is not yet using.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Once a related solved problem is in hand, which questions does the author ask next?
options: Can you check the result? Can you derive it differently?
What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition of the problem?
Have you used all the data? Is the condition used?
Could you use it? Could you use its result? Could you use its method?
optionExplain: Those questions come after a result has been reached.
Those questions help to understand the problem first.
Those test a solution plan, not the use of a related problem.
Right: these ask how the old problem can serve.
questions.explain: The author says that, knowing the solution but not how to use it, we ask: Could you use it? Could you use its result? Could you use its method?
questions.rule: Ask whether to use it, its result, or its method.
questions.teaches: With a solved related problem we ask: Could you use it? Could you use its result? Could you use its method?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A lawyer finds an old case related to her current one. Which related case is the more welcome, by the author?
options: One with a remote connection but a famous name
One whose connection with the present case is close and whose outcome is easy to follow
One with a close connection but a tangled argument that nobody has managed to follow
One chosen because it was won by the same side
optionExplain: Fame is not the criterion.
Right: it is still more welcome if the connection is close and the solution simple.
A simple solution makes it more useful.
The side that won does not matter here.
questions.explain: The author says it is still more welcome if the connection is close and the solution simple.
questions.rule: Prefer a close connection and a simple solution.
questions.teaches: A related solved problem is still more welcome if the connection is close and the solution is simple.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: You introduce a second problem B to help with problem A. Which statement fits a problem B that you recall from before?
options: You know how to use it, but you must still solve it
You know neither its solution nor its use
You know its solution, but you do not yet know how to use it for A
You know both, so A is already solved
optionExplain: That fits a newly invented problem.
A recalled problem has a known solution.
Right: its solution is known; the use remains to be found.
Then no work would remain.
questions.explain: A recalled problem has a known solution and an unknown use. The card next sets it against an invented one.
questions.rule: Recalled: solution known, use unknown. Invented: use known, solution unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Match each helper problem with what you know about it.
pairs: Its solution is known; its use is not yet known
Its use is known or strongly suspected; its solution is not
Either kind, once the difficulty is overcome
It is used in the same way for the proposed problem
questions.explain: The difference lies in the relation to B: solution known and use unknown, versus use known and solution unknown.
questions.rule: Know which half of the job is left.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Sort each situation: is B recalled, or invented?

items.t: I solved a similar puzzle last week but cannot see how to use it now
I make up an easier puzzle that, if solved, would show me the way
I remember the textbook solution but not how it applies
I suspect a simpler version would help, but I have not solved it
The full solution of B is on my shelf; my task is to find a link
I think the link is clear, but B still needs to be proved

questions.explain: A recalled problem has a known solution and an unknown use. An invented one has an expected use and an unsolved solution.
questions.rule: Recalled: solved, use unclear. Invented: use clear, unsolved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Which difficulty remains for a recalled problem B, and which for an invented one?
options: Recalled: how to use B. Invented: how to solve B
Recalled: how to solve B. Invented: how to use B
Both: how to prove that A is true
Neither: both are solved the moment B is chosen
optionExplain: Right: the difficulty sits in different places.
The two are swapped.
Neither case concerns the truth of A as such.
Choosing B does not solve either.
questions.explain: The author says our difficulty concerning B makes all the difference between the two situations.
questions.rule: Different difficulty, same later use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Suppose the difficulty with B is overcome in each case. What is the use of B for A, by the author?
options: Different: a recalled B gives its result, an invented one its method
Only a recalled B can supply a method
The same in both cases: we may use the result or the method
Neither, since B is then no longer related to A
optionExplain: The author says the use is the same in both.
Both can supply either.
Right: once the difficulty is overcome, B is used in the same way.
B remains related to A.
questions.explain: The author says that when the difficulty is overcome, we may use B in the same way in both cases.
questions.rule: Overcome the difficulty, and the use is alike.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A coach wonders whether a method that worked for a sprinter fits a hurdler. If it does, what may she take over?
options: The result, the method, or, with luck, both
Only the result, never the method
Only the method, not the final result
Nothing, because the athletes differ
optionExplain: Right: the author lists these three uses.
The method may be used as well.
The result may be used too.
A related case can still be a source of method or result.
questions.explain: The author says we may use the result or the method and, if we are lucky, we may use both.
questions.rule: Use B's result, its method, or both.
questions.teaches: We may use the result or the method of B, and, if we are lucky, both.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: In the invented case, what does the author say we know about how to use B?
options: We know nothing about its use until B is solved
We know it only by recalling a textbook
We know it only after A is solved
We know, or at least strongly suspect, how to use it
optionExplain: The author says the use is known or suspected.
That describes the recalled case.
The use is expected before A is solved.
Right: the use is known or strongly suspected.
questions.explain: The author writes that for an invented B we know, or at least suspect strongly, how to use it.
questions.rule: Invented: use known or strongly suspected.
questions.teaches: With an invented auxiliary problem we know, or at least suspect strongly, how to use it, but not yet how to solve it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: You can find the circle through three plane points and must find the sphere through four points of space. What is a good start?
options: Start again with no reference to the plane problem
Ask what in space corresponds to each element used in the plane solution
Use the plane method unchanged, ignoring the third dimension
Wait for a new idea to arrive on its own, since the plane problem differs in dimension
optionExplain: That throws away the solved problem.
Right: link the problems by corresponding elements.
Space needs counterparts, not an unchanged copy.
The old problem already offers one.
questions.explain: The old problem suggests elements to look for in the new one. The card next gives the author's example.
questions.rule: Find the counterpart in the new problem of each key element of the old.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: To find the sphere circumscribed about a tetrahedron, the author recalls the circle circumscribed about a ____.
questions.explain: The plane problem of the circle about a triangle is the old problem he recalls.
questions.rule: Plane problem first, then space.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A square-based pyramid has 8 edges. How many perpendicular bisecting planes of its edges are there, one per edge?
optionExplain: This counts the sides of the square base, not the pyramid's edges.
Right: one for each edge.
This counts the vertices, not the edges.
This counts each edge twice.
questions.explain: The plane problem used one bisecting line per side. For the pyramid, the counterpart is one bisecting plane per edge, so 8.
questions.rule: One counterpart per element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: True or false: the plane problem's bisecting lines of the sides have their counterparts in the bisecting planes of the edges in the new problem.
questions.explain: The author introduces perpendicular bisecting planes of the edges as the corresponding auxiliary elements.
questions.rule: Sides to edges, lines to planes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: After introducing the corresponding elements, how does the author say the solid problem is worked out?
options: Only after a new method is found for space that does not rely on the plane solution
By measuring a model of the tetrahedron
By proving a new theorem for the plane first
Easily, by following the analogous solution in plane geometry
optionExplain: He follows the old plane solution.
No model is mentioned.
The plane problem is already solved.
Right: the old solution guides the new.
questions.explain: The author says that after the idea of the bisecting planes, we can easily work out the solution of the solid problem, following the analogous solution in plane geometry.
questions.rule: Follow the old solution step by step.
questions.teaches: Once the corresponding elements are introduced, the solution of the solid problem can be worked out easily by following the analogous plane solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A cook can scale a sauce recipe by adjusting the pan size and must now scale a cake. Which first step follows the author?
options: Ask which elements of the sauce method have counterparts in the cake method
Use the sauce method on the cake exactly as written
Start with a new recipe that ignores the sauce
Scale only the cooking time and keep the ingredients, since the sauce method fixed the amounts
optionExplain: Right: link the problems by corresponding elements.
Counterparts may differ.
The solved sauce case is a guide.
That ignores elements of the old method.
questions.explain: The cook treats the sauce as the old problem and looks for a counterpart of each key element in the cake, as the author does with the circle and the sphere.
questions.rule: Let the old problem tell you what to look for.
questions.teaches: The intention of using a formerly solved problem influences how we see the present one: we introduce into it elements corresponding to important elements of the old.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: You know how to find the area of a right triangle but face an ordinary triangle. What may make the known solution usable?
options: Wait for a formula for ordinary triangles to appear from some other source or textbook
Treat the triangle as a rectangle
Add a line, the height, that splits the triangle into two right triangles
Remove one side of the triangle
optionExplain: Waiting does not use what you know.
That changes the problem.
Right: an auxiliary element makes the old solution fit.
Removing a side destroys the figure.
questions.explain: A well-chosen extra line can connect the new problem to the old one. The card next states the author's question.
questions.rule: Add the element that lets the old solution apply.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: Should you introduce some ____ element in order to make its use possible?
questions.explain: This is the author's question when thinking about using a formerly solved problem.
questions.rule: Ask about an auxiliary element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: You can find the area of any triangle. For a quadrilateral, which auxiliary element lets you use the triangle result?
options: A circle around the quadrilateral
A second quadrilateral of the same size
A vertical line through the centre only
A diagonal, which cuts the quadrilateral into two triangles
optionExplain: A circle does not reduce it to known areas.
That doubles the problem.
That may not cut into triangles.
Right: the diagonal brings in triangles.
questions.explain: The diagonal is the auxiliary element that makes the known solution applicable.
questions.rule: Add the element that lets the old solution apply.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: True or false: an auxiliary element is justified only if it makes the use of the formerly solved problem possible.
questions.explain: The author introduces auxiliary elements to make use of the related problem possible.
questions.rule: Judge an element by what it enables.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: In the author's example, what auxiliary elements are introduced for the solid problem?
options: The centres of the faces of the tetrahedron, joined to the opposite vertices of the solid
The perpendicular bisecting planes of the edges of the tetrahedron
The medians of the tetrahedron's faces
Spheres touching each face
optionExplain: The text names bisecting planes.
Right: they correspond to the bisectors of the plane problem.
Medians are not mentioned.
No such spheres appear.
questions.explain: The author introduces the perpendicular bisecting planes of the edges as auxiliary elements, in analogy with the bisectors of the sides of a triangle.
questions.rule: Auxiliary elements come from the old problem.
questions.teaches: In the solid problem the auxiliary elements introduced are the perpendicular bisecting planes of the edges of the tetrahedron.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.section: Here Is a Problem Related to Yours and Solved Before
questions.q: A theorem about triangles is proved; your new claim concerns quadrilaterals, so you consider a diagonal. What does this mirror in the author's wording?
options: A guess that has been proved false, but which could still help as an auxiliary element
A problem that is unrelated but easy
A theorem related to yours and proved before, made usable by an auxiliary element
A figure that was drawn inexactly
optionExplain: The related theorem has been proved.
The theorem is related.
Right: the same remark applies to theorems.
Exactness is not the issue.
questions.explain: The author states a version of the remark for theorems: here is a theorem related to yours and proved before.
questions.rule: Make a related theorem usable by adding an element.
questions.teaches: The same approach applies to a theorem related to yours and proved before.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A branch of study asks how people come to discover or invent methods. What would the author call it?
options: Heuristic, or ars inveniendi
Rhetoric, the art of persuading an audience
Logic, the study of valid proof alone
Arithmetic, the study of number operations
optionExplain: Right: the study of discovery and invention.
Rhetoric concerns persuasion, not discovery.
Logic checks proofs; heuristic aims at finding them.
Arithmetic does not study discovery.
questions.explain: Heuristic studies discovery and invention. The card next gives the author's description.
questions.rule: Heuristic studies how to find solutions, not how to check them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Heuristic is also called ars ____.
questions.explain: Ars inveniendi means the art of invention, one of the names the author gives.
questions.rule: Heuristic = ars inveniendi.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which activity belongs to heuristic as the author describes it?
options: Listing which theorems have been formally proved, with the dates and the names of their authors
Checking each line of a finished proof for errors
Studying the methods a solver uses to come upon a proof
Memorising multiplication tables
optionExplain: That is a record of results, not of discovery.
That is verification, not discovery.
Right: methods and rules of discovery and invention.
That trains recall, not invention.
questions.explain: Heuristic aims to study the methods and rules of discovery and invention.
questions.rule: Heuristic studies how to find solutions, not how to check them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Match each name with what the author says about it in relation to heuristic.
pairs: Made the most famous attempts to build a system
An attempt to revive heuristic in a modern, modest form
questions.explain: The author lists traces in Euclid's commentators and Pappus, systems by Descartes and Leibnitz, Bolzano's detailed account, and his own modest revival.
questions.rule: Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz, Bolzano.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: How does the author describe the present booklet in relation to heuristic?
options: As an attempt to revive heuristic in a modern and modest form
As the first complete system of heuristic ever written, replacing all earlier attempts
As a refutation of Descartes and Leibnitz
As a history of logic and psychology
optionExplain: Right: modern and modest.
Others tried before, and he is modest.
He mentions them as earlier attempts.
It is about solving problems, not history.
questions.explain: The author says the booklet is an attempt to revive heuristic in a modern and modest form.
questions.rule: The book is a modest revival of heuristic.
questions.teaches: The author presents the booklet as an attempt to revive heuristic in a modern and modest form.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A student asks why most textbooks have so little on how to find solutions. What does the author's description suggest?
options: Heuristic has been refuted and abandoned as false by every serious logician of recent years
Heuristic is detailed in every textbook of logic
Heuristic is still the main subject of modern philosophy
Heuristic has often been outlined but seldom presented in detail, and is as good as forgotten today
optionExplain: He calls it forgotten, not refuted.
He says it is seldom presented in detail.
He says it is as good as forgotten today.
Right: that is how he describes its fate.
questions.explain: The author says the study was often outlined, seldom presented in detail, and as good as forgotten today.
questions.rule: Heuristic is a neglected study.
questions.teaches: Heuristic was often outlined, seldom presented in detail, and as good as forgotten in the author's day.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: You suspect a pattern but have no proof. Which attitude toward your reasoning is sound?
options: It is worthless until a full proof exists
It is plausible and useful for finding the answer, but it is not yet certain
It is already certain because it feels strong and the pattern has held in the cases seen
It is only decoration and can be skipped
optionExplain: Plausible reasoning helps to discover the solution.
Right: provisional reasoning serves discovery.
Feeling strong is not certainty.
It is the means of discovering the answer.
questions.explain: Provisional reasoning serves discovery and awaits proof. The card next gives the author's term.
questions.rule: Heuristic reasoning is the scaffolding, and the proof is the building.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: We need heuristic reasoning when we construct a strict proof as we need scaffolding when we erect a ____.
questions.explain: The author's comparison: heuristic reasoning is to proof as scaffolding is to a building.
questions.rule: Scaffolding for the proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: An engineer makes a rough estimate before the detailed calculation. How would the author view this estimate?
options: As a rigorous result that makes the later detailed calculation unnecessary and can replace it
As heuristic reasoning, a plausible guide that the exact calculation later confirms or corrects
As an error to be avoided in careful work
As a proof of the final design
optionExplain: A rough estimate is not strict.
Right: provisional and plausible, for discovery.
The author regards such reasoning as good in itself.
It proves nothing by itself.
questions.explain: A rough estimate is provisional and plausible, and serves to find the answer ahead of strict work.
questions.rule: Plausible now, proved later.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Sort each description: heuristic reasoning, or rigorous proof?

items.t: Provisional and plausible only
Final and strict
Serves to discover the solution
Gives complete certainty
Settles for a more or less plausible guess
Complete once the solution is complete

questions.explain: Heuristic reasoning is provisional, plausible and for discovery; a strict proof is final and gives certainty.
questions.rule: Provisional versus final.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, complete certainty is attained before the complete solution has been obtained.
questions.explain: Certainty comes only when we have obtained the complete solution; before then we must often settle for a plausible guess.
questions.rule: Certainty comes with the complete solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A detective sees that three burglaries share one method and a fourth matches, so she suspects one thief. What reasoning is this, by the author?
options: Rigorous proof, because several cases agree and the method of the thief is the same each time
Pure calculation, with no guesses
Rhetoric, aimed only at persuading others
Heuristic reasoning, based on induction from cases and on analogy between them
optionExplain: Agreement of cases is not proof.
She is making a plausible guess.
Her aim is to discover who the thief is.
Right: it is often based on induction or analogy.
questions.explain: The author says heuristic reasoning is often based on induction, or on analogy.
questions.rule: Induction and analogy are common sources.
questions.teaches: Heuristic reasoning is often based on induction or on analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: True or false: heuristic reasoning is bad in itself and should be avoided.
questions.explain: The author says heuristic reasoning is good in itself; the fault lies in mixing it up with proof. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Say which part is plausible and which is proved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What is bad is to mix up heuristic reasoning with ____ proof.
questions.explain: The fault is in the confusion, not in the heuristic reasoning.
questions.rule: Do not mix the two.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A report contains a plausible argument for a new design's safety. What is the honest way to present it?
options: State that the argument makes safety plausible, and that full proof or testing is still needed
State that safety is proved, since the argument is persuasive and the readers will prefer certainty
Omit the argument, since it is not a proof
Present it without saying whether it is plausible or proved
optionExplain: Right: it labels the argument for what it is.
That sells heuristic reasoning for proof.
The argument is good in itself.
That leaves the confusion in place.
questions.explain: The honest course is to use the argument and to say what it shows and what it does not.
questions.rule: Say which part is plausible and which is proved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Sort each statement: honest labelling, or confusion of heuristic reasoning with proof?

items.t: This pattern held in ten cases, so it is plausible but not proved
Ten cases agree, therefore the law is proved
The sketch below suggests the answer; the proof follows later
The sketch proves the answer, with no further argument needed
It seems likely; I have not yet shown it
It is certain because it seems so likely

questions.explain: Honest labelling keeps plausible and proved apart; the others treat a plausible argument as a proof.
questions.rule: Never relabel plausible as proved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which does the author count as worse: mixing up heuristic reasoning with proof, or selling it for proof?
options: Mixing them up is worse than selling it
They are equally bad
Selling heuristic reasoning for rigorous proof is worse
Neither is bad when the argument is plausible
optionExplain: The author ranks selling as worse.
He says one is worse.
Right: the author says what is worse is to sell it for proof.
He says both are faults.
questions.explain: The author says that mixing up heuristic reasoning with rigorous proof is bad, and that selling heuristic reasoning for rigorous proof is worse.
questions.rule: Selling it as proof is the worse fault.
questions.teaches: Mixing up heuristic reasoning with rigorous proof is bad, and selling it for rigorous proof is worse.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A teacher says lectures should show no plausible argument without a proof attached. What does the author's view imply?
options: The advice is right, since plausible arguments mislead readers and should be kept out of lectures
The advice is right, since proofs are always short
The advice is wrong, since plausible arguments are proofs
The advice is too strict, since heuristic reasoning is good in itself when it is kept distinct from proof
optionExplain: He calls heuristic reasoning good in itself.
Length is not the issue.
They are not proofs.
Right: the fault is confusion, not the reasoning.
questions.explain: The author says heuristic reasoning is good in itself; the fault lies only in mixing it up with, or selling it as, rigorous proof.
questions.rule: Good in itself; faulty only when confused with proof.
questions.teaches: Heuristic reasoning is good in itself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A textbook gives a plausible argument for a formula and wants to be helpful. What is best?
options: Call the argument a proof so students trust it
Say plainly that the argument is plausible and that a strict proof comes later
Leave out the argument and state the formula only, since an unproved argument has no place in class
Give the argument without saying anything about its status
optionExplain: That misleads the learner.
Right: openness about status helps the learner.
The argument prepares the proof and aids understanding.
Ambiguity can do harm.
questions.explain: Honest labelling lets a plausible argument teach. The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Say openly that an argument is heuristic, and what it leaves unproved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A heuristic argument presented with taste and ____ may be useful.
questions.explain: Taste and frankness are the conditions under which the author calls it useful.
questions.rule: Present it with taste and frankness.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: A lecturer must introduce an idea that she cannot yet prove in full. Which presentation follows the author?
options: Give the argument and let the class assume it is proved
Refuse to give any argument until a full proof is ready, however long the class has to wait for it
Give a plausible argument, say it is only that, and indicate where the strict argument will come
Present it as a proof, apologising quietly afterwards
optionExplain: That leaves the status ambiguous.
A plausible argument can prepare the way.
Right: open, with its limits stated.
That is the ambiguity he warns against.
questions.explain: The argument is useful when its status is clear.
questions.rule: Say openly that an argument is heuristic, and what it leaves unproved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Sort each teaching move: does it follow the author's advice, or break it?

items.t: Calls a plausible argument heuristic and states its limits
Hints that a plausible argument is a proof without saying so
Says openly that a strict proof will follow
Hides doubts about the argument from the class
Uses a heuristic argument to prepare the way for the proof
Pretends that the argument needs no further proof

questions.explain: The author wants openness about advantages and limits, and he warns against ambiguity.
questions.rule: Be open about status.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: What does the author say a frank heuristic argument usually contains?
options: Certain germs of the rigorous argument
The complete rigorous proof in short form
Nothing that the rigorous argument will use
Only the final result with no reasoning
optionExplain: Right: it prepares for the strict proof.
It is not a proof.
He says it contains germs of it.
It contains reasoning, which can become strict.
questions.explain: The author says a heuristic argument usually contains certain germs of the rigorous argument and so may prepare for it.
questions.rule: Heuristic arguments hold the germs of proof.
questions.teaches: A heuristic argument usually contains certain germs of the rigorous argument, which it prepares.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Examine Your Guess to Heuristic Reasoning
questions.q: Which subject does the author single out as one whose teaching could be essentially improved by openness about heuristic reasoning?
options: Geometry as taught to young children, who need the most help with arguments that are not strict
History as taught to law students
Calculus as taught to engineers and physicists
Languages as taught to adults
optionExplain: He does not name geometry here.
History is not mentioned.
Right: he names it.
Languages are not mentioned.
questions.explain: The author says the teaching of certain subjects, especially calculus to engineers and physicists, could be essentially improved.
questions.rule: Calculus teaching is his example.
questions.teaches: The author names the teaching of calculus to engineers and physicists as an example that could be essentially improved by open heuristic arguments.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: You have worked long on a problem and are no closer. Which response does the author recommend?
options: Keep repeating the same attack until your effort finally wins
Solve some related problem that is easier, then come back to yours
Put the problem aside for good, since failure shows it is insoluble
Copy a solution from a similar problem without checking it fits
optionExplain: Persistence feels virtuous, but the author advises a way around the obstacle when the direct way is blocked.
Right: an easier success gives consolation and builds courage.
One failure shows only that you have not solved it yet; the author does not call such problems insoluble.
Copying unexamined skips the thinking the related problem is meant to prompt.
questions.explain: When direct effort stalls, the author suggests an easier related problem. The card next gives his reasons.
questions.rule: When the proposed problem resists you, solve some easier related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: The author tells you to try some related problem first.
questions.rule: Try a related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: A baker cannot work out stock levels for 30 products across four shops. What follows the author's advice?
options: Order extra of everything for every shop to avoid working it out
Wait until a colleague produces the whole table for all 30 products
Work out all four shops at once but skip the least popular items
Work out stock for two products in one shop, then return to the task
optionExplain: That avoids the problem instead of going around it with an easier related one.
Waiting hands the work off; the author wants you to devise an easier problem yourself.
Dropping items changes the task and does not build on a solved simpler case.
Right: the small case is a related, easier problem and success there gives a route back.
questions.explain: Two products in one shop is a related problem that is easier but has the same shape. Solving it shows how to handle the full task.
questions.rule: When the proposed problem resists you, solve some easier related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: True or false: Once the easier related problem is solved, the original problem is solved as well.
questions.explain: Solving the related problem is a step; the author says you may then find courage to attack the original again, so the original still needs work.
questions.rule: The related problem is a means, not the goal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: According to the author, in what does human superiority consist when an obstacle cannot be overcome directly?
options: Going around it by devising a suitable auxiliary problem
Applying more force until the obstacle gives way
Choosing only problems that can be solved at once
Recognising early which problems are too hard to try
optionExplain: Right: the author names this as a mark of human superiority.
Force is the direct attack that the passage says is not enough.
Avoiding hard problems is the opposite of the passage, which speaks of obstacles you cannot overcome directly.
Giving up early is not the superiority the author means; he praises devising an auxiliary problem.
questions.explain: The author says human superiority consists in going around an obstacle that cannot be overcome directly, in devising some suitable auxiliary problem when the original appears insoluble.
questions.rule: Devising an auxiliary problem is going around an obstacle.
questions.teaches: The author calls devising a suitable auxiliary problem, when the original seems insoluble, the mark of human superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: A manager cannot fix late deliveries across a whole company. After fixing them for one small team, what should she do next?
options: Treat the company-wide problem as solved, since one team improved
Stop, because the small team was never the real problem
Return to the company-wide problem, using what the small team showed
Repeat the small-team fix for the next team without re-examining the whole
optionExplain: A related success does not settle the original problem.
The small team was a stepping stone; the aim stays with the original.
Right: the author expects you to attack the original problem again after the easier success.
Repeating the fix team by team is a new related problem; the whole still has to be faced.
questions.explain: The detour is meant to be a route back. After the easier success you attack the original problem again.
questions.rule: The detour ends with a return to the original problem.
questions.teaches: After the easier success you are expected to return and attack the original problem again, with new courage.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: You cannot recall any problem like yours. What else can you do to find an easier one?
options: Wait for a similar problem to come to mind on its own
Look for a problem with an identical answer
Ask for the solution and then work backwards
Change your own problem to create an easier one
optionExplain: Waiting leaves invention out; the author says you should invent one.
Needing an identical answer already requires the solution you lack.
Asking for the solution replaces the thinking the exercise is meant to build.
Right: making a variation of the problem yourself is the author's suggestion.
questions.explain: The author asks you to invent a related problem, not merely remember one. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: If you do not remember a suitable related problem, invent one by varying your own problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: The questions about a related problem share one aim: the ____ of the problem.
questions.explain: The common aim is the variation of the problem.
questions.rule: Related-problem questions aim at varying the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: A hiker cannot plan food for a 21-day trek with eight people. Which move invents a related problem?
options: Pack the same food as last year without doing any planning
Plan the food for a 2-day outing with two people
Plan the food for a 30-day trek with twenty people
Ask the other seven hikers which food they like best
optionExplain: That repeats an old answer; it does not create a new problem.
Right: shrinking days and people gives a simpler problem of the same kind.
A larger trek is also a variation, but it makes the task harder, not more accessible.
Preferences are data for the original; they do not make a different, easier problem.
questions.explain: Reducing days and people is a specialization. It keeps the structure of the original but makes it easy enough to solve.
questions.rule: If you do not remember a suitable related problem, invent one by varying your own problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: Which are named as means of varying a problem? Select all that apply.
options: Repeating the question aloud
Waiting for inspiration
Generalization
Specialization
Analogy
optionExplain: Repeating the question varies nothing.
Waiting is not a way of varying the problem.
Right: widening the problem is one means.
Right: narrowing it to a special case is one means.
Right: using a similar problem is one means.
questions.explain: The author lists generalization, specialization and analogy, and adds others that are ways of decomposing and recombining.
questions.rule: If you do not remember a suitable related problem, invent one by varying your own problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: True or false: The author wants you to invent a related problem before you try to recall one you already know.
questions.explain: He hopes you have already tried the question whether you know a related problem. Inventing comes when recall has not helped.
questions.rule: Recall first; invent when recall fails.
questions.teaches: Recalling a known related problem comes first; inventing one is the step taken when recall does not help.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.section: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem
questions.q: A spreadsheet formula fails in some of 5,000 rows. Which choice uses decomposing and recombining?
options: Test the formula on 50 rows at a time, then combine the findings
Delete the failing rows and carry on with the remaining ones
Re-enter the whole formula again from memory and run it
Ask which colleague wrote the sheet and what they intended
optionExplain: Right: splitting the data into parts and recombining the findings is decomposing and recombining.
Deleting rows removes the symptom and builds no related problem.
Re-entering from memory varies nothing about the problem.
Finding the author may help, but it is not a variation of the problem.
questions.explain: Splitting a problem into parts and putting the findings together is one of the further ways, beyond generalization, specialization and analogy, to vary a problem.
questions.rule: Parts and recombination are a way to vary a problem.
questions.teaches: Decomposing and recombining is a further family of ways to vary a problem, listed with generalization, specialization and analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Which statement about mathematical induction is closest to the author's?
options: It is the same process as induction, applied to numbers only
It collects many special cases to suggest a general law
It proves theorems of a certain kind, and does not find laws
It is used in every science to discover general laws
optionExplain: The author says there is very little logical connection between them.
Collecting cases to suggest a law is induction, not mathematical induction.
Right: it is a proof method for theorems of a certain kind.
Induction is used in all sciences; mathematical induction only in mathematics.
questions.explain: The names suggest one idea, but the processes differ. The card next gives each one its job.
questions.rule: Keep the two names apart: induction discovers general laws, mathematical induction proves certain theorems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Induction discovers general laws from instances; ____ induction proves theorems of a certain kind.
questions.explain: Induction discovers laws from particular instances; mathematical induction proves theorems of a certain kind.
questions.rule: Induction finds; mathematical induction proves.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Sort each activity by the method it uses.

items.t: A botanist infers a growth rule after examining many leaves
Showing that a statement about n carries over to n + 1
Spotting that the first five totals are all squares and guessing a law
Proving a formula for all whole numbers by passing from each to the next
A chemist suspects a rule after several repeated experiments
Using a verified step from one integer to the next to cover every integer

questions.explain: Induction works from observed instances to a conjectured law. Mathematical induction proves a statement about integers by passing from n to the next one.
questions.rule: Keep the two names apart: induction discovers general laws, mathematical induction proves certain theorems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: Mathematical induction is a strong form of induction, so the two are closely linked in logic.
questions.explain: The author says there is very little logical connection, only some practical connection.
questions.rule: Same family of names, different logic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: According to the author, why does mathematical induction carry the name induction?
options: The assertion proved often came from induction, so the proof complements it
Both methods rest on one and the same logical principle of reasoning
Mathematical induction is the rigorous last stage of the same method
The first users of the method were physical scientists in laboratories
optionExplain: Right: the name is a random circumstance, since the assertion often arises by induction.
The author denies a close logical connection.
The two differ in kind; the proof method is not a stage of induction.
The author gives no history of this kind; he gives a circumstance in how the assertions arise.
questions.explain: The assertion to prove may come from any source. In many cases, as in the cube sums, it is found by induction, so the proof appears as a mathematical complement to induction.
questions.rule: The shared name is a random circumstance.
