That is a wider relation than the special suggestion.
Complicated ones come last.
questions.explain: The general suggestion lets in problems sharing any common point; the special suggestion insists on a common unknown.
questions.rule: The special suggestion insists on a common unknown.
questions.teaches: Related problems may share objects, notions, data or part of the condition; the special suggestion insists on one particular common point, the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: You must find the diagonal of a 6 by 8 rectangle. What helps?
options: Find the area of the rectangle before anything else
Treat the diagonal as the side of a right triangle
Draw a circle of radius 6 around one of the corners
Double both sides of the rectangle and then measure
optionExplain: Area is a different unknown.
Right: a right triangle with legs 6 and 8 uses a familiar result.
A circle brings in nothing useful here.
Doubling changes the problem.
questions.explain: The diagonal is a length, and triangles give familiar results about lengths. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: If a familiar result needs a part your figure lacks, introduce a suitable auxiliary element such as a triangle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Should you introduce some auxiliary ____ in order to make their use possible?
questions.explain: The author asks whether you should introduce some auxiliary element.
questions.rule: Introduce what the familiar result needs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: On a map, points sit at (1, 2) and (7, 10) in kilometres. What distance follows the pattern?
options: 14 km, from adding the legs of the triangle
8 km, taking the longer leg as the distance
48 km, from multiplying the legs together
10 km, from a right triangle with legs 6 and 8
optionExplain: Adding the legs forgets that a diagonal is shorter.
The longer leg is not the distance.
Multiplying gives an area.
Right: the legs are 6 and 8 and 36 + 64 = 100.
questions.explain: The auxiliary right triangle has legs 7 - 1 = 6 and 10 - 2 = 8, so the distance is 10 km.
questions.rule: If a familiar result needs a part your figure lacks, introduce a suitable auxiliary element such as a triangle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: To use the triangle plan, you must already know three parts of the new triangle.
questions.explain: It is not absolutely necessary; if you foresee that the missing parts can be obtained, you already have a plan.
questions.rule: Foreseeing the missing parts is enough to start.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Which kind of triangle makes these side-of-triangle problems particularly simple?
options: The right triangle
The equilateral triangle
The obtuse triangle
The triangle of unequal sides
optionExplain: Right: right triangles are particularly simple.
The author does not name it.
The author does not name it.
Unequal sides are not simpler.
questions.explain: The simple problems differ in their data, and all of them are particularly simple for right triangles.
questions.rule: Right triangles are the simplest case.
questions.teaches: These side-of-triangle problems differ in their data, and all are particularly simple for right triangles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: To find the height of a tree, you can measure its shadow and the sun's angle. What does the author say about such a start?
options: It fails unless all three parts are measured first
It is no plan at all, only a hope of being lucky
Foreseeing how the missing parts can be got is essential progress
It works only when the triangle is a right triangle
optionExplain: All three parts are not necessarily required at once.
The author calls it a plan of the solution.
Right: foreseeing counts as a plan.
Right triangles are simplest but not the only case.
questions.explain: If we foresee that the missing parts can be obtained somehow, we have made essential progress, we have a plan of the solution.
questions.rule: Foresight of the missing parts gives a plan.
questions.teaches: If you foresee that the missing parts can be obtained somehow, you have made essential progress and have a plan of the solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: The unknown is the volume of a tetrahedron. What would you look for?
options: The perimeter of the base of the tetrahedron
The sum of all the angles of the solid
The longest edge of the tetrahedron on its own
The area of a base and the altitude
optionExplain: The perimeter is not what a volume needs.
Angles are not enough.
One edge is not enough.
Right: base area and altitude give the volume.
questions.explain: The kind of unknown suggests what to find. The card next lists four.
questions.rule: Write the problem as given-find-the-unknown, and let the kind of unknown suggest your plan.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Match each unknown to the plan it suggests.
questions.explain: Each plan comes from a simple familiar problem with the same unknown.
questions.rule: Write the problem as given-find-the-unknown, and let the kind of unknown suggest your plan.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Given the four sides of a field and one diagonal, find a corner angle. Which plan follows?
options: Obtain the angle by finding the area of the field
Obtain it as an angle of a triangle, using the diagonal
Obtain the angle by measuring all four sides again
Obtain the angle by constructing a point first
optionExplain: The area is a different unknown.
Right: the diagonal cuts the field into triangles.
The sides are already given.
Constructing a point is for a different unknown.
questions.explain: The unknown is an angle, so the plan is to obtain it in a triangle, and the diagonal supplies one.
questions.rule: Write the problem as given-find-the-unknown, and let the kind of unknown suggest your plan.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: Following such a plan means you will meet no difficulties.
questions.explain: You may run into difficulties, but you have some idea to start with, which is a great advantage.
questions.rule: A plan is a start, not a guarantee.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: How many of the problems to find in less advanced classes can be started in this way, according to the author?
options: Only a few of them
Exactly half of them
Almost all of them
Only those with a figure
optionExplain: The author says almost all.
He gives no such share.
Right: the solution of almost all such problems can be started this way.
Figures are not a condition.
questions.explain: The solution of almost all problems to find usually proposed in less advanced classes can be started by thinking of a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown.
questions.rule: Almost all elementary problems to find can be started this way.
questions.teaches: The solution of almost all problems to find usually proposed in less advanced classes can be started by this suggestion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A treasure is buried at a given distance from a tree and a rock. What plan does the unknown suggest?
options: The point lies where two circles meet, one around each landmark
The point is the side of some triangle drawn on the map
The point is the base of a tetrahedron built over the map
The point cannot be found from two distances alone
optionExplain: Right: a point to construct is an intersection of two loci.
The unknown is a point, not a length.
The unknown is not a volume.
Two distances fix the point.
questions.explain: The loci are circles, and what remains is to disentangle such loci from the proposed condition.
questions.rule: A point to construct is an intersection of loci.
questions.teaches: What remains for a point to construct is to disentangle two loci, each a circle or a straight line, from the proposed condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: What can knowing a solved problem with the same unknown do?
options: Make every problem trivial
Make the data unnecessary
Turn a hard problem into an easier one
Make an auxiliary element unnecessary
optionExplain: Not every problem becomes trivial.
Data are still used.
Right: it may make all the difference.
Auxiliary elements may still be needed.
questions.explain: The author says it may make all the difference. The card next gives his example.
questions.rule: Check what you know: having a solved problem with the same unknown can make all the difference.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Archimedes found the area of the surface of a ____ with given radius.
questions.explain: The area of the surface of the sphere was found by Archimedes.
questions.rule: Archimedes solved the sphere problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Dana must find the surface area of a sphere inside a cube of edge 6 that touches the cube's faces. She knows the sphere result. What remains?
options: Express the radius through the cube's edge; it is 3
Find the surface area of the sphere from the beginning
Find the volume of the cube before anything else
Find the length of the edge of the sphere itself
optionExplain: Right: the radius is half the edge.
The known result removes this need.
Volume is not the unknown.
A sphere has no edge.
questions.explain: Once the sphere result is known, the problem reduces to finding the radius, 6 divided by 2 = 3.
questions.rule: Check what you know: having a solved problem with the same unknown can make all the difference.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: Archimedes had a simpler solved problem with the same unknown to use for the sphere.
questions.explain: The author says there was scarcely a simpler problem with the same unknown, and certainly none Archimedes could have used.
questions.rule: No simpler same-unknown problem existed for him.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: How does the author rate Archimedes' solution?
options: An easy exercise for a beginner
A solution copied from earlier published work
A minor result of little importance
One of the most notable achievements
optionExplain: The author calls the solution a notable achievement, so it is far from an easy beginner's exercise.
No earlier work is mentioned.
He calls it notable.
Right: this is how the author puts it.
questions.explain: The author regards the solution as one of the most notable mathematical achievements.
questions.rule: The sphere solution was a notable achievement.
questions.teaches: Archimedes' solution may be regarded as one of the most notable mathematical achievements.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A team knows a standard method for pricing a service but must now price an unusual one. What does the contrast with Archimedes suggest?
options: The remaining step will then be trivial to do
Even then the remaining step may be hard, far easier than the first solution
A known standard method makes no difference to the difficulty
Only first solutions of a problem are ever really difficult
optionExplain: The author says the remaining step is not exactly easy.
Right: the remaining step is not exactly easy but cannot be compared with the original difficulty.
He says it may make all the difference.
Later steps can also be hard.
questions.explain: The author says the radius step is not exactly easy but cannot be compared with the difficulty of Archimedes' problem.
questions.rule: A known result lowers the difficulty; it does not remove it.
questions.teaches: Even with the sphere result known, the inscribed-sphere problem is not exactly easy, but its difficulty cannot be compared with that of Archimedes' problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: No problem you know has exactly your unknown. What next?
options: Stop working
Look for a problem with a similar unknown
Choose a problem with a different kind of unknown
Wait for new data
optionExplain: You can still look further.
Right: similar-unknown problems can guide you.
A different kind is a more distant relation.
The data are not the issue.
questions.explain: A close cousin can still guide. The card next shows Archimedes' case.
questions.rule: If none has the same unknown, look for a solved problem with a similar unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Archimedes approximated the sphere using two cones and several ____ of cones.
questions.explain: The composite solid consisted of two cones and several frustums of cones.
questions.rule: Archimedes used cones and frustums.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A homeowner must find the area of an oval pond. She knows the areas of rectangles and circles. Which is the best similar-unknown problem?
options: The volume of a bucket
The cost of the water
The depth of the pond
The area of a circle
optionExplain: A volume is a different unknown.
The cost is not an area.
Depth is not an area.
Right: a circle shares the unknown, an area, in a similar shape.
questions.explain: The circle is the nearest known case with an area unknown.
questions.rule: If none has the same unknown, look for a solved problem with a similar unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: A problem with a similar unknown is as closely related as one with the same unknown.
questions.explain: Problems with a similar unknown are less closely related than those with the same unknown.
questions.rule: Same is closer than similar.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: How did Archimedes use the cones and frustums in his solution?
options: As an approximation to the sphere
As a full replacement for the sphere
As an exact copy of the sphere
As a check on the sphere's radius
optionExplain: Right: a composite solid of two cones and several frustums approximated the sphere.
It was an approximation, not a replacement.
It was not exact.
The check on the radius is not mentioned.
questions.explain: His solution uses as approximation to the sphere a composite solid consisting of two cones and several frustums.
questions.rule: Simpler shapes approximate the harder one.
questions.teaches: Archimedes approximated the sphere by a composite solid consisting of two cones and several frustums of cones.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A planner must estimate delivery times for a new city. No data exist, but three similar cities do. How does the author describe such similar problems?
options: As easy to use as cases with an identical unknown
As useless, since the unknown differs
Less easy to use in general, but valuable guides
As proofs of the answer for the new problem
optionExplain: They are less closely related.
The author says they may be valuable.
Right: less closely related, yet valuable guides.
They guide; they do not prove.
questions.explain: Problems with a similar unknown are less easy to use in general but may be valuable guides nevertheless.
questions.rule: Similar cases guide but do not settle.
questions.teaches: Problems with a similar unknown are less easy to use in general, but they may be valuable guides nevertheless.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: You must prove that two angles are equal. Which earlier theorem is likely to help most directly?
options: One about the lengths of the sides of triangles
One about the area of a circle of given radius
One about the volume of a cone with given height
One whose conclusion says that angles are equal
optionExplain: Different conclusion.
Different conclusion.
Different conclusion.
Right: same conclusion.
questions.explain: Matching the conclusion gives the closest help. The card next explains.
questions.rule: To prove a theorem, look at its conclusion and recall proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: For a problem to prove, look at the ____.
questions.explain: The advice for a problem to prove is to look at the conclusion.
questions.rule: Look at the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: You must prove that a quadrilateral's opposite sides are equal. Which recalled theorem fits the author's method best?
options: A theorem that begins with a quadrilateral
A simple theorem ending with two sides being equal
A theorem that ends with a statement about a circle
A theorem about the area of a triangle
optionExplain: Starting with a quadrilateral matches a hypothesis.
Right: look for the same conclusion.
Ending with a circle is a different conclusion.
Area is a different subject.
questions.explain: The conclusion is that sides are equal, so recall theorems that end that way.
questions.rule: To prove a theorem, look at its conclusion and recall proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Sort each recalled theorem by whether it matches a target conclusion that two angles are equal.

items.t: If two triangles are congruent, the corresponding angles are equal
If a triangle has two equal sides, its base angles are equal
If two lines cross, the vertical angles are equal
If two triangles are congruent, the corresponding sides are equal
If a figure is a square, its area is the side squared
If a number is even, its square is even

questions.explain: The first three end with equal angles; the others end differently.
questions.rule: To prove a theorem, look at its conclusion and recall proved theorems with the same or a similar conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: What does the author say of related theorems that do not share the conclusion?
options: They never help, whatever their relation to the theorem
They help more than theorems with the same conclusion do
They may help, but same-conclusion theorems serve most directly
They must be proved a second time before any use
optionExplain: The author says they have a chance.
He says the most immediate service is from same conclusion.
Right: any related proved theorem may help.
No such requirement is stated.
questions.explain: Any theorem proved in the past which is in some way related has a chance to be of service; we expect the most immediate service from theorems with the same conclusion.
questions.rule: Same conclusion helps most directly.
questions.teaches: Any related theorem proved earlier has a chance to be of service, but theorems with the same conclusion are expected to serve most immediately.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: You must prove two angles in a figure are equal, but the figure has no triangles. What does the book's plan require?
options: Introduce triangles containing the angles and prove them congruent
Measure the two angles directly with a protractor instead
Give up on the congruence theorem and look for another route
Prove that two of the sides of the figure are parallel
optionExplain: Right: the congruent-triangles theorem needs triangles.
Measurement is not a proof.
The theorem is the plan.
Parallelism is a different matter.
questions.explain: The author says we must introduce a pair of triangles containing those angles and prove that they are congruent.
questions.rule: Introduce the triangles the theorem needs.
questions.teaches: The plan requires introducing a pair of triangles containing those angles and proving them congruent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: In simple cases, which recalled problems usually suffice?
options: Only the hardest ones that you have met
Only problems taken from another subject entirely
The most elementary ones with the same unknown
Only problems that you have never solved yourself
optionExplain: Hard ones are not needed.
Another subject is not required.
Right: elementary ones usually suffice.
Solved problems are the point.
questions.explain: The author says the most elementary ones are usually sufficient. The card next puts it together.
questions.rule: Recall problems with the same or a similar unknown, and in simple cases the most elementary ones suffice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: Trying to recollect problems with the same unknown is an obvious and ____ device.
questions.explain: The author calls it an obvious and common-sense device.
questions.rule: It is a common-sense device.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A student must find an angle. Which approach follows the advice for a simple case?
options: Recall the simplest familiar problem whose unknown is an angle
Search for the most obscure angle problem that you can find
Avoid all the known problems and start from nothing at all
Try constructing a point from the meeting of two loci
optionExplain: Right: elementary same-unknown problems usually suffice.
The most obscure is not elementary.
Known problems are the resource.
A different unknown.
questions.explain: The simplest same-unknown problem usually gives the plan in a simple case.
questions.rule: Recall problems with the same or a similar unknown, and in simple cases the most elementary ones suffice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: True or false: Our reading: for a much harder problem, the simplest recalled problem may not be enough.
questions.explain: The author ties the sufficiency of the most elementary problems to simple cases, so harder cases may call for more than the simplest recalled problem. This is our reading.
questions.rule: The elementary shortcut is for simple cases.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: What does the author say about how widely known this device is?
options: It is already universally taught in schools
It is a very recent invention of the author
It is known only to teachers of mathematics
It is surprising that it is not more widely known
optionExplain: He says it is not widely known.
He says it is obvious and common-sense.
He says neither students nor teachers can ignore it.
Right: he finds it rather surprising.
questions.explain: The author finds it rather surprising that such a simple and useful device is not more widely known, and thinks it was not stated before in full generality.
questions.rule: A simple device may be little known.
questions.teaches: The author finds it surprising that this simple, useful device is not more widely known, and thinks it was not even stated before in full generality.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: A tutor says her student needs not worry about asking for problems with the same unknown. What does the author say?
options: Only teachers of mathematics need to use it
Neither students nor teachers can afford to ignore it
Only advanced students of mathematics need to use it
It is optional for everybody in every class
optionExplain: Both are named.
Right: neither can afford to ignore it.
The author speaks of less advanced classes.
He says they cannot afford to ignore it.
questions.explain: The author says neither students nor teachers of mathematics can afford to ignore the proper use of the suggestion: Look at the unknown.
questions.rule: Students and teachers should both use it.
questions.teaches: Neither students nor teachers of mathematics can afford to ignore the proper use of the suggestion: look at the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A researcher wants to build a science of problem-solving that helps teachers. What should she study first?
options: A catalogue of the final answers to famous problems, arranged by topic so students can look them up
The school subjects in which students score lowest
The mental operations that usually help people when they solve problems
A fixed script that every student must recite when stuck
optionExplain: Answers are products; they say little about the process that led to them.
Weak scores show where help is needed, not which mental steps would supply it.
Describing those steps is the natural base for any advice a teacher could give.
A script is a rule to apply, not an understanding of the process behind it.
questions.explain: The aim is to understand the process of solving, especially the steps that typically help. The card next shows this.
questions.rule: Study the useful mental operations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Modern heuristic tries to understand the process of solving problems, especially the typically useful mental ____.
questions.explain: The author names the mental operations typically useful in solving problems as the focus.
questions.rule: Focus on the useful mental operations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A school wants to apply heuristic to its mathematics classes. Which plan is closest to the author's practical aim?
options: Describe the helpful mental steps so teachers can encourage them
Add more drill so every student sees more solved problems
Replace problems with lectures that give the final formulas
Test students more often so that weak ones are found early
optionExplain: This matches the aim: a better understanding of useful steps should improve teaching.
Practice helps, but the aim is to understand and teach the mental steps, not to add volume.
Formulas give results; the aim here is the process that finds them.
Testing finds weakness; it does not describe or teach the helpful operations.
questions.explain: The practical aim is to improve teaching through an understanding of typically useful mental operations.
questions.rule: Understand the steps, then teach them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two statements fit the aim of modern heuristic as the author states it?
options: It replaces practice with the study of logic alone
It tries to understand the mental operations typically useful in solving problems
It hopes its understanding could influence teaching for the better
It aims to list every theorem of elementary geometry
optionExplain: The author wants logic, psychology and experience used together, not logic alone.
Right: the author's stated focus is the mental operations typically useful in solving problems.
Right: the practical aim he states is a good influence on teaching, above all of mathematics.
A theorem list is a body of results, not a study of the process.
questions.explain: Heuristic studies the process and hopes to improve teaching. It does not catalogue theorems or rely on logic alone.
questions.rule: Process first, teaching second.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How does the author describe the present book in relation to the programme of modern heuristic?
options: As the finished, complete system of heuristic
As a rival to the older writers on the subject
As a handbook meant only for teachers of geometry
As a first attempt toward realising that programme
optionExplain: The author claims no completeness; he calls the book a first attempt.
He draws on the older writers rather than opposing them.
The book is meant for teachers and students more broadly, not only geometry.
He calls it a first attempt, which also explains its modest, elementary scope.
questions.explain: The author says the book is a first attempt toward realising the programme of modern heuristic.
questions.rule: A first attempt, not a final system.
questions.teaches: The author calls the present book only a first attempt toward realising the programme of modern heuristic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A teacher meets a hint in the list and wants a fuller explanation of the mental operation behind it. Where does the author say to look?
options: Only in the closing pages, where all the operations are repeated in a single summary table
In the Second Part, and for some operations in the more thorough First Part
Nowhere in this book; the hints are meant to stand without further comment or later explanation
In a separate book that the author promises to write
optionExplain: No closing summary of all operations is described.
The author says some operations are described again in the Second Part and some are discussed more thoroughly in the First Part.
The author points to further treatment of the operations.
The author names parts of this same book.
questions.explain: Some operations are described again in the Second Part, and some are more thoroughly illustrated in the First Part.
questions.rule: Follow the list into the other parts.
questions.teaches: Operations hinted at in the list are described again in the Second Part, and some are discussed and illustrated more fully in the First Part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which basis would you trust most for a study of how people solve problems?
options: Logic alone, since proof is the only certain knowledge
Logic, psychology and earlier writers, resting on real experience of solving
Introspection by one gifted mathematician, who reports carefully on his own methods of working
The opinions of the most experienced classroom teachers
optionExplain: Logic leaves out the psychological side of how solutions are found.
A mix of sources, grounded in experience, covers both the formal and the human side.
One mind is a thin sample; experience of others solving is also needed.
Teachers' opinions are one source but not a basis taken alone.
questions.explain: A serious study uses several sources but rests on experience. The card next gives the author's list.
questions.rule: Use many sources, rooted in experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a serious study of heuristic should take into account both the logical and the psychological background.
questions.explain: The author says both backgrounds should be considered, along with older writers and unbiased experience.
questions.rule: Logic and psychology together.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A new teacher wants to start a heuristic project. Which first step follows the author's advice on sources?
options: Read only one famous textbook and copy its method
Ignore earlier writers, since their methods are out of date
Decide on a theory first and test only what supports it
Watch pupils solving problems and note which steps help them
optionExplain: This neglects experience and the other sources named.
The author says the older writers should not be neglected.
The author asks for unbiased experience, not a theory defended in advance.
The author names experience of watching others solving as part of the base.
questions.explain: Experience in solving and in watching others solve is the base, and no source should be neglected.
questions.rule: Start from unbiased experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which of these does the author name among the sources not to neglect? Select all that apply.
options: Unbiased experience of solving problems and of watching others solve
Older writers such as Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano
Only the findings of experimental laboratories
Rules that never fail, collected by earlier masters
optionExplain: Right: the author names unbiased experience of solving and of watching others solve as a basis.
Right: he names the older writers Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano among the sources.
He does not restrict the sources to laboratory findings; experience and the older writers count too.
He says infallible rules of discovery lie beyond serious research, so he does not offer them as a source.
questions.explain: Older writers and experience are named. Infallible rules are not a source.
questions.rule: Name the sources.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which older writers does the author name as ones a study of heuristic should not neglect?
options: Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano
Euclid, Newton, Gauss and Cauchy
Plato, Aristotle, Kant and Hegel
Archimedes, Fermat, Euler and Hilbert
optionExplain: Right: these are the four older writers the author names as ones not to neglect.
Great mathematicians, but not the four named for heuristic.
Great philosophers, but not those named here.
Great mathematicians, but not those named here.
questions.explain: The author names Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano as older writers on the subject.
questions.rule: Four older writers on heuristic.
questions.teaches: The older writers the author names on the subject of heuristic are Pappus, Descartes, Leibnitz and Bolzano.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A group studies how nurses handle unusual cases. Following the author's approach, what should it look for?
options: Rules that apply only to the nursing cases studied, since each field has its own manner of solving
Rules that guarantee a good outcome in every case
Features of handling problems that would also appear outside nursing
Only the cases in which an experienced nurse failed
optionExplain: This would tie the study to its subject matter.
The author does not promise infallible rules.
The heuristic aim is general features independent of subject matter.
Unbiased experience includes successes as well as failures.
questions.explain: General features, independent of subject, are the target.
questions.rule: Seek what carries across subjects.
questions.teaches: Heuristic aims at general features of problem handling that are independent of the subject matter of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A reference list is grouped in paragraphs and a hint in the middle of one interests you. How would you find the matching article?
options: Search the hint itself as an article title
Read all articles in alphabetical order until it appears
Ask which page number the hint is on and look there
Use the paragraph's opening words as the title to look up
optionExplain: The hint is inside a paragraph and need not be a title.
This works but wastes time and misses the built-in key.
Page numbers do not point to the explanatory article.
When articles are named after paragraph openings, the opening words are the key.
questions.explain: The next card shows the system the author sets up.
questions.rule: Look up the paragraph's first words.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: To find the article for an item of the list, look up the title that equals the ____ sentence of the paragraph containing it.
questions.explain: The first sentence of each of the fifteen paragraphs is the title of an article.
questions.rule: First sentence is the key.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A manual's paragraphs each open with a question, and its articles carry those questions as titles. For a line inside the paragraph opening with How do I reset it, which article do you consult?
options: The article named after the line's first word
The article titled How do I reset it
The last article in the index
The article named after the manual itself
optionExplain: Only the paragraph's first sentence is the title.
The opening question is the title of the article.
Position in the index has no link to the paragraph.
The manual's name is not a section article.
questions.explain: The method uses the paragraph's opening, not the line itself.
questions.rule: Paragraph opening, not item.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Put the steps for tracing a hint in the list to its explanation in order.
items: Find the hint inside the list
Note the first words of the paragraph that holds it
Look up the Dictionary article with those words as its title
If that article only cross-refers, follow the reference to the full explanation
questions.explain: The key is the paragraph opening; a cross-reference may carry you one step further.
questions.rule: Hint, paragraph, title, cross-reference.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Besides the fifteen articles titled by the list's paragraphs, the Dictionary has twelve principal articles. What do those twelve treat?
options: Aspects of the process of solving, such as progress, variation, problems to find and to prove, notation and figures
The fifteen paragraphs of the list, one article each
Short lives of the mathematicians whose problems appear
Problems with hints and solutions for practice
optionExplain: Right: the introduction says the twelve principal articles study aspects of the process of solving problems.
The fifteen list-titled articles are a different group.
The Dictionary is about solving, not biography.
Practice problems are in Part IV, not in the principal articles.
questions.explain: Besides the fifteen articles titled from the list's paragraphs, twelve principal articles study aspects of the process of solving problems.
questions.rule: Twelve principal articles treat aspects of solving.
questions.teaches: The Dictionary has twelve principal articles on aspects of solving problems, besides the fifteen titled by the list's paragraphs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The list has the suggestion to go back to definitions inside the paragraph that opens with a question about restating the problem. What does the author say you find under that title?
options: A cross-reference to the article on definition, where the suggestion is explained
The full explanation of the suggestion, set out in that paragraph with no need to look elsewhere
A list of problems that were solved by going back to definitions, with their solutions
A note that the suggestion has no article
optionExplain: He gives this as the example of the lookup.
The article under that title sends the reader on to another article.
The author describes no such list under that title.
Every item can be traced to an article.
questions.explain: The restating-the-problem entry points on to the article on definition.
questions.rule: Follow the cross-reference.
questions.teaches: Under the title of the restating-the-problem paragraph, the reader finds a cross-reference to the article on definition, where the suggestion to go back to definitions is explained.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: While stuck, you restate the problem, split it into parts, and look for a similar one. What do these moves share?
options: Each puts off the real work until later
Each repeats the same step again and again
Each looks at the problem from a different side
Each asks someone else to supply the answer
optionExplain: They are real work on the problem, not delay.
The moves differ from one another.
They are all ways of turning the problem over to see it differently.
They are things the solver does alone.
questions.explain: Turning a problem over in the mind is variation of the problem. The card next shows its forms.
questions.rule: Vary the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Rolling the problem over and over in the mind, viewing it from different sides, is the essence of ____ of the problem.
questions.explain: The author makes variation of the problem essential to the work.
questions.rule: Variation is essential.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student keeps the same problem but cuts the condition into two parts, treats them one at a time, then puts them together. Which kind of variation is it?
options: Decomposing and recombining
Generalization
Specialization
Analogy
optionExplain: Splitting and joining the elements is exactly this.
Generalization widens the problem; here it is split and rejoined.
Specialization narrows to a special case, which did not happen.
Analogy brings in a similar problem, which did not happen.
questions.explain: Splitting and joining the elements is decomposing and recombining.
questions.rule: Split and rejoin.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each move as a way to vary a problem (as the author names them) or not.

items.t: Go back to a definition of a term
Generalize the problem
Specialize it
Use an analogous problem
Copy the answer from the back of the book
Stop thinking and wait for luck

questions.explain: Definition, generalization, specialization and analogy are named. The last two are not.
questions.rule: Four named ways to vary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What may variation of the problem lead the solver to, according to the author?
options: A guarantee that the problem has a solution
A proof that the first approach was wrong
A final answer to the problem without any further work by the solver on the details
Auxiliary elements, or a more accessible auxiliary problem
optionExplain: Variation gives no such guarantee.
Variation does not by itself show that.
Variation opens routes; it is not the answer.
Both are named as results of variation.
questions.explain: Variation may lead to auxiliary elements or to a more accessible auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: Variation opens new routes.
questions.teaches: Variation of the problem may lead to auxiliary elements, or to the discovery of a more accessible auxiliary problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student must use the list on a theorem whose truth is unknown. What does the author say about the list for such a problem?
options: It applies without any change to both kinds of problem, since all problems are alike in structure
It is specially adapted to problems to find and some questions must be changed for problems to prove
It cannot be used on problems to prove at all
It is adapted to problems to prove and must be changed before use on problems to find
optionExplain: Someone might think one list fits all problems, but he says some questions must be revised for problems to prove.
Right: the list is specially adapted to problems to find, and for problems to prove some questions must be changed.
He does not rule the list out for proofs; he says it can be revised for them.
This reverses his statement: the list is adapted to problems to find, not to problems to prove.
questions.explain: The list suits problems to find; for problems to prove some questions change.
questions.rule: Adapt the list for the kind of problem.
questions.teaches: The list is specially adapted to problems to find, and some of its questions and suggestions must be changed to apply to problems to prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You spot a pattern in the first three cases of a problem. What is the sound next move?
options: Announce the pattern as proved since three cases fit
Treat it as a guess and test it against more cases
Drop the pattern since guessing is unscientific
Wait until someone else confirms the pattern
optionExplain: Three cases make a hunch, not a proof.
A guess is useful for discovery but needs examination.
Guessing is part of discovery, so dropping the pattern throws away a useful lead that should be tested.
Examination is the solver's own job.
questions.explain: The next card shows how guessing and checking fit together.
questions.rule: Guess, then examine.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You must guess, but also ____ your guess.
questions.explain: The author joins the two: guess, but examine the guess.
questions.rule: Guess and examine.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student finds that a formula fits five table values and writes the word proved. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because five agreeing cases are enough for a proof in mathematics
The student should not have used a formula, since formulas are not allowed in a proof
Tables can never be used in mathematics
Fitting some cases supports a guess but does not prove it
optionExplain: Any finite number of cases leaves room for failure.
Using a formula is fine; the fault lies in calling it proved.
Tables are fine as evidence for a guess.
Plausible support is not a proof.
questions.explain: A guess fitting some cases is only plausible.
questions.rule: Do not take plausible for proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two lines go against the author's attitude to heuristic reasoning?
options: Line 1: 'I guess the pattern holds in general'
Line 4: 'Never guess, since guesses can be wrong'
Line 3: 'Let me test it on a new case'
Line 2: The pattern fits, so the theorem is now proved
optionExplain: This line allows a guess, which is the stage heuristic reasoning starts from, so it fits his attitude.
Right: he says to guess and then examine the guess, so a ban on guessing goes against his view.
Testing a guess on a new case is the examining he asks for, so this line fits his attitude.
Right: treating a pattern that merely fits as a proof takes plausible reasoning for demonstration, which he warns against.
questions.explain: Taking plausible for proof, and refusing to guess, both fail.
questions.rule: Guess, then check.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How does the author describe heuristic reasoning in relation to the discovery of a solution?
options: Provisional and only plausible, yet important in discovering the solution
Final and certain, and the only reliable route that a solver can take to a discovery
Harmful, and best kept out of any serious inquiry
Irrelevant to discovery, though it can be useful for teaching beginners how to think about problems
optionExplain: Right: he calls heuristic reasoning provisional and only plausible, yet important in discovering the solution.
He calls heuristic reasoning provisional, not final and certain; certainty belongs to demonstrative reasoning.
He calls it important for discovery, so he would not keep it out of serious inquiry.
He says it is important for discovery, not merely a teaching aid for beginners.
questions.explain: Provisional, merely plausible, yet important for discovery.
questions.rule: Provisional but important.
questions.teaches: The author calls heuristic reasoning provisional and merely plausible, yet important in discovering the solution; it must not be taken for a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A manager has a hunch about why sales fell. By the author's attitude to guessing, what is a fair way to treat it?
options: As the cause, since managers know their markets
As worthless, since a hunch is not evidence
As a guess worth following, to be examined before anyone acts on it
As something only a committee may propose
optionExplain: A hunch has not been examined, whoever has it.
Guesses are part of discovery; they need examining.
A guess is useful in discovery but needs examining.
Nothing in the text restricts who may guess.
questions.explain: The book discusses the nature of heuristic arguments only briefly and says the discussion could go further.
questions.rule: A hunch earns a check.
questions.teaches: The book discusses the nature of heuristic arguments only briefly and says that the discussion could go further.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Would a study of how people solve problems include puzzles and everyday practical problems?
options: No, only serious mathematical problems count
Only puzzles, since they are games
Only if a calculation can settle them
Yes, such problems belong within its scope
optionExplain: Restricting the field to serious mathematical problems would shrink it; the author includes puzzles and practical problems.
Puzzles are included but they are not the only problems covered.
The subject is wider than calculation.
Their solving shows the same kind of behaviour.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's wide scope.
questions.rule: Wide scope.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author holds that infallible rules of discovery lie within the reach of serious research.
questions.explain: He says infallible rules of discovery are beyond the scope of serious research.
questions.rule: No infallible rules.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student asks for a rule that is guaranteed to find the solution of any problem. What would the author say?
options: Such a rule exists and is printed in the list at the front of the book for all solvers to use
No such infallible rule is within serious research; there are useful questions and suggestions
Such a rule exists, but it is far too long to print in a book of this size
The student should give up on solving problems
optionExplain: The author says no such infallible rule exists, and the list is not one.
Right: he says infallible rules of discovery lie beyond serious research, though useful questions and suggestions exist.
He denies that such a rule exists.
Heuristic offers useful guidance.
questions.explain: No infallible rules, only useful guidance.
questions.rule: Guidance, not guarantees.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each topic to the way the Dictionary treats it.
pairs: An article devoted mainly to psychology
A second article devoted mainly to psychology
Preserved in the wisdom of proverbs
questions.explain: Two articles deal mainly with psychology; logical patterns got no technical article; old wisdom is in proverbs.
questions.rule: Know what is in and out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What reason does the author give for leaving some points out of this first short exposition?
options: They have already been published in full elsewhere, so repeating them here would be needless
They have no use in teaching
They could appear too subtle, too technical or too controversial
They need computers that did not yet exist, so they could not be tested in a first exposition
optionExplain: He gives no such reason; the points are left out because they might appear too subtle, not because they are published elsewhere.
He does not say the omitted points are useless in teaching; his reason concerns how they would appear in a first account.
Right: he says they could appear too subtle, too technical or too controversial for a first short exposition.
He gives no such reason; lack of computers is not mentioned as a cause of the omissions.
questions.explain: Too subtle, too technical or too controversial for a first account.
questions.rule: Choose points for a first account.
questions.teaches: Points that could appear too subtle, too technical or too controversial were left out of this first short exposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A chess teacher wonders whether heuristic's ideas about solving even apply to chess problems. What does the author say about such puzzles?
options: Puzzles are within the scope of heuristic
Puzzles lie outside heuristic
Only puzzles fit heuristic
Only chess puzzles are excluded
optionExplain: Right: the author names puzzles among the sorts of problems that lie within the scope of heuristic.
He says the opposite: puzzles are named as inside the scope of heuristic.
He says all sorts of problems fit, not only puzzles.
He describes no exclusion of chess or of any other kind of puzzle.
questions.explain: Practical problems and puzzles fall within heuristic.
questions.rule: Puzzles count.
questions.teaches: The author emphasises that all sorts of problems, especially practical problems and even puzzles, are within the scope of heuristic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You study alone and have no teacher. How might a written classroom dialogue still help you?
options: Memorise the teacher's words and recite them
Skip the dialogue and read only the answers
Ask yourself the teacher's questions in turn
Wait for a teacher to read it to you
optionExplain: Reciting the teacher's words is not the same as thinking through the problem; the value lies in the questions.
The dialogue carries the useful steps and questions, so reading only the answers would miss them.
Right: the dialogue's questions can be used in self-talk, the way a teacher would put them to you.
A reader can use the questions without a teacher, so waiting for someone to read them aloud is not needed.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's view of self-dialogue.
questions.rule: Question yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The author describes thinking as a sort of ____ discourse, a conversation of the thinker with himself.
questions.explain: He calls thinking mental discourse.
questions.rule: Thinking is mental discourse.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student stuck on a word problem asks herself what she is asked to find and what is given. Which idea is she using?
options: A self-dialogue modelled on the teacher's questions
A rule that always yields the answer
A replacement for understanding the problem
A way to avoid the problem
optionExplain: Right: asking herself what is asked and what is given is a self-dialogue modelled on the teacher's questions.
No question guarantees an answer; the questions guide the work but do not replace thinking.
The questions aid understanding of the problem, so they do not replace it.
She is working on the problem by questioning it, not avoiding it.
questions.explain: She is talking herself through, as the dialogues model.
questions.rule: Use the model on yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: If a solver follows a dialogue's questions in a problem of a different kind, the dialogue will give the answer step by step.
questions.explain: A dialogue is a model of progress and not a script that fits every problem.
questions.rule: Model, not script.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: For whom does the author say the dialogues may serve as models?
options: Only a teacher, since a solver alone has nobody to talk to
Only a student, since a teacher already knows how to ask
Only an examiner, who sets the questions
Both a teacher guiding a class and a solver working by himself
optionExplain: The author says the lone solver may also use them.
He says the teacher may take them as models too.
Examiners are not named among those for whom the dialogues may serve as models.
Both uses are named by the author.
questions.explain: The dialogues are models both for guiding a class and for a person working alone.
questions.rule: Models for class and for self.
questions.teaches: The author says the dialogues may serve as models both to a teacher guiding a class and to a problem-solver working by himself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A programmer debugging alone wants to use the author's idea. What would follow his advice?
options: Look for a teacher to take over the debugging
Put the teacher's kind of questions to herself, step by step, and answer them
Avoid questions so as to keep a clear mind
Write the expected answer first and fit the steps to it
optionExplain: The idea is that the solver can play both parts.
This is thinking as a conversation with oneself.
Questions are what drive the dialogue.
This reverses the dialogue's progress from question to solution.
questions.explain: The dialogues show the progress of a solution, so a solver who talks with himself may progress along a similar line.
questions.rule: Talk it through.
questions.teaches: Because the dialogues show the progress of the solution, a solver who talks with himself may progress along a similar line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A teacher wants advice written for teachers rather than for students. How could a dictionary's table of contents help?
options: By listing articles in the order they were written
By grouping articles by the reader they are written for
By marking the hardest articles with a star
By giving only page counts
optionExplain: Order of writing says nothing about who the article is for.
Groups by audience let a reader pick quickly.
Difficulty is not the same as audience.
Length does not show the intended reader.
questions.explain: The author does name such groups; the card next lists them.
questions.rule: Groups guide choice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each article to the purpose the author gives it.
questions.explain: These are the author's own groupings.
questions.rule: Match article to purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student wants to learn how an argument by contradiction works. Which group of articles should she consult first?
options: The history articles, since they cover great thinkers
The technical-term articles, since contradiction is a term
The articles for teachers, since proofs are taught
The methodical articles, which include indirect proof
optionExplain: History tells who thought what, not how the method runs.
Terms such as lemma are explained there, but the method of indirect proof is a methodical topic.
Teacher articles discuss teaching, not the method itself.
Indirect proof is named in the methodical group, which explains how it works.
questions.explain: Reductio ad absurdum and indirect proof is a methodical article.
questions.rule: Methods sit in the methodical group.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each article by the group the author gives it.

items.t: Setting up equations
Test by dimension
Working backwards
Corollary
Bolzano
Lemma

questions.explain: The first three are methodical; Corollary and Lemma explain terms and Bolzano is history.
questions.rule: Know the groups.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say about the articles on the intelligent problem-solver, the intelligent reader and the future mathematician?
options: They address students somewhat more ambitious than average
They address teachers who guide a class of pupils and need advice for teaching routine work
They explain technical terms for beginners
They give the history of the subject
optionExplain: This is the group they belong to.
Teachers are served by routine problems and diagnosis.
Terms are explained under condition, corollary and lemma.
History is under Descartes, Leibnitz, Bolzano and heuristic.
questions.explain: These three articles are aimed at somewhat more ambitious students.
questions.rule: Match article to reader.
questions.teaches: The articles on the intelligent problem-solver, the intelligent reader and the future mathematician address students somewhat more ambitious than the average.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A reader opens the Table of Contents of a reference book and sees that several of its articles are marked with daggers. By the author's convention, what do daggers mean?
options: Those articles are the hardest in the book
Those articles are meant for teachers only
Those articles contain only cross-references
Those articles were added in a later edition
optionExplain: Daggers do not signal difficulty.
Teacher articles are not marked this way.
A dagger does not mark cross-reference articles; it marks articles meant for a different group of readers.
The author does not use daggers to mark articles added later.
questions.explain: Daggers mark pure cross-reference articles.
questions.rule: Daggers mean cross-reference only.
questions.teaches: Some articles contain only cross-references, and these are marked with daggers in the Table of Contents.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A book on general methods uses only school-level maths examples. What is the most sensible reading?
options: The method works only in school mathematics, because the examples are all taken from that field
The author could not handle harder problems
The examples were picked at random
The examples are a convenient choice and the method is meant to reach further
optionExplain: The stated aim is generality, so this misreads it.
Harder problems may be the very background of the book.
A deliberate choice, with reasons, is more likely.
Easy examples serve as a doorway into a general method.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's reasons.
questions.rule: Examples are a choice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author says that nonmathematical problems, though seldom quoted as examples, are not completely forgotten.
questions.explain: He states this directly while admitting that the examples are mainly elementary mathematical.
questions.rule: Others are not forgotten.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A chemist finds only school-level maths in the book. What does the author suggest an expert can do?
options: Wait for a separate edition written especially for chemists, with examples from their science
Add examples from her own experience to bring out the same points
Conclude that the method cannot cover chemistry, since its examples are drawn from mathematics
Replace the method with the rules of her own field
optionExplain: The author does not promise a separate edition for chemists; he suggests the expert can supply examples from his own science.
He invites experts to supply their own examples.
This clashes with the aim of generality.
The method is meant to be general, not replaced.
questions.explain: Experts can add examples from their own experience.
questions.rule: Bring your own examples.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The real background of the exposition, which is not directly quoted, consists of more advanced ____ problems.
questions.explain: The author says more advanced mathematical problems are never directly quoted but form the background.
questions.rule: Advanced problems are the background.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which modern authors does the writer name with gratitude, besides those mentioned under heuristic?
options: Ernst Mach, Jacques Hadamard, William James and Wolfgang Kohler
Isaac Newton, Carl Gauss, Leonhard Euler and Paul Dirac
John Locke, David Hume, Immanuel Kant and John Mill
Euclid, Apollonius, Aristaeus and Pappus
optionExplain: Right: Mach, Hadamard, James and Kohler are the four modern authors he thanks.
Great scientists, but not named in this list.
Great philosophers, but not named here.
These are ancient names that come up in the entry on Pappus.
questions.explain: He names a physicist-philosopher, a mathematician and two psychologists.
questions.rule: Four named debts.
questions.teaches: The writer acknowledges his debt to Ernst Mach, Jacques Hadamard, William James and Wolfgang Kohler.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A reader asks why the book does not use medical examples. Which of the author's remarks gives the best reply?
options: Medical problems cannot be studied by heuristic, because they lack the clear concepts of mathematics
Medical problems are too easy to need any method, so examples from medicine would teach little
Elementary mathematical problems offer all the desirable variety and are accessible and interesting
The author found medical problems uninteresting and left them out for that reason alone
optionExplain: Nothing in the text says medical problems resist heuristic; non-mathematical problems are said not to be forgotten.
No such claim is made; the choice of examples is not based on how easy medical problems are.
Right: elementary mathematical problems offer all the desirable variety and are accessible and interesting.
The author does not call medical problems uninteresting; his stated reason concerns the merits of elementary mathematics.
questions.explain: Accessibility and variety explain the choice.
questions.rule: Choose examples for access.
questions.teaches: The author says elementary mathematical problems present all the desirable variety and that their solution is particularly accessible and interesting.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What makes adding several large numbers in Roman numerals only so much harder than in the usual digits?
options: The Roman symbols give no convenient column layout for the work
Roman numerals cannot represent numbers as large as these, so the sum has to be found some other way
The sums come out different in Roman numerals, because the symbols have different values from digits
Roman numerals are used only by experts
optionExplain: Place value in digits makes the steps routine.
They can represent them; the labour of working with them is the point.
The values are the same; only the writing differs.
Familiarity, not expertise, is the difference.
questions.explain: The notation carries part of the work. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: Notation carries load.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author asks readers to add large numbers without Arabic numerals to see how much a well-chosen notation helps.
questions.explain: He uses Roman numerals such as MMMXC as the experiment.
questions.rule: Try it without.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Using digits, what is XLVII + CXXIX?
optionExplain: This is 10 short of the sum, as if one ten were lost when adding 47 and 129.
This is 10 too many, as if one ten were counted twice when adding 47 and 129.
This is 20 too many, which is what you get from reading XLVII as 67.
Right: XLVII is 47 and CXXIX is 129, and 47 + 129 = 176.
questions.explain: XLVII is 47 and CXXIX is 129, and 47 + 129 = 176.
questions.rule: Translate, then add.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The five numerals MMMXC, MDXCVI, MDCXLVI, MDCCLXXXI and MDCCCLXXXVII stand for which total?
optionExplain: Reading MMMXC as 2990 would lose the total by a hundred.
Reading XC as 110 instead of 90 gives this.
Reading MDXCVI as 1696 adds a hundred.
questions.explain: Convert each numeral and add: 3090 + 1596 + 1646 + 1781 + 1887 = 10000.
questions.rule: Check the total by digits.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Modern computers, using the ____ notation, have a great advantage over the ancient computers.
questions.explain: The author contrasts modern computers using the decimal notation with ancient ones who lacked a convenient way of writing numbers.
questions.rule: Notation helps the computer.
questions.teaches: Modern computers, using the decimal notation, have a great advantage over the ancient computers who had no convenient manner of writing numbers.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the author's view, what advantage does an average modern student have over a Greek mathematician such as Archimedes?
options: Greater natural genius than the Greek mathematician, who lacked the advantage of modern schooling
Knowledge of problems that the Greek never met
Better access to measuring instruments for areas and volumes, which the Greeks did not possess
Familiarity with the notation of algebra, analytic geometry and calculus when solving area and volume problems
optionExplain: The author does not compare natural talent; the student's advantage lies in the notation received.
The problems are those that exercised Archimedes.
Measuring instruments are not mentioned; the advantage he names is the modern system of numerals and signs.
He names these notations as an immense advantage.
questions.explain: Notation is a gain, though not a gain in genius.
questions.rule: Notation is a lever.
questions.teaches: An average modern student who knows the usual notation of algebra, analytic geometry and calculus has an immense advantage over a Greek mathematician in solving problems of areas and volumes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A friend says that no hard thinking is possible without words. Looking at a mathematician who works with figures and symbols, what is the best reply?
options: Hard thinking can go on with figures or symbols, so signs in general help
Agree, since only words can carry meaning and a figure or a symbol is only a picture or a mark
Disagree, since thinking needs no support of any kind, whether words, figures or symbols
Agree, because mathematicians always speak aloud
optionExplain: Figures and symbols can carry thinking.
Symbols and figures carry meaning for the mathematician, so they are more than a picture or mark.
Signs of all kinds do assist the mind, so thinking is not unsupported.
Speaking aloud is not what the author requires; he points to signs and symbols as supports of thought.
questions.explain: The card next gives a milder version of the claim.
questions.rule: Signs assist reason.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Setting up equations appears as a sort of ____ from ordinary language into the language of mathematical symbols.
questions.explain: The author calls it a translation.
questions.rule: Setting up is translation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Translate into symbols: 'Three times a number, decreased by 4, equals twice the number.'
optionExplain: This subtracts 4 before multiplying by 3.
This turns twice the number into half of it.
Three times the number minus 4 equals twice the number.
This attaches the 4 to the wrong quantity.
questions.explain: Translate piece by piece: 3x, minus 4, equals 2x.
questions.rule: Translate each phrase.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: A student translates the sentence, a number plus its square is 12, as x + 2x = 12, and this is a correct translation.
questions.explain: The square of x is x times x, written x^2; 2x is double x. The correct translation is x + x^2 = 12.
questions.rule: Translate faithfully.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How does the author say mathematical notation compares with the rules of ordinary grammar?
options: It has exceptions in the way ordinary grammar does, though it has fewer of them in practice
Its rules suffer no exception, unlike those of ordinary grammar
It has rules that bend to the reader's taste, so that each reader may apply them differently
It has no rules and depends on context
optionExplain: He says the rules of mathematical notation have no exception at all, so fewer exceptions is not his claim.
Right: he says the rules of mathematical notation suffer no exception, unlike those of ordinary grammar.
He stresses rules without exception, so they do not bend to the reader's taste.
He calls mathematical notation a language with rules, so it does not depend on context in place of rules.
questions.explain: Concise and precise with rules that have no exceptions.
questions.rule: A language without exceptions.
questions.teaches: Mathematical notation is a language well adapted to its purpose, concise and precise, with rules that, unlike those of ordinary grammar, suffer no exception.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The philosophers held that words are indispensable to reason. How did the author amend that claim?
options: By saying that reason needs no signs at all, since the mind can work without words or symbols
By saying that only mathematical signs help reason, and that words never assist the mind at all
By saying that signs of all kinds, not only words, are indispensable to reason
By saying words are the only reliable signs
optionExplain: He says signs are indispensable.
He widens the claim to signs of all sorts, words included.
Right: he widens words to signs, saying signs of all kinds are indispensable to reason.
He brings words into line with other signs.
questions.explain: Words are one kind of sign among others.
questions.rule: Signs, not only words.
questions.teaches: The author improves the philosophers' claim by saying that the use of signs, and not only words, appears to be indispensable to the use of reason.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You face a word problem with five unknown amounts. What is the best use of your first minutes?
options: Decide the names for the unknown amounts, which also clarifies what they are
Start calculating with whatever letters come to hand
Search for a similar solved problem before reading this one closely
Draw a decorative figure to calm yourself
optionExplain: Naming sharpens the picture of the problem.
Starting with whatever letters come to hand risks mixing up the five unknowns later.
Understanding the problem comes first.
A figure should serve the problem.
questions.explain: The card next shows why choosing the notation is a step.
questions.rule: Choose with care.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, time spent on choosing the notation may be well repaid by time saved later by avoiding hesitation and confusion.
questions.explain: He says so directly in the entry on notation.
questions.rule: Time spent now saves time later.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A problem involves a train's speed, travel time and distance, plus the same quantities for a bicycle. What is a sound first step?
options: Use one letter for all the speeds and another for all the times, to keep the notation short
Skip naming and compute with words in the margins, deciding on symbols once the answer appears
Choose distinct symbols for each of the six quantities and note what each stands for
Wait until the answer is found to name anything
optionExplain: One letter for several things breaks the rule of a good notation.
Naming is the step that clarifies the problem.
Distinct, recognisable symbols avoid confusion.
This reverses the order the author advises.
questions.explain: Careful choice of symbols helps you see which elements need denoting.
questions.rule: Name each element.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student rushes into a problem with a few arbitrary letters. What does the author predict is likely?
options: Hesitation and confusion later that careful choice would have avoided
A faster solution, since time was saved by not choosing a notation carefully at the start
No effect at all, since the letters carry no meaning beyond what the solver gives them
A guaranteed wrong answer
optionExplain: Right: he says careful choice of notation avoids hesitation and confusion later on.
He argues the opposite: time saved by careless choice is lost later in hesitation and confusion.
The meaning of the letters matters to the solver, so careless letters do have an effect.
He promises no particular outcome such as a guaranteed wrong answer; he predicts hesitation and confusion.
questions.explain: Careless choice may cost time later.
questions.rule: Rushing costs later.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Choosing a suitable notation may contribute essentially to ____ the problem.
