questions.explain: Choosing notation makes us think sharply of the elements to be denoted, which helps us to understand the problem.
questions.rule: Notation aids understanding.
questions.teaches: Choosing a suitable notation may contribute essentially to understanding the problem, because it makes us think sharply of the elements to be denoted.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A software team renames variables x1, x2, x3 to price, quantity, tax before debugging. Which author's remark does this echo?
options: Notation is a matter of taste and does not matter to the quality of the work that follows
Time spent choosing the notation is repaid by less hesitation and confusion
Signs must never be changed once they have been chosen, even for another problem
Words are better than signs for reasoning, so names should replace all the letters
optionExplain: He says notation should be chosen carefully, so it is not a matter of taste that leaves the work unaffected.
Right: clear names such as price, quantity and tax repay the time spent choosing them with less hesitation and confusion.
He allows a sign to take a different meaning in a different problem, so signs may be changed.
He stresses signs as aids to thought, so he does not say names should replace all letters.
questions.explain: A symbol can have a different meaning in a different problem, so each problem needs its choice.
questions.rule: Name for the problem at hand.
questions.teaches: The same letter may be used in a different meaning in a different problem, so notation has to be chosen afresh for each new problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which quality would you most want in a set of symbols that you must use for an hour?
options: That the symbols are unusual, so that no other writer uses them
That each symbol is easy to remember and never stands for two things
That the symbols are long, so that each one says a great deal
That the symbols change alphabet from one step to the next, to keep the work fresh
optionExplain: Rarity does not help the solver; a good sign should remind us at once of its object.
Right: a good sign is easy to remember and unambiguous, so it never stands for two things.
Length adds writing and does not make a sign easier to remember.
Switching alphabets without reason adds confusion and breaks the order of the signs.
questions.explain: The card next lists the author's qualities.
questions.rule: Memorable, unambiguous.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each feature as something a good notation has or something it avoids.

items.t: Easy to remember
Unambiguous
Order of signs suggests order of things
Harmful second meanings
Same symbol for two objects in one inquiry
Hard to recognise

questions.explain: The author asks for the first three and warns against the last three.
questions.rule: Qualities and faults.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which choice of letters for the sides of a triangle best suggests their connection to its vertices A, B, C?
options: p opposite A, k opposite B, w opposite C
A, B, C for the sides as well
1, 2, 3 for the sides and vertices alike
a opposite A, b opposite B, c opposite C
optionExplain: The letters show no link with the vertices.
One alphabet would be used for different objects.
The same signs would be used for different objects.
Matching letters link sides and vertices.
questions.explain: Order and connection of signs should suggest the order and connection of things.
questions.rule: Letters should hint the link.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two of these does the author list among the qualities of a good notation? Select two.
options: It is easy to remember
It is as short as the writer can make it, whatever it expresses
It takes advantage of useful second meanings
It uses a new symbol for each step of the work
optionExplain: Right: the author asks for a notation that is easy to remember.
Brevity is not on his list; a very short sign may express too little, and he asks for signs chosen for good reasons.
Right: he asks us to take advantage of useful second meanings of words and signs.
He prefers one sign per object and warns against using several wantonly, so a new symbol for each step goes against him.
questions.explain: Easy to remember and useful second meanings are named; more symbols and whim are not.
questions.rule: Name the qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say about using more than one sign for the same object?
options: It is not forbidden and can be advantageous, but needs particular care
It is forbidden in every case, since one object must have exactly one sign in all writing
It is always better than using one sign
It is harmless and needs no particular care, since several signs make a formula easy to read
optionExplain: Right: using more than one sign for the same object is not forbidden and can be advantageous, but needs particular care.
He says it is not forbidden, so a ban in every case goes beyond his words.
He says one sign is usually better.
He asks for particular care, so it is not harmless.
questions.explain: Different signs for the same object are allowed; the same sign for different objects is not.
questions.rule: One-to-one is the usual rule.
questions.teaches: It is not forbidden to use different symbols for the same object, but such cases require particular care and several signs should not be used wantonly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A spreadsheet uses 'T' for both temperature and time in the same model. Which quality of a good notation does this break?
options: Being pregnant
Being easy to remember
Being unambiguous
Suggesting order of things
optionExplain: Pregnant concerns how much a notation expresses; the fault here is double meaning.
The letter T is easy to remember; the fault is its two meanings.
One sign stands for two objects.
The fault is not about the order of signs.
questions.explain: The same symbol must not denote two different objects in the same inquiry.
questions.rule: One symbol, one object.
questions.teaches: It is inadmissible for the same symbol to denote two different objects in the same inquiry, though it may be used in a different meaning in a different problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In one problem, you have named a rectangle's width a. A second quantity appears. What should you do with the letter a?
options: Reuse a for the new quantity as well, since both quantities are lengths and a suits both
Use a for the larger of the two quantities
Drop the letter a altogether and use words, since letters are likely to be confused in a problem
Keep a for the width and choose another letter for the new quantity
optionExplain: Both would then be indistinguishable.
Which one is larger may change as the work goes on.
Letters are shorter and fine when kept distinct.
One letter, one meaning in the same problem.
questions.explain: The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: One meaning per symbol.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author allows the letter a to be used in a different meaning in a different problem.
questions.explain: The ban holds within one inquiry only.
questions.rule: Different problem, different meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In a problem about a cone, a student uses r for the radius and, later, r for the rate of filling. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw, because the context of the problem makes it clear which meaning is intended
One symbol stands for two different objects in the same inquiry
The flaw is that r is not an initial
The flaw is the use of a letter rather than a number, since letters are less exact
optionExplain: Context is not enough; the rule is a strict one.
This is the ambiguity the author forbids.
Initials are fine, but r is taken twice.
Letters are the normal choice for quantities.
questions.explain: Use one symbol for one object within one problem.
questions.rule: Change one of the r's.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which writing of the product of a and b breaks the rule of unambiguous signs?
options: Writing a·b, with a raised dot between the two letters, for the product of a and b in the problem
Writing ab, with the two letters side by side and no sign between them, for the product
Writing a x b for the product and also using x for an unknown in the same problem
Writing a×b alone, with no other use of the multiplication sign anywhere in the problem
optionExplain: A raised dot is a normal sign for the product and has no second job in this problem.
Writing the letters side by side is a normal way to write a product and clashes with nothing here.
Right: the multiplication sign and the unknown x now share one symbol, so the sign has a second meaning in the same problem.
The cross is a normal sign for the product, and since nothing else uses it here, no clash arises.
questions.explain: The author notes a x b, a·b and ab all denote the product; a clash arises when a sign gets a second job.
questions.rule: Do not give a sign two jobs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The author does not forbid using different ____ for the same object, as in a x b, a·b and ab for a product.
questions.explain: Several signs for one object are allowed; one sign for several objects in the same inquiry is not.
questions.rule: One object may have several signs.
questions.teaches: The product of a and b may be written as a x b, a·b or ab: using different signs for the same object is not forbidden, though it needs care.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A chemist writes C for carbon in one equation and C for concentration in the next line of the same working. By the author's rule, what should she do?
options: Keep both, since chemistry readers will guess from context
Drop symbols and write only in words for the rest of the working, to avoid any possible clash
Give concentration another symbol, since one symbol must not denote two objects in one inquiry
Use C for carbon in every later problem too, even if that makes it a different meaning each time
optionExplain: Readers should not have to guess.
Words are not required; the fix is to give the two quantities different signs.
The ban applies within the inquiry.
Reuse in later problems is fine; the issue is within this one.
questions.explain: Within one inquiry, one symbol names one object.
questions.rule: Rename the clash.
questions.teaches: A symbol that clashes within one inquiry should be replaced for one of the objects, while the same letter may serve in a different meaning in a different problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You need symbols for price, quantity and total in a shop problem. Which choice makes them easiest to recognise?
options: p, q and T, the initials of the things named
x, y and z, the standard unknowns
a, b and c, since they come first in the alphabet
Greek letters, since they are less common
optionExplain: Right: initials such as p, q and T recall the objects they stand for.
They carry no hint of what they stand for here.
They suggest givens, not a particular meaning.
Rarity does not make them memorable.
questions.explain: The card next explains why initials help.
questions.rule: Initials remind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A simple device to make signs easily recognisable is to use ____ as symbols.
questions.explain: The author names initials as the simple device.
questions.rule: Use initials.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A problem has a rate r and also a radius. Which is the best fix, following the author's remark?
options: Use r for both quantities and rely on the context to show which one is meant in each formula
Rename the rate and use r for the radius instead, since the radius is the more important object
Replace both quantities by numbers from the start, so no letters are needed
Keep r for the rate and choose a different sign for the radius
optionExplain: The ambiguity rule forbids one letter for two quantities, and context alone does not remove the risk.
Possible, but the author keeps r for the rate and moves the radius.
Letters are needed for general unknowns, so replacing both by numbers loses the generality of the problem.
The letter is taken, so another sign is needed.
questions.explain: A letter cannot serve both; the author lets r stand for the rate.
questions.rule: Handle clashes explicitly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: With initials r (rate), t (time) and V (volume), what does a reader likely think when meeting the letter t in a formula?
options: Temperature, since t is the usual symbol for it
Time, since t is the initial
A triangle's side
A constant
optionExplain: Nothing in this problem points to temperature; the initial t recalls time here.
Right: the letter t is the initial of time, which recalls the object.
Nothing about the letter t suggests the side of a triangle; no such prompt is given.
t was introduced for the time, so the initial does not suggest a fixed constant.
questions.explain: A good sign immediately reminds us of the object.
questions.rule: Signs remind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the author's example the radius could not be called r, because r was already used to denote a rate.
questions.explain: Initials cannot be used in every case; here r was taken by the rate.
questions.rule: Letters may be taken.
questions.teaches: In the author's example the radius could not be called r, since r was already taken to denote a rate.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A coach records Distance, Duration and Dose in one sports study. All three begin with D. What does the author's remark suggest?
options: Use D for all three and keep the context in mind, since all three are quantities in the same study
Give up symbols and describe each quantity in words every time it appears in the study
Choose letters at random so that no initial can be mistaken for the object it names
Initials alone will not do; use other means to keep the signs recognisable
optionExplain: This violates the ambiguity rule.
Giving up symbols loses their help; symbols remain useful if the letters are chosen with care.
Random letters lose the recognisability that initials give, so the object is not recalled.
Clashing initials need another device.
questions.explain: There are other means to make signs recognisable besides initials.
questions.rule: When initials clash, find another device.
questions.teaches: There are still other means to make symbols easily recognisable, besides initials; the next cards discuss them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A problem gives three lengths and asks for an unknown length. Which choice of letters best shows which are given and which unknown?
options: a, b, c for the given lengths and x for the unknown
p, d, s for the givens and q for the unknown
x, y, z for the givens and a for the unknown
x for all four lengths, given and unknown
optionExplain: The start and end of the alphabet mark givens and unknowns.
The letters follow no pattern that shows their roles.
This reverses the usual convention.
One letter would stand for several objects.
questions.explain: The card next gives the convention.
questions.rule: Start for givens, end for unknowns.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Letters at the beginning of the alphabet generally denote given quantities, and letters at the end denote ____.
questions.explain: The author states this convention.
questions.rule: Unknowns at the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A budget problem gives annual income and annual rent, and asks for monthly savings. Which letters follow the convention?
options: x and y for income and rent, a for the savings
z and a for income and rent, b for the savings
a and b for income and rent, x for the savings
m for all three amounts
optionExplain: This reverses the roles of early and late letters.
Z and a follow no alphabetical pattern, so they hide that income and rent play the same role.
Givens early in the alphabet, the unknown late.
One sign would name several objects.
questions.explain: Early letters for givens, late letters for unknowns.
questions.rule: Givens first, unknowns last.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student sets up a : b = x : y for two rectangles. Which two of her remarks match the intended reading of the letters?
options: a and b are constants, and x and y are variables
a stands to b as x stands to y
a stands to x as b stands to y, which is the same statement
The letters tell nothing about which are given
optionExplain: The early pair is given and the late pair unknown.
a precedes b as x precedes y, suggesting the same relation.
Pairing across the colon reads the proportion differently.
Their position in the alphabet does tell.
questions.explain: The letters hint that a, b are constants and x, y variables, with matching order.
questions.rule: Order mirrors relation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the proportion a : b = x : y, a and x are horizontal and b and y vertical. What do the letters suggest about a and x?
options: That a and x are unrelated, since they are different letters standing for different lengths
That a is larger than x, since a comes earlier in the alphabet and so names the bigger length
That a and b are unknowns, since they form the first pair of letters in the proportion
That a is to b as x is to y, the same relation
optionExplain: The matching positions in the two ratios link a with x and b with y, so they are not unrelated.
The alphabet order of letters does not tell size, so nothing suggests a is larger than x.
In this proportion a and b are given constants, not unknowns.
Right: matching positions suggest that a is to b as x is to y, the same relation.
questions.explain: a precedes b as x precedes y, suggesting that a is in the same relation to b as x is to y.
questions.rule: Position hints relation.
questions.teaches: In the author's example a and x are horizontal, b and y vertical, and a : b = x : y, so the order of the letters matches the relation of the lengths.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A tank problem must keep the horizontal length, the horizontal width and the vertical height apart because only the height matters for pressure. Which notation does the author prefer when roles differ?
options: a, b, c, because successive letters make it plain that the three lengths of the tank are all given
The initials l, w, h
x, y, z
a, a1, a2
optionExplain: Successive letters stress that the three play the same role, which is not the case here.
Initials tell which length is which.
The letters x, y, z suggest unknowns, not three lengths with different roles.
These suggest the three lengths are alike.
questions.explain: When the three lengths play different roles and it matters which is horizontal and which vertical, l, w, h might be preferable.
questions.rule: Different roles, different letters.
questions.teaches: If the three lengths play different roles and it is important to know which are horizontal and which vertical, the notation l, w, h might be preferable to a, b, c.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In a geometry problem you have points, lines and angles to name. What scheme keeps their kinds apart at a glance?
options: The letter x for everything, with subscripts added only when asked
Numbers for points and letters for lines
A different style of letter for each kind of object
Whatever letters come first in the alphabet
optionExplain: Using x for everything hides the kinds of object instead of showing them.
Numbers do not mark categories the way alphabets can; a number tells nothing about whether it names a point or a line.
Right: a different style of letter for each kind of object shows the kind at a glance.
Taking whatever letters come first follows no pattern, so the kind of object is not shown.
questions.explain: The card next describes the author's scheme.
questions.rule: Alphabets mark categories.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each geometric object to the usual style of letter.
pairs: Small Roman letters a, b, c
Small Greek letters alpha, beta, gamma
questions.explain: These are the author's three alphabets.
questions.rule: Know the three alphabets.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A triangle has vertices P, Q, R. By the scheme, what are good names for its sides?
options: Small Roman letters p, q, r
Small Greek letters
Capital letters P, Q, R again
The numbers 1, 2, 3
optionExplain: Sides are lines, and matching letters link them to the vertices.
Small Greek letters are conventionally used for angles, not for sides.
Capitals already name the points.
Numbers show no link to the vertices.
questions.explain: Sides are lines, so small Roman letters; matching letters show the relation.
questions.rule: Match letters across categories.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the standard triangle notation, the small letter a names the side opposite the vertex A.
questions.explain: The author states it is understood that a is the side opposite the vertex A.
questions.rule: a faces A.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the standard notation of a triangle, which angle is called alpha?
options: The angle at the vertex B
The angle opposite the side b
The angle at the vertex A
The angle between sides a and b
optionExplain: B pairs with the angle beta, so the angle at vertex B is not alpha.
The side b lies opposite vertex B, whose angle is beta, so this is not alpha.
Right: by the convention alpha is the angle at vertex A.
The angle between sides a and b lies at vertex C, so it is gamma.
questions.explain: The angle at A is called alpha.
questions.rule: Alpha belongs to A.
questions.teaches: It is understood that a is the side opposite the vertex A and that the angle at A is called alpha.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In a study of two teams, you must name team captains and their deputies, who are each closely tied to one captain. Which idea from the author fits?
options: Use corresponding letters from two alphabets, such as A and a
Use the same letter in the same alphabet for both captain and deputy, with a subscript for the deputy
Use unrelated letters so that nothing about the pairing is suggested by the notation at all
Use numbers only, since numbers are neutral and cannot be confused with any other symbol
optionExplain: Related objects of different categories get matching letters.
The same sign would then denote two different objects.
This throws away the relation that matters.
Numbers do not display categories as alphabets can.
questions.explain: If two objects of different categories have an important relation, choose corresponding letters of their alphabets.
questions.rule: Pair letters for related objects.
questions.teaches: If two objects belong to different categories but have a particular relation important to the problem, we may denote them by corresponding letters of the respective alphabets, as A and a, B and b.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Two ways of writing that two triangles are similar exist: one fixes which vertex matches which, the other does not. Which is more useful?
options: The one that omits the matching, because it is shorter
Both are equal, since the figure is always at hand
The one that omits the matching, since vertices do not matter
The one that fixes the matching, because more can be read from it
optionExplain: Shortness loses the matching of vertices, so the shorter form says less.
The point is to work without the figure.
The matching decides which angles are equal.
More information in the sign means more consequences.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's term.
questions.rule: More expressed, more useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A notation expressing more than another is called more ____.
questions.explain: The author calls a notation that expresses more more pregnant.
questions.rule: Pregnant means expressive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle EFG with vertices matched in order. AB = 6, BC = 9, EF = 4. What is FG?
optionExplain: This uses FG = 4 x 6 / 9, inverting the ratio.
AB : BC = EF : FG gives 6 : 9 = 4 : FG, so FG = 4 x 9 / 6 = 6.
This multiplies 9 by 6 / 4, matching AB with FG.
This copies BC without scaling; FG is not equal to BC, since the second triangle is smaller.
questions.explain: Corresponding sides: AB goes with EF and BC with FG.
questions.rule: Match in the written order.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle EFG with the vertices matched in the order written. Which two statements follow?
options: AB : BC = EF : FG
AB : BC = FG : EF
The angle at A equals the angle at G
The angle at A equals the angle at E
optionExplain: Right: with the vertices matched in order, AB and BC correspond to EF and FG, so the ratios are equal.
This swaps the second ratio: AB goes with EF and BC with FG, not the other way.
A corresponds to E, not G, so these two angles are not the ones matched.
Right: A corresponds to E, so the angles at A and at E are equal.
questions.explain: Matched in order: A to E, B to F, C to G.
questions.rule: Order tells the matching.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What was the drawback of the older way of writing similarity of triangles, according to the author?
options: It could not express the similarity of two triangles at all, so the figure always had to be drawn
The reader had to look at the figure or remember the derivation to see which vertex corresponded
It required special letters that the reader had to learn for each new book before using the formula
It confused similarity of triangles with congruence, so that a reader could not tell them apart
optionExplain: The old form could express the similarity, but it said less than the modern form does.
Right: the reader had to look at the figure or remember the derivation to see which vertex corresponded to which.
The text mentions no need to learn special letters for each book.
The text mentions no confusion of similarity with congruence.
questions.explain: The older notation expressed less and did not allow definite consequences.
questions.rule: Older form said less.
questions.teaches: In older books the matching order of vertices was not part of the formula, so the reader had to look at the figure or remember the derivation to know which vertex corresponded to which.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: One recipe app gives flour to sugar as the ratio 3 to 1 with no units; another gives 300 g of flour to 100 g of sugar. Which is more pregnant?
options: The first, because it is shorter and a shorter sign is always the more pregnant one
Neither, because a ratio is a ratio and both say the same thing about the recipe
The first, because ratios of small whole numbers are easier to remember than ratios of larger ones
The second, because it lets you draw more consequences, such as the amounts
optionExplain: Brevity is not pregnancy; the second ratio says more, and a shorter sign may say less.
The two do not say the same: they differ in the consequences that can be drawn from them.
Memorability is a separate quality of a notation; pregnancy is about how much the sign expresses.
Right: the second lets you draw more consequences, such as the actual amounts, so it expresses more.
questions.explain: A notation that expresses more can support more consequences.
questions.rule: More said, more drawn out.
questions.teaches: The modern notation for similarity reflects the order and connection of things more fully than the older one, and so it can serve as the basis for more consequences.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student defines e as the edge of a cube in a problem that also involves natural logarithms. What is the risk?
options: The traditional meaning of e may interfere and mislead
There is no risk, because any letter can be given any meaning that the writer chooses for it
The letter e cannot be used for anything in geometry, since it is reserved for analysis
The problem becomes unsolvable
optionExplain: e already stands for the base of natural logarithms.
Readers bring the traditional meaning with them.
It can be used; the risk is the clash of meanings.
The clash of e is a risk of confusion, but the problem does not become unsolvable; it only needs a different letter.
questions.explain: The card next explains second meanings.
questions.rule: Mind traditional meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The letter i usually stands for the imaginary unit, the square root of ____.
questions.explain: The text gives i as the imaginary unit, the square root of minus one.
questions.rule: i is root of -1.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A physics problem needs a symbol for a rate of interest. Which choice follows the author's advice about traditional symbols?
options: Use pi, because it looks like a p and so reminds the reader of percent in the problem
Use e, because it is a short letter that is quick to write in a long calculation
Avoid pi and e for it, since they have rooted traditional meanings
Use i, because interest begins with i and the letter recalls its object at once
optionExplain: The traditional meaning could interfere.
e is the base of natural logarithms, so a clash may occur.
They are better used only in their traditional meaning.
i is the imaginary unit; a clash may occur.
questions.explain: It is on the whole better to use such symbols only in their traditional meaning.
questions.rule: Keep rooted symbols for their role.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: When is a second meaning of a symbol helpful rather than harmful, according to the author?
options: When it blends with the present meaning of the symbol so that both are read at once by the reader
When the reader is unaware of the earlier use of the symbol and so cannot be misled by it
Never; second meanings of symbols are harmful in every case and should be avoided by the writer
When a notation used before helps to recall a procedure and the present meaning is kept distinct
optionExplain: Blending is what causes trouble: two meanings read at once confuse the reader.
The help arises from recalling the earlier use, so a reader unaware of it gains nothing.
He says second meanings can be very helpful if used with tact, so they are not harmful in every case.
Right: used with tact, an earlier notation recalls a procedure while the present meaning is kept distinct.
questions.explain: Separate the present meaning clearly from the former one.
questions.rule: Use tact.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, harmful second meanings of symbols give less trouble to a beginner than to an experienced mathematician.
questions.explain: The beginner has not yet studied many subjects, so fewer associations clash; the mathematician has more to deal with.
questions.rule: Experts meet more clashes.
questions.teaches: Harmful second meanings of symbols give less trouble to the beginner who has not yet studied many subjects than to the mathematician.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In every problem, a physics student writes force as F, mass as m and acceleration as a. What advantage of notation does this show?
options: It makes the notation more pregnant than any other, since each symbol now carries its own history
It removes the need to define symbols in each new problem, since the reader knows them already
A standing notation helps in recalling formulas and procedures used on former occasions
It guarantees that no symbol will ever carry a second meaning, since each is fixed for good
optionExplain: Pregnancy concerns how much a sign expresses, not how often it is reused.
Definitions still matter where the usage differs.
Constant symbols make earlier work easy to recall.
Standing symbols are second meanings of a helpful sort.
questions.explain: We remember our formulas in some standing notation, so keep it when you can.
questions.rule: Keep a standing notation.
questions.teaches: We remember our formulas in some standing notation, so a notation used on several former occasions may assist us in recalling formerly used procedures.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A bright student resists learning algebraic notation. What is the most likely reason?
options: She finds it arbitrary and a burden on memory, and sees no reward for it
She lacks the intelligence to learn it, and so she fails to see why anyone would bother with it
She has never met a mathematical problem that was hard enough to need a language of symbols
She believes that numbers are always better than symbols, and has weighed the evidence on both sides
optionExplain: This is the author's explanation.
The author says intelligent students may share this aversion.
The aversion has little to do with how many problems she has met.
The text describes no belief that numbers are always better than symbols, nor any weighing of evidence.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's explanation.
questions.rule: Doubt is reasonable without reward.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, an intelligent student may be justified in disliking algebra if he is not given opportunity to see for himself that symbols assist the mind.
questions.explain: He says the student is justified in that case.
questions.rule: Show the compensation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student keeps asking why she must learn letters instead of working with numbers. Which response follows the author's advice?
options: Tell her she will understand when she is older and has met more of mathematics, so she should wait
Insist that notation is arbitrary and must be learned by rote, like the spelling of words in school
Give her a problem that is far easier in symbols, so she meets the benefit herself
Skip algebra for her entirely, since she dislikes it and will not be asked to use it later
optionExplain: This offers no compensation now.
The author grants that it is arbitrary, but a burden needs a reward.
Experience convinces; argument does not.
The aim is to convince her, not to skip it.
questions.explain: To help him to such experience is an important task of the teacher.
questions.rule: Let her feel the benefit.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Two notations are available and each has an advantage. What does the author say should decide?
options: Experience and taste, informed by the known advantages and disadvantages, and a good reason for the choice
The notation used in the largest number of textbooks, since that is the one readers will meet most
The shorter notation in every case, since brevity saves effort and space on the page of the work
A coin toss, since all notations are equal and no reason can be given for preferring any of them
optionExplain: Right: the choice rests on experience and taste, informed by the known advantages and disadvantages, and on a good reason.
Popularity is not offered as the reason.
Brevity is one consideration only.
He says they differ and a reason is needed.
questions.explain: We should choose carefully and have some good reason.
questions.rule: Choose with a reason.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Checking a formula by extensive discussion of its ____ is recommended as a particularly instructive exercise.
questions.explain: The author recommends discussing a formula's properties at length as an instructive exercise.
questions.rule: Discuss the formula.
questions.teaches: Checking a formula by extensive discussion of its properties is recommended as a particularly instructive exercise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A teacher wonders whether motivating symbols is an easy task. What does the author say?
options: It is easy and needs little thought, since a student who sees one example will see the point at once
It is an important task, one of the teacher's most important, but not an easy one
It is unimportant compared with covering the syllabus, which is the first duty of every teacher
It is a task for the student alone, since only the student can decide to find symbols useful
optionExplain: He denies that motivating symbols is easy, so a single example cannot be assumed to be enough.
Right: he calls it an important task, one of the teacher's most important, but not an easy one.
He calls the task important, so it cannot be set aside as less important than the syllabus.
He gives the task to the teacher, not to the student alone.
questions.explain: He calls motivating symbols an important task, one of the teacher's most important, but not an easy one.
questions.rule: Important but hard.
questions.teaches: The author says that helping students experience how symbols assist the mind is one of the teacher's most important tasks, but not an easy one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A body of doctrine is said to be for those who have studied the ordinary Elements and want to solve problems. Which description fits?
options: A first textbook of arithmetic for beginners who have not yet met the ordinary geometry of the Elements
A guide to solving mathematical problems for readers who already know the basics
A history of Greek mathematics, giving the lives and the discoveries of the main Greek geometers
A set of tables for astronomers, giving the positions of stars and planets for use in navigation
optionExplain: A first arithmetic book would not presuppose the Elements, which this doctrine does.
Right: it is a guide to solving problems that builds on the Elements.
It is about solving problems, not history.
Tables of star positions are not the doctrine; nothing like it is described.
questions.explain: The card next names the author and the study.
questions.rule: Know the audience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Pappus lived probably around A.D. ____.
questions.explain: The text gives about A.D. 300.
questions.rule: About A.D. 300.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A reader asks what Pappus's study was good for. Which statement matches his claim?
options: It is useful for every sort of human activity, from farming to war, as well as for mathematics
It is a purely historical study of how earlier Greeks solved problems, with no use for new ones
It replaces the ordinary Elements, so that a student need not first study the Elements at all
It is useful for solving mathematical problems and for this alone
optionExplain: The rendering says the study is useful for solving mathematical problems and for this alone, not for every human activity.
It is a practical doctrine for solving problems, not a purely historical study.
It comes after the Elements, so it does not replace them.
Right: it is useful for solving mathematical problems and for this alone, in his own wording.
questions.explain: It is for those who studied the Elements and want to solve mathematical problems.
questions.rule: Know the claim.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two men does Pappus name, with Aristaeus the elder, as makers of the work?
options: Descartes
Euclid, the author of the Elements
Apollonius of Perga
Archimedes of Syracuse
optionExplain: Descartes lived long after Pappus, so he cannot be among the makers Pappus names.
Right: Pappus names Euclid, the author of the Elements, among the makers.
Right: Pappus names Apollonius of Perga among the makers.
Archimedes is not named in this passage.
questions.explain: The three named are Euclid, Apollonius and Aristaeus the elder.
questions.rule: Three named authors.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which three English renderings does the author mention for the Greek name analyomenos?
options: Treasury of Analysis, Art of Solving Problems, Heuristic
Book of Proofs, Art of Logic, Mathematics of the Elements, offered as the three possible names
Method of Exhaustion, Geometry, Algebra, offered as the three possible names of the study
Analysis, Synthesis, Construction, which are the procedures taught rather than names of the study
optionExplain: Right: these are the three renderings the author mentions, and he prefers the last, Heuristic.
These names do not occur among the renderings of the Greek title.
These are not renderings of the Greek name; they are names of mathematical subjects.
These are the procedures the report teaches, not names for the study itself.
questions.explain: The three renderings are Treasury of Analysis, Art of Solving Problems and Heuristic.
questions.rule: Three names.
questions.teaches: The author renders analyomenos as Treasury of Analysis, as Art of Solving Problems, or as Heuristic, and he prefers the last term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A modern translator wants a literal English text of Pappus's report. Where does the author say a good translation is easily accessible?
options: In the author's own appendix, where the literal Greek text is set out line by line with notes
Only in the Greek original, since no translation of the report has been made into English
In T. L. Heath's edition of Euclid's Elements
In a work by Descartes, who copied out the report with a commentary on each of its parts
optionExplain: He gives a free rendering of the report, not a literal text set out line by line.
He says an accessible translation exists, so the Greek original is not the only source.
Right: he points to T. L. Heath's edition of Euclid's Elements.
He does not cite Descartes as copying out the report.
questions.explain: A good English translation is in Heath's Euclid.
questions.rule: Cite the translation.
questions.teaches: A good English translation of Pappus's report is easily accessible in T. L. Heath's The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements, while the text given here is a free rendering.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You want to prove a statement. Which opening move works backwards?
options: Start from a known fact and wander forward from it until you happen to reach the statement
Verify the statement for one example and stop there, since one example settles the matter
Wait for the answer from a friend, who may already know how the statement can be reached
Assume the statement and ask what it would follow from
optionExplain: This moves forward, not backward.
One example does not settle a statement and is not a method that works backwards from it.
Waiting for a friend is not a method of reasoning about the statement.
Right: assume the statement and ask what it would follow from, which works back from the required.
questions.explain: The card next names this move.
questions.rule: Assume, then ask what precedes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In analysis, we start from what is ____, take it for granted, and draw consequences from it.
questions.explain: Analysis begins with what is required.
questions.rule: Begin with the required.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: To get a bridge across a river, a team first asks what would make a crossing possible, then what would allow that, and so on. Which procedure is it?
options: Synthesis, which builds forward from known facts
Analysis, working back from the required result
Guessing, which looks for no antecedents
Specialisation, which narrows the problem
optionExplain: Synthesis builds forward from known facts and comes second, after the analysis.
Each step asks for the antecedent.
Guessing looks for no antecedents, whereas the team keeps asking what would allow each step.
Specialisation narrows the problem to a special case, which is not what the team does.
questions.explain: Analysis asks what could precede the desired result.
questions.rule: Ask for antecedents.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Order the stages of an analysis.
items: Assume what is required as already done
Ask from what antecedent it could be derived
Ask what could be the antecedent of that antecedent
Reach something already known or admittedly true
questions.explain: Analysis passes from antecedent to antecedent until known ground appears.
questions.rule: Backwards chain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Besides analysis, what two other names does the text give for this procedure?
options: Progressive reasoning and constructive solution
Direct proof and indirect proof
Solution backwards and regressive reasoning
Induction and deduction
optionExplain: These names belong to synthesis, which goes forward, not to analysis.
Direct and indirect proof are different notions that do not name analysis.
Right: the text calls analysis also solution backwards and regressive reasoning.
Induction and deduction are different notions that do not name analysis.
questions.explain: Analysis is also solution backwards or regressive reasoning.
questions.rule: Three names.
questions.teaches: Analysis is also called solution backwards, or regressive reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A detective starts from the fact that the safe was opened and asks what must have happened immediately before, then before that. Which feature of analysis does this show?
options: Passing from antecedent to antecedent from the thing to be explained
Moving from a known fact straight to the conclusion, without asking what lay behind the event
Doubting that anything was done, so that no consequences can be drawn from the opened safe
Counting the suspects and ranking them by their opportunity, without any chain of antecedents
optionExplain: Right: the detective passes from antecedent to antecedent, starting from the thing to be explained.
Moving from a known fact straight to the conclusion is synthesis, not analysis.
Analysis assumes that what is required was done, so it does not doubt that anything happened.
Ranking suspects by opportunity involves no chain of antecedents, which is the mark of analysis.
questions.explain: Analysis proceeds from what is required back to what is known.
questions.rule: Work backwards.
questions.teaches: Analysis can end at a point already known, which then serves as the starting point of synthesis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An analysis has ended at a fact you already know. What is the next step?
options: Start analysing the known fact again, to see whether it too rests on something simpler still
Discard the known fact as trivial and look for a harder fact to serve as the starting point
Go from that fact forward through the steps found, to the required result
Repeat the analysis from a different required result, in case the first chain was a mistake
optionExplain: The analysis has ended at a known fact, so analysing that fact again would be needless.
The known fact is the starting point of the finished solution, so it should not be discarded.
Right: go from that fact forward through the steps found, to the required result.
The chain was found by a sound analysis, so repeating it is not necessary.
questions.explain: The card next names this synthesis.
questions.rule: Retrace forward.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Synthesis is also called constructive solution, or ____ reasoning.
questions.explain: The text names synthesis progressive reasoning.
questions.rule: Progressive reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An analysis of a geometry problem ended at the fact that two sides are equal, which is known. Which is the synthesis?
options: Start from the equal sides and derive each earlier step in turn until the required result
Start from the required result and assume it, then ask what could precede it in the argument
Show again that the two sides are equal, using the same argument as before without any new step
Test a few special cases of the problem to see whether the required result seems to hold in them
optionExplain: Right: starting from the equal sides and reversing the steps found retraces the analysis.
Starting by assuming the required result and asking what could precede it is the analysis itself.
The equal sides are the starting point, so merely showing them again adds no new step to the solution.
Testing special cases is a different procedure and is not the synthesis.
questions.explain: Synthesis starts where analysis ended.
questions.rule: Retrace forward.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In synthesis the order of derivation is the reverse of the order followed in the analysis.
questions.explain: Synthesis goes from the last point of the analysis back to the beginning.
questions.rule: Reverse order.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say the same objects do in analysis and in synthesis?
options: They are different in each
They appear only in the analysis
They appear only in the synthesis
They fill both, but in reverse order
optionExplain: The same objects appear in both, so it is wrong to say they differ in each.
They appear in the synthesis as well as in the analysis.
They appear in the analysis as well as in the synthesis.
Right: the same objects fill both procedures, but in reverse order.
questions.explain: The same objects fill the analysis and the synthesis.
questions.rule: Same objects, reversed.
questions.teaches: The same objects fill the analysis and the synthesis, but the order is reversed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A cook finds, by working back from the dish, that she needs to chop onions first. Which part does she carry out when she starts cooking?
options: The analysis, again, since she must ask once more what comes before the onions on her list
The synthesis, which retraces the analysed steps in forward order
A new problem, since cooking is a different matter from the thinking that came before it
A specialisation, since she now cooks one particular dish instead of dishes in general
optionExplain: The analysis is already done, so she need not ask again what comes before the onions.
Right: starting to cook retraces the analysed steps in forward order, which is the synthesis.
It is the same problem, now being executed, not a new one.
She is carrying out one found plan, not specialising to a particular case.
questions.explain: Synthesis carries out the plan found in the analysis.
questions.rule: Execute the plan.
questions.teaches: Synthesis is the step in which the plan found by analysis is carried through.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: From an unproved claim A you derive B, then C, and C turns out false. What do you conclude about A?
options: A is true, since B was derived from it and so A must be well founded in the first place
A is false, since a false consequence cannot come from a true A
Nothing at all can be said about A, since a false consequence leaves its truth undecided
C must be re-derived and A kept, since a consequence that is false has probably been mistaken
optionExplain: Derivation from A proves nothing about A itself.
A consequence of A is false, so A fails.
A false consequence is enough to settle A, since a true claim cannot lead to a falsehood.
C's falsity is not in doubt in the question.
questions.explain: The card next states the logic of this analysis.
questions.rule: False consequence, false A.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the analysis of a problem to prove, if the last theorem L is true, then A is also true provided all our derivations are ____.
questions.explain: The proviso is that the derivations are convertible.
questions.rule: Convertible derivations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: To test a theorem T you derive U, then V, and V is a well-known true theorem. Every step is reversible. What follows?
options: T is false, since V is already known and so cannot have anything to do with the truth of T
Nothing follows, since V is only a consequence of T and a consequence proves nothing at all
U must be false, since it stands between T and the known theorem V in the chain of reasoning
T is true, and you prove it by going back from V to U to T
optionExplain: The truth of V does not refute T; a true consequence does not make T false.
With reversible steps it proves T.
Nothing in the chain shows that U is false; U is a step on the way from T to V.
The reversible chain lets you retrace.
questions.explain: Reversible steps carry truth back from L to A.
questions.rule: Retrace from the known.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Put the steps of proving a theorem A by Pappus's analysis and synthesis in order.
items: Derive B from A, then C from B, and so on
Reach a last theorem L about which definite knowledge exists
Find that L is true
Prove the theorem before L from L, and retrace until A is proved
questions.explain: The analysis runs forward from A to L; the synthesis returns from L to A.
questions.rule: Down the chain, back up.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does Pappus say follows if the final theorem L of the analysis is false?
options: A has been proved false
Nothing about A
A is true but unprovable
The derivations must have been wrong
optionExplain: A false consequence of A disproves A.
The text says A is false, so something can be said about A.
The text says A is false, not that it is true but unprovable.
The conclusion stands if the derivations are sound.
questions.explain: If L is false, then A is false, because a true claim cannot have a false consequence.
questions.rule: False end, false start.
questions.teaches: If the last theorem L reached by the analysis is false, then the original theorem A has been proved false.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A manager reasons: if the new policy A were true, sales would double, and then profits would double; profits did not double. What does the pattern of Pappus suggest?
options: The policy claim is proved, because the reasoning from the claim to the consequence was sound
Profits are irrelevant, since only sales were mentioned in the original claim about the policy
The policy claim is refuted, provided the reasoning from A to the consequence is sound
The policy claim is neither true nor false, since profits depend on many things besides policy
optionExplain: A false consequence does not prove the claim.
They are the false last step of the chain.
False consequence refutes the claim.
A false consequence decides it, if the steps are sound.
questions.explain: A false consequence disproves the assumption, if the derivations are sound.
questions.rule: Test by consequences.
questions.teaches: The analysis of a problem to prove aims at establishing true theorems, but it can also end by showing the theorem false.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You want a number x with a complicated property. Which way of starting follows Pappus?
options: Wait to find x by luck, trying numbers that come to mind until one happens to have the property
Check numbers at random from a long list, and stop when one of them seems to have the property
Declare that no such x can exist at once, since the property seems too complicated to be met
Assume such an x exists and ask what other unknown it depends on
optionExplain: Waiting for luck, with numbers tried as they come to mind, is not a method of analysis.
Random checking from a long list is not a method, and it may never find x.
Declaring that no such x exists, without analysis, is not justified.
Right: assume such an x exists and ask what other unknown it depends on, linking x to a simpler unknown.
questions.explain: The card next gives the chain from x to z.
questions.rule: Chain of unknowns.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the analysis of a problem to find, we first find the last unknown z, then, knowing z, we find the unknown that ____ z in the analysis.
questions.explain: We retrace our steps from z back.
questions.rule: Work back.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: To find the side x of a square with a given diagonal, you note that x depends on x squared, and that x squared is half the squared diagonal. In Pappus's terms, what is the last unknown?
options: The diagonal, which was already given
x squared, which can be found by a known method
x, the original unknown
The area of the circle through the vertices
optionExplain: It is given data, not an unknown.
The easiest unknown, found first.
x is the first unknown, found last.
Nothing in the problem points to it.
questions.explain: The last unknown of the analysis is found first in the synthesis.
questions.rule: Find the last unknown first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In an analysis you reach a last unknown z, and no z satisfies the condition imposed on it. What follows for the original problem?
options: It has a solution that is hard to find
It has two solutions
It has no solution
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: The chain says otherwise: if the last unknown cannot exist, no solution exists.
The chain gives no ground for two solutions.
Right: if z does not exist, then x does not exist, so the original problem has no solution.
The chain gives a definite answer, so something can be said.
questions.explain: If no z satisfies the condition, then no x can exist, so the original problem has no solution.
questions.rule: Check the last unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the analysis of a problem to find, Pappus assumes that there is an x satisfying the condition, although we do not yet know whether such a thing is possible.
questions.explain: The assumption is provisional: we assume an x exists in order to derive the next unknown from it.
questions.rule: Assume x exists.
questions.teaches: In the analysis of a problem to find we do not yet know whether a thing satisfying the condition is possible, but we assume there is an x satisfying it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A planner asks: to reach city X on time, I must catch train Y; to catch Y, I must leave by time Z. Which move comes first in carrying out the plan?
options: Settle X first, since the whole plan was built to reach X and everything else follows from it
Settle Y first, since the train is the middle of the chain and links the departure to the arrival
Settle Z, the last unknown, then Y, then X
Wait to see what happens on the day and decide each step as it comes, with no plan fixed beforehand
optionExplain: Settling X was the start of the analysis, not of carrying out the plan.
Y is the middle of the chain, so it cannot be settled before the last unknown.
Right: in carrying out the plan one settles the last unknown Z first, then Y, then X.
Deciding each step as it comes, with no plan, is not a method.
questions.explain: The synthesis finds z, then y, then x.
questions.rule: Last unknown first.
questions.teaches: After the analysis the unknowns are found in the reverse order: z first, then y, and finally x.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An equation contains 4 to the power x and 2 to the power x together. What substitution might simplify it?
options: Let y be 2 to the power x, since 4 to the power x is y squared
Let y be x squared, so that the exponents are turned into ordinary powers that are easy to handle
Divide through by x, since x occurs in every term of the equation and so can be removed
Take logarithms of both sides at once, which turns the powers into products that can be combined
optionExplain: This turns both terms into powers of y.
This does not simplify the exponents.
x is an exponent, not a factor, so dividing by x does not remove it from the terms.
This does not simplify a sum of powers.
questions.explain: The card next works the example.
questions.rule: Substitute y.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the example, with y = 2^x, which equation in y does 8(4^x + 4^-x) - 54(2^x + 2^-x) + 101 = 0 become?
optionExplain: This treats 4^x as 2y, but 4^x = (2^x)^2 = y^2.
This writes 4^x as y to the fourth, but it is y squared.
The signs stay plus, because 4^x and 4^-x are added in the original equation.
Right: 4^x = y^2 and 4^-x = 1/y^2, so the equation becomes 8(y^2 + 1/y^2) - 54(y + 1/y) + 101 = 0.
questions.rule: Square the substitution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: With z = y + 1/y, y^2 + 1/y^2 equals z^2 - 2. Which quadratic in z results from 8(y^2 + 1/y^2) - 54(y + 1/y) + 101 = 0?
optionExplain: This forgets the -2 correction in y^2 + 1/y^2 = z^2 - 2.
This adds 16 instead of subtracting.
This subtracts 16 twice, giving 69 where the correct constant is 85.
questions.rule: Remember the -2.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: For z = 5/2 the values of y are 2 and 1/2, so the values of x = log base 2 of y are 1 and ____.
questions.explain: y = 2 gives x = 1 and y = 1/2 gives x = -1, since 2^-1 = 1/2.
questions.rule: Solve in reverse.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which of these values solve the original equation 8(4^x + 4^-x) - 54(2^x + 2^-x) + 101 = 0?
optionExplain: Right: the equation is unchanged when x changes sign, so -2 works as well as 2.
17/4 is a value of z = y + 1/y, not of x.
5/2 is a value of z = y + 1/y, not of x.
questions.explain: The solutions are 1, -1, 2 and -2; the values 5/2 and 17/4 belong to z.
questions.rule: Walk back to x.
questions.teaches: The synthesis runs z = 5/2, 17/4; then y = 2, 1/2, 4, 1/4; and finally x = 1, -1, 2, -2, the opposite of the order of invention.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Another equation: 3(9^x + 9^-x) - 10(3^x + 3^-x) + 14 = 0. With y = 3^x and z = y + 1/y, which quadratic in z appears?
optionExplain: This forgets the -2 correction in y^2 + 1/y^2 = z^2 - 2.
This adds 6 instead of subtracting.
This subtracts 12 instead of 6, because 3 x 2 = 6 is the correction.
questions.explain: Same two substitutions, new numbers.
questions.rule: Reuse the pattern.
questions.teaches: The analysis ends when the problem has been reduced to one the solver knows how to solve, such as a quadratic equation, provided the solver is acquainted with its solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A man cannot wade a swollen creek. He thinks: a fallen tree would let me cross; a tree across the water needs a tree to fall. Which kind of reasoning is this?
options: Guessing the answer without reasoning
Copying another man's crossing
Working backwards from the wished-for result
Waiting for the water to fall
optionExplain: He does not guess; he reasons from the goal to what he needs.
He is not copying another man's crossing; he plans a crossing himself.
Right: working backwards from the wished-for result, each need leads to the one before it.
Waiting for the water to fall is not reasoning about the problem.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's name for it.
questions.rule: From goal to means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the creek story, the analysis consists in thoughts, the synthesis in ____.
questions.explain: The author says thoughts for analysis and acts for synthesis.
questions.rule: Thoughts then acts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A hiker wants to light a fire in the rain. She thinks: I need dry wood; dry wood is under the log; to lift the log I need a lever. Which is the first physical act?
options: Lighting the fire with the dry wood, since that is the goal for which she made her whole plan
Taking the dry wood from under the log, since that is the object she needs for the fire
Lifting the log, since it is the obstacle that stands between her and the dry wood she needs
Finding the lever, the last item of her analysis
optionExplain: That is her original goal and the last act.
That comes after the log is lifted.
That comes after the lever is found.
Synthesis starts with the last found.
questions.explain: The act order is reversed from the order of thought.
questions.rule: Start with the last item.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the creek story, walking across the creek is both the first desire from which the analysis starts and the last act with which the synthesis ends.
questions.explain: The order is reversed, so the object that opens the analysis closes the synthesis.
questions.rule: Same end, opposite order.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say the primitive man may become if he finishes his analysis?
options: The first mathematician, since he reasoned about means and ends in a way later called analysis
The founder of a city, since the bridge would bring settlers across the creek to live there
The inventor of the bridge and of the axe
The discoverer of fire, since the axe would give him wood to burn on the other bank of the creek
optionExplain: The author does not call him the first mathematician.
The author does not say he would found a city.
Right: the author says he may become the inventor of the bridge and of the axe.
The author does not credit him with the discovery of fire.
questions.explain: He may invent the bridge and the axe.
questions.rule: Analysis can invent.
questions.teaches: If the primitive man succeeds in finishing his analysis he may become the inventor of the bridge and of the axe.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student wants to call the creek story 'mathematics'. What does the author's use of the example show about analysis?
options: The procedure is not restricted to mathematics
The procedure is useful only for engineering, since the creek story is a problem of building
The procedure is a joke, since a primitive man cannot be said to carry out an analysis
The procedure works only for primitive men, who have no formal methods of their own to use
optionExplain: The creek is not a mathematical problem.
Not so; the author says the procedure is not restricted to mathematical problems.
Not so; the author takes the story seriously.
Not so; it is a general procedure.
questions.explain: Generality and independence of the subject matter are important.
questions.rule: Beyond mathematics.
questions.teaches: The procedures described by Pappus are not restricted to geometric problems, nor even to mathematical problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A builder first sketches how the pieces must fit and only then cuts timber. Which pairing fits analysis and synthesis?
options: Cutting is the analysis and sketching is the synthesis, since the cut is the first act on the timber
Both are the same step, since the sketch and the cut are two parts of a single piece of work
Sketching is the analysis, cutting and assembling the synthesis
Neither applies to building, since the procedure belongs to geometry and not to craft
optionExplain: Reversed: sketching how the pieces must fit is the analysis, and cutting is carrying out the plan.
The two differ as invention differs from execution, so they are not the same step.
Right: sketching how the pieces fit is the analysis, and cutting and assembling is the synthesis.
The procedure applies beyond geometry, so craft work such as building also fits the pairing.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's pairing.
questions.rule: Plan, then do.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each term to what the author says it is.
pairs: Order of calculation in the example
Opposite to the order of invention
questions.explain: Analysis is invention and devising a plan; synthesis is execution; the order of calculation reverses the order of invention.
questions.rule: Invent, then execute.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the algebra example the solver found y = 2^x and z = y + 1/y, then computed z, y, x. Which step is the invention?
options: Seeing the two substitutions
Finding z = 5/2 from the quadratic, which is the first value that the calculation delivers
Finding x = 1 from y = 2, which is the last step of the calculation and gives the answer
Checking the roots by putting them back into the equation, which confirms the whole work
optionExplain: Right: seeing the two substitutions is the idea, and the idea is the invention.
Finding z = 5/2 from the quadratic is a calculation once the substitutions are seen.
Finding x = 1 from y = 2 is the last calculation, not the idea that made the solution possible.
Checking the roots by putting them back is a calculation, not an invention.
questions.explain: The substitutions needed a good idea; the rest is patience and attention.
questions.rule: Ideas first, calculation later.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the algebra example the order of calculation in the synthesis is the same as the order in which the substitutions were invented.
questions.explain: The calculation runs z, then y, then x, the opposite of the order of invention.
questions.rule: Reverse order.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say the problem-solver needs in order to finish the algebra example after the analysis?
options: Another substitution, since the quadratic in z is still hard and needs one more clever idea
A new theory of equations, since the roots y and x need a method not yet available to the solver
A computer, since the numbers are awkward and the work would take too long by hand
No new idea, only patience and attention in calculating
optionExplain: The analysis ended with the quadratic in z, which needs no further clever idea.
No new theory of equations is needed; the quadratic is solved by familiar means.
The author mentions no computer; the numbers can be handled by hand.
Right: no new idea is needed, only patience and attention in calculating.
questions.explain: Execution needs care, not a new idea.
questions.rule: Careful work finishes it.
questions.teaches: After the analysis the problem-solver needs no new idea to finish, only some patience and attention in calculating the various unknowns.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student is told to submit the plan for an essay before writing it. Which pair does the author's contrast fit?
options: The writing is the analysis and the plan is the synthesis, since writing is where the thinking happens
The plan is analysis-like invention; the writing is synthesis-like execution
Both are analysis, since planning and writing are alike in that each asks what must come before
Both are synthesis, since both are acts of putting something together for a reader
optionExplain: Reversed: writing is the execution, which is synthesis-like, and the plan is the analysis-like invention.
Right: the plan is the analysis-like invention, and the writing is the synthesis-like execution.
Only the plan is analysis-like; the writing is the execution of the plan.
Only the writing is synthesis-like; the plan is the stage of invention.
questions.explain: Analysis is devising a plan, synthesis carrying through the plan.
questions.rule: Plan then write.
questions.teaches: The paraphrase of Pappus hints a little more distinctly than the original at the natural connection between analysis and synthesis: analysis comes naturally first and synthesis afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A friend says that assuming a problem solved is cheating, because you have not solved it. What is the best reply?
options: It is cheating, but cheating of that sort is allowed in mathematics when a problem is hard
The assumption is provisional, and if wrong the analysis will reveal that
It is not an assumption but a proof, since the solved problem is shown to be solved at once
It is needed only for geometry, where figures make the solved problem easy to picture
optionExplain: It is not cheating, because the assumption is only provisional and is tested in the analysis.
Right: the assumption is provisional, and if it is wrong the analysis will reveal that.
It is only an assumption, not a proof that the problem is solved.
The procedure applies widely, beyond geometry.
questions.explain: The card next gives four reasons.
questions.rule: Provisional assumption.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The assumption that a problem is solved is made in order to start the ____.
questions.explain: The text says the assumption is made just to start the analysis.
questions.rule: To start the analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You want a number x with certain properties and begin by supposing that such an x exists. If none exists, what will the analysis do?
options: Produce a false solution, because the assumed object cannot be told from a real one at the end
Prove that you cheated by assuming the problem solved, and so undo all the work done so far
Stop with no result at all, because no chain of consequences can be built on an object that does not exist
Lead eventually to a final problem that has no solution
optionExplain: It would reveal that there is no solution, not give a false one.
It proves nothing of the kind; the assumption is only provisional.
It reaches a final problem that has no solution, which is a result, not a stop with nothing.
Right: the analysis leads eventually to a final problem that has no solution, which shows the original has none.
questions.explain: If there is no such object, the analysis is bound to lead to a final problem with no solution.
questions.rule: The assumption is harmless.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each reason as one the author gives for assuming the problem solved, or not.

items.t: It is harmless
It is useful for examining the condition
It is natural
It guarantees a solution exists
It replaces proof
It is required by law

questions.explain: Harmless, useful and natural are the three; the others are not claimed.
questions.rule: Three reasons.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Why does the author say the assumption is useful when examining the condition?
options: To see the relations the condition prescribes between x and the data, we have to picture x as existent
