It lets us skip the condition of the problem, since the assumed object already satisfies it by definition
It proves that the unknown x exists, so that the rest of the work is only a matter of finding it
It reduces the number of data that must be taken into account, since the unknown stands in for several
optionExplain: The relations need x to be pictured.
The condition remains to be examined.
It proves nothing about existence; the assumption is provisional.
The assumption does not reduce the number of data; it lets us picture the unknown so that the condition can be examined.
questions.explain: How could we visualise the relations without visualising x as existent?
questions.rule: Picture the unknown.
questions.teaches: To examine the condition we must represent the relations it prescribes between x and the data, and we cannot do so without conceiving x as existent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A designer imagines the finished app on a phone screen before deciding how to build it. Which of the author's three words best describes that imagining?
options: Harmless, because the finished app exists somewhere already and so cannot do any damage to the plan
Provisional, because the app is still unfinished and the picture of it may change as work goes on
Natural, as the man pictures himself on the tree
Convertible, because each feature of the app can be turned back into a step of the building work
optionExplain: This does not match: the harm in question is about a false assumption.
Related, but the best match is the idea that such a picture is natural to the thinker.
Right: the designer sees the problem as solved, as the man pictures himself on the tree.
A different notion: convertible steps are about reversing derivations.
questions.explain: Imagining the solved problem is natural.
questions.rule: Picture the goal.
questions.teaches: In the creek story the primitive man imagines himself walking on a fallen tree and crossing the creek long before he actually can: he sees his problem as solved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: You are asked to prove a claim A that you cannot yet decide. Which attitude lets you begin?
options: Refuse to use A in any step until it has been proved by someone else
Wait for a teacher to tell you whether A is true before you spend any effort on it
Prove the opposite of A first, since a contradiction is the only safe way to begin
Draw consequences from A as if true, and see where they lead
optionExplain: You cannot start an analysis that way.
Waiting for a teacher to decide whether A is true leaves the work undone; the solver can begin by exploring consequences.
That is not required in order to begin.
Right: draw consequences from A as if true and see where they lead.
questions.explain: The card next states the attitude.
questions.rule: Explore consequences.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: Assuming a theorem A true in an analysis means that A is thereby proved.
questions.explain: It is only an invitation to draw consequences; the proof still has to be built.
questions.rule: Assumption is not proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: To analyse the claim 'the angles of every triangle add up to two right angles', a student draws a line through one vertex and reasons from the claim to see what it implies. Which attitude is shown?
options: Reluctance to use an unproved theorem in any step of the work, since it has not yet been shown true
Willingness to draw consequences from an unproved theorem
Certainty that the theorem is false, so that the student looks for the place where it breaks down
Indifference to the theorem, which the student treats as neither worth proving nor worth disproving
optionExplain: That is the opposite attitude: the student is willing to draw consequences from the unproved theorem.
Right: drawing consequences from an unproved theorem is the attitude of analysis.
She is not sure the theorem is false; she is exploring what it implies.
She is not indifferent; she is working on the theorem to prove it.
questions.explain: Drawing consequences is how analysis begins.
questions.rule: Be willing.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which person, in the author's view, will be unable to start an analysis?
options: One who assumes the theorem true and then checks the consequences against what is already known
One who asks what could be the antecedent of the theorem, and then of that antecedent
One who shrinks from drawing consequences from an unproved theorem
One who aims at a proof in the end and treats the assumption as a stage on the way to it
optionExplain: This is the correct method, so this person can start.
This is the method of analysis, so this person can start.
He says such people cannot start.
This is the aim, so this person can start.
questions.explain: A person who refuses to draw consequences cannot begin.
questions.rule: Do not shrink.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: People with a certain mental ____ or a certain philosophy may shrink from drawing consequences from an unproved theorem.
questions.explain: The author says such people cannot start an analysis.
questions.rule: Some temperaments resist.
questions.teaches: People with a certain mental character or a certain philosophy may shrink from drawing consequences from an unproved theorem, but such people cannot start an analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A lawyer assumes for a moment that her client was in the shop at noon and asks what else must then be true. Which method does she use?
options: Synthesis from established facts, moving forward from what is known to the claim about the client
A proof that the client was in the shop at noon, since she has now shown that he could have been
Analysis of a problem to prove, drawing consequences of the assumption
A guess with no further steps, since she supposes something and leaves it at that
optionExplain: She starts from an assumption, not from established facts.
It is only an assumption, not a proof.
Right: she assumes the claim and draws its consequences, which is analysis of a problem to prove.
She does not stop at the supposition; she asks what else must then be true.
questions.explain: The assumption opens the analysis; the consequences are tested.
questions.rule: Assume and test.
questions.teaches: The paraphrase explains the analysis of problems to prove in words quite different from those of the original, with no intended change of sense.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: From a claim A you derive B, from B you derive C, and C is true. Why can you not yet conclude that A is true?
options: The steps may not be reversible, so C's truth need not carry back to A
A consequence of A can never be useful to know, since only the premises of a claim can establish it
A must first be shown false, since only a false claim can be properly replaced by a proved one
B must have been wrong, since a true C would not have followed from a doubtful B in a sound chain
optionExplain: Reversal is what the proof needs.
True consequences can help when the steps are reversible.
A need not be shown false first; the gap is that the steps may not be reversible.
Nothing suggests that B is wrong.
questions.explain: The card next states the proviso.
questions.rule: Check reversal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The proviso that all derivations are ____ is an interpolation in the paraphrase of Pappus.
questions.explain: The author says the original contains nothing of the sort.
questions.rule: Convertible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student solves the square root of (x + 6) = x by squaring and gets x = 3 or x = -2. Which action follows the lesson of convertible steps?
options: Accept both roots, since the algebra of squaring and solving the quadratic was done correctly
Reject both roots, since squaring was used and any root found that way is bound to be suspect
Accept only the larger root without any check, since the smaller one is likely to be spurious
Substitute each root in the original equation, since squaring is not reversible
optionExplain: Correct algebra does not make squaring reversible.
x = 3 does satisfy the original equation.
Luck, not reasoning, would then decide.
Squaring can add false roots; here x = -2 fails.
questions.explain: Square root of 9 is 3, so x = 3 works; the square root of 4 is 2, not -2, so x = -2 fails.
questions.rule: Check non-reversible steps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: Pappus's original text states that the derivations of the analysis must be convertible.
questions.explain: The author says the proviso is an interpolation; the original contains nothing of the sort.
questions.rule: Not in the original.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author report about the lack of the proviso in the original text?
options: It was praised by Pappus himself, who was careful to state it in the text of his own report
It was observed and criticised in modern times
It was never noticed by anyone until the author wrote his paraphrase of the original report
It was supplied by Euclid in a later edition of the Elements, which added the proviso
optionExplain: Pappus never stated the proviso, so he cannot have praised it.
Right: the lack of the proviso was observed and criticised in modern times.
The author says it was observed and criticised, not unnoticed.
No claim is made that Euclid supplied the proviso in a later edition.
questions.explain: Modern critics saw the gap: Pappus did not state the proviso that the steps be reversible.
questions.rule: A noticed gap.
questions.teaches: The lack of such a proviso in the original text was observed and criticised in modern times.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student reduces proving P to proving Q, then Q to R, and R is known. But Q does not follow from R. What does the chain lack?
options: A longer chain of reductions, since more steps would give more chances to find a link between them
Convertible steps, so that the chain can be retraced from R back to P
A different letter for each claim, since the confusion lies in using the same symbols for P, Q and R
A figure that shows Q and R together, since a figure can usually supply a missing implication
optionExplain: Length does not help; the missing link does.
Retracing needs reversible steps.
Using different letters for each claim does not mend the gap, which lies in a step that cannot be reversed.
A figure cannot supply a missing implication.
questions.explain: The original seems to aim at a chain of equivalent auxiliary problems, a more general procedure.
questions.rule: Chain of equivalents.
questions.teaches: The original text seems to aim at the description of a somewhat more general procedure, the construction of a chain of equivalent auxiliary problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A geometry book has a short section on analysis and synthesis; no other book in the course mentions them. What might that suggest?
options: That analysis is a method special to geometry, so that other courses have no need to mention it
That Pappus wrote only about geometry, so that the method was never meant for other subjects
That other subjects have no use for making plans, because only geometry has problems to solve
A tradition that confines the idea to geometry, though it is more general
optionExplain: The author calls this a lack of understanding.
The paraphrase says mathematical where the original says geometrical, to stress its reach.
Other subjects do have problems to solve and plans to make, so analysis is not limited to geometry.
The idea is wider than its usual home.
questions.explain: The card next explains that the procedures are not tied to one subject.
questions.rule: Wider than geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The paraphrase says mathematical problems where the original means ____ problems.
questions.explain: The change stresses that the procedures are not restricted to geometry.
questions.rule: Not just geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A teacher says analysis belongs only in the geometry unit. What would the author reply?
options: The procedures are not even restricted to mathematical problems
The teacher is right, because analysis was invented for geometry and has no other proper home
Analysis belongs only to algebra, where an equation can be assumed solved and then reduced step by step
Analysis belongs only to the history of mathematics, as a curiosity of the Greek geometers
optionExplain: Right: the procedures are not even restricted to mathematical problems, let alone to geometry.
The author denies that analysis has no other proper home than geometry.
The author says the procedures are not restricted to one branch of mathematics such as algebra.
The author treats analysis as a living procedure, not a curiosity of Greek geometers.
questions.explain: Generality and independence of the subject matter are important.
questions.rule: Not only geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which of these is a difference between the paraphrase and Pappus's original, according to the author?
options: The paraphrase omits the analysis of problems to find, which the original treated at length
The paraphrase is a literal translation of the original, with every phrase kept in its Greek order
The paraphrase introduces the symbols A, B, ..., L and x, y, ..., z
The paraphrase removes the idea of synthesis, which the original did not mention at all
optionExplain: The paraphrase includes the analysis of problems to find.
The paraphrase is a free rendering, not a literal translation.
The original has no such symbols.
It keeps synthesis, which the original does mention.
questions.explain: The paraphrase uses more definite terminology.
questions.rule: Know the differences.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, the restriction of analysis and synthesis to textbooks of geometry shows a current lack of understanding.
questions.explain: Because the procedures are general, confining them to geometry textbooks shows the lack of understanding.
questions.rule: A narrow tradition.
questions.teaches: That analysis is restricted to textbooks of geometry shows a current lack of understanding of its generality, in the author's view.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A medical school teaches 'start from the diagnosis you wish to reach and ask what would lead to it' only in its geometry-based statistics course. What would the author say?
options: The procedure is rightly tied to geometry, because geometry is where Pappus first described it
The procedure is general and should not be tied to one subject
The procedure is wrong for medicine, because diagnosis is a matter of experience and not of method
The procedure is out of date, because it was devised before the modern sciences existed
optionExplain: The author denies that the procedure is tied to one subject because Pappus first described it in geometry.
Right: the procedure is general and should not be tied to one subject.
The author says the procedure is independent of the subject, so it is not wrong for medicine.
The author presents it as still useful, so it is not out of date.
questions.explain: The procedures are independent of the nature of the subject.
questions.rule: General method.
questions.teaches: In these matters generality and independence from the nature of the subject are important.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Two cooks follow the same recipe. One adds the full salt even though the stock is already salty; the other tastes first. Whose habit is more like mastery?
options: The cook who adds the full salt, since the recipe says so and she has followed it to the letter
Neither of them, since recipes ought to be dropped altogether by a cook who is a real master
The cook who tastes first, since she lets the purpose guide the rule
Both of them, since both follow the recipe and neither of them breaks any of its instructions
optionExplain: This is applying the rule rigidly.
Dropping the recipe is not mastery; the master uses the rule and notices where it does not fit.
Judgment about when the rule fits.
One follows it with no judgment.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's contrast.
questions.rule: Judgment over letter.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Pedantry and mastery are opposite attitudes toward ____.
questions.explain: The entry opens with this statement.
questions.rule: Attitudes toward rules.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student begins every problem with the words Let x be the unknown, even when a quantity already has a standard letter. What is this?
options: Pedantry: applying a habit regardless of whether it fits
Mastery, because the rule is followed exactly and without exception in every problem the student meets
Good luck, because the habit happens to work in most of the problems that the student meets
Heuristic, because the student is asking a question that helps to start the problem
optionExplain: The rule is applied without noticing the case.
Mastery involves judging when the rule fits.
The habit is not luck; it is a rigid habit that happens to work in most problems, which is the pedant's way.
The aim of heuristic is judgment, not ritual.
questions.explain: Mastery notices where a rule fits.
questions.rule: Notice the fit.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each habit as pedantry or mastery.

items.t: Applying a rule the same way in every case
Following the words of the rule even where they defeat its purpose
Using a rule without understanding why it works
Noticing the cases where a rule fits
Letting the purpose of the action guide how the rule is used
Applying a rule with natural ease and judgment

questions.explain: The first three are pedantry; the last three are mastery.
questions.rule: Fit before force.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How does the author describe the successful kind of pedant?
options: Someone who never understood the rule he applies, but follows it with great conscientiousness
Someone who adapts the rule to each case and notices where it fits and where it does not
Someone who understood a good rule at the start and later applied it rigidly
Someone who breaks every rule he is given and trusts only his own sense of what is best
optionExplain: That is the poor fool, who never understood the rule he follows.
That is the master, who adapts the rule to each case.
Right: the successful pedant understood a good rule at the start and later applied it rigidly, and succeeds because the rule fits many cases.
Breaking every rule is not pedantry at all.
questions.explain: Some pedants chose a good rule and fail only occasionally.
questions.rule: Two kinds of pedant.
questions.teaches: Some pedants are quite successful: they understood their rule at least in the beginning, before they became pedants, and chose a good one that fits in many cases and fails only occasionally.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A pilot follows a checklist step by step in normal flight, but when an alarm shows that the next step would worsen the fault, she stops and thinks. Which attitude is this?
options: Mastery: the purpose guides the use of the rule
Pedantry: she should continue
Carelessness: she dropped the checklist
Ignorance: she does not know the rule
optionExplain: Right: the purpose guides her use of the rule, which is mastery rather than pedantry.
Continuing would be applying the rule blindly, which is the pedant's way.
She uses the checklist with judgment, so she has not dropped it carelessly.
She knows the rule well, so this is not ignorance.
questions.explain: A master never lets the words of the rule obscure the purpose of the action or the opportunities of the situation.
questions.rule: Purpose beats letter.
questions.teaches: A master never lets the words of the rule obscure the purpose of the action or the opportunities of the situation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student recites every question of a problem-solving list, in order, for every problem. How would the author likely judge it?
options: As ideal, since the list is complete and a student who recites all of it will meet every need
As harmless, since all the questions help and none of them can do any damage to the work
As cheating, since the student is not thinking but only repeating what is printed in the book
As pedantic, since the questions are used by rigid habit
optionExplain: The list is a guide, not a ritual.
Ritual use can waste effort and hide the case.
Cheating is not the author's concern here.
The author warns against asking questions indiscriminately.
questions.explain: The card next states how the author wants the list used.
questions.rule: Use with judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The proper use of the questions and suggestions must be learned by trial and error, by failure and success, by ____ in applying them.
questions.explain: The entry says the list is not to be applied by rigid habit.
questions.rule: Learn by experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A teacher wants to help a stuck student. Which approach follows the author?
options: Run through the whole list from the first question, so that no helpful suggestion is overlooked
Say what grows from a sympathetic understanding of the student's difficulty
Give the student the answer at once, since the stuck student will otherwise lose heart
Ask the same question each time, so that the student learns to expect it and to answer promptly
optionExplain: Running through the whole list from the first question is indiscriminate and ignores the student's difficulty.
Right: the teacher should say what grows from a sympathetic understanding of the student's difficulty.
The aim is to help the student work, so handing over the answer defeats it.
Asking the same question each time is rigid habit, not a response to the student.
questions.explain: What you say should come from sympathetic understanding.
questions.rule: Respond to this student.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author holds that a question from the list should be asked whether or not it suits the case, so that the habit is kept up.
questions.explain: He says the list must never be used indiscriminately.
questions.rule: No rigid habit.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: For whom does the author say the questions and suggestions of the list may be helpful?
options: Problem-solvers only, since a teacher already knows the questions and has no need of a list
Both problem-solvers and teachers
Teachers only, since a student who works alone cannot make use of questions put to a class
Examiners, who must set problems and judge the answers of students in a fair way
optionExplain: Teachers are named too, so it is not for problem-solvers only.
Right: the entry says the list may be helpful to both problem-solvers and teachers.
Problem-solvers are named too, so it is not for teachers only.
Examiners are not named in the entry.
questions.explain: Both problem-solvers and teachers.
questions.rule: Two users.
questions.teaches: The questions and suggestions of the list may be helpful both to problem-solvers and to teachers, but first they must be understood and their use learned.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A coach gives a young athlete a list of tips. What does the author's advice imply about how the coach should apply them?
options: Repeat all the tips at every session, so that the athlete hears each one often enough to remember it
Withhold all the tips, since an athlete should find out everything for himself by trial
Give the tips in alphabetical order, one a day, so that none is skipped and none is repeated
Use a tip only when the athlete's situation calls for it
optionExplain: Repeating all the tips every time is indiscriminate use, which the author warns against.
The list is useful if used with judgment, so withholding every tip is not his advice.
Giving tips in alphabetical order is rigid habit, not a response to the athlete.
Right: use a tip only when the athlete's situation calls for it, not by rigid habit.
questions.explain: The step you try next should be prompted by attentive consideration of the problem.
questions.rule: Prompt by the case.
questions.teaches: The step the solver tries next should be prompted by an attentive and open-minded consideration of the problem before him.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A person who relies on rules asks for one rule to remember above all others. Which would suit the author's view?
options: Think about the problem yourself before applying any other rule
Ask the first question of the list each time, whatever the problem and whatever the state of the work
Do without any rule at all, and meet each problem with nothing but your own bare intelligence
Do whatever the teacher says in every case, since the teacher knows the problems better than you
optionExplain: Right: think about the problem yourself before applying any other rule.
Asking the first question each time whatever the state of the work is the pedant's habit.
The author accepts the use of rules with judgment.
The author puts your own thinking first.
questions.explain: The card next quotes the author's rule.
questions.rule: Think first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The author's closing rule for those inclined to be pedants is to use your own ____ first.
questions.explain: These are the entry's closing words of advice.
questions.rule: Brains first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A student stuck on a problem opens the book to the list at once. What would the author suggest she do first?
options: Ask the teacher at once what the first step should be, since the teacher knows the best opening
Copy a similar solution from the book and change the numbers until the work comes out right
Look at the problem and think about it herself
Stop working on the problem until the next lesson, when a teacher can show how it is done
optionExplain: Her own thinking comes first, so asking the teacher at once is not the first step.
Copying a similar solution is not what the author recommends.
Right: she should look at the problem and think about it herself first.
Stopping until the next lesson is not what the author recommends.
questions.explain: She should first use her own brains on the problem, before turning to the list.
questions.rule: Think first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The rule to use your own brains first tells the solver to refuse any list of questions.
questions.explain: It sets an order: own thinking first, then the list if it helps.
questions.rule: Order, not ban.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What kind of person is this rule offered to?
options: One who is an expert in the field and who has used the list for many years without difficulty
One who dislikes rules and prefers to rely only on his own judgment in every problem he meets
One who teaches only and never has to solve a problem of his own, so that rules are all he has
One who is inclined to be a pedant and must rely upon some rule
optionExplain: The entry does not offer the rule to experts of long standing.
The entry offers the rule to one who relies on rules, not one who dislikes them.
The entry does not offer it only to teachers who never solve problems.
Right: it is offered to one who is inclined to be a pedant and must rely upon some rule.
questions.explain: The advice is for those inclined to pedantry.
questions.rule: The audience is the pedant.
questions.teaches: The closing rule is offered to those inclined to be pedants who feel they must rely upon some rule.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A new manager follows a thick handbook line by line. Which advice from the entry fits her best?
options: Follow the handbook more strictly, so that no rule is overlooked and every case is handled alike
Think about the situation first, and use the handbook where it helps
Burn the handbook and rely on instinct, since a rule book is only a crutch for the unskilled
Ask a colleague about each decision before acting, since two heads are better than one on a rule
optionExplain: Following the handbook more strictly is the pedant's way, which the entry warns against.
Right: she should think about the situation first and use the handbook where it helps.
The author does not tell her to drop rules, only to think first.
Her own thinking should come first, before asking a colleague about each decision.
questions.explain: Own brains first, rules second.
questions.rule: Think then consult.
questions.teaches: The closing advice sets the order of use: one's own brains come first, and any rule comes after.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An engineer asks what the unknown is in a bridge design. Is that question out of place for a practical problem?
options: Yes, since only mathematicians have unknowns and an engineer works with materials and not with unknowns
Yes, since engineers rely only on experience and the question belongs to the study of mathematics
No, the same basic questions apply, though the answers are less sharp
No, since every practical problem has one exact unknown that the engineer can state in a single line
optionExplain: Practical problems have unknowns too.
Experience and questions work together.
Motives and procedures are the same.
The unknowns are many and loosely bounded.
questions.explain: The card next states the author's view.
questions.rule: Same motives.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, practical engineering problems usually involve mathematical problems.
questions.explain: He says so in the opening paragraph.
questions.rule: Practical involves mathematical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A farmer must decide where to dig an irrigation channel. Which of the list's questions still applies, as the author would say?
options: What is the unknown? What are the data? What is the condition?
None of them, since farming is not mathematics and its problems call for another kind of thinking
Only the question about the figure, since irrigation can be pictured but not set out in words
Only the questions about proofs, since a farmer must be sure that the channel will work
optionExplain: Right: the questions about the unknown, the data and the condition carry over to the farmer's problem.
The same motives and procedures apply to practical problems, so the questions are not limited to mathematics.
All the main questions can be asked, not only the one about the figure.
The channel is a problem to find, not a problem to prove, so the questions about proofs are not the ones that apply.
questions.explain: The principal motives and procedures are essentially the same.
questions.rule: Ask the same questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In a practical problem, unknowns, data and conditions are more complex and less ____ defined than in a mathematical problem.
questions.explain: The author calls this perhaps the main difference between the two kinds of problem.
questions.rule: Less sharp.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which example of a practical problem does the author choose to illustrate his points?
options: The construction of a dam across a river
The design of a bridge over a river, with its spans, its piers and the loads it must carry
The planning of a school timetable, with its rooms, its teachers and the hours of each class
The building of a house, with its foundations, its walls and the materials that go into them
optionExplain: Right: he uses the construction of a dam, which needs no special knowledge to understand.
The author's example is a dam, not a bridge.
The author's example is a dam, not a school timetable.
The author's example is a dam, not a house.
questions.explain: He uses the dam, which needs no special knowledge to understand.
questions.rule: The dam example.
questions.teaches: The author's example of an impressive practical problem is the construction of a dam across a river, which men attempted in almost prehistoric times in the valley of the Nile.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A hospital team plans a new ward. Which view of the author's would they rely on?
options: Drop all the questions of the list, since a hospital ward is not a mathematical matter in any way
Insist that every condition of the plan be stated exactly before any work is allowed to start
Solve only the mathematical part of the plan and leave the rest to the judgment of the staff
Treat unknowns, data and conditions as many and less sharply defined, but ask the usual questions
optionExplain: The same motives and procedures apply to a practical problem, so the questions are not dropped.
Practical conditions are less sharply defined.
The problem is not only mathematical.
Right: in practical problems the unknowns, data and conditions are more numerous and less sharply defined, but the usual questions still apply.
questions.explain: Practical problems are less sharply defined than purely mathematical ones.
questions.rule: Ask, tolerate blur.
questions.teaches: In a practical problem the unknowns, data and conditions are more complex and less sharply defined than in a mathematical problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Why does the question about the condition of a dam resist an answer in one short sentence?
options: Because the dam has no condition of any kind, and so there is nothing for a sentence to say about it
Because there are many conditions, some pulling against others
Because only engineers can state conditions, and an ordinary reader cannot follow such a statement
Because the conditions of a problem are the same as its data and cannot be told apart from them
optionExplain: There are conditions, and many of them.
Right: there are many conditions, some pulling against others, which resists a one-sentence answer.
Anyone can understand the conditions of a dam.
Conditions and data differ; a condition links the unknown to the data.
questions.explain: The card next lists the many conditions of the dam.
questions.rule: Many conditions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each item into unknown or condition for the dam problem.

items.t: The exact location of the dam
The materials used
The shape and dimensions
Provide electric power
Help to control floods
Disturb navigation as little as possible

questions.explain: Location, materials and shape are things to be found; the rest are requirements.
questions.rule: Find versus require.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which of these is a datum, not an unknown or a condition, for the dam?
options: The shape of the dam, which has to be settled in the course of the design and is not given beforehand
The annual rainfall and height of floods
Provide irrigation water for the farms below the dam, which is one of the purposes it must serve
The location of the dam along the river, which must be chosen by the designer after the survey
optionExplain: The shape of the dam is settled during the design, so it is an unknown.
Right: annual rainfall and the height of floods are meteorological data, given or collected for the design.
Providing irrigation water is one of the purposes the dam must serve, so it is a condition.
The location along the river is chosen by the designer, so it is an unknown.
questions.explain: Data are what is given or collected: topographical, geological, meteorological, economic.
questions.rule: Data are given.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each kind of datum to what it concerns.
pairs: The vicinity of the river and its tributaries
Precipitation and the height of floods
Value of flooded ground and cost of materials and labour
questions.explain: These are the four kinds the author lists.
questions.rule: Four kinds of data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How does the author say the conditions of the dam may conflict?
options: All the conditions are consistent, so that each can be fully satisfied without costing any other
Only cost and speed conflict, because every other condition can be met in full at the same time
The conditions conflict only in mathematics, since in real life one can always satisfy all of them
It should serve power, irrigation and flood control while disturbing navigation, fish and scenery as little as possible
optionExplain: Several pull in opposite directions.
More than cost and speed conflict; the author names several further aims that pull against each other.
They conflict in the real problem too.
Some conditions work against others.
questions.explain: Some needs must be satisfied and others hurt as little as possible.
questions.rule: Balance competing aims.
questions.teaches: The dam should also cost as little as possible and be constructed as quickly as possible, besides satisfying the other needs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A city plans a new tram line. Which is an unknown in the sense used for the dam?
options: The route, the stops and the type of track
The budget limit for the whole scheme, which the planners must not exceed
The expected number of riders on the line, which the planners must estimate before they begin
The requirement to disturb as few residents as possible while the line is being built
optionExplain: Right: the route, the stops and the type of track are things to be decided, so they are unknowns.
A budget limit that must not be exceeded restricts the solution, so it is a condition.
The expected number of riders is estimated beforehand, so it is a datum.
Disturbing as few residents as possible restricts the solution, so it is a condition.
questions.explain: Unknowns are the things to be found.
questions.rule: Name the unknowns.
questions.teaches: In so large a project it is necessary to satisfy many important economic needs and to hurt other needs as little as possible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An ancient builder has no formula for water pressure but has seen floods break dams. What does he rely on?
options: Nothing at all, so that he cannot solve the problem until someone gives him a formula for pressure
An exact calculation of the stress inside the dam, made from the laws of fluids and solids
Experience and stories about dams, pictured as pressure against the dam
A guarantee that the dam will stand, which his experience of other dams is able to give him
optionExplain: He can act on his experience of floods without a formula, so he is not left with nothing.
He lacks the concepts of fluids and solids needed for an exact calculation.
Common-sense interpretation of experience.
Experience offers no guarantee, only a basis for judging what is likely to stand.
questions.explain: The card next details the knowledge on which builders and engineers rely.
questions.rule: Experience first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The ancient Egyptian dam-builder had precise, quantitative, scientific concepts of fluid pressure.
questions.explain: He had none; modern engineers have them.
questions.rule: No exact concepts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A modern engineer needs to know how a certain river carries silt. How does the author describe such knowledge?
options: Fully scientific and exact, with the precision of a theory of fluid pressure, and settled by calculation
Purely mathematical, since erosion and silt can be handled by the theory of elasticity alone
Unneeded in modern engineering, which now rests wholly on exact theory and leaves no room for experience
Of a rather empirical character, not quite at a precise scientific level
optionExplain: He says it is not quite at that level.
He calls it empirical, not mathematical.
He says the engineer does use it.
Right: such knowledge is of a rather empirical character, not quite at a precise scientific level.
questions.explain: The engineer also uses knowledge that has not yet reached a precise scientific level.
questions.rule: Empirical knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two items does the author list among the engineer's empirical knowledge?
options: The theory of elasticity
Erosion by flowing water
The strength of steel beams
The transportation of silt
optionExplain: The theory of elasticity is a theory the engineer applies, not an item of empirical knowledge.
Right: erosion by flowing water is named among the engineer's empirical knowledge.
The strength of steel beams is not named as empirical knowledge in this passage.
Right: the transportation of silt is named among the engineer's empirical knowledge.
questions.explain: Erosion and silt are named, with the plasticity of certain materials.
questions.rule: Know the examples.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What stock of knowledge does the modern engineer use besides a scientific theory of strength of materials?
options: Only the oral tradition of earlier builders, handed down from master to apprentice without being written
His own experience and the mass of engineering experience stored in technical literature
Only the opinion of clients, who know what a dam should do for the farms and towns below it
Nothing besides theory, since the theory of strength of materials is sufficient for the whole design
optionExplain: The author names technical literature, not only oral tradition handed from master to apprentice.
Right: the engineer uses his own experience and the mass of engineering experience stored in technical literature.
The author does not name clients' opinions as a stock of knowledge.
The engineer has more than theory: he also has experience.
questions.explain: Experience and literature complete the theory.
questions.rule: More than theory.
questions.teaches: The modern engineer has a scientific theory of the strength of materials, his own experience, and the mass of engineering experience stored in special technical literature.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A nurse faces an unusual symptom with no textbook rule for it. Which parallel does the author's passage offer?
options: She should wait for a theory to be worked out before she acts, since an unusual symptom needs one
She should ignore the symptom until a textbook rule appears that covers an unusual case like it
Like the Egyptian builder, she must draw on experience where exact concepts are lacking
She should use mathematics only, since a rule that is not in a textbook cannot be known at all
optionExplain: Waiting for a theory is not the parallel; experience can act now, as the builder's did.
Ignoring the symptom is not advised; the parallel is to draw on experience.
Right: like the Egyptian builder, she draws on experience where exact concepts are lacking.
Mathematics alone is not enough.
questions.explain: Knowledge in practical problems is more complex and less sharply defined.
questions.rule: Use experience.
questions.teaches: The knowledge needed and the concepts used are more complex and less sharply defined in practical problems than in mathematical problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A team must reduce 'waste' in a factory but nobody agrees what counts as waste. What should they do first?
options: Clarify what waste means, as part of the problem
Start cutting costs at random
Wait until the notion becomes clear itself
Declare the problem unsolvable
optionExplain: Right: they should clarify what waste means, because that is part of the problem.
Cutting costs at random ignores that the hazy notion must be cleared first.
The notion does not become clear by itself; clarifying it is work.
The problem can be solved once the notion is clarified, so declaring it unsolvable is wrong.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Clarify first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In solving a practical problem we are often obliged to start from rather ____ ideas.
questions.explain: The author uses the word hazy for notions that must be clarified as part of the problem.
questions.rule: Hazy start.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Before Pasteur, the notion of infection was hazy. Which approach does the author's remark suggest for a researcher then?
options: Skip the notion of infection and test possible cures only, since cures are what the physician needs
Assume that the notion of infection is already clear and go on to design the experiments needed
Treat clarifying the notion of infection as part of the problem
Rely on mathematics alone, since a hazy notion in medicine can be cleared by calculation
optionExplain: Without the notion, progress is limited.
It was hazy, so that assumption would mislead.
Right: clarifying the hazy notion of infection is part of the problem, as the author advises.
Mathematics alone cannot clarify it.
questions.explain: Clarification of concepts can become an important part of the problem.
questions.rule: Clarify concepts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The question 'Have you taken into account all essential notions involved in the problem?' is useful for all sorts of problems, but its use varies with the notions involved.
questions.explain: True: the question is useful for all sorts of problems, but how it is used varies with the notions involved.
questions.rule: Question works everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say about the starting concepts of a mathematical problem?
options: They are very clear and fairly well ordered in our mind
They are hazy and have to be clarified before the solution can begin, as in a practical problem
They are unnecessary, since a mathematical problem is solved by calculation from the data alone
They are the same as in practical problems, vague at the start and clarified in the course of the work
optionExplain: Contrast with the practical case.
That describes the practical case; mathematical problems start from clearly stated concepts.
Not so; concepts are the base of the problem.
He contrasts the two kinds of problem.
questions.explain: Mathematical problems start from clear concepts.
questions.rule: Clear versus hazy.
questions.teaches: In solving a mathematical problem we start from very clear concepts that are fairly well ordered in our mind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A school wants to improve student wellbeing but has no agreed meaning of the term. Which step matches the author's advice?
options: Buy new equipment for the pupils first, since material help is quick and easy for everyone to see
Ask other schools for the answer, since a school with the same aim must have settled the question
Set a numerical target for the whole school at once, so that progress can be measured from the first term
Clarify what wellbeing is to be taken to mean, as part of the problem
optionExplain: New equipment before the meaning is agreed is premature, since nobody knows what it should achieve.
Another school's answer does not settle what this school means; the author does not advise it.
A numerical target needs the concept of wellbeing to be clear first.
Right: clarify what wellbeing is to be taken to mean, as part of the problem.
questions.explain: Clarifying hazy notions is part of the problem.
questions.rule: Clarify first.
questions.teaches: Medical science is in a better position to check infectious diseases today than before Pasteur, when the notion of infection was rather hazy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A designer could keep gathering more soil data without end. When should she stop?
options: Never, until every uncertainty has been removed and the ground is known as well as a person can know it
When further data would hardly change the form of the solution
Immediately, before starting, since a designer can always work from what is known without more survey
When the budget for the survey is exhausted, whatever may be known or unknown about the ground then
optionExplain: The data are inexhaustible, so waiting until every uncertainty is removed means never stopping.
Appreciable influence is the test.
Some data are essential, so starting with no survey at all leaves the design unsupported.
A reason, but not the author's test.
questions.explain: The card next gives the test for when to stop collecting data.
questions.rule: Appreciable influence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In practical problems we ask: did you use all the data which could contribute ____ to the solution?
questions.explain: The author's modified question.
questions.rule: Appreciable data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A planner has 200 minor facts about a site. How should she treat them?
options: Use all 200 of them equally, so that none is neglected and the plan rests on the full evidence
Use those that could influence the plan appreciably and neglect the rest
Use none of them, since minor facts cannot change a plan that rests on the main facts
Use the first ten she meets, since the order of discovery is as good a guide as any other
optionExplain: Using all 200 equally is not practical, because most minor facts do not change the plan.
Right: use the facts that could influence the plan appreciably and neglect the rest.
Some minor facts may matter, so using none of them is a mistake.
The order in which facts are found is not a principled test of what matters.
questions.explain: Draw the line where influence becomes slight.
questions.rule: Draw the line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: How do the questions about using all the data and the whole condition apply to a purely mathematical problem?
options: They are optional, since a solver may leave out a datum that seems to have no bearing on the answer
They apply only to practical problems, where data are many and some of them can be left out
They are replaced by guesses about which data matter, since a mathematical problem is too exact
They cannot be missed, since all data and clauses are essential
optionExplain: In a perfectly stated problem every datum is essential, so it cannot be left out.
They apply to mathematical problems too, not only practical ones.
A mathematical problem is exact enough that no guessing about the data is needed.
Right: in a perfectly stated mathematical problem all data and clauses are essential, so none can be missed.
questions.explain: A perfect mathematical problem uses all data.
questions.rule: Math: all data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author quotes a proverb about sailing without danger in his discussion of how a solver must stop collecting data and neglect something.
questions.explain: The proverb says that anyone who wants to sail without danger must never put to sea, so complete safety cannot be had.
questions.rule: Act despite risk.
questions.teaches: The book quotes a proverb about sailing without danger while discussing why data collection must stop somewhere.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A doctor must choose a treatment with imperfect test results. Which attitude matches the author's?
options: Wait until the evidence is perfect and no doubt remains, so that the treatment is chosen with certainty
Ignore all the evidence and treat the patient by general rule, since tests can never be trusted
Weigh the relevant evidence, stop collecting at some point and accept a margin of uncertainty
Use only the first test that comes back and treat on it, since further tests would only delay
optionExplain: The author says we must draw the line somewhere, so waiting for perfect evidence is not his view.
Some evidence matters, so ignoring all of it is wrong.
Right: weigh the relevant evidence, stop collecting at some point and accept a margin of uncertainty.
Stopping at the first test is not a principled place to stop collecting evidence.
questions.explain: We cannot help neglecting something.
questions.rule: Stop and accept margin.
questions.teaches: Quite often there is a great surplus of data which have no appreciable influence on the final form of the solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A colleague says practical work needs a different mindset from mathematics. What would the author most likely say?
options: The attitude must be entirely different, since practical work faces real materials and real costs
Practical work needs no experience, since it can be done by following the rules of the trade
Mathematics needs no experience, since it works from definitions and does not use past cases
The attitude is the same; the kind of knowledge needed differs
optionExplain: The author says the motives are the same, so the attitude is not entirely different.
Practical work needs experience, so following trade rules alone is not enough.
Mathematics also draws on experience, so saying it needs none is wrong.
Right: the attitude is the same, and what differs is the kind of knowledge needed.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's view that the attitude is the same in both kinds of problem.
questions.rule: Same attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The author says the difference between practical and mathematical problems probably lies in the nature of the knowledge needed, not in our attitude toward the problem.
questions.explain: That is his view: the same motives and procedures apply in practical and in mathematical problems.
questions.rule: Knowledge, not attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: An architect and a mathematician both tackle new problems. Which question can both ask, per the author?
options: Is this a problem to prove, so that it is a matter of showing that an assertion is true or false
Have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form?
Did you check the answer to six digits, so that no error can be hidden in the last place
Is the problem in a textbook, so that the answer can be looked up when you are stuck
optionExplain: Whether a problem is one to prove is a distinction, not a question both would ask.
Right: both can ask whether you have seen the same problem in a slightly different form.
Checking to six digits is not a question the author names as shared.
Looking the answer up in a textbook is not a question the author names.
questions.explain: Both rely on experience with similar problems.
questions.rule: Shared questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Solvers of both kinds of problem rely on their experience with ____ problems.
questions.explain: The author says that in both cases we rely on experience with similar problems.
questions.rule: Experience with similar problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which two questions does the author name as ones we often ask in both kinds of problem?
options: Have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form? Do you know a related problem?
What is the unknown? What is the answer? These two questions start every inquiry into a problem
Is it possible? Is it worth the cost? These two questions are asked before work begins
Who will pay for it? Who will build it? These two questions are asked of every practical task
optionExplain: Right: these are the two questions the author names as often asked in both kinds of problem.
What is the unknown is a common first question, but this pair is not the one he names.
Questions about cost and possibility are not the pair he names.
Questions about who will pay and who will build are not the pair he names.
questions.explain: These two questions are from the list and are asked in both kinds of problem.
questions.rule: Two familiar questions.
questions.teaches: In solving a problem of either kind we often ask: Have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form? Do you know a related problem?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A software team treats each bug report as if it were new. Which remark of the author's fits?
options: Always start from zero, since every bug report is different and no past report can help with it
Ask the client to solve it, since the client knows best how the program is supposed to behave
Rely on experience with similar problems and ask if you have seen it before
Avoid asking questions of the report, since each question leads away from the fault itself
optionExplain: Starting from zero ignores experience, which the author says to use.
Asking the client to solve the problem is not his advice.
Right: rely on experience with similar problems and ask whether you have seen it before.
Avoiding questions is not his advice; questions are what lead toward the fault.
questions.explain: Related experience helps, so one asks whether the new problem has been seen before in another form.
questions.rule: Recall similar cases.
questions.teaches: The question 'Have you seen the same problem in a slightly different form?' belongs to the list of suggestions that apply to practical problems as well.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A designer neglects some minor conditions of a real problem before calculating. What follows for the accuracy she should demand of the mathematics?
options: Not extreme accuracy, since the model is already approximate
Perfect accuracy, since mathematics is exact and an exact method should be applied to every model
No calculation at all, since a model that neglects data cannot be calculated with any value
Accuracy beyond the data, since the computation can always be carried to as many places as wished
optionExplain: Right: the model is already approximate, so extreme accuracy in the mathematics is not called for.
The model is not exact, so demanding perfect accuracy from the mathematics adds nothing.
Calculation still serves even if the model neglects minor data.
Carrying accuracy beyond the data is pointless, since the model cannot be better than its inputs.
questions.explain: The card next gives the author's view.
questions.rule: Match accuracy to model.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In mathematical problems derived from practical problems, we usually content ourselves with an ____.
questions.explain: The author says approximation.
questions.rule: Content with approximation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A builder's calculation of beam load is exact to six digits but the load estimate is uncertain by 10 percent. How would the author judge it?
options: Admirable, since more digits are always better and a builder should compute everything as finely as possible
Wrong, since the answer is approximate and a builder should not use approximate answers in design
Irrelevant, since the beam will hold anyway and the builder has no need to calculate its load
Reasonable to accept lower accuracy and a simpler computation
optionExplain: The input is rough, so the digits are wasted.
Approximate answers are accepted in design when the data are approximate, so this is not wrong.
The point is not whether the beam holds, but that six-digit accuracy is wasted on a 10 percent uncertainty.
Accuracy beyond the data is wasted.
questions.explain: Gain in simplicity what we lose in accuracy.
questions.rule: Do not over-calculate.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: If minor data are neglected in setting up a mathematical problem, it is reasonable to allow slight inaccuracy in the computations.
questions.explain: True: once minor data are neglected, slight inaccuracy in the computations is reasonable.
questions.rule: Allow slight inaccuracy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What theory does the author say the modern engineer applies to calculate the resistance of a concrete dam?
options: The theory of probability
The theory of elasticity
The theory of relativity
The theory of numbers
optionExplain: The author does not name the theory of probability for the resistance of a dam.
Right: he names the theory of elasticity for calculating the resistance of a concrete dam.
The author does not name the theory of relativity here.
The author does not name the theory of numbers here.
questions.explain: It applies fairly well to constructions in concrete.
questions.rule: Elasticity.
questions.teaches: The engineer applies the theory of elasticity, which applies fairly well to constructions in concrete, to calculate the resistance of the projected dam.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A weather service simplifies its model by ignoring tiny local effects. Which author's remark does this support?
options: Weather problems are not practical problems, since nobody builds or designs anything with a forecast
Neglecting minor data makes a slight inaccuracy reasonable when simplicity is gained
Models should include every detail, since a neglected effect may be the one that matters most
Approximation is a mistake, since a forecast should be as exact as the physics allows it to be
optionExplain: Weather forecasting is a practical problem, since a forecast serves practical ends.
Right: neglecting minor data makes a slight inaccuracy reasonable when simplicity is gained.
He allows minor data to be neglected, so he does not say every detail should be included.
He accepts approximation, so he does not call it a mistake.
questions.explain: We gain in simplicity what we lose in accuracy.
questions.rule: Simplify with care.
questions.teaches: A practical engineering problem usually leads to a mathematical problem, as with the dam, where the application of a theory needs a good deal of mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A map-maker assumes the earth is a perfect sphere although it is slightly flattened. Is this assumption reasonable?
options: No, because every assumption in a problem must be exact or else the answer cannot be trusted
No, because the earth is shaped like a cube and a sphere is far from the truth
Yes, because the earth is a perfect sphere and the flattening is only a rumour among map-makers
Yes, if the error is small compared with the gain in simplicity
optionExplain: Approximations are accepted when the error is small, so exactness is not required of every assumption.
The earth is nearly a sphere, not a cube.
The earth is not a perfect sphere; it is slightly flattened.
Right: the assumption is reasonable if the error is small compared with the gain in simplicity.
questions.explain: The card next gives the numbers.
questions.rule: Small error, big gain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In the author's model, a ball with 25 feet across at the equator is about ____ inch(es) shorter between its poles.
questions.explain: The author says about one inch.
questions.rule: About an inch.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A ball 25 feet (300 inches) across at the equator is about 1 inch shorter between the poles. What fraction of the diameter is the shortfall?
options: About 1/300, roughly 0.33 percent
About 1/25, 4 percent
About 1/12, 8.3 percent
About 1/3000, 0.033 percent
optionExplain: Right: 1 divided by 300 is about 0.0033, which is 0.33 percent.
This mixes feet and inches: 1/25 compares one inch with 25 inches, not with 300 inches.
This divides by 12 only, treating the diameter as 12 inches.
This is a slip of a decimal place: 1/3000 would be ten times smaller than the real shortfall.
questions.rule: Convert units first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the author's model ball, 25 feet across at the equator, the distance between the poles is exactly 25 feet.
questions.explain: The earth is flattened at the poles, so the distance between the poles of the model is about one inch less than 25 feet.
questions.rule: The sphere is only close.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say we gain and lose by assuming the earth is a sphere?
options: We gain accuracy and lose simplicity, since a sphere is a more exact figure than the true shape
We lose both accuracy and simplicity, since the sphere is not the shape of the earth at all
We gain nothing at all, since the true shape of the earth can be drawn as easily as a sphere
We gain much in simplicity and do not lose a great deal in accuracy
optionExplain: That reverses the point: the sphere gains simplicity and loses little accuracy.
He does not say that both accuracy and simplicity are lost.
The sphere gives a real gain in simplicity, so it is wrong to say nothing is gained.
Right: we gain much in simplicity and do not lose a great deal in accuracy.
questions.explain: A sphere makes the map easier to draw.
questions.rule: Gain simplicity.
questions.teaches: By assuming the earth is a sphere we gain much in simplicity and do not lose a great deal in accuracy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A civil engineer treats a gently sloping road as flat in a rough cost estimate. Which idea from the earth example does this match?
options: Insisting on exact shapes in every estimate, however rough, so that no neglected curve can distort the result
Accepting a small error for a large gain in simplicity
Avoiding all models and measuring the road itself, since a model can only lead the estimator astray
Using traditional symbols in their traditional meaning, since a reader expects them to mean the same
optionExplain: Insisting on exact shapes is the opposite of the approximation idea.
Right: accepting a small error for a large gain in simplicity matches the earth example.
Avoiding all models is not the earth example, which accepts a model with a small error.
Keeping traditional symbols is a different topic from approximation.
questions.explain: A good approximation costs little accuracy.
questions.rule: Simplify when error is small.
questions.teaches: The surface of the earth is not at all a mathematically defined surface, and we definitely know that the earth is flattened at the poles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A detective story asks who did it. What sort of problem is this?
options: A problem to prove, since the culprit must be proved guilty
A pure puzzle with no unknown
A problem to find, with the culprit as the thing sought
A problem with no data
optionExplain: The aim is first to find who, so it is a problem to find rather than one to prove.
There is an unknown, so it is not a puzzle without one.
Right: it is a problem to find, with the culprit as the unknown, the thing sought.
The clues are the data, so it is not a problem with no data.
questions.explain: The card next defines the term.
questions.rule: The unknown is sought.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Sort each task as a problem to find or not.

items.t: Locate the murderer in a mystery story
Find the best move in a chess position
Construct a triangle from three given sides
Show that the square of an even number is even
Decide whether a witness's claim is true
Prove the theorem of Pythagoras

questions.explain: The first three seek an object; the last three assert or ask for a conclusion.
questions.rule: Seek an object.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A puzzle asks for a five-letter word that fits clues across and down. In the author's terms, what is the unknown?
options: The word to be found
The clues given across and down, which tell the solver something about each word to be found
The crossword grid itself, with its squares and the black cells that separate the words from each other
The solver, who fills in the letters one by one and tries each word against the clues
optionExplain: Right: in certain riddles the unknown is a word, so the word to be found is the unknown.
The clues across and down are the data.
The grid is part of the condition, not the unknown.
The solver is not the unknown; the unknown is the thing to be found.
questions.explain: The unknown is what is sought.
questions.rule: Name the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which of these is another name the author gives the unknown of a problem to find?
options: The hypothesis, which is the part of the problem that states what is assumed at the start
The conclusion, which is the part of the problem that states what has to be shown at the end
The quaesitum, or thing sought
The corollary, which is a theorem that follows easily from one that has already been proved
optionExplain: The hypothesis belongs to problems to prove, not to problems to find.
The conclusion belongs to problems to prove, not to problems to find.
Right: the quaesitum, or thing sought, is another name for the unknown.
A corollary is a different notion, a theorem that follows easily from another.
questions.explain: The unknown is the thing sought or required.
questions.rule: Other names.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: We may try to find, obtain, acquire, produce or ____ all imaginable kinds of objects as the unknown of a problem to find.
questions.explain: The author lists these verbs to show how varied the unknown can be.
questions.rule: Many verbs for the unknown.
questions.teaches: We may try to find, to obtain, to acquire, to produce, or to construct all imaginable kinds of objects as the unknown of a problem to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A town wants to find a site for a new library. Which kind of problem is it, and what is the unknown?
options: A problem to prove; the unknown is the proof
Not a problem; nobody can know
A problem to find; the unknown is the town
A problem to find; the unknown is the site
optionExplain: No proof is wanted, so it is not a problem to prove.
It is a problem, since an unknown, the site, is to be found.
The town is given, so the town is not the unknown.
Right: it is a practical problem to find, and the unknown is the site.
questions.explain: Problems to find may be practical or theoretical.
questions.rule: Practical unknown.
questions.teaches: Problems to find may be theoretical or practical, abstract or concrete, serious problems or mere puzzles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A court must decide whether a witness's statement is true and say why. What kind of problem is this?
options: A problem to find, since the truth of the statement is the unknown that the court has to discover
A problem to prove, since a statement must be established or refuted
Not a problem at all, since a court records what the witnesses say and weighs it by custom
A puzzle, since the court is asked to guess which of the two sides is telling the truth
optionExplain: The aim is to decide on a stated claim, so the truth of the statement is not an unknown to be found.
Right: it is a problem to prove, since a statement must be established or refuted with grounds.
It is a problem, since the court must reach a conclusion with grounds.
It is not a puzzle, because the court must give grounds and not just guess.
questions.explain: The card next defines the term.
questions.rule: Prove or refute.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The aim of a problem to prove is to show ____ that an assertion is true, or else that it is false.
questions.explain: A problem to prove asks for a conclusive answer: to show that an assertion is true, or else that it is false.
questions.rule: Conclusive answer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: 'Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is even.' Which kind of problem is it?
options: A problem to find the sum of two odd numbers, since the sum is the thing the task asks for
A problem to prove, with a stated assertion
A problem to find an odd number, since the two numbers in the statement have not been named
Neither kind of problem, since the task is a rule of arithmetic that needs only to be learned
optionExplain: The sum is not what is wanted; no number is sought, only a stated assertion to be shown.
Right: the task states an assertion to be shown true, so it is a problem to prove.
No odd number is sought; the problem asks for a demonstration about all odd numbers.
A rule of arithmetic is still something to prove; this is one of the two kinds of problem.
questions.explain: The assertion is stated; the task is to show it true or false.
questions.rule: Assertion, then proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: In the author's account, a problem to prove may end by showing the assertion false.
questions.explain: He says either true or false must be shown conclusively.
questions.rule: Either outcome.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Why does the author ask only to prove the theorem of Pythagoras, without adding a request to disprove it?
options: Because disproof is not part of any problem to prove, which asks only for a proof of the stated claim
Because the theorem of Pythagoras has already been disproved, so that only a proof can still be asked for
Because disproof is easier than proof, so that a student can be left to find it without being asked
Because the chances of disproving that theorem are rather slight
optionExplain: Disproof is part of such problems, as the author says, so this is not his reason.
The theorem of Pythagoras has not been disproved, so this is not the reason.
Disproof being easier is not his reason.
Right: his reason is that the chances of disproving that theorem are rather slight.
questions.explain: It would be better in some respects to include disproof.
questions.rule: Slight chance.
questions.teaches: The author neglects the possibility of disproving in the request to prove the theorem of Pythagoras because the chances for disproving that theorem are rather slight.
