questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A manager must decide whether a rumour about a supplier is true, and give grounds. How does this compare with the judge's problem?
options: It is the same kind, a problem to prove
It is a problem to find a supplier, since the manager has to discover who is behind the rumour
It is not a problem, since a rumour is a matter of opinion and needs no grounds to be settled
It is a puzzle, since the manager has to choose between two answers on the strength of a hunch
optionExplain: Right: deciding whether the rumour is true and giving grounds is a problem to prove, like the judge's.
The supplier is known, so it is not a problem to find a supplier.
It is a problem, since it needs grounds, so it cannot be left as opinion.
It is not a puzzle, because grounds are required and not a hunch.
questions.explain: Judge and manager need conclusive grounds.
questions.rule: Same kind.
questions.teaches: The judge has to find out whether the assertion is true and, moreover, give as good grounds as possible for his finding.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: In 'Construct a triangle whose sides have given lengths a, b, c', which is the unknown?
options: The lengths a, b, c
The sides being equal to a, b, c
The triangle
The number three
optionExplain: The lengths a, b, c are the data.
The requirement that the sides be equal to a, b, c is the condition.
Right: the triangle is the thing sought, so it is the unknown.
The number three is not an element of the problem.
questions.explain: The card next names all three parts.
questions.rule: Unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each part to its role.
pairs: The link between data and unknown
What is to be proved from the hypothesis
questions.explain: These are the principal parts of the two kinds.
questions.rule: Name the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: 'If a triangle has two equal angles, then it has two equal sides.' What is the hypothesis?
options: It has two equal sides
The triangle
Nothing; it has no parts
A triangle has two equal angles
optionExplain: That the triangle has two equal sides is the conclusion, not the hypothesis.
The triangle is the subject, not the hypothesis.
The theorem does have parts: it splits naturally into hypothesis and conclusion.
Right: the if-part, that a triangle has two equal angles, is the hypothesis.
questions.explain: The if-clause is the hypothesis.
questions.rule: If-part, then-part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: The problems of constructing a triangle from three given sides and from three given altitudes have the same unknown and the same data, but different conditions.
questions.explain: In both the unknown is a triangle and the data are three lengths; the condition linking them differs.
questions.rule: Same data, new condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Which theorem does the author give as hard to split into a hypothesis and a conclusion?
options: The theorem of Pythagoras
The sum of the angles of a triangle is two right angles
There are an infinity of prime numbers
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular
optionExplain: The theorem of Pythagoras splits naturally into hypothesis and conclusion.
The sum of the angles of a triangle splits naturally into hypothesis and conclusion.
Right: that there are an infinity of prime numbers is his example of a theorem hard to split.
The diagonals of a rhombus being perpendicular splits naturally into hypothesis and conclusion.
questions.explain: Not all theorems split naturally.
questions.rule: Not every theorem splits.
questions.teaches: Not all mathematical theorems can be split naturally into hypothesis and conclusion, and the theorem that there are an infinity of prime numbers is the author's example.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A bank wants to know whether a customer's claim of a stolen card is true. Which pair of parts would a problem to prove about it have?
options: A hypothesis (the facts assumed) and a conclusion (the claim to be established)
An unknown and data, since the bank has to find out what happened to the card and from what facts
A figure and a notation, since the bank will draw the events on a diagram and give them labels
A lemma and a corollary, since the bank will prove an auxiliary claim and then draw a result from it
optionExplain: Right: a problem to prove has a hypothesis, the facts assumed, and a conclusion, the claim to be established.
An unknown and data are the parts of a problem to find, not of a problem to prove.
A figure and a notation are aids, not the principal parts.
A lemma and a corollary are terms for theorems, not the principal parts.
questions.explain: Problems to prove have hypothesis and conclusion.
questions.rule: Hypothesis, conclusion.
questions.teaches: Mathematical problems to prove of the usual kind have as principal parts the hypothesis and the conclusion of the theorem to be proved or disproved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A list question reads: 'Look at the unknown! Think of a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown.' You have a theorem to prove. What would the matching advice be?
options: Look at the hypothesis and think of a familiar theorem with a similar hypothesis
Look at the figure and redraw it
Look at the conclusion and think of a familiar theorem with a similar conclusion
Look at the proof of another theorem
optionExplain: The unknown corresponds to the conclusion, not to the hypothesis.
Redrawing the figure is not the matching advice for this question.
Right: the conclusion plays the unknown's role, so look at it and think of a familiar theorem with a similar conclusion.
Looking at another proof is not the matching advice.
questions.explain: The card next gives the table of parallels.
questions.rule: Unknown becomes conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: Match each question for a problem to find with its counterpart for a problem to prove.
pairs: Did you use the whole condition?
Did you use the whole hypothesis?
questions.explain: These are the author's pairs: unknown with conclusion, and condition with hypothesis.
questions.rule: Pair the questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: For the theorem 'if the four sides of a quadrilateral are equal, the diagonals are perpendicular', which is the counterpart of 'Separate the various parts of the condition'?
options: Separate the various parts of the hypothesis
Separate the various parts of the conclusion
Separate the sides of the quadrilateral from each other
Separate the theorem from its proof
optionExplain: Right: the hypothesis takes the place of the condition, so one separates its parts.
The conclusion plays the role of the unknown, not of the condition.
Separating the sides of the quadrilateral from each other is not the counterpart.
Separating the theorem from its proof is not the counterpart.
questions.explain: The condition's counterpart is the hypothesis.
questions.rule: Condition becomes hypothesis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: For a theorem, keep only a part of the hypothesis, drop the other part, and ask whether the ____ is still valid.
questions.explain: This is the counterpart of keeping a part of the condition and asking how far the unknown is determined.
questions.rule: Weaken the hypothesis, test the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author's counterpart ask about changing the parts of a problem to prove?
options: Whether the proof can be shortened by changing some of its steps so that the argument is easier to follow
Whether the theorem can be replaced by its converse, which may be easier to prove than the original
Whether the hypothesis, the conclusion or both can be changed so that they are nearer to each other
Whether the conclusion can be dropped altogether so that only the hypothesis remains to be examined
optionExplain: The question is about the parts of the theorem, not about the proof.
Converses are not mentioned here.
Right: the counterpart asks whether the hypothesis, the conclusion or both can be changed so that they are nearer to each other.
Dropping the conclusion would leave nothing to prove.
questions.explain: The new hypothesis and the new conclusion should be nearer to each other.
questions.rule: Bring them nearer.
questions.teaches: For a problem to prove the counterpart asks whether you could change the hypothesis, or the conclusion, or both if necessary, so that the new hypothesis and the new conclusion are nearer to each other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A lawyer wonders whether a weaker premise would still yield the same conclusion. Which list question is this?
options: Look at the unknown, and try to think of a familiar problem with the same or a similar unknown
Keep only a part of the hypothesis; is the conclusion still valid?
Draw a figure, and introduce suitable notation for the elements that the weaker premise concerns
Did you use the whole condition, so that no clause of the premise has been left out of the argument
optionExplain: That question is about the unknown, which corresponds to the conclusion, not to a weaker premise.
Right: keeping only a part of the hypothesis and asking whether the conclusion is still valid is this move.
That question is about drawing a figure and notation, not about weakening a premise.
That question is about using the whole condition, which is the opposite of weakening it.
questions.explain: Weakening the hypothesis is a standard move.
questions.rule: Weaken and test.
questions.teaches: Another question for a problem to prove is: could you think of another hypothesis from which you could easily derive the conclusion?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A school course has mostly find-the-number tasks while a university course has mostly show-that tasks. What does this suggest about the two levels?
options: The university course is the easier of the two, since showing a statement is true is simpler than finding
The school course is the more advanced, since finding a number needs more skill than showing a claim
The two courses are the same in kind, since both ask the student to reach a definite conclusion
Elementary courses lean toward problems to find, advanced ones toward problems to prove
optionExplain: There is no reason to think the university course is easier.
That reverses the pattern: elementary courses lean toward problems to find.
The two courses differ in emphasis, so they are not the same in kind.
Right: elementary courses lean toward problems to find, advanced ones toward problems to prove.
questions.explain: The card next states the author's remark.
questions.rule: Find then prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, problems to prove are more important in advanced mathematics than in elementary mathematics.
questions.explain: That is the statement the author makes about the emphasis of elementary and advanced courses.
questions.rule: Prove for advanced.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A textbook for beginners has 90 percent find-type tasks. How would the author view this?
options: As fitting, since problems to find matter more at elementary level
As an error, since a book for beginners ought to give as many tasks of proof as tasks of finding
As proof that the book is really an advanced one, since problems to find mark the advanced level
As unimportant, since the proportion of find and prove tasks does not matter to a beginner
optionExplain: Right: it is fitting, since problems to find matter more at elementary level.
He does not require equal numbers of both kinds in a beginner's book.
Problems to find mark the elementary level, so this does not show an advanced book.
The author gives the proportion importance, so he would not call it unimportant.
questions.explain: Problems to find dominate elementary mathematics.
questions.rule: Beginners seek objects.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: The author's list is specially adapted to problems to ____.
questions.explain: It must be revised for problems to prove.
questions.rule: Adapted to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: What does the author say the book needs to do to apply the list to problems to prove?
options: Throw the list out and start again, since a list built for one kind of problem is of no use to another
Use it without any change, since the same questions apply equally well to both kinds of problem
Add a section on proof at the end and leave the rest as it stands, since the list is complete
Revise it and change some of its questions and suggestions
optionExplain: The list is of use for proof with changes, so throwing it out is not his advice.
He says changes are needed, so using the list unchanged is wrong.
Adding a section at the end and leaving the rest as it stands is not what he says.
Right: he says the list must be revised and some of its questions and suggestions changed.
questions.explain: A revision of the list is needed, with some questions and suggestions changed, for problems to prove.
questions.rule: Revise the list.
questions.teaches: We have to revise the list and change some of its questions and suggestions in order to apply it also to problems to prove.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Modern Heuristic to Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.section: Problems to Find, Problems to Prove
questions.q: A mixed-ability class meets a worksheet with both find and prove tasks. What does the author's remark suggest a teacher should do?
options: Use the same list wording for both kinds of task, so that the pupils learn one set of questions
Use the list as is for find tasks and adapt it for prove tasks
Avoid the prove tasks until the pupils are older, because the list does not suit them at all
Avoid the find tasks, because the list is built for proof and not for finding an unknown
optionExplain: The list must be changed for prove tasks, so one wording for both is not suitable.
Right: use the list as it stands for find tasks and adapt it for prove tasks.
The list can be revised for prove tasks, so they need not be avoided until the pupils are older.
The list suits find tasks as it stands, so avoiding them is wrong.
questions.explain: Adapt the list to each kind: as it stands for find tasks, revised for prove tasks.
questions.rule: Adapt to the kind.
questions.teaches: In the present book problems to find are emphasised more than problems to prove, though the other kind matters more in advanced mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: By the time a hard problem is solved, your picture of it holds much more than at the start. What was mostly added?
options: New facts learned from sources outside your own head
A stronger feeling of certainty that the answer is within reach
Relevant knowledge you already had but had not yet brought to mind
A tidier restatement of the data in the same words as before
optionExplain: Plausible, since looking things up feels like gaining material; but the book's account puts the gain inside memory.
Prevision does grow, but a feeling is not material added to the conception of the problem.
Right: according to Polya, the addition is largely material extracted from memory. The card next gives it a name.
Restating can help, but it rearranges what is there and adds no knowledge.
questions.explain: Polya says what has been added is what we succeeded in extracting from memory. The card next names this activity.
questions.rule: Mobilize first: recall the earlier problems, theorems and definitions that bear on this problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Extracting relevant items from your memory while solving a problem is called ____.
questions.explain: Polya calls the extraction of relevant elements from memory mobilization.
questions.rule: Mobilization: extract the relevant items from memory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A student stares at a task: find the number of diagonals of a decagon. Which move is mobilization?
options: Draw the decagon very large and neat so that every vertex and line is easy to see
Decide in advance that the answer must be a round number such as 30 and work toward it
Check the final count against the answer printed at the back of the book before starting
Ask which related problems, formulas or definitions about polygons are already known
optionExplain: Drawing helps but is not recall; it brings no stored knowledge to the table.
A guess about the answer is not material taken from memory.
That is checking a result, which belongs after the solving, not to bringing knowledge into play.
Right: this reaches into dormant knowledge for material that may bear on the task.
questions.explain: Mobilization draws on formerly solved problems, theorems and definitions. Drawing or guessing may follow, but only recall adds stored knowledge.
questions.rule: Ask what you already know that touches this problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A tutor says: 'A solved problem contains nothing that was not in its statement.' Which reply fits Polya's account?
options: Wrong: it also contains facts about the world that no one in the room had known before
Wrong: the finished conception includes recalled items such as earlier problems and theorems
Right: the statement already holds everything, and solving only decodes what is there
Right for routine problems only, since hard ones need entirely new theorems invented
optionExplain: The book speaks of material the solver already held but had not used, not new knowledge for everyone.
Right: that is what the solver added by extracting material from memory.
The statement is a starting point; the book says much more stands in the conception at the end.
Polya does not say hard problems need invented theorems; he says recalled material fills the gap.
questions.explain: The book states that the conception of the problem is much fuller at the end, and the addition is mobilized memory.
questions.rule: The solution picture is richer than the statement; the difference is recalled knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: a solver who recalls many facts but does not link them to the aim of the problem has completed both mobilizing and organizing.
questions.explain: The book treats extraction from memory as one half; the facts must also be combined into a well adapted whole. Our reading: mobilizing helps when its facts are aimed at the problem.
questions.rule: Isolated facts are not a solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which suggestion from the book's list is aimed directly at mobilization?
options: Look at the unknown, and try to think of a familiar problem with a similar unknown
Could you restate the problem still differently, using other words for its parts?
Did you use the whole condition, and have you taken all its parts into account?
Is the condition sufficient to determine the unknown, or is it insufficient or redundant?
optionExplain: Right: it sends you to memory for a known problem sharing the unknown.
This is aimed at varying the problem, a different aspect of progress.
This asks whether enough material has been collected or used; it checks coverage, not recall.
This tries to foresee the nature of the solution, not to retrieve anything.
questions.explain: Polya names questions such as 'Have you seen it before?' and 'Look at the unknown!' as aimed at mobilizing formerly acquired knowledge.
questions.rule: Questions about related problems and the unknown pull knowledge out of memory.
questions.teaches: Among the suggestions aimed directly at mobilization, the book lists: 'Look at the unknown! And try to think of a familiar problem having the same or a similar unknown.'

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver has recalled five relevant theorems but has not solved the problem. What is still missing?
options: A sixth theorem, since five recalled theorems cannot be enough for any problem
A faster way of reciting the theorems from memory whenever the problem comes up
More confidence that the problem has an answer, since the facts are already there
An argument connecting the recalled items into a whole adapted to the problem
optionExplain: Another fact may help, but the shortfall described is connection, not count.
Speed of recall is not the gap; the facts are already in hand.
Confidence may grow with progress, but it does not turn facts into an argument.
Right: recall provides parts; the combining step builds the solution. The card names it.
questions.explain: Polya says it is not enough to recollect isolated facts; their combination must be adapted to the problem. The card next gives this its name.
questions.rule: After recalling, build the argument: connect the materials into a whole adapted to the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: The adapting and combining activity that connects recalled materials into a well adapted whole is called ____.
questions.explain: Polya names the combining and adapting of recalled material organization.
questions.rule: Organization: combine the recalled facts into a whole that fits the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A cook has recalled how to make dough, a sauce and a filling, and still has no dinner. Which move is organization?
options: Look up a fourth recipe for dessert to add to the stack of recipes already known
Reread each recipe slowly to make sure that every one of them is remembered accurately
Wait until a better idea for the evening comes of itself, then cook whatever suits it
Decide the order and timing so the dough, sauce and filling come together as one dish
optionExplain: More material is mobilization-like; it does not combine what is held.
Better recall is not connection; the parts are already known.
Waiting adds nothing; organization is something the cook does.
Right: this links the recalled parts into a whole that serves the aim.
questions.explain: Organization is the act of linking recalled parts. Here the cook plans the dish; recalling more would not do it.
questions.rule: Recalled parts become a solution when they are connected.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each activity: is it mobilization or organization?

items.t: Recalling a theorem about similar triangles
Remembering how a formerly solved problem went
Recalling the definition of a term in the problem
Building an argument that links the theorem to the unknown
Fitting the old problem's method to the new data
Working the recalled pieces into one connected chain

questions.explain: Mobilization extracts items from memory. Organization adapts and combines them into a whole fitted to the problem.
questions.rule: Mobilize to get the pieces; organize to join them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: if a solver fails to organize, recalling more and more facts is guaranteed to finish the solution.
questions.explain: Without combining, extra facts remain isolated. Polya says recollecting isolated facts is not enough. Our reading: additional recall helps only when it feeds an argument.
questions.rule: More facts do not replace connecting them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: In the book's list, which question aims at organization, the use of material already collected?
options: Have you seen this very problem before, perhaps in a slightly different form?
Could you restate the problem in other words, so that it looks different?
Could you use the result or the method of a related problem solved before?
Is it possible to satisfy the condition, and is the condition contradictory?
optionExplain: This asks for recall, a mobilizing question.
This varies the problem rather than assembling material.
Right: it asks whether collected material can be built into the solution.
This is a question about foreseeing the solution's nature, not about using collected material.
questions.explain: Polya says some typical situations are those where we think the right material has been collected and we work for better organization; the question about using a related problem's result or method belongs there.
questions.rule: A related solved problem is used by its result or its method.
questions.teaches: The book says that when we think the right material is collected, a suggestion to organize it is: could you use the related problem's result, or its method, or introduce an auxiliary element to make its use possible?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which description of working at a problem with concentration seems most accurate?
options: You first collect every fact you know, then start thinking about how to join them
You connect the pieces first and look for the facts afterwards
You wait without thinking until the whole solution appears
You recall facts that seem connected with your purpose, and connect them as you recall
optionExplain: This two-phase picture is tempting but the book says the two cannot really be separated.
Connection needs recalled material to work on, so this order fails.
Polya's account describes active working, not waiting.
Right: recall and combination go together. The card gives the book's reasoning.
questions.explain: Polya says mobilization and organization can never be really separated; the card gives his reason.
questions.rule: While working, recall facts connected with your purpose and connect them as you go.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: According to Polya, mobilization and organization are two ____ of the same complex process.
questions.explain: He calls them two aspects of one process, which has still many other aspects.
questions.rule: Mobilization and organization are aspects of one process.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A student plans: 'Monday, I only list all theorems I know; Tuesday, I only try connecting them.' What does Polya's account suggest?
options: The plan is ideal, because giving each task its own day keeps the two tasks clean and apart
The split is artificial: recall during work is guided by purpose, and connecting uses what was recalled
The plan fails only because Monday's list of theorems will probably be too short to be useful
The plan works if the theorems are listed in alphabetical order, so that none is missed
optionExplain: The book says the two cannot be separated; tidy scheduling does not make them separate in practice.
Right: the two go together while working.
The objection is to splitting, not to length.
Order of listing does not touch the point that recall is guided by purpose.
questions.explain: Because we recall facts with a purpose in mind, the recalling is already pulled toward combination.
questions.rule: While working, recall facts connected with your purpose and connect them as you go.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya claims mobilization and organization together are the whole of progress in solving a problem.
questions.explain: He says they are but two aspects of one complex process with still many other aspects, such as the changing conception of the problem.
questions.rule: Mobilization and organization are not the whole story.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Besides mobilization and organization, which further aspect of progress does the book go on to describe?
options: The mode of conception of the problem changes as we view it from different sides
The solver's memory slowly improves with every hour of practice at similar problems
The teacher's instructions become clearer and clearer as the solver asks more questions
The data of the problem are replaced by simpler numbers wherever that is possible
optionExplain: Right: Polya names the changing conception as another aspect.
The book does not list this as an aspect of progress within one solution.
Teaching is a different topic; the aspects concern the solver's work.
Replacing data may be a tool but is not named as the aspect of progress here.
questions.explain: Polya says the first two are but aspects of one process with many others; the next he names is the change of conception.
questions.rule: Progress also shows as a changing conception.
questions.teaches: Polya names a further aspect of progress: our mode of conception changes, and we could make hardly any progress without variation of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver is stuck after repeating the same view of a problem. What does Polya say we can hardly do without?
options: Repeat the same view more carefully
Reduce the problem to its numerical data only
Look at the problem from different sides, varying it
Wait for the memory to supply the missing fact
optionExplain: Repetition polishes one view and does not change it.
Data alone drop the other parts of the problem, not the standpoints.
Right: variation is how conceptions improve. The card gives the reason.
Mobilization matters, but this question asks about changing the conception.
questions.explain: Polya says we could make hardly any progress without variation of the problem.
questions.rule: When your first conception stalls, vary the problem: another standpoint, another side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says we could make hardly any progress without ____ of the problem.
questions.explain: The needed activity is variation of the problem.
questions.rule: Progress needs variation of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Someone cannot decide where to place a new shop. Which step is a variation of the problem in Polya's sense?
options: Ask the same question again, louder, in the same words
Pick the street with the cheapest rent without further thought
Restate it as: where do the customers I want already walk?
Copy the location a competitor chose and stop
optionExplain: Repeating the question does not change the standpoint.
This drops part of the problem instead of viewing it differently.
Right: a new standpoint on the same problem.
Copying may be a solution but it is no variation of the question.
questions.explain: A restatement that exposes another side of the problem is a variation; repeating it or dropping parts is not.
questions.rule: When your first conception stalls, vary the problem: another standpoint, another side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, the solver's conception of the problem at the end is likely to be fuller than at the outset.
questions.explain: Polya states that enriched with the materials recalled and worked into it, our conception is much fuller at the end than at the beginning.
questions.rule: Expect the conception to grow.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which suggestion from the list is aimed at variation of the problem by a specified means?
options: Asking whether you have used all the data, and whether the whole condition has been used in the working
Looking at the unknown and trying to recall a familiar problem that has a similar unknown
Going back to the definition, or using analogy, generalization, specialization or decomposing and recombining
Asking whether the condition is contradictory, redundant, insufficient or sufficient
optionExplain: This is about coverage of the data, not about varying the problem.
Recalling a familiar problem with a similar unknown is mobilization, not a means of varying the problem.
Right: these are the specified means the book names.
That is a foresight question about the solution's nature.
questions.explain: Polya says many questions aim at variation by specified means: going back to the definition, analogy, generalization, specialization, decomposing and recombining.
questions.rule: Variation has named means.
questions.teaches: The book lists the specified means of variation: going back to the definition, using analogy, generalization, specialization, and decomposing and recombining.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: When you feel you are getting nearer to a solution, how sure should you treat that feeling, according to Polya?
options: As a plausible guess that guides the work but is not certainty
As proof that the solution is correct, since seeing better means knowing better
As worthless, since only facts that are already certain can be used in solving
As evidence that the problem is routine, since its steps are now visible to you
optionExplain: Right: a plausible foresight is useful but provisional. The card explains.
Seeing better is not having proved anything.
Polya says we could never find the certain solution without plausible considerations.
Foresight is part of all problem solving; it does not mark the problem as routine.
questions.explain: Polya says we do not foresee with certainty, only with a certain degree of plausibility.
questions.rule: Use plausible foresight to guide you, then confirm it by complete argument.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya calls the reasoning that uses plausible, provisional considerations ____ reasoning.
questions.explain: He writes that we need heuristic reasoning because only complete solutions give certainty.
questions.rule: We need heuristic reasoning to reach certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A programmer suspects that a caching trick might fix a slowdown but has not tested it. How should she treat the suspicion?
options: As settled, so that she can report the slowdown as fixed in the next status note
As useless, so she should ignore it until some other test has proved it for her
As a plausible lead to try and confirm, not yet a conclusion
As a good reason to stop looking at other causes of the slowdown from now on
optionExplain: An untested lead is not a result, so reporting the slowdown as fixed would be premature.
Provisional guesses are how a solver moves toward something provable.
Right: use it to steer, then verify.
Plausibility is not proof, so other causes stay open.
questions.explain: Plausible foresight guides the work; a complete argument or test gives certainty.
questions.rule: Use plausible foresight to guide you, then confirm it by complete argument.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each statement: does it match Polya's view of foresight, or contradict it?

items.t: We see the goal better as our examination advances
Foresight comes with some degree of plausibility
Certainty arrives with the complete solution
A plausible hunch is as good as a finished proof
Provisional guesses should be avoided until certainty is secured
We foresee the whole solution exactly from the start

questions.explain: Polya says foresight grows as we work and is plausible, never certain, until the solution is complete. Without plausible guesses the certain solution could not be found.
questions.rule: Guess plausibly, then secure it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: The book lists examples of what a lucky solver may foresee. Which one is named?
options: That a certain known theorem might be used
That the answer must be a whole number
That the problem has exactly one solution
That the teacher will approve the method
optionExplain: Right: it is one of the three named examples.
The book does not give this as an example of foresight.
This is not among the foreseen items named.
This is unrelated to the solver's foresight about the solution.
questions.explain: Polya gives three examples: a known theorem might be used, a formerly solved problem might help, and going back to the meaning of a technical term might be necessary.
questions.rule: Foresee which theorem, problem or term may matter.
questions.teaches: Polya names examples of foresight: that a known theorem might be used, that a formerly solved problem might help, or that going back to the meaning of a technical term might be necessary.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A supervisor asks whether you have made progress. Which reply gives the supervisor most to go on?
options: I have recalled the relevant theorem, I see the task as an angle question, and I expect the last step to use it
I have worked on it for two hours without any break at all, and I intend to keep going until it is completely done
I feel much more confident than I did at the start, though I cannot say what has changed
I have filled three pages with calculations, and the pages show how much I have tried
optionExplain: Right: it names the substance of progress. The card lists the signs.
Time spent is effort, not a sign of advance.
Confidence alone says nothing about what has changed.
Volume of writing does not show advance toward the solution.
questions.explain: Progress shows in material mobilized and organized, in a changed conception, and in clearer foresight.
questions.rule: Judge progress by what is mobilized and organized, how the conception has changed, and what you now foresee.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya defines progress as advancing mobilization and organization, evolution of the conception, and increasing ____ of the final steps.
questions.explain: The third sign is increasing prevision of the steps that will constitute the final argument.
questions.rule: Progress includes growing prevision of the final steps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: After an hour, a pupil can say: 'I have not changed my picture of the problem, recalled nothing new and foresee nothing.' What is the fair verdict?
options: Substantial progress, because an hour has passed
Some progress, since staying calm counts as organization
None of Polya's three signs of progress is present
Progress of the abrupt kind, to be followed by a bright idea
optionExplain: Time passing is not one of Polya's three signs; an hour with no change of picture shows no progress.
Staying calm is not organization of knowledge, which is only one of the signs Polya names.
Right: no mobilization, no change of conception, no prevision.
A bright idea is a sudden reorganization; the statement describes no change at all.
questions.explain: With no knowledge brought up, no new conception and no foresight, Polya's account finds no sign of advance.
questions.rule: Judge progress by what is mobilized and organized, how the conception has changed, and what you now foresee.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which are signs of progress toward a solution in Polya's account? Select all that apply.
options: The statement of the problem has been copied out more neatly
Knowledge relevant to the problem is better mobilized and organized
The solver conceives the problem differently and more adequately
The solver has used more paper than at the start
The solver foresees more of the steps of the final argument
optionExplain: Neat copying does not change the substance.
Right: the first sign.
Right: the second sign.
The amount of paper used says nothing about knowledge, conception or foresight, so it is not a sign.
Right: the third sign.
questions.explain: Polya lists mobilization and organization, evolution of the conception, and increasing prevision as progress.
questions.rule: Judge progress by what is mobilized and organized, how the conception has changed, and what you now foresee.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: According to Polya, how can progress arrive?
options: Only in small steps, since leaps are accidents that tell us nothing about the solver's work
Only in leaps, since small steps are not real advance toward the solution at all
Only when a teacher confirms each step, since the solver cannot judge progress alone
Steadily by small imperceptible steps, and now and then abruptly by leaps and bounds
optionExplain: He names leaps, the bright ideas, as a normal case.
He names small steady steps as a kind of advance.
Progress is described from the solver's work, not from approval.
Right: both kinds occur.
questions.explain: Polya says we may advance steadily by small imperceptible steps, but now and then we advance abruptly.
questions.rule: Progress can be steady or abrupt.
questions.teaches: Polya says we may advance steadily, by small imperceptible steps, but now and then we advance abruptly, by leaps and bounds.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Suddenly you see a problem in a new way and the next steps become visible. What would Polya call this?
options: A bright idea: a sudden reorganization of the way the problem is conceived
A routine problem, since its remaining steps became visible all at once to the solver
A reductio ad absurdum, since you changed your mind about the way the problem stands
An error of foresight, since foresight is only plausible and so cannot be trusted
optionExplain: Right: that is his definition. The card gives the details.
A routine problem is one solved by a formerly solved pattern, not a sudden insight.
This is a method of proof, not a sudden change of outlook.
Plausible foresight is not an error, and a bright idea includes a confident one.
questions.explain: Polya describes a bright idea as a sudden advance toward the solution.
questions.rule: Prepare for the bright idea by working on understanding and planning, and carry it through when it comes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A bright idea is an abrupt and momentous change of our ____ on the problem, a sudden reorganization of how we conceive it.
questions.explain: Polya describes the bright idea as an abrupt and momentous change of outlook, with a just emerging confident prevision of the steps.
questions.rule: A bright idea is a sudden change of outlook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A team debugging a failure says: 'We saw it differently: it is not a code fault but a timing fault, and now the fix is clear.' What is this?
options: Steady progress by small imperceptible steps, since the team kept working on it
A bright idea: an abrupt reorganization of how the problem is conceived
Mobilization only, since they recalled one fact about timing and then used it
A routine problem solved by substituting the data into a known general solution
optionExplain: Small imperceptible steps are the other kind of progress; here the change of view was abrupt and momentous.
Right: the outlook changed suddenly and the steps became foreseeable.
The reorganized view is more than a recalled fact.
Nothing was substituted into a ready general solution.
questions.explain: Seeing the problem a new way and foreseeing the steps is a bright idea.
questions.rule: Prepare for the bright idea by working on understanding and planning, and carry it through when it comes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: according to Polya, the questions on the list mention the bright idea directly.
questions.explain: He says they do not mention it directly, yet all are concerned with it.
questions.rule: The list never names the bright idea but serves it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: How does Polya relate the four phases of solving to the bright idea?
options: Understanding the problem produces the idea by itself, so the later phases only check it and cannot add to it
Looking back prevents the idea, because it shows that the first plan was probably wrong
Devising a plan replaces the idea, because a good plan is complete and needs no insight
Understanding prepares for it, devising a plan tries to provoke it, carrying out follows it, looking back exploits it
optionExplain: Understanding prepares for the idea but does not produce it.
Looking back tries to exploit it better.
Devising a plan tries to provoke the bright idea; it does not replace it, and a good plan may still wait for one.
Right: each phase has its relation.
questions.explain: The questions are all about the bright idea: preparing, provoking, carrying through, exploiting.
questions.rule: Each phase stands in a relation to the bright idea.
questions.teaches: Polya says that in understanding the problem we prepare for the bright idea, in devising a plan we try to provoke it, we then carry it through, and in looking back we try to exploit it better.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver feels all needed material is probably at hand but cannot fit it together. Which question suits best?
options: Could you use the result or method of a related problem you solved before?
Have you seen this problem before, or the same problem in a slightly different form?
Could you restate the problem differently, or restate it still differently again?
Is the condition sufficient, insufficient, redundant or even contradictory?
optionExplain: Right: it asks how to use what is at hand. The card sorts the others.
This asks for more recall, but the material is already at hand; the gap is in fitting it together.
A variation question; useful, but this solver's difficulty is organizing what they hold.
This tries to foresee the nature of the solution.
questions.explain: When the right material seems collected, the questions about using a related problem's result or method serve organization.
questions.rule: Diagnose your situation first, then pick the question that matches it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Match each situation to the kind of question that suits it.
pairs: You think you have not collected enough
Did you use all the data and the whole condition?
You want to look at the problem another way
You want to foresee the nature of the solution
Is the condition sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory?
You want to recall formerly acquired knowledge
Do you know a related problem or a useful theorem?
questions.explain: Each group of questions is aimed at one part of progress: more material, variation, foresight, or recall.
questions.rule: Pick the question by the situation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver realises she overlooked one clause of the problem. Which question from the list fits her moment?
options: Could you restate it still differently?
Did you use the whole condition?
Do you know a theorem that could be useful?
Look at the unknown
optionExplain: A variation question; she has a more specific lead.
Right: a question for when material may be missing.
Recall may help later; her clue is an unused part.
The unknown is not the trouble in this case.
questions.explain: Unused data or condition signals missing material, and the question about using the whole condition addresses it.
questions.rule: Diagnose your situation first, then pick the question that matches it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each question: is it aimed at mobilizing knowledge or at checking for missing material?

items.t: Have you seen it before?
Do you know a related problem?
Do you know a theorem that could be useful?
Did you use all the data?
Did you use the whole condition?
Have you taken into account all essential notions involved?

questions.explain: The first three ask you to retrieve what you know. The last three ask whether something the problem contains has been left unused.
questions.rule: Recall questions fetch; coverage questions check.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: according to the book, the questions Is the condition sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory aim at foreseeing the nature of the solution.
questions.explain: Polya places 'Is it possible to satisfy the condition? Is it sufficient to determine the unknown? Or insufficient? Or redundant? Or contradictory?' among questions that try to foresee the nature of the solution sought.
questions.rule: Some questions test what kind of solution is possible.
questions.teaches: Polya says some questions try to foresee the nature of the solution: whether the condition can be satisfied, and whether it is sufficient, insufficient, redundant or contradictory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Why does Polya try to describe progress in general if we already judge it in single cases?
options: To make the study of heuristic somewhat complete, he must clarify what progress is in general
Because judging progress in single cases is usually mistaken and needs a formula to correct it
Because a general account lets teachers skip the supervision of the students' own work
Because progress cannot be recognised at all unless it is first defined in a formula
optionExplain: Right: that is his stated reason. The card has the detail.
He says we judge such cases with fair confidence.
The general account does not replace supervision.
He offers no formula, only a descriptive account.
questions.explain: Polya says we are used to judge progress in concrete cases, but a study of heuristic needs the general step.
questions.rule: Do not stop at feeling you can judge progress; state in general what it consists of.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya's second question about a solver's work asks what the essential ____ was.
questions.explain: The two questions of the entry are about progress and the essential achievement.
questions.rule: Ask about progress and about the essential achievement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A hiking guide can tell any walker whether they are on the route, but has not written down what being on the route means. What would Polya's reasoning suggest?
options: Leave it unwritten, since concrete judgments are enough for any book
Write that it cannot be defined and skip it
Try to clarify in general what being on track consists of
Define it by the speed of walking alone
optionExplain: Polya insists a complete study must undertake the step.
He says the step is hard, not impossible.
Right: the same step he takes for progress.
That would be a quick formula; Polya's account has several aspects.
questions.explain: Judgment in cases does not replace a general statement when a study aims at completeness.
questions.rule: Do not stop at feeling you can judge progress; state in general what it consists of.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya's two questions about a solver's work ask for different things. Which pair is right?
options: Progress asks whether the work has advanced; achievement asks for the essential gain
Progress asks for the answer to the problem; achievement asks for the proof of that answer
Progress concerns the teacher's point of view; achievement concerns the student's own view
Progress is judged only at the end of the work; achievement is judged during the work
optionExplain: Right: the first asks about advance, the second about the main gain.
Neither is a request for answer or proof.
Both can be asked of oneself or of a student.
He says we ask these questions while solving.
questions.explain: Have you made any progress? What was the essential achievement? Both are put during and after solving.
questions.rule: Do not stop at feeling you can judge progress; state in general what it consists of.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A team lead wants to ask what the essential achievement of a piece of work was. Who, according to Polya, may put such questions?
options: Only a teacher marking finished work, once the student has handed in the whole solution for grading
Only the solver, after the answer is found and the whole solution is written down
The solver to themself while solving, or a supervisor to a student whose work they supervise
Only a researcher who is studying heuristic and who has not worked the problem
optionExplain: He also names the solver's own use while solving.
Polya says we may put such questions to ourselves while solving, not only after the solution is written.
Right: both uses are named.
He says everyday solvers and supervisors ask them.
questions.explain: We may address questions of this kind to ourselves when we are solving a problem or to a student whose work we supervise.
questions.rule: Progress questions are asked by solvers and supervisors alike.
questions.teaches: Polya says we may address the questions about progress and achievement to ourselves when we are solving a problem, or to a student whose work we supervise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: In the puzzle 'rearrange the letters of DRY OXTAIL IN REAR into one word', what is the unknown?
options: The four given words
The number of letters, fifteen
The rule that the word is a common one
A single word
optionExplain: They are given, so they are the data.
This is a fact about the condition, not the thing sought.
This is a likely feature of the condition, not what must be found.
Right: the thing to find. The card sets out data and condition as well.
questions.explain: The question is what the unknown is: here a word.
questions.rule: On a puzzle, begin as on any problem: what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: The anagram DRY OXTAIL IN REAR uses a total of ____ letters.
questions.explain: Counting 3 + 6 + 2 + 4 letters in the four words gives fifteen.
questions.rule: Count the letters the condition fixes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A puzzle asks you to rearrange the letters of SILENT into another word. Which description of the condition is right?
options: The new word has more than six letters, so extra ones may be added
The new word uses exactly the six letters of SILENT, each once
The new word must rhyme with SILENT
The new word is SILENT, since it uses all its letters
optionExplain: Rearranging uses the given letters only, so no extra letters may be added.
Right: this is what the answer must satisfy.
The puzzle states no rhyme; its condition concerns the letters that must be used.
The unknown is a rearrangement into a word, which here is something else.
questions.explain: The condition says the new word must use exactly the given letters.
questions.rule: On a puzzle, begin as on any problem: what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: according to Polya, several questions of the list are pertinent and stimulating on an anagram puzzle, even though it is not a mathematical problem.
questions.explain: He uses the anagram to test the claim that the list is independent of subject-matter and finds several of its questions pertinent.
questions.rule: The list is independent of the subject-matter.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which pair of statements about the anagram puzzle puts data and condition correctly?
options: Data: the fifteen letters. Condition: the answer is made from the four given words and is a plausible English word
Data: the four words. Condition: the answer uses their fifteen letters and is a probable English word
Data: the word that is to be found. Condition: the answer is made from the four words
Data: none are given. Condition: the answer is an English word of any length at all
optionExplain: This swaps data and condition: the fifteen letters belong to the condition, and the four words are the data.
Right: data are given, the condition constrains the unknown.
The word to be found is the unknown, so it cannot be listed among the data.
The four words are the data, so saying none are given misreads the puzzle.
questions.explain: Unknown: a word. Data: the four words. Condition: the fifteen letters and a not too unusual English word.
questions.rule: On a puzzle, begin as on any problem: what is the unknown, what are the data, what is the condition?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: For the anagram DRY OXTAIL IN REAR, how does Polya answer the suggestion to draw a figure?
options: By drawing a picture of the objects named in the words
By sketching the alphabet in order
By marking out fifteen blank spaces, one for each letter
By drawing no figure, since puzzles have none
optionExplain: The words name no object that could be drawn; the figure Polya suggests concerns the letters.
Alphabetical order is not the point; the figure is a row of places to be filled.
Right: the figure is a row of blanks.
He does draw one: a row of blanks serves as the figure of a word puzzle.
questions.explain: The count is 3 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 15 letters, so fifteen blanks.
questions.rule: A figure for a word puzzle is a row of blanks.
questions.teaches: Polya answers the suggestion 'Draw a figure' for the anagram by marking out fifteen blank spaces.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: You restate an anagram by listing its letters with vowels in one group and consonants in another. Which feature does this make easy to see?
options: The meaning of the word that the letters will spell, once they are put in order
About how many syllables the answer word will have
The language that the answer word comes from, judging by the letters used
The first letter of the answer word, since the groups are already in order
optionExplain: Letters alone do not reveal the meaning.
Right: vowel count points to syllables. The card works the example.
The grouping says nothing about language.
Position is not shown by grouping.
questions.explain: Separating vowels and consonants shows the number of vowels, hence syllables.
questions.rule: Restate the puzzle as a set of letters, with vowels apart from consonants, and read off what that shows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Counting Y as a vowel, the letters of DRY OXTAIL IN REAR contain ____ vowel letters.
questions.explain: The vowels are A, A, E, I, I, O, Y: seven. The other eight letters are consonants.
questions.rule: Count the vowels.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A puzzle asks for one word from the nine letters A,A,C,E,E,I,N,S,T. The vowels are A,A,E,E,I (five). What does this suggest?
options: The word has exactly nine syllables, one for each of the nine letters in the puzzle
The word has four syllables, because the count of consonants fixes the syllables
The word probably has about five syllables, unless diphthongs cut the count
No word can be formed at all, because five vowels are too many for one word
optionExplain: Syllables follow vowels, not every letter.
Consonants do not set the syllable count; syllables follow the vowels.
Right: same reasoning, with the same caveat.
The count gives no verdict on existence.
questions.explain: Five vowels suggest five syllables, with fewer if diphthongs are present.
questions.rule: Restate the puzzle as a set of letters, with vowels apart from consonants, and read off what that shows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya says the alphabetical order of the letters is the important thing when separating vowels from consonants.
questions.explain: He says separating vowels from consonants is important and the alphabetical order is not.
questions.rule: Group by vowel or consonant, not by order.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: If the desired word contains diphthongs, what happens to Polya's count of seven syllables?
options: It has more than seven syllables
It still has exactly seven, diphthongs make no difference
The word has fewer than seven syllables
It has no syllables
optionExplain: Diphthongs merge vowels; they do not add syllables.
His claim is conditional on there being no diphthongs.
Right: his statement is seven syllables unless there are diphthongs.
A word has syllables whatever its letters.
questions.explain: Two vowel letters in a diphthong sound together, so the count drops.
questions.rule: Restate the puzzle as a set of letters, with vowels apart from consonants, and read off what that shows.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya calls the letter form of DRY OXTAIL IN REAR an equivalent restatement. What else does he say about it?
options: It is a weaker problem that only approximates the original and so cannot help
It is a stronger problem that adds new conditions to the original one
It may be an advantageous restatement, because it shows another aspect of the problem
It is useless unless the letters are first put into alphabetical order
optionExplain: He calls the restatement equivalent, so it is not weaker and loses nothing from the original.
No condition is added; equivalent means the restated problem asks exactly the same thing.
Right: an equivalent restatement can still be advantageous because it shows another aspect of the problem.
Alphabetical order is not important here.
questions.explain: Equivalent restatements can still help by showing a new aspect.
questions.rule: Equivalent does not mean useless.
questions.teaches: Polya notes that the equivalent restatement may be an advantageous one (he refers to AUXILIARY PROBLEM, 6), because it shows another aspect of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: You cannot find the long word for an anagram. Which step is a sensible next try?
options: Form shorter words from some of the letters, then try longer ones
Give up until a flash of insight arrives, since no method can find the word
Choose any word of fifteen letters and test only that one against the puzzle
Reorder the given letters alphabetically and read the answer off the result
optionExplain: Right: build up from partial words. The card adds more such moves.
Waiting for a flash of insight is giving up; Polya wants the solver to keep trying related problems.
Random guessing ignores the letters given.
Alphabetical order is not the point of the puzzle.
questions.explain: Related problem: words from some of the letters. The card extends this.
questions.rule: Try a related problem or a part, and keep only a part of the condition if needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: The suggestion is to solve some related problem first; here, forming words from some letters.
questions.rule: Solve a related problem first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: You are scheduling a 12-person meeting with conflicting diaries and cannot find a slot. Which move parallels 'keep only part of the condition'?
options: Invite everyone to every possible time and see who comes to which meeting
Find a time that suits the 8 core attendees first, then see who can be added
Cancel the meeting and discard the whole condition, then start the plan afresh
Wait for someone else to propose a slot and then accept whatever time it is
optionExplain: This ignores the condition rather than relaxing part of it.
Right: satisfy part of the condition, then extend.
Dropping the whole condition is not keeping part of it; the aim is to satisfy one part and then extend.
This is passivity, not a variation of the condition.
questions.explain: Keep part of the condition, satisfy it, and build toward the full one.
questions.rule: Try a related problem or a part, and keep only a part of the condition if needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each move: part of the book's suggestion for the anagram, or not suggested?

items.t: Form words with some of the given letters
Think of a usual ending for a long word
Think of a long word with an X and a Y and few consonants
Pick the longest dictionary word and check it
Assume the answer is a short common word
Stop after the first failed trial

questions.explain: Polya suggests related problems, a part of the problem, and keeping part of the condition. He treats the word as long, probably compound or with a usual ending.
questions.rule: Build from parts and endings.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: forming longer and longer words from the given letters is expected to bring us nearer to the desired word.
questions.explain: Polya says the more letters we use the nearer we may come to the desired word.
questions.rule: Longer partial words bring you nearer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya writes two ending patterns for the long word, with blanks before them. Which are they?
options: ATION and ELY
ING and ED
MENT and NESS
ABLE and ISH
optionExplain: Right: ATION and ELY are the two usual endings Polya writes for the long word.
ING and ED are common endings in general, but they are not the two Polya writes for this word.
MENT and NESS are usual endings too, but Polya does not write them in this passage.
ABLE and ISH are possible endings, yet Polya writes ATION and ELY instead.
questions.explain: Polya writes ATION and ELY.
questions.rule: Think of usual endings.
questions.teaches: Polya writes two possible usual endings for the long word: ATION and ELY, leaving blanks for the rest of the letters.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver is about to give up on a hard puzzle. What can a list of problem-solving questions realistically offer?
options: The solution itself, provided that the right question is chosen from the list
A guarantee that the puzzle has an answer if only the solver keeps on asking
A new trial, aspect or variation that may keep them thinking
A good reason to postpone the problem to another day, when it may seem easier
optionExplain: Polya says the list does not hand over solutions without effort.
A list of questions cannot promise that a puzzle has an answer; it only offers new things to try.
Right: this is the book's modest claim. The card spells it out.
Postponing is dropping; the list aims to prevent that.
questions.explain: The questions keep the ball rolling.
questions.rule: When about to drop a problem, ask a list question to find a new trial.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says the list's questions can help to keep the ball ____.
questions.explain: The phrase is that the questions keep the ball rolling.
questions.rule: The list keeps work moving.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A friend says: 'I asked all the questions from the list and still have no answer, so the list is useless.' What fits Polya's view?
options: The friend is right, since a good list of questions would have given the answer by now if it were any use
The list cannot work magic; it helps by suggesting new trials, and effort still has to continue
The friend should ask the same questions again in the same words until one works
The friend has proved that the puzzle has no solution, since every question failed
optionExplain: Polya rejects the expectation that a list could do this.
Right: the claim is modest.
Repeating the same questions in the same words adds no new trial, so it will not break the deadlock.
Failure to find an answer proves nothing about existence.
questions.explain: Polya says the questions cannot give solutions without effort.
questions.rule: When about to drop a problem, ask a list question to find a new trial.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya claims the list provides the solution of all possible puzzles without effort on the solver's part.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: the questions cannot work magic and the reader must keep trying.
questions.rule: No magic, only stimulus.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Which reading of 'keep the ball rolling' matches the passage?
options: They speed up the arithmetic so that the solver reaches the end of the work sooner
They decide which problems are worth solving and which should be dropped at once
They replace the solver's memory, so that nothing has to be recalled any more
The questions offer a new trial or aspect when we are inclined to drop the problem
optionExplain: The passage is about thinking, not speed.
No sorting of problems by worth is described; the questions help us continue, not decide what to drop.
Memory is still needed; the questions prompt recall of what we know, they do not replace it.
Right: they stop us dropping the problem.
questions.explain: When discouraged by lack of success, the questions may suggest a new trial, a new aspect, a new variation, a new stimulus.
questions.rule: The list stimulates; it does not solve.
questions.teaches: Polya says that when discouraged by lack of success we are inclined to drop the problem, and the questions may then suggest a new trial, a new aspect, a new variation of the problem, a new stimulus.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Which pair correctly describes reductio ad absurdum and indirect proof?
options: Reductio proves a claim true by direct forward steps from known facts; indirect proof shows that some assumption is absurd
Reductio shows an assumption false by deriving an absurdity; indirect proof shows a claim true by refuting its opposite
They are the same procedure under two names, used by different schools of mathematicians
Reductio is used in speech and debate, while indirect proof is used only in writing
optionExplain: The two roles are swapped: indirect proof, not reductio, is the one that establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.
Right: this is the standard split. The card gives the book's wording.
Polya calls them different but related, so treating them as one procedure blurs a distinction he draws.
Neither is tied to speaking or writing; the difference lies in what each one shows.
questions.explain: Reductio refutes an assumption; indirect proof establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.
questions.rule: Reductio ad absurdum refutes an assumption by an absurd consequence; indirect proof establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Indirect proof establishes the truth of an assertion by showing the falsity of the ____ assumption.
questions.explain: Indirect proof proves a claim by refuting its opposite.
questions.rule: Indirect: refute the opposite to establish the claim.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A detective argues that it did not rain overnight: if it had, the road would be wet, but the road is dry. Which procedure is this?
options: Direct proof, because the dry road is an observed fact that supports the claim directly
Irony, because the supposition that it rained is stressed until it looks absurd
A routine problem solved by substituting the data into a general solution
Indirect proof, with a reductio inside: the opposite is refuted by an absurd consequence
optionExplain: The road is used to refute a supposition, not to prove the claim directly.
Irony resembles the reductio in manner but this is a proof.
Nothing is substituted into a ready solution.
Right: the claim is established by refuting its opposite.
questions.explain: The opposite (it rained) is assumed, an impossible consequence is drawn, and the claim follows. Both procedures appear together.
questions.rule: Reductio ad absurdum refutes an assumption by an absurd consequence; indirect proof establishes a claim by refuting its opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each description: does it fit reductio ad absurdum alone or indirect proof?

items.t: Shows the falsity of an assumption
Derives a manifest absurdity from the assumption
Resembles irony that overstresses an opinion
Establishes the truth of an assertion
Works by refuting the opposite assumption
Resembles demolishing an opponent to establish a candidate

questions.explain: Polya's likeness for reductio is irony, for indirect proof a politician demolishing a rival. Reductio targets a false assumption; indirect proof targets the truth of a claim.
questions.rule: Reductio refutes; indirect proof establishes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: Polya counts both procedures as effective tools of discovery that come readily to an intent mind.
questions.explain: He says so, while noting that a few philosophers and many beginners dislike them.
questions.rule: Both are natural tools of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Why, according to Polya, do some people dislike these two procedures?
options: They are known to produce false results in a good number of the cases they are applied to
Satirical people and tricky politicians, whom they resemble, do not appeal to everybody
They need advanced mathematics that a beginner lacks and cannot easily be taught
