They were invented too recently in the history of mathematics to be trusted yet
optionExplain: He treats them as effective tools; the dislike is not based on false results.
Right: he gives this as the understandable reason.
The objection is not about the level of mathematics here.
The book cites Euclid's old proof, so recent invention cannot be the reason for the dislike.
questions.explain: The dislike is understandable because irony and the politician's trick do not appeal to everyone.
questions.rule: Part of the dislike follows the likeness to irony and tricks.
questions.teaches: Polya says reductio and indirect proof are disliked by a few philosophers and many beginners, which is understandable since satirical people and tricky politicians do not appeal to everybody.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: You have tried many ways to use each digit 0 to 9 once and reach a sum of exactly 100. Every try misses. What is the sound conclusion?
options: It is certainly impossible, because you have tried so many sets and none of them worked
The puzzle is badly worded and needs no solution, so the trials can stop here
You may suspect it is impossible, but only a proof settles it
Keep trying random sets, since a proof of impossibility cannot be found for such a puzzle
optionExplain: Failed trials do not prove impossibility.
The condition is clear enough to examine.
Right: failure builds suspicion, not certainty. The card works the puzzle.
Polya says a proof is easy with the right attitude.
questions.explain: The suspicion leads to the problem: prove that both parts cannot be satisfied at the same time.
questions.rule: Satisfy each part of the condition alone, then, if both together keep failing, ask whether it can be proved impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: State the two parts of the condition in the digit puzzle.
questions.a: First, each of the ten digits 0 to 9 must be used exactly once in writing the numbers. Second, the numbers must sum to exactly 100.
questions.rule: Satisfy each part of the condition alone, then, if both together keep failing, ask whether it can be proved impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A solver offers 17 + 26 + 35 + 48 + 9 + 0. Which part of the condition does it meet?
options: The digit part, since each of 0 to 9 appears once, but not the sum part: the total is 135
The sum part, since the numbers can be added to give exactly 100 as the puzzle requires of them
Both parts, because the numbers are all different from one another
Neither part, since 0 cannot be written as a number on its own in the set
optionExplain: Right: digits 1,7,2,6,3,5,4,8,9,0 each appear once; the sum is 135.
The total is 135, not 100, so the sum part fails.
Different numbers do not ensure each digit is used once, and the sum is wrong.
0 is allowed as a digit and as a number here; the digit part is met.
questions.explain: 17+26+35+48 = 126, and 126+9+0 = 135. All ten digits occur exactly once.
questions.rule: Satisfy each part of the condition alone, then, if both together keep failing, ask whether it can be proved impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each attempt by what it achieves.
groups: Each digit once, sum is not 100
Sum is 100, digits not each used once
questions.explain: The first three use each of the ten digits once (their sums are 180, 99 and 135). The last three reach 100 but repeat or omit digits: 31 repeats the 1 and lacks 0; 50+49+1 omits several digits; 75+25 repeats 5.
questions.rule: One part is easy; both together are hard.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Which pair shows that each part of the condition alone is easy to meet?
options: 19+28+30+7+6+5+4 meets the sum rule, because it adds up to exactly 100 when the terms are summed
Any two numbers whatever meet both parts at once if the digits are well chosen
19+28+37+46+50 uses each digit once; 19+28+31+7+6+5+4 sums to 100 but breaks the digit rule
The number 100 on its own meets both parts of the condition at once
optionExplain: It sums to 99, not 100, so it does not even meet the sum part that this option claims.
Polya shows that each part alone is easy but both together resist, so 'any two numbers' overclaims.
Right: one for each part.
The numbers 1,0,0 repeat 0 and omit most digits.
questions.explain: The text shows 19, 28, 37, 46, 50 for the first part alone (sum 180) and a sum of 100 that repeats the 1 and omits the 0 for the second.
questions.rule: Each part alone is easy.
questions.teaches: Polya shows the first part alone is easy with the set 19, 28, 37, 46, 50 (sum 180), and the second part alone with 19 + 28 + 31 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 100, which repeats the figure 1 and omits 0.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: You doubt a condition can be satisfied. What does Polya say you must do to show it conclusively?
options: Examine the situation in which all parts are supposedly satisfied and find a definitely wrong point in it
Assume that the situation is possible and trust that assumption, then build the rest of the work on top of it
List all the attempts that have failed so far and count how many of them there were
Drop one part of the condition, solve the rest, and report that result instead
optionExplain: Right: the contradiction must be located. The card gives the reason.
An assumption is examined, not trusted; trusting that the situation is possible cannot show it impossible.
Failed attempts support suspicion only; they do not locate a definite wrong point.
This changes the problem; it does not show the original impossible.
questions.explain: Only by facing the situation closely can we hope to perceive a definitely wrong point.
questions.rule: To show a condition cannot be met, assume it is met and look for a definite wrong point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: To show conclusively that a situation is impossible, we must lay our hand upon some ____ wrong point in it.
questions.explain: Polya says we must lay our hand upon some definitely wrong point.
questions.rule: Find the definite wrong point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Your colleague claims a database can hold 5 million rows of 2 KB each in a 1 GB file. You suspect it cannot. Which approach follows Polya?
options: Suppose it can, then work out what that requires and look for a clear contradiction
Refuse to calculate anything at all, since a claim so doubtful cannot possibly be true in any case
Try to build the database and see whether it fails when it is filled with rows
Reduce the rows to 1 million without checking and report that the claim is fine
optionExplain: Right: face the hypothetical. (5 million x 2 KB is about 10 GB.)
Without examining the supposition, nothing is shown.
A failed trial supports suspicion but does not prove it.
This changes the claim rather than testing it.
questions.explain: 5,000,000 x 2 KB = 10,000,000 KB, about 10 GB, which exceeds 1 GB. The hypothetical situation yields a clear wrong point.
questions.rule: To show a condition cannot be met, assume it is met and look for a definite wrong point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: while examining a situation you suspect is impossible, you should treat it as already known to be impossible.
questions.explain: Polya says to keep an open mind and face the situation; the examination is meant to find out.
questions.rule: Keep an open mind while examining.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A strong student finds the digit problem above her head. What does Polya say about it?
options: It needs advanced theory that she has not yet met in her studies, so she should read more mathematics first
It cannot be answered at all, since the puzzle has a solution waiting to be found
The answer is easy enough with the right attitude: examine the situation in which both parts hold
She should give it up, since even good students fail it and a proof is out of reach
optionExplain: He says the answer is easy enough with the right attitude, so no advanced theory is needed.
The puzzle has no solution; the proof is the answer.
Right: the difficulty lies in the attitude.
He says quite good students may find it hard, not that it should be dropped.
questions.explain: Quite good students may find the problem above their heads, yet the answer is easy with the right attitude.
questions.rule: The right attitude makes the proof easy.
questions.teaches: Polya says quite good students may find the digit problem above their heads, yet the answer is easy enough if we have the right attitude, namely to examine the situation in which both parts are satisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: In a set of numbers using each digit 0 to 9 once, what is the sum of all ten digits?
optionExplain: This is the sum 1 to 10, not the digits 0 to 9.
Right: 0+1+...+9 = 45. The card builds on this.
This is the target sum, not the sum of the digits.
90 is double the digit sum 45, as if each digit were counted twice.
questions.explain: The ten digits add to 45.
questions.rule: From the supposed situation derive an equation; if it has no admissible solution, the situation is impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: The ten figures add to 45. If the figures in the tens place add to t, the figures in the units place add to ____.
questions.explain: The ten figures add to 45 and the tens figures add to t, so the units figures add to 45 - t.
questions.rule: Tens plus units equals 45.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Suppose the target sum were 108 instead of 100. With the same condition, what does the equation 10t + (45 - t) = 108 give for t?
options: t = 63/9 = 8, an integer
t = 153/9 = 17, so the target is also impossible
t = 7, an integer, so no absurdity appears
optionExplain: 63/9 = 7, not 8, so this slips in the division.
This forgets to subtract the 45: it divides 108 by 9 as if the equation were 9t = 108.
This adds 45 instead of subtracting it: 9t = 108 - 45, not 108 + 45.
Right: 9t + 45 = 108 gives 9t = 63 and t = 7.
questions.explain: 9t = 108 - 45 = 63, so t = 7. An integer, so this route gives no contradiction for 108. (The tens figures could be, for example, 1+2+4.)
questions.rule: Check the value of t against what t must be.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: With the same ten-digit condition, for which target sum does the equation give a whole-number t?
optionExplain: 9t = 65 gives t = 65/9, which is not whole.
Right: 9t + 45 = 99 gives t = 6.
9t = 55 gives t = 55/9, which is not whole; this is the absurdity of the book.
9t = 75 gives t = 25/3, which is not whole.
questions.explain: Only targets of the form 9t + 45 with whole t work. 99 gives t = 6; 100, 110 and 120 do not. Indeed the book's 99 example uses tens figures 1, 2, 3.
questions.rule: From the supposed situation derive an equation; if it has no admissible solution, the situation is impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: the value t = 55/9 is a problem because t is a sum of whole-number figures and so must be a whole number.
questions.explain: t adds figures in the tens place, each a whole number, so t is a whole number; 55/9 is about 6.11.
questions.rule: The solution must be admissible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: What type of equation does Polya find for t, and what does it show?
options: A quadratic equation whose two roots are both negative and so cannot be sums
A first-degree equation that gives t = 6, which is an integer and so causes no trouble
A first-degree equation whose solution, t = 55/9, is not an integer
A system with infinitely many whole-number solutions, so nothing can be refuted
optionExplain: The equation is first degree, not quadratic: t appears only to the first power.
t = 6 belongs to target 99; for 100 the value is 55/9, which is not an integer.
Right: it is linear in t, and its solution t = 55/9 is not a whole number, which is the absurdity.
Only one value of t emerges, and it is not an integer.
questions.explain: The equation 10t + 45 - t = 100 is of the first degree and gives t = 55/9.
questions.rule: A linear equation can still refute.
questions.teaches: Polya calls the equation for t one of the first degree, and says the value found, 55/9, is not an integer although t should be, so something is definitely wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A chain of correct deductions from a supposition ends in something absurd. What does it show?
options: The deductions must contain an error, however carefully checked
The supposition cannot be true
The conclusion is true, since it follows logically
The problem has no answer, whatever the supposition
optionExplain: If they are correct, the fault lies elsewhere.
Right: sound steps from a true supposition cannot end in an absurdity.
An absurd result is not a truth; it shows that the supposition behind it was wrong.
Only the supposition is rejected, not the problem as a whole.
questions.explain: Polya: our original supposition must be wrong.
questions.rule: If every step is sound and the end is absurd, blame the starting supposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: After reaching a manifest absurdity, Polya concludes that the original ____ must be wrong.
questions.explain: The conclusion falls on the supposition from which the derivation started.
questions.rule: Blame the supposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Assume a lift can carry 12 people of 70 kg each within its 600 kg limit. Correct arithmetic gives 840 kg. What follows?
options: The arithmetic must be wrong and has to be redone until the total fits the limit
The limit of the lift must be changed to 840 kg so that the claim stays true
The result shows that the lift is unsafe for any group of people in general
The assumption is refuted: such a load cannot be within the limit
optionExplain: The arithmetic is correct; redoing it will not change it.
Changing the limit alters the problem instead of explaining the absurdity that was found.
The conclusion concerns only this combination.
questions.explain: 12 x 70 = 840 kg exceeds 600 kg, so the supposed situation cannot occur.
questions.rule: If every step is sound and the end is absurd, blame the starting supposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each statement: does it follow Polya's reasoning about a reductio, or break it?

items.t: Each step from the supposition is checked and found correct
The absurd end shows the supposition false
The proof goal is to show the parts of the condition incompatible
The absurd end shows the deductions were mistaken
A single absurdity shows the unknown does not exist in any form
The supposition is kept since the steps were correct

questions.explain: Only when the steps are sound does the absurdity fall on the supposition; the supposition is the one thing discarded.
questions.rule: Sound steps, absurd end: reject the supposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: if the same derivation had begun from a supposition that could be true, the same correct steps could still end in an absurdity.
questions.explain: Correct reasoning from a true supposition cannot end in a manifest absurdity. Our reading: this is what makes the absurdity a verdict on the supposition.
questions.rule: Absurdity points to a false starting point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya's remarks on the reductio say we want to prove a situation cannot arise. What must we do, and in what spirit?
options: Avoid the situation altogether and argue only from its opposite, which seems far more likely to be true
Examine the hypothetical situation in which all parts are satisfied, although it appears extremely unlikely
Examine the situation only if it looks likely enough to be worth the effort
Examine the situation in general terms only, without going into any detail of it
optionExplain: He says to examine the unlikely situation, not to avoid it.
Right: that is the general trend.
He applies it to extremely unlikely situations.
Vague, general treatment cannot reveal a definite wrong point; the situation has to be examined in detail.
questions.explain: The general trend: face the hypothetical situation in which all parts are satisfied, however unlikely.
questions.rule: Face even the extremely unlikely situation.
questions.teaches: Polya says the procedure that succeeded is reasonable in general: we must examine the hypothetical situation in which all parts of the condition are satisfied, although such a situation appears extremely unlikely.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: You are not sure whether a problem has a solution. How should you start?
options: Express that all parts of the condition hold and follow the working, letting it show which is true
First decide whether a solution exists at all, and only then begin the working on the problem itself
Assume that there is no solution and look only for contradictions in the problem
Assume that there is a solution and ignore any contradiction that comes up
optionExplain: Right: the start is the same either way. The card explains.
This needs the answer before starting.
The same steps may find a solution; assuming otherwise closes that off.
Contradictions are exactly what may appear.
questions.explain: The investigation starts in both cases in the same way.
questions.rule: Start by writing down that every part of the condition holds, and see what comes out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya calls the procedure ____ because it hopes either to find the unknown or to show the condition cannot be satisfied.
questions.explain: He says our procedure is open-minded.
questions.rule: Keep both hopes alive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A scheduler writes: 'Task A takes 3 days, B takes 4 days, both must finish within 5 days using one worker.' What does writing this equation show?
options: It assumes from the outset that the plan fails and looks for a way to prove that it must fail
It starts the same whether a plan exists or not; the sum 7 > 5 then reveals impossibility
It assumes the plan works and so is unable to detect that the plan fails
It proves the plan works, because the equation could be written down at all
optionExplain: The setup assumes only that the conditions hold.
Right: the setup is neutral, the result decides.
The same neutral setup does detect failure, because an absurd outcome shows the condition cannot be met.
Writing the equation proves nothing by itself; what follows from it decides.
questions.explain: 3 + 4 = 7 days exceeds 5, so the supposed plan is impossible. The setup was the same either way.
questions.rule: Start by writing down that every part of the condition holds, and see what comes out.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: the equation for t in the digit puzzle could have been set up without any suspicion that the condition was impossible.
questions.explain: Polya says we could have arrived at the same equation without suspecting that something was wrong with the condition.
questions.rule: The equation is neutral.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya compares an analysis that ends in disproving a theorem to what?
options: A reductio ad absurdum, as the entry on Pappus remarks
A direct proof that confirms the theorem by a chain of forward steps
A routine problem with the data substituted into a known general solution
An indirect proof of the theorem by refuting the opposite assumption
optionExplain: Right: an analysis that disproves the proposed theorem, or shows a problem to find has no solution, is a reductio.
It ends in disproving, so it is not a direct proof that confirms the theorem.
No substitution is described; the analysis ends in disproof, not in applying a ready formula.
It disproves a theorem and does not prove it, so 'indirect proof of the theorem' is not Polya's comparison.
questions.explain: Compare PAPPUS: an analysis ending in disproof is actually a reductio.
questions.rule: An analysis that disproves is a reductio.
questions.teaches: Polya says that an analysis which ends in disproving the proposed theorem, or in showing that the proposed problem to find has no solution, is actually a reductio ad absurdum (compare PAPPUS).

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: How would you begin to prove that the list of primes has no end?
options: List the primes in order until one of them can be seen to be the last
Check that 100 is not prime and then stop, because the series is clear
Suppose it ends with a last prime and look for something definitely wrong
Assume that the series ends and then accept that assumption as true
optionExplain: Listing cannot show a list stops or continues.
One non-prime says nothing about the whole series.
Right: examine the opposite. The card carries it out.
Accepting the assumption without testing it would prove nothing.
questions.explain: Face the situation in which there is a last prime P.
questions.rule: To prove a claim indirectly, assume its opposite and ask what is definitely wrong with it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A prime is a number greater than 1 that cannot be resolved into smaller ____.
questions.explain: Primes are greater than 1 and cannot be resolved into smaller factors; 1 is excluded.
questions.rule: Primes have no smaller factors.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya decomposes 630 into primes. Which is the correct decomposition?
options: 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 9
2 x 5 x 7 x 9
2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7
optionExplain: The product is 1890, and 9 is not prime.
9 is not prime, so this is not a decomposition into primes.
14 is not prime (2 x 7), so this is not a decomposition into primes.
Right: 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 630, five prime factors.
questions.explain: 630 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7. Each factor is prime.
questions.rule: To prove a claim indirectly, assume its opposite and ask what is definitely wrong with it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: Polya suggests that if the series of primes ended somewhere, the world of integers would appear too poor in a manner of speaking.
questions.explain: He says that if it ended, all integers could be decomposed into a finite number of ultimate elements and the world would appear too poor.
questions.rule: A finite set of ultimate elements would seem too few.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya says the problem of proving infinitely many primes appears inaccessible. What makes it workable?
options: Finding the largest prime known so far and showing that it must therefore be the last prime of all
Computing the primes up to a very large bound and seeing that they go on
Proving that composite numbers are rare enough for primes to continue
It is extremely unlikely that there is a last prime P, so that situation is faced squarely
optionExplain: A largest known prime is not a last prime.
A finite computation cannot show the series is infinite.
Rarity of composites is not the argument.
Right: the unlikely opposite is examined.
questions.explain: Though the problem appears inaccessible, the unlikely situation of a last prime is examined.
questions.rule: Examine the unlikely opposite.
questions.teaches: Polya says the problem is very different from elementary problems of the usual kind and appears at first inaccessible, yet it is extremely unlikely that there should be a last prime P.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Suppose 2, 3, 5 were all the primes. Which number built from them leaves remainder 1 on division by each?
optionExplain: 10 is divisible by 2 and 5, so the sum leaves remainder 0, not 1.
30 is divisible by each of 2, 3 and 5, so it leaves remainder 0.
Right: 30 is divisible by each, so 31 leaves remainder 1.
29 leaves remainder 1 on division by 2 and 4 on division by 5, so not 1 for every prime.
questions.explain: The product is a multiple of every listed prime, so adding 1 leaves remainder 1.
questions.rule: Multiply all the supposed primes, add 1, and note that none of them divides the result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Q = (2 x 3 x 5 x ... x P) + 1 is divided by any of the primes 2, 3, 5, ... P. The ____ is 1.
questions.explain: The product part is divisible by each of the primes, so the remainder is always 1.
questions.rule: Product plus 1 leaves remainder 1.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Take the supposed primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Q = 30031. What does Polya's argument say about Q?
options: Q has a prime divisor outside 2 to 13, since each of those leaves remainder 1; in fact 30031 = 59 x 509
Q must itself be prime, since nothing on the list divides it, and so 30031 is a prime number as well
Q is divisible by 13, since 13 is the last prime on the list and goes into Q
Q cannot be divided by anything at all, so the whole argument fails here
optionExplain: Right: both 59 and 509 are primes outside the list.
Q need not be prime; here 30031 = 59 x 509, so it has prime divisors outside the list.
Dividing Q by 13 leaves remainder 1, so 13 does not divide Q.
Q is divisible by some prime; it just cannot be one of the listed ones.
questions.explain: 2x3x5x7x11x13 = 30030; adding 1 gives 30031 = 59 x 509. Each listed prime leaves remainder 1. A prime divisor lies outside the list.
questions.rule: Multiply all the supposed primes, add 1, and note that none of them divides the result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: Polya's argument shows that the product of the supposed primes plus 1 must itself be prime.
questions.explain: It need only be prime or divisible by some prime; for 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 11 x 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 x 509 it is not prime.
questions.rule: Q needs a prime divisor, not primality.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Under the supposition that P is the last prime, why does Polya say Q = (2 x 3 x ... x P) + 1 cannot be a prime?
options: Because Q is greater than P, and P is supposed to be the last prime
Because Q leaves remainder 1 when it is divided by 2, so it is not divisible
Because Q is odd, and an odd number cannot be a prime in this argument
Because Q is the product of the listed primes, so it has many divisors
optionExplain: Right: so Q must be divisible by a prime, yet none of the supposed primes divides it.
A remainder of 1 does not rule out primality.
Odd numbers can be prime, and the argument does not rest on oddness.
Q is that product plus 1, not the product.
questions.explain: Q greater than the supposed last prime P cannot be a prime, so it must have a prime divisor in the list, and that is the absurdity.
questions.rule: Larger than the last prime means not prime.
questions.teaches: Polya reasons that Q is greater than P and therefore, allegedly, Q cannot be a prime; consequently Q must be divisible by a prime, and the only primes at our disposal are 2, 3, 5, ..., P.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: How would you describe the proof that the series of primes has no end, by supposing a last prime and reaching an absurdity?
options: A direct proof, because it names an explicit prime that is not on the list
A reductio only, since it proves no theorem and only refutes a supposition
An indirect proof whose refutation of the opposite is a reductio ad absurdum
A routine problem about decomposing integers into primes by a known pattern
optionExplain: It argues through a supposed opposite.
It does prove the theorem, through the opposite.
Right: the two combine. The card names the parts.
No formerly solved pattern is substituted.
questions.explain: The theorem is established by disproving its opposite, which is disproved by an absurdity.
questions.rule: In an indirect proof, disprove the opposite by deriving an absurdity from it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: In Euclid's proof, the supposition that is refuted is that there is a last ____.
questions.explain: Euclid supposes a last prime P, derives an absurdity, and so refutes the supposition; this establishes that the series of primes has no end.
questions.rule: The proof is Euclid's.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A detective proves: the butler did not do it. Suppose he did; then the study door was locked from inside; it was found open. Contradiction. Which structure is this?
options: A direct proof, because it begins from the facts of the case and moves forward step by step to the claim
A routine problem, because the steps are the standard steps of such an inquiry
Neither, because it proves nothing about the butler and only refutes a story
The claim is established by refuting its opposite, which is refuted by an absurd consequence
optionExplain: It begins with the supposition that the butler did it.
No formerly solved problem is being followed.
It establishes the claim by refuting the opposite.
Right: indirect proof with a reductio inside.
questions.explain: Opposite supposed, absurdity derived, opposite rejected, claim established.
questions.rule: In an indirect proof, disprove the opposite by deriving an absurdity from it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each part of Euclid's proof by its role.

items.t: The theorem: the series of primes never ends
The contradictory opposite: the series ends somewhere
Concluding the theorem because the opposite was disproved
Supposing a last prime P exists
Showing Q has no prime divisor in the supposed list
Seeing that Q must be prime or have a prime divisor

questions.explain: The indirect proof frames the theorem and its opposite; the reductio is the working inside, from the supposition to the absurdity.
questions.rule: Indirect frames; reductio works inside.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: in Euclid's proof the contradictory opposite of the theorem is that the series of primes ends somewhere.
questions.explain: The theorem says the series never ends; its contradictory opposite says it ends, and the proof refutes that opposite.
questions.rule: Opposite of 'never ends' is 'ends somewhere'.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A proof shows a number is irrational by supposing it is a fraction and reaching an absurdity. Does Polya treat combining indirect proof with reductio as unusual?
options: No: he says this combination is also very typical
Yes: it occurs only in Euclid's proof of the primes
Yes: the two procedures exclude each other
No: but only because both are routine problems
optionExplain: Right: Polya says the combination of indirect proof with reductio is also very typical, not unusual.
He calls the combination typical, not unique.
They are different but related and combine.
Whether a problem is routine is another question; Polya's point here is about combining the two proof procedures.
questions.explain: Thus we have combined indirect proof with reductio ad absurdum; this combination is also very typical.
questions.rule: The combination is typical.
questions.teaches: Polya says that in Euclid's proof indirect proof is combined with reductio ad absurdum, and that this combination is also very typical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Which objection to reductio ad absurdum does Polya state?
options: It produces a wrong theorem in a good many of the cases in which it is applied, so its results are unreliable
We must attend to a false assumption while following it, though we want to retain the true theorem
It cannot be used in mathematics at all, since mathematics needs direct proofs
It is too short to be convincing to anyone who has not seen it before
optionExplain: He does not claim this; the theorem it proves is true.
Right: this is the practical objection. The card has the detail.
Reductio is used in mathematics, in Euclid's proof for instance, so this is not the objection Polya states.
Length is not the objection; lengthy reductios are the problem.
questions.explain: Listening to such a proof we focus on a false assumption which we should forget.
questions.rule: Put the objection in its strongest form: what we must attend to is false, what we want to keep is true.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: The objection says we are obliged to focus attention on a ____ assumption instead of the true theorem.
questions.explain: The assumption started from is false.
questions.rule: The proof dwells on a false assumption.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A teacher says: 'My pupils remember the supposition from the proof of the primes instead of the theorem.' Which objection does this illustrate?
options: That the proof is too hard to be correct, so the pupils cannot learn from it
That the theorem being proved is false, which the proof was meant to reveal
That pupils dislike mathematics and so do not bother to remember any proof
That a reductio keeps attention on the false assumption rather than the true result
optionExplain: The objection concerns attention, not correctness.
The theorem is true; the supposition is false.
This is not the objection Polya states.
Right: this is the objection in practice.
questions.explain: What pupils retain is the false supposition, which they should have forgotten.
questions.rule: Put the objection in its strongest form: what we must attend to is false, what we want to keep is true.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each phrase: part of the objection or part of Polya's later reply?

items.t: We should store only true things in memory
A reductio's consequences are all false
Attention stays on what we should forget
A proof found by reductio can be rearranged into a pleasant form
Indirect proofs can often be converted into direct ones
Reductio is a valuable tool for discovery

questions.explain: The objection concerns what we hold in mind. Polya's reply distinguishes uses and points out that proofs can often be rearranged or converted.
questions.rule: State the objection, then weigh it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: a reader who only studies the final true theorem of an indirect proof avoids the objection.
questions.explain: The objection concerns following the proof, where the false assumption must be kept in mind. Our reading: skipping to the theorem skips the understanding of why it holds.
questions.rule: The proof must be followed to be understood.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya says it is difficult to retain something true from a reductio. Why can we not forget the falsehoods at once?
options: Because falsehoods are easy to remember, and so they will stay in the memory of the reader anyway
Because all points must be remembered sharply and correctly during the study of the proof
Because false assumptions turn out to be true when the proof is finished
Because forgetting is impossible for adults once they have studied a proof
optionExplain: Ease of memory is not his point; the falsehoods have to be held in mind to follow the argument.
Right: we need the false steps to follow the argument.
The false assumptions remain false when the proof is finished; they are only used along the way.
He does not argue that adults cannot forget; we need the false steps to follow the proof.
questions.explain: We should forget at once but cannot, since all points must be remembered during the study.
questions.rule: We must hold the false in mind to follow the proof.
questions.teaches: Polya says the objector would forget the falsehoods as quickly as possible, but this is not feasible because all points must be remembered sharply and correctly during the study of the proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Should Polya's objection lead us to abandon reductio ad absurdum entirely?
options: Yes, since it asks the reader to hold falsehoods in mind through the whole proof
No, because the objection is baseless and the written form is always pleasant
Yes, but only in mathematics, where the false suppositions can be listed
No: it is a valuable tool of discovery even if a long written reductio can be painful
optionExplain: He says abandoning the procedure entirely would be foolish, since it is a valuable tool of discovery.
He grants the objection some force for exposition.
He does not restrict the abandonment to mathematics.
Right: his view distinguishes the uses. The card has the details.
questions.explain: He distinguishes the research use from the exposition use.
questions.rule: Use reductio freely to find results; when writing for others, consider whether a gentler form exists.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya distinguishes the use of reductio as a tool of ____ and as a means of exposition.
questions.explain: He names research (discovery) and exposition as the two uses.
questions.rule: Two uses: research and exposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A textbook author must present a three-page proof by contradiction. Which choice follows Polya's remarks?
options: Keep the long form as it stands, since the proof is correct and the reader can be expected to follow it
Delete the proof from the book and state only the result that it establishes
Repeat the word hypothetically in every line, so that no reader is ever misled
Try to rearrange it so that the contradiction is compressed into a few sentences or disappears
optionExplain: Correct is not the same as pleasant.
The proof is the purpose of the exposition.
This is what makes the long reductio tedious.
Right: reduce the strain on the reader.
questions.explain: Polya says a reductio found by long search can often be put in a more pleasant form, even compressed to a few striking sentences.
questions.rule: Use reductio freely to find results; when writing for others, consider whether a gentler form exists.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Sort each remark: about reductio as a tool of discovery, or as a means of exposition?

items.t: It may bring a decision when other means seem exhausted
It presents itself naturally to an intent mind
It is not foolish to rely on it
It can become tedious through repeated 'hypothetically'
It may cause an inner discord in reader or listener
Long ones can be painful

questions.explain: For discovery Polya is positive; for exposition he concedes a long reductio is not an unmixed blessing.
questions.rule: Praise for discovery, caution for exposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: What does Polya say experience shows about converting indirect proofs?
options: Conversion is rarely possible, so an indirect proof usually has to stay indirect
There is usually little difficulty in converting an indirect proof into a direct proof
Conversion makes the proof wrong, since a direct form needs different premises
Conversion is possible only for the proof about primes and for no other proof
optionExplain: He says usually little difficulty.
Right: so the two contentions are not opposed.
Conversion keeps the proof correct; it only rearranges it into a more pleasant form.
The remark is general and not limited to the proof about primes.
questions.explain: There is no essential opposition between recognizing the tool and rearranging the proof.
questions.rule: Experience says conversion is usually easy.
questions.teaches: Polya says experience shows there is usually little difficulty in converting an indirect proof into a direct proof, or rearranging a long reductio into a more pleasant form.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: You have proved a result by contradiction. Which next step does Polya recommend?
options: Stop, since a correct proof needs no further thought once it has been found
Look back and ask whether you can derive the result differently
Repeat the proof aloud several times until it feels natural to say it
Discard the proof and wait for a direct one to appear without effort
optionExplain: He urges looking back even at a correct proof, so stopping at once misses a chance to learn more.
Right: from the look-back phase. The card shows why.
Repetition does not create another derivation.
The proof is the starting point for finding another.
questions.explain: The recommended question: Can you derive the result differently?
questions.rule: Once a result is found indirectly, look back for a direct route.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: After a result is found by reductio or indirect proof, ask: Can you ____ the result differently?
questions.explain: The question is whether the result can be derived differently.
questions.rule: Ask for a different derivation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A student proves a claim about integers by contradiction and re-reads it, marking steps that do not use the assumption. What is she doing?
options: Checking the spelling of her answer and the layout of the proof before handing it in
Replacing the proof by an experiment that tests the claim on many integers
Carving out the part independent of the false assumption, in line with Polya's look-back
Hiding the fact that the proof was indirect so that readers will trust it more
optionExplain: Her aim is structural, finding which parts do not depend on the assumption, not tidiness.
Her aim is another derivation of the claim, not a test on many integers.
Right: that part contains positive information.
The aim is to find what is true without the assumption.
questions.explain: Polya's rearrangement carves out the part of the argument independent of the initial false assumption.
questions.rule: Once a result is found indirectly, look back for a direct route.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: according to Polya, a familiar reader of both procedures should still look back after a successful reductio.
questions.explain: He says we should not fail to look back at the solution even when we have succeeded by either method.
questions.rule: Looking back is for every success.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Which of the following does Polya say is true about the information in the rest of the digit reductio?
options: Nothing in it is true, since the whole argument rests on a false supposition from beginning to end
Part of the argument is independent of the false assumption and contains positive information
All of it is true, since every one of the steps is correct in itself
Only the final absurdity is true, since it is the one thing that is observed
optionExplain: He extracts a true part of the argument instead of calling it all false.
Right: that is what he carves out.
The situations faced are impossible; only a part is independent of them.
The absurdity is not a truth; it is the sign that the supposition was false.
questions.explain: Reconsidering what we have done, we may carve out a part of the argument independent of the initial false assumption.
questions.rule: Find the part that does not depend on the false assumption.
questions.teaches: Polya says that in rearranging a reductio we can carve out a part of the argument which is independent of the initial false assumption and contains positive information.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Every set of one- and two-figure numbers using the ten digits once has a total of 10t + (45 - t). Which fact about that total follows?
options: It equals 10(t + 5), a multiple of 10
It equals 9(t + 5), so it is a multiple of 9
It equals 45, whatever t is
It equals 9t + 40, one less than a multiple of 9
optionExplain: The coefficient on t is 9, not 10, so the total is not a multiple of 10.
t changes the total; only the multiple-of-9 form stays fixed.
The constant is 45, giving 9(t + 5), not 9t + 40.
questions.rule: Show that every achievable sum is a multiple of 9, then compare the target.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: The sum of the numbers is 10t + (45 - t), which simplifies to 9(t + ____).
questions.rule: The sum simplifies to a multiple of 9.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Using the rearranged argument, which of these targets can a set using each digit once NOT reach?
options: 99, because 99 leaves remainder 1 when it is divided by 9 and so is excluded
110, because it is not a multiple of 9: it leaves remainder 2
108, because 108 is greater than 100 and the target must be at most 100
126, because 126 is an even number and sums of digits cannot be even
optionExplain: 99 = 9 x 11 is a multiple of 9, so it is not excluded.
Size is not the issue; 108 = 9 x 12 is a multiple of 9, so it is not excluded.
Parity is irrelevant; 126 = 9 x 14 is a multiple of 9, so it is not excluded.
questions.explain: Reachable sums are multiples of 9: 99 = 9 x 11, 108 = 9 x 12, 126 = 9 x 14. 110 is not a multiple.
questions.rule: Show that every achievable sum is a multiple of 9, then compare the target.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: A student writes: 'Sums reach every multiple of 9, so 100 is out only by luck.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: the argument shows that every multiple of 9 can in fact occur as a sum of such a set of numbers
The argument is wrong, since 100 is a multiple of 9 and so the sum is reachable
The argument needs a supposition about the last prime before it can be used at all
The argument excludes 100 because it is not a multiple of 9; whether every multiple is reachable is a separate question
optionExplain: It only shows that sums are multiples of 9.
100 = 9 x 11 + 1 is not a multiple of 9, so the sum is not reachable.
The prime proof is a separate argument and is not needed here.
Right: the argument proves a necessary condition, not that all multiples occur.
questions.explain: The direct argument is a necessary condition for the sum; 100 fails it.
questions.rule: Show that every achievable sum is a multiple of 9, then compare the target.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: Polya says the new presentation of the digit argument still contains a reductio ad absurdum.
questions.explain: He says the reductio which led to the discovery vanished from the new presentation.
questions.rule: The direct form hides no supposition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: In the rearranged argument, what does Polya say a reader who knows casting out nines can do?
options: Prove that every multiple of 9 can be reached
See the whole argument at a glance
Replace the sum 100 by 99 without changing the problem
Avoid checking the tens figures altogether
optionExplain: The argument concerns which totals cannot be reached; it does not show that every multiple of 9 occurs.
Right: the divisibility by 9 shows the point.
Changing the target from 100 to 99 changes the puzzle instead of explaining it.
The tens figures are still the heart of the form 9(t + 5).
questions.explain: By the way, a reader acquainted with casting out nines can see the whole argument at a glance.
questions.rule: Casting out nines shows it at once.
questions.teaches: Polya remarks that a reader acquainted with the procedure of casting out nines can see the whole argument at a glance.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: As a problem to find, what does the statement that the series of primes has no end mean?
options: Given any finite set of primes, find a prime different from all of them
Find the largest prime, which would end the series at the greatest one known
List every prime in a single sweep, so that the whole series is written out
Check that every number beyond some point is a prime, so no gaps appear
optionExplain: Right: restating the claim as a task. The card builds the answer.
This is the opposite claim: the series would end at a largest prime.
The list cannot be finished, so the whole series cannot be written out in one sweep.
Not every number is prime, so checking that all numbers beyond some point are prime is not the claim.
questions.explain: The problem to prove becomes a problem to find a new prime.
questions.rule: Restate 'prove it never ends' as 'given the primes so far, find a new one', and use a prime divisor of the product plus 1.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Polya converts the problem to prove into a problem to ____ a new prime N.
questions.explain: The problem becomes: being given the primes 2, ..., P, find a new prime N.
questions.rule: From prove to find.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Given the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, Q = 30031. Which choice is a valid N in Polya's recipe?
options: 30031, since Q is always prime
13, the largest listed prime
59, a prime divisor of 30031
1, since it divides everything
optionExplain: Q is not prime here; 30031 = 59 x 509.
Division by 13 leaves remainder 1, so 13 does not divide Q.
Right: 59 divides Q and is not on the list.
1 is not counted as a prime, so it cannot be N.
questions.explain: 30031 = 59 x 509; 59 is its smallest prime divisor and differs from 2 to 13.
questions.rule: Restate 'prove it never ends' as 'given the primes so far, find a new one', and use a prime divisor of the product plus 1.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: True or false: in the converted proof, if Q happens to be prime then N = Q.
questions.explain: Polya states this case explicitly: if Q is a prime, then N = Q.
questions.rule: Q is its own prime divisor when prime.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Applying the recipe starting from the primes 2, 3, 5 gives Q = 31. What is N?
options: 31, since Q is itself prime
2, since it is the smallest prime
5, the last listed prime
30, the product of the list
optionExplain: Right: 2 x 3 x 5 + 1 = 31, which is prime.
Dividing 31 by 2 leaves remainder 1, so 2 is not a divisor of Q.
31 divided by 5 leaves remainder 1, so 5 does not divide Q.
30 is composite and not a prime divisor of 31.
questions.explain: 31 is prime, so N = Q = 31.
questions.rule: Restate 'prove it never ends' as 'given the primes so far, find a new one', and use a prime divisor of the product plus 1.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: What does Polya say the converted proof gives us?
options: A formula that lists all the primes in order, one after the other, from the start
A definite procedure for prolonging the series of primes again and again, without limit
A proof that Q is itself a prime for every finite set of primes that is chosen
A reason to distrust the original proof, which is now seen to have been wrong
optionExplain: It gives a new prime each time, not a complete listing in order.
Right: nothing indirect remains.
Q may be composite, so the procedure gives a new prime divisor, not a proof that Q is prime.
He says it is fundamentally the same proof.
questions.explain: Nothing is indirect in it; no impossible situation needs to be considered.
questions.rule: The converted proof is constructive.
questions.teaches: Polya says the converted proof gives a definite procedure of prolonging again and again the series of primes without limit, with nothing indirect in it, though fundamentally it is the same as the indirect proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: After a lesson solving quadratic equations in general, a student is asked to solve x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 by substituting numbers into the general solution. What kind of problem is this?
options: A problem needing a bright idea
A routine problem
A reductio ad absurdum
A puzzle needing variation of the problem
optionExplain: The method is given, so no sudden idea is needed.
Right: the answer to the related-problem question was handed over. The card has the definition.
No supposition is refuted.
The student is not asked to vary the problem.
questions.explain: Substitution into a formerly solved general problem is the book's first example of routine.
questions.rule: Judge routine by whether the solution is a substitution into a known general solution or a copy of a conspicuous example.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A routine problem can be solved by substituting special ____ into a formerly solved general problem.
questions.explain: The first way: substitute special data into a formerly solved general problem.
questions.rule: Routine: substitute the data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: The class has solved three problems of the form: a train covers D km in T hours; find the speed. The next one repeats the form with new numbers. What is it?
options: A problem that needs a bright idea about trains before the speed can be found
A problem with a redundant condition, since the distance is given twice over
A reductio ad absurdum, since the speed is found by refuting a supposed speed
A routine problem: it follows a conspicuous example step by step without originality
optionExplain: The pattern is already shown in the three solved problems, so no bright idea is needed.
Nothing suggests redundancy; the distance is given once.
No impossible situation is examined, so this is not a reductio.
Right: the pattern is followed step by step.
questions.explain: Following a well-worn example step by step is the second route to a routine problem.
questions.rule: Judge routine by whether the solution is a substitution into a known general solution or a copy of a conspicuous example.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each situation: routine problem or not routine?

items.t: Solving a quadratic after the general solution was explained
Solving six similar equations just after six similar ones were solved
Copying a worked example with new numbers
Proving the primes never end, with no method given
Solving the digit puzzle with no model to follow
Finding a word from the letters of an anagram

questions.explain: The routine cases supply a general solution or a conspicuous example. The others require judgment or invention.
questions.rule: Routine is a matter of what has been shown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: a problem that is routine for a student who has seen the model solution may not be routine for one who has not.
questions.explain: Our reading: Polya defines routine by whether the problem can be solved by substitution into a known general case or by following an example, which depends on what the student has been shown.
questions.rule: Routine depends on what has been shown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: What question does a teacher answer for the student by setting a routine problem?
options: Do you know a related problem?
What is the unknown?
Can you check the result?
Could you restate the problem?
optionExplain: Right: the related problem is thrust under the student's nose.
The unknown remains for the student to identify.
Checking the result is a separate question that a routine problem does not answer for the student.
Restating is not supplied by a routine problem.
questions.explain: The teacher thrusts an immediate and decisive answer to: Do you know a related problem?
questions.rule: Routine problems pre-answer the related-problem question.
questions.teaches: Polya says that in setting a routine problem the teacher thrusts under the nose of the student an immediate and decisive answer to the question: Do you know a related problem?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A course sets only exercises that repeat a worked model with new numbers. How does Polya judge such teaching?
options: Routine problems have no place in teaching, since they use no judgment at all
Routine problems are ideal and should fill the whole course from start to end
Routine problems are fine so long as the numbers in them are made large
Some routine problems may be necessary, but giving no other kind is inexcusable
optionExplain: He says even many may be necessary.
He calls an exclusive diet inexcusable.
Size does not change the objection.
Right. The card states his reasoning.
questions.explain: Necessary in part, inexcusable alone.
questions.rule: Mix routine exercises with problems that call for judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says teaching mechanical routine alone falls below the level of the ____.
questions.explain: He compares with the cookbook: kitchen recipes still leave something to the cook.
questions.rule: Even a cookbook leaves room for the cook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A maths teacher wants to keep routine practice but add something more. Which addition fits Polya?
options: Problems in which the student has to decide which method to use
More routine problems of the same pattern, but with larger numbers in them
The same routine problems again, but now with a strict time limit on them
The answers printed beside each problem, so the student can check as she goes
optionExplain: Right: they use judgment.
Still no judgment: larger numbers make the same pattern longer, not more thoughtful.
Speed does not add judgment; the student still follows a fixed pattern.
Printed answers let the student skip thinking about how to get them.
questions.explain: To use judgment and inventive faculties a student needs problems where the method is not handed over.
questions.rule: Mix routine exercises with problems that call for judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: How does a mathematical recipe differ from a kitchen recipe, in Polya's comparison?
options: Kitchen recipes leave something to the imagination and judgment of the cook; mathematical recipes do not
Mathematical recipes give the student a good deal more freedom than kitchen recipes ever give the cook
Kitchen recipes cannot be followed at all without some judgment from the cook
Both kinds of recipe leave no room for judgment, and the cook follows them
optionExplain: Right: a kitchen recipe leaves something to the cook's imagination and judgment; a mathematical routine recipe leaves none.
He says mathematical recipes give the student none of the freedom a cook has.
They leave some to the cook; they can be followed.
He distinguishes the two kinds of recipe, so they do not both leave no room for judgment.
questions.explain: That is why drilling mathematical recipes alone is below cookbook level.
questions.rule: Mix routine exercises with problems that call for judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya says routine problems have no place in teaching mathematics.
questions.explain: He says routine problems, even many, may be necessary, but making students do no other kind is inexcusable.
questions.rule: Routine problems are fine in moderation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: What does Polya say the student needs for a routine problem?
options: A fresh bright idea each time, since no two routine problems are quite alike
A thorough grasp of the proof behind the general solution, which the student must reproduce before substituting
An original approach to the problem, since the method is not supplied
A little care and patience in following a cut-and-dried precept
optionExplain: No bright idea is needed, because the method has been given and only has to be followed.
The student only substitutes data into the formula; reproducing its proof is not needed.
Originality is absent from a routine problem; the precept is followed as it stands.
Right: a routine problem needs only care and patience in following a cut-and-dried precept.
questions.explain: A cut-and-dried precept is followed without any trace of originality.
questions.rule: Routine asks for care and patience.
questions.teaches: Polya says the student of a routine problem needs nothing but a little care and patience in following a cut-and-dried precept.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: What is Polya's attitude to the idea of infallible rules for solving all mathematical problems?
options: They would be more desirable than the philosophers' stone, but there is no magic and they remain a dream
They exist and are collected in his list of questions, which is meant to solve every mathematical problem
They exist but are too complicated to be taught to students at any level
They are not wanted, since problems ought to be left unsolved in the end
optionExplain: Right: the card gives his comparison.
He says the list cannot work magic, so it does not solve every problem.
He denies their existence: no unfailing rules for all problems exist.
He says such rules would be highly desirable, so they are wanted, though out of reach.
questions.explain: He compares the hope with the alchemists' search for the philosophers' stone.
questions.rule: Do not wait for an infallible method; do what is typically useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says infallible rules of discovery would be more desirable than the philosophers' ____.
questions.explain: The comparison is with the philosophers' stone, sought by alchemists.
questions.rule: Infallible rules are like the philosophers' stone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A website promises 'a three-step method guaranteed to solve any maths problem'. How would Polya react?
options: With approval, since such rules would be the true aim of any sound heuristic
With a request for an even shorter method that would work for every problem
By adopting it as the first rule of discovery in his own list of questions
With scepticism: unfailing rules for all problems are an old dream that will not be fulfilled
optionExplain: He says a reasonable heuristic cannot aim at unfailing rules.
Length is not his concern; the objection is that no short method could be unfailing for every problem.
His first rule is a joke about brains and luck.
Right: Polya treats unfailing rules for all problems as an old dream, so he would greet the promise with scepticism.
questions.explain: No unfailing rules applicable to all problems exist.
questions.rule: Do not wait for an infallible method; do what is typically useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A reader takes 'sit tight and wait till you get a bright idea' as Polya's real advice. What is the error?
options: None: waiting quietly for the bright idea is exactly the method that he recommends to every solver of problems
The error is that he advises hurry, and the reader has taken him to say wait
It is a jest reminding us that some aspirations are hopeless; his actual advice is to study useful procedures
The error is that he rejects bright ideas, which he thinks the solver should avoid
optionExplain: He offers the sit-tight rule rudely, as a jest, and does not recommend waiting.
He does not advise hurry; the jest is about waiting passively.
Right: the sit-tight rule is a jest; his real advice is to learn the procedures that are typically useful.
He values bright ideas highly; the point is that waiting is no method of getting one.
questions.explain: The two rules are a rude reminder, which then leads to what heuristic can honestly do.
questions.rule: Do not wait for an infallible method; do what is typically useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya says infallible rules for solving all mathematical problems would be more desirable than the philosophers' stone.
questions.explain: He says so, and adds that there is no such thing as magic.
questions.rule: Desirable, but out of reach.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: An author proposes one master method that solves every problem of every kind. How does Polya classify the search for such unfailing rules?
options: As the true aim of any sound heuristic that is worth the name of a method
As a project already completed in his own list of questions and suggestions
As an old philosophical dream that will never be more than a dream
As a task for the alchemists to finish once they find the philosophers' stone
optionExplain: He says a reasonable heuristic cannot aim at it.
His list does not claim to be unfailing.
Right: he calls the search for unfailing rules an old philosophical dream that will never be more than a dream.
The alchemists sought the stone in vain.
questions.explain: To find unfailing rules applicable to all sorts of problems is an old philosophical dream.
questions.rule: Unfailing rules are a dream.
questions.teaches: Polya calls the search for unfailing rules applicable to all sorts of problems an old philosophical dream that will never be more than a dream.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: What may a reasonable heuristic study, once unfailing rules are out of reach?
options: Procedures that always work, whatever kind of problem is being solved
Procedures that are used only by geniuses and cannot be taught to others
Procedures that replace the need for thinking about the problem itself
Procedures that are typically useful in solving problems
optionExplain: Procedures that always work are the unfailing rules that cannot be had.
Polya says every sane person interested in the problem uses them.
Polya does not offer procedures that replace thinking about the problem itself.
Right. The card gives the details.
questions.explain: Typically useful procedures, hinted by stereotyped questions.
questions.rule: Learn the typical useful moves and the questions that call them to mind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says the useful procedures are hinted by stereotyped ____ and suggestions.
questions.explain: He mentions stereotyped questions and suggestions.
questions.rule: The hints are stereotyped questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A chess coach wants to write down ideas for finding good moves. Which approach matches Polya's idea of heuristic?
options: A rule that finds the best move every time, whatever the position on the board
A single question that decides the best move in every position that arises
A neatly ordered collection of typically useful questions and moves, with no guarantee
A ban on asking questions during play, so the coach's advice is not diluted
optionExplain: A rule that finds the best move every time is the dream of unfailing rules.
The aim is a collection, not one question.
Right: a neatly ordered collection of typically useful questions and moves, with no guarantee, is what Polya means.
Questions are the means of heuristic, so banning them would defeat the collection.
questions.explain: A collection of questions stated with generality and neatly ordered.
questions.rule: Learn the typical useful moves and the questions that call them to mind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each claim: Polya's aim for heuristic, or the dream he rejects?

items.t: Study typically useful mental operations
Collect stereotyped questions and suggestions
State them with generality and neat order
Find rules that solve every problem
Replace the solver's effort by a procedure
Rival the philosophers' stone

questions.explain: The first three describe what heuristic can provide. The last three are the infallible-rules dream.
questions.rule: Aim at typical usefulness, not infallibility.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya expects his collection of questions to rival the philosophers' stone.
questions.explain: He says such a collection may be less desirable than the stone but can be provided.
questions.rule: The list is modest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: According to Polya, who puts the stereotyped questions and suggestions?
options: Intelligent people to themselves and intelligent teachers to their students
Only the authors of mathematical textbooks, to the readers of their books
Only students to their teachers, when they are stuck and need some help
Only computers, which ask them while searching for a solution to a problem
optionExplain: Right: intelligent people put them to themselves and intelligent teachers put them to their students.
He says intelligent people generally put these questions, not only textbook authors.
It is teachers who question students, and intelligent people who question themselves.
Computers are not mentioned in the passage on these questions.
questions.explain: They are hinted by questions intelligent people put to themselves and intelligent teachers to their students.
questions.rule: Questions flow from solver and teacher.
questions.teaches: Polya says the stereotyped questions and suggestions are those which intelligent people put to themselves and intelligent teachers put to their students.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: You have two points to make to your team. What does Polya's second rule of style advise?
options: Say both together to save time, since the listener can keep up with two points
Say first one, then the other, not both at the same time
Say neither until you are sure which one of the two points matters more
Say the shorter one only, and leave the other for some later occasion
optionExplain: This is what the rule warns against: two things said at the same time.
Right: his wording in short.
