Waiting until you are sure which point matters more is not the advice; both are said, one after the other.
Dropping one point is not the advice; the rule asks for both, taken in turn.
questions.explain: Control yourself and take the points in turn.
questions.rule: Have something to say, and say two things one after the other, not both at once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: The first rule of style, Polya says, is to have ____ to say.
questions.explain: The first rule is to have something to say.
questions.rule: First, have something to say.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A report's introduction both defines the terms and argues the main claim in the same sentences. Which edit follows the rule?
options: Merge the definitions into the argument more tightly so both appear together
Delete the definitions altogether and let the reader work them out alone
Move both the definitions and the argument to a footnote at the page end
Define the terms first, then argue the claim in the following paragraphs
optionExplain: This does both at once, which is what the rule warns against.
Deleting the definitions drops a thing that has to be said.
A footnote does not put the two in order; they should be said one after the other.
Right: one thing, then the other.
questions.explain: Taking the two in turn is the rule.
questions.rule: Have something to say, and say two things one after the other, not both at once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A writer says: 'Rule two means a document may contain only one topic.' What is the mistake?
options: None: the rule limits a document to a single topic from the first page to the last page of it
The rule asks for as many topics as possible in each paragraph written
The rule applies only to speeches and has nothing to say about writing
The rule is about order: take two things one after the other, not both at the same time
optionExplain: The rule asks for order, not a limit on topics.
It asks for neither many nor few topics, only for order.
It is not limited to speeches; the rule covers anything you have to say.
Right: the rule is about order, taking two things one after the other.
questions.explain: Our reading: the rule asks for ordering, not for a single topic.
questions.rule: Have something to say, and say two things one after the other, not both at once.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: after Polya's first rule of style, a text with nothing to say can be rescued by good style.
questions.explain: Our reading: the first rule puts having something to say before style; the second rule concerns how to order what there is.
questions.rule: Content first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: In Polya's wording of the second rule of style, what must you do when, by chance, you have two things to say?
options: Control yourself, then say first one, then the other
Say only the more important of the two and drop the other from your talk
Hurry through both of them so that the listener cannot lose the thread
Wait for the listener to ask about each one before you say anything at all
optionExplain: Right: self-control is the first step.
Neither point is dropped; both are said, one after the other.
Hurry is not his advice; he asks for self-control and an orderly sequence.
Waiting for a question is not mentioned; the speaker is expected to say both points.
questions.explain: The rule is: control yourself when, by chance, you have two things to say; say first one, then the other, not both at the same time.
questions.rule: Control yourself and take them in turn.
questions.teaches: Polya's wording of the second rule of style is to control yourself when, by chance, you have two things to say: say first one, then the other, not both at the same time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: What does Polya's second rule of teaching add to the first?
options: Teach a little more than you know, so that the pupils keep learning with you
Teach less than you know, to be safe against any question from the class
Know exactly the same as what you teach, so that nothing is left unsaid
Know a little more than what you are supposed to teach
optionExplain: This is the reverse: the second rule asks for more knowledge than the lesson, not that pupils learn with you.
Teaching less than you know is not his advice; the second rule asks for a little more.
The second rule asks for more than the first, not exactly the same.
Right. The card places it beside the first.
questions.explain: First, know it; second, know a little more.
questions.rule: Know what you are supposed to teach, and a little more.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Polya says the first rule of teaching is to know what you are ____ to teach.
questions.explain: The first rule of teaching is to know what you are supposed to teach; the second is to know a little more.
questions.rule: Know what you are supposed to teach.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A tutor prepares only the worked examples of one chapter and freezes when a student asks why a step is allowed. Which rule did she break?
options: Know a little more than what you are supposed to teach
Know what you are supposed to teach and stay strictly within the lesson
Teach only what is written on the page, which the pupils can then check
Say first one thing, then the other, as the rule of style would advise
optionExplain: Right: the second rule.
She knew the exercises; the gap was beyond them.
This is not one of Polya's rules; his rules ask for more than the page.
That is a rule of style, about ordering two things to say, not about knowing the subject.
questions.explain: The second rule asks for a little more knowledge than the lesson itself.
questions.rule: Know what you are supposed to teach, and a little more.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each statement: in line with Polya's rules of teaching, or against them?

items.t: Know what you are supposed to teach
Know a little more than you teach
Do not think all rules for teachers are useless
Prepare only the exact page and nothing beyond it
Know less than the lesson requires and rely on the book
Treat all rules of conduct for teachers as useless

questions.explain: He wants subject knowledge and a little more, and says rules of conduct for teachers are not completely useless.
questions.rule: Subject plus a little more.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya thinks all rules of conduct for teachers are completely useless.
questions.explain: He says he does not think so, otherwise he would not have dared to write a whole book about the conduct of teachers and students.
questions.rule: Rules for teachers are not useless.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A school adopts a thick handbook of classroom-conduct rules but hires a maths teacher who has not studied mathematics. How does Polya's remark apply?
options: The handbook is enough, because Polya holds that a good manner of teaching can replace subject knowledge
The handbook is worthless, because Polya thinks all rules of conduct for teachers are completely useless
The hire is acceptable if she stays one page ahead of the class in the textbook
Conduct rules are not useless, yet first things come first: a mathematics teacher should know some mathematics
optionExplain: Polya says no such thing; subject knowledge is the first rule of teaching, and manner cannot replace it.
He does not think all rules of conduct for teachers are useless, otherwise he would not have written a book about them.
Staying a page ahead falls short of the second rule: she must know a little more than what she teaches.
Right: rules of conduct have value, but a mathematics teacher should first know some mathematics.
questions.explain: Polya does not dismiss rules of conduct for teachers, but he adds that it should not be forgotten that a teacher of mathematics should know some mathematics.
questions.rule: First things come first: know the subject.
questions.teaches: After saying that rules of conduct for teachers are not completely useless, Polya adds: it should not be forgotten that a teacher of mathematics should know some mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: When you have understood a problem as a whole, which step does Polya describe next?
options: Choose an answer at once and test it against the problem to see if it fits
Consider the whole problem again, in the same words as the first time
Consider its principal parts, the unknown, the data and the condition, each by itself
Drop the data and keep only the condition, which is the only part to study
optionExplain: Guessing the answer is not the described step.
He moves to detail, not back to the whole.
Right. The card carries on from there.
He considers each part by itself, not dropping any.
questions.explain: From the whole to the principal parts, each by itself.
questions.rule: Go from whole to parts to parts of parts, as far as needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Having understood the condition as a whole, we separate its various ____ and consider each by itself.
questions.explain: The separating step takes the parts of the condition.
questions.rule: Separate the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A trip must arrive by 6 pm, cost under 100 euros and avoid motorways. Which step separates the parts of the condition?
options: Picking a destination at random and then asking whether it meets the rest
Writing the budget as the only datum and letting the other two wait
Listing the three requirements apart and considering each one
Combining all three requirements into one vague wish about a good trip
optionExplain: This is a guess, not a separation, and it ignores the parts of the condition.
This isolates one datum, not the parts of the condition.
Right: three parts of the condition.
This blurs the parts into one wish instead of separating them.
questions.explain: Arrive by 6 pm; spend under 100 euros; avoid motorways. Each can be examined alone.
questions.rule: Go from whole to parts to parts of parts, as far as needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A solver has understood the whole problem and its main parts but has no helpful idea. What does Polya say comes next?
options: Go into further detail: consider each datum by itself, and separate the condition into parts
Abandon the problem, since the main parts are understood and nothing came of it, and try another one
Go back to the statement and read it aloud again, hoping an idea will come
Choose the answer by a rough estimate and then adjust the data to fit it
optionExplain: Right: when the parts are in mind but no idea comes, Polya says to go into further detail.
Abandoning the problem is not what he advises; he asks for finer analysis first.
Repetition is not a finer analysis of the problem.
Choosing the answer by a rough estimate does not analyse the parts and then adjusting data changes the problem.
questions.explain: When parts are well in mind but no idea occurs, go into further detail.
questions.rule: Go from whole to parts to parts of parts, as far as needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya says separating the parts of the condition is a step in decomposing and recombining.
questions.explain: He says the suggestion provokes a step we take when trying to see the problem distinctly, and it is a step in DECOMPOSING AND RECOMBINING.
questions.rule: Separating is a step in decomposing and recombining.
questions.teaches: Polya says the suggestion to separate the parts of the condition provokes a step we take when trying to see the problem distinctly in finer and finer detail, and it is a step in decomposing and recombining.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A condition says: the rectangle has perimeter 20 and its length is twice its width. What does separating its parts ask you to write?
options: Two statements: the perimeter is 20, and the length is twice the width
One statement merging both parts into a single sentence about the rectangle
The area of the rectangle, worked out from the perimeter alone
A guess of the dimensions, to be corrected later by trial and error
optionExplain: Right. The card shows how.
The aim is to separate the parts, so merging them into one sentence undoes the step.
The area is not part of the condition, which gives only the perimeter and the ratio of sides.
A guess of the dimensions is not a part of the condition; it is a trial to be tested later.
questions.explain: Two parts, two statements.
questions.rule: Write each separated part of the condition down in its own statement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Separate the various parts of the condition. Can you ____ them down?
questions.explain: The attached question is: Can you write them down?
questions.rule: Ask it when setting up equations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: 'The rectangle has perimeter 20 and length twice its width.' Writing the two parts as 2(l + w) = 20 and l = 2w, what are l and w?
options: l = 10 and w = 5
l = 8 and w = 4
l = 5 and w = 10
optionExplain: With l = 10 and w = 5 the perimeter would be 30, not 20.
Right: 2(3w) = 20 gives w = 10/3 and l = 20/3.
With l = 8 and w = 4 the perimeter would be 24, not 20.
With l = 5 and w = 10 the length is not twice the width.
questions.rule: Write each separated part of the condition down in its own statement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A pupil writes one equation for a rectangle with perimeter 20 and length twice the width: l + w = 20. What is the error?
options: None: the equation l + w = 20 holds, since the perimeter is the length plus width
The perimeter is 2(l + w), and the second part, l = 2w, was not written at all
The equation uses letters, whereas the problem gives only numbers to work with
The equation is too long, because the condition should be written in one symbol
optionExplain: The sum of length and width is half the perimeter, 10, so l + w = 20 is wrong.
Right: the perimeter is 2(l + w), and the second part, l = 2w, was not written at all.
Letters are fine, as they stand for the unknown lengths.
The condition has two parts, so one equation is too short, not too long.
questions.explain: Two parts must be separated and written: 2(l + w) = 20 and l = 2w.
questions.rule: Write each separated part of the condition down in its own statement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: according to Polya, we often have the opportunity to ask 'Can you write them down?' when setting up equations.
questions.explain: He links the question to setting up equations.
questions.rule: Setting up equations invites this question.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Anna is twice as old as Ben, and in 5 years their ages will add up to 40. On which kind of occasion does Polya say we often ask: can you write the parts down?
options: Only when checking a finished answer
Only when the unknown is a word
When setting up equations, as here
Only when the problem has no solution
optionExplain: He links the question to setting up equations, not to checking a finished answer.
It is not restricted to word puzzles; it applies whenever a condition has parts.
Right: each part becomes an equation.
It is not restricted to impossible cases; it applies to problems with solutions too.
questions.explain: The ages give a = 2b and (a + 5) + (b + 5) = 40, so 3b = 30, b = 10, a = 20.
questions.rule: Setting up equations invites the question.
questions.teaches: Polya says we often have the opportunity to ask 'Can you write them down?' when we are setting up equations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Sort each event: steady progress or a bright idea?

items.t: Recalling a related theorem and fitting it in, step by step
Slowly noticing that the data are enough to fix the unknown
Each day a few more steps of the argument become clear
Suddenly seeing the whole figure as half of a rectangle and foreseeing all the steps
An abrupt reorganization of how the problem is conceived
A brain-wave that makes the plan clear at once

questions.explain: Steady progress comes by small imperceptible steps; a bright idea is an abrupt reorganization with a sudden prevision of the steps.
questions.rule: Steady steps or a sudden leap.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: True or false: Polya expects the general description of progress to be easy to obtain from the many concrete cases we can already judge.
questions.explain: He says the step from concrete cases to a general description is not easy at all.
questions.rule: The general account is the hard step.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Had the target sum been 99, what would the trial 19 + 28 + 30 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 show?
options: Only the sum part is met, since the total is 99 but some digits are repeated
Only the digit part is met, because the total must still be checked against 100
Neither part is met, since a number such as 30 cannot begin with a zero digit
Both parts are met: each digit 0 to 9 occurs once and the total is 99
optionExplain: The ten digits also occur once each, so the digit part is met.
The sum is also 99, so the sum part is met.
The number 30 contains 0 as a units figure, and 0 is used only once.
Right: the digits 1,9,2,8,3,0,7,6,5,4 are all different and 19+28+30+7+6+5+4 = 99.
questions.explain: Changing the target to 99 changes the puzzle: the same trial now satisfies both parts. For 100 it cannot.
questions.rule: Satisfy each part of the condition alone, then, if both together keep failing, ask whether it can be proved impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Suppose the primes were only 2, 3, 5, 7. Q = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 + 1 = 211. What does the argument show?
options: 211 is divisible by 7, so the prime 7 cannot be the last prime on the list of all the primes
211 is composite, so 2, 3, 5 and 7 must be all the primes there are
211 has no listed prime divisor, so a prime outside the list exists; here 211 is itself prime
The argument fails here, because 211 is an odd number and the proof needs even Q
optionExplain: Dividing 211 by 7 leaves remainder 1, so 7 does not divide it.
211 is prime, and the list is not complete.
Right: 210 + 1 = 211, with remainder 1 for 2, 3, 5 and 7.
Oddness is not relevant; the argument looks at the remainders left by the listed primes.
questions.explain: 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 210, so Q = 211, which leaves remainder 1 for each listed prime; 211 is prime and outside the list.
questions.rule: Multiply all the supposed primes, add 1, and note that none of them divides the result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Does the rearranged argument rule out a total of 126 for a set of numbers using each digit once?
options: Yes: 126 exceeds 100, and the puzzle's totals cannot go beyond the number 100 under any condition
Yes: 126 is an even number, and the totals of such sets are always odd
Yes: any total other than 100 is excluded by the argument as it stands
No: 126 = 9 x 14 is a multiple of 9, so the argument does not exclude it (t would be 9)
optionExplain: Size is not the condition; the argument looks at multiples of 9, not at the limit 100.
Parity is not the condition; the argument looks at multiples of 9.
Only totals that are not multiples of 9 are excluded, and 126 is a multiple of 9.
Right: the argument excludes only totals that are not multiples of 9.
questions.explain: 9(t + 5) = 126 gives t = 9, an integer. The argument does not forbid 126.
questions.rule: Show that every achievable sum is a multiple of 9, then compare the target.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Reductio ad Absurdum and Indirect Proof
questions.q: Order the steps that turn the indirect proof into a construction.
items: Ask what 'the series of primes never ends' means
Restate it as: given primes 2, ..., P, find a new prime
Form Q as the product of the primes plus 1
Take a prime divisor of Q as the new prime N
questions.explain: The meaning of 'never ends' is that one more prime always exists; this gives a problem to find; Q supplies a number whose prime divisors are all new.
questions.rule: Prove-to-find, then reuse Q.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: A teacher wants to pass on the right attitude of mind toward problems. What does Polya say she should have done?
options: Memorized a list of attitudes to recite
Acquired that attitude herself
Asked pupils to acquire it first
Taught only from the textbook
optionExplain: He does not mention reciting a list; he asks that the teacher have the attitude herself.
Right: a teacher who wants to impart the right attitude toward problems should have acquired it herself.
Asking pupils to acquire it first puts the burden on them; the teacher needs the attitude herself.
The second rule asks for more than the textbook, and the attitude cannot be taken from it.
questions.explain: A teacher wishing to impart the right attitude of mind toward problems should have acquired that attitude himself.
questions.rule: Teach the attitude you have.
questions.teaches: Polya says a teacher of mathematics should know some mathematics, and a teacher wishing to impart the right attitude of mind toward problems should have acquired that attitude himself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Progress and Achievement to Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.section: Separate the Various Parts of the Condition
questions.q: Put these steps of understanding a problem in the order Polya describes.
items: Understand the problem as a whole
Consider the unknown, the data and the condition, each by itself
Consider the various data, each datum by itself
Separate the parts of the condition and consider each by itself
questions.explain: He moves from the whole to the principal parts, then to each datum, then to the parts of the condition.
questions.rule: Whole, parts, finer parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A student stares at a word problem and cannot begin. Which diagnosis is most useful?
options: Arithmetic speed is the cause, so more timed drills on sums will fix the trouble
Writing equations is a separate talent, so practice cannot build it in a weaker student
Find out whether the gap is in grasping the statement or in knowing how to write such ideas in symbols
The problem is badly set, so the student should skip it and move on to an easier one
optionExplain: Plausible if the student is slow, but speed with sums does not tell you what the sentence means or how to write it.
This treats the difficulty as fixed; the book treats it as a translation difficulty that can be located and worked on.
Right: two different gaps can look alike from outside, and each needs a different cure.
Skipping avoids the difficulty rather than locating it.
questions.explain: A student stuck at the start may lack understanding of the statement or the notation to express it. The card next names both.
questions.rule: Ask which of two things is missing: understanding the condition, or knowing the forms of mathematical expression.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: According to the author, setting up equations is like ____ from one language into another.
questions.explain: Setting up equations expresses in mathematical symbols a condition stated in words, which is translation from ordinary language into the language of formulas.
questions.rule: Setting up equations is translation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Maria says in her own words that a number exceeds 20 by 7, yet writes 7x = 20. Which requirement is she missing?
options: Familiarity with mathematical forms: she understands the sentence but cannot write it as x = 20 + 7
Understanding of the condition: she must reread the sentence until she grasps it
Both requirements, since a wrong equation shows nothing was understood
Neither: a single slip in writing shows only that she was hurried
optionExplain: Right: her own restatement shows the sentence is understood, so the missing piece is the way mathematics expresses 'exceeds by'.
Her own restatement shows she does grasp the sentence, so rereading would not help.
A wrong equation does not prove the sentence was misunderstood; her words show it was understood.
This may be true of a given slip, but writing 7x for 'exceeds by 7' looks like a gap in the forms, which repeated attempts will not fix.
questions.explain: Two requirements, two possible gaps: the diagnosis comes from what the student can do with the words before writing symbols.
questions.rule: Locate the gap by asking the student to restate the condition in words first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each complaint by which of the two requirements for translation it points to.

items.t: I cannot say in my own words what the problem asks
I know what 'is 5 less than' means but not how to write it as an equation
I cannot tell which quantities are given and which are wanted
I see the relation between the quantities but do not know how to write a product of two lengths

questions.explain: The first and third complaints are about grasping the statement; the second and fourth are about the language of formulas.
questions.rule: Name the gap before choosing a cure.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A reader fluent in algebraic notation meets a condition she has not understood. By the translation comparison, what follows?
options: She succeeds, because the second requirement is the only one that matters in practice for equations
She succeeds after a few tries, because fluent notation will itself expose what the sentence means
She fails only on conditions that contain idioms, while plain conditions pose her no problem at all
She still cannot set up the equations, as a translator who does not grasp the English sentence cannot render it in French
optionExplain: The comparison gives the two requirements equal standing; fluency in notation does not replace understanding.
Notation does not show what the sentence means; the meaning has to come from reading the condition.
Even a plain condition must be understood before it can be translated; idioms only add difficulty.
Right: both requirements are needed. Skill in the target language cannot stand in for understanding the source.
questions.explain: What if one requirement is removed? The translation fails: each of the two is necessary.
questions.rule: Ask which of two things is missing: understanding the condition, or knowing the forms of mathematical expression.
questions.hint: Think of a translator who knows French perfectly but has not understood the English sentence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A teacher notices pupils failing to set up equations. Which use of the translation comparison fits the author's view?
options: Use it only for pupils' difficulties, since teachers do not face difficulties of translation themselves
Use it to see which of the two kinds of difficulty a pupil has, understanding the condition or knowing the forms
Use it to show that equations are a foreign language that only gifted pupils can ever learn to speak
Use it to justify handing pupils the finished equations to copy until they feel at home in the language
optionExplain: The author names teachers as well as students among those whose difficulties the comparison clarifies.
Right: the author says the comparison may clarify difficulties often felt by both students and teachers.
Nothing in the comparison says the language is for a few; translation is learnt by anyone who meets both requirements.
Copying finished equations leaves both requirements unmet.
questions.explain: The comparison, used by Newton in his Arithmetica Universalis, helps to clarify difficulties felt both by students and by teachers.
questions.rule: Ask which of two things is missing: understanding the condition, or knowing the forms of mathematical expression.
questions.teaches: The comparison of setting up equations with translation clarifies difficulties felt both by students and by teachers.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A condition in words resists being written down piece by piece. What is the best move?
options: Write each word as a symbol in the order the words appear, translating the sentence word for word
Restate the condition in a rearranged form, guided by its meaning, that can be written in symbols
Drop the part you cannot translate and solve the rest of the problem first, then come back to it
Guess an equation that looks about right from the numbers in the statement and adjust it afterwards
optionExplain: Word order may differ from the order of the mathematical relations, so the symbols come out wrong.
Right: meaning, not word order, carries the condition into symbols.
A dropped part is part of the condition; the solution of the rest will not satisfy it.
Guessing skips the understanding the translation needs.
questions.explain: When wording does not match mathematical forms, meaning has to lead. The card next explains.
questions.rule: If a part will not translate directly, restate it by its meaning in a form notation can express.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the translation comparison, a part of a condition that cannot be written down at once is like an ____.
questions.explain: Idioms cannot be put into French word for word; the translator looks to the whole meaning. Parts of a condition that will not go into symbols directly call for the same move.
questions.rule: Parts that resist word-for-word translation need their meaning restated.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: After spending a third of her savings on a book, Lena had 24 euros left. Which restatement is ready for an equation?
options: Her savings minus one third equal 24 euros
One third of her savings equals 24 euros
Her savings divided by 24 equal one third
Two thirds of her savings equal 24 euros
optionExplain: Copying the order of the words subtracts a bare fraction from an amount, which does not mean anything.
This confuses the part spent with the part left; one third is what she spent.
This uses the same numbers but does not follow from any reading of the sentence.
Right: what is left is two thirds of the savings, so (2/3)S = 24 and S = 36 euros.
questions.explain: Restating by meaning turns 'spent a third, then had 24' into a relation notation can express.
questions.rule: Ask what the left-over amount is a part of, then write that.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each rewrite by whether it follows the meaning of the sentence or copies its word order.

items.t: Cara is twice as old as Ben was 3 years ago: Cara's age equals 2 times (Ben's age minus 3)
Cara is twice as old as Ben was 3 years ago: C = 2B - 3, putting the numbers in the order the words come
Five less than a number is 12: the number minus 5 equals 12
Five less than a number is 12: 5 - n = 12, following the order of the words
Mia has 4 more than three times Joe's amount: M equals 3 times J, plus 4
Mia has 4 more than three times Joe's amount: M = 4 + 3 + J, reading the numbers as they appear

questions.explain: Each wrong rewrite puts the words in order but changes the relation. The right ones say what the quantities are first and then join them.
questions.rule: Rearrange so that the relation, not the order of the words, is preserved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which condition needs no rearranging before it can be written in symbols?
options: Two numbers have sum 78 and product 1296
A prism with square base has volume 63 cubic inches and surface area 102 square inches
A point is symmetrical to a given point with respect to a given line
After giving away a fifth of her marbles she had 12 left, and the question asks for the original number
optionExplain: Right: the book says this one splits almost automatically into parts that can be written down at once. Our reading: the others have parts that must first be restated.
The prism needs knowledge of how volume and surface are calculated before it can be translated.
Symmetry about a line has to be restated through its definition before it can be written.
A fifth given away has to be restated as four fifths left before an equation is possible.
questions.explain: Where the wording already matches notation, rearranging is not needed.
questions.rule: If a part will not translate directly, restate it by its meaning in a form notation can express.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A reader is rewording a hard condition and has two faithful versions. Which one should she prefer?
options: The one closest to how she would say it aloud, since natural speech keeps the meaning best
The one with the fewest words, since a shorter version leaves less room for a slip of meaning
The one that uses the forms notation can express, such as equal quantities, sums and products
The one that keeps the original sentence order, since that order is the order of the relations
optionExplain: Speech-like wording can be perfectly accurate and still fit notation badly.
A short version may leave out relations that notation needs to see.
Right: the author says that, while rearranging the condition, we should keep an eye on the resources of mathematical notation.
Keeping the order is the word-for-word habit the rearranging is meant to break.
questions.explain: The rearranging is steered by what mathematical notation can express, not by ordinary phrasing.
questions.rule: If a part will not translate directly, restate it by its meaning in a form notation can express.
questions.teaches: While rearranging a condition before writing formulas, we should keep an eye on the resources of mathematical notation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A rectangle has perimeter 30 and its length is 3 more than its width. Which first step helps most?
options: Try widths at random until some length turns up that fits both facts of the statement
Write one long equation that holds every word of the statement, so nothing is left out
Find the area first, since the area is the usual goal for problems about rectangles
Split the statement into two claims and ask of each whether it can be written down
optionExplain: Trying values may work but gives no method and no equations.
A single equation hides which part of the condition each symbol carries.
The area is not asked for and does not appear in the condition.
Right: two separate claims each give a short equation.
questions.explain: Splitting a condition into parts is the first move. The card next gives the full routine.
questions.rule: Understand the condition, separate its parts, and test each part with 'Can you write it down?'

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Put the author's routine for a condition in order.
items: Understand the condition
Separate the various parts of the condition
Ask of each part: can you write it down?
Write down the parts that can be expressed in symbols
questions.explain: The routine runs from understanding to separating to testing each part with the question, and only then to writing.
questions.rule: Understand, separate, ask, write.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A garden is twice as long as it is wide and its fence has length 54 m. Which parts are ready to be written down?
options: length x width = 54, and length = 2
length = 2 x width, and 2 x (length + width) = 54
length + width = 54, and width = 2 x length
length = 2 + width, and length + width = 54, where length is two more than width
optionExplain: This uses the fence length as an area and treats 'twice' as the number 2.
Right: width 9 and length 18 satisfy both conditions, since 2 x 27 = 54.
This turns the fence into half-perimeter and reverses the roles of length and width.
'Twice as long' is multiplication, not addition, and the fence goes round all four sides.
questions.explain: Two parts, each stated in the form of a relation between quantities already named.
questions.rule: Name the unknowns first, then read the statement one claim at a time.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each part of a condition by whether it can be written down at once.

items.t: The sum of two numbers is 78
The product of two numbers is 1296
A prism with square base has volume 63
The surface of the prism has area 102
One number is 5 more than the other
A point is symmetrical to another about a given line

questions.explain: Sums, products and 'more than' are already relations notation expresses. Volume, surface and symmetry have to be restated in terms of known formulas or definitions first.
questions.rule: Test each part: can it be written as it stands?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A condition splits into one part that can be written at once and one that cannot. What does the author's routine suggest?
options: Drop the second part, since the first part alone will give an answer to the problem
Wait for a second expert to translate the second part, since the first part is already done, which saves you the effort of working it out
Write the first part and keep working on the second by restating it in terms you can express
Replace the whole condition by the first part, since that is the part that can be written
optionExplain: The answer from the first part alone would not satisfy the whole condition.
Nothing in the routine hands the difficulty to another person; it asks 'can you write them down?' of each part.
Right: every part belongs to the condition; the part that resists has to be restated until it can be written.
Replacing the condition changes the problem.
questions.explain: What if one part resists? The routine keeps all parts and works on the resistant one.
questions.rule: Understand the condition, separate its parts, and test each part with 'Can you write it down?'

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A manager asks for a vendor with cost under 5000, delivery within 3 weeks, and reliable service. Which part resists being written down?
options: Reliable service: it must be restated in terms that can be checked before it can be written down
Cost under 5000, since a limit needs a rule for turning words into a number first
Delivery within 3 weeks, since a time span cannot be written as a quantity in the usual way, and the same for every duration measured in days
None, since all three parts are written down in the same way and with the same ease
optionExplain: Right. The book says that in difficult cases the condition has parts that cannot be immediately translated into symbols, so the division and restatement need thought.
A cost limit is already a statement about a number.
A duration is a number of weeks and can be written as it stands.
The first two parts are written at once; the third is not.
questions.explain: Some parts of a condition cannot be immediately translated into mathematical symbols.
questions.rule: Understand the condition, separate its parts, and test each part with 'Can you write it down?'
questions.teaches: In difficult cases the condition has parts that cannot be immediately translated into symbols, and the appropriate division is less obvious.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How would you lay out the work for the problem: two numbers have sum 78 and product 1296?
options: Statement in parts on one side, and symbols for each part opposite it on the other
One line of symbols written straight away, with the words of the statement kept in your head
A table of trial pairs, adding each pair in turn to test whether the sum comes out right
A single long sentence mixing words and symbols, so the translation stays inside the statement
optionExplain: Right: facing columns keep each part with its translation.
Words kept in the head lose the link between each part and its symbols.
Trial pairs may find the answer but do not set up the equations.
Mixed sentences blur which part of the condition each symbol carries.
questions.explain: The card next shows the layout the author uses.
questions.rule: Write the statement in parts on the left and its translation opposite each part on the right.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the author's layout the original statement is on the ____ and the translation into symbols on the right.
questions.explain: The original sits on the left of the vertical line and the algebraic translation on the right.
questions.rule: Original left, translation right.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two numbers have difference 9 and product 190. Which right-hand column mirrors the statement?
optionExplain: A difference has been replaced by a sum.
The numbers 9 and 190 have been swapped between the two parts.
Right: 19 and 10 fit, since 19 - 10 = 9 and 19 x 10 = 190.
The product has been replaced by a sum.
questions.explain: Each row must face the part it translates; the match shows if a part was misread.
questions.rule: Read each phrase on the left and check the symbol facing it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: if a phrase on the left has no matching symbols on the right, the condition has not been fully used.
questions.explain: Each part of the condition must be translated; an untranslated phrase means that a part of the condition is missing from the equations.
questions.rule: Every part on the left needs an entry on the right.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The sum-and-product problem and the square-based prism problem are both set out in columns. How do the left columns differ?
options: The prism's left column is shorter, since the prism has fewer parts than the sum-and-product problem
In the first the statement splits as it stands; in the prism the left side is first rearranged and expanded
The sum-and-product left side has been rearranged, while the prism's left side is the original wording, with only the lengths of the columns differing
They do not differ at all; only the symbols on the right-hand side differ between the problems
optionExplain: The prism's left side is longer, because the parts of the condition are spelled out.
Right. The book says the prism's left side is an essentially rearranged and expanded statement of the problem, ready for translation.
It is the other way round: the sum-and-product statement is almost untouched.
The left sides differ in how far the wording had to be rearranged.
questions.explain: A condition that cannot be written down immediately gets a rewritten left column.
questions.rule: Write the statement in parts on the left and its translation opposite each part on the right.
questions.teaches: For the prism problem the left-hand column holds an essentially rearranged and expanded statement of the problem, ready for translation into algebraic language.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A clerk sets a shop rule (late fee of 2% of the balance for each month late) beside a spreadsheet formula. Which pairing follows the layout?
options: The whole sentence faces the finished total, with nothing written in between to show the steps
The formula is written first and the sentence is fitted to it later, whatever the sentence says
Only the percentage is paired with a symbol, since the remaining words are only wording
Each phrase on one side faces its own piece of the formula: 2% faces 0.02, the balance faces B, each month faces the month count
optionExplain: A single pairing hides whether each part was translated.
The statement comes first; the translation is built from its parts.
Words such as 'for each month' also carry a relation to be written.
Right: the layout carries over to any rule stated in words. The book's example is one where the verbal statement splits almost automatically into parts that can be written at once.
questions.explain: Phrase by phrase, each part of the verbal statement meets its symbols.
questions.rule: Write the statement in parts on the left and its translation opposite each part on the right.
questions.teaches: When the verbal statement splits almost automatically into successive parts, each part can be immediately written down in mathematical symbols.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A prism with square base has volume 63 cubic inches and surface area 102 square inches. What are the unknowns?
options: The volume and the surface area, which are the measurements we are given
The numbers 63 and 102, which are the values to be found
The side of the base and the altitude
The prism itself, because it is the thing described
optionExplain: These are the data; they are given, not sought.
The numbers are given, so they are data.
Right: we are asked for the breadth and the height, which can be called x and y.
The prism is the object; the unknowns are the quantities to find.
questions.explain: The unknowns are what we are asked to find, the data what we are given. The card next gives the routine.
questions.rule: Name the unknowns, the data and the condition; then separate the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each item of the prism problem by whether it is an unknown or a datum.

items.t: The side of the square base
The altitude of the prism
The volume, 63
The area of the surface, 102

questions.explain: The sides of the prism are what is wanted; the volume and the area are given.
questions.rule: Unknowns are what you find; data are what you are given.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A rectangle has area 96 and perimeter 40. Which list names unknowns, data and condition correctly?
options: Unknowns: length and width. Data: 96 and 40. Condition: the rectangle must have area 96 and perimeter 40
Unknowns: area and perimeter. Data: length and width. Condition: area equals length plus width
Unknowns: the numbers 96 and 40. Data: the rectangle. Condition: length times width
Unknowns: length, width and area. Data: perimeter only. Condition: the rectangle must be a square, because a square has equal sides
optionExplain: Right: the sides are sought, the two numbers are given, and the condition links them (l = 12 and w = 8 satisfy it).
This reverses unknowns and data and states a wrong relation.
The numbers are given, not sought, and the relation chosen is only one fragment.
Area is given, and nothing in the statement says the rectangle is a square.
questions.explain: Unknowns are the sides, data the two numbers, and the condition ties them together.
questions.rule: Ask what is sought, what is given and what must hold.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The condition of the prism problem separates into ____ parts: one about the volume, one about the surface area.
questions.explain: The volume and the area of the surface are two separate requirements, so the condition has two parts, each giving an equation.
questions.rule: One requirement, one part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Suppose the prism problem gave only the volume. What changes in the naming and separating?
options: Nothing changes, since a single datum is enough to fix both unknowns of the prism
The unknowns would change to the volume and the base area, which would now be sought
The condition could no longer be written in symbols at all, since one part is too few
The condition would have one part, so the data would be one number and fewer equations would result
optionExplain: Two unknowns generally need two relations; one datum gives one.
The unknowns are still the sides of the prism.
One part is easier to write, not impossible.
Right: one requirement gives one part; our reading is that two unknowns would then be left under-determined.
questions.explain: What if a datum is removed? The condition loses a part and the set of equations shrinks with it.
questions.rule: Name the unknowns, the data and the condition; then separate the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A reader says the prism's condition divides easily into two parts, yet cannot write them down at once. Is that a contradiction?
options: Yes: parts that are easy to separate can always be written down at once as equations
No: the division is easy to see, but the parts cannot be written immediately without more knowledge
Yes: if the writing is hard the division itself must be wrong and should be made again
No: hard writing means that some of the data are missing from the statement
optionExplain: The book gives this very case as a counter: easy division, but not an immediate translation.
Right. The book says we can scarcely hesitate in dividing the condition into the volume part and the area part, but we cannot write those parts at once.
The division is right; what is missing is the knowledge to write each part.
The data are all present; the knowledge of how to compute volume and area is what is needed.
questions.explain: The division into volume and area parts is easy to see, yet each part still needs geometry (how volume and surface are calculated) before it can be written in symbols.
questions.rule: Name the unknowns, the data and the condition; then separate the condition.
questions.teaches: We can scarcely hesitate in dividing the prism's condition into its volume part and its area part, but we cannot write those parts down immediately.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: To write the volume of a square-based prism as an equation in x and y, what do you need to know?
options: The numerical value of the volume, which is given
How the volume of a prism is calculated from its base and altitude
How to solve equations, which the translation itself requires
The surface area, since volume and surface determine each other, so one of them can be had from the other
optionExplain: The value is given, but it is not enough to write an equation in x and y.
Right: the translation uses the rule base area times altitude.
Solving is a later step; the translation needs the formula first.
The surface is a different requirement, written by its own equation.
questions.explain: Translating needs subject knowledge as well as notation. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Know the subject's formulas, restate each part with them, then translate.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the prism's condition can be written as equations at once, without knowing how volume and surface are calculated.
questions.explain: The book says we must know how to calculate the volume and the various parts of the surface; with that knowledge the parts can be restated and then written.
questions.rule: Subject knowledge comes before translation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A box with no lid has a square base of side x and height y, volume 100 and outer surface 130. Which equations fit?
options: x squared times y = 100, and 2 x squared + 4xy = 130
xy = 100, and x squared + 4xy = 130
x squared times y = 100, and 4xy = 130
x squared times y = 100, and x squared + 4xy = 130
optionExplain: This counts both a top and a bottom, which suits a closed box and not this one.
The volume is base area times height, so the base area x squared must appear.
This leaves out the square base from the surface.
Right: the base counts once and the four sides add 4xy. No lid means no top square.
questions.explain: Restating the surface with the lid removed changes one term of the area equation.
questions.rule: Count the faces that the box actually has.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A student restates a closed square-based prism of base side x and height y. Which lines contain an error?
options: The surface equals the area of the base times the altitude
Volume = area of base times altitude = x squared times y
Surface = two squares of side x plus four rectangles x by y = 2 x squared + 4xy
Each side rectangle has area x squared
optionExplain: Wrong: that product is the volume, not the surface.
Correct: the base is a square, so its area is x squared.
Correct: top and bottom squares plus four sides.
Wrong: a side rectangle has base x and altitude y, so its area is xy, not x squared.
questions.explain: The two errors confuse the side faces with the square base and confuse surface with volume. The two correct lines follow the geometry.
questions.rule: Check each restatement against the figure.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Of what does the surface of a closed prism with square base of side x and altitude y consist, according to the book?
options: Two squares with side x and four rectangles, each with base x and altitude y
Four squares with side x and two rectangles of base x and altitude y, as the faces of a prism with a square base are counted
One square with side x and four triangles of base x and altitude y
Six rectangles, each with base x and altitude y
optionExplain: Right: the sum of these six pieces is the area, 2 x squared + 4xy.
This swaps the counts: the square faces are top and bottom only.
A prism with square base has rectangular, not triangular, sides.
Top and bottom are squares of side x, not rectangles x by y.
questions.explain: The six faces of a closed square-based prism are the square top and bottom and four side rectangles; adding their areas gives 2x squared plus 4xy.
questions.rule: Know the subject's formulas, restate each part with them, then translate.
questions.teaches: The surface of the square-based prism consists of two squares with side x and four rectangles, each with base x and altitude y, whose sum is the area.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A pupil is stuck turning a tax rule (20% of income above 12,000) into a formula. Which diagnosis follows the prism example?
options: She needs a better notation, since the idea itself is already clear to her from the wording
She should drop the wording and guess a formula from sample incomes and taxes instead
She needs to know how the tax is calculated; with that, the statement can be easily restated and then written
She should look for a different condition that is easier to write down in symbols
optionExplain: Notation is not the missing piece; the knowledge of the rule is.
Guessing skips the restating that connects the wording to the formula.
Right. In the book's case, once we know that much geometry, we can easily restate both parts so the translation into equations is feasible.
Replacing the condition changes the problem being solved.
questions.explain: Subject knowledge makes the restating easy, and the restating makes the translation feasible.
questions.rule: Know the subject's formulas, restate each part with them, then translate.
questions.teaches: If we know the needed geometry, we can easily restate both parts of the condition so that the translation into equations is feasible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A condition can be cut into parts in many ways. Which cut is best for setting up equations?
options: The cut with the fewest parts, since fewer parts mean fewer equations, and with them fewer chances for an error of translation
The cut that follows the order of the words in the statement
The cut closest to a textbook definition of the idea involved
One whose parts can be expressed in the mathematical language you will use
optionExplain: A short list can still consist of parts that cannot be written.
Word order may split the condition at points that are hard to express.
A definition can be correct and still use words notation does not have.
Right: a part you cannot write adds nothing to the equations.
questions.explain: A condition can be cut up in several ways; the card next says which cut serves equations.
questions.rule: A division is good only if each of its parts can be written in the language you are using.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: a division of a condition that is logically unobjectionable is bound to be useful for setting up equations.
questions.explain: The author says a decomposition may be logically unobjectionable and nevertheless useless, because its parts are not fit for the language of the equations.
questions.rule: Correct is not the same as writable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A rectangle with one side 4 is to have the area of a square of side 6. Which decomposition is fit for writing?
options: The rectangle can be cut up and rearranged into the square
The rectangle's area, 4 times w, equals the square's area, 6 times 6
The two shapes cover equal ground on the plane
The rectangle is a squashed version of the square
optionExplain: This may be true of equal areas but it does not give a relation among numbers.
Right: 4w = 36 gives w = 9. The other three are true or helpful ideas but give nothing to write.
This restates 'equal area' in words with no formula.
This is a picture, not a relation between sides.
questions.explain: Each part of a fit decomposition becomes a relation among the quantities.
questions.rule: Use the formula that connects the quantities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which comments on decomposing a condition match the book?
options: The parts must be fit for expression in the language we are using
The more parts, the better the decomposition
A decomposition can be logically sound and still useless
Any decomposition covering the whole condition will do
optionExplain: Right: the language of analytic geometry in the book's example.
Wrong: the book asks for fit, not for a count of parts.
Right: this is the author's warning.
Wrong: covering the whole is necessary but the parts must also be writable.
questions.explain: The book asks for decompositions that are fit for expression. Covering the condition or having many parts does not ensure it.
questions.rule: Fit for expression is the test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the symmetric-point problem, what does the author say is the essential difficulty?
options: Finding the coordinates of the given point, which the statement does not give in numbers
Solving the equations once they have been written, which needs the whole algebra of the pair, which is the real difficulty of the problem
Dividing the condition into parts each of which can be expressed in the language of analytic geometry
Proving that a symmetric point exists at all for every choice of the line and the point
optionExplain: The point's coordinates are given as a, b.
The solving is a later step; the passage is about setting up.
Right: the difficulty lies in the translation, in finding the right parts.
The problem takes it for granted that the point is to be found.
questions.explain: The nature of the difficulty must be well understood: it lies in the division itself.
questions.rule: A division is good only if each of its parts can be written in the language you are using.
questions.teaches: A decomposition of the condition into parts may be logically unobjectionable and nevertheless useless; what is needed is a decomposition into parts fit for analytic expression.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A product owner writes that the app should feel fast. Which split helps a tester who writes numeric checks?
options: Pages load in under 2 seconds on the test device, and a tap responds within 100 ms
Users are not annoyed by waiting, which is the aim the owner actually has in mind
The app compares well with others in the same category, as a customer would judge it
Users call it fast when they are asked in a survey, so that their words settle it
optionExplain: Right: these parts are fit for the tester's language, numbers and thresholds. Our reading: the others are fair statements but give nothing to write as a check.
A correct goal, but not expressed in numbers.
A comparison is a different language and gives no number.
A survey word is a report, not a relation the tester can write.
questions.explain: The choice of parts depends on the language you will write in.
questions.rule: A division is good only if each of its parts can be written in the language you are using.
questions.teaches: What is needed is a decomposition into parts fit for expression in the language we are going to use; here the book's language is that of analytic geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A point Q is the mirror image of P across a line. Which pair of facts fixes Q?
options: PQ is perpendicular to the line, and the midpoint of PQ lies on the line
PQ is parallel to the line, and Q is as far from the origin as P, which together are enough to name the mirror image
The line passes through both P and Q
Q is as far from the origin as P is, and nothing else
optionExplain: Right: these two facts together locate Q uniquely.
A parallel join is not the mirror relation, and equal distance from the origin holds only for lines through the origin.
If the line passed through both points, they would be on the mirror itself, and P would be its own image.
Equal distance from the origin does not use the line; many points satisfy it.
questions.explain: A mirror image is fixed by perpendicularity and by the midpoint on the line. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: Express symmetry about a line as perpendicularity of the joining line plus its midpoint lying on the line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The line joining a point and its mirror image is ____ to the mirror line.
questions.explain: The joining line meets the mirror line at a right angle, and the midpoint of the joining segment is on the mirror line.
questions.rule: Joining line perpendicular; midpoint on the mirror.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The line is y = 2x and the point is (5, 0). Which point is its mirror image?
optionExplain: Its midpoint (0, 0) lies on the line, but the join is horizontal, not perpendicular.
This satisfies the perpendicular relation but is the foot of the perpendicular, on the line itself; the midpoint is (3, 1), not on the line.
Right: the slope of the join is 4 / (-8) = -1/2, perpendicular to 2, and the midpoint (1, 2) is on y = 2x.
Its midpoint (2.5, 2.5) is not on y = 2x.
questions.explain: Both relations must hold. A point that meets one of them is not enough.
questions.rule: Check both relations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: For a line y = mx + n and a point (a, b), which statements about the sought point (p, q) hold?
options: The points (a, b) and (p, q) have equal y-coordinates
The joining line has slope m, parallel to the given line
The midpoint of the joining segment satisfies the equation of the given line
The slope of the joining line is -1/m, the negative reciprocal of m
optionExplain: Wrong: this holds only when the mirror line is vertical.
Wrong: parallel lines would never meet the mirror at the midpoint.
Right: the midpoint is on the line.
Right: this is perpendicularity in coordinates.
questions.explain: Perpendicular slope and midpoint on the line are the two relations; parallel joins and equal y-coordinates are not general.
questions.rule: Negative reciprocal slope, midpoint on the line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which two questions does the author say guide the search for a fit decomposition of the symmetric-point condition?
options: What is the length of the segment joining the points, and what is the angle of the given line
What is meant by symmetry with respect to a line, and which relations are simple in analytic geometry
Which figures are symmetric and which are not, and how many axes of symmetry each of them has, and with how much each figure resembles a mirror image
Where the mirror image is drawn on the page, and in which quadrant of the plane it falls
optionExplain: Lengths and angles are not the two questions.
Right: the author concentrates on the first question but should not forget the second.
That asks about figures in general, not about this condition.
Drawing positions do not help to set up equations.
questions.explain: The definition gives the geometric parts; the notation limits which ones are usable.
questions.rule: Express symmetry about a line as perpendicularity of the joining line plus its midpoint lying on the line.
questions.teaches: We concentrate upon the question of what is meant by symmetry with respect to a line, but should not forget the other question: which geometric relations can be expressed easily in analytic geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A decorator wants the mirror image of a lamp at (2, 6) across the wall line y = x. Which setup follows the two relations?
options: Slope of the join is 1 and the midpoint is on y = x, which gives (6, 6)
Slope of the join is -1 and the midpoint is the origin, which gives (-2, -6)
The join is horizontal and the midpoint is on y = x, which gives the point (6, 6)
Slope of the join is -1 (perpendicular to slope 1) and the midpoint is on y = x, which gives (6, 2)
optionExplain: A join of slope 1 would be parallel to the mirror, not perpendicular.
The midpoint need not be the origin; it only has to be on the line.
A horizontal join is perpendicular only to a vertical mirror.
Right: (2, 6) to (6, 2) has slope -1 and midpoint (4, 4) on y = x. In coordinates the book writes the two parts as slope -1/m and (b + q)/2 = m(a + p)/2 + n.
questions.explain: The join from (2, 6) to (6, 2) has slope -1, perpendicular to the wall of slope 1, and its midpoint (4, 4) lies on y = x, so both relations hold.
questions.rule: Express symmetry about a line as perpendicularity of the joining line plus its midpoint lying on the line.
questions.teaches: In coordinates the two parts read: (q - b)/(p - a) = -1/m for the perpendicular join, and (b + q)/2 = m(a + p)/2 + n for the midpoint on the line y = mx + n.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sailing west into unknown waters, a crew sees a bird. How should they take it?
options: As proof that land lies straight ahead
As meaningless, since birds fly anywhere over open sea, so the sight tells the crew nothing at all
As a favorable but uncertain sign that land may be near
As a warning to turn back at once
optionExplain: A bird raises hope but does not prove land, as the crew learned.
Birds are more frequent near land than on the open sea, so the sight carries some information.
Right: birds are more common near shore, but the crew was disappointed by them more than once.
Nothing about a bird suggests danger; it is a sign of possible land.
questions.explain: A bird is an indication, not a proof. The card next shows how the crew read signs.
questions.rule: Watch eagerly for signs that the solution is near.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: On 11 October 1492 the ____ multiplied: sandpipers, a green reed, a cane and more, and next day land was sighted.
questions.explain: Several different signs came one after another that day, unlike the single birds and seaweed that had disappointed the crew before.
questions.rule: Signs multiplied before land was sighted.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A developer chasing a bug sees one log line pointing to module X. Later two unrelated checks also point to X. How does the second event change things?
options: The signs have multiplied, so the case for looking in X gets stronger, though X is still not certain
It proves that X contains the bug, because three clues cannot all be pointing wrongly
It changes nothing, because one sign is as good as three and the first line already said it
It shows the first log line was wrong, because new clues replace the older clue in weight
optionExplain: Right: like the crew on 11 October, the developer finds more signs agreeing; confidence rises without being proof.
More signs make the conclusion more plausible, but the crew's experience shows signs can still mislead.
The author says signs multiply and confidence rises; one sign does not weigh as much as three.
Nothing in the new checks contradicts the first line.
questions.explain: Like the crew on 11 October, the developer now has several agreeing signs, which raises confidence in X more than one line did, though none of them proves it.
questions.rule: Count how many independent signs agree.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: on the voyage, the crew's early signs, such as birds, all turned out to be followed by land soon after.
questions.explain: They were repeatedly disappointed. Only on 11 October did the signs multiply and the next day brought land.
questions.rule: Early signs did not guarantee land.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Besides birds, which other things did the crew read as possible signs of land and then find disappointing?
options: Changes in the color of the sea and the stars at night
Fish that followed the ships and warm winds
Distant lights seen on the horizon
Floating seaweed and low banks of cloud
optionExplain: These are not the signs the account names.
The account does not name fish or winds.
Lights on the horizon do not appear in the account.
Right: seaweed and low cloud banks were also watched for, with disappointment.
questions.explain: The crew tried several kinds of sign and were disappointed by some of them.
questions.rule: Watch eagerly for signs that the solution is near.
questions.teaches: The crew thought floating seaweed or low banks of cloud might indicate land, and were again disappointed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A job seeker gets a friendly reply from one firm. Another firm calls the next day; a third asks for references. How does this fit the author's picture?
options: As proof of an offer, since three friendly replies cannot all be wrong about the firms
As signs multiplying: encouraging, and the author says this holds for undertakings of any kind
As irrelevant, since only a signed contract counts and everything before it is only noise
As relevant only to sea voyages, since signs of progress belong to explorers, not to ordinary affairs
optionExplain: Three signs are encouraging but not proof; the author says they only cheer us.
Right. The author says that whether the undertaking is important or unimportant and the problem of any kind, we watch for signs of progress.
Signs are what a person has before any final proof, and the author treats them as useful.
The author says the undertaking may be important or unimportant, the problem of any kind.
questions.explain: The watching for signs is not limited to mathematical problems.
questions.rule: Watch eagerly for signs that the solution is near.
questions.teaches: Our undertaking may be important or unimportant and our problem of any kind; when we work intensely we watch eagerly for signs of progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In a mate-in-two puzzle, a distant knight seems useless. You find a move that brings it into play. How do you react?
options: With suspicion, since a useless piece should stay out, because a piece that does nothing should not be disturbed
With new hope, since a well-built puzzle has no spare piece
With certainty that this is the solution
With indifference, since one piece cannot matter
optionExplain: The reverse is true: an idle piece is unusual in a well-built puzzle.
Right: the correct solution uses every piece, so a move that uses the knight resembles it.
A move using the knight is encouraging but not proven to give mate.
A designed puzzle has no superfluous piece, so one piece matters a good deal.
questions.explain: Using a piece that looked idle is a good sign. The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: A candidate that uses a datum the others ignored resembles the true solution in that respect.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In a well-constructed chess problem there is no ____ piece.
questions.explain: Because every piece belongs to the problem, the correct solution uses all of them.
questions.rule: No piece is superfluous in a well-built problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A logic puzzle has five clues. Candidate A uses clues 1 to 4 and ignores clue 5. Candidate B uses all five. Which looks more promising?
options: A, since fewer assumptions make a stronger answer
They are equally promising until one is checked
A, since the unused clue can be a distractor
B, since a well-stated puzzle uses every clue
optionExplain: Fewer clues used is a worse sign when the puzzle is well-stated.
They are not equally likely: only one has the property the true solution must have.
A distractor is possible in a badly built puzzle; the book's sign applies to well-stated problems.
Right: B shares the property that the true solution must have. It is a sign, and still needs checking.
questions.explain: Use of all data is a mark of the true solution in a well-stated problem.
questions.rule: Count how many data each candidate uses.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A candidate move brings the idle knight into play but the black king escapes. What does the sign say now?
options: The sign was only a plausible indication and this candidate has failed; look for another move that uses the knight
The sign proves the candidate right, so the king must somehow be able to escape after all
The puzzle is badly built, since a sign that points to a failing move cannot be a good one
The knight should be ignored from now on, since it has led the search into a failure
optionExplain: Right: a sign makes a candidate plausible, not certain; a failed test sends you on.
A sign cannot override a test that fails.
Our reading: a failed candidate does not show the puzzle is bad; the author's rule is for well-built puzzles.
The sign says the true solution uses the knight; it does not say to drop the knight.
questions.explain: A sign makes a candidate plausible, but a test that fails decides against it; the sign still tells you the true move should use the knight.
questions.rule: A candidate that uses a datum the others ignored resembles the true solution in that respect.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which of these claims about the sign are justified?
options: A move that uses the knight must be the correct one
A move that uses the knight might be the correct one
A move that leaves the knight idle is less likely to be the solution
A move that uses the knight shows the puzzle has a flaw
optionExplain: Not justified: the sign only makes it plausible.
Justified: it shares the property of the true solution.
Justified: the true solution uses all the pieces.
Not justified: the knight belongs to a well-built puzzle.
questions.explain: The sign makes a move plausible and idle pieces suspect; it does not make a move certain.
questions.rule: Plausible, not certain.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: An accountant reconciling a ledger cannot explain one odd entry of 40 units. A candidate explanation accounts for it along with the others. Why is that encouraging?
options: Because a candidate that explains more entries is always right, however many it leaves out
Because odd entries are always errors that ought to be removed before the sums are made
