In a well-stated problem all the data should be used and connected with the unknown
Because 40 units is a small amount and does not matter for the reconciliation at all
optionExplain: It is encouraging but not always right; a candidate can still fail the check.
Dropping the odd entry would leave a datum unused, which is the opposite of the sign.
Right. The book says that at least in well-stated problems we should use all the data and connect each with the unknown.
Size does not decide; unused data in a well-stated problem are a warning.
questions.explain: The accountant is applying the principle that in a well-stated problem every datum should be used and connected with the unknown; an entry left unexplained is a warning.
questions.rule: A candidate that uses a datum the others ignored resembles the true solution in that respect.
questions.teaches: In well-stated problems we should use all the data and connect each of them with the unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: While building an area formula for a triangle, a square root of b + c - a appears. Why might that cheer you?
options: It contains all three side lengths, as the true formula must, but this is not what makes it encouraging
It shows the answer is a whole number
It makes the formula shorter than rival formulas
It becomes unreal exactly when no triangle with those sides exists
optionExplain: Containing the letters is not enough; the point is how it behaves when the sides cannot form a triangle.
Nothing about a square root makes values whole.
Brevity is no sign of correctness.
Right: the expression is unfit for real values exactly where the true area expression must fail.
questions.explain: The square root is a sign because of how it behaves for impossible sides. The card gives details.
questions.rule: Take it as a good sign when your expression breaks down in just the circumstances where the true one must.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The square root of b + c - a becomes ____ when b + c is less than a.
questions.explain: A square root of a negative number is imaginary. That is exactly when the three lengths cannot form a triangle.
questions.rule: Imaginary when b + c < a.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: For sides a = 5, b = 2, c = 2, what does b + c - a equal, and what does it say?
options: 1, so the square root is real, as a triangle with these sides exists and has an area, exactly as the true formula would
-1, so the square root is imaginary, as it should be since no triangle has these sides
-1, so the formula is wrong because it cannot handle these particular side lengths
4, so the formula gives a real area for this triangle, because b + c is 4
optionExplain: That is the sign error: 2 + 2 - 5 is -1, not 1.
Right: 2 + 2 - 5 = -1. The formula fails where the triangle does not exist, which is the sign.
The failure is the good sign: the true expression must also fail for these lengths.
4 is the sum b + c, not b + c - a.
questions.explain: With a = 5, b = 2, c = 2 no triangle exists, and the quantity b + c - a is negative, so the square root fails exactly where the true area expression must fail.
questions.rule: Substitute and look at the sign of the quantity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Candidate formulas for a triangle's area have a square root of (a - b - c) or of (b + c - a). Which gives the good sign?
options: The root of a - b - c: it is real for every triangle that exists
Both, since each contains the three side lengths
The root of b + c - a: it fails exactly when no triangle exists
Neither, since a root can never behave like an area
optionExplain: It is imaginary whenever a triangle exists, which is the wrong way round.
Having the three letters is not the test; what matters is where the expression fails.
Right: for a real triangle a - b - c is negative, so the first would fail where a triangle exists, the reverse of the sign.
An expression with a root can represent area, as the true formula does.
questions.explain: A sign works when the failures of the formula match those of the answer.
questions.rule: Take it as a good sign when your expression breaks down in just the circumstances where the true one must.
questions.hint: For which sides does each expression become negative?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: if b + c is not greater than a, a formula for the triangle's area is bound to become illusory.
questions.explain: No triangle has such sides, since the sum of any two sides exceeds the third; the restriction is part of the condition and the whole condition should be used.
questions.rule: A restriction in the condition limits the formula too.
questions.teaches: The given lengths cannot be quite arbitrary: b + c must exceed a. This restriction is an essential part of the condition, and we should use the whole condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A candidate formula for the time to empty a tank is volume / (outflow - inflow). The true answer is meaningless when inflow is at least outflow. Is the candidate encouraging?
options: Yes: it breaks down in exactly those circumstances, as the true answer must, though that does not prove it
No: a formula that breaks down anywhere is wrong, so it cannot be a good candidate
Yes: because it breaks down in the same place, it is now proved to be correct
No: formulas for a time cannot have a denominator, since time is never divided
optionExplain: Right: the candidate has an important property in common with the true answer, which makes it plausible.
Breakdown where the true answer breaks down is the sign, not a fault.
Matching the true answer where it breaks down makes the candidate plausible, not proved; it could still be wrong elsewhere.
A denominator is allowed; here it vanishes where it should.
questions.explain: A candidate that breaks down in exactly the circumstances in which the true answer must break down shares an important property with it; that is plausible evidence, not proof.
questions.rule: Take it as a good sign when your expression breaks down in just the circumstances where the true one must.
questions.teaches: A formula that becomes unfit to represent a real quantity under exactly those circumstances under which the desired expression is bound to become illusory has an important property in common with the true formula.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Stuck on a proof about solids, you suddenly recall a plane theorem of the same kind. How should you take it?
options: As encouraging: it may be the lemma you need
As a distraction from the real problem
As proof that the solid result is true
As evidence that the solid problem is too hard
optionExplain: Right: solid-geometry problems often rest on analogous plane problems.
Analogy is a guide, so the recall is relevant.
The plane theorem does not prove the solid one; it may supply a step.
The recollection suggests a way forward, not an obstacle.
questions.explain: An analogous problem is a hopeful sign. The card next says why.
questions.rule: When an analogous problem comes up unprompted, treat it as a good sign.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The solution of a problem in solid geometry often depends on an analogous problem in ____ geometry.
questions.explain: The author refers to analogy: plane problems are often the stepping stone for solid ones.
questions.rule: Solid problems often rest on plane analogues.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Counting the arrangements of 6 distinct books is hard. While thinking, the case of 3 books comes up by itself. What does that suggest?
options: Nothing, since the 3-book case is a different problem
That the 6-book answer must be double the 3-book one
A simpler analogous problem has emerged; it may show the pattern to use
That the problem should be abandoned for the easy case
optionExplain: Analogy is one of the main sources of invention; it is relevant.
No rule of doubling is suggested; the sign is only a lead.
Right: the author says that if an analogous problem emerges spontaneously we naturally feel that we are approaching the solution.
The easy case is a step, not a replacement.
questions.explain: A simpler analogous problem that appears unprompted is a lead: it may show the pattern, though it still has to be used and checked on the real problem.
questions.rule: Ask what the simpler case could teach about the harder one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: after finding an analogous plane theorem, the author could say he had proved the solid theorem.
questions.explain: He says he had good reason to be convinced, but the plane theorem only looked like the lemma he needed; the sign is plausible, not proof.
questions.rule: A lemma that looks right still has to be shown to work.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: On the day he gave up, what did the author already have, compared with the beginning?
options: A finished proof lacking a single line, which he then supplied the next morning
A much clearer notion of how the proof should look and how the gap should be filled
A list of theorems in plane geometry, from which he chose the one that fitted
No new insight, only fatigue, which a night's rest then removed before the idea came
optionExplain: The proof was not finished; a gap remained.
Right: he could not fill the gap, but he understood its shape much better the next morning.
He had not yet recalled the plane theorem.
He says he had a much clearer notion than at the outset.
questions.explain: Even a failed day can leave a clearer picture of what is needed.
questions.rule: When an analogous problem comes up unprompted, treat it as a good sign.
questions.teaches: When the author gave up that day he had a much clearer notion than at the outset of how the proof should look and how the gap should be filled, though he could not fill it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A cook cannot scale a recipe for 40 guests. A simpler case, scaling for 4, comes to mind. What does the author's advice say?
options: Ignore the 4-guest case, since the cook should solve the real 40-guest case first and directly, whatever easier cases may turn up along the way
Use only the 4-guest recipe, since that case is simpler and the large case is not needed
Wait until a similar recipe for a large party has been found in a cookery book
If other means fail, try to imagine an analogous problem, and welcome one that appears by itself
optionExplain: Setting it aside throws away a possible lead.
Staying with the easy case does not solve the real one.
The analogue that emerges spontaneously can be used at once.
Right: analogy is one of the main sources of invention, so a spontaneous analogue is welcome.
questions.explain: When other means fail, imagining an analogous problem is a recommended move, and one that arrives unprompted is welcome as a sign of progress.
questions.rule: When an analogous problem comes up unprompted, treat it as a good sign.
questions.teaches: Analogy is one of the main sources of invention: if other means fail we should try to imagine an analogous problem, and if one emerges spontaneously we naturally feel elated.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If land is near, birds are often seen. Now birds are seen. What can be concluded?
options: Land is near, since birds come from land
Nothing, since birds also live over open sea
Probably land is near, but not for certain
Land is not near, since birds were not seen before
optionExplain: Treating the sign as proof is the fallacy the author warns of.
Birds are more common near shore, so the sight changes the odds.
Right: birds are a sign, not a proof.
The sight of birds does not tell against land.
questions.explain: A sign supports a probable conclusion. The card next gives the book's wording.
questions.rule: Conclude from a sign with 'probably', never with 'certainly'.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: without the word probably, the birds-and-land conclusion would be an outright fallacy.
questions.explain: From 'if land is near we often see birds' and 'we see birds' it does not follow with certainty that land is near.
questions.rule: Add probably.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If a student understands a lesson, she usually answers well. She answered well. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Probably she understands it, though she may have guessed or been given help
She understands it, since good answers need understanding
She does not understand it, since good answers can be copied
No conclusion at all can be drawn
optionExplain: Right: the answer is a sign of understanding and no more.
Good answers can also come from copying or a guess, so treating them as proof of understanding goes beyond what the sign supports.
Possible copying lowers confidence, but does not reverse the sign.
A sign supports a probable conclusion; denying that would discard it.
questions.explain: A good answer is what understanding would produce, so understanding becomes more likely, but guessing or help could also produce it, so probably is the right strength.
questions.rule: Choose the conclusion with the right qualifier.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each conclusion by whether it is an indication only or follows with certainty.

items.t: We see birds, so probably land is near
A square has four equal sides; this is a square, so it has four equal sides
Its sails are wet, so probably it rained
All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal
Sandpipers appeared, so probably we are close to shore

questions.explain: Conclusions from signs are indications. Those that follow from a general rule applied to a case are certain.
questions.rule: Sign gives indication, rule gives certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Suppose the crew had treated every bird sighting as certain proof of land. What would the author expect?
options: They would have reached land sooner
They would have stopped at once and turned back
Nothing, since birds near land are always seen first
They would have been fooled and disappointed, as they were many times
optionExplain: Certainty about signs does not bring land sooner.
Turning back is not what treating a sign as proof leads to.
Birds were seen many times without land.
Right: they saw birds many times and were disappointed; one fallacy leads to repeated frustration.
questions.explain: Taking each bird as proof would have led the crew to expect land again and again, and they were disappointed many times; the signs only made land more likely.
questions.rule: Conclude from a sign with 'probably', never with 'certainly'.
questions.teaches: Columbus and his companions saw birds many times and were disappointed later; only once came the day on which they saw sandpipers followed by the day of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A manager sees sales rise after a new poster and says the poster caused it, for certain. How does the author's reasoning treat this?
options: As proof, since the rise followed the poster and a later event cannot cause an earlier one
As an indication only: the rise makes the poster's effect more credible, not certain
As worthless, since sales vary for many reasons and a single rise can tell us nothing
As proof of the opposite, since a rise that follows a poster shows the poster did harm
optionExplain: The rise coming after the poster fits the pattern, but that gives plausibility only: sales rise for many other reasons too.
Right: the pattern if the poster works then sales rise; they did, so the poster's effect becomes more credible.
Throwing the sign away would be what the author calls a still greater mistake.
Nothing in a rise after a poster points to harm; the sign points toward the poster working, only weakly.
questions.explain: The rise in sales is what an effective poster would produce, so its effect is more credible, yet sales rise for other reasons too, so the conclusion stays an indication.
questions.rule: Conclude from a sign with 'probably', never with 'certainly'.
questions.teaches: Such a conclusion is a reasonable and natural suggestion, but by no means a demonstrative proof: it is only an indication, a heuristic suggestion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A colleague says: either follow every sign you see or ignore signs and rely on proof. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing is wrong with it; one of the two extremes is the safe course for a careful worker
Both extremes fail: following blindly gets you fooled, and ignoring signs stops progress
Only the first is wrong, since signs are worthless and proof is the only thing to rely on
Only the second is wrong, since signs never mislead a person who reads them with care
optionExplain: Neither extreme is safe by the author's account.
Right: the author warns against both.
Ignoring signs is called a greater mistake than trusting them as certain.
Signs can mislead, as the crew's birds did.
questions.explain: Good practice lies between the two. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Use signs as guides, check them, and keep your own judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If you neglect heuristic conclusions altogether, you will make no ____ at all.
questions.explain: The most important signs of progress are heuristic, so neglecting them stops the work.
questions.rule: Neglect signs and you make no progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A hunch says a bug lives in module X. A fix there changes nothing. What follows from follow, but keep your eyes open?
options: Keep changing X until the symptom disappears, since the hunch was a sign and signs are right
Throw away every hunch from now on, since one hunch has now been shown to be wrong
Ask someone else to decide, since your own judgment has now been shown to be unreliable
Check the evidence behind the hunch and keep other places open, rather than dropping or clinging to it
optionExplain: This treats the hunch as certain and keeps tinkering, which is the risk of taking a heuristic conclusion as fixed truth.
That neglects heuristic conclusions altogether.
The book says never renounce your judgment.
Right: the sign guided the first try; the result is new evidence.
questions.explain: The hunch guided the first try; its failure is new evidence, so the sensible course is to check what the hunch rested on while keeping other places open.
questions.rule: Use the hunch, then look at what happens.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which attitudes toward signs match the author?
options: A sign is only a plausible indication, not certainty
A strong enough sign makes the conclusion certain
A sign should be dropped as soon as it is shown to be uncertain
Follow a sign, but keep looking at the evidence
optionExplain: Right: following a sign while still examining the evidence is the author's own advice.
Does not match: a sign never becomes proof.
Does not match: uncertain signs still guide work.
Right: trust but look is the form in which the author gives the advice.
questions.explain: The author keeps signs as guides while denying them the status of proof.
questions.rule: Trust but look.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: According to the author, which is the greater mistake: taking a heuristic conclusion as certain, or disregarding such conclusions entirely?
options: Disregarding them entirely
Taking one as certain
They are equally bad
Neither, since both are harmless
optionExplain: Right: the author calls it a still greater mistake, since without them there is no progress.
Being fooled is a mistake, but the author calls the other greater.
The author ranks them: one is a still greater mistake.
Neither is harmless: being fooled wastes effort, and neglecting signs stops progress, and the author ranks the second as worse.
questions.explain: Ignoring heuristic conclusions entirely is the worse mistake.
questions.rule: Use signs as guides, check them, and keep your own judgment.
questions.teaches: The author calls disregarding heuristic conclusions entirely a still greater mistake than taking them as certain, and says the most important signs of progress are heuristic.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A pilot sees an instrument reading that points to a fuel leak, but no other gauge agrees. What fits the advice?
options: Ignore it, since one gauge in disagreement with all the others is likely to be unreliable
Act at once as if the leak were certain, since a reading that points to danger must be obeyed
Take the reading seriously, check the other gauges, and use her own judgment
Let the gauge decide and stop thinking, since an instrument is more reliable than a pilot
optionExplain: Ignoring is the greater mistake in the author's account.
Acting as if the leak were certain treats a single sign as proof, which risks being fooled by a faulty gauge.
Right: trust the sign enough to look further, and keep judgment.
Handing the decision to the gauge gives up her own judgment, which the author says never to renounce.
questions.explain: One reading is a sign, not proof: take it seriously enough to check the other gauges, and keep using her own judgment. The book puts it as: Trust but look.
questions.rule: Use signs as guides, check them, and keep your own judgment.
questions.teaches: Follow, but keep your eyes open: trust but look, and never renounce your judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Why is bringing one more datum into play felt as progress?
options: Because more data always make a problem easier, so each added datum is a gain
Because a datum once used is a datum removed from the problem, which leaves less to do
Because it shortens the solution, and a shorter solution is the sign of a better one
Solving is finding the connection between the data and the unknown, and every datum should be connected with it
optionExplain: More data do not make a problem easier by themselves.
A datum used remains part of the problem.
The reason is not length of solution.
Right: using all the data is part of finding the connection.
questions.explain: Progress is judged by whether the step is one a solution needs.
questions.rule: Feel progress where a useful step has succeeded: one more datum, one more clause, or an analogue.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Match each sign of progress to the reason the author gives for it.
pairs: One more datum brought into play
To solve a problem is to connect the data with the unknown
One more clause of the condition taken into account
We should use the whole condition
Analogy is one of the main sources of invention
questions.explain: Each sign is justified by the usefulness of the step behind it: data are to be connected with the unknown, the whole condition is to be used, and analogy is a source of invention.
questions.rule: A sign is justified by the usefulness of the step behind it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Planning a trip, you have a budget, a date and a mood. Your tentative plan now includes the budget, which it ignored before. What does that suggest?
options: Nothing at all, since a budget is an outside matter that cannot affect the shape of a plan, however well the plan is otherwise built
A condition that the plan must satisfy has been taken into account, which counts as progress
The plan is now certain to work, because every clause of the condition is covered by it
The plan was wrong from the start and is now useless, because it had ignored a clause
optionExplain: The budget is a clause the plan has to meet.
Right: using one more clause of the condition is a forward step, not a guarantee.
The sign is plausible, not certain.
The plan is improved by a step in the right direction.
questions.explain: The budget is a clause of the condition, so a plan that now respects it has taken one more clause into account, which is a step in the right direction though not a guarantee.
questions.rule: Compare the clauses the plan covers before and after.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each event by whether it is a justified sign of progress.

items.t: A data point not used before is now connected with the unknown
A clause of the condition is now respected by the formula
A simpler related problem comes to mind
You have worked for an hour on the same line
You wrote more pages than yesterday

questions.explain: The justified signs correspond to useful operations on data, condition or related problems. Time spent and pages written do not.
questions.rule: Judge by useful operations, not by effort spent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author says that to each typical mental operation corresponds a certain sign. What follows for the list of questions?
options: The list becomes unnecessary
Only the first questions give signs
The list can be read a second way, as a list of signs of progress
Signs are separate from the list and unrelated to it
optionExplain: The list still tells you what to do.
Each question, once its operation succeeds, gives a sign.
Right: success of a typical operation is felt as progress.
The signs come from the same operations.
questions.explain: Because each typical operation has a sign when it succeeds, the list that tells you what to try can also be read as a list of signs of progress.
questions.rule: Feel progress where a useful step has succeeded: one more datum, one more clause, or an analogue.
questions.teaches: If a typical useful mental operation succeeds, its success is felt as a sign of progress, so the list of questions, appropriately read, also lists signs of progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A coach reviews a student's draft essay and sees that the new outline covers every point of the assignment brief. How does the author's pattern read it?
options: A favorable sign: one more clause of the condition is now taken into account
A guarantee that the essay will earn top marks, since every point of the brief is covered
No sign at all, since only the final text of the essay counts and an outline is not the essay
A sign that the brief is too simple, since an outline can cover all of its points so easily
optionExplain: Right: the brief is the condition, and covering its points is a useful step.
A step in the right direction is not a guarantee.
Signs come before the final result and guide work.
Nothing suggests the brief is simple.
questions.explain: The pattern applies outside mathematics: clause, datum or analogue.
questions.rule: Feel progress where a useful step has succeeded: one more datum, one more clause, or an analogue.
questions.teaches: Taking into account one more clause of the condition is justly felt as progress, as a move in the right direction, because we should use the whole condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You finally find a notation that you can easily remember. Is that progress?
options: Yes: it is a step forward, though not the solution
No, until an equation is written
Yes, because the problem is now solved
No, since notation is only a matter of taste, and the choice of one makes no difference to the work
optionExplain: Right: a notation easy to retain is a sign of progress.
Progress can be made before equations appear.
Progress is not the same as solution.
A good notation is useful, according to the author.
questions.explain: Typical operations are signs. The card next lists more.
questions.rule: When a typical useful operation succeeds, treat it as a sign of progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which of these events does the author count as signs of progress?
options: Finishing the problem sheet quickly
Disposing the data so that any one is easy to recall
Visualizing the condition as a whole
Understanding what the unknown is
optionExplain: Not counted: speed through other work is not a sign for this problem.
This is on the list: orderly data that can be recalled easily is one of the steps the author counts as progress.
Counted: it may mean an essential advance.
This is on the list: seeing the condition as a whole may mean an essential advance, the author says.
questions.explain: The first three are operations from the book's list; speed on other work is not.
questions.rule: Signs are tied to operations on the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Stuck on a puzzle, you recall a puzzle solved last month that has the same unknown. How should you read that?
options: As a waste of time, since each puzzle is new and an old solution cannot help with a new one
As a proof that the same method works, since the unknown is the same in both of the puzzles
As a possible decisive move: recalling a related solved problem is a sign of progress
As a sign only if the two puzzles are of equal difficulty, since otherwise nothing carries over
optionExplain: Related problems are one of the main resources.
A related solved problem is a lead; it does not prove that the same method will work on the new puzzle.
Right: the author says recalling a related problem solved before may be a decisive move.
Difficulty need not match; relation to the unknown matters.
questions.explain: Recalling a related problem solved before may be a decisive move; it gives a lead to try, not a proof that the old method works here.
questions.rule: Ask what the old solution shares with the new problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the author counts separating the condition into appropriate parts as possibly an important step forward.
questions.explain: Separating the condition into parts is on his list of operations whose success is felt as a sign of progress.
questions.rule: Separating the condition is a step forward.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author describe the questions and suggestions of the list, and the signs connected with them?
options: Technical and needing special training, since reading signs is a skill taught in advanced courses
Simple, obvious, plain common sense; no occult science is needed to read the signs
Hard to learn but rewarding, since the list demands long study before any of it can be used
Reserved for the exceptionally talented, since only they can read the signs of progress at all
optionExplain: The author says the opposite: no special training is needed, only a little common sense and some experience.
Right: the author says a little common sense and a little experience are all that is needed.
He calls the signs simple and obvious, so they are not hard to learn, though experience improves the reading.
Talent helps, but ordinary reading needs common sense.
questions.explain: The author calls the questions of the list and the signs connected with them simple, obvious common sense; reading them takes a little common sense and experience, no occult science.
questions.rule: When a typical useful operation succeeds, treat it as a sign of progress.
questions.teaches: The questions of the list and the signs of progress connected with them are simple, obvious, plain common sense; reading such signs takes no occult science, only a little common sense and a little experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A teacher says a student's careful list of what is given and what is wanted shows no progress, since nothing is solved. How would the author respond?
options: The teacher is right, since only the final results count and nothing is solved yet
It is progress only after the answer is found, since progress can be judged only afterwards
It is progress only for the exceptionally talented, since ordinary students cannot read such signs
It is progress: understanding the unknown and disposing the data are signs
optionExplain: Results are not the only progress.
The author counts the steps as signs while the work goes on, so they are felt before the answer is found.
Common sense is enough to read these signs.
Right: clear understanding of the unknown and orderly data are listed signs.
questions.explain: Understanding the unknown and disposing the data in order are listed signs of progress, so the teacher is wrong to say nothing has been achieved before the answer.
questions.rule: When a typical useful operation succeeds, treat it as a sign of progress.
questions.teaches: Understanding the nature of the unknown means progress, and disposing the data so that we can easily recall any one also means progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: While working, you feel a plan is well-balanced although you cannot say why. What is it?
options: Noise, to be ignored until you have a reason
A guarantee that the plan works
A real but vague sign of progress, to be followed with care
A proof the plan has no defects
optionExplain: The author says the feeling frequently leads in the right direction.
A strong sense that a plan is balanced does not guarantee success; the author treats it as an indication to follow with care.
Right: the author says behind vague words there is a feeling we follow with confidence.
A feeling cannot prove a plan free of defects; the author asks only that we follow such feelings while staying alert.
questions.explain: The card next treats such feelings.
questions.rule: Notice the pace of progress and the mood of the situation as signs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: When progress is rapid we are elated; when it is slow we are ____.
questions.explain: We feel keenly the pace of progress even when we cannot name a distinct sign.
questions.rule: We feel the pace of progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A writer says of her draft: It is not so good; something is lacking and spoils the harmony. How should this be read?
options: As a vague sign of slow progress, worth following up by looking for what is lacking
As meaningless noise, since she cannot say what is lacking and gives no reason for it
As proof that the draft is bad, since a feeling of something lacking is a firm verdict
As a sign that the draft is finished, since a sense of harmony only comes at the end
optionExplain: Right: such nuanced phrases express a feeling that usually points in the right direction.
The author treats such feelings as real indications.
A feeling is an indication, not proof.
Lacking harmony points the other way.
questions.explain: The remark that something is lacking and spoils the harmony expresses a real feeling about slow progress, which suggests looking for what is lacking.
questions.rule: Ask what could be missing.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the author says feelings of progress are less trustworthy than explicit signs and so should be set aside.
questions.explain: He says we follow the feeling with confidence and that it leads frequently in the right direction; he asks only that we treat it like other signs.
questions.rule: Treat feelings as signs, not as proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What does the bracketed passage suggest about the nature of the guiding feelings?
options: They are random moods with no cause, which come and go whatever the state of the work
They are the same as the explicit operations of the list, only described in vaguer words
They are produced by the problem's difficulty, so a harder problem produces stronger feelings, with no activity other than the problem behind them
They may be connected with obscure mental activities that are more psychological and less logical
optionExplain: He thinks they have a basis, though not a logical one.
The explicit signs are tied to definite operations; the feelings to more obscure ones.
He does not tie them to difficulty.
Right: the author suspects they relate to other, more obscure mental activities.
questions.explain: Explicit signs are tied to definite mental operations, so the author suspects that guiding feelings are tied to other, more obscure and more psychological activities.
questions.rule: Notice the pace of progress and the mood of the situation as signs.
questions.teaches: Since the explicit signs are connected with the success or failure of definite mental operations, the guiding feelings may be similarly connected with other, more obscure, more psychological and less logical, mental activities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A runner feels the pace of training is right this week, but cannot say why. How does the author's approach treat this?
options: As worthless, since it has no numbers behind it and nothing in it can be written down
As a vague but real indication to be followed with some care
As proof that the training plan is perfect, since a right feeling cannot lead one astray
As relevant only to mathematicians, since signs of progress belong to problem solving alone
optionExplain: The author says such feelings are unmistakable and often lead right.
Right: the pace of progress is felt even when no distinct sign can be pointed out.
A good feeling about the pace of training does not prove the plan perfect; it is an indication, to be checked against results.
The author speaks of anyone working intently.
questions.explain: Even when no distinct sign can be pointed out, a worker keenly feels the pace of progress; such a feeling is a vague but real indication, to be followed with care.
questions.rule: Notice the pace of progress and the mood of the situation as signs.
questions.teaches: When we work intently we feel keenly the pace of our progress, and such differences can be felt quite clearly without being able to point out any distinct sign.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A very strong feeling suddenly tells you the solution is found. What do you do?
options: Trust it fully, since strong feelings are rarely wrong
Follow it, while checking it with a grain of doubt
Distrust it completely, since it has no reason behind it
Wait a week before looking at it again
optionExplain: The author notes people are sometimes fooled by their inspirations.
Right: inspiration is a sign like others.
Rejecting it would waste a real sign.
Waiting a week does not examine the idea; a test of the inspiration is what the advice asks for.
questions.explain: Inspiration is a sign. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: Follow inspiration, and keep a grain of doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: People usually cannot doubt their inspirations and are sometimes ____ by them.
questions.explain: A strong sudden feeling is hard to doubt and so can mislead.
questions.rule: Inspirations can fool.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Waking up sure that you have the key to a stuck proof, what is the best next step?
options: Submit it at once; the feeling is proof enough
Forget it, since feelings are unreliable
Wait for another inspiration to confirm it
Write the proof out and test it, treating the certainty as a lead
optionExplain: Strong feelings do sometimes fool, which is why the author adds a grain of doubt and a check.
Discarding the feeling is the greater mistake.
Another feeling would not test anything.
Right: follow the inspiration and keep your eyes open.
questions.explain: Waking with strong certainty is an inspiration; follow it by writing the proof out and testing it, since people are sometimes fooled by their inspirations.
questions.rule: Follow inspiration, and keep a grain of doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each reaction to a sudden strong feeling by whether it follows the author's advice.

items.t: Follow the feeling, but with a grain of doubt
Test the idea it suggests before relying on it
Treat it as certain because it is so strong
Dismiss it because it came without a reason

questions.explain: The advice is to follow and test. Dismissing and over-trusting both break it.
questions.rule: Trust, but keep your eyes open.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the author's picture, how did past ages regard a sudden good idea, and what is it worth by his account?
options: As a gift of the gods, which must be deserved by work or at least by a fervent wish
As a chance event with no connection to effort, which comes or does not come by luck
As a sign of exceptional talent only, which ordinary workers could never expect to meet
As the final proof of the idea, since a sudden good idea needs no further checking
optionExplain: Right: the passage on subconscious work says the gift must be deserved.
The author ties the idea to work or wish.
He does not tie it to talent alone.
A sudden good idea may be wrong, so it is not final proof; the author says only that it must be deserved by work or wish.
questions.explain: Past ages saw a sudden good idea as a gift of the gods, one that must be deserved by work or at least by a fervent wish.
questions.rule: Follow inspiration, and keep a grain of doubt.
questions.teaches: Past ages regarded a sudden good idea as an inspiration, a gift of the gods, and the author says you must deserve such a gift by work, or at least by a fervent wish.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A salesperson feels certain that a particular client will sign. How does the advice read?
options: Skip the check on the client and go ahead, since the feeling of certainty is so strong
Ignore the feeling, since feelings have no place in sales and only figures should count
Follow the feeling in planning the next step, and keep checking the client's actual signals
Cancel the meeting to avoid a disappointment, since the feeling may well be a false one, since a client who seems sure may still not sign
optionExplain: People are sometimes fooled by their inspirations.
The author treats feelings as signs worth following.
Right: always follow your inspiration, with a grain of doubt.
Nothing in the advice says to withdraw.
questions.explain: The salesperson should use the feeling to plan the next step while checking the client's actual signals, which is following inspiration with a grain of doubt.
questions.rule: Follow inspiration, and keep a grain of doubt.
questions.teaches: Always follow your inspiration, with a grain of doubt: treat guiding feelings and inspirations just as we treat the more explicitly expressible signs of progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You have a plan whose first steps are clear but whose later steps are not. How should you proceed?
options: Do all the planned steps at once to finish quickly, trusting the plan from start to end
Wait until the whole road is clear before starting, so that no effort is ever wasted
Start, and never change course whatever happens, since a plan is only worth its being kept
Start cautiously and watch for signs, going on faster as they multiply
optionExplain: Doing everything at once risks effort on a plan that may not work.
Waiting delays the work, and the road becomes clearer only by going on.
The point of watching signs is to be able to change course.
Right: signs let you adjust boldness to evidence.
questions.explain: Signs set the pace. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Let the frequency of signs set how boldly you proceed along a plan.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Put these stages of following a plan in the order the author describes.
items: Start out cautiously in the direction the plan indicates
Keep a lookout for signs of progress
If signs are rare, become more hesitant
If signs multiply, move on with increasing confidence
questions.explain: The author starts cautiously, looks for signs, and lets their frequency set confidence: hesitation when rare, confidence when they multiply.
questions.rule: Start, look, adjust.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You follow a study plan for a new subject. After two weeks no sign of progress appears: tests are no better and the material is not clearer. What does the advice suggest?
options: Continue unchanged, since signs are only a distraction and the plan itself is what counts
Grow more hesitant, and if the lack of signs continues, consider turning back to try another approach
Conclude that the subject is beyond you, since no sign of progress means no ability at all
Double the hours without changing the method, since the lack of signs shows too little effort, and then see whether signs appear
optionExplain: The advice is to watch the signs and adjust.
Right: lack of signs for a long time is a reason to try another road.
A missing sign is not proof of inability.
More of the same ignores the warning.
questions.explain: A long absence of signs is a warning of a blind alley; the sensible response is growing hesitation and, if it persists, trying another road.
questions.rule: Ask what the absence of signs warns of.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: as signs along a road multiply, the worker's hesitation fades and he moves on with increasing confidence.
questions.explain: This is how Columbus and his companions moved before sighting San Salvador; frequent signs raise confidence, rare ones raise hesitation.
questions.rule: Frequent signs, growing confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Besides raising confidence, what two services does the author say signs perform?
options: They give the final answer and show how to check it once the answer is found
They remove the need for a plan and for experience, since they say what to do next
Their absence may warn of a blind alley, and their presence may concentrate effort on the right spot
They reveal who else has solved the problem and when they did it, to save repeating work
optionExplain: Signs do not give the answer itself.
A plan and experience are still needed.
Right: signs save time by warning of dead ends and focusing effort.
Signs say nothing about other solvers.
questions.explain: Signs perform two services: their absence may warn of a blind alley and save useless exertion, and their presence may make us concentrate effort on the right spot.
questions.rule: Let the frequency of signs set how boldly you proceed along a plan.
questions.teaches: The absence of signs may warn us of a blind alley and save us time and useless exertion; their presence may cause us to concentrate our effort upon the right spot.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A startup tests a product idea with ten customers. Two of them ask when it will launch; none buys. How would the author read the signs?
options: Cautiously: some signs exist, so continue carefully and watch whether more appear
As proof that the idea is wrong, since none of the ten customers bought the product
As proof that the idea is right, since two of the customers asked when it would launch
As no information at all, since ten customers are too few to tell anything of the market
optionExplain: Right: rare or indistinct signs mean hesitation, not abandonment, and not full confidence.
A few weak signs do not prove failure.
Two customers asking about the launch are a weak sign of success, which calls for caution rather than certainty.
Some signs exist, even weak ones, so the result gives some information; it is just not strong.
questions.explain: Two interested customers and no sale are rare, indistinct signs, which call for hesitation and a watch for more signs, not for stopping and not for full confidence.
questions.rule: Let the frequency of signs set how boldly you proceed along a plan.
questions.teaches: If the signs are rare or indistinct, I become more hesitant, and if for a long time they fail to appear altogether, I may lose courage, turn back, and try another road.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A sign led you to abandon a path, and someone else, following it farther, made a discovery. What does that show?
options: Signs can mislead in a single case, though they guide right in most
Signs are useless and should be ignored
Anyone who follows a path to the end will succeed
The other person was only lucky
optionExplain: Right: this was the author's experience, and he still advises using signs.
One failure does not make signs useless.
Following farther sometimes works, but not for everyone.
The other man also read a sign the author had failed to notice.
questions.explain: A sign can deceive once. The card next gives the author's story.
questions.rule: Accept that signs may fail in one case while guiding right on the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Signs may misguide us in any single case, but they guide us right in the ____ of them.
questions.explain: A hunter who misreads sometimes is still right on average, or he could not make a living by hunting.
questions.rule: Right on the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A founder gave up on a niche market because early surveys showed little interest. A competitor stayed and later did well. What does the author's story suggest?
options: Early surveys are worthless and should never be used to decide what to do about a market
The competitor must have had better surveys, since only better evidence could lead to success
The absence of signs misled the founder this time, though such signs usually guide right
The founder should have ignored every sign, since a sign cannot tell anything about a market
optionExplain: One failure does not make signs worthless.
The competitor may have read a sign the founder missed, as in the author's story.
Right: like the author, the founder abandoned a path for lack of signs and was wrong.
Ignoring all signs is the greater mistake.
questions.explain: The founder, like the author, gave up for lack of signs and was wrong this time; this shows signs can mislead in a single case, yet they guide right in most cases.
questions.rule: Remember signs guide right in most cases.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which two kinds of failure of signs does the author describe?
options: Finding that signs are right every time for experts
Seeing no signs on a road that later turns out to be easy
Following a road cheered by favorable signs into an insurmountable obstacle
Giving up a path because signs were absent, though someone else later succeeded on it
optionExplain: Not described: even experts are right on average, not every time.
Not described as such; the author describes giving up and a later discovery.
Described: favorable signs can also mislead.
Described: the author recalls his regret at leaving a path that another man later followed to a discovery.
questions.explain: The author names the false negative (abandoning a good path) and the false positive (an unsuspected obstacle).
questions.rule: Signs can fail both ways.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the author's account, what did the man who came after him on the abandoned path have?
options: A better theory of the problem, which explained why the path was worth following
More perseverance, and he read correctly a sign the author had failed to notice
Help from an expert, who told him what lay a little farther along the path
Nothing but luck, since the path would have led to the discovery for anyone who walked it
optionExplain: The account credits perseverance and the reading of a sign, not a theory of the problem.
Right: the author says he not only had more perseverance but also read a sign correctly.
The account names no expert helper; the man succeeded through his own perseverance and his reading of a sign.
The author attributes it to perseverance and a sign read correctly.
questions.explain: The man who went on had more perseverance and read correctly a sign the author had missed, so both persistence and sign-reading mattered.
questions.rule: Accept that signs may fail in one case while guiding right on the whole.
questions.teaches: The man who followed the path a little farther not only had more perseverance than the author but also read correctly a certain sign which the author had failed to notice.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A scientist drops a research line when early experiments show no sign of an effect. Which lesson from the hunter fits?
options: Signs are never wrong, so the drop is certain to be right and need not be reconsidered
A hunter can ignore traces, so the scientist can ignore experiments that show no effect
Drops are always mistakes, so the research line should be kept whatever the first results, and no early result should be allowed to change that
Signs are right on average, so the drop is reasonable, but it may be wrong in this single case
optionExplain: The author says signs may misguide in a single case.
The hunter reads traces; he does not ignore them.
The author says signs are right on average, so drops are often fine.
Right: the hunter must be right on average to make a living, yet may misread traces now and then.
questions.explain: Like the hunter, the scientist relies on signs that are right on average, so the drop is reasonable, though it may be wrong in this single case.
questions.rule: Accept that signs may fail in one case while guiding right on the whole.
questions.teaches: A hunter may misinterpret the traces of his game now and then but he must be right on the average, otherwise he could not make a living by hunting.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What is the main advantage of an expert over a beginner in reading signs of progress?
options: She never misreads a sign
She needs fewer signs because she works faster
She knows more signs, and knows them better
She ignores signs and relies on rules
optionExplain: Experts are right on average, not always.
The passage speaks of knowing signs, not of working faster; speed is not named as the expert's advantage.
Right: the author says that may be her main advantage.
Experts read signs; they do not ignore them.
questions.explain: Experience gives knowledge of signs. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Practice on many problems until you recognise what nearing a solution looks like.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: It takes ____ to interpret the signs correctly.
questions.explain: Columbus's seasoned companions could read the sea near shore, and the expert knows how a nearing solution looks and feels.
questions.rule: Signs are read with experience.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two debuggers see the same odd log pattern. One recognises it from past incidents as typical of a cache fault; the other sees nothing special. How does the author explain the difference?
options: The first has experience of how such situations look and so reads the sign
The first has a lucky guess
The second has lower talent in all things
The pattern is a sign only to experts, so it is not a real sign
optionExplain: Right: like the hunter who sees how fresh a trace is, she knows the sign.
Her reading rests on known signs, not luck.
The author separates experience from extraordinary sensibility.
A sign is real; the beginner fails to see it.
questions.explain: The expert who has seen similar situations before knows which patterns are signs and reads them, where the beginner sees nothing in the same data.
questions.rule: Ask who knows the signs better.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, the expert's main advantage may be knowing more signs and knowing them better than the inexperienced.
questions.explain: He writes that the expert knows more signs than the inexperienced and knows them better; his main advantage may consist in such knowledge.
questions.rule: Experts know more signs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What further advantage does the author attribute to the exceptionally talented?
options: A larger memory for formulas, so that more of the facts of a subject are ready to hand
A tendency to ignore signs and rely on proof, since proof is more certain than any sign, which is the habit of a careful mind
Immunity to deceptive signs, so that a gifted solver is never misled in a single case
A sort of extraordinary mental sensibility that feels subtle signs or notices their absence
optionExplain: The passage does not mention memory.
They read signs, with more sensibility.
The passage does not call the talented immune to deceptive signs; all signs can mislead in a single case.
Right: they detect differences that the less talented cannot perceive.
questions.explain: Beyond experience, the exceptionally talented may have an extraordinary mental sensibility, feeling subtle signs of progress or noticing their absence.
questions.rule: Practice on many problems until you recognise what nearing a solution looks like.
questions.teaches: The main advantage of the exceptionally talented may consist in a sort of extraordinary mental sensibility, feeling subtle signs of progress or noticing their absence where the less talented cannot perceive a difference.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A sommelier tastes a wine and says it is a year or two from its peak. A novice tastes only wine. Which line of the passage matches this?
options: Columbus's crew saw birds many times and were disappointed when no land followed
The expert hunter notices traces of game and even their freshness where the inexperienced one sees nothing
The author rested overnight and then found the solution to the problem that had stopped him
Signs may misguide in a single case but they are right on average over many cases
optionExplain: That line is about repeated disappointment, not about expert reading.
Right: the expert appraises fine features of signs that the beginner misses.
That line is about subconscious work, not expertise.
That line is about reliability, not experience.
questions.explain: Like the expert hunter who tells even how fresh a trace is, the sommelier appraises fine features of a sign that a novice cannot perceive.
questions.rule: Practice on many problems until you recognise what nearing a solution looks like.
questions.teaches: An expert hunter notices traces of game and appraises even their freshness or staleness where the inexperienced one is unable to see anything.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If a pipe leaks, the water bill rises. The bill has risen. Which conclusion fits best?
options: There is a leak
A leak has become more credible
There is no leak, since many things raise a bill
A leak has become less credible
optionExplain: Other causes can raise a bill; the conclusion is not certain.
Right: the rise is what a leak would produce, so the leak gains credibility.
The sign pushes toward a leak, not away from it.
A bill that rose supports the leak, never undermines it.
questions.explain: A sign raises credibility. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: From if A then B and B true, conclude that A is more credible, not that A is true.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The pattern: if A then B; B is true; therefore A becomes more ____.
questions.explain: Written out, the conclusion says that A becomes more credible; it expresses a change in confidence, not a proof that A is true.
questions.rule: A becomes more credible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If the cake is done, a skewer comes out clean. The skewer comes out clean. What do we conclude?
options: The cake is done, since a clean skewer is what a done cake always gives and nothing else
The cake being done is less credible, since a clean skewer can also come from other causes
Nothing can be said about the cake, since a clean skewer proves neither done nor not done
The cake being done is more credible, though not certain
optionExplain: That is the fallacy of treating the sign as proof.
The reverse direction is not licensed.
The syllogism says something: credibility rises.
Right: this is the heuristic syllogism with A as done and B as clean skewer.
questions.explain: With A as the cake being done and B as the clean skewer, B true makes A more credible, but other causes of a clean skewer keep it from being certain.
questions.rule: Identify A and B.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each line by its role in the pattern if A then B; B true; A more credible.

items.t: If we are approaching land, we often see birds
Now we see birds
It becomes more credible that we are approaching land
If the cake is done, the skewer is clean
A cake being done becomes more credible

questions.explain: The first two lines give the premises, and the line under them the conclusion.
questions.rule: Two premises above, one conclusion under the line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the schematic If A then B / B true / A more credible, what does the horizontal line stand for?
options: The word therefore, expressing the implication that links premises to conclusion
The word because, linking the conclusion to a cause that explains the premises above it
A division between true and false statements, with the true ones above and the false below
A break between the two premises, marking where one premise ends and the other begins
optionExplain: Right: the line expresses the implication between premises and conclusion.
The line sits under the premises and marks therefore, not a cause.
It does not divide truth from falsity.
It separates premises from conclusion.
questions.explain: In the schematic form the line under the premises stands for therefore and expresses the implication that links the premises to the conclusion.
questions.rule: From if A then B and B true, conclude that A is more credible, not that A is true.
questions.teaches: In the schematic statement the horizontal line stands for the word therefore and expresses the implication, the essential link between the premises and the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If an employee is thriving, she volunteers for new tasks. She volunteered for a task. What can the manager say?
options: She is certainly thriving, since a thriving employee is the only kind that volunteers
She is probably not thriving, since volunteering is often a sign of someone who is over-eager
It is more credible that she is thriving, but she may volunteer for other reasons
Volunteering tells the manager nothing, since employees volunteer for all kinds of reasons
optionExplain: Volunteering is a sign of thriving, not a certain proof, since people volunteer for other reasons too.
The sign points toward thriving, not away from it; volunteering raises the credibility of the claim.
Right: the pattern gives direction but not certainty.
Volunteering is a sign, and a sign does shift credibility, even though it does not settle the matter.
questions.explain: Volunteering is what thriving would produce, so thriving becomes more credible; she may volunteer for other reasons, so it is not certain.
questions.rule: From if A then B and B true, conclude that A is more credible, not that A is true.
questions.teaches: The two statements above the horizontal line are called the premises, the statement under the line the conclusion, and the whole pattern a heuristic syllogism.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: During a long voyage, crew members' confidence about finding land rises and falls. What causes the shifts?
options: Orders from the captain about what to believe, which the crew followed whatever they saw
The calendar, since land is nearer as the days pass and the crew counted them one by one
Random mood unrelated to what they see, which carried hope up and down at no particular cause
Incidents, major or minor, that they relate to the question: are we approaching land?
optionExplain: The account ties beliefs to events, not orders.
Days passing do not tell by themselves.
Moods follow incidents they relate to the question.
Right: each incident changes confidence, differently for each person.
questions.explain: Signs move confidence. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Treat a sign as a reason to move your confidence, not as a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the improved wording of the heuristic conclusion stresses a change in the level of confidence.
questions.explain: More credible expresses a ground for a change in confidence, which is the essential role of this kind of reasoning.
questions.rule: Signs change confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two investors read the same encouraging report on a firm. One raises her confidence a lot, the other a little. Is either wrong?
options: Yes: only one correct amount of confidence exists, and the other investor has misjudged it
Not necessarily: the report gives a reason to raise confidence, and the amount depends on each person
Yes: both are wrong, since a report cannot give a reason to change anyone's confidence
Yes: the one who changed less is ignoring the report and should follow the other investor
optionExplain: The premises fix direction, not amount.
Right: the author says people's beliefs fluctuate differently according to background and character.
The report gives a reasonable ground for change.
A smaller change is still a change.
questions.explain: The report gives both investors a reason to raise confidence, so they agree on direction; how far to raise it depends on background and unstated reasons, so a difference in amount is not an error.
questions.rule: Ask what the sign fixes and what it leaves open.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Suppose the crew had no belief at all that land lay westward. What would the author expect?
options: They would have sailed faster, since a crew without belief in land would not have waited
They would have been more confident in every sign, since they had nothing to lose by hoping
They would not have started the voyage, since they gave the conjecture some credence
They would have seen more birds, since birds come to a ship when its crew is not watching
optionExplain: Nothing links speed to belief here.
Without a conjecture there is nothing for signs to support.
Right: the passage says they must have given some credence to the conjecture, or they would not have started.
Birds near the ship do not depend on what the crew believes; belief governs the start of the voyage and the reading of signs.
questions.explain: Confidence needs something to move: the crew gave the conjecture some credence at the start, or they would not have set out.
questions.rule: Treat a sign as a reason to move your confidence, not as a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The whole dramatic tension of the voyage was due to the fluctuations of ____.
questions.explain: The crew's confidence rose and fell as events occurred or failed to occur, and that fluctuation is what made the voyage dramatic.
questions.rule: Signs move confidence.
questions.teaches: The whole dramatic tension of the voyage is due to the fluctuations of confidence as events occurred or failed to occur.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A scientist has a conjecture and each new experiment either supports or fails to support it. What does the author's picture say her confidence does?
options: Rises and falls with the results, according to each event's bearing on the conjecture
Stays fixed until a proof arrives, since only a proof can justify any change in confidence
Rises with every experiment whatever the result, since each experiment adds to what she knows
Is set by the majority view of her field, so she should hold the confidence others hold
optionExplain: Right: this is the pattern the author found in the voyage.
Confidence in a conjecture moves with evidence.
Results that do not support the conjecture lower confidence.
The author speaks of each person's own fluctuating belief.
questions.explain: As with the crew, each result bears on the dominating question: does the conjecture hold? Her confidence rises and falls with the events accordingly.
questions.rule: Treat a sign as a reason to move your confidence, not as a verdict.
questions.teaches: Columbus and his men related every incident, major or minor, to their dominating question: Are we approaching land? Their confidence rose and fell as events occurred or failed to occur.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What do circumstantial evidence, inductive evidence and an inventor's signs have in common?
options: None gives strict certainty, yet each helps in gaining new knowledge
Each proves its conclusion beyond doubt, which is why such evidence is accepted in courts
Each is used only in law, because circumstantial evidence is a legal term and not a general one
Each is useless outside mathematics, because other fields need a proof before they can act
optionExplain: Right: these are two essential points of plausible reasoning.
They lack the certainty of strict demonstration.
Such evidence appears in law, science, everyday affairs and invention, so it is not limited to one field.
The author says the opposite: they are indispensable outside pure mathematics and logic.
questions.explain: Evidence of this kind is uncertain but useful. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Treat heuristic, inductive and circumstantial evidence as plausible reasoning: uncertain but needed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author names the reasoning behind such evidence, for lack of a better term, ____ reasoning.
questions.explain: He considers heuristic, inductive and plausible and accepts plausible, to avoid stretching existing terms.
questions.rule: Plausible reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A detective builds a case from fibres, a timeline and a motive, with no confession. Which description fits?
options: Demonstration, since there are three kinds of evidence and they all point to the same person
Worthless, since there is no confession and no confession means no case can be built at all
Plausible reasoning: no strict demonstration, but it can still yield new knowledge
A mathematical proof, since the pieces fit together without a gap into one complete picture
optionExplain: Several kinds of evidence still do not make a strict demonstration.
Such evidence is useful and sometimes indispensable.
Right: circumstantial evidence is one of the author's examples.
A proof in mathematics is demonstrative.
questions.explain: Circumstantial evidence is one of the author's examples of plausible reasoning: it lacks strict certainty yet can still add new knowledge.
questions.rule: Ask whether the conclusion follows with certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which two points do all kinds of plausible evidence share, according to the author?
options: They are replaced by demonstration once a problem is understood
They are useful in acquiring essentially new knowledge
They are valid only in the physical sciences
They lack the certainty of strict demonstration
optionExplain: Not so: they are indispensable for knowledge about the physical world.
Right: usefulness in acquiring essentially new knowledge is the second point the author names.
Not so: the author includes everyday affairs and law.
Right: lacking the certainty of strict demonstration is the first point the author names.
questions.explain: The two points are no certainty and usefulness for new knowledge.
questions.rule: No certainty, but useful for new knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: For what kind of knowledge does the author call this reasoning indispensable?
options: Only knowledge of the history of science, where evidence of this kind is the only kind there is
Any knowledge not purely mathematical or logical, any knowledge concerned with the physical world
Only knowledge that can be proved in a few lines, since longer arguments can no longer be trusted
Only knowledge concerning future events, since only the future is open to plausible guesses
optionExplain: No restriction to history is made.
Right: outside pure mathematics and logic, plausible reasoning is indispensable.
Proof in a few lines is demonstration.
The sentence covers knowledge of the physical world generally.
questions.explain: The author says this evidence is indispensable for any knowledge that is not purely mathematical or logical, in particular knowledge of the physical world.
questions.rule: Treat heuristic, inductive and circumstantial evidence as plausible reasoning: uncertain but needed.
questions.teaches: Such evidence is indispensable to any not purely mathematical or logical knowledge, to any knowledge concerned with the physical world.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A statistician says a drug works because trials show benefits for most patients. Where does this fit in the author's picture?
options: It is demonstration, since numbers are exact and an exact number cannot give a doubtful result
It is outside the author's list of evidence, which names only signs, law and the inductive sciences
It is useful only in mathematics, where the numbers are, and nowhere in the physical world
Statistical evidence is plausible reasoning: not strictly certain, but useful for new knowledge
optionExplain: Numbers do not make the inference a strict demonstration.
He names statistical evidence invoked in many and diverse subjects.
He says it is useful beyond mathematics.
Right: the author lists statistical evidence among his kinds.
questions.explain: Statistical evidence is on the author's list: it is not a strict demonstration, but it is useful in acquiring essentially new knowledge.
questions.rule: Treat heuristic, inductive and circumstantial evidence as plausible reasoning: uncertain but needed.
questions.teaches: Statistical evidence invoked in many and diverse subjects belongs, with the inventor's signs, the lawyer's circumstantial evidence and the scientist's inductive evidence, among the kinds of plausible reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If it rained, the street is wet. The street is dry. What follows?
options: It probably did not rain
It rained, since streets dry quickly
It did not rain, with certainty
Nothing follows
optionExplain: The conclusion is certain, not just probable.
Rain would make a street wet, so a dry street argues against rain; the idea that it rained reverses the reasoning.
Right: this is the demonstrative pattern.
A wet street is what rain would cause, so a dry street rules it out.
questions.explain: Dry street gives a certain conclusion. The card next sets it beside its heuristic twin.
questions.rule: From if A then B, B false gives A false; B true gives only A more credible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each conclusion by whether it is demonstrative or heuristic.

items.t: A is false (from if A then B, and B false)
A is more credible (from if A then B, and B true)
It did not rain (street is dry)
Rain is more credible (street is wet)

questions.explain: B false gives A false with full support; B true gives only a push toward A.
questions.rule: False B kills A; true B only helps A.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If the shop is open, its lights are on. You see the lights off. What can you conclude, and with what strength?
options: The shop is not open, with certainty
The shop is probably not open
The shop is not open, but only more credibly so
Nothing, since lights can be off for other reasons
optionExplain: Right: if the shop were open the lights would be on; they are not, so it is not open.
The conclusion is certain, not probable.
That strength belongs to the heuristic pattern.
The premise says if open then lights on.
questions.explain: If the shop were open the lights would be on, and they are off, so the shop is not open; a false B gives A false with full support.
questions.rule: Look at whether B is true or false.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What is the difference in logical nature between conclusions A false and A more credible?
options: A false is vague and weakly supported, while A more credible is sharp and fully expressed
There is no difference in logical nature, only in how strongly the conclusion is worded
A more credible is fully supported by the premises, as A false is fully supported
A false is of the same nature as the premises and fully supported; A more credible is vaguer and less fully expressed
optionExplain: The reverse is true: the demonstrative conclusion is sharp and fully supported, the heuristic one is vaguer.
They are on different logical levels.
The premises support the direction only.
Right: the heuristic conclusion differs in kind from the premises.
questions.explain: A false is of the same logical nature as the premises and fully supported by them, while A more credible is vaguer, less sharp and not fully supported.
questions.rule: From if A then B, B false gives A false; B true gives only A more credible.
questions.hint: Which conclusion could two people not dispute?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The statements B false and B true are exactly opposite but of similar ____ nature, on the same level.
