questions.explain: The two second premises are on the same logical level; the great difference arises only in the conclusions.
questions.rule: Premises alike in kind, conclusions unlike.
questions.teaches: The statements B false and B true are exactly opposite to each other but of similar logical nature, on the same logical level; the great difference arises in the conclusions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A test for a fault: if the part is faulty, the light blinks. The light blinked. Which reading follows the book?
options: The part is faulty with certainty, since a blink is what a faulty part produces
A fault is more credible, but the blink could have another cause
The part is certainly not faulty, since a blink is a sign that the fault was found and fixed
A blink means the part cannot be faulty, because a faulty part would not respond at all
optionExplain: That treats the heuristic pattern as a demonstration.
Right: B true gives only a heuristic conclusion.
A blink does not rule out the fault.
A blink is what a faulty part produces, so it points toward the fault; it does not rule the fault out.
questions.explain: The blink is B true, so by the heuristic pattern a fault is more credible, but another cause for the blink is possible.
questions.rule: From if A then B, B false gives A false; B true gives only A more credible.
questions.teaches: The demonstrative pattern is called the modus tollens of the hypothetical syllogism; the heuristic pattern shares its first premise, if A then B, but differs in the second premise and the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two reasonable people accept the premises of a heuristic syllogism. On what can they differ?
options: Whether the conclusion became more or less credible
How much more credible the conclusion becomes
Whether the premises mean anything
Nothing, since the premises settle everything
optionExplain: For any reasonable person the direction is fixed: more credible.
Right: the premises fix the direction only.
Premises are accepted by hypothesis.
That holds for demonstration, not for heuristic reasoning.
questions.explain: The amount is not fixed. The card next gives the author's image.
questions.rule: Agree on direction from the premises; do not expect agreement on the amount.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author compares a heuristic conclusion to a ____, which has direction and magnitude.
questions.explain: The conclusion pushes us in a direction with a certain strength.
questions.rule: Direction and magnitude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two doctors accept that a symptom is more common with a disease and that the patient has it. One is slightly more convinced, the other strongly. Who is unreasonable?
options: The more convinced doctor, since the premises fix the amount and she has gone beyond it
The less convinced doctor, since the premises fix the amount and he has fallen short of it
Both of them, since signs of this kind cannot change a physician's belief in any amount
Neither necessarily: they agree on direction and may differ in amount for unstated reasons
optionExplain: The premises do not fix the amount.
The same reasoning applies in reverse: the premises leave the amount open, so the less convinced doctor is not unreasonable either.
Signs do change belief; the author says they make the conclusion more credible, only the amount is left open.
Right: magnitude is not implied by the premises.
questions.explain: The doctors share the direction, since the symptom makes the disease more credible, but the premises do not fix the amount, so neither need be unreasonable.
questions.rule: Separate the direction from the amount.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each feature by whether the premises fix it in a heuristic syllogism.

items.t: The direction: A becomes more credible, not less
How much more credible A becomes
That a reasonable person will not find A less credible
How strongly different people feel about A

questions.explain: Direction follows from the premises; magnitude depends on temperament, background and unstated reasons.
questions.rule: Direction yes, amount no.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: in a demonstrative syllogism two people who accept the premises can reasonably disagree about the conclusion.
questions.explain: If both accept the premises they cannot reasonably disagree about the conclusion, however different their tastes or convictions.
questions.rule: Demonstration compels; plausible reasoning only nudges.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A school board reads a study showing a small gain for a new method. A teacher thinks it a strong reason to adopt; a parent a mild one. Which statement fits the book?
options: Both may be reasonable, since the study fixes direction but not how much weight it deserves
The teacher is right because she knows more, so her weighting should be adopted by all, and the parent should accept it
The parent is wrong because mild reasons count for nothing in a decision of this kind
They should agree on the weight, since the evidence is the same for both of them
optionExplain: Right: in heuristic reasoning, magnitude depends on stated and unstated reasons.
Knowledge may matter but does not fix the amount.
A mild reason still counts: it pushes in the same direction, only with less weight than the teacher gives it.
Same evidence does not force same weight in plausible reasoning.
questions.explain: The study makes the new method more credible for anyone reasonable, but how much weight it deserves is left open, so teacher and parent can both be reasonable.
questions.rule: Agree on direction from the premises; do not expect agreement on the amount.
questions.teaches: The conclusion of a heuristic syllogism is not fully expressed and not fully supported by the premises: the direction is expressed and implied, the magnitude is not.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Both premises of a plausible argument stay true. Can the conclusion still be lowered?
options: No: if the premises stand, the conclusion stands
Yes, but only if a premise turns out false
Yes: new information outside the premises can make it less credible
No: conclusions can only rise in credibility
optionExplain: That is true of demonstration only.
A premise need not fail; other grounds may count.
Right: the premises are only part of the basis.
New grounds can lower the conclusion, which is the point: the premises are not the whole basis.
questions.explain: Plausible conclusions rest on more than their premises. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Hold heuristic conclusions open to revision, though the premises stand.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: in a demonstrative syllogism the premises give a full basis, so if they stand the conclusion stands.
questions.explain: In a heuristic syllogism, by contrast, the premises are only the visible part of the basis.
questions.rule: Demonstration: premises are a full basis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If a cake is done, the skewer is clean; it is clean, so done is more credible. Then you learn the oven ran far too hot. What happens?
options: The conclusion is unchanged since the premises hold
The first premise is refuted
The conclusion becomes certain
Both premises stand, yet the done conclusion may now be less credible
optionExplain: That is only so for demonstration.
The premise if done then clean is not refuted.
The hot oven does not make it certain.
Right: new information in the invisible part can lower trust while both premises stand.
questions.explain: The hot oven is information outside the premises: both premises still stand, yet trust in the cake being done is lowered.
questions.rule: Ask what else bears on the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which statements about the basis of a heuristic conclusion match the book?
options: New information leaving the premises intact cannot change the conclusion
The premises are the visible, fully expressed part
An unexpressed part may include inarticulate feelings or unstated reasons
Once the premises are accepted nothing can overturn the conclusion
optionExplain: Does not match: new information that leaves the premises intact can still lower trust in the conclusion.
Matches: the unexpressed part includes inarticulate feelings and unstated reasons, which the author calls the invisible part.
Matches: the premises are the fully expressed, visible part of the basis, according to the author.
Does not match: commotions in the invisible part can.
questions.explain: Heuristic conclusions can be shaken from the invisible part of their basis.
questions.rule: Visible premises, invisible rest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author says the conclusion may be shaken by commotions in what?
options: The premises, which must fail first before the conclusion can be shaken in any way
The invisible parts of its foundation, although the premises stand quite firm
The conclusion's wording, which can be changed so that the premises no longer support it
The reader's memory of the premises, which fades so that the conclusion loses its basis
optionExplain: The premises can stand firm while the conclusion is shaken, so they need not fail first.
Right: the invisible part carries weight too.
The wording of the conclusion is not what the author blames; the shaking comes from the unseen part of its foundation.
Memory of the premises is not at issue; the premises stand, and other grounds lower the conclusion.
questions.explain: The premises are only the visible part of the basis; commotion in the invisible part can shake or overturn the conclusion while the premises stand.
questions.rule: Hold heuristic conclusions open to revision, though the premises stand.
questions.teaches: The conclusion may be shaken and even overturned completely by commotions in the invisible parts of its foundation, although the premises, the visible part, stand quite firm.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A manager concluded that a hire is capable from a strong interview. Later she learns the interviewee was coached on every question. What does the book's picture say?
options: The conclusion stands, since the interview is unchanged
The interview must be redone as a rule
The premises may stand yet new grounds lower trust in the conclusion
Interviews carry no information
optionExplain: That is demonstration; here other grounds count.
The book does not say a redo is required.
Right: the interview still happened, but trust in the conclusion drops.
Interviews remain signs; the coaching lowers trust in this one without making interviews useless.
questions.explain: Revise plausible conclusions in the light of new information.
questions.rule: Hold heuristic conclusions open to revision, though the premises stand.
questions.teaches: Behind any reason clarified there are many others that remain obscure and are perhaps still more important; heuristic reasons are important although they prove nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You must decide whether a claim holds for all triangles. Which first move uses specialization?
options: Test it on one particular triangle you can easily handle
Prove it for all triangles at once, with no examples, relying on the general argument to settle every triangle
Ask a teacher for the answer
Replace triangles by all polygons
optionExplain: Right: a single object from the set is a special case.
That is the general problem, the opposite of specializing.
Asking is not a move on the problem.
Moving to all polygons enlarges the set instead of shrinking it.
questions.explain: Specialization shrinks the set. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: Pass from the whole set to a smaller set or a single member of it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Specialization is passing from a given set of objects to a ____ set, or to a single object contained in it.
questions.explain: The special case lies inside the given set: a smaller set, or a single object contained in it.
questions.rule: Smaller set, or one object.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A rule claims that every prime number is odd. You pick the prime 2 to test it. What does the move accomplish?
options: It specializes to one object of the set and refutes the claim, since 2 is prime and even
It generalises the claim to all numbers, so that the claim is now tested on a larger set
It proves the claim for odd primes only, since the single prime 2 is left out of the claim
It changes the problem into a different one, so the claim about primes is no longer tested
optionExplain: Right: one object from the set already settles it.
Choosing one object narrows, not widens, the claim.
The claim concerned all primes; a single failure refutes it.
The problem is the same; the case is smaller.
questions.explain: Choosing the prime 2 passes from the set of all primes to one of its members, and since 2 is even the claim is refuted.
questions.rule: Ask which one object to take.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: testing a statement on a special case that complies with it proves the statement for the whole set.
questions.explain: A complying case may give a hint or an impression that the statement could be true, but a proof for the set needs more.
questions.rule: A special case that complies is a hint, not a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Besides finding solutions and refuting claims, what further use of specialization does the author mention?
options: Writing the final answer in short form
Choosing which problem to solve first
Testing a solution you have already found
Replacing the data by approximate numbers
optionExplain: Nothing in the passage suggests it.
The passage does not discuss choice of problems.
Right: the author refers to the question: can you check the result?
Approximation is not discussed in the passage; its other use is in testing a solution that has been found.
questions.explain: Besides solving problems, specialization can be used to test a solution already found, which the author links to the question Can you check the result?
questions.rule: Pass from the whole set to a smaller set or a single member of it.
questions.teaches: Specialization can be useful in testing the solution; the author refers to the question Can you check the result?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A manager thinks a pricing rule works for every product line. How could she apply specialization?
options: Apply the rule to the company as a whole and see the total, which covers every product line
Try the rule on one product line, preferably a simple or unusual one, and see whether it holds
Wait until all product lines report their results, and only then judge whether the rule holds, with one more report to come in from each of the lines
Rewrite the rule so that it always holds, and then apply the new rule to each product line
optionExplain: The whole company is the large set, not a special case, so it does not specialize the question.
Right: one member of the set is a special case; a failure would refute the rule.
Waiting for all lines to report tests nothing; a single line can be tested at once.
Rewriting the rule to always hold avoids the test; specialization is meant to find out whether the rule holds.
questions.explain: One product line is a single member of the set of lines; trying the rule on it is specialization, and a failure would refute the rule.
questions.rule: Pass from the whole set to a smaller set or a single member of it.
questions.teaches: If the object we examine complies with a general statement we may possibly derive a hint from it, and if it does not comply, the statement is refuted and our task finished.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You meet a theorem about triangles with a conclusion unlike any you know. Nothing comes to mind. What might you try?
options: Give up, since an unfamiliar theorem cannot be tested
Assume it is true because it is printed
Look for a general proof before any example
Test it on a special triangle you know well, such as the equilateral
optionExplain: Special cases are what you try when nothing else occurs.
Printed claims can be false, as this very one turns out to be.
A general proof is the hard path; a test comes first here.
Right: a well-known special case costs little.
questions.explain: A familiar special case gives a start. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: With an unfamiliar assertion, try the best-known special case first.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the equilateral triangle with longest altitude H, the inscribed radius r equals H divided by ____.
questions.explain: In the equilateral triangle the inradius is a third of the altitude and the circumradius is two thirds of it.
questions.rule: Equilateral: r = H/3, R = 2H/3.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In an equilateral triangle with side 6 the altitude H is about 5.196. What is r + R compared with H?
options: Greater than H, so the assertion fails already at the first special case that is tried
Half of H, so the assertion holds easily and with plenty of room to spare
Equal to H, so the assertion r + R at most H holds, with equality
Twice H, so the assertion fails by a wide margin at the equilateral case
optionExplain: The sum of a third and two thirds of H is exactly H, not more.
Half of H would need r + R to equal H/2.
Right: r = H/3 is about 1.732 and R = 2H/3 is about 3.464, whose sum is H.
Twice H would need r + R to equal 2H.
questions.explain: In the equilateral triangle r is a third of H and R two thirds of H, so r + R equals H and the assertion r + R at most H holds, with equality.
questions.rule: Add one third and two thirds.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: if the equilateral case had given r + R larger than H, the assertion would be refuted.
questions.explain: One case that does not comply is enough to refute a general statement about all triangles.
questions.rule: One non-complying case refutes.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What did the author note about the unfamiliar triangle assertion before testing it?
options: He could scarcely remember a theorem about triangles with a similar conclusion
It was a well-known theorem that he had met many times in other books and problems
It had been proved earlier in the same chapter, so he took its truth for granted
It followed at once from the angle sum, so no test was needed before using it
optionExplain: Right: its unusual shape is why a test came first.
The author calls the assertion unusual, so it was not a theorem he knew well.
No proof is given before the test.
No such argument from the angle sum is given; the assertion is tested on special cases instead.
questions.explain: He found the assertion unusual, since he could scarcely recall a theorem with such a conclusion, which is why he tested a special case when nothing else occurred to him.
questions.rule: With an unfamiliar assertion, try the best-known special case first.
questions.teaches: The proposed theorem is of an unusual sort: we can scarcely remember any theorem about triangles with a similar conclusion, so if nothing else occurs to us we may test some special case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A reader meets an odd-looking rule in a tax guide, with nothing similar she knows. Which approach fits?
options: Accept it as printed, since a published guide has already been checked by its authors
Wait for a lawyer to explain it, since only a lawyer can say what a tax rule really means
Test it on the most complicated case she can find, since a hard case shows more than an easy one
Try the rule on the simplest case she can calculate by hand and see what it gives
optionExplain: Printed rules need to be tested like any assertion.
Waiting for a lawyer does not test the rule; a simple hand calculation can show what it gives right now.
The author starts with the best-known special case.
Right: a simple, well-known case is the first thing to test.
questions.explain: Nothing similar comes to mind, so test the rule on the simplest case she can work by hand, as the author tests the best-known special triangle.
questions.rule: With an unfamiliar assertion, try the best-known special case first.
questions.teaches: The best known special triangle is the equilateral triangle, for which r is H/3 and R is 2H/3, so that in this case the assertion is correct.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A claim holds for the equilateral triangle. What would you test next?
options: Nothing; one case that complies proves it
Other special cases, such as isosceles triangles with extreme angles
Only the equilateral case again, with a different size
Any convenient number, to see whether the claim looks plausible
optionExplain: A case that complies is not a proof; the author asks for further special cases to be varied and tested.
Right: vary the case and look at the extremes.
Changing the size of an equilateral triangle changes nothing in shape.
A convenient number does not test the claim; the author asks for special cases at the extremes of the family.
questions.explain: After the first case, vary it. The card next says how.
questions.rule: Look at the extreme cases of a family, since a rule must hold there too.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the isosceles family, the two extreme cases are the angle at the vertex becoming 0 degrees and becoming ____ degrees.
questions.explain: At 0 degrees the base vanishes; at 180 degrees the triangle is flat and its heights vanish.
questions.rule: Extremes: 0 and 180 degrees.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the angle-to-0 limit, the book finds r = 0 and R = H/2. What does that say about r + R compared with H?
options: r + R is 0, so the assertion fails, because both radii shrink to nothing at that limit
r + R is H/2, less than H, so the assertion is verified in that limit
r + R is 2H, so the assertion fails, because the circumradius R is twice the altitude there
r + R equals H, so only equality holds there and the assertion is verified only barely
optionExplain: In that limit r is 0 but R is H/2, so the sum is H/2, not 0.
Right: 0 + H/2 = H/2, below H.
R is H/2 in the limit, half of H, so r + R cannot be twice H.
The sum is H/2, which is less than H, so strict inequality holds and not only equality.
questions.explain: At the limit r is 0 and R is H/2, so r + R is H/2, which is less than H, so the assertion holds at that extreme.
questions.rule: Add the two values.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: for an angle at the vertex near 180 degrees, all heights vanish while R grows without bound, so the assertion fails.
questions.explain: In that limit H goes to 0 and R becomes unbounded, so r + R cannot stay at most H.
questions.rule: Flat triangles break the assertion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author treat the extreme cases the assertion fails in, once he sees that very flat triangles also fail?
options: He insists the extreme cases are the only valid test and that flat triangles are not triangles, and so the failure of the assertion there does not count
He says the assertion is true after all, since the failure appears only in the limit case
He says a failure in a limit case proves nothing, since limit cases are not triangles
He says the extreme cases may be officially disregarded, since flat but genuine triangles already fail
optionExplain: Genuine flat triangles also give a failure.
The assertion is false, since very flat isosceles triangles break it; it is not true after all.
The failure proves the assertion false, regardless of extremes.
Right: the failure is shown for genuine, very flat isosceles triangles.
questions.explain: The extreme case was only the start; very flat but genuine isosceles triangles also break the assertion, so the extremes need not be treated as unorthodox.
questions.rule: Look at the extreme cases of a family, since a rule must hold there too.
questions.teaches: The assertion is also false for very flat isosceles triangles whose angle at the vertex is nearly 180 degrees, so we may officially disregard the extreme cases that appear not quite orthodox.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A bakery rule says the price per slice falls as cakes get bigger. Which test uses extreme cases?
options: Check a one-slice cake and a very large cake, to see whether the rule still holds
Check three medium cakes, which are typical of what the bakery makes and sells every day
Check the cake the bakery sells most, since a common cake is the one that matters in practice
Check no cakes at all and trust the rule, since a rule about price needs no checking
optionExplain: Right: the extremes are most likely to expose an overlooked exception.
Medium cases are least likely to expose a failure.
A common case rarely fails because the rule was probably made with such cases in mind; extremes are the likely failures.
Skipping tests leaves the rule unexamined.
questions.explain: The extremes, one slice and a very large cake, are the cases most likely to break a rule that seems to hold in the middle of the range.
questions.rule: Look at the extreme cases of a family, since a rule must hold there too.
questions.teaches: An extreme case can reveal a refutation because such cases are apt to be overlooked by the inventors of generalizations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Someone says: this rule has an exception, and that proves the rule. What is the best response?
options: Agreed: exceptions confirm rules, so a rule with an exception is made stronger by it
Rules with exceptions are true about half of the time, so the rule may still be used
One exception refutes a general rule; the saying is a joke on loose logic
An exception matters only if there are at least two of them, since one can be a slip
optionExplain: The saying is a joke on a certain laxity of logic, not serious logic; one exception refutes a general rule.
Truth does not come in halves: a general statement with an exception is simply refuted.
Right: logic needs only one non-complying object.
One exception is enough to refute; waiting for a second adds nothing to the logic.
questions.explain: A general statement fails with a single counterexample. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Specialize to an object that does not comply; one is enough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: An object that does not comply with a general statement is called a ____.
questions.explain: The most usual and in some respects the best method to refute a general statement is to exhibit such an object.
questions.rule: Exhibit a counterexample.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The number 2 to the power p, minus 1, is prime for p = 2, 3, 5 and 7, and equals 2047 for p = 11. Is it prime for every prime p?
options: Yes: four successes establish the pattern
Yes: 2047 is prime because 11 is prime
Cannot be decided without trying all primes, since the general case has infinitely many cases to try
No: 2047 = 23 x 89, so p = 11 is a counterexample
optionExplain: Successes do not prove a general statement.
2047 equals 23 times 89, so it is not prime and the claim fails for p = 11.
One counterexample already refutes it.
Right: 3, 7, 31 and 127 are prime but 2047 is not. One counterexample settles it.
questions.explain: The four successes suggest a pattern, but 2047 is 23 times 89, so one counterexample refutes the claim for all primes p.
questions.rule: Look for the one object that does not comply.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each argument by whether it correctly handles a general claim.

items.t: The claim fails at n = 40, so it is refuted
The claim holds for n = 1 to 39, so it must hold for n = 40
The claim holds in ten tests, so it is proved for all cases
The claim has one exception, so it cannot be called a general rule

questions.explain: One failure refutes a general claim, while any number of successes, even 39 of them, leaves the next case open.
questions.rule: Failure refutes, success only hints.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: If the tested object does comply with the statement, what might you still gain?
options: A full proof of the statement, since one complying object shows that every object complies
A hint: the impression that the statement could be true, and a suggestion where to seek the proof or the counterexample
A guarantee that all objects in the set comply, because the one tested was a typical member
Nothing at all, since only objects that fail the statement can tell us anything about it
optionExplain: A complying object proves nothing about the set.
Right: the author says an object that complies can still give hints.
No guarantee follows from one case.
Complying cases still teach: they may give the impression that the statement could be true or point to where to look next.
questions.explain: A case that complies cannot prove the statement, but it may give the impression that it could be true and suggest where to look for the proof or the counterexample.
questions.rule: Specialize to an object that does not comply; one is enough.
questions.teaches: If the object examined complies with the statement we may receive the impression that the statement could be true, after all, and some suggestion in which direction to seek the proof, or which other special cases to test.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A school claims that all its pupils pass the swimming test. A visitor finds one pupil who failed. What follows?
options: The claim is true for the rest, so it stands
The claim needs several failures to be refuted, since a single failure may be a slip of the test
The claim is refuted; that pupil is a counterexample
The failure proves the claim by exception
optionExplain: The claim was all pupils, and it stands refuted.
One is enough, however many pupils there are.
Right: one object that does not comply refutes an all-statement.
Exceptions refute; they do not prove.
questions.explain: The school claimed that all pupils pass; one pupil who did not is an object that fails to comply, and that is enough to refute the claim.
questions.rule: Specialize to an object that does not comply; one is enough.
questions.teaches: If we take matters seriously, one exception is enough to refute irrefragably any would-be rule or general statement.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A claim is said to hold for all birds. Which test would be most informative?
options: An unusual bird, such as a penguin
A sparrow, the usual bird
Any common bird, since birds are alike
No test, since birds are alike
optionExplain: Right: an unusual case has the best chance of refuting the claim.
A common bird will comply with almost any claim made about birds, so it tests little.
A common bird is a weak test since claims tend to be built around ordinary members.
Birds differ; extreme cases show it.
questions.explain: Unusual members test a rule hardest. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Choose the case most likely to break the rule; if it survives, trust the rule more.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the author's example, a statement meant for all mammals must hold even for the unusual mammal, the ____.
questions.explain: The whale is an extreme case of a mammal, so it tests the statement.
questions.rule: Extreme members test the rule.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A student claims that the square of every whole number is larger than the number itself. Which test is most informative?
options: Try 1, the smallest positive whole number, an extreme member of the set
Try 1000, a large whole number, since big numbers are the ones that matter most in practice
Try a whole number picked at random from a list, since a random pick is a fair sample
Try 17, a number of moderate size, since moderate numbers are neither too easy nor too odd
optionExplain: Right: 1 squared is 1, which is not larger than 1, so the claim fails at the extreme. Large and moderate numbers comply.
Large numbers satisfy the claim easily, so this test could hardly refute it.
A random pick is likely to be an ordinary member of the set, and ordinary members comply.
A moderate number such as 17 squares to 289, which complies, so the test learns nothing.
questions.explain: Prospective exceptions test the rule: choose the member most likely to break it.
questions.rule: Look for the extreme member of the set.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: a statement that is verified even in its most extreme case gains strong inductive evidence, according to the author.
questions.explain: The prospect of refutation was strong there, so surviving counts for much, though it is still not a proof.
questions.rule: Surviving a strong test gives strong evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author reshape the saying that the exception proves the rule?
options: Exceptions never matter to rules, whatever exceptions they may happen to have
Rules prove their exceptions
Prospective exceptions test the rule
The rule proves itself
optionExplain: Exceptions matter because one of them refutes a rule; they are the very thing a rule has to survive.
That reverses the idea: rules do not prove their exceptions; likely exceptions test the rules.
Right: the improved saying treats likely exceptions as tests.
Rules are tested, not self-proving.
questions.explain: The author keeps the old saying but changes its sense: likely exceptions are tests that a rule must survive, not confirmations of it.
questions.rule: Choose the case most likely to break the rule; if it survives, trust the rule more.
questions.teaches: Because extreme cases are apt to be overlooked by the inventors of generalizations, there is a good chance of refuting the statement there; the saying is reshaped as prospective exceptions test the rule.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A new bridge design is claimed to carry any load up to 40 tonnes. Which trial gives the strongest evidence if the bridge passes?
options: Several 5-tonne loads at the center
A single 40-tonne load at the weakest point of the span
A 20-tonne load spread over the deck
A long observation without any load
optionExplain: These loads are far from the limit.
Right: the extreme load in the hardest spot is the likeliest to break the design.
A mid-range load does not strain the claim.
Without any load there is no test; the bridge must actually be loaded for the claim to be tried.
questions.explain: The strongest evidence comes from the test most likely to refute the claim, so the extreme load at the weakest point is the telling trial.
questions.rule: Choose the case most likely to break the rule; if it survives, trust the rule more.
questions.teaches: If the general statement is verified even in the extreme case, the inductive evidence derived from this verification will be strong, just because the prospect of refutation was strong.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A problem can be given with positions and speeds chosen in many ways, and you cannot see one method. What might help?
options: Solve it only for the case you are given and ignore the others, since the other cases can be dealt with when they come up
Add more data to make it more varied
Memorize the answer for each possible choice
Look for a more special case in which one of the data is trivial
optionExplain: The problem requires a solution for whatever data are given.
More variety makes the problem harder, and the difficulty here is already too much variety.
There are too many choices to memorize.
Right: a special case reduces the variety.
questions.explain: A more special problem is an entry. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask for a more special problem, such as one datum set to a trivial value.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the ships problem, the extreme special case is the one in which one ship lies at ____.
questions.explain: A ship at anchor has zero speed, so the problem becomes easier.
questions.rule: One speed set to zero.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A ship at anchor is at point B. Another ship moves along a straight line. What is their shortest distance?
options: The distance from B to the starting point of the moving ship
The distance from B to the point where the moving ship stops
The length of the perpendicular from B to the straight line of the moving ship
Half the length of the moving ship's path
optionExplain: The starting point need not be the nearest.
The end of the journey need not be the nearest.
Right: the nearest point of a line to a given point is the foot of the perpendicular.
Half of the path has no meaning for the shortest distance; the nearest point of a line is the foot of the perpendicular.
questions.explain: With the second ship at anchor, the shortest distance from it to the moving ship is the perpendicular to the line of the moving ship.
questions.rule: Use the line-to-point result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes a more special problem related to the ships problem.

items.t: One ship stays at anchor
Both ships travel along the same straight line
The ships may change speed during the voyage
The ships move on a curved course

questions.explain: A more special problem restricts the data; changing speed or course makes the problem more general.
questions.rule: Special means more restricted.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author describe the feeling that leads to the idea of a more special problem?
options: A feeling of too much variety in the data, A, B, P and Q, which may be chosen arbitrarily
A feeling that the data are insufficient, since the speeds and positions are not given enough
A feeling that the problem is too easy, since only two straight courses are involved
A feeling that the answer is already known, since the shortest distance is the perpendicular
optionExplain: Right: the four points can be arbitrary, and the same solution has to fit all possibilities.
The data are sufficient, but varied; the difficulty is how many ways they can be chosen.
The problem is not too easy; the feeling is of too much variety, which makes the method hard to see.
The answer is not known; the feeling is of not yet seeing how one solution fits all choices of data.
questions.explain: The four points A, B, P and Q can be chosen arbitrarily, and the same solution must fit them all; this feeling of too much variety leads to asking for a more special problem.
questions.rule: Ask for a more special problem, such as one datum set to a trivial value.
questions.teaches: The difficulty has a peculiar nuance, too much variety: the points A, B, P and Q may be chosen arbitrarily, and the required solution must apply to all these possibilities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A scheduling rule has to work for any number of workers and any shifts, and you cannot see the pattern. What does the ships example suggest?
options: Wait for more details about the workers and shifts before trying anything on the problem
Write a separate rule for each possible case, and join the rules together when finished
Drop the requirement of generality, and build a rule that works for the present roster only, leaving the harder general case aside
Try a more special case, such as one worker or one shift, solve it, and look for a way to use it
optionExplain: More details add to the variety instead of reducing it, and they delay trying a special case.
That does not yield a general rule.
Generality is the point of the task; the special case is used to get an entry into the general problem.
Right: the extreme special case may be too simple to look relevant, but it can have a role to play.
questions.explain: The roster problem has too much variety, so try one worker or one shift; the extreme special case may look too simple to matter and yet have a part to play.
questions.rule: Ask for a more special problem, such as one datum set to a trivial value.
questions.teaches: The extreme special case, which could appear as too simple to be relevant, may have a role to play: it is a bright idea if it emerges with the premonition that there is more ahead.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two ships move at constant speeds. You know how to find the shortest distance if one is at rest. What might you do to use that?
options: Make both ships stop, so that their distance can be read off from the fixed positions
Give both ships the same extra motion so that one comes to rest
Ignore the second ship, and find the shortest distance of the first ship to a fixed point
Average the two speeds, and let both ships travel at that average on their own courses
optionExplain: Stopping both changes the problem.
Right: adding the same motion to both does not change their distance.
Ignoring a ship changes the problem.
Averaging does not give a rest case.
questions.explain: Common motion preserves distances. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Add a common motion that brings one ship to rest, and use the special result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: giving both ships the same uniform motion leaves their relative positions and shortest distance unchanged.
questions.explain: A common motion carries both along together, so their distances do not change.
questions.rule: Common motion keeps relative distances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Ship A starts at (0, 0) moving 5 east; ship B starts at (10, 6) moving 2 east. What is their shortest distance, and when?
options: 10, at the start
6, at 10/3 time units after the start
6, at 10 time units after the start
11.66, at 3 time units after the start
optionExplain: The distance at the start is about 11.66, not 10, and it is not the smallest.
Right: relative to B, A moves 3 east, passing level with B after 10/3 units, at distance 6.
A moves relative to B at 3 per unit, so it covers 10 in 10/3 units, not 10.
11.66 is the distance at the start, not the shortest.
questions.explain: Subtract B's velocity from both ships: B is at rest, A moves 3 east relative to B, and the shortest distance is the perpendicular, 6, reached after 10/3 time units.
questions.rule: Switch to B's frame.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Both ships have the same velocity. What happens to the distance?
options: It shrinks steadily, since two ships travelling together approach one another in time
It grows steadily, since two ships travelling at the same speed draw ever farther apart
It oscillates, since ships keep changing their distance as the moments of time go by
It stays constant, since relative to either ship the other is at rest
optionExplain: No relative motion exists to shrink it.
No relative motion exists to grow it.
Nothing in constant velocity oscillates.
Right: if the velocities are equal, subtracting one makes both at rest, so the distance is constant. Our reading: this limiting case shows the method at its edge.
questions.explain: What if the two speeds are the same? Relative motion vanishes.
questions.rule: Add a common motion that brings one ship to rest, and use the special result.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The velocity added to both ships, which makes use of the special result possible, is called the ____ element.
questions.explain: It is introduced into the problem only to make the use of the special result possible.
questions.rule: An auxiliary element makes a known result usable.
questions.teaches: The velocity, opposite to that of the second ship and of the same amount, added to both ships is the auxiliary element that makes the use of the special result possible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two cyclists ride at constant speeds on straight roads. How would you find when they are closest, using the ships idea?
options: Subtract one cyclist's velocity from both, treat that cyclist as at rest, and take the perpendicular distance
Compute both cyclists' paths separately and compare them at the moments when they cross
Wait until they meet and measure the distance there, since that is when they are closest
Take the average of their speeds and use it for both cyclists on their separate roads
optionExplain: Right: the relative-motion trick works for any two uniform motions.
That does not reduce the case to the rest case.
They may never meet; the minimum is wanted.
Averaging the speeds does not bring either cyclist to rest, so the perpendicular-distance result is not reached.
questions.explain: Subtract one cyclist's velocity from both so that cyclist is at rest, then the shortest distance is the perpendicular to the other's relative path.
questions.rule: Add a common motion that brings one ship to rest, and use the special result.
questions.teaches: Rest is a special case of motion, and motion is relative, so whatever the given velocity of the second ship may be, we can consider it as being at rest.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You solve an easy special case of a hard problem. What else do you need to solve the hard problem?
options: Nothing more; the special case already solves the original problem, so the work is done
A harder special case, because only a more difficult case can stand in for the original
A remark that carries you from the special case back to the original problem
A new problem unrelated to the original, which will then settle both of them at once
optionExplain: The special case is less ambitious; a link is needed.
A harder case is not the issue; an easier special case suffices if a link back is found.
Right: the supplementary remark is the link.
An unrelated problem would not help.
questions.explain: Two remarks are needed. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Solve the special problem, then find the remark that links it back.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Put the author's two steps for crossing from a problem to its solution in order.
items: Invent an advantageous auxiliary problem, a special case of the original
Solve the auxiliary problem
Discover the supplementary remark linking the auxiliary problem to the original
Use that remark to pass to the solution of the original problem
questions.explain: First the stepping stone is chosen, then used, then the link back to the shore is found and crossed.
questions.rule: Stone, link, shore.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: To tile a 7-by-9 floor, you first solve a 1-by-9 strip. What makes the strip a stepping stone rather than the answer?
options: Strips are always wrong at first, so a strip is a poor choice of auxiliary problem
The floor is easier than the strip, so the strip adds a difficulty that was not there
No remark is needed, since a strip is itself a floor of the same kind and size
You still need a remark showing how 7 such strips make up the floor
optionExplain: Strips are not wrong at first; a strip is a good stepping stone if a remark links it to the floor.
The floor is harder, as the original problem.
A strip alone is not the floor, so a remark is needed to carry the result from strips to the floor.
Right: the supplementary remark links the special case to the original.
questions.explain: The strip is the stepping stone; the supplementary remark is that seven such strips side by side make up the floor.
questions.rule: Find what connects the two.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each item of the ships solution by whether it is the auxiliary problem or the supplementary remark.

items.t: The ships problem with one ship at anchor
Motion is relative, so relative distances do not change
The shortest distance from a ship at rest to the path of the other
Subtracting a common velocity from both ships brings one to rest

questions.explain: The special problem is the stepping stone; the relativity remark carries us back to the original.
questions.rule: Stone is the special problem; link is relativity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author explain that the easier auxiliary problem can help despite being much less ambitious?
options: Because the auxiliary problem is harder than it looks, and it hides the work of the original
Because a substantial supplementary remark on the relativity of motion was added to pass back to the original
Because the original problem was easy after all and needed no help from a special case
Because specialization always proves the general case, whatever special case may be chosen
optionExplain: The auxiliary problem was immediate.
Right: the link carried the weight.
The original looked hard, which is why a special case was sought; it was not easy after all.
Specialization does not prove the general case.
questions.explain: The auxiliary problem was immediate, but the original became solvable because a substantial supplementary remark, on the relativity of motion, carried the result back.
questions.rule: Solve the special problem, then find the remark that links it back.
questions.teaches: The original problem looked hard and the solution of the auxiliary problem was immediate; we could solve the original on the basis of the auxiliary one because in reducing it we added a substantial supplementary remark.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A coder solves a bug for a single input, then must fix it for all inputs. What is the supplementary remark?
options: The list of all the inputs tried, which shows that the fix worked on each of them
A faster computer, which would allow every input to be tried in a short time
An argument showing why the fix for that input carries over to every other input
A longer test run, with more inputs, which would raise the number of cases covered
optionExplain: A list of tried inputs does not link.
Hardware has no bearing on whether the single-input fix carries over to the other inputs.
Right: the remark links the single case back to the general problem.
A longer test gives more cases but not the reason the fix generalises, so it is not the supplementary remark.
questions.explain: The fix for one input is the stepping stone; the link is an argument showing why it carries over to every other input.
questions.rule: Solve the special problem, then find the remark that links it back.
questions.teaches: To sum up, we used the less difficult, less ambitious, special, auxiliary problem as a stepping stone in solving the more difficult, more ambitious, general, original problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A teacher introduces coordinates in space. Which choice makes them concrete?
options: Treat a corner of the classroom as the origin and its floor and walls as coordinate planes
Write the equations on the board without any example, so that the abstract form is seen at once
Ask students to memorize the definition of coordinates, and test them on it the next day
Use only imaginary points far away from the room, so that no example gets in the way
optionExplain: Right: the classroom provides a rectangular system at hand.
Writing equations without any example keeps the matter abstract, which is what the author wants to avoid.
Memorizing does not make it concrete.
Far imaginary points stay abstract.
questions.explain: A room can serve as a model. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Present abstract mathematics concretely.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: In the author's classroom example, a corner of the room serves as the ____ of coordinates.
questions.explain: The floor and two walls are the coordinate planes and the edges the axes.
questions.rule: Corner is origin.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A teacher wants to show a rectangular box with sides 3, 4 and 5 in a lesson. What is the simplest concrete choice, following the author?
options: Use a classroom or a real box as the example
Draw only the formula for its volume, since the formula is what matters in the lesson
Avoid solids until later
Refer to a figure in another book
optionExplain: Right: the classroom itself serves as the rectangular parallelepiped.
A formula without an object keeps the box abstract, while a real box or the classroom makes it concrete.
The author says nothing should be omitted that may bring mathematics home.
A real object at hand is better than a remote figure.
questions.explain: The classroom or a real box serves as the rectangular parallelepiped, which makes the solid concrete for the students.
questions.rule: Look around the room.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the author regards the classroom examples as deep proofs that replace abstract reasoning.
questions.explain: He calls them simple tricks but says nothing should be omitted that has some chance to bring home mathematics to the students.
questions.rule: Concrete illustrations help; they are not proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the teacher illustrate a surface of revolution?
options: By spinning a globe on the desk so that the curve on it turns into a surface
By cutting a cone out of paper and unrolling it to show the curve that made it
By drawing a curve with chalk on the door and opening the door slowly
By drawing a circle on the board and shading in the region that the circle encloses
optionExplain: A globe is not in the passage; the author uses a chalk curve on a door that is opened slowly.
A paper cone is not in the passage; it is the door turning that sweeps out the surface.
Right: the moving door sweeps the curve into a surface.
A static circle does not show revolution.
questions.explain: Drawing a curve on the door and opening it slowly lets the students see the curve sweep out a surface of revolution.
questions.rule: Present abstract mathematics concretely.
questions.teaches: Explaining the notion of a surface of revolution, the teacher draws a curve with chalk on the door and opens it slowly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A finance trainer explains compound interest. Which approach follows the passage?
options: Give the general formula only, and trust the learners to see what it means for themselves
Give a concrete case: a small deposit and a table of its balance year by year
Avoid examples altogether to keep the subject pure, and leave illustrations to the learners
Tell the learners to read a book first and come back to the formula when they have done so
optionExplain: The formula alone keeps the matter abstract, whereas the author wants mathematics presented concretely.
Right: Mathematics being a very abstract science should be presented very concretely.
Avoiding examples is the reverse of the advice.
The advice is to present concretely now.
questions.explain: A small deposit and a table of balances year by year gives a concrete case, in line with presenting a very abstract science very concretely.
questions.rule: Present abstract mathematics concretely.
questions.teaches: Mathematics being a very abstract science should be presented very concretely, and nothing should be omitted that has some chance to bring home mathematics to the students.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You have worked hard on a problem without success. What might happen after a night's rest?
options: The problem will be solved for certain
Nothing can change, since you did not work during the night
The problem will seem harder because you forgot details
A bright idea may appear and the solution come easily
optionExplain: The experience is common, not certain.
Many people find the problem clarified, even though they did not work on it.
Forgotten details are not what the author reports.
Right: this is a familiar experience, though not a guarantee.
questions.explain: A rest can bring the idea. The card next gives the author's story.
questions.rule: A problem returned after a break may be clarified and nearer to its solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author could not recall a name one evening, and next morning it came to him without any ____.
questions.explain: He remembered everything about the author except the name, and the name came when he thought of the annoyance again.
questions.rule: Names and solutions can return without effort.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A student cannot start an essay beginning and gives up for the evening. Next morning a good first sentence comes at once. How does the author read this?
options: As luck, unrelated to the evening's effort, since good first sentences come at random
As proof that essays write themselves, since the writer did nothing during the night
As an example of a problem returning clarified after an absence, which seems like subconscious work
As a sign that the assignment was too easy, since a good start came at once next day
optionExplain: The author ties it to prior work, not luck.
It followed from effort, not from nothing.
Right: the beginning of an annoying letter is one of the author's own examples.
Ease at the end does not mean ease at the start.
questions.explain: The beginning of an annoying letter is one of the author's own examples of a problem returning clarified after an absence, as if by subconscious work.
questions.rule: Look for the pattern: stuck, rest, idea.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the author says the kind of problem matters greatly for whether it returns clarified after a break.
questions.explain: He says the nature of the problem matters little: a forgotten word, a crossword clue, a letter beginning or a mathematical solution may come this way.
questions.rule: The kind of problem matters little.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What does the author say about who clarified the problem during the interval?
options: Oneself, working at it subconsciously, though psychologists have begun to find another answer
A friend who happened to mention it, whose remark set off the idea in the solver
Nobody; the problem solved itself while it lay forgotten and out of the solver's mind
The unconscious mind of an expert only, since ordinary people lack the training for it, while the rest of us can only wait and see
optionExplain: Right: it is difficult to give any other answer, he says, though another answer may become more satisfactory.
No friend is mentioned; the author says the clarifying was done by oneself, working at it subconsciously.
A problem cannot solve itself; someone clarified it.
He does not restrict this to experts.
questions.explain: The author says it is difficult to give any other answer than that oneself, working at it subconsciously, did the clarifying, though psychologists have begun another account.
questions.rule: A problem returned after a break may be clarified and nearer to its solution.
questions.teaches: After prolonged absence a problem may return into consciousness essentially clarified; who clarified it is oneself, working at it subconsciously, although psychologists have discovered the beginnings of another answer.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A programmer fails to find a bug on Friday and finds it in five minutes on Monday. Which statement fits the author?
options: The weekend must have fixed the code, since the code had been left alone for two days
The programmer was lazy on Friday, and found the bug on Monday when working properly
It shows that bugs only exist on Fridays, which are the days when errors creep in
It is an everyday case of a problem coming back improved after an interruption
optionExplain: The code did not change; the programmer's view did.
The author counts it as a general experience, not laziness.
Nothing supports a pattern of Fridays.
Right: the author counts a few days' interruption as one of the ways it happens.
questions.explain: Failing on Friday and succeeding on Monday is the kind of return after a few days' interruption the author describes.
questions.rule: A problem returned after a break may be clarified and nearer to its solution.
questions.teaches: It often happens that you have no success at all with a problem even though you work very hard, and then when you come back after a night's rest or a few days' interruption a bright idea appears and you solve the problem easily.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: You have been forcing a hard problem for hours with no gain. Which advice does the author give?
options: Force harder, since effort always pays in the end and a break only wastes time
Leave it alone for a while, after settling some small point
Abandon it permanently, since hours of work without a gain show it cannot be solved
Switch to a different problem every five minutes, so that none of them grows stale
optionExplain: That is the mistake the author warns against.
Right: there is a limit beyond which we should not force conscious reflection.
The author advises coming back later, not abandoning the problem for good.
Quick switching is not his advice.
questions.explain: Rest has a place. The card next says how.
questions.rule: Rest a problem when forcing it stops helping, after settling some small point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the old advice take counsel of your pillow means sleeping on a problem can help.
questions.explain: An interval of rest may give more tomorrow with less effort.
questions.rule: Sleeping on a problem can help.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: At the end of a long evening on a puzzle you are stuck. What should you do before quitting, per the author?
options: Throw away all your notes, so that tomorrow you start again from a clean sheet of paper, and begin afresh as though no work had been done
Settle some small point or elucidate some aspect, so you quit with a sense of achievement
Leave the question entirely undefined, so that the mind is free of it for the night
Promise yourself to solve it by morning, so that the pressure keeps you working on it
optionExplain: Throwing away the notes destroys the achievement that makes the problem come back improved.
Right: a problem set aside with something achieved comes back more easily.
A vague quitting gives nothing to return to.
Promises put tension without achievement.
questions.explain: Settling a small point before quitting means the problem is put aside with some achievement, which makes it more likely to come back improved.
questions.rule: Make one small point firm.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each plan for a stuck evening by whether it follows the author's advice.

items.t: Settle one small point, then rest until tomorrow
Write down what is now clear about the question, then stop
Keep forcing thought past the point where nothing new comes
Put the problem aside with no result and no note of where you are

questions.explain: The advice combines rest with some achievement before quitting.
questions.rule: Rest, but not empty-handed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: What condition does the author put on setting a problem aside if we wish to return to it later?
options: We must have solved at least half of it, so that the remainder is not too large to take up
We must tell someone else about it, so that another mind can also keep it in view
We must have worked on it for a full day, so that the effort can be said to be enough
We should not set it aside without the impression of some achievement
optionExplain: No fraction of the problem has to be solved; a little point settled is enough.
Telling someone is not part of the advice; the achievement is the point.
No set duration is required; some small point settled is what counts.
Right: at least some little point should be settled.
questions.explain: To come back to a problem later with profit, do not set it aside without the impression of some achievement; at least a little point should be settled.
questions.rule: Rest a problem when forcing it stops helping, after settling some small point.
questions.teaches: It is desirable not to set aside a problem to which we wish to come back later without the impression of some achievement; at least some little point should be settled when we quit working.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A violinist cannot master a passage after an hour of repeating it. What fits the advice?
options: Stop forcing it, make sure one bar is now secure, and return tomorrow
Repeat it a hundred more times tonight, since effort past the point of tiring still pays
Never play the piece again, since a passage that resists an hour will resist for good
Play something unrelated and forget the passage, so that it is no longer on the mind
optionExplain: Right: there is a limit to forcing, and rest with a small gain helps.
That forces conscious effort past its limit.
The passage is meant to be revisited.
Forgetting loses the point of coming back.
questions.explain: After an hour of forcing, stopping with one bar secure follows the advice to rest with some achievement and return, since more forcing gains little.
questions.rule: Rest a problem when forcing it stops helping, after settling some small point.
questions.teaches: Allowing an interval of rest to the problem and to ourselves, we may obtain more tomorrow with less effort; if today will not, tomorrow may.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A student has not tried a hard problem but plans to sleep on it. What will likely happen, by the author's account?
options: The solution will come in the morning, since sleep does the work that the student has not done
He will wake with a partial answer, since the night gives a start even without any effort
Nothing much: rest helps only after conscious effort and real desire
Sleeping is as good as working, since the mind keeps on solving problems while one rests
optionExplain: It would be too easy if that were so.
Partial answers come after effort.
Right: the subconscious work needs conscious effort to start.
The author says sleep does not replace work.
questions.explain: Effort must come first. The card next says why.
questions.rule: Strive and care first; rest afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Conscious effort and ____ seem necessary to set the subconscious work going.
questions.explain: Only problems we desire passionately, or worked at with great tension, come back improved.
questions.rule: Effort and tension start the process.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Two students leave a puzzle for the night. One worked on it for hours and wants the answer badly; the other glanced at it. Which is more likely to find it improved in the morning?
options: The second, since a mind that has glanced at a puzzle only is fresher than one that has worked
Both equally, since sleep is the cause of the idea and how much one worked does not matter
Neither, since sleep never helps a person to find the answer to a problem
The first, since conscious effort and passionate desire set the subconscious work going
optionExplain: A glance does not start the process.
Sleep alone is not the cause; the author says conscious effort and tension are needed to set the work going.
The author reports that sleep can help after work.
Right: the author says only such problems come back improved.
questions.explain: Only problems we desire passionately, or worked at with great tension, come back improved, so the student who worked hard is the more likely to find it improved.
questions.rule: Who worked, who wanted?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, one could solve difficult problems by sleeping and waiting for a bright idea.
questions.explain: He says it would be too easy if that were so; conscious effort and tension seem necessary.
questions.rule: Sleep does not replace work.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author's argument end up justifying that effort is needed before rest works?
options: He cites a laboratory experiment on sleep and problem solving that is described in the entry, with results that the entry sets out
At any rate, it would be too easy otherwise, since hard problems could then be solved by sleeping
He appeals to a law of psychology that says sleep always brings out the answer to a puzzle
He relies on the testimony of famous writers who said they had solved problems in sleep
optionExplain: No laboratory experiment is cited at this point; the author argues from what would follow if effort were not needed.
Right: his argument is partly a plausibility remark.
No law of psychology is cited here; he even says psychologists have only begun to find another answer.
No testimony of writers is cited here; the argument is that it would be too easy otherwise.
questions.explain: The author argues that it would be too easy otherwise, since difficult problems could then be solved just by sleeping and waiting for an idea.
questions.rule: Strive and care first; rest afterwards.
questions.teaches: Only problems whose solution we passionately desire, or for which we have worked with great tension, come back improved; at any rate, it would be too easy if it were not so, since we could solve difficult problems by sleeping and waiting for a bright idea.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: An entrepreneur wants a name for a product and has brainstormed hard for days without success. A friend says: stop and let it come. How does this fit the author?
options: It does not fit: a rest only works for mathematicians
It fits only if she does nothing more about it, ever
It fits: after strong effort and desire, a rest may bring the idea
It does not fit: names cannot be remembered by resting
optionExplain: The author says the nature of the problem matters little.
Nothing says never to work on it again.
Right: the author's examples include a forgotten name and a letter beginning.
A forgotten name is the author's first example.
questions.explain: She has worked hard and wants a name badly, which is the condition under which a rest may let the idea come, as with the author's forgotten name.
questions.rule: Strive and care first; rest afterwards.
questions.teaches: Past ages regarded a sudden good idea as an inspiration, a gift of the gods, which we must deserve by work or at least by a fervent wish.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which describes the general, logical sense of symmetry?
options: A whole is symmetric if it has interchangeable parts
A figure that looks the same when turned upside down
A figure with equal sides
A figure drawn on a grid
optionExplain: Right: in the general sense interchangeability is what matters.
That is a special case of geometry only.
Equal sides are not the definition.
A grid has nothing to do with the definition; symmetry in the general sense is about interchangeable parts.
questions.explain: Interchangeable parts define it. The card next gives both meanings.
questions.rule: Geometric symmetry is about a plane or a point; the general sense is about interchangeable parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Elementary solid geometry considers symmetry with respect to a plane and symmetry with respect to a ____.
questions.explain: The plane is the plane of symmetry and the point the center of symmetry.
questions.rule: Plane and point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A vase is cut by a vertical plane into two halves that are mirror images. Which kind of symmetry is this?
options: Symmetry with respect to a plane
Symmetry with respect to a point only
Logical symmetry with no geometric meaning
No symmetry, because the halves are separate
optionExplain: Right: this is the statue example.
A point of symmetry is a different relation.
The geometric meaning is the more usual one.
The halves being interchangeable is the symmetry.
questions.explain: Cutting the vase by a vertical plane into mirror halves shows symmetry with respect to a plane, the plane of symmetry.
questions.rule: Ask what exchanges the halves.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the human body is completely symmetrical, since its two sides look alike from outside.
questions.explain: The author says the body appears fairly symmetrical but in fact is not, since many interior organs are unsymmetrically disposed.
questions.rule: Appearances can hide asymmetry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: How does the author describe a statue that is completely symmetrical with respect to a vertical plane?
options: It has four planes of symmetry
It has no center of symmetry
Its two halves appear completely interchangeable
It can be turned around any axis
optionExplain: The passage gives no count of planes; the statue is symmetric about one vertical plane.
Centers of symmetry are discussed separately.
Right: complete symmetry means interchangeable halves.
Rotation about an axis is not mentioned; the statue example concerns a vertical plane.
questions.explain: Complete symmetry about a vertical plane means the two halves appear completely interchangeable.
questions.rule: Geometric symmetry is about a plane or a point; the general sense is about interchangeable parts.
questions.teaches: A statue may be completely symmetrical with respect to a vertical plane so that its two halves appear completely interchangeable.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A seesaw balanced with two equal children can be swapped left to right without changing the balance. Which sense of symmetry is closer?
options: The geometric sense with a center of symmetry
The general sense: the two children are interchangeable parts
Neither, since seesaws are not figures
The geometric sense with a plane only
optionExplain: A center of symmetry is a point relation.
Right: interchangeable parts is the general meaning, usable outside geometry. Our reading: a seesaw is only an illustration.
The general sense is not limited to figures.
The plane sense applies to geometric figures.
questions.explain: Interchangeable parts define the general sense, so it reaches beyond geometry; the seesaw is our own illustration, not the book's.
questions.rule: Geometric symmetry is about a plane or a point; the general sense is about interchangeable parts.
questions.teaches: In a more general acceptance of the word, a whole is termed symmetric if it has interchangeable parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which expression is unchanged when any two of x, y, z are swapped?
options: x squared y + y squared z + z squared x
x + 2y + 3z
xy + yz + 2zx
yz + zx + xy
optionExplain: Swapping x and y changes this sum to y squared x + x squared z + z squared y.
Different letters have different coefficients.
The last term has an extra coefficient.
Right: every pair appears with the same role.
questions.explain: A symmetric expression is unchanged by swaps. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Look for parts that can be swapped without changing the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the expression yz + zx + xy is unchanged when any two of x, y, z are interchanged.
questions.explain: Swapping x and y gives xz + zy + yx, the same sum, and the same holds for any other pair.
questions.rule: A symmetric expression is unchanged by any swap of its letters.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: For x = 1, y = 2, z = 3, compare x squared y + y squared z + z squared x with the same sum after swapping x and y. What do you find?
options: The sums are both 23, so the expression is symmetric under this swap
The sums are both 25, so the expression is symmetric under this swap
The sums are 23 and 25, so this expression is not symmetric
The sums are 14 and 14, so the expression is symmetric under this swap
optionExplain: The first sum is 23 but the swapped one is 25; equal values would be needed for symmetry.
The swapped sum is 25 but the original is 23; equal values would be needed for symmetry.
Right: 1*1*2 + 2*2*3 + 3*3*1 = 23 and, with x and y swapped, 2*2*1 + 1*1*3 + 3*3*2 = 25. One swap that changes the value is enough to show it is not symmetric.
14 is the value of x + 2y + 3z or similar sums, not of either arrangement here.
questions.explain: A single swap that changes the value shows the expression is not symmetric.
questions.rule: Compute both sums with the given values.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Which expressions are unchanged when any two of x, y, z are interchanged?
