options: x + 2y + 3z
x + y + z
x squared y + y squared z + z squared x
x squared + y squared + z squared
optionExplain: Not symmetric: the letters have different weights.
Symmetric: every letter plays the same role.
Not symmetric: swapping x and y changes it.
Symmetric: each letter appears in the same way.
questions.explain: Symmetric means any swap leaves the expression unchanged; cyclic or weighted forms fail.
questions.rule: Swap any two and compare.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The author says symmetries differ in two respects. Which?
options: The number of interchangeable parts and the operations which exchange the parts
The size and the color of the parts, and the material from which the whole is made
The age and the material of the whole, and the place in which the whole is found
The length and the weight of the parts, and the order in which they are listed
optionExplain: Right: the cube has many interchangeable parts, the expression has three letters.
Size and color are not what the author names; the differences are in the number of parts and in the exchanging operations.
Age and material are not mentioned.
Length and weight are not mentioned.
questions.explain: The cube has many interchangeable parts, the expression only three letters; kinds of symmetry also differ in the operations that exchange the parts.
questions.rule: Look for parts that can be swapped without changing the whole.
questions.teaches: There are many kinds of symmetry; they differ in the number of interchangeable parts, and in the operations which exchange the parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A soccer league table treats all 20 clubs by the same rules, so any two clubs can swap names in the rules without change. In the general sense, is the rule set symmetric?
options: No, because soccer is not geometry, so the idea of symmetry cannot be used about it
No, because the clubs differ in size and in strength, so they are not interchangeable
Only if there are exactly 6 clubs, because 6 is the number of faces of a cube
Yes in the general sense: the clubs are interchangeable parts under the rules
optionExplain: The general sense is not limited to geometry.
Size differences do not affect the rules' interchangeability.
The number 6 belongs to the cube's faces, not to the definition.
Right: interchangeability is what makes a whole symmetric. Our reading: this is an illustration of the general sense, not an example from the book.
questions.explain: The clubs play the same role under the rules, so they are interchangeable parts; this is our illustration of the general sense.
questions.rule: Look for parts that can be swapped without changing the whole.
questions.teaches: A cube has high symmetry: its 6 faces are interchangeable with each other, and so are its 8 vertices, and so are its 12 edges.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A problem has three quantities that play identical roles. Which handling is wise?
options: Pick one quantity and process it first, with a special trick
Treat all three in the same way, without favouring one
Ignore the symmetry and handle each as if unrelated
Remove two quantities from the problem
optionExplain: Favouring one breaks a natural symmetry.
Right: symmetric roles call for symmetric treatment.
Ignoring symmetry wastes it, since interchangeable parts can be treated alike to save work.
Removing quantities changes the problem.
questions.explain: Treat symmetrically what is symmetrical. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: Treat symmetrically what is symmetrical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Try to treat symmetrically what is symmetrical, and do not destroy ____ any natural symmetry.
questions.explain: The author asks us not to break a natural symmetry without reason.
questions.rule: Do not destroy natural symmetry wantonly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The expression a*b + b*c + c*a must be bounded in terms of a, b and c. Which plan respects the symmetry?
options: Set a to zero first, then look at what is left, since a simpler case comes first
Use the same step on each pair of letters, so no letter is favoured
Solve for a in terms of b and c, and then substitute the result into the other terms
Replace b by a and c by a at once, which favours a and gives a single quantity to handle
optionExplain: That removes the symmetry at the start.
Right: every letter plays the same role, so every pair is handled alike.
Solving for a first singles out a, which breaks the symmetry between the three letters.
Replacing b and c by a favours a, so the three letters are no longer treated alike.
questions.explain: Every letter plays the same role, so apply the same step to each pair and do not favour any letter.
questions.rule: Check that no letter gets special treatment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, noticing the interchangeable parts of a symmetric problem may be profitable.
questions.explain: It often pays to treat the parts which play the same role in the same fashion.
questions.rule: Noticing symmetry pays.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: The symmetry entry sends the reader to AUXILIARY ELEMENTS, section 3. For which advice?
options: To introduce a notation that is easy to retain and that can be recalled without effort
To test an assertion on its extreme cases and see whether it survives them or not
To break a natural symmetry as early as possible, so that the parts are handled one by one
To treat in the same fashion those parts of a problem that play the same role
optionExplain: Notation is a different topic; the cross reference is for treating alike the parts with the same role.
Extreme cases belong to specialization.
The entry says not to destroy natural symmetry wantonly.
Right: the cross-reference supports treating alike what plays the same role.
questions.explain: The cross reference is for the advice to treat in the same fashion the parts that play the same role.
questions.rule: Treat symmetrically what is symmetrical.
questions.teaches: The book refers the reader to AUXILIARY ELEMENTS, section 3, for the advice to treat in the same fashion those parts which play the same role.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A committee must give tasks to four identical-role members. Which approach follows the advice?
options: Rotate tasks so each member is treated alike over time
Give the hardest task to one member always
Remove symmetry by choosing a leader at random each day
Ignore the roles and assign by mood
optionExplain: Right: identical roles call for like treatment.
Giving the hardest task to one member favours that member, which breaks the equal treatment the advice asks for.
Random leaders break the equal treatment.
Mood-based assignment ignores the symmetry.
questions.explain: Four members of identical role should be treated alike, for instance by rotating tasks, not by favouring one.
questions.rule: Treat symmetrically what is symmetrical.
questions.teaches: If a problem is symmetric in some ways we may derive some profit from noticing its interchangeable parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A pair of gloves is symmetrical. How do people put them on?
options: Both at the same moment, using both hands together
Right first, because most people favour the right hand
One after the other, not both at once
Left first, to keep the stronger hand free
optionExplain: Few people can manage both gloves at the same moment; the author says nobody handles the pair quite symmetrically.
No fixed order is implied; the point is that one glove goes on after the other.
Right: we are compelled to treat what is symmetrical unsymmetrically.
No fixed order is implied; either hand may go first, so long as it is one after the other.
questions.explain: A limit of symmetry. The card next gives the point.
questions.rule: Treat unsymmetrically only when compelled; test results for the symmetry the problem has.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: True or false: the author admits that we are sometimes compelled to treat unsymmetrically what is symmetrical by nature.
questions.explain: The author gives the pair of gloves as his example: they are symmetrical, yet nobody puts both on at once.
questions.rule: Symmetry cannot always be kept.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A problem treats the unknowns x, y and z alike in every condition, yet a solver's answer gives 2, 2 and 9. What does symmetry suggest?
options: The answer is correct, since any three numbers can be a solution
The answer is wrong, since symmetric problems have equal unknowns only
Symmetry has no bearing on checking, since it is a property of figures
The answer deserves a check, since it treats equal roles unequally
optionExplain: Equal roles make an unequal answer unusual, though not impossible, so the check should not be skipped.
Our reading: a symmetric problem may still have an asymmetric answer, so equal unknowns are not required.
The author says symmetry may be useful in checking results, and the general sense applies to problems, not only figures.
Right: symmetry is useful in checking results. Our reading: unequal values can be correct, so this is a prompt to check, not a verdict.
questions.explain: Equal roles making an unequal answer is a reason to check; our reading is that an asymmetric answer can still be correct.
questions.rule: Compare the answer with the symmetry of the data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Sort each case by whether symmetric treatment is kept or has to be given up.

items.t: Applying the same step to each of three equal-role letters
Putting on a pair of gloves
Adding the three terms of yz + zx + xy in any order
Reading the two words of a sentence, one after the other

questions.explain: Where the activity has to be done in sequence, we are compelled to break the symmetry.
questions.rule: Sequence breaks symmetry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: Besides guiding how to treat a problem, what further use of symmetry does the author mention?
options: Finding the unknown directly from the data
Checking results once they are found
Choosing a suitable notation for the problem
Sorting problems into those with and without solutions
optionExplain: Symmetry guides treatment of the parts; it does not give the unknown by itself.
Right: the entry says symmetry may also be useful in checking results, and points to the section on checking.
Notation is the topic of another entry, not of this remark.
Nothing in the entry classifies problems by symmetry.
questions.explain: The symmetry entry says symmetry may also be useful in checking results and points to a section on checking.
questions.rule: Treat unsymmetrically only when compelled; test results for the symmetry the problem has.
questions.teaches: Symmetry may also be useful in checking results; the entry sends the reader to section 14 on checking.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Setting Up Equations to Symmetry
questions.q: A recipe divides a bill equally among three friends, but only one can pay at the till. What does the gloves example suggest?
options: All three must pay at the same instant, because equal shares call for equal timing too
The shares should be unequal, because one person pays first and so carries more of the bill
The act of paying must be unsymmetrical in time, though the shares stay symmetric
Symmetry has no place in sharing, since the act of paying is already unsymmetrical in time
optionExplain: That is what the gloves example denies.
Equal roles do not call for unequal shares.
Right: the process is sequential even if the shares are equal. Our reading: the bill is a fresh illustration.
Equal shares keep the symmetry of the roles; only the act of paying is sequential.
questions.explain: The roles stay symmetric, with equal shares, even though the act of paying must happen one person after another.
questions.rule: Treat unsymmetrically only when compelled; test results for the symmetry the problem has.
questions.teaches: A pair of gloves is certainly symmetrical; nevertheless, nobody handles the pair quite symmetrically, nobody puts on both gloves at the same time, but one after the other.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Why might a book about solving problems avoid a familiar word and coin a new one?
options: The familiar word is too old for modern readers to understand, so only recent words can be trusted
New words make a method look more scientific than it is, and that appearance is the reason given
The familiar word is used in different senses by different authors, so readers may take it the wrong way
A familiar word has never been used by earlier writers on the subject, so a new one is needed
optionExplain: Age is not the issue; the trouble is that the word carries more than one meaning.
The book gives no such motive; it is worried about confusion, not appearance.
Right: shared words with several meanings mislead, so a plain new term can be safer.
Earlier authors did use such words, which is exactly why they clash.
questions.explain: A word that different writers use in different ways can mislead a reader. The card next shows how the book handles this.
questions.rule: Ambiguity, not age, is the reason to drop a term.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The author says terms for solving problems are often ____ because different authors use the same word in different meanings.
questions.explain: Ambiguity is the book's complaint: the same word is used in different senses.
questions.rule: One word, several meanings, is the trouble.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, no technical terms exist for solving problems because people rarely do it and so have not discussed it.
questions.explain: The author says the opposite: the activity is familiar to everybody and often discussed. It is hard to describe, and there has been no systematic study.
questions.rule: Familiar does not mean easy to name.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A team handbook uses the word review for a code check, for a weekly meeting and for a written report. What fits the book's approach?
options: Give each meaning its own term, or fix one meaning for the word and say which one is meant
Keep the word as it is and let each reader work out the meaning from the context of the passage
Drop all technical words and describe everything loosely, so that no word can carry a second meaning
Define the word once at the start and then go on using it freely in all three senses afterwards
optionExplain: Right: this is what the book does, introducing new terms or avoiding a word when meanings collide.
Guessing is the very risk the author warns about when meanings differ.
Loose description loses precision; the book still wants clear terms.
A definition that is then broken by mixed use recreates the ambiguity.
questions.explain: The book answers ambiguity by separating meanings, either with new terms or by avoiding the clashing word.
questions.rule: Separate the meanings or keep to one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: According to the author, what risk does a reader run when meeting the list of terms for the first time?
options: Mistaking every old term for a new one, because the list does not label which terms are which
Being confused by it, unless their ideas about problems are already anchored in examples
Learning the avoided terms well and forgetting the retained ones, because the list is too long
Believing that all the terms in the list have only one meaning, because the author defines them
optionExplain: The list does separate new, avoided and retained terms, so labels are not the problem.
Right: the author warns that the discussion may confuse a reader whose notions are not anchored in examples.
Nothing in the text suggests a memory trap; the warning is about understanding.
The list is about ambiguity, so it does not push readers toward single meanings.
questions.explain: The author advises reading the terms with worked examples in mind, because terminology without examples is hard to hold.
questions.rule: Anchor terms in examples.
questions.teaches: The author warns that the terminology discussion may confuse a reader whose notions are not well anchored in examples.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A cookbook introduction lists words it uses in a special sense, some it avoids and some it keeps despite two meanings. What does this copy from the book?
options: A strict ban on every word that has more than one meaning, whatever its use in the field
A list that includes only words the author invented personally, with a reason for each invention
A rule that retained words must be used in all their meanings, so that none is ever lost
The list of new, avoided and retained terms, with ambiguity as the reason for each choice
optionExplain: The author keeps some ambiguous old terms, so there is no total ban.
The book also lists old terms it avoids, not only new ones.
Keeping a term does not mean using every sense; the author separates them.
Right: the book sorts terms into new, avoided and retained, and ambiguity is its concern.
questions.explain: The book's list has three groups: new terms used, old terms avoided and old terms retained despite ambiguity.
questions.rule: Say which terms are new, avoided or kept.
questions.teaches: The author's list contains three kinds of entry: new terms used, old terms avoided, and old terms retained despite their ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which description matches analysis as Pappus defined it?
options: Start from the unknown or the conclusion and work backwards toward the data or the hypothesis
Separate a chemical compound into the substances it is made of, one by one, and name each
Start from the data and work forward step by step until the unknown is reached at the end
Divide an argument into its premises and its conclusion, and judge each one in turn on its merits
optionExplain: Right: Pappus's analysis works backwards from what is wanted toward what is given.
This is chemical analysis, one of the other meanings that made the word unsafe.
Going forward from the data is the opposite direction.
This is logical analysis, another meaning of the same word.
questions.explain: Pappus's sense has a direction: from the unknown backwards to the data. The card next lists what the book does about the word.
questions.rule: Analysis in Pappus's sense runs backwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Pappus's analysis starts from the unknown (or the conclusion) and works backwards toward the ____ (or the hypothesis).
questions.explain: The data (or hypothesis) are where the backward path ends.
questions.rule: Unknown back to data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A route planner starts at the destination and traces roads back until it reaches the traveller's start. Which old term fits?
options: Progressive reasoning, used by some authors in the old meaning of synthesis
Chemical analysis, because it breaks the route into small parts
Regressive reasoning, used by some authors in the old meaning of analysis
Hypothesis, because the destination is assumed in advance
optionExplain: That term was sometimes used for the opposite direction, from the data toward the unknown.
Chemical analysis is another sense of the word and has no direction from a goal.
Right: working backwards from the goal is the direction of analysis, which regressive reasoning named.
Hypothesis is a part of a theorem, not a way of reasoning.
questions.explain: Working back from the goal to the givens is analysis in Pappus's sense; some authors called it regressive reasoning.
questions.rule: Backward from the goal is regressive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Match each term to what the book says about it.
pairs: Defined neatly by Pappus; acquired other meanings, so avoided
Well defined by Pappus, but avoided like its counterpart
Used by some in the old meaning of synthesis; avoided
Used by some in the old meaning of analysis; avoided
questions.explain: All four are avoided, each for the same family of reasons: several authors have used them with different senses.
questions.rule: Four terms, one reason: shifting meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The book calls the old use of progressive reasoning defensible. Why does it avoid the term anyway?
options: The old use is a mathematical mistake that the book corrects by dropping the word in favour of a better one
Defensible use can still be one of several meanings, and the book wants a vocabulary without clashes
Pappus himself rejected the term in his own writing, and the author is following that rejection here
The term is unnecessary because the method it names is not used in solving problems at all
optionExplain: The book does not call it a mistake; it calls the usage defensible.
Right: the book says the usage is defensible, yet the term is avoided.
Pappus is cited as defining analysis and synthesis, not as rejecting these terms.
The method is used in the book; only the label is dropped.
questions.explain: Avoidance is not condemnation: a term can be defensible and still be left out because several authors give it different senses.
questions.rule: Defensible is not the same as unambiguous.
questions.teaches: The author calls the old use of progressive reasoning defensible, yet avoids the term; avoiding a term does not mean it is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A manual avoids the word upstream because it has two meanings. It also uses the pair word downstream. What does the book's treatment of synthesis suggest?
options: Keep the counterpart, since a word with a clear meaning of its own never needs to be removed
Keep the counterpart but redefine it to mean the opposite of upstream, so that the pair stays balanced
Drop the counterpart only if readers complain about it, since its own meaning is clear
Drop the counterpart too, even if its own meaning is clear, for the same reasons
optionExplain: The book shows a clear word being dropped because it forms a pair with an avoided one.
Redefining a word does not fix a pair whose partner is ambiguous.
The book gives no reader-complaint test; it gives reasons based on the pair.
Right: the book avoids synthesis, though Pappus defined it well, for the same reasons as analysis.
questions.explain: Synthesis, defined well by Pappus and worth conserving, is still avoided with its counterpart analysis.
questions.rule: A pair of terms may be dropped together.
questions.teaches: Synthesis is avoided although Pappus's meaning deserves to be conserved, for the same reasons as its counterpart, analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A problem has a condition with two separate requirements. What is the best name for each requirement?
options: Another condition, since each requirement is itself a condition in the usual way of speaking
A hypothesis, since a requirement is something that is assumed in order to start
A clause of the condition, so the word condition stays for the whole
A datum, since each requirement is something that is given in the statement of the problem
optionExplain: This is common usage, but it is the ambiguity the book finds embarrassing.
Hypothesis belongs to theorems to prove, not to the requirement of a problem to find.
Right: the book would reserve condition for the whole and give the parts another name.
Data are the given objects, not the requirements that link them to the unknown.
questions.explain: Using one word for whole and part is the problem; the card next names the book's fix.
questions.rule: Whole: condition; part: clause.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The book suggests calling each part of a whole condition or hypothesis a ____.
questions.explain: The suggested technical term is clause.
questions.rule: Parts get a separate word.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A contract's payment section has three requirements. Following the book's idea, how should a careful reader describe the section and its requirements?
options: Each requirement and the section are all called the payment section, so one name serves all
The payment section is the whole, and each requirement is a clause of it
Only the largest requirement is counted as part of the section; the others are ignored
The section is dropped from the discussion and only the separate requirements are talked about
optionExplain: One name for all of them keeps the ambiguity.
Right: one name for the whole and another for its parts removes the ambiguity.
The book never suggests ignoring parts; it wants them named.
Dropping the whole loses the link that the term for the whole provides.
questions.explain: The remedy is a second word for the parts, so statements about the whole and about a part cannot be confused.
questions.rule: Name the whole and the parts separately.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: The author finds the term hypothesis unclear even when it is applied to the whole assumption of a theorem.
questions.explain: He calls the term perfectly clear and satisfactory in that meaning; the difficulty is that each part is also called a hypothesis.
questions.rule: The whole sense is clear; the part sense collides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Condition is called clear, useful and unavoidable. What does that imply for the ambiguity in its use for parts?
options: The term is kept and the ambiguity is fixed by a separate word for the parts, not by dropping the term
The term must be dropped, since an ambiguous term cannot be useful to anyone who reasons carefully
Only the plural form should be used for the whole, and the singular kept for each part
The parts should be called conditions and the whole should be called a super-condition instead
optionExplain: Right: the author keeps terms that are unavoidable and repairs them.
The author keeps condition because it cannot be avoided.
No plural rule is mentioned.
The book proposes a fresh word, clause, not a compound of the same one.
questions.explain: Some ambiguous terms stay because they are unavoidable; the repair is a new word for the parts.
questions.rule: Keep what is unavoidable and repair it.
questions.teaches: The author calls condition a clear, useful and unavoidable term, so he keeps it and suggests a separate word for its parts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A rulebook says every rule is made of smaller rules, all called rule. Which fix copies the book's remedy for condition and hypothesis?
options: Call every smaller piece a rule and every larger piece a rule too
Replace the word rule by hypothesis throughout
Keep rule for the whole and call each smaller piece a clause
Number the rules and ban the word rule
optionExplain: That repeats the ambiguity.
Hypothesis is another term with the same whole-and-part problem.
Right: reserve one word for the whole and give the pieces their own.
Numbering can help in practice, but the book's remedy is a separate technical word.
questions.explain: The same word for a whole and for its parts is the trouble in both condition and hypothesis; clause is the book's example of a fix.
questions.rule: One word per level.
questions.teaches: The book notes that the same remedy, calling each part a clause or something similar, applies to hypothesis as to condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Why replace old names for the two kinds of problem with new ones?
options: The old names were invented by the author himself and were never used by anyone else
The old names changed meaning in modern usage, so they no longer mark the distinction
The old names refer only to problems from geometry, so they do not suit other branches
The old names are too short to describe the two kinds, so longer names are needed
optionExplain: The old names came from Latin versions of Greek texts, not from the author.
Right: current usage confused them.
Nothing in the text limits them to geometry.
Length is not the issue; shifting meaning is.
questions.explain: Meaning drift, not length or origin, is the reason. The card next gives the Latin names and the replacement.
questions.rule: Replace terms whose meaning has drifted.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Match each Latin name to what it named in Latin versions of Greek texts.
pairs: Both kinds of problem under one common name
questions.explain: Propositio covered both kinds; problema meant a problem to find and theorema a problem to prove.
questions.rule: Three Latin names, two kinds.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A textbook author writes: This theorem asks you to find the length of the side. Judged by the old Euclidean meanings, what is odd?
options: A theorema was a problem to prove, so asking for a length mixes the two kinds
A theorema was a problem to find, so the sentence asking for a length is correct as it stands
A theorema named both kinds of problem, so no mistake is possible in the sentence
Euclid never used the word theorem at all, so the sentence cannot be judged by his usage
optionExplain: Right: old usage kept the two kinds apart; a theorem asked for a proof.
That reverses the Latin names: problema meant a problem to find.
The common name for both kinds was propositio, not theorema.
The Latin version names theorema, so the word was in use.
questions.explain: In the old scheme, theorema meant problem to prove and problema meant problem to find.
questions.rule: Find: problema. Prove: theorema.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a reader trained in modern mathematical language can read proposition, problem and theorem in their Euclidean sense without confusion.
questions.explain: He says that meaning has completely changed in modern language, which is why he introduced new terms.
questions.rule: Modern usage is not Euclidean usage.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: How does the author describe his own feeling about replacing the historical terms?
options: He did it eagerly, since the old terms were wrong from the start and deserved to be removed
He did it casually, because terms matter little to the method and any names would serve
He did it under pressure from mathematicians who disliked Latin and wanted modern names
He introduced the new pair regretfully, since the old meaning was confused beyond redemption
optionExplain: He speaks of regret, and the terms were not wrong in their own era.
He treats the matter seriously enough to explain it.
No such pressure is mentioned.
Right: the text says regretfully, and says confusion made it justified.
questions.explain: Replacement is a last resort: the author takes it only because current usage has made the old words useless.
questions.rule: Replace old words only when they cannot be rescued.
questions.teaches: The author introduced problem to find and problem to prove regretfully, because current usage had confused the historical terms beyond redemption.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A law student must keep two kinds of case apart, but the words for them have drifted. Which step copies the book's approach?
options: Keep the old words and trust readers to remember the old senses when they meet them
Drop the distinction altogether, since the words for the two kinds are unclear now
Introduce a clear pair of names and say why the old words no longer work
Use the old words for both kinds together, as propositio did in the Latin versions
optionExplain: The book says that is the failure: current usage confuses the old senses.
The distinction between the two kinds remains important in the method.
Right: the book retires the words and states the reason.
Propositio did cover both, but the point of the new pair is to separate them.
questions.explain: A new pair of terms is justified when the old names have drifted beyond repair, and the book says so openly.
questions.rule: Retire drifted names and explain why.
questions.teaches: Old-fashioned mathematical language still keeps the Euclidean meanings of proposition, problem and theorem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Someone says: The solution took three days, and it is a beautiful solution. What is unclear?
options: The two uses name different things, the work and its result, apart from the objects satisfying the condition
Nothing is unclear, since both uses name the same answer to the problem
The word solution can only be used for the roots of an equation, not for work or results
Beauty cannot be a property of mathematics, so the phrase beautiful solution is meaningless
optionExplain: Right: solution can mean the process, the result of the process, or the object satisfying the condition.
The two uses differ: one is about time spent, the other about elegance.
The book uses an equation as an example, not as a restriction.
The book accepts beautiful solution as ordinary usage; it is not condemned.
questions.explain: Solution has several meanings that a single sentence may mix. The card next sorts them.
questions.rule: Check what the word names.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: In its purely mathematical meaning, a solution is any object satisfying the ____ of a problem to find.
questions.explain: The solution is an object, not a process; it satisfies the condition.
questions.rule: Solution means object satisfying the condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The equation x squared minus 3x plus 2 equals 0 has roots 1 and 2. In the book's pure sense, what are 1 and 2?
options: Its data, because they were given to us at the start of the problem
Its solutions, because each satisfies the condition of the problem to find
Its conditions, because they limit which numbers the equation allows
Its work, because they come from the process of solving the equation
optionExplain: The data of the problem are the coefficients; the roots are what we find.
Right: roots are the objects satisfying the equation, hence its solutions.
The condition is the equation itself.
Work is the process; the roots are an object.
questions.explain: In the pure sense, a solution is an object. Check by substitution: 1 gives 1 minus 3 plus 2 equal to 0, and 2 gives 4 minus 6 plus 2 equal to 0.
questions.rule: Roots are solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each term by what the book does with it.

items.t: Analysis
Synthesis
Progressive reasoning
Regressive reasoning
Problem to find
Problem to prove
Condition
Hypothesis

questions.explain: The four reasoning terms are avoided; the two new kinds of problem are introduced, and condition and hypothesis are kept, with clause as the remedy for parts.
questions.rule: Avoided: four reasoning terms.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: What does the author say can happen when one sentence calls the object, the work and the result all solution?
options: The sentence becomes clearer, since the repetition ties the three together
The sentence becomes wrong, but only for a reader who is not a mathematician
The sentence cannot be too clear, since the reader cannot tell which meaning is meant
The sentence is unchanged, since mathematicians use the three meanings together without confusion
optionExplain: Repetition of one word for three things hides distinctions.
The problem concerns clarity, not the reader's training.
Right: the text says the sentence cannot be too clear.
The text says mathematicians do use the meanings together, but warns about the sentence.
questions.explain: Mathematicians use all three meanings, which is the source of the muddle when they meet in one sentence.
questions.rule: Three meanings in one sentence blur.
questions.teaches: Mathematicians themselves use solution in all three meanings, along with the purely mathematical one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A software report says: The fix was hard, and the fix is elegant, and the fix removes the fault. What does the book's warning suggest?
options: Repeat fix throughout, since using the same word every time makes the report consistent
Replace fix by solution, since solution has only one meaning in a technical report
Leave the sentence alone, since three meanings of one word never confuse a careful reader
Use one word for the code change and other words for the effort and the result
optionExplain: Consistency of word is what hides the three meanings.
Solution itself has three meanings in the book.
The warning says confusion is likely, not that it never happens.
Right: separate the object, the work and the result.
questions.explain: The book's advice: when object, work and result are all in play, give each its own word.
questions.rule: One word, one role.
questions.teaches: The book speaks of a difficult solution when solution means the work of solving, and of a beautiful solution when it means the result of that work.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student writes the area of a circle of radius r (in metres) as 2 pi r. What is suspicious about it?
options: The number 2 should be 4, since areas are larger than lengths
Pi should not appear in an area formula
The radius should be cubed, since an area needs a higher power than a length
Area should be in square metres, but 2 pi r comes out in metres
optionExplain: Changing a number cannot repair a mismatch of dimension; a numerical factor has dimension 1.
Pi appears in the correct area formula; the problem is how the radius enters.
A cube would give a volume; the area needs the square, so the power of r is the real issue.
Right: the dimensions on the two sides do not match.
questions.explain: Dimensions alone show something is off: a length cannot equal an area. The card next states the test.
questions.rule: Lengths, areas and volumes cannot be equated.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Quantities can be added only if they have the same ____.
questions.explain: Only quantities of the same dimension can be added.
questions.rule: A sum needs one dimension.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Radius r and height h are lengths in cm. Which candidate for the total surface area of a closed cylinder passes the test?
optionExplain: Right: r times (r plus h) is a length times a length, and pi and 2 have dimension 1.
Two lengths add to a length, not to an area, so the result has the wrong dimension.
An area cannot be added to a length.
Four lengths multiplied give cm to the fourth power.
questions.explain: Compute each side: 2 pi r (r+h) is cm times cm, which is cm squared, the dimension of area.
questions.rule: Check each side and each sum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Lengths a, b, h are in cm. Sort each candidate formula for an area by whether it passes the test.

items.t: a * b + h
a squared + b * h
a + b + h
a * b * h
pi * a squared

questions.explain: A formula for area must give cm squared. Products of two lengths pass; adding a length to an area, adding lengths only, or multiplying three lengths do not.
questions.rule: Area means cm squared.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: In the frustum formula, the square root of \((R-r)^2+h^2\) appears. Why does it have the dimension of a length?
options: The square root of any sum is a pure number, so the root has dimension 1 and no unit
Both terms are cm squared, so the sum is cm squared, and its square root is cm
Squares of lengths cancel out of the sum, leaving only a plain number under the root
Square roots remove the dimension of whatever quantity stands under them, leaving a number
optionExplain: A root of a quantity with dimension still has a dimension unless the quantity is a pure number.
Right: sum of two cm squared terms stays cm squared, and the root halves the power.
Squares add; they do not cancel.
Roots halve the power but do not remove it.
questions.explain: A root is a power one half, and the rule for powers applies: cm squared to the power one half is cm.
questions.rule: Powers of dimensions follow the power rule.
questions.teaches: The dimension of a power follows a rule like that for products, so a square root of an area has the dimension of a length.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A free-fall distance s (cm) depends on g (cm sec to the minus 2) and time t (sec). Which formula passes the test?
options: \(s=g t\), since g times t is a distance covered in that time
\(s=g+t\), since both are quantities describing the motion of the body
\(s=\tfrac12 g t^2\), since cm sec to the minus 2 times sec squared is cm
\(s=g/t^2\), since dividing by time squared removes the time from the answer
optionExplain: g times t is cm per sec, a speed.
Acceleration and time have different dimensions, so they cannot be added.
Right: g times t squared gives cm, and one half has dimension 1.
g over t squared is cm per sec to the fourth.
questions.explain: The test applies to physics as well as geometry, and the author says it is even more important there.
questions.rule: The test matters most in physics.
questions.teaches: The author says the test by dimension is even more important in physics than in geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You recall two expressions for a sphere's area and volume but not which is which. What could settle it?
options: Compare the powers of the radius: area is a square, volume is a cube, so match them
Pick the expression with the larger coefficient as the volume, since volume is the bigger quantity
Pick the expression with a fraction in it as the area, since area is usually the smaller one
Nothing short of looking up a textbook can settle it, since both expressions contain pi
optionExplain: Right: area has dimension length squared and volume length cubed.
Coefficients do not carry dimension, so size of the coefficient says nothing.
A fraction has dimension 1, so it cannot signal area.
Dimensions give a quick check without a textbook.
questions.explain: The powers of the length decide. The card next states where the test can be used.
questions.rule: Area: square. Volume: cube.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: On which can the dimension test be used? Select all that apply.
options: Only the final answer of a finished problem
An intermediate result in your own work
Only formulas printed in a reliable textbook
A formula you recollect but are unsure of
A formula you have guessed
optionExplain: The text applies it also to intermediate results.
Right: the test needs only a formula, not a finished problem.
Source does not matter to the test.
Right: a recalled formula can be checked in a moment.
Right: a guess can be tested before it is trusted.
questions.explain: The test does not depend on where a formula comes from, so it applies to recollected and guessed formulas and to results at any stage.
questions.rule: Test at any stage.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student's answer for the volume of a cube of edge a is \(6a^2\). What does the test show?
options: The result passes, because 6 is a pure number and a squared is a length measure
The result fails only if a is not measured in centimetres, and passes in other units
The result is in cm squared, so it cannot be a volume; it matches a surface area instead
The result is correct, since an edge appears squared and that gives volume
optionExplain: The number 6 has dimension 1, but a squared decides the dimension.
The mismatch holds in whatever unit of length is used.
Right: a volume must be cm cubed, and 6a squared is cm squared (it is in fact the total surface area).
Squares belong to areas, not volumes.
questions.explain: A cube's volume needs the third power of the edge. The test spots the wrong power at once.
questions.rule: Wrong power, wrong dimension.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: The dimension test can be used only when the whole problem is finished and the final formula is known.
questions.explain: It applies equally to intermediate results, so mistakes can be caught while the work is still in progress.
questions.rule: Use it midway too.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A teacher marks an examination paper with a wrong formula in line 5. How can the test help, according to the author?
options: It is useless on another person's work, as it needs your own notation and your own symbols
It gives the correct formula, so the student's wrong line can be replaced at once
It works only on the last line of a paper, where the final result stands
It helps trace where the mistake entered, since it works on the work of others
optionExplain: Dimensions are visible in anyone's work.
It shows that a formula is wrong, not what the right one is.
It works on any line that carries a formula.
Right: the author calls the test very suitable for tracing mistakes in examination papers.
questions.explain: The test is a tool for checking other people's work as well as your own.
questions.rule: Use it on other people's work too.
questions.teaches: The author recommends the test as very suitable for tracing mistakes in examination papers, that is, in the work of others.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A hobbyist designs a spherical tank and half-remembers its surface and volume as \(4\pi r^2\) and \(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\). What does the test tell them?
options: The first has dimension cm squared, so it is the area; the second has cm cubed, so it is the volume
The two cannot be told apart, since both contain pi and a numerical fraction
The larger result is always the volume, so one compares their sizes
Both are volumes, since r is a length and a length cubed gives a volume
optionExplain: Right: matching the powers of the radius removes the doubt.
Pi has dimension 1, so it carries no hint, but the powers of r do.
Which is larger depends on the radius; only the dimension is reliable.
Dimension decides: squared is an area.
questions.explain: The author gives exactly this pair as his example of how the test removes doubt about recollected formulas.
questions.rule: Powers of the radius tell area from volume.
questions.teaches: The author's example is the pair \(4\pi r^2\) and \(4\pi r^3/3\) for a sphere, where the test shows which is area and which is volume.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A pendulum's wire is made four times as long, with everything else unchanged. How does the period change?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It quadruples
It increases sixteen-fold
optionExplain: Length matters: the period depends on length and gravity.
Right: the period grows with the square root of the length, as the card shows.
Quadrupling would mean the period grows in proportion to length.
Sixteen times would need the period to grow as the square of the length.
questions.explain: The period grows as the square root of the length, so four times the length gives twice the period. The card shows how dimensions give that.
questions.rule: Period grows as the square root of length.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: To fix the exponents m and n, the powers of each basic unit must be ____ on both sides of the dimension equation.
questions.explain: Matching powers of cm and of sec gives two equations for the two exponents.
questions.rule: Match the powers on both sides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A body falls from rest through a height h (cm) with gravity g (cm sec to the minus 2). Its speed v is c times h to the m times g to the n. Find m and n.
options: m = 1 and n = 1
m = 1 and n = 0
optionExplain: That gives cm squared per sec squared; the powers do not match.
Right: cm per sec equals cm to (m+n) times sec to (-2n), so -2n = -1 and m+n = 1.
These are the pendulum exponents; the speed needs sec to the minus 1, not plus 1.
That leaves no sec at all, so the time dimension is missing.
questions.explain: Matching sec: -2n = -1, so n = 1/2. Matching cm: m + n = 1, so m = 1/2. The speed has the form c times the square root of g h.
questions.rule: Match each unit separately.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Using the form T = c times the square root of l over g, match each change of the wire length to the change of the period.
questions.explain: The period varies as the square root of the length: the roots of 4, 9 and 16 are 2, 3 and 4.
questions.rule: Take the square root of the length factor.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Before using dimensions to find the form of T, what must the argument already know?
options: The numerical value of the constant c, since the exponents depend on it
That the swing is exactly harmonic at all angles, which the argument takes for granted
That T depends on l and g alone, which mechanical considerations show
The mass of the swinging body in grams, since the period depends on how heavy it is
optionExplain: The test does not give c; it cannot be an input.
Nothing is assumed about all angles; the formula is limited to small oscillations.
Right: the author starts from the statement that mechanical considerations show T depends on l and g alone.
Mass is not among the quantities T depends on.
questions.explain: The method only sorts exponents among quantities already known to matter.
questions.rule: List the relevant quantities first.
questions.teaches: The dimension argument starts from the statement, supplied by mechanical considerations, that T depends on l and g alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A rope stretches a lot as a weight swings on it. Which feature of the simple pendulum no longer holds?
options: The pendulum is supposed to hold a small body, and a stretching rope can hold one
The body is supposed to be heavy, and the weight on the rope is still heavy
The pendulum is supposed to hang under gravity, and the stretching rope still hangs so
The wire is supposed to have an invariable length
optionExplain: The size of the body is not what changed.
The body is still heavy.
Gravity still acts.
Right: a large stretch breaks the invariable length.
questions.explain: The simple pendulum is a small heavy body hung on a wire of invariable length and negligible weight.
questions.rule: Know the model's assumptions.
questions.teaches: The book's simple pendulum is a small heavy body suspended by a wire whose length is regarded as invariable and whose weight is regarded as negligible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A formula for an area passes the dimension test. What does this show?
options: That no dimension error was found, though a wrong numerical factor could remain
That the formula is correct, since a wrong formula would have failed the test
That the numerical factors in it are right, since the test checks the whole expression
That the formula is correct for all sizes of the figure, large or small
optionExplain: Right: passing rules out one kind of error only.
Passing does not prove correctness.
A wrong numerical factor has dimension 1 and passes unseen.
The range of validity is another thing the test cannot show.
questions.explain: The test removes only errors that show in the dimensions. The card next lists what it misses.
questions.rule: Passing is not proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The dimension test gives no information about the value of the numerical ____ in the pendulum formula.
questions.explain: The constant is a pure number, so it has dimension 1 and the test cannot see it.
questions.rule: Constants are invisible to dimensions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student's formula for the area of a circle of radius r is \(3.14\,r^2\cdot 2\). It passes the test. What follows?
options: The factor 2 is right, since the formula passed the dimension test as written
The factor 2 is wrong, but the test cannot detect it
The formula fails, since 3.14 is not a length and so cannot be a factor
The formula is right whenever r is measured in centimetres, whatever the factor
optionExplain: Passing is only necessary for correctness, not sufficient.
Right: all the numerical factors have dimension 1.
Pure numbers have dimension 1; they need not be lengths.
The unit chosen for r does not matter.
questions.explain: The area is 3.14 r squared; the extra 2 is a pure number the test cannot flag.
questions.rule: Pure numbers are invisible.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each claim by whether the dimension test alone can settle it.

items.t: Area given in cm cubed is wrong
A length cannot be added to an area
The exponents of l and g in the pendulum formula
The constant c is 2 pi
A missing factor of one half
The pendulum formula is exact for large swings

questions.explain: Dimensions fix the powers of the quantities involved but not the numerical constants or the range of validity.
questions.rule: Exponents yes; constants and ranges no.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Dimensions gave T proportional to the square root of l/g. What does the author add about the formula?
options: The constant is 1, and the formula is exact for any swing
The constant is 2 pi, and the formula is exact only for infinitely small oscillations, otherwise approximate
The constant is 2 pi, and the formula is exact for every swing
The constant is unknown, and the formula is valid only for heavy bodies
optionExplain: The constant is not 1.
Right: c is 2 pi, and the validity limit is small oscillations.
The formula is valid only for small oscillations, and only approximately.
The constant is known, and the limit concerns the size of the swing, not heaviness.
questions.explain: The test does not give either of these facts; they come from fuller mechanical treatment.
questions.rule: Constants and ranges need other means.
questions.teaches: The constant c in the pendulum formula is 2 pi, and the formula is valid only approximately, exactly for infinitely small oscillations.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: An engineer wonders whether a quick dimension argument is worth doing when the full result needs advanced mathematics. What does the book say?
options: It can replace the advanced treatment completely, since it gives the form of the result
It is worthless, since it cannot give constants or the range where a formula holds
It lets one foresee an essential part of the result quickly with elementary means, in many similar cases
It works only for pendulums, where the dependence on length and gravity is simple
optionExplain: The author says it cannot yield everything.
The author values it despite that limitation.
Right: despite its limitations the test foresees an essential part of the result.
The text says this holds in many similar cases.
questions.explain: The test is a quick first look, not a replacement for the full treatment.
questions.rule: Use dimensions for a quick forecast.
questions.teaches: Despite its limits, the dimension test lets us foresee quickly and with elementary means an essential part of a result whose exhaustive treatment needs much more advanced means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You have finished a hard problem after hours of work. What is the most valuable next step?
options: Review the solution and your path to it, asking what the key idea was and what slowed you
Start the next problem at once, while your energy and your concentration last
Memorise the final answer, so that you can recall it later when it is needed
Show the answer to a friend, and move on if it matches what the friend has
optionExplain: Right: reflection on the finished work is where the learning is.
Starting at once skips the step that turns one solved problem into skill.
The answer alone is the least reusable part of the work.
A matching answer says the result is right, not what the work taught.
questions.explain: Reflection on the solution and the path to it is the step this entry stresses. The card next says why.
questions.rule: Look back before moving on.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: For the future mathematician, the most important part of the work is to ____ back at the completed solution.
questions.explain: The author stresses looking back at the finished solution and the course of the work.
questions.rule: Look back.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You solved a scheduling puzzle by trying every case. Which follow-up best matches the author's advice?
options: Write the answer out neatly and file it, so that it is complete and tidy for later
Ask whether a short intuitive idea explains the answer at a glance, and whether another method reaches it
Check the arithmetic again and leave the method alone, since the method already worked
Ask only how fast you solved it compared with other people who tried the puzzle
optionExplain: Filing the answer stops the reflection the author values.
Right: the author suggests looking for simple intuitive ideas and for different derivations.
Rechecking arithmetic is a check on the result, not a look at the method.
Speed against others is not among the things the author suggests observing.
questions.explain: Two of the author's questions: can you see it at a glance, and can you derive the result differently.
questions.rule: Seek the glance and a second route.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each activity by whether the author lists it as part of looking back at a solution.

items.t: Meditate on the decisive idea and on what hampered or helped you
Look for a simple intuitive way to see the result
Try to derive the result in a different way
Put the notes away so the solution does not bias the next problem
Rewrite the proof in the most formal style available
Rank yourself against other solvers

questions.explain: The author's looking back is about the difficulty, the decisive idea, intuition and other derivations. Hiding the solution, formal rewriting and ranking are not on his list.
questions.rule: Study the work itself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: According to the author, what can the future mathematician do with a freshly completed solution besides studying it?
options: Forget the method on purpose, so that it does not limit later thinking about new problems
Keep the answer and discard the method, which was only a tool for getting the answer
Compare the problem with problems solved before and invent new problems he can solve on the basis of the completed work
Move on to a harder problem without reviewing the easier one, since reviewing is slow
optionExplain: The author wants the method kept and developed.
The method is what carries over to other problems.
Right: the author lists comparison with earlier problems and the invention of new, solvable problems.
Reviewing is the point of the activity.
questions.explain: A finished problem is a source of new problems and links to old ones.
questions.rule: Solved problems breed new ones.
questions.teaches: The author suggests comparing the present problem with problems formerly solved, and inventing new problems that can be solved on the basis of the freshly completed work.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A programmer fixes a hard bug. Which habit copies the author's idea of digesting solved problems?
options: Close the ticket and avoid thinking about the bug again, since it is now fixed for good
Memorise the exact lines that were changed, so they can be pasted in next time
Record only how many hours it took, so that future estimates can be better
Write down what the root cause was, what misled them and what trick they can reuse
optionExplain: Closing without review leaves no knowledge to use.
The exact lines are the least general part.
Time spent does not tell you what to reuse.
Right: the author hopes digesting a solved problem as fully as possible gives well-ordered knowledge, ready to use.
questions.explain: Digesting solved problems as completely as possible yields well-ordered knowledge, ready to use.
questions.rule: Digest it into knowledge.
questions.teaches: By digesting the problems he solved as completely as he can, the future mathematician may acquire well-ordered knowledge, ready to use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A talented beginner asks how to become a mathematician. Which plan does the author favour?
options: Imitate a good model, solve problems in your line, and discover your own taste
Work only from current textbooks, so that nothing outdated or unfashionable is learned
Avoid copying anyone at all, so that every idea she has stays entirely her own
Solve every available problem equally and develop no preferences, to stay open to all
optionExplain: Right: imitation and practice, then taste.
The author wants good authors read too, not textbooks alone.
He says that one learns by imitation, as everybody does.
He wants the learner to discover likes and dislikes, not to hide them.
questions.explain: Imitation of a good model plus practice, leading to a taste of one's own, is the author's plan. The card next gives details.
questions.rule: Imitate, practise, discover taste.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The future mathematician learns, as everybody does, by imitation and ____.
questions.explain: The author names imitation and practice as the way of learning.
questions.rule: Imitate and practise.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Maya finds that she is drawn to one author's way of writing proofs. What does the author advise?
options: Change authors often, so that no single style takes hold of her way of working
Keep reading that author and imitate his ways, since she feels drawn to that author's ways
Avoid that author, because liking a style makes her uncritical of his mistakes
Wait until she knows the whole field before she chooses any model to imitate
optionExplain: The author wants her to settle on one whose ways she is inclined to imitate.
Right: the advice is to read good authors until one is found whose ways attract imitation.
He does not fear the attraction; he wants it.
He does not make her wait; imitation and practice come first.
questions.explain: Following a natural inclination toward a good author is the author's recommended route to a personal style.
questions.rule: Follow the natural pull toward a good model.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each piece of advice by whether it fits the author's description of how a future mathematician learns.

items.t: Compete with a capable friend
Observe a stimulating teacher
Choose problems that are in your line
Read only current textbooks
Avoid imitation so that your style stays original
Hide your likes and dislikes from yourself

questions.explain: The author lists a model, a stimulating teacher, a capable friend and good authors, and asks the learner to find his likes and dislikes.
questions.rule: Models, teachers, friends and good authors.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Does the author think that being a clever problem-solver is enough for a future mathematician?
options: Yes; cleverness at solving problems is all that mathematics needs from a person
Yes, provided the problems he solves are all of the same kind, so he gains speed
No; in due time he should solve significant problems and first find which kind of problems suits his gift
No; he should stop solving problems and spend his time studying theory instead
optionExplain: The text says cleverness is not enough.
The text does not ask for a single kind only; it asks him to find the kind that suits him.
Right: the text says a clever problem-solver is not enough.
The text asks him to solve problems, and significant ones.
questions.explain: Skill at solving is the base; the aim is significant problems of a kind that fits the person's gift.
questions.rule: Cleverness is not enough.
questions.teaches: The author says that being a clever problem-solver is not enough: in due time the future mathematician should solve significant problems, and first find out which kind of problems his native gift suits.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A young cook wants to find a personal style. Which step copies the author's advice for the future mathematician?
options: Seek out and enjoy what seems simple, instructive or beautiful, and cook in that line
Cook only the dishes that the market currently favours, since those will sell best
Cook what is easiest to prepare, whatever the taste, so that no effort is wasted
Cook the same dish every day until it is perfect, and then add nothing else to it
optionExplain: Right: the author tells the learner to enjoy and seek what seems simple, instructive or beautiful.
The author does not tie choices to current fashion.
Ease is not his criterion; simplicity, instruction and beauty are.
He asks for a taste and a line, not endless repetition of one task.
questions.explain: The first important discovery is one's own likes, dislikes and taste.
questions.rule: Find your own line.
questions.teaches: The author tells the future mathematician to enjoy and seek what seems to him simple, instructive or beautiful, and to make his first important discovery: his likes and dislikes, his taste, his own line.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A learner has a list of useful questions for problem-solving. What is the best way to use it?
options: Work through the list from top to bottom on every problem, so that nothing is missed
Ask a question when the problem in front of you suggests it, based on your own careful judgment
Memorise the list and recite it to yourself before starting on each problem
Leave the list to teachers, who need it more than learners and use it better
optionExplain: A fixed order ignores the problem at hand.
Right: judgment about the problem decides which question to ask.
Reciting does not give understanding of what each question is for.
The learner is exactly the user the list is for.
questions.explain: A question is asked because the situation calls for it. The card next explains how understanding grows.
questions.rule: Let the problem choose the question.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The intelligent problem-solver asks none of the questions unless prompted by careful consideration of the problem and by his own unprejudiced ____.
questions.explain: The prompt comes from the solver's own judgment about the problem at hand.
questions.rule: Judgment decides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A developer stuck on a bug has a list of questions. Which choice follows the author's advice?
options: Pick the question that resembles one that worked in a similar earlier situation
Ask every question on the list in order until one of them happens to work
Ask the first question again and again, regardless of what the bug looks like
Avoid the list altogether, because it is not tailored to this particular bug
optionExplain: Right: the solver should recognise whether the present situation is similar to one where a question succeeded.
Running through the whole list ignores the situation.
The author does not say to repeat one question blindly.
The author wants the list in hand, to be used by judgment.
questions.explain: Recognising similarity between situations is the solver's task, not the list's.
questions.rule: Match the question to the situation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: Reading the explanations and examples that go with a question is enough to reach real understanding of its use.
questions.explain: The author says one may suspect the proper use but cannot attain real understanding until one meets the procedure in one's own work and finds it useful.
questions.rule: Understanding comes from use.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A skilled solver repeats the same stereotyped question again and again without noticing. What might the question be doing?
options: It replaces thought by habit, and the solver should break the habit as soon as possible
It is a sign that the solver has not understood the problem and is stalling
It summons the mental attitude suited to a phase of the work
It is only a way to fill time while the solver waits for an idea to come
optionExplain: The author presents the habit as part of the solver's mental attitude.
Nothing suggests lack of understanding.
Right: the author says the question may be part of the attitude suited to a phase, summoned by asking it.
The question has a purpose: it summons an attitude.
questions.explain: Asking the right question can be a way of putting oneself in the right frame of mind.
questions.rule: A pet question can set the attitude.
questions.teaches: The intelligent problem-solver may not be conscious of repeating the same stereotyped question; he knows it is part of the attitude suited to a phase of the work, and summons that attitude by asking it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A pianist asks, before each practice, which bar is hardest, and does not know why. How does the author's account describe such a habit?
options: It is a mistake, since a person must be able to give a conscious reason for any habit
It is useful only if other pianists share it, which shows that the habit is sound
It is useful only after it has been written down in a list of questions
It can be the solver's own question, part of an attitude he summons, perhaps without being conscious of repeating it
optionExplain: The author says he may not be conscious of it at all.
Whether others share it is not his test.
The list is not a precondition; the person discovered the question himself.
Right: such habits may serve as attitude-setters without the person being aware.
questions.explain: A personal question can work even when its use is not articulated.
questions.rule: Habits may carry method.
questions.teaches: The intelligent problem-solver may have discovered such questions himself, or heard one and discovered its proper use himself, and may not be conscious of asking them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which of these does a successful problem-solver need beyond understanding the problem?
options: Concentration on it and a real wish to solve it
A large number of other problems done first, to build up the needed stamina
A teacher who is present throughout the work to say whether each step is right
A complete list of formulas set out in advance, so that nothing has to be recalled
optionExplain: Right: concentration and desire.
Other problems help in other ways but are not what the entry names.
Teachers help; the entry stresses the solver's own attitude.
Formulas do not replace attention and wish.
questions.explain: Understanding is the start; attention and desire carry the work. The card next says so.
questions.rule: Understand, concentrate, want.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Besides understanding the problem, the solver must ____ upon it and earnestly desire its solution.
questions.explain: Concentration is named next to desire.
questions.rule: Concentrate.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Tom understands a puzzle fully but drifts when working at it and does not care how it ends. What is missing?
options: A fuller understanding of the problem, since understanding is the root of success
Concentration and desire to obtain the solution
A longer list of questions to ask, since more questions give more chances
A teacher to give the answer, so that the puzzle can be finished quickly
optionExplain: He already understands it fully.
Right: understanding is present; concentration and desire are not.
More questions will not help someone who does not care.
The answer from outside does not supply his own desire.
questions.explain: The author insists that understanding alone is not enough.
questions.rule: Understanding alone is not enough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a solver whose understanding is complete will succeed whatever his interest.
questions.explain: Concentration and desire are needed as well as understanding.
questions.rule: Understanding does not do the work alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student says: I understand it, but I cannot summon any real desire to solve it. What does the author advise?
options: Force the work through, since desire follows effort
Ask a teacher to want it for him
Better leave the problem alone
Work on it only half-heartedly to save time
optionExplain: The author does not suggest forcing it.
A teacher cannot supply the student's desire.
Right: if real desire cannot be summoned, the solver does better to leave the problem alone.
Half-hearted work is what the author advises against.
questions.explain: The author's practical conclusion: without real desire it is better not to start.
questions.rule: No desire, no problem.
questions.teaches: If he cannot summon up real desire for solving the problem, the solver would do better to leave it alone.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A manager offers a developer a puzzle-like task they find dull. What follows from the author's last sentence on the topic?
options: Success needs only a clear specification of the task, set out in writing
Success needs only the right reference book on the shelf, open at the right page
Success needs only a deadline, since pressure produces concentration by itself
Success needs the person to throw their whole personality into the task
optionExplain: A specification helps understanding, not desire.
A book informs but does not make the person care.
A deadline is pressure, not wholehearted involvement.
Right: the author calls throwing the whole personality into the problem the open secret of success.
questions.explain: The open secret of real success is to throw your whole personality into your problem.
questions.rule: Whole personality.
questions.teaches: The author calls it the open secret of real success to throw your whole personality into your problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You read a proof in which every line follows from the one before, yet you keep wondering why it goes this way. What is missing for you?
options: A visible purpose for the steps
A check that each line is correct
A longer list of definitions
A figure printed beside every line
optionExplain: Right: correctness is present; purpose is not.
You already see that each line is correct.
Definitions would not tell you what the steps are for.
A figure may help but does not by itself give a purpose.
questions.explain: A reader can follow correctness and still be lost for lack of purpose. The card next names both wishes.
questions.rule: Correctness and purpose are two needs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which two things does the intelligent reader of a mathematical book desire? Select both.
options: To see the whole proof printed on one page
To see that the present step is correct
To see the author's name on every lemma
To see the purpose of the present step
optionExplain: Layout is not among the wishes.
Right: correctness of the step.
Names are not among the wishes.
Right: the purpose of the step.
questions.explain: The two wishes are correctness and purpose of the present step.
questions.rule: Correct and purposeful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: In a textbook proof, step 4 introduces a new quantity without explanation. You can verify step 4. What should an intelligent reader still ask?
options: Whether step 4 can be skipped, since it checks out and the proof would still stand
What step 4 is for, and why it was worth introducing the new quantity
Who first introduced that quantity in the literature, and in which year
Whether the author enjoys such quantities and uses them for their own sake
optionExplain: A step that checks is not therefore pointless; the reader still wants its purpose.
Right: purpose is the second wish.
History is not what the reader needs to follow the argument.
