Taste is not a reason for the step.
questions.explain: Having verified a step, the intelligent reader asks what it is for.
questions.rule: After correct, ask for purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: A reader who has checked that every step of a proof is correct has therefore seen everything an intelligent reader wants.
questions.explain: Correctness is only the first wish. The second is to see the purpose of each step.
questions.rule: Two wishes, not one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: What usually happens to a listener who can see no purpose in the present step?
options: He protests loudly and forces the lecturer to explain the step in more detail
He guesses the purpose for himself and goes on with confidence to the next step
He is dismayed and bored and loses the thread of the argument
He becomes more attentive to the next step, in the hope that it will explain this one
optionExplain: Protest is what the doubter of correctness does.
He cannot suspect any reason, so he cannot guess.
Right: the author says he does not protest but is just dismayed and bored, and loses the thread.
The author describes the opposite: the thread is lost.
questions.explain: Missing purpose is the silent failure of exposition: the listener leaves without objecting.
questions.rule: Silent loss of the thread.
questions.teaches: A listener who sees no purpose in the present step usually cannot even formulate a clear objection; he does not protest, is just dismayed and bored, and loses the thread of the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: In a company meeting an analyst shows slides of correct calculations. Which statement fits the author's view of the audience?
options: The audience wants only the conclusion, so the purposes of the steps are irrelevant to it
The audience wants only to check the arithmetic, line by line, and nothing else
The audience wants only to see the data tables, which settle everything for it
The audience, like a lecture audience, wants to see that each step is right and what it is for
optionExplain: The author wants steps and purposes to be visible.
Correctness is only one of the two wishes.
Tables alone give neither correctness nor purpose.
Right: the author says the intelligent listener has the same wishes as the reader.
questions.explain: The two wishes belong to readers and listeners alike.
questions.rule: Same wishes for listener and reader.
questions.teaches: The intelligent listener to a mathematical lecture has the same two wishes as the intelligent reader.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A blackboard proof is free of errors, but students are lost. What is the likeliest cause?
options: They cannot see why the steps are taken, so the proof is hard to follow
The proof is too short to count as a proof, so the students cannot rely on it
The students did not check each line, so they could not see that it was correct
Proofs are always lost on students, whatever the way in which they are presented
optionExplain: Right: correctness does not give purpose.
Length is not the issue.
Students may check every line and still be lost.
The author says the fault lies in the presentation, not in the nature of proofs.
questions.explain: A correct derivation is hard to use without visible purposes. The card next says what is also needed.
questions.rule: Correct is not enough.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: To write and speak correctly is necessary, but it is not ____.
questions.explain: Correctness is required but does not by itself make an argument accessible.
questions.rule: Necessary, not sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A tutor's derivation of a formula has no mistakes but each move arrives unannounced. Which repair follows the author?
options: Add more lines, so that the proof is more complete and leaves no step out
Speak more slowly while presenting the very same steps in the very same order
Say what each move is for, so students see the motive behind it
Ask the students to memorise the derivation line by line, so that they can repeat it
optionExplain: Completeness is not the problem; the proof is already correct.
Speed is not the cause of the missing purpose.
Right: motives and purposes are what is missing.
Memorising is not understanding and leaves the motive unseen.
questions.explain: The repair is to emphasise purpose and motive.
questions.rule: Show the motive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each feature of a presentation by whether it helps or leaves the audience lost.

items.t: Says why the first step was chosen
Shows what each step is for
Lists correct steps one after another without comment
Gives no hint how anyone could have found the argument
Points out what the next step will achieve
Assumes the audience will trust correctness alone

questions.explain: The author asks for visible purpose and for a way to find the argument; bare correctness is not enough.
questions.rule: Purpose helps; bare correctness leaves lost.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Besides unclear purpose, what other failing can make a correct derivation inaccessible?
options: The derivation uses too many symbols, which makes the reading slow and hard
The reader gets no suggestion about how he could find such an argument by himself
The derivation is shorter than the reader expects, so it seems to leave parts out
The derivation has no numbered equations, so the reader cannot refer back to it
optionExplain: Symbols are not named as the problem.
Right: the author names the lack of any suggestion how the argument could be found by the reader himself.
Length is not named.
Numbering is not named.
questions.explain: A good presentation hints at how the argument could be discovered.
questions.rule: Hint at how to find it.
questions.teaches: A correct derivation can be uninstructive if the reader cannot derive from the presentation any suggestion as to how he could find such an argument by himself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A senior engineer's install guide lists correct commands, but newcomers cannot see why. Which gap does this show?
options: The guide has too few commands, so some steps are missing from the procedure
The newcomers read too slowly, so they do not take in the commands in time
The commands are not correct, so the newcomers cannot make the procedure work
The reader cannot understand how it was humanly possible to find such steps
optionExplain: The commands are enough.
Speed of reading is not the issue.
The guide is stated to be correct.
Right: the author lists this as a way for correct exposition to stay inaccessible.
questions.explain: A correct exposition fails when readers cannot see how its steps could have been found.
questions.rule: Make the finding visible.
questions.teaches: A derivation is inaccessible if the reader cannot understand how it was humanly possible to find such an argument.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Midway through an argument, a step suddenly uses a condition that was ignored so far. What reason would a good author give?
options: That condition has not been used yet, and a complete argument should use all the data
Authors like to introduce new material at random, to keep the reader on alert
The earlier steps were wasted effort, and the author now starts again from scratch
The condition is easier than the others, so the author saves it for the end
optionExplain: Right: an unused datum is a good reason to bring it in.
The step has a reason; it is not random.
Earlier steps were not wasted.
Ease is not the reason.
questions.explain: Unused data call for use. The card next names the question that brings this out.
questions.rule: Look for the unused datum.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The question is: Did we use all the ____?
questions.explain: The question asks about the data of the problem.
questions.rule: Use all the data.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You read a proof and cannot see why the author considers the side AB at this point. What can you ask?
options: Whether AB is the longest side in the figure, since the longest side matters most
Whether AB is a datum that has not been used yet
Whether AB was named first in the text, since first-named items come first in proofs
Whether the author likes the side AB and has used it in other proofs before
optionExplain: Length is not the question.
Right: if AB is an unused datum, that explains the step.
Order of naming is not a reason.
Preference is not a reason.
questions.explain: The question turns a puzzling step into a reasoned one.
questions.rule: Is it an unused datum?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: Only the author or teacher can use the question did we use all the data; a reader cannot.
questions.explain: The reader or listener can use the same question to understand the author's reason for considering an element.
questions.rule: Readers can use it too.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: What effect can the question have on a reader who understands a step through it?
options: He may feel that the step is unnecessary and could be removed from the proof
He may feel that the author has hidden something that the reader is not meant to see
He may feel that, asking this question, he could have discovered the step himself
He may feel that he must reread the whole book from the beginning to be sure
optionExplain: The question explains the step; it does not discredit it.
The question reveals the reason, not a secret.
Right: understanding the motive makes the step feel discoverable.
Nothing suggests rereading.
questions.explain: The goal is to give the reader the feeling that he could have found the step.
questions.rule: Feel that you could have found it.
questions.teaches: By asking did we use all the data, a reader may feel that he could have discovered the step by himself.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A teacher wants to make the purpose of a proof step clear. What do the questions of the list offer her?
options: A way to avoid explaining motives, by supplying a ready question instead
A way to shorten the proof, by leaving out the steps that need an explanation
A way to test students instead of teaching them, by marking the answers they give
A way to emphasise the purpose and motives of the argument
optionExplain: The point is to explain motive.
Shortening is not mentioned.
The questions explain; they are not only tests.
Right: the author says such questions may be useful to author and teacher in emphasising purpose and motives.
questions.explain: The questions help the writer and the teacher to bring out why each step is taken.
questions.rule: Questions bring out motive.
questions.teaches: The questions and suggestions of the list may be useful to the author and the teacher in emphasising the purpose and the motives of the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A fly keeps flying at a closed window; a mouse in a trap tries bar after bar. What is the main difference?
options: The mouse varies its trials, while the fly repeats the same one
The mouse is stronger than the fly, and so it manages to get through the bars
The fly tries harder than the mouse, and this is why the fly keeps going at the glass
The mouse tries only once while the fly tries many times, so the fly is the persistent one
optionExplain: Right: variation of trials separates them.
Strength is not the point.
The fly repeats but does not vary.
The mouse also tries many times.
questions.explain: The point is variation of the trials. The card next says how this applies to problems.
questions.rule: Vary the trials.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Whoever follows try, try again with more success does so because he ____ his problem more intelligently.
questions.explain: The difference lies in how intelligently the problem is varied.
questions.rule: Vary the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Jo cannot open a jar and twists harder each time. Sam taps the lid, runs hot water over it and tries a cloth grip. Who follows the book's advice?
options: Jo, since persistence is what try, try again means
Sam, who changes the way of attack when one fails
Neither, since the advice does not apply to jars
Both equally, since each keeps trying
optionExplain: Jo repeats one trial as the insect does.
Right: Sam varies the trials as the mouse does.
The advice is about trying with variation, and a jar is a case.
Only one of them varies.
questions.explain: Persistence with variation, not mere repetition, is the lesson.
questions.rule: Persist by varying.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each move on a stuck problem by whether it varies the problem or repeats the attempt.

items.t: Restate the problem in other words
Try a special case first
Look at the problem from another side
Run the same method again with more force
Try the next pair of bars
Return to the same blocked window

questions.explain: Restating, trying a special case and trying the next pair of bars are variation; pushing again the same way or going back to the blocked window is repetition.
questions.rule: Change something between trials.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: How does the author say our conception of the problem changes between the start and the end of the work?
options: It stays the same from start to end, and only the method of attack changes
It becomes simpler because details are dropped one by one as the work goes on
It becomes fuller and more adequate, and we try various standpoints to get there
It becomes narrower as unlikely sides are ruled out, until one side remains
optionExplain: The conception itself changes.
The text speaks of fuller, not simpler.
Right: we move from the initial conception toward a more adequate one by viewing the problem from different sides.
The text speaks of viewing from different sides, not narrowing.
questions.explain: Variation is how the initial view of a problem develops into a better adapted one.
questions.rule: Views improve through variation.
questions.teaches: At the end of the work, our conception of the problem is fuller and more adequate than at the outset, and to reach it we try various standpoints and view the problem from different sides.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A shop sells poorly through one channel. What does the author's image of attacking a fortress suggest?
options: Attack the strongest wall, since the side that is pushed hardest is the one that gives way
Wait outside until the fortress opens by itself, since waiting costs nothing at all
Repeat the first attack with a bigger force, since the first attack was well chosen
Try several sides to find the accessible one, since success depends on choosing the right aspect
optionExplain: The author wants the accessible side.
Waiting does not solve a problem.
Repeating is the insect's way.
Right: success depends on choosing the right aspect, attacking from the accessible side.
questions.explain: To find which aspect is right, the author tries various sides: he varies the problem.
questions.rule: Find the accessible side.
questions.teaches: Success in solving a problem depends on choosing the right aspect, on attacking the fortress from its accessible side; to find which, we try various sides and aspects, that is, we vary the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You are stuck on a problem and cannot recall anything useful. Why might restating it differently help?
options: The new wording puts other things in your mind, which may call up relevant knowledge
The new wording makes the problem easier by itself, since an easier problem is solved faster
The new wording forces you to forget your earlier failures, which were holding you back
The new wording gives you the answer as a hint, because the words are chosen to do so
optionExplain: Right: what is in mind affects what is recalled.
A restated problem is the same problem; the benefit is in what it brings to mind.
The book does not appeal to forgetting.
Restating does not hand over the answer.
questions.explain: What is in mind decides what is recalled. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: What you think about shapes what you recall.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The author says we remember things by a kind of "action by contact", called mental ____.
questions.explain: Mental association links what is in mind now with what it touched before.
questions.rule: Association is memory by contact.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You must find the area of an odd-shaped plot and nothing comes to mind. Which restatement is likeliest to call up useful knowledge?
options: Read the same statement once more, aloud, so that every word is heard properly
Think of the plot as a rectangle with pieces added and removed
Rewrite the same words in the same order, in a neater hand, on a clean page
Wonder how large the plot looks, and compare it with other plots you have seen
optionExplain: Reading the same words in the same way brings in nothing new.
Right: the rectangle brings in new points that may touch known facts about areas.
The same words bring the same contacts.
Guessing at size recalls no method.
questions.explain: A change of aspect adds points that may contact knowledge, as the rectangle recalls area rules.
questions.rule: New points, new contacts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each statement by which reason for varying a problem it illustrates.

items.t: What is in mind now tends to recall what touched it before
An unchanging object tires attention
A new question reconquers flagging interest
New contacts with earlier knowledge become possible
Without progress we may lose the problem altogether
Elements relevant to the problem are extracted from memory

questions.explain: The memory reason is about contacts between what is in mind and what is stored; the attention reason is about interest fading when the object does not change.
questions.rule: Memory: contacts. Attention: change.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: From one point of view, how does the author describe progress in solving a problem?
options: As finding facts that no one has known before, which are then added to the problem
As ignoring what we already know, so as to look at the problem with fresh eyes
As mobilising and organising knowledge we already have, and working the needed elements into the problem
As waiting patiently for a flash of insight, which cannot be forced by any means
optionExplain: The text says knowledge is already acquired.
The text says we draw on memory.
Right: progress appears as mobilisation and organisation of formerly acquired knowledge.
The text describes work, not waiting.
questions.explain: Variation matters because progress means drawing the right knowledge into the problem.
questions.rule: Progress is mobilising what you know.
questions.teaches: From a certain point of view, progress in solving a problem appears as mobilisation and organisation of formerly acquired knowledge, which we extract from memory and work into the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A scientist needs hours of intense concentration but tires when staring at one point. How does the author reconcile the two?
options: Avoid concentration, since concentration tires the mind and so defeats its own purpose
Concentrate on the same point until tired, then stop and leave the problem for good
Change problems entirely every few minutes, so that no one problem tires the mind
Concentration is needed for any worthwhile problem, so keep the object changing to keep attention alive
optionExplain: He says that concentration is needed.
Staying on one point is what tires us.
Changing aspects of the same problem, not the problem itself, is advised.
Right: the author says no worthwhile problem is solved without intense concentration, and that the object must unceasingly change.
questions.explain: We cannot hope to solve any worthwhile problem without intense concentration; so the attention must be fed by changing aspects.
questions.rule: Concentrate, but vary what you look at.
questions.teaches: We cannot hope to solve any worthwhile problem without intense concentration, yet we tire of attention on one point, so the object of attention must unceasingly change.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A square frustum has a lower side a and an upper side b. If b grows until it equals a, what is the volume?
options: It is the volume of a prism with square base a and height h, that is a squared times h
It is a squared times h divided by 3, the volume of a pyramid on the same base
It is zero, since the top and the bottom coincide and leave no solid at all
It is a squared times h divided by 2, halfway between the pyramid and the prism
optionExplain: Right: equal sides make a prism.
That is the pyramid value for b equal to 0.
The solid has height h, so it is not empty.
One half belongs to no case of this problem.
questions.explain: Equal base sides make the sides vertical, so the solid is a prism. The card next uses this.
questions.rule: b = a gives a prism.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: When b shrinks to 0, the frustum becomes a ____ whose volume is a squared times h divided by 3.
questions.explain: A zero upper side leaves a pyramid.
questions.rule: b = 0 gives a pyramid.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which candidate for the frustum's volume gives a squared h for b = a and a squared h over 3 for b = 0?
options: \(hab\)
optionExplain: With b = a it gives \(a^2h\), but with b = 0 it gives \(a^2h/4\), not \(a^2h/3\).
With b = 0 it gives \(a^2h/2\), not \(a^2h/3\).
Right: with b = a it gives \(3a^2h/3\), and with b = 0 it gives \(a^2h/3\).
With b = 0 it gives 0, not \(a^2h/3\).
questions.explain: Only the first candidate meets both limiting values; the test cannot prove it right but can reject the others.
questions.rule: Check each limiting case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Sort each statement by the limiting case of the frustum it describes.

items.t: The solid is a prism
The volume is a squared times h
The upper base equals the lower base
The solid is a pyramid
The volume is a squared times h over 3
The upper base shrinks to a point

questions.explain: Equal bases give a prism with volume base times height; a vanishing upper base gives a pyramid with one third of that.
questions.rule: Prism: a squared h. Pyramid: a squared h over 3.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Besides finding properties of the result, what else does varying the data in this example do?
options: It adds to the interest of the problem and may suggest using the known results for prism and pyramid
It gives the final formula directly, since the limiting values fix the whole formula
It proves that a formula exists, which is needed before one can look for it
It removes the need to know any volume formulas, since the limits do all the work
optionExplain: Right: the author says it contributes to interest and may suggest using the quoted results.
The limits do not by themselves produce the formula.
Existence is not the point.
The problem presupposes familiarity with the prism and pyramid formulas.
questions.explain: The variation raises interest and points to the known results.
questions.rule: Variation also invites known results.
questions.teaches: The variation of the data contributes first of all to the interest of the problem, and may suggest using the known results about prism and pyramid.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student proposes the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides a and c and height h as (a + c) h. Which variation exposes the error?
options: Let h become very large: the area then grows without bound, as it should for any formula
Let a and c be swapped: the formula is unchanged, so it must be symmetric and so correct
Let c become 0: the figure becomes a triangle of area ah/2, but the formula gives ah
Let c equal a and h equal 0: the area is 0 in both formulas, so they cannot be told apart
optionExplain: Growth in h is consistent with both formulas.
Symmetry in a and c does not test the factor.
Right: the limiting case contradicts the formula.
Both give 0 at h = 0, so this case does not separate them.
questions.explain: It is an advantage to foresee properties of the result: when the formula is found, we can test it against them.
questions.rule: Test formulas against limiting cases.
questions.teaches: It is an advantage to foresee properties of the result; when we have found the final formula, we can test it, which gives an answer in advance to the question: can you check the result?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You know the four sides of a trapezoid, bases a and c, legs b and d. Which simple figure with known sides could help construct it?
options: A triangle whose sides are b, d and the difference of the two bases
A square whose side is the sum of all four sides, which can be built from the data
A circle whose diameter is the longer base, which can be built from the data
A rectangle whose sides are the two bases a and c, which can be built from the data
optionExplain: Right: sliding one leg gives such a triangle.
No such square is built from the data.
No circle is determined by these data in this way.
A rectangle on the bases a and c does not use the legs.
questions.explain: The triangle with sides b, d and a minus c can be built from the data. The card next shows how the book finds it.
questions.rule: Look for a buildable triangle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: When c grows to equal a, the trapezoid becomes a ____.
questions.explain: Equal parallel sides make a parallelogram.
questions.rule: c = a gives a parallelogram.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Bases are a = 9 and c = 7, legs b = 1 and d = 1. Can the trapezoid be constructed by this method?
options: Yes: the triangle has sides 1, 1 and 2 and can be drawn, so the trapezoid follows
No: the triangle would have sides 1, 1 and 2, and 1 + 1 equals 2, so it collapses
Yes: any four lengths whatever give a trapezoid, so the method always works
No: the two bases must be equal for the method to work, and here they are not
optionExplain: Sides 1, 1 and 2 form no proper triangle.
Right: a triangle needs the sum of two sides to exceed the third.
Not every set of four sides gives a trapezoid.
The method needs unequal parallel bases, so this is not the reason.
questions.explain: The triangle has sides b, d and a minus c, which are 1, 1 and 2. Since 1 + 1 = 2, it degenerates. Our reading: this limit is our own check, not the book's.
questions.rule: Check that the triangle exists.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: The first attempt, shrinking c to 0, failed because a triangle is too hard to construct.
questions.explain: The triangle is easy to construct; the data supply only two of its sides, a and d, and three are needed.
questions.rule: Check that the data fit the figure.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: What does the author find, looking back, about the failed first attempt?
options: It was useless and should be forgotten, since it did not lead to the construction
It proved that the construction is impossible, since the triangle lacked a side
It was not useless: it gave an opportunity to think of constructing a triangle as a means to the end
It gave the final construction at once, so the second attempt was not needed
optionExplain: He says the opposite.
It showed only that this particular triangle lacked data.
Right: the book says there was some idea in it.
The second try gave the construction.
questions.explain: Failure can leave a useful idea behind.
questions.rule: Keep the good idea of a failed try.
questions.teaches: Looking back, the first, failed attempt was not useless: there was some idea in it, in particular the thought of constructing a triangle as a means to the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A planner's first route plan fails because it assumes a shorter road than exists. How does the trapezoid example say to proceed?
options: Discard the failed plan and start again from nothing, since it taught nothing about the problem
Modify the failed plan, as the author varied c first down and then up
Repeat the failed plan with a different shorter road, and hope that the result is different
Give up the problem, since the first plan has shown that no route can be found
optionExplain: The second trial was a modification of the first.
Right: the second try came by modifying the first.
Repeating a wrong assumption is the insect's way.
The author arrives at success.
questions.explain: The successful trial came by modifying the unsuccessful one: c was first decreased, then increased.
questions.rule: Modify the failed try.
questions.teaches: The author arrived at the second, successful trial by modifying the first, unsuccessful trial: he varied c, first trying to decrease it, then to increase it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Your first three attempts at a problem have failed. What is a sensible next move?
options: Modify one of the failed attempts, looking for the good idea in it
Repeat the best of the failed attempts with more care, since care may be what was missing
Conclude that the problem has no solution, since three attempts have failed already
Pick an easier problem and forget this one, since time is better spent on that one
optionExplain: Right: a failed attempt can be modified into a better one.
Repeating changes nothing in the approach.
Failure of attempts does not show absence of a solution.
Dropping the problem gives up what was learned.
questions.explain: Failure carries information. The card next shows how the book uses it.
questions.rule: Modify what failed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A more successful trial may come by modifying an ____ one.
questions.explain: A good idea may lie inside an unsuccessful trial.
questions.rule: Modify what failed.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A student's attempt to prove a claim for n = 3 gives only arithmetic. What should she do with it, following the book?
options: Delete it, since an attempt that did not prove the claim has nothing left to teach
Look for the idea in the attempt and restate the claim in the light of it
Repeat it for n = 4 in exactly the same way, to see whether the outcome changes
Wait for the teacher to supply the proof, so as not to waste any more time on it
optionExplain: Deleting discards what it showed.
Right: learn by failure and keep varying.
Repeating the same way is the insect's method.
The author wants the solver to keep working.
questions.explain: Vary, restate and transform until something useful appears.
questions.rule: Keep varying.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which list names the modes of varying a problem that the author calls typically useful?
options: Counting, measuring, estimating, rounding, plotting, averaging, and similar steps of calculation
Memorising, copying, repeating, timing, ranking, checking, and similar habits of study
Going back to the definition, decomposing and recombining, auxiliary elements, generalization, specialization, analogy
Doubling, halving, squaring, inverting, summing, subtracting, and similar operations on numbers
optionExplain: These are operations on numbers, not modes of varying a problem.
These are study habits, not modes of variation.
Right: these six modes are named in the entry.
These are arithmetic operations.
questions.explain: The six typical modes are the entry's own list.
questions.rule: Six typical modes.
questions.teaches: Certain modes of varying the problem are typically useful: going back to the definition, decomposing and recombining, introducing auxiliary elements, generalization, specialization, and the use of analogy.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Match each move on a stuck problem to the mode of variation it illustrates.
pairs: Replace a term by its definition
Split the figure into parts and join them in a new way
Draw an extra line in the figure
questions.explain: Each move is one of the typical modes listed in the entry.
questions.rule: Name the mode.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: After several tries, a team has reduced a hard scheduling task to a smaller one it can solve. What does the book call what we attain?
options: A final proof that the task is impossible, which ends the search for good
A longer version of the original task, which has more cases but the same difficulty
A copy of the original task in new words, which is no easier than the original
A more accessible auxiliary problem, whose result helps solve the original
optionExplain: Nothing in the text says that.
The auxiliary problem is easier to reach.
A copy would gain nothing.
Right: what is attained after various trials is very often a more accessible auxiliary problem.
questions.explain: In the trapezoid, the triangle was such an auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: Aim for an accessible auxiliary problem.
questions.teaches: What we attain after various trials is very often a more accessible auxiliary problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A teacher watches a student making steady progress on a problem. What is best?
options: Say nothing and let the student work alone
Ask a guiding question every minute
Give the answer to save time
Stop the student and test his understanding
optionExplain: Right: asking is for when help is needed.
Needless questions interrupt a student who is progressing.
The student's independence matters.
Testing interrupts progress.
questions.explain: Independence is valued while progress lasts. The card next says when to step in.
questions.rule: No help without need.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: When work goes well, asking extraneous questions would hamper our spontaneous ____.
questions.explain: Spontaneous progress should not be interrupted.
questions.rule: Do not interrupt progress.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: You have been stuck for twenty minutes and nothing occurs to you. What does the author suggest?
options: Keep staring at the same point until an idea appears, since the idea must come in time
Drop the problem for good, since twenty minutes without an idea shows it is too hard
Think of a general idea or a question of the list that might help, one that may show a new aspect
Ask nothing and wait until someone else offers help, since help should come from outside
optionExplain: Staring at one point is what tires attention.
The aim is to keep interest alive, not to drop the problem.
Right: a blocked solver should look for a question that may show a new aspect.
The solver can supply the question himself.
questions.explain: When blocked, any question with some chance of showing a new aspect is welcome.
questions.rule: Blocked: ask.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: A tutor should offer a hint every minute even when the pupil is progressing, to keep the pupil interested.
questions.explain: While the pupil progresses, interest is alive and the pupil needs no help; letting him work alone is better for his independence.
questions.rule: Let progress run.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Why should the teacher try to find a suitable question when the student is stuck?
options: Because the student may tire of the problem, drop it, or lose interest and make a blunder from sheer indifference
Because stuck students can never succeed alone and must always be given the next step
Because a teacher who stays silent while a student is stuck is plainly a bad teacher
Because the list has to be used a fixed number of times in the course of a lesson
optionExplain: Right: the author names the danger of tiredness and indifference.
The text does not say they can never succeed.
No such rule is given.
No fixed count is given.
questions.explain: The danger when work stalls is loss of interest, and a question can revive it.
questions.rule: Help prevents loss of interest.
questions.teaches: When the student is stuck there is danger that he will get tired of his problem and drop it, or lose interest and make some stupid blunder out of sheer indifference.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A team lead sees a developer stuck in debugging. Which question fits the author's advice?
options: Only a question that gives the answer directly, so that the developer loses no more time
Only a question taken from the same list in its fixed order, one after the other
Only a question about the developer's progress rate, so that the lead can plan ahead
Any question that has some chance of showing a new aspect of the problem
optionExplain: The question need not give the answer.
Order of the list is not required.
Progress rate does not show a new aspect.
Right: any question that may show a new aspect is welcome.
questions.explain: Any question with some chance of showing a new aspect is welcome; it may reconquer interest and keep us thinking.
questions.rule: Any aspect-showing question helps.
questions.teaches: Any question is welcome that has some chance of showing a new aspect of the problem; it may reconquer our interest and keep us working and thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A farmer wants a rectangular pen of area 96 square metres using 40 metres of fence. What is the unknown?
options: The two side lengths of the pen
The 40 metres of fence, since it is the number that the farmer cares about most
The area of 96 square metres, since the farmer wants a pen with that much space
The shape of the pen, since the farmer has not yet decided what shape to build
optionExplain: Right: the side lengths are what we want to find.
That is a given quantity.
That is a given quantity too.
The shape is given as a rectangle.
questions.explain: The unknown is what we seek. The card next adds data and condition.
questions.rule: The unknown is what you seek.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Match each question to the principal part of a problem to find that it points to.
pairs: By what is the unknown linked to the data?
questions.explain: The three questions point to unknown, data and condition.
questions.rule: Unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Find the diagonal of a rectangle with sides 6 and 8. Which identification of the parts is right?
options: Unknown: the sides; data: the diagonal; condition: the area of the rectangle
Unknown: the diagonal; data: the sides 6 and 8; condition: the diagonal joins opposite corners
Unknown: the area; data: the diagonal; condition: the sides of the rectangle
Unknown: the corner; data: the sides; condition: the area of the rectangle
optionExplain: This swaps unknown and data.
Right: the diagonal is wanted, the sides are given, and the condition links them (the diagonal is 10).
The area is not asked for.
A corner is not asked for.
questions.explain: The diagonal is the square root of 36 plus 64, which is 10. Naming the parts first makes the link clear.
questions.rule: Name unknown, data, condition.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Which questions are ways of asking about the unknown? Select all that apply.
options: What is given?
What is required?
What have you?
What do you want?
What are you supposed to seek?
optionExplain: That asks about the data.
Right: required means unknown.
That asks about the data.
Right: what you want is the unknown.
Right: what you seek is the unknown.
questions.explain: The book gives several wordings for each question; seek, want and required point to the unknown, given and have to the data.
questions.rule: Different words, same part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: After the start of the work, should the three questions be asked again?
options: No; they are only for understanding the statement at the start, and then they are done with
No; asking them twice shows that the problem has not been understood the first time
Yes, but only when a teacher is present to ask them on the solver's behalf
Yes; the parts may be needed again and again, so the questions may be repeated in later phases
optionExplain: They are not limited to the start.
Repeating is normal for a solver who focuses on the parts.
They are for the solver himself.
Right: the book says the questions are often repeated in later phases of the solution.
questions.explain: The solver has to focus on the unknown and data again and again.
questions.rule: Return to the parts as often as needed.
questions.teaches: Because consideration of the principal parts may be necessary again and again, the questions may be often repeated in the later phases of the solution.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A coach wants to check whether a pupil has understood a puzzle. Which use of the three questions fits the author?
options: Answer them for the pupil, to save time, and then move on to the solution itself
Skip them, since they apply only to arithmetic and not to puzzles of this kind
Ask the pupil to answer them in his own words, since a pupil who understands the problem can do so
Ask them only after the puzzle is solved, as a check on the pupil's memory
optionExplain: The pupil should answer.
They apply to any problem to find.
Right: the teacher can use the questions to test the understanding of the problem.
They are meant for the start and later phases.
questions.explain: The author says that the teacher can use these questions to test the understanding of the problem, and the student should be able to answer them clearly.
questions.rule: Test understanding by asking.
questions.teaches: The teacher may use these questions to test the understanding of the problem; the student should be able to answer them clearly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Find two numbers whose sum is 20 and whose product is 96. How might you adapt the question what is the unknown?
options: Ask what the unknowns are, since there are two numbers to find
Ask what the unknown is, and expect a single number, since the question stays the same
Ask what the conclusion is, since there are two numbers that the problem leads to
Ask what the hypothesis is, since the sum and product are assumed in the problem
optionExplain: Right: with two numbers sought, the plural fits (they are 8 and 12).
There are two numbers, not one.
Conclusion is for problems to prove.
Hypothesis is for problems to prove.
questions.explain: The questions bend to the problem. The card next gives the book's variants.
questions.rule: Adapt the number.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The principal parts of a problem to prove are the hypothesis and the ____.
questions.explain: Hypothesis and conclusion are the principal parts of a problem to prove.
questions.rule: Hypothesis and conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: Prove: if a triangle has two equal angles, then it has two equal sides. What is the hypothesis?
options: The triangle has two equal sides, since that is the fact on which the proof rests
The triangle has two equal angles
The triangle exists as a figure in the plane, since otherwise nothing can be proved
The triangle is drawn on paper with a ruler, since the figure is part of the statement
optionExplain: That is the conclusion.
Right: the hypothesis is what we assume; the equal sides are the conclusion.
Existence is not the stated assumption.
The drawing is not part of the theorem.
questions.explain: What do you assume? The two equal angles. What is to be shown? The two equal sides.
questions.rule: Assume the if-part, conclude the then-part.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: True or false: For a problem to prove, the right first question is: what is the unknown?
questions.explain: A problem to prove has a hypothesis and a conclusion as principal parts, so the fitting questions are what is the hypothesis and what is the conclusion.
questions.rule: Ask the questions of the right kind.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: The questions may need a variation of verbal expression. What alternative does the author give for a problem to prove?
options: What do you want? What are you supposed to seek? What is required of you?
What do you assume? What are the various parts of your assumption?
What is given? What have you? What are the data that you have at hand?
What is the first datum? What is the second datum? What are the further data?
optionExplain: Those ask about the unknown.
Right: these are the author's alternatives for the hypothesis.
Those ask about the data.
Those fit a problem to find.
questions.explain: The hypothesis can be asked about as what you assume, and its parts as parts of your assumption.
questions.rule: Hypothesis: what do you assume?
questions.teaches: For a problem to prove the questions may be varied as: What do you assume? What are the various parts of your assumption?

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Terms, Old and New to What Is the Unknown?
questions.q: A contract dispute must show that a supplier breached terms. Which question is the analogue of what is the hypothesis?
options: What facts do you assume are given as the basis?
What number are you looking for, and what do you want it to be in the end?
Which side do you want to win, and what would the outcome be for each side?
What was the supplier's price, and how does it compare with other prices?
optionExplain: Right: assumed facts correspond to the hypothesis.
That is the unknown of a problem to find.
Wanting a result is not the hypothesis.
Price is only one possible datum.
questions.explain: It may be desirable to consider some datum by itself, and the questions are adapted to do so.
questions.rule: Ask what you assume.
questions.teaches: It may be desirable to consider some datum by itself, so the questions are modified to ask about the first datum, the second datum, and so on.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student finds geometry theorems evident and skips their proofs. What would you guess the entry says such a student misses?
options: Nothing, since a true theorem is fully learned once it is believed
Only the marks, since proofs are asked for in examinations
Something beyond the facts themselves, which the later headings name
Only the history, since proofs record who found each result first
optionExplain: Believing a fact feels like learning it, but the entry gives several reasons proofs matter beyond the fact.
Exams may reward proofs, but the entry's reasons are about evidence, system and memory.
Right: the entry argues that proofs teach more than the facts they establish.
The entry is not about credit; its reasons concern what proofs do for understanding.
questions.explain: The entry gives several reasons a student gains from proofs beyond the facts. The card next sets out the question it starts from.
questions.rule: Before you decide how much proof to teach or learn, ask which proofs serve a purpose instead of assuming all or none.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Which policies does the entry set against each other when it asks what is preferable? Select all that apply.
options: No proof at all
Proofs for everything
Some proofs only
Proofs only for students who ask
Proofs only in examinations
optionExplain: Right: this is the first policy it names.
Right: this is the second policy it names.
Right: and then it asks which proofs, if only some.
No such policy is considered; it sounds fair but the entry weighs only the three amounts.
Examinations are not discussed as a criterion in the entry.
questions.explain: The entry compares no proof, proofs for everything and some proofs, and asks which ones if only some.
questions.rule: Name the options before choosing among them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A tutor must decide whether to prove each rule in a unit. In the spirit of the entry, what should the tutor ask first?
options: Whether the rules are true, since true rules need no proof
Whether the learners are as quick at geometry as Newton was, since only they need proofs
Which proofs earn their place, and what each one would give the learner
Whether the time allows full proofs, and if not, to drop all of them
optionExplain: Truth is not the issue: Newton saw that theorems were true and the entry still asks why prove them.
Talent is not the criterion; the entry looks at what proofs give a learner.
Right: the entry treats the choice as a question of purpose, proof by proof.
This jumps to the all-or-none choice the entry is trying to avoid.
questions.explain: The entry does not pick all or none; it asks what proofs give and then which ones deserve a place.
questions.rule: Judge proofs by what they give, one by one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: Even if the Newton story is invented, the question of why we teach proofs remains.
questions.explain: The entry says the question remains whether or not the story is authentic.
questions.rule: A doubtful story does not remove its question.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: According to the story, what happened to Newton's view of Euclid's proofs?
options: He kept thinking proofs were superfluous for evident results
He praised the theorems but still rejected the proofs
He gave up geometry for physical science
Years later he changed his opinion and praised Euclid
optionExplain: This was his student view; the story says it changed.
The story has him praise Euclid, not split theorems from proofs.
The story says nothing about leaving geometry.
Right: this is the story's ending.
questions.explain: The story reports a reversal: the student who skipped proofs later praised Euclid. A first impression that proofs are idle can change with experience.
questions.rule: Early scorn for proofs may not last.
questions.teaches: In the story Newton changed his opinion many years later and praised Euclid.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A manager asks whether to explain why each safety rule exists or only list the rules. How does the entry's way of thinking help?
options: Ask workers to vote, since the entry settles it by majority
List the rules only, because workers can see for themselves that the rules are sensible
Explain every rule in full, since a partial explanation is worthless
Treat it as the none, all or some question and weigh the reasons for explaining
optionExplain: The entry gives reasons, not a vote.
This repeats the student's view that evident things need no explanation.
The entry later defends incomplete proofs, so all-or-nothing is not its position.
Right: the entry works toward its answer through five considerations rather than one rule.
questions.explain: The entry answers in five steps: complete proofs, logical system, mnemotechnic system, cookbook system, incomplete proofs. Our reading: the same weighing fits a rule list with or without reasons.
questions.rule: Weigh the reasons for each level of explanation.
questions.teaches: The entry answers its question through five considerations: complete proofs, logical system, mnemotechnic system, cookbook system and incomplete proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: In everyday life and in courts, we regularly meet proofs that leave no gaps at all.
questions.explain: The entry doubts that such proofs are found outside mathematics. The card next shows where it says to look.
questions.rule: Study proofs in plane geometry to learn what a proof with no gaps looks like.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A complete proof must leave no gaps, no loopholes and no ____ whatever.
questions.explain: A proof that leaves any uncertainty is, for the strict logician, no proof at all.
questions.rule: No gaps, no loopholes, no uncertainty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Which argument would the strict logician of the entry accept as a complete proof?
options: Ten experts agree the claim is correct and none can name a counterexample
The claim held in every one of a hundred trials, so it is proved
The argument is so convincing that no reader has yet thought to ask a question about any step
Each step follows from statements already accepted, and no step is left doubtful
optionExplain: Agreement of experts is strong evidence, but doubt can remain; it is not a complete proof.
Many trials give confidence, yet a case could still fail.
Persuasiveness is not completeness; a gap may simply be unnoticed.
Right: it leaves no gap or uncertainty.
questions.explain: The strict logician asks only whether every step is secure. Evidence, authority and persuasion do not meet that standard.
questions.rule: Completeness means every step is secure.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, plane geometry still offers the best opportunity to acquire the idea of rigorous proof.
questions.explain: Because everyday life rarely supplies proofs without gaps, the entry points to plane geometry as the place to learn the standard.
questions.rule: Learn rigour in plane geometry.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: According to the entry, where did humanity chiefly learn the idea of a strictly complete proof, with a little exaggeration?
options: From the courts, where evidence is weighed step by step
From experimental sciences, which test claims repeatedly
From Euclid and his Elements
From logicians' treatises written after Euclid
optionExplain: The entry lists legal procedure among places where complete proofs are scarce.
The entry lists physical science among those places too.
Right: the entry names one man and one book.
The entry credits Euclid, not later logicians.
questions.explain: The entry says humanity learned the idea from one man and one book, Euclid and the Elements, adding that this is a slight exaggeration.
questions.rule: Euclid's Elements is the source of the idea.
questions.teaches: With a little exaggeration, the entry says humanity learned the idea of strictly complete proof from Euclid and his Elements.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A judge says the evidence proves guilt beyond doubt. Given the entry's doubts, is that a complete proof in the logician's sense?
options: Yes, because a court is the strictest judge of truth that society has, and it hears all evidence
Yes, if the judge is experienced enough
Probably not, since the entry doubts legal procedure can reach a standard with no gaps
No, because only geometry can ever be proved by any method
optionExplain: Courts are careful, but the entry puts legal procedure among the doubtful cases.
Experience of the judge is not the test; completeness of the proof is.
Right: the entry lists legal procedure among places where such proofs are scarcely found.
The entry says scarcely, not never, and does not rule out other fields entirely.
questions.explain: The entry asks whether everyday life, legal procedure or physical science can meet the high standard and answers 'scarcely'. Our reading: so a verdict beyond reasonable doubt is a different, weaker standard.
questions.rule: Beyond doubt in practice is not the same as complete in logic.
questions.teaches: The entry names everyday life, legal procedure and physical science as places where complete proofs are scarcely found.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In a triangle ABC, a line through A is drawn parallel to BC. What do you expect this line to help show?
options: That the triangle must have two equal sides
That the three sides add up to a fixed length
That the three angles of the triangle add up to a straight angle
That the triangle's area is half a rectangle's
optionExplain: The parallel line says nothing about side lengths.
Sides have no fixed total; the line concerns angles.
Right: the two base angles reappear at A beside the angle already there.
That is a different result; the line is used for angles.
questions.explain: The line brings the base angles up to the vertex. The card next walks through the proof.
questions.rule: To prove the angle sum of a triangle, draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and match the angles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the proof, the angles at B and C equal angles at A because ____ angles between parallel lines are equal.
questions.explain: Alternate angles between the parallel line and the sides are equal, which carries the base angles up to A.
questions.rule: Alternate angles let the base angles move to the vertex.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A triangle has angles of \(50^\circ\) and \(65^\circ\). Using the proof, what is the third angle?
options: \(75^\circ\), since the two given angles are not equal
\(45^\circ\), since the angles must fill \(160^\circ\)
\(115^\circ\), since the third angle is the sum of the others
\(65^\circ\), since the three angles must fill \(180^\circ\)
optionExplain: Equality plays no role in the sum; 50 + 65 + 75 = 190.
The straight angle is 180, not 160.
50 + 65 = 115 is the sum of two angles, not what remains of 180.
questions.explain: The three angles fill a straight angle, so \(180 - 50 - 65 = 65\).
questions.rule: The angles fill 180 degrees.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student draws the extra line through A but makes it cut across the triangle instead of parallel to BC. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since any line through A works equally well
The triangle then has more than three angles, which breaks the count the proof relies on
The sum becomes more than two right angles
The alternate angles no longer equal the base angles, so they cannot be moved up to A
optionExplain: Any line through A makes some angles, but only a parallel gives equal alternate angles.
The number of angles in the triangle does not change.
The sum of the triangle's angles stays the same; it is the proof that fails.
Right: parallelism is what makes alternate angles equal.
questions.explain: Equal alternate angles are what the proof needs, and they come from parallel lines. Without parallelism the matching fails.
questions.rule: The parallel line is the key move.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says a student who has not met this particular angle-sum fact has missed something grave.
questions.explain: The entry says missing a particular geometric fact matters little; missing proofs matters more. A proof you can see teaches more than the fact.
questions.rule: A fact can be looked up; the habit of proof is the loss.
questions.teaches: The entry says a student who missed a particular geometric fact did not miss much, because the facts may have little use later in life.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student finishes school knowing many geometry facts but no proofs. What does the entry say the student lacks?
options: Only a few facts, which are easily looked up
A true standard with which to compare evidence offered in modern life
The patience to read long books
Skill at arithmetic, which proofs train
optionExplain: The entry says missing particular facts costs little; the loss lies elsewhere.
Right: the entry says proofs supply that standard.
The entry does not tie proofs to patience.
The entry makes no claim about arithmetic.
questions.explain: The entry says the loss is the idea of strict reasoning. The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: Learn a few geometric proofs to gain a true standard for judging evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Without having understood geometric proofs, the entry says a person lacks a true ____ with which to compare alleged evidence.
questions.explain: Proofs give a standard of evidence; without one every claim looks as good as another.
questions.rule: Proofs give a standard of evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A friend says a diet is proven because three people on a forum lost weight. Following the entry, what does a standard from proofs let you do?
options: Accept it, since any evidence is as good as another
Reject every claim that is not stated and proved as a geometry theorem, however sound
Compare the claim with real evidence and see it falls far short of proof
Wait for a teacher to decide which claims are true
optionExplain: Without a standard, this is exactly the temptation; the entry warns of it.
The entry asks for a standard of comparison, not a ban on non-geometric claims.
Right: the entry says the standard lets us compare alleged evidence with the real thing.
The point is to have the standard yourself.
questions.explain: The standard from proofs lets us see how far a claim is from real evidence. Our reading: it shows the gap; it does not decide the whole matter.
questions.rule: Set claims beside a real proof to see the gap.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: According to the entry, which loss is the more serious for a student, and why?
options: Missing particular facts, since facts are what a student is tested on and later uses
Missing both equally, since a proof only restates the fact
Missing neither, since later life needs neither
Missing proofs, since they are the best simple examples of true evidence
optionExplain: The entry says missing a particular fact is little loss.
The entry separates the two, ranking proofs higher.
The entry says the facts may have little use but the reasoning idea matters.
Right: the entry weighs proofs above particular facts.
questions.explain: The entry says a student who lacked some geometric facts missed little, but one who lacked proofs missed the best simple examples of evidence.
questions.rule: Proofs matter more than particular facts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry's argument depends on the student needing the geometric facts later in life.
questions.explain: The entry says the facts may have little use later. Its argument rests on the standard of evidence and reasoning that proofs give.
questions.rule: The value is the standard, not the stock of facts.
questions.teaches: The entry says the particular geometric facts may be of little use in later life, so its case for proofs does not rest on them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What do you think made Euclid's Elements more than a collection of geometric facts?
options: The pictures that accompany each fact
The large number of facts it gathered in one place
The order of the propositions, each resting on what precedes it
The fame of its author, which gave it authority
optionExplain: Figures help, but the entry stresses the ordering.
Quantity is not what the entry values.
Right: the entry points to the ordering as the main merit.
The entry rates the system, not the fame.
questions.explain: The entry stresses the order and logical dependence. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Read a deductive subject as a system in which each proposition is tied to earlier ones by a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In Euclid's system, each proposition is linked to the foregoing axioms, definitions and propositions by a ____.
questions.explain: Proofs are the links; without them the order is only a list.
questions.rule: Proofs are the cement of the system.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student reads a chapter of a physics text and wants to know whether it forms a system. What would show it?
options: The chapter lists many results under tidy headings
Each result is derived from earlier ones in the text, so the order can be traced
The chapter uses the formal tone of a geometry book
The chapter has the most citations of any chapter in the book, each pointing to a source
optionExplain: Tidy listing is a collection, not a system.
Right: this is how Euclid's propositions are placed.
Tone does not make dependence.
Citations show sources, not logical dependence.
questions.explain: A system is shown by dependence: each item rests on earlier ones. Our reading: the same test applies outside geometry.
questions.rule: A system shows its order by dependence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says Euclid's main achievement was arranging the propositions into a logical system.
questions.explain: The entry credits the ordered arrangement of propositions into a logical system as his main achievement.
questions.rule: Credit Euclid with the system.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The entry calls Euclid's geometry the first and greatest example of a logical system. What does it say about other sciences?
options: They have all succeeded, and the debate is over
They have no use for logical systems
Only physics may imitate it, because only physics uses figures and diagrams to support its reasoning
They try to imitate it, though whether psychology or jurisprudence should is debatable
optionExplain: The entry calls the question debatable.
The entry says they try to imitate.
The entry gives no such restriction.
Right: this is how the entry states it.
questions.explain: The entry says other sciences have tried and are trying to imitate Euclid, and that whether sciences far from geometry should is debatable.
questions.rule: Imitating Euclid is debated.
questions.teaches: Other sciences try to imitate Euclid's system; whether very distant ones such as psychology or jurisprudence should is a debatable question.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student wants to join the debate on whether law should be built like Euclid. What does the entry say she needs first?
options: No preparation, since the debate is about opinion
A degree in law, since only trained lawyers are competent to judge such a question at all
A new system for law, to compare with Euclid
Acquaintance with the Euclidean system, since competence in the debate requires it
optionExplain: The entry says competence requires acquaintance.
The entry names acquaintance with Euclid, not a degree.
The entry asks for knowledge of Euclid first.
Right: the entry says so directly.
questions.explain: The entry says nobody can take part in the debate with competence who is not acquainted with the Euclidean system. This is a reason to learn Euclid even for fields far from geometry.
questions.rule: Know the model before debating imitating it.
questions.teaches: The entry says nobody can debate competently whether other sciences should imitate Euclid without being acquainted with the Euclidean system.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student must remember two geometry facts but has no time for logic. Which approach would you guess helps most?
options: Repeat each fact on its own until it sticks
Memorise the page numbers where they appear
Link the facts through a simple proof or figure that connects them
Skip the facts and keep only the formulas
optionExplain: Isolated items are laboriously acquired and easily forgotten.
This helps lookup, not retention of the facts.
Right: connected facts stick better than isolated ones.
The entry's point is that connection aids memory, not that facts are dropped.
questions.explain: The entry says isolated items are easily forgotten. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When only the facts are wanted, attach them to a simple proof or system so they connect.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Connected facts are better retained than ____ facts.
questions.explain: A connection gives each fact a hook; an isolated item has none.
questions.rule: Connect facts to remember them.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A language teacher gives 30 unrelated verb forms to memorise. Following the entry, what would help?
options: Drop the pattern, because only a strictly logical system can really aid the memory of a learner
Add more forms so repetition fixes them all
Let learners pick the forms they like
Group them into a pattern that links related forms, even one not based on logic
optionExplain: The entry says the system need not be logical.
More isolated items are harder, not easier.
Choice is not a connection among the items.
Right: any simple, natural, durable connection is welcome.
questions.explain: The entry welcomes any connection that unites facts simply, naturally and durably, even without logic.
questions.rule: Any simple connection helps memory.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, a system meant only to aid memory need not be founded on logic.
questions.explain: The entry says the system need not be founded on logic; it must only aid the memory effectively.
questions.rule: A memory system need not be logical.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say about simple proofs from a purely mnemotechnic point of view?
options: They are harmful, since they add facts to remember
They are useless, since memory is helped only by repetition
They may still be useful, especially simple ones
They are useful only if complete
optionExplain: The entry says they connect facts instead.
The entry says proofs may be useful.
Right: even a memory system may include proofs.
The entry's example is a simple figure, not a full proof system.
questions.explain: The entry says even from a mnemotechnic viewpoint proofs, especially simple ones, may be useful.
questions.rule: Simple proofs aid memory.
questions.teaches: Even from the point of view of a purely mnemotechnic system, proofs, especially simple ones, may be useful.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In a first-aid course the instructor gives each step with the reason it protects the patient. Which feature of the entry does this match?
options: The cookbook, which gives each step of a recipe with no reasons for any of them
The logician's demand for no uncertainty
Connecting facts to reasons makes them interesting and durable, as proofs do
The incomplete proof sold as a complete one
optionExplain: The cookbook gives no reasons.
That is the complete-proof standard, not a memory aid.
Right: reasons link steps as proofs link facts.
Nothing in the course pretends incompleteness.
questions.explain: The entry says connected facts are better retained. Our reading: the same holds for steps and their reasons.
questions.rule: Reasons make steps stick.
questions.teaches: The entry says that facts presented in some connection and system are retained better because isolated items are laboriously acquired and easily forgotten.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Engineering students have little time for difficult proofs in calculus. What do you expect happens if all proofs are cut?
options: The students invent their own proofs for the missing steps
Nothing is lost, since engineers only apply the results
The students learn faster and remember more
The procedures are poorly understood and the rules are soon forgotten
optionExplain: This would be nice, but the entry predicts the opposite effect.
Application feels like the goal, but the entry says unmotivated procedures are not understood.
Less to read feels like faster learning, but unconnected rules fade.
Right: rules without reasons fail to stick.
questions.explain: The entry warns that rules without reasons are forgotten. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Do not teach a subject to be understood as a cookbook; give the reasons for the rules, not only the rules.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The cookbook gives a description of ingredients and procedures but no ____ for its prescriptions.
questions.explain: The cookbook gives no proofs or reasons for its recipes; the pudding itself is the test.
questions.rule: A cookbook gives rules without reasons.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A software course teaches ten commands without saying why any works. By the entry's reasoning, what is likely?
options: Students will remember them all, since commands are short
Students will not understand the commands and will soon forget them
Students will understand, since using a command a few times teaches its logic
Students will do better than with a full theory
optionExplain: Short items are still isolated; the entry says isolated items are forgotten.
Right: unmotivated procedures are not understood and unconnected rules are forgotten.
Use may help, but the entry says procedures without proofs are not understood.
Nothing in the entry supports this.
questions.explain: The entry's two warnings apply: commands taught without reasons are unmotivated and unconnected.
questions.rule: Teach the reason with the rule.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A professor says: Cooks use recipes without proofs, so a calculus course can follow the same system. What is the flaw?
options: Cooks in fact learn the chemistry behind each recipe before they ever cook from it, unlike students
Calculus has no procedures, so there is nothing to compare
Recipes are written down and consulted, not kept in memory, but a course must be understood
Recipes are always more complex than calculus procedures
optionExplain: The entry says the cookbook gives no reasons for its recipes.
The entry discusses calculus procedures and rules.
Right: the entry gives this as the reason the cookbook needs no system.
The entry makes no complexity comparison.
questions.explain: The entry says a cookbook need not have a logical or mnemotechnic system since recipes are written or printed and not retained in memory. A calculus course must be retained.
questions.rule: Written recipes need no memory aid; a course does.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry predict for a calculus course in which all reasoning is barred?
options: It becomes a more efficient list of rules that is easy to apply
It becomes a course that can be tested by its results, the way a pudding is tested
It becomes a course of pure logic that engineers can follow
It may easily become an incoherent inventory of indigestible information
optionExplain: The entry calls such a list indigestible.
The entry says mathematics cannot be tested exactly like a pudding.
Cutting proofs removes logic, not adds it.
Right: this is the entry's own forecast.
questions.explain: The entry says mathematics cannot be tested in the same manner as a pudding; barring all reasoning risks an incoherent inventory of indigestible information.
questions.rule: Without reasoning a course is an inventory.
questions.teaches: The entry says a calculus course that bars all reasoning may easily become an incoherent inventory of indigestible information.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says a printed collection of recipes fails if it gives no reasons for its recipes.
questions.explain: The entry says the cookbook may serve its purpose perfectly. The failure arises only when a textbook follows the cookbook system too closely.
questions.rule: A cookbook is fine as a cookbook; a course should not copy it.
questions.teaches: The entry says a cookbook may serve its purpose perfectly; the trouble starts when a textbook or instructor follows its system too closely.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A class meets a theorem whose proof is far beyond them. Which approach would you guess the entry favours?
options: Skip the theorem until the class can follow a full proof
Show the easier connected facts that make it plausible, and say it is not a full proof
State the theorem and ask the class to take it on authority
Present the easy facts as if they were the complete proof
optionExplain: This avoids the dilemma but loses what the theorem could give meanwhile.
Right: the entry favours reasonable use of incomplete proofs.
