This is the cookbook route the entry warns about.
The entry calls selling an incomplete proof as complete worse than confusing them.
questions.explain: The entry endorses incomplete proofs in their place. The card next describes them.
questions.rule: Use an incomplete proof, honestly labelled, to give a result interest, plausibility and coherence when a complete proof is out of reach.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Incomplete proofs do not replace complete ones; their purpose is to lend interest and ____ to the presentation.
questions.explain: They give a result interest and a place in the learner's mind, not logical certainty.
questions.rule: Incomplete proofs give interest and coherence.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What do the facts about degrees 1 and 2, and the easy upper bound, support for an equation of degree 7?
options: That exactly 7 roots exist, since the proof is now complete
That at least 7 roots exist, shown by the same bound
At most 7 different roots is shown, and exactly 7 becomes plausible but not proved
Nothing, since examples with small degrees say nothing at all about larger degrees, however regular the pattern
optionExplain: The facts are not a complete proof; the entry says so.
The bound gives at most, not at least.
Right: the upper bound is the easily shown part and the rest is made plausible.
They do not prove it, but the entry says they give plausibility.
questions.explain: The easy part gives at most \(n\) different roots; the equality for \(n=7\) rests on the pattern for \(n=1,2\), which is plausible but not a proof.
questions.rule: Small cases make plausible, not proved.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: A textbook may call a few easy facts about a theorem a complete proof of it if the facts make the theorem plausible.
questions.explain: The entry says such facts are not a complete proof, and selling an incomplete proof as complete is worse than confusing the two.
questions.rule: Label plausible arguments as incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say about the basis on which mathematicians accepted the Fundamental Theorem for about 250 years?
options: Repeated experiment in physical science
A complete proof given by Euclid
Little more than the plausible facts shown to students, and no complete proof
A vote among the leading mathematicians of the age, who agreed to accept it as true
optionExplain: The entry cites no experiments.
The entry says no complete proof was in hand.
Right: the entry says they believed it without complete proof.
The entry mentions no vote.
questions.explain: The entry notes that for about 250 years mathematicians believed the theorem without a complete proof, on little more basis than the students' facts.
questions.rule: Plausibility has carried real mathematics.
questions.teaches: For about 250 years mathematicians believed the Fundamental Theorem without a complete proof and without much more basis than the plausible facts shown to students.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student notes that the angle sums of a triangle, a four-sided figure and a five-sided figure follow a regular pattern and guesses a general rule. What does the entry call such a step?
options: A complete proof by induction on the number of sides
A plausible argument from observation and analogy, a source of conjectures
A cookbook rule with no reasoning at all
A logical system in the manner of Euclid, with every claim derived from earlier ones
optionExplain: A pattern on three cases is not a proof.
Right: the entry says discovery often starts from observation, analogy and induction.
The student has observed a pattern and reasoned from it.
The student has not derived the rule from earlier propositions.
questions.explain: The entry says analogy is an important source of conjectures and that discovery often starts from observation, analogy and induction.
questions.rule: Observation and analogy start discoveries.
questions.teaches: The entry calls analogy an important source of conjectures and says discovery in mathematics and science often starts from observation, analogy and induction.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The first idea of a proof usually arrives with every detail already in place.
questions.explain: The entry says the first idea of a proof is very frequently incomplete. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When you present a proof, start with its germ, the main idea in its simplest form, and add the details afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The most essential remark of a proof, its main connection, is called its ____.
questions.explain: The germ is the main idea; details are filled in afterwards.
questions.rule: The germ is the main connection.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Which opening best presents the germ of a proof that the sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is \(n^2\)?
options: Check the claim for \(n=1,2,3\) and then stop
List all the axioms of arithmetic that any proof of the claim could ever make use of
State that the claim is true because textbooks say so
Show rows of 1, 3, 5, ... squares that wrap one another into a growing square
optionExplain: Checking cases is evidence, not the connecting idea.
This is detail without the main connection.
Authority is not a germ.
Right: it states the central picture and leaves the algebra for later.
questions.explain: The wrapping squares show why the sum is a square; the algebra is a detail that can follow.
questions.rule: Lead with the connection, not the checks.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a proof giving only the germ may be much more instructive than a proof with complete details.
questions.explain: The entry says such a proof, although incomplete, may be much more instructive than a proof presented with complete details.
questions.rule: A bare germ can teach more than a full proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Besides the main idea, what must an author with the gift of presenting only the germ also do?
options: Replace the details with a figure only
Hide the remaining details so the reader finds them alone
Supply every detail in footnotes
Indicate the nature of the remaining details
optionExplain: The entry does not say a figure replaces details.
The entry wants the nature of the details indicated.
That would be the complete proof, not a germ.
Right: the entry says so.
questions.explain: The entry says some authors, but not many, can present just the germ in its simplest form and indicate the nature of the remaining details.
questions.rule: A good germ points to what is missing.
questions.teaches: Only a few authors have the gift of presenting just the germ in its simplest form while indicating the nature of the remaining details.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A mentor explains a hard algorithm by stating its key insight and saying that edge cases still need care. Which remark of the entry does this match?
options: A complete proof fully replaces the germ
Details come afterwards and are often troublesome, so the key idea comes first
Details are unimportant and may be dropped
Only experts can ever follow an incomplete proof, so it should be kept from beginners
optionExplain: The entry says the germ is the essential part.
Right: the entry says details must be provided afterwards and often prove troublesome.
The entry says they must be provided afterwards.
The entry says incomplete proofs may be more instructive.
questions.explain: The entry says the germ is there first and details must be provided afterwards, often with trouble.
questions.rule: Insight first, details after.
questions.teaches: Once the germ is found, the details must be provided afterwards and are often troublesome.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A teacher gives a partial argument for a theorem. What would you ask of the teacher?
options: That the teacher hide the gaps to avoid confusing students
That the teacher make it as long as a complete proof
That the argument be marked as incomplete
That the teacher drop the theorem
optionExplain: Hiding gaps is the abuse the entry fears.
Length does not make a proof complete.
Right: marking prevents readers mistaking it for a full proof.
The entry supports using partial arguments honestly.
questions.explain: The entry's first rule is to indicate the incompleteness. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Whenever a proof is incomplete, indicate it as such, somewhere and somehow.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: If a proof is incomplete, it must be ____ as such, somewhere and somehow.
questions.explain: The first rule is that the incompleteness be indicated.
questions.rule: Indicate incompleteness.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A tutor sketches a proof in class. Which action follows the first rule?
options: Writing 'QED' to give it a finished look
Leaving the gaps unmentioned so no one is distracted
Giving the sketch extra detail until it looks complete, whether or not it is
Saying aloud that the sketch leaves out steps and is not a full proof
optionExplain: This hides the gaps.
Silence about gaps breaks the rule.
Looking complete is not being complete.
Right: it indicates incompleteness somehow.
questions.explain: The rule needs only that the incompleteness be indicated; saying so aloud does that.
questions.rule: Say that it is incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What second condition does the entry set on an author or teacher who presents an incomplete proof?
options: He must have published a proof of the theorem himself
He must himself know very well a complete proof of the theorem
He must show students the complete proof afterwards
He must be a recognised authority on the subject, with published work on it
optionExplain: Knowing a proof is enough; publishing is not required.
Right: he is not entitled otherwise.
The entry does not require this.
The entry asks for knowing the complete proof, not status.
questions.explain: The entry says an author or teacher is not entitled to present an incomplete proof unless he knows a complete one himself.
questions.rule: Know the full proof before sketching it.
questions.teaches: An author or teacher is not entitled to present an incomplete proof for a theorem unless he himself knows a complete proof of it very well.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Sort these practices: do they follow the entry's rules for incomplete proofs, or break them?

items.t: A teacher says the argument is a sketch and she knows the full proof
A textbook gives a plausibility argument labelled as incomplete by an author who has studied the full proof
A teacher presents a partial argument as a full proof
A teacher presents a partial argument without knowing how a full proof goes
An author hesitates between shame and pretending the argument is complete
A lecturer says the argument is incomplete and the missing part is the hard one

questions.explain: The rules are that incompleteness be indicated and that the presenter know a complete proof. The second and fourth fail one rule each, and hesitating between shame and pretence fails the first.
questions.rule: Indicate it, and know the complete proof.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: An analyst presents a model's forecast as certain, though the key step was assumed rather than checked. Which remark of the entry fits?
options: A forecast cannot be an incomplete proof
Assumed steps are harmless if the forecast turns out to be right in the end, so honesty about gaps is optional
Only mathematicians face this problem
To confuse them is bad, and to sell one for the other is worse
optionExplain: The analogy is about presenting unchecked steps as checked.
The entry's rules concern honesty about gaps, not outcomes.
The entry's rules are about proofs, but the reasoning carries over.
Right: the entry ranks confusion below selling.
questions.explain: The entry says confusing the two is bad and selling one for the other worse. Our reading: the same honesty applies outside mathematics.
questions.rule: Do not sell the unfinished as finished.
questions.teaches: The entry says that to confuse incomplete proofs with complete ones is bad, and to sell one for the other is worse.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A course has little time and its students will apply the subject. Which proof treatment would you guess the entry recommends?
options: No proofs, since students will only apply the results
Complete proofs for every result, whatever the time
Reasonable use of incomplete proofs, marked as such
Only proofs that appear on the final test
optionExplain: This is the cookbook the entry warns against.
This ignores the entry's practical limits.
Right: it avoids both heavy proofs and the cookbook.
The entry does not choose by test content.
questions.explain: The entry sees incomplete proofs as the way between heavy proofs and the cookbook. The card next gathers the options.
questions.rule: Match the proof treatment to the aim: complete proofs for strict reasoning and system, simple proofs for memory, incomplete proofs where full ones are too heavy, never the bare cookbook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Match each aim to the proof treatment the entry links with it.
pairs: Acquire the ideas of evidence and strict reasoning
Understand a subject as a connected deductive structure
Help facts connect and be remembered
Rules with no reasons, as in a recipe book
Lend interest and coherence when full proofs are too heavy
questions.explain: Each heading of the entry names a treatment with its own end.
questions.rule: Each treatment serves its own end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A school wants all pupils to leave with the idea of strict reasoning. What does the entry say it must do?
options: Teach many geometric facts and skip proofs
Offer a cookbook of formulas with practice
Reserve a place for geometric proofs
Teach only incomplete proofs
optionExplain: The entry says facts matter little compared with proofs.
The cookbook gives no reasons.
Right: the entry draws this conclusion for general education.
Incomplete proofs do not replace complete ones.
questions.explain: For the idea of strict reasoning, the entry requires geometric proofs in general education.
questions.rule: Strict reasoning needs real proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, a course with little time that does not aim at general logical ideas should drop proofs entirely.
questions.explain: The entry says that even then proofs may be useful, as a memory device, especially simple proofs.
questions.rule: Even short courses can use simple proofs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say is the best way of handling the dilemma between too heavy proofs and the level of the cookbook?
options: Full proofs for everything, taught slowly
Reasonable use of incomplete proofs
Dropping calculus from engineering courses
Replacing proofs with worked numerical examples
optionExplain: The entry says this is the heavy extreme.
Right: this is its stated suggestion.
The entry does not suggest this.
The entry does not suggest this.
questions.explain: The entry says the best way may be to make reasonable use of incomplete proofs.
questions.rule: Between heavy proofs and a cookbook, use honest incomplete proofs.
questions.teaches: The entry names reasonable use of incomplete proofs as the best way of handling the dilemma between too heavy proofs and the level of the cookbook.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: An online course for nurses on dosage calculation has little time and wants dependable memory. Which choice is closest to the entry's advice?
options: Leave the rules for learners to discover
List the rules alone, as in a cookbook, since learners will look them up when needed
Prove every rule completely from basics
Give each rule with a short reason, and mark any shortcut as one
optionExplain: The entry does not recommend discovery in place of instruction.
Rules without reasons are quickly forgotten.
Time rules this out, as with the engineers.
Right: reasons connect, and shortcuts should be indicated.
questions.explain: The entry's cases of limited time point to connected, short justifications. Our reading: nursing is outside the entry, but the reasoning carries over.
questions.rule: Short reasons beat bare rules.
questions.teaches: The entry says even when no special importance is attached to general logical ideas, proofs may be useful as a mnemotechnic device.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: How far would you trust proverbs as a guide to solving problems?
options: Fully, since they hold the wisdom of many generations
As lively descriptions of method, which can conflict and need judgment
Not at all, since they contradict one another
Only those that appear in several languages
optionExplain: Age feels like authority, but the entry calls it foolish to treat proverbs as authoritative.
Right: this is the entry's balanced view.
Contradiction is real, but the entry says it would be a pity to disregard them.
The entry gives no such test.
questions.explain: The entry values proverbs without making them law. The card next gives its view.
questions.rule: Read proverbs as vivid descriptions of how people solve problems, not as authority.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Many a proverb can be matched with another giving exactly ____ advice.
questions.explain: Because proverbs can be paired with opposites, they cannot serve as a consistent system.
questions.rule: Proverbs can contradict one another.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student meets two proverbs, one urging haste and one urging care, and asks which is right. What does the entry suggest?
options: Follow the one that is older, since it has lasted longer and been tested by more people
Follow the one that more people know
Treat each as describing a procedure that fits some circumstances, and judge
Reject both, since contradictory sayings are useless
optionExplain: Age is not the entry's test.
Popularity is not the entry's test.
Right: the entry allows great latitude of interpretation.
The entry values them as descriptions.
questions.explain: The entry says there is great latitude of interpretation, so a proverb is a description to be fitted to the case.
questions.rule: Fit the proverb to the circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry presents the proverbs on solving problems as a consistent scientific system.
questions.explain: The entry says there is no such system in them: they contain inconsistencies, obscurities and opposite pairs.
questions.rule: Proverbs are not a system.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: How does the entry arrange the proverbs it quotes?
options: Under the main phases of the solution emphasized in the book's list
In alphabetical order by their first words
By the country each proverb comes from, beginning with the oldest nations
From the most to the least famous
optionExplain: Right: it uses the phases of the solution as headings.
The entry gives numbered phases, not an alphabetical list.
The entry does not cite origins.
The entry does not rank them.
questions.explain: The entry says it quotes proverbs illustrating the main phases of the solution: understanding, planning, carrying out and looking back.
questions.rule: The proverbs follow the phases of solution.
questions.teaches: The entry quotes proverbs to illustrate the main phases of the solution from the book's list, which are understanding, devising a plan, carrying out the plan and looking back.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A manager reads a proverb about a common planning mistake. How might it be useful, going by the entry?
options: As a binding rule to apply to the plan, since proverbs capture settled wisdom about planning
As a graphic description of a usual error to watch for, not as a rule to obey
As proof that the mistake never occurs when the proverb is known
It has no use, since planning needs data not sayings
optionExplain: The entry calls this foolish.
Right: the entry says proverbs describe usual tricks and usual errors.
The entry makes no such claim.
The entry says disregarding proverbs would be a pity.
questions.explain: The entry says proverbs characterise strikingly the typical procedures, the points of common sense, the usual tricks and the usual errors.
questions.rule: Use proverbs to see the usual errors.
questions.teaches: Proverbs characterise the typical procedures, points of common sense, usual tricks and usual errors in solving problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A group starts on a task without agreeing what the finished result should be. What would you expect?
options: They may stray from the problem and drop it
They will find the best route faster by trying things
They will succeed because enthusiasm overcomes vagueness
They will finish early since there is nothing to check against
optionExplain: Right: an unclear end loses the thread.
Trying may help later, but with no end in view they lack a direction.
Enthusiasm does not tell them what to aim at.
With no aim there is nothing to measure progress by.
questions.explain: The entry says an unclear end invites straying. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: Understand the problem and keep its end clearly in mind before you begin to act.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The proverb in the entry says that one who understands the problem badly will also give a ____ answer.
questions.explain: The entry quotes this proverb for understanding the problem first.
questions.rule: Understand ill, answer ill.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: You are handed a vague assignment by a manager. Which first move follows the entry?
options: Start on the part you know best and see where it leads before asking anything of anyone
Restate what the finished result must be and check it with the manager
Collect as many related documents as possible
Ask a colleague what they would do
optionExplain: This acts before the end is clear.
Right: it fixes the end before acting.
Collecting may help later, but it does not fix the end.
A colleague cannot say what the manager wants.
questions.explain: Before acting, make the end clear to yourself, as the proverb 'Think on the end before you begin' advises.
questions.rule: Fix the end before you start.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, people who ignore the advice to understand the aim tend to hold back from acting.
questions.explain: The entry says they start speculating, talking and even acting fussily without having understood the aim.
questions.rule: Unclear aims do not stop action; they misdirect it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What else besides understanding does the entry say a difficult problem needs?
options: A quick start, since delay kills the chance
A helper to share the work, since a difficult problem rarely yields to one person
A reward promised in advance
A strong desire to solve it, for with such desire there is a chance
optionExplain: Speed is not what the entry asks for; it asks for desire as well as understanding.
The entry's point is the solver's own desire, not a helper sharing the work.
Reward is not the entry's point; the desire to solve the problem is what gives a chance.
Right: the entry says there is no chance without it.
questions.explain: The entry says it is not enough to understand the problem; we must also desire its solution, as in 'Where there is a will there is a way'.
questions.rule: Understanding needs wanting.
questions.teaches: Besides understanding the problem, we must desire its solution: there is no chance of solving a difficult problem without strong desire, but with it there is a chance.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A meeting jumps to suggesting fixes before anyone has said what the problem is. Which comment of the entry applies?
options: People often speculate and act without understanding the aim, though the advice is old
Early fixes are best, since a fix shows what the problem is
The meeting is right, since a clear aim too early would spoil the creativity of the group
Only the chair needs to understand the aim
optionExplain: Right: the entry describes this habit and calls the advice old.
The entry says to see the end first.
The entry makes no such claim.
The entry asks everyone who works at the problem to understand it.
questions.explain: The entry notes that the advice 'respice finem' is old and that people nevertheless often fail to heed it.
questions.rule: Name the aim before the fixes.
questions.teaches: The advice to see the end before beginning is old, the Latin saying being 'respice finem', yet not everybody heeds it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Your first attempt at a hard problem fails. Which next step is the most promising?
options: Try a different means, adapted to the circumstances
Repeat the same attempt with more force
Stop, since a failure shows the problem is unsolvable
Wait for inspiration to arrive on its own
optionExplain: Right: variation widens the chances.
The same trial rarely yields a different result.
One failure shows only that this means failed.
The entry says luck is deserved by diligence.
questions.explain: The entry says to try different means. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Keep trying after a failure, but vary the means and keep a second plan in reserve.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Try all the keys in the ____.
questions.explain: The entry quotes this to urge varying one's trials.
questions.rule: Vary the trials.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student's method for a puzzle has failed three times. By the entry, what should she do?
options: Repeat the same method until it works, since perseverance kills the game
Switch to a different method rather than repeat the same one
Give the puzzle to someone else at once
Wait until she feels sure the method is right
optionExplain: Perseverance must include variation.
Right: if we have failed, we must try something else.
The entry advises varying her own trials first.
Waiting does not change the method.
questions.explain: The entry says it is not enough to try repeatedly; we must try different means.
questions.rule: Vary, not only repeat.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says changing from one scheme to another can be overdone and cost time.
questions.explain: The entry quotes an ironical comment on doing and undoing for this fault.
questions.rule: Vary, but do not flit.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say keeps us from blundering when we try different means?
options: Having the most expensive tools available
Working alone without consulting others
Trying every possible means in turn, in the hope that one of them is the right one
Not losing sight of our aim, since fishing is for catching, not angling
optionExplain: Expensive tools are not the entry's point; keeping the aim in sight is.
Working alone is not what the entry advises against blundering; the fishing proverb about keeping the aim is.
The entry warns against changing too often.
Right: the entry offers this proverb.
questions.explain: The entry says we are likely to blunder less if we do not lose sight of the aim: the end of fishing is catching, not angling.
questions.rule: Keep the aim in view while varying.
questions.teaches: We are likely to blunder less if we do not lose sight of our aim, as in 'The end of fishing is not angling but catching'.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A builder's planned timber is out of stock, so she redesigns the shelf around the boards the yard has. Which remark of the entry fits?
options: We must do as we may if we cannot do as we would, adapting the plan
A plan should not change once made, as a wise man holds his course whatever happens
She should wait for the planned timber, since waiting kills the game
She should give up, since the first plan has failed
optionExplain: Right: the entry quotes this advice with 'Cut your coat according to the cloth'.
The entry says a wise man changes his mind and a fool never does.
The entry does not praise waiting for ideal conditions here.
The entry advises trying something else instead.
questions.explain: The entry says we must adapt our trials to the circumstances and do as we may if we can't do as we would.
questions.rule: Adapt the plan to what you have.
questions.teaches: If we cannot do as we would, we must do as we may; our trials must be adapted to the circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What may make an expert better than a beginner at finding ideas?
options: Having far more ideas than the beginner
Appreciating and using the ideas that come, even modest ones
Waiting until an idea looks impressive
Avoiding ideas that come from memory
optionExplain: The entry says the expert perhaps has no more ideas.
Right: the entry suggests the expert does not need more ideas.
Inconspicuous ideas are exactly the ones that matter.
The entry says we work hard to extract help from memory.
questions.explain: The entry says the expert appreciates what he has. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Notice and use the modest ideas that come to mind, and look for opportunities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The expert has perhaps no more ideas than the inexperienced, but ____ more what he has.
questions.explain: Appreciation, not number, marks the expert.
questions.rule: Appreciate the idea you have.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: During a discussion a student says, almost as an aside, that two columns in a table differ by 2 in every row. What should the teacher do?
options: Move on, since the remark is not part of the plan
Note it only if the student sounds confident that the remark is correct
Ask what follows if the difference is 2 in every row, since it may be useful
Wait until a clever student says the same
optionExplain: This is how inconspicuous ideas are lost.
Confidence is not the criterion.
Right: an inconspicuous remark may carry the idea.
The entry values modest ideas.
questions.explain: The entry says helpful ideas present themselves inconspicuously, so the skill is to notice them.
questions.rule: Follow up the modest remark.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says the expert perhaps has no more ideas than the beginner but appreciates them more.
questions.explain: The entry says the expert perhaps has no more ideas but appreciates and uses them better.
questions.rule: Appreciation, not supply.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What second explanation of the expert's advantage does the entry offer?
options: That the expert is continually on the lookout for opportunities
That the expert has a better memory than the beginner for similar past problems
That the expert avoids all risk
That the expert uses more tools
optionExplain: Right: the entry says 'or, possibly' this.
The entry does not claim better memory.
Avoiding risk is not offered as the expert's advantage; the entry says he watches for opportunities.
More tools are not the second explanation; it is the expert's constant watch for chances.
questions.explain: The entry offers it as a possibility alongside appreciation: he is continually on the lookout, and the proverb 'Have an eye to the main chance' fits.
questions.rule: Keep a lookout for chances.
questions.teaches: The expert's advantage may also lie in continually being on the lookout for opportunities.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A teacher's projector breaks, so she turns the class to the windows and teaches shadows from the sunlight. Which proverb of the entry fits?
options: Do and undo, the day is long enough
A wise man will make tools of what comes to hand
Where there is a will there is a way
Diligence is the mother of good luck, and perseverance kills the game
optionExplain: This mocks changing schemes without end.
Right: she makes a tool of what came to hand.
This is about wanting a solution, not using chance.
This proverb about diligence and perseverance concerns effort, not using what comes to hand.
questions.explain: The entry says a wise man makes more opportunities than he finds and makes tools of what comes to hand.
questions.rule: Use what comes to hand.
questions.teaches: A wise man will make more opportunities than he finds, and will make tools of what comes to hand, and turn chance into good fortune.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: When should you begin carrying out a plan?
options: When it is ripe, judged by yourself
As soon as it is made, to avoid losing momentum
Only once success is guaranteed
When someone else tells you the time has come
optionExplain: Right: neither early nor late.
Rashness is the fault the entry warns of.
If you will sail without danger you must never put to sea.
The entry says we must use our own judgment.
questions.explain: The entry warns against both haste and delay. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Start carrying out the plan when it is ripe, neither rashly nor after endless hesitation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Look before you ____.
questions.explain: The proverb urges care before action.
questions.rule: Do not start rashly.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A founder has a prototype but keeps polishing it for a year, afraid of risk. Which remark of the entry fits?
options: Look before you leap, so keep polishing until no flaw is left and nothing can go wrong
A wise delay makes the road safe in every case
If you will sail without danger you must never put to sea; do not hesitate too long
The plan is ripe only when others say it is
optionExplain: This takes only one side.
Delay is wise only when it is wise.
Right: waiting for no danger means never starting.
The entry asks for our own judgment.
questions.explain: The entry balances 'Look before you leap' against not hesitating too long.
questions.rule: Delay only as long as it helps.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, the right moment to begin must be determined by our own judgment.
questions.explain: The proverbs pull both ways, so the entry says we must use our judgment to determine the moment.
questions.rule: Judgment decides the moment.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: If a plan cannot be made fully safe, what advice for acting does the entry quote?
options: Do the likeliest and hope the best
Do nothing and hope for better
Do the unlikeliest and hope the worst
Do what others do and hope for the same
optionExplain: Right: this proverb follows the warning against hesitating.
Waiting is the fault in question.
The quoted advice is to hope for the best from the likeliest course, not to pick the unlikeliest and hope for the worst.
The quoted proverb advises acting on the likeliest course, not copying what others do.
questions.explain: The entry quotes 'Do the likeliest and hope the best' after warning against hesitating too long.
questions.rule: When certainty is out of reach, do the likeliest.
questions.teaches: When delay is no longer wise, the entry quotes 'Do the likeliest and hope the best'.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A manager is sure a new product will sell because she badly wants it to. Which failure does the entry point to?
options: She is hesitating too long and so missing the best moment to begin the launch
We soon believe what we desire, the most usual failure of judgment
She is acting after due reflection
She is relying on a second proof
optionExplain: She is certain, not hesitating.
Right: wishing shapes the judgment of the moment.
Her certainty comes from desire.
No second proof is described.
questions.explain: The entry names 'We soon believe what we desire' as the most common fallacy, and the usual failure of our judgment.
questions.rule: Distrust a judgment colored by wishes.
questions.teaches: The most common fallacy and usual failure of our judgment about the right moment is that we soon believe what we desire.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A plan gives only an outline. How do you make sure it works?
options: Examine each detail in turn to see it fits
Trust the outline, since details follow of themselves
Check only the first and last steps
Ask others to check the whole at once
optionExplain: Right: the outline does not show the details.
Details often hide the trouble.
The middle steps may fail.
Step-by-step checking is the entry's advice.
questions.explain: The entry says to examine each detail one after the other. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Carry out the plan step by step, checking each detail in turn.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Step after step the ____ is ascended.
questions.explain: The proverb stands for going step by step.
questions.rule: Go step by step.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A builder worked out her design backwards from the finished roof: the roof needs walls, the walls need a foundation, the foundation needs dug ground. In what order does she build?
items: Dig the ground
Lay the foundation
Raise the walls
Put on the roof
questions.explain: She found the design from the roof back to the ground, but she builds from the ground up: the reverse of the order of invention.
questions.rule: Build in the reverse of the order of finding.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A planner finds a plan by working from the goal back to the start, then tries to carry it out in the order she found the steps. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the order found is also the order of doing, so she may start where she began
She does the steps in the wrong order, since execution often reverses invention
She should skip the last step found, since it came first
She should carry out all steps at once
optionExplain: The entry says the order is frequently reversed.
Right: the entry states this.
Every step is needed.
The entry says to do it step by step.
questions.explain: The entry says we must arrange the steps in the proper order, which is frequently the reverse of the order of invention.
questions.rule: Reverse the order of invention to execute.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the proverb What a fool does at last, a wise man does at first say about order?
options: The wise man leaves the hardest step for last, so that easier ones build confidence
The fool works faster than the wise man
What is found last in the search often has to be done first in the work
The wise man never repeats a step
optionExplain: The proverb says the opposite.
Speed is not discussed.
Right: it illustrates the reversed order.
Repetition is not discussed.
questions.explain: The entry quotes it as an illustration of arranging steps in the proper order, which often reverses the order of invention.
questions.rule: Last found, first done.
questions.teaches: The proper order of carrying out is frequently just the reverse of the order of invention, as in 'What a fool does at last, a wise man does at first'.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A technician traces a fault from the broken output back to a faulty cable. In what order should the repair and test proceed?
options: Test the broken output first, since it was noticed first and is the thing that needs fixing
Replace nothing until every stage is tested at once
Start from the middle of the chain and move randomly
Replace the cable first, then check the later stages in their working order
optionExplain: The fault was noticed first, but the cause lies earlier in the chain.
The entry advises step by step.
No plan of order is followed.
Right: the first thing found last is done first.
questions.explain: Tracing back to the cause is the order of invention; the repair follows the reverse order.
questions.rule: Fix the cause first, then verify forward.
questions.teaches: Working out a plan from the end and carrying it out from the beginning are opposite orders.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: Once a problem is solved, nothing more needs to be done on it.
questions.explain: The entry treats looking back at the completed solution as an important and instructive phase. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Look back at the completed solution and re-examine it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: He thinks not well that thinks not ____.
questions.explain: The proverb praises second thoughts.
questions.rule: Think again.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student has finished an exam question. Which action follows the entry?
options: Hand it in at once, since further thought on a finished solution only wastes the time left for other questions
Copy the answer a second time exactly
Re-examine the solution, perhaps by another route, to see whether the result holds
Erase the working so it cannot be questioned
optionExplain: Second thoughts are best.
Repeating does not re-examine.
Right: looking back may supply additional confirmation.
Looking back needs the working.
questions.explain: The entry says to look back and see whether additional confirmation can be found.
questions.rule: Re-examine the finished work.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, re-examining a solution may reveal an additional confirmation of the result.
questions.explain: The entry presents looking back as an instructive phase that can supply such confirmation.
questions.rule: Re-examination can confirm.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What must be pointed out to the beginner about additional confirmation?
options: That it is valuable, since two proofs are better than one
That it is unnecessary if the first proof was carried out with great care
That it must replace the first proof
That it can only be found by experts
optionExplain: Right: the entry says so, with 'It is safe riding at two anchors'.
The entry says two proofs are better than one.
It supplements it.
The entry gives no such restriction.
questions.explain: The entry says it must be pointed out to the beginner that additional confirmation is valuable: two proofs are better than one.
questions.rule: Two proofs beat one.
questions.teaches: It must be pointed out to the beginner that additional confirmation of a result is valuable: two proofs are better than one.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A pilot cross-checks the altitude on two independent instruments before landing. Which proverb of the entry fits?
options: A fool looks to the beginning, a wise man regards the end
It is safe riding at two anchors
Do and undo, the day is long enough
We soon believe what we desire
optionExplain: This concerns understanding the aim.
Right: two independent confirmations give more safety.
This mocks changing schemes.
This concerns wishful judgment.
questions.explain: The entry uses riding at two anchors for having two proofs of one result.
questions.rule: Independent confirmation adds safety.
questions.teaches: The entry quotes 'Second thoughts are best' as part of its comment that looking back at the completed solution is important and instructive.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Which question list would you expect the entry to call your five best friends when you need advice?
options: What, Why, Where, When and How
Who, Whom, Whose, Which and Whether
Yes, No, Maybe, Never and Always
Plan, Do, Check, Act and Repeat
optionExplain: Right: these are the five question words in the entry's proverb.
These are not in the entry.
These are answers, not questions.
This is a different method not in the entry.
questions.explain: The entry's proverb names five question words. The card next gives the full set.
questions.rule: Keep four short reminders: the end suggests the means, ask What, Why, Where, When and How, doubt only what is worth doubting, and look around after a first discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The end suggests the ____.
questions.explain: Knowing the aim helps to find the means that reach it.
questions.rule: The end suggests the means.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Match each synthetic proverb to what it asks of a problem solver.
pairs: Use the aim to find the way to it
Ask What, Why, Where, When and How
Question the problem from many sides
Doubt only what is worth doubting
Do not spread doubt over everything
Look around after your first discovery
Search nearby for more like it
questions.explain: Each proverb is a compact attitude; the matches follow the wording of each.
questions.rule: Each proverb is a short rule of attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student doubts everything the textbook says, including simple definitions. Which synthetic proverb does this breach?
options: The end suggests the means
Do not believe anything but doubt only what is worth doubting
Look around when you have got your first mushroom or made your first discovery
Ask What, Why, Where, When and How
optionExplain: This is about using the aim.
Right: doubt should be spent where it is worth it.
This is about searching nearby.
This is about questions.
questions.explain: The proverb asks for selective doubt. Our reading: doubting every definition spends doubt where it is not worth it.
questions.rule: Be selective in doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Why does the entry stop quoting traditional proverbs and write its own?
options: Traditional proverbs are all false
The author wanted to avoid the inconsistency between proverbs that give opposite advice and obscurities
More traditional proverbs would add only variations; the systematic aspects are beyond their scope
No further proverbs exist
optionExplain: The entry never says so.
The entry's reason is scope and repetition.
Right: the entry says so.
The entry says many others could be quoted.
questions.explain: The entry says many other proverbs would scarcely furnish new themes, and the more systematic aspects of solution are hardly within the Wisdom of Proverbs.
questions.rule: Traditional proverbs have limited scope.
questions.teaches: The entry says further traditional proverbs would offer only variations on themes already mentioned, and the more systematic aspects of solving lie outside the scope of proverbs.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A researcher finds her first bug and says she will check the neighbouring code for similar ones. Which synthetic proverb fits?
options: Look around when you have got your first mushroom; they grow in clusters
Do not believe anything but doubt only what is worth doubting
The end suggests the means, so work back from the aim to find the way to it
Your five best friends are What, Why, Where, When, How
optionExplain: Right: discoveries tend to come in clusters.
This is about selective doubt.
This is about aims.
This is about questions.
questions.explain: The entry says to look around after a first discovery because mushrooms, like discoveries, grow in clusters.
questions.rule: Look near a first discovery for more.
questions.teaches: A first discovery often has companions nearby: the entry says mushrooms and discoveries grow in clusters.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: You must bring up exactly 6 quarts from a river with only a 4-quart pail and a 9-quart pail. What do most people try first?
options: Start with the empty pails and try filling and emptying them in various ways
Work out the last pouring step first
Mark a scale on the sides of the pails and read off 6
Fetch a third container to measure with
optionExplain: Right: this is how most people work on the puzzle.
This is working backwards, which the entry says only some people do.
The pails have no scale; imagining one does not help.
The puzzle allows only the two pails.
questions.explain: Most people work forward from the data. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Recognise forward trial and error from the data as the usual first attack, and do not count on it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Starting from the given situation and moving toward the unknown is working ____.
questions.explain: Forward work goes from the data to the unknown.
questions.rule: Forwards runs from data to unknown.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: With a 7-quart and a 3-quart pail, you fill the 7-quart pail and pour into the 3-quart pail until it is full. How much is left in the 7-quart pail?
options: 3 quarts, since the small pail now holds 3
4 quarts, since \(7-3=4\)
5 quarts, since \(7-2=5\)
10 quarts, since \(7+3=10\)
optionExplain: The 3 quarts are in the small pail; the large keeps 7 - 3.
Right: the small pail takes 3 quarts, leaving 4.
This subtracts 2, which has no source here.
Pouring moves water; it does not add it.
questions.explain: \(7-3=4\): this forward step gives a quantity you can measure, though not necessarily the one you want.
questions.rule: A forward step gives measurable amounts.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, working forwards by trial and error may succeed, but usually by accident after many trials.
questions.explain: The entry says we may succeed after many trials, accidentally.
questions.rule: Forward trying succeeds by accident.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: According to the entry, what do most people do when a forward trial fails?
options: Give up the puzzle at once
Check the figure for a scale of lines and read the required amount from it
Ask for the answer
Start again from the empty pails and try something else
optionExplain: The entry says they start again.
The imagined scale is a separate idea.
Asking for the answer is not what most people do; they empty and fill the pails and start again.
Right: this is the entry's description.
questions.explain: The entry says we empty and fill, and when we do not succeed, we start again, trying something else.
questions.rule: Restart and try again is the forward habit.
questions.teaches: Most people confronted with the puzzle empty and fill, and when they fail, start again from the empty containers and try something else.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A person hunting a lost key tries random places for an hour. What does the entry say exceptionally able solvers do instead of long trials?
options: They do not spend long in such trials but turn round and work backwards
They try the same places over and over again, but more systematically than at first
They wait for the key to appear
They ask others to search
optionExplain: Right: this is how the entry distinguishes them.
This is the forward habit.
The entry describes no waiting.
The entry describes their own method.
questions.explain: The entry says exceptionally able people, or those taught more than routine operations, do not spend long in such trials but start working backwards.
questions.rule: Able solvers turn round sooner.
questions.teaches: Exceptionally able people, or those who learned more than routine operations in mathematics classes, do not spend much time in forward trials but start working backwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: You cannot see how to get exactly 6 quarts with a 4-quart and a 9-quart pail. What is a sensible way to make progress?
options: Find some other amount the pails can measure, and see whether it helps
Wait until the pails show a scale
Assume the puzzle is a trick and impossible
Fill both pails and compare the amounts
optionExplain: Right: a related quantity may open the way.
They never will; the pails have no marks.
One failure shows nothing of the kind.
Without a plan, comparing teaches little.
questions.explain: The entry suggests solving a related problem when the proposed one resists. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Picture exactly what you are given, and if the unknown is out of reach, aim for a related quantity you can reach.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: If you cannot solve the proposed problem, try to solve first some ____ problem.
questions.explain: A related problem may supply a result or method for the main one.
questions.rule: Try a related problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: With an 11-quart and a 4-quart pail, you fill the 11-quart pail and pour 4 quarts away twice. How much is left?
options: 7 quarts, since \(11-4=7\)
4 quarts, since the small pail holds 4
3 quarts, since \(11-4-4=3\)
15 quarts, since \(11+4=15\)
optionExplain: This removes 4 only once.
The small pail's size is not the amount left in the large pail.
Right: each pouring removes 4 quarts.
Pouring away does not add water.
questions.explain: \(11-4-4=3\): a related amount the pails can measure.
questions.rule: Repeated pouring measures a remainder.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says that because the pails have no scale, no exact amount can be measured with them.
questions.explain: A full pail is a measure: filling the 9 and pouring into the 4 leaves exactly 5 quarts.
questions.rule: A full container measures without marks.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Which of the book's own questions does the entry attach to the hint of finding something useful in the data?
options: Can you check the result, or derive it differently?
Could you derive something useful from the data?
Can you use the result for another problem?
Do you know a theorem that could be useful?
optionExplain: This belongs to looking back.
Right: it appears in parentheses beside the related-problem hint.
This belongs to looking back.
This is a different question of the list.
questions.explain: The entry places this question with the advice to try a related problem if the proposed one cannot be solved.
questions.rule: Ask what the data can give.
questions.teaches: Beside the related-problem hint the entry quotes the question 'Could you derive something useful from the data?', one of the book's own questions.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A cook has a 5-cup and a 3-cup measure and needs exactly 2 cups. What do the entry's hints suggest as a first move?
options: Play around: fill the 5-cup and pour into the 3-cup, which leaves 2
Estimate 2 cups by eye and accept the error, since an exact amount is not needed
Find a 2-cup measure instead
Fill the 3-cup measure twice
optionExplain: Right: a related result reaches the target.
The problem asks for an exact amount.
The puzzle limits the tools.
That gives 6 cups, not 2.
questions.explain: The entry says 'let us play around a little'; here \(5-3=2\) at once.
questions.rule: Playing around may hit the target.
questions.teaches: The entry lets the solver play around a little with the given tools before looking for a method.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the six-quart puzzle, which picture would you hold in mind to start from the end?
options: The large pail holding exactly 6 quarts and the small pail empty
Both pails empty at the river bank
The large pail full and the small pail full
The small pail holding 6 quarts
optionExplain: Right: it is the desired final situation.
This is the starting situation.
Both pails full is not the desired end; the aim is exactly six quarts in the large pail.
The small pail holds only 4.
questions.explain: Working backwards begins with the desired final situation. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Picture the goal as already reached, as clearly as you can, and start your thinking from that picture.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Pappus says: start from what is required and assume what is sought as already ____.
questions.explain: Assuming the goal reached gives a definite situation to reason from.
questions.rule: Assume the sought thing found.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A traveller must reach an airport by 9 a.m. Which question follows from starting at the goal?
options: What is the first thing I could do after waking, and where does that lead?
How could I be at the airport at 9, and what must precede that?
What time does the airport open?
Which airline is cheapest?
optionExplain: This starts from the data, not from the goal.
Right: it pictures the goal reached and asks for its antecedent.
This does not start from the goal situation.
This is another problem.
questions.explain: Start from being at the airport by 9, then ask what, immediately before, would make that possible.
questions.rule: Start from the reached goal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Sort these opening moves: do they work forwards from the data, or backwards from the goal?

items.t: Fill the large pail and see what pouring does
Picture 6 quarts in the large pail and the small pail empty
Ask from what situation that picture could be reached
Try this and that with the two empty pails
Empty the small pail and start again
Assume what is sought as already found

questions.explain: Forward moves act on the given pails; backward moves begin with the pictured goal and ask what precedes it.
questions.rule: Forwards uses the data; backwards uses the goal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: By what other name is the method of working backwards known in the entry?
options: The method of induction, described by Euclid
The method of the cookbook, described by Gauss
The method of analysis, described by Pappus
The method of synthesis, described by Newton
optionExplain: Euclid is not the source named.
Neither is correct.
Right: the entry gives this name and source.
The entry names analysis and Pappus.
questions.explain: The entry calls working backwards the method of analysis and says Pappus gave an important description of it.
questions.rule: Working backwards is analysis.
questions.teaches: Working backwards is also called the method of analysis, and Pappus gave an important description of it.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A wedding must start at 4 p.m. on Saturday. A planner works from that moment back to the invitations. Which remark of the entry fits?
options: Backward planning is possible only for mathematical puzzles
Backward planning needs a genius
Backward planning works only with a picture
Even quite primitive problems may lead to working backwards
optionExplain: The entry says it suits non-mathematical problems too.
The entry says it does not.
The entry gives no such condition.
Right: the entry says so.
questions.explain: The entry says that quite primitive problems may lead naturally to working backwards.
questions.rule: Planning from the deadline is working backwards.
questions.teaches: Quite primitive problems may lead naturally to working backwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: To end with 6 quarts in the 9-quart pail, what situation could come immediately before?
options: The 9-quart pail full and 1 quart in the 4-quart pail
The 9-quart pail holding 6 and the small pail full
The 9-quart pail empty and the small pail full
The 9-quart pail holding 3 and 3 in the small pail
optionExplain: Right: pouring 3 into the small pail leaves 6.
Then 6 is already in the large pail, so nothing remains to be done.
You cannot reach 6 from this by one pouring.
The small pail holds 4, and 6 does not follow in one move.
questions.explain: With 1 quart in the small pail, pouring from the full large pail fills the small pail with 3 more quarts and leaves \(9-3=6\). The small pail is then emptied into the river.
questions.rule: From the goal, ask from what foregoing situation it could be obtained, and repeat for each answer until you reach something you can do.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Pappus: let us inquire from what ____ the desired result could be derived.
questions.explain: The antecedent is the situation just before the goal.
questions.rule: Ask for the antecedent.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: With a 5-quart and a 3-quart pail, the goal is 4 quarts in the 5-quart pail. What situation could come immediately before?
options: The 5-quart pail full and 1 quart in the 3-quart pail
The 5-quart pail full and 2 quarts in the 3-quart pail
The 5-quart pail holding 4 and the small pail full, ready to be emptied
The 5-quart pail empty and 4 quarts in the small pail
optionExplain: Then 2 quarts would be poured and 3 would be left.
Right: pouring 1 quart into the small pail leaves \(5-1=4\).
It already holds 4 in the large pail, so nothing remains to be done.
The small pail holds only 3.
questions.explain: The small pail with 2 quarts has room for \(3-2=1\) quart, so pouring from the full 5 leaves 4.
questions.rule: Ask what must hold just before the goal.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the 5- and 3-quart puzzle, with the 5-quart pail full and 2 quarts in the small pail, you pour from the big into the small until the small is full. What is left in the big pail?
options: 3 quarts
2 quarts
5 quarts
4 quarts
optionExplain: The small pail takes 1 quart, not 2.
That is the amount in the small pail before pouring.
Some water is poured, so the big pail loses some.
Right: one quart fits in the small pail.
questions.rule: Compute the pouring to confirm the link.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The entry says situations like large pail full and 1 quart in the small can be replaced by small pail holds 1 and anything in the large. Why?
options: The pails are cylinders of equal base, so their contents are interchangeable
Pappus proved it
The river holds unlimited water, so the large pail can be filled afresh
Water poured into the river returns later
optionExplain: The entry gives the shapes but not as the reason.
No proof is attributed to Pappus here.
Right: the supply makes the large pail's content free to reset.
The reason is the unlimited supply, not return.
questions.explain: The entry says that since the amount of water in the river is unlimited for our purpose, the situations in Figs 26, 27 and 28 are the same for our purpose: any one gives the others.
questions.rule: An unlimited supply makes some situations equivalent.
questions.teaches: Because the water in the river is unlimited, the situations 'large full with 1 in small', '1 in small' and '1 in large' each give the others.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: With a 5-quart and a 3-quart pail, put these steps in the order that ends with 4 quarts in the 5-quart pail.
items: Fill the 5-quart pail
Pour into the 3-quart pail until full, leaving 2
Empty the 3-quart pail into the river
Pour the 2 quarts into the 3-quart pail
Fill the 5-quart pail again
Pour into the 3-quart pail until full, leaving 4
questions.explain: The goal needs 2 quarts in the small pail with the big pail full. Getting that 2 comes from the first pouring. Reversing the backward chain gives these six steps.
questions.rule: Perform the backward chain in reverse.
questions.teaches: Hitting upon the key antecedent, here 1 quart in the small pail, is not easy, and few persons take that step without much foregoing hesitation.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: You have discovered, working backwards, the chain: 6 in the large pail needs 1 in the small pail, which needs 1 left in the large pail. In what order do you perform it?
options: Start with the last item discovered and end with the first
Start with the first item discovered and end with the last
Do all three at once
Do only the first
optionExplain: Right: performance is the reverse of discovery.
This repeats the order of discovery, which ends at the start.
They depend on one another.
The others are needed too.
questions.explain: The entry says all that is left is to reverse the process. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When the backward chain reaches something you can do, perform the operations in the reverse order of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The sequence is discovered in ____ order but performed in the opposite order.
questions.explain: The chain is found from the goal back, then run forward.
questions.rule: Find backwards, perform forwards.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Put these steps of the six-quart solution in the order they are performed.
items: Fill the big pail and pour 4 away twice, leaving 1 quart in it
Pour that 1 quart into the small pail
Fill the big pail from the river
Pour from the big pail into the small until the small is full, leaving 6
questions.explain: The last link found backwards is performed first: reach 1 quart, move it, refill, then pour 3 more quarts.
questions.rule: Perform the chain from its last-found link.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A solver finds the chain backwards and then tries to perform the first link she discovered first. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: performing in order of discovery works equally well
That link needs steps performed earlier, which she has not yet done
She has skipped the river, so the pails cannot be filled at the start
She should have used a larger pail
optionExplain: The first found is the final goal state.
Right: the first link found is the last performed.
The river is not the issue.
The size of the pails is not the issue.
questions.explain: The first link found is the goal-side step, which can only be performed after the others.
questions.rule: Do not perform in the order of discovery.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: From which point does the entry say the performance must start?
options: The point reached first in the analysis, which is the goal itself
The midpoint of the chain
The point reached last of all in the analysis
Any point, since the chain is a loop
optionExplain: This is the goal itself.
The entry names an end point.
Right: Pappus says this.
The chain is not a loop.
questions.explain: The entry says all that is left is to reverse the process and start from the point reached last of all in the analysis, as Pappus says.
questions.rule: Start where the analysis stopped.
questions.teaches: Following Pappus, the performance starts from the point which was reached last of all in the analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A developer finds a release plan backwards: the release needs passing tests, which need a clean build, which needs the code merged. In what order does she act?
options: Release, run the tests, build, then merge the code last of all
Build, merge, release, test
Run the tests, merge, build, release
Merge the code, build, run the tests, release
optionExplain: This is the order of discovery.
The release must follow the tests.
Tests need a build to run on.
Right: reverse of discovery.
questions.explain: The release plan was found from the goal back; it is carried out in the reverse order.
questions.rule: Reverse the chain to act.
questions.teaches: Retracing the steps from the point reached last in the analysis finally derives what was required.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: Working backwards is a method only a genius could invent or use.
questions.explain: The entry says anybody can use it with a little common sense. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Use working backwards as a common-sense procedure within everyone's reach, for any kind of problem.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Working backwards is a ____-sense procedure within the reach of everybody.
questions.explain: It needs only the natural question of what could come just before.
questions.rule: Common sense suffices.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A hiker wants to be at a summit by noon. Which move follows the method in a common-sense way?
options: Ask what time she must leave the last hut, and the hour before that
Walk fast and hope to arrive by noon, trusting her pace over the whole climb
Postpone deciding until she reaches the summit
Carry heavier bags to be safe
optionExplain: Right: she asks from what position the goal can be reached.
This is a forward effort without the backward question.
This cannot help planning.
This does not use the goal as a starting point.
questions.explain: The backward question is what is natural: from what foregoing position could we get there?
questions.rule: Ask 'from where could I get there?'

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says the tradition crediting Plato with the method of analysis may not be quite reliable.
questions.explain: The entry says the tradition may not be quite reliable and the procedure was surely practised before Plato.
questions.rule: Common sense preceded its name.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say some Greek scholar may have regarded as an achievement worthy of Plato's genius?
options: To invent the cookbook of mathematics, which gives rules and procedures without reasons
To discover the sum of angles in a triangle
To state the procedure in general terms as typically useful in all problems
To measure six quarts of water
optionExplain: The cookbook is a separate entry.
This is a different theorem.
Right: the achievement is generalising it.
This is the puzzle, not the achievement.
questions.explain: The entry says what the scholar may have admired is stating the procedure in general terms and stamping it as typically useful.
questions.rule: Generalising a habit is an achievement.
questions.teaches: The Greek achievement was to state the procedure in general terms and mark it as typically useful in mathematical and nonmathematical problems.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A cook, trained in no method, plans a dinner by asking what must be done immediately before serving, then before that. How does the entry see her?
options: She does not use working backwards, since she is not a mathematician by training
She uses it only if she has read Pappus
She is inventing a new method
She uses the common-sense procedure that others practised before Plato
optionExplain: The entry says it applies to nonmathematical problems.
The entry says no study is needed.
The entry says it was common practice.
Right: the entry says so.
questions.explain: The entry says we can hardly doubt it was practised by mathematicians and nonmathematicians before Plato.
questions.rule: Backwards planning is old and ordinary.
questions.teaches: Working backwards was in all likelihood practised by mathematicians and nonmathematicians before Plato.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Why might a bright student resist working backwards?
options: It means turning away from the goal and reversing the natural order
It needs a very high intelligence
It uses mathematics that students have not met
It rewards guessing over thought
optionExplain: Right: a psychological difficulty.
The entry says it does not take a genius.
It needs only common sense.
The entry does not say that the method rewards guessing; it says that reversing the order feels unnatural.
questions.explain: The entry names a psychological difficulty. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Expect resistance to turning away from the goal, and present working backwards carefully.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: There is a certain psychological ____ in turning around and going away from the goal.
questions.explain: The direct path pulls us on.
questions.rule: Turning round is psychologically hard.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A teacher wants to introduce working backwards to a class. Following the entry, what should she do?
options: Present it quickly, since able students will grasp it without any help from her
Present it carefully, since an able student may otherwise fail to grasp it
Present it only to the weakest students
Avoid the method, since it is unnatural
optionExplain: The entry warns they may not.
Right: the entry says so.
The entry says even an able student may fail to grasp it, so it is not meant only for the weakest.
The entry values the method.
questions.explain: The entry says a psychological repugnance to the reverse order may prevent a quite able student from understanding the method if it is not presented carefully.
questions.rule: Present the reverse order carefully.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry says anybody can solve a concrete problem by working backwards with a little common sense.
questions.explain: The entry says anybody can do it with a little common sense, though turning round has a psychological difficulty.
questions.rule: The obstacle is habit, not ability.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Besides going away from the goal, what else does the entry say makes the turn hard?
options: Having to count the water in each pail with great accuracy
Having to draw a figure
Having to wait for help
Proceeding without looking continually at the aim
optionExplain: It does not list counting.
It does not list drawing.
It does not list waiting.
Right: the entry lists it among the difficulties.
questions.explain: The entry lists turning round, going away from the goal, proceeding without looking continually at the aim and not following the direct path to the end.
questions.rule: Do not look only at the goal.
questions.teaches: Working backwards means proceeding without looking continually at the aim and not following the direct path to the desired end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A hiker will not descend to a lower valley even though the pass can only be reached through it. Which difficulty of the entry does this show?
options: The pull of the direct path makes going away from the goal feel wrong
A lack of strength for the climb after a long and tiring day on the mountain
A mistake about arithmetic
A fear of animals
optionExplain: Right: it fits the described repugnance.
The scenario is about direction.
No arithmetic is involved.
No animals are involved.
questions.explain: The entry describes the difficulty in going away from the goal. Our reading: the detour is sometimes the only route.
questions.rule: A detour away may be the way.
questions.teaches: There is a difficulty in not following the direct path to the desired end, which the entry compares to the hen's difficulty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Food lies right beyond a fence that is open at one end. Which animal would you guess finds the problem hardest?
options: A hen
A dog
A chimpanzee
A four-year-old child
optionExplain: Right: she runs back and forth.
The dog goes around the end.
The chimpanzee finds it easy.
The child finds it easy.
questions.explain: The entry reports the hen has surprising difficulty. The card next gives the setup.
questions.rule: When food is in plain view but a fence blocks the direct path, turn away from it and go around the end.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The problem turns out to be surprisingly difficult for a ____.
questions.explain: The hen runs back and forth excitedly on her side.
questions.rule: The hen struggles.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A dog is placed very close to the food behind the fence. What does the entry say may happen?
options: It goes straight around the end at once, whatever the distance to the food may be
It may lose time barking, scratching or jumping at the fence before it turns
It never gets to the food
It waits calmly for the fence to open
optionExplain: The entry says it is not always smooth.
Right: the solution is less smooth when the points are close.
The dog does solve the problem.
The entry describes barking and scratching.
questions.explain: The entry says that, especially when D and F are close, the dog may lose time before it conceives the bright idea of going around.
