questions.rule: Closeness to the goal hinders turning round.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: According to the entry, a chimpanzee finds the fence problem very easy.
questions.explain: The entry says the problem is very easy for a chimpanzee or a four-year-old child.
questions.rule: Some animals turn round easily.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: How may the hen eventually reach the food, according to the entry?
options: By accident, after much running
By planning her route in advance, as the dog does
By watching the dog and copying its path
By jumping over the fence at last
optionExplain: Right: the book says she may succeed, after much running, accidentally.
The book describes no planning by the hen; she runs back and forth.
The book does not say she learns from another animal.
The book does not mention jumping over the fence.
questions.explain: The entry says she may succeed, after much running, accidentally, if she gets there at all.
questions.rule: Trying about can succeed by chance.
questions.teaches: The hen may reach the food after much running, by accident, if she gets there at all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A manager keeps pushing the same sales pitch harder at a client who has said no. Which animal's behaviour does the entry's picture resemble?
options: The dog dashing around the end of the fence
The hen running back and forth against the fence
The chimpanzee turning around and going straight to the food
The child with a toy
optionExplain: The dog turns away from the goal.
Right: she presses the direct path.
The chimpanzee turns.
The child finds the way around.
questions.explain: Our reading: pushing the direct path harder is the hen's behaviour; the entry suggests turning round.
questions.rule: When blocked, turn around.
questions.teaches: Going around an obstacle is what we do in solving any kind of problem, so the experiment has a sort of symbolic value.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A hen presses against a fence beside food and a dog goes around it. Which human way of solving does the hen's behaviour resemble?
options: Trying again and again until a lucky accident, without insight
Calmly planning the route before moving
Working backwards from the food
Asking others how the fence works
optionExplain: Right: she muddles through.
The hen shows no planning.
Working backwards means turning away from the goal.
The hen asks nobody.
questions.explain: The entry compares the hen to people who muddle through. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Compare your own way of solving with the dog's and the hen's: muddling through or turning round with insight.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: The hen acted like people who solve their problem by ____ through.
questions.explain: She tried again and again, succeeding by lucky accident.
questions.rule: The hen muddles through.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A student tries many formulas at random on an exam problem and finally one works, without knowing why. Which animal does the entry compare her with?
options: The hen
The dog that turns round quickly
The chimpanzee
The child with a toy
optionExplain: Right: success by lucky accident without insight.
The student shows no quick insight.
The entry says the chimpanzee solves it easily.
The child solves it easily.
questions.explain: The entry compares muddlers who succeed by accident to the hen.
questions.rule: Random trials, lucky success.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: Match each behaviour in the experiment to the human way of solving it resembles.
pairs: The hen running back and forth until a lucky accident
The dog barking and scratching before turning
Working forwards before turning round, as with the pails
The dog that inspects briefly and dashes around
questions.explain: The entry draws these parallels between the animals and ways of solving problems.
questions.rule: Each animal stands for a way of solving.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say of imagining a scale on the pails?
options: It was the key idea of the solution, from which the pouring followed
Almost useless scratching, showing that what we seek lies deeper
It was an example of the hen's lucky accident
It was the first step of working backwards
optionExplain: The entry calls it almost useless.
Right: it compares the scale to scratching.
The entry compares it to scratching, not luck.
It was a forward attempt.
questions.explain: The entry calls imagining a scale a sort of almost useless scratching.
questions.rule: A scale only shows the answer is deeper.
questions.teaches: Imagining a scale on the pails was a sort of almost useless scratching, showing only that what we seek lies deeper under the surface.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A colleague repeatedly fails at a task by pushing straight at it. Following the entry, how should you regard him?
options: With contempt, since he lacks the insight that even the dog showed at the fence
With envy, since he works so hard
With indifference, since the task is his
Not with blame, since turning round and leaving the goal is truly difficult
optionExplain: The entry says not to blame the hen.
The entry does not praise this.
The entry asks for understanding the difficulty.
Right: the entry says we should not blame the hen.
questions.explain: The entry says there is an obvious analogy between the hen's difficulties and ours.
questions.rule: The difficulty is shared.
questions.teaches: The entry says we should not even blame the hen for her clumsiness, since there is an obvious analogy between her difficulties and ours.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A single simple experiment, briefly reported, suggests a striking analogy. What should you do?
options: Note the analogy but be ready to recheck and revalue it
Build a general theory on it at once
Ignore it entirely, as one case proves nothing
Accept it because the experiment used animals
optionExplain: Right: the entry accepts analogies with care.
The entry warns against this.
The entry sees no disadvantage in noticing analogies.
The kind of subject is no guarantee.
questions.explain: The entry accepts analogies with care. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Notice analogies from one sketchy experiment, but treat them as hypotheses to be rechecked and revalued.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: We should be prepared to recheck and ____ the analogies.
questions.explain: Analogies are provisional until rechecked.
questions.rule: Recheck analogies.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A news item says one small study found that a habit raised memory scores, and urges everyone to adopt it. What does the entry's caution suggest?
options: Adopt it at once, since a study has been done and the result looks promising
Treat it as a suggestion to recheck, not as a settled theory
Reject it, since one study means nothing
Wait for the headline to be repeated
optionExplain: One study is not a theory.
Right: one sketchy study cannot bear a big theory.
The entry sees no harm in noticing analogies.
Repetition of a report is not rechecking.
questions.explain: The entry asks us not to build a big theory on one simple, sketchily reported experiment.
questions.rule: One study suggests; it does not settle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: True or false: The entry holds that the hen experiment alone supports a big theory of how people solve problems.
questions.explain: The entry says we should not build a big theory on one simple, sketchily reported experiment.
questions.rule: Do not overclaim from one case.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: What does the entry say is the sort of value the experiment has for solving problems?
options: The value of a complete proof, since the experiment shows how every solver behaves
The value of a measurement
No value at all
A symbolic value, since going around an obstacle is what we do in any problem
optionExplain: It is not a proof.
It is not a measurement.
It has symbolic value.
Right: it says so.
questions.explain: The entry says going around an obstacle is what we do in solving any kind of problem, so the experiment has a sort of symbolic value.
questions.rule: The experiment is a symbol, not a proof.
questions.teaches: Going around an obstacle is what we do in solving any kind of problem, so the fence experiment has a sort of symbolic value.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: A teacher sees a pupil solve a problem smoothly after a brief look and concludes the pupil has superior insight. What does the entry's caution suggest?
options: The smooth solution gives the impression of insight, rightly or wrongly, so test it on more cases
Dismiss the pupil's success as chance because no visible effort was shown over several minutes
Dismiss the pupil's success as chance because no effort showed
Reward the pupil at once without looking at any further work
optionExplain: Right: the entry says the dog gives this impression, rightly or wrongly.
One smooth case is not enough.
Noticing the pattern does no harm; dismissing it is also unsupported.
This ignores rechecking.
questions.explain: The entry says the dog who turned round after a brief inspection gives, rightly or wrongly, the impression of superior insight. Our reading: that is a hypothesis to recheck.
questions.rule: A smooth solution suggests insight; it does not prove it.
questions.teaches: The dog who turns round after a brief inspection gives, rightly or wrongly, the impression of superior insight.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Where would you guess the book explains a hint from its list in more depth?
options: In the Dictionary article named by the opening words of the hint's list paragraph
In the Foreword by John Conway, which reviews the list hint by hint in turn, answering each likely question
In Part IV, where every solution comments on the hint it uses and why
Nowhere, since each hint is meant to explain itself to a good reader
optionExplain: Right: the list has fifteen paragraphs and the Dictionary has an article titled by each one.
The Foreword by John Conway is a general introduction to the book; it does not review the hints one by one.
Part IV poses problems with hints and solutions, but it is not organised around the list's items.
The book says the list is explained and illustrated; treating hints as self-explanatory ignores the Dictionary.
questions.explain: The Dictionary has an article for each paragraph of the list, titled by its opening words. The card next shows how the parts fit.
questions.rule: Each list paragraph has a Dictionary article named by its first sentence.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each part of the book to the use the card recommends.
pairs: Watch a teacher put the list's questions to students
Hear a solver talk through the phases with himself
Visit an article when a point arises in your own work
Practise on problems and compare with hints and solutions
questions.explain: Each part has its own use: watching, self-talk, consulting and practising. Reading all four in one way loses what each offers.
questions.rule: Watch, talk, consult, practise.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader wants to learn more about the hint Go back to definitions. Where does the book's design send her?
options: To an article titled Go back to definitions, since the Dictionary gives every single hint of the list its own entry
To the article named by the opening of the hint's paragraph, Could you restate the problem?, which refers on to Definition
To the Part II dialogue, which defines each term of the list in turn
To Part IV, where each solution names the hint it relies on
optionExplain: The Dictionary has one article per list paragraph, not one per hint, so no such entry exists.
Right: the hint sits in that list paragraph, so its opening sentence names the article, and a cross-reference leads on to Definition.
The dialogue shows the phases as self-talk; it is not a glossary of the list's terms.
Part IV gives problems, hints and solutions; it does not index the list's hints.
questions.explain: The hint is inside the list paragraph that opens with Could you restate the problem?, so the article with that title is the entry point, and it points on to Definition.
questions.rule: Find the hint's paragraph, take its first sentence, read that article.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader wants one article that explains how the Dictionary's main articles connect. Which does the introduction point to?
options: Progress and Achievement, which the author says to read fairly early
Heuristic, the article that gives the history of the word
Modern Heuristic, the key article of the Dictionary
Variation of the Problem, since every article varies the problem
optionExplain: The author does advise reading it early, but as a topic article, not as the map of the whole Dictionary.
That article gives the history of the term, not the plan of the Dictionary.
Right: the introduction calls it the key article, explaining the connection of the main articles and the plan of the Dictionary.
Variation is one principal aspect among several; it does not explain how all the articles fit.
questions.explain: The introduction names Modern Heuristic as the key article. It explains how the main articles connect and also tells how to find information on particular items of the list.
questions.rule: Read Modern Heuristic to see the plan of the Dictionary.
questions.teaches: The introduction calls Modern Heuristic the key article: it explains the connection of the main articles and the plan underlying the Dictionary, and gives directions for finding information about particular items of the list.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The Dictionary is meant to be read from first to last, following the order of the four phases.
questions.explain: The Dictionary is arranged alphabetically and its text is condensed, so it is meant to be visited with a question from your own work. Our reading: the order of the phases belongs to the list, not to the Dictionary.
questions.rule: Visit the Dictionary with a question; do not read it as a course.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A self-taught learner thinks Part I is for teachers only. How does the introduction's account of viewpoint answer her?
options: The whole book keeps the teacher's viewpoint from start to finish, so a self-taught learner gains little from it
Only the dialogue in Part II speaks to a solver working alone
The student's viewpoint dominates Part I, so teachers should skip it
Part I leans to the teacher's side, but most of the book, above all the Dictionary, takes the solver's viewpoint
optionExplain: The introduction says otherwise: the teacher's view predominates only in Part I.
The solver's viewpoint also runs through the Dictionary, not only Part II.
The introduction says the teacher's view is the preponderant one in Part I.
Right: the introduction says the teacher's view predominates in Part I while most of the time the viewpoint is that of a person anxious to solve a problem.
questions.explain: Part I looks at the situation mostly from the teacher's side, but the list is equally useful to a solver working alone, and the Dictionary mostly takes the viewpoint of a person who is neither teacher nor student.
questions.rule: The book is for the solver alone as well as for the teacher.
questions.teaches: The introduction says the teacher's viewpoint predominates in Part I, but most of the time, especially in the Dictionary, the viewpoint is that of a person who is neither teacher nor student but anxious to solve the problem.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which trouble would a teacher most likely answer with the question Can you check the result?
options: The student cannot say what the problem asks or what is given
The student is glad to get an answer and never examines it
The student rushes into calculations without any plan
The student cannot recall a theorem needed for the proof
optionExplain: That is the first phase, where the unknown, data and condition are the questions.
Right: the question belongs to the last phase and aims at failure to look at the result.
That is a planning trouble, met by questions about related problems and the unknown.
That is a planning trouble too; checking the result does not supply a missing theorem.
questions.explain: Can you check the result? is a question of the fourth phase. The card next links each trouble to the phase and question that fit.
questions.rule: Match the question to the phase where the trouble lies.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each phase to the typical trouble the book finds in it.
pairs: Incomplete understanding of what is asked
Rushing in with no plan, or waiting clumsily for an idea
Never checking the result at all
questions.explain: Each phase has its own typical trouble, and naming the trouble tells you which questions of the list to press.
questions.rule: One phase, one typical trouble.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Priya states the unknown, data and condition correctly, then sits waiting for an idea. Which question aims at her trouble?
options: Ask her to look at the unknown and recall a problem with a similar unknown
Ask her again what the unknown is, what the data are and what the condition is
Ask her whether she can check the result and derive it a second way
Ask her whether she can use the result of this problem for another problem
optionExplain: Right: she has passed the first phase, and the open trouble is in planning, where this question points.
She has already answered these; repeating them aims at a trouble she does not have.
She has no result yet, so this fourth-phase question has nothing to work on.
That also needs a finished solution, which she lacks.
questions.explain: Priya understands the problem; what she lacks is a plan. The list's planning questions, beginning with the unknown and related problems, fit her.
questions.rule: Understood but stuck: ask the planning questions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a helper should add a list question whenever a student is working well, to keep him on track.
questions.explain: When the student progresses he needs no help, and asking nothing is better for his independence. The same holds when you work alone: do not hamper spontaneous progress with extraneous questions.
questions.rule: Questions are for blocked progress, not for steady progress.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the author, what danger faces a student whose progress is blocked and who gets no new question?
options: Becoming so dependent on the teacher's questions that he never learns to work alone
Skipping the check of the result because the answer is close
Tiring of the problem and dropping it, or blundering out of indifference
Repeating one question until it loses its meaning
optionExplain: The author worries about dependence when help is too heavy, not about a blocked student left without a question.
That is a fourth-phase fault; the danger named here comes while the student is stuck.
Right: the author names loss of interest as the danger, which a new question may avert.
Nothing in the text links a blocked student to overused questions.
questions.explain: When progress is blocked there is danger of tiring of the problem and dropping it, or making a stupid blunder from indifference. Any question with a chance of showing a new aspect may revive interest.
questions.rule: A question to a blocked student protects his interest.
questions.teaches: When progress is blocked there is danger that the student will tire of the problem and drop it, or lose interest and make a stupid blunder out of sheer indifference, so any question that may show a new aspect is welcome.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A supervisor sees a new analyst make silly blunders and work exasperatingly slowly. By the author's diagnosis, what should she try first?
options: Set more drill problems of the same kind to build speed
Give a grade, so the analyst sees how far behind he is
Check each step of his work for him, since carelessness in carrying out is the cause
Stir the analyst's interest in the task before offering technical help
optionExplain: Drill treats the symptom; the author traces such blunders to the missing wish to understand.
The author prefers a diagnosis of good and bad points to a grade, and a grade does not stir interest.
Carelessness in carrying out is a different fault; here the author points back to the first phase.
Right: the author says the trouble is almost always lack of desire to solve, or even to understand, the problem.
questions.explain: Silly blunders and slowness point back to the first phase: without desire the analyst has not understood the task. Interest comes first, and some time to settle down.
questions.rule: Silly blunders: first stir the wish to understand.
questions.teaches: When a student makes silly blunders or is exasperatingly slow, the trouble is almost always that he has no desire to solve or even to understand the problem, so the teacher should first stir his curiosity and allow him time to settle down.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You face a problem and no idea comes. What would you guess the book suggests trying first?
options: Recall a problem you have solved with a similar unknown
Carry out the most promising calculation at once and see what comes
Wait quietly for the idea to arrive on its own
Replace the problem at once by a much broader one
optionExplain: Right: it uses what you already know, and it is the book's first move.
Calculating without a plan is the fault the book warns against.
Waiting clumsily for an idea is itself named as a planning fault.
Broadening is a variation, which the book puts after recall has failed.
questions.explain: The book starts with recall, narrowed by looking at the unknown. The card next gives the whole order.
questions.rule: Recall before you reinvent.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these moves in the order the book suggests when no plan comes.
items: Ask whether you know a related problem
Look at the unknown and recall a problem with the same or a similar one
Restate the problem or go back to definitions
Solve first a more accessible related problem
Ask whether you used all the data and the whole condition
questions.explain: The order runs from recalling something known, through varying the problem and solving an auxiliary problem, to the check that brings you back to the original.
questions.rule: Recall, vary, auxiliary problem, check.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Dev must find the shortest route through five shops. He recalls a solved problem: the shortest path between two towns. What is his next question?
options: Can he check his answer for the route by deriving it in a second way?
Should he drop it as unhelpful, because the two unknowns are not quite identical?
Can he state a wider problem about every map in the country?
Could he use its method or its result, perhaps adding an auxiliary element?
optionExplain: There is no answer yet; this question belongs to the last phase.
The book also invites a similar unknown, so a near match is worth exploiting.
Widening is a variation tried when recall fails; he has just recalled something useful.
Right: the book follows recall with exactly this question about result, method and an auxiliary element.
questions.explain: A recalled problem is luck to be exploited. The book asks whether its result or method can be used, and whether an auxiliary element would make that possible.
questions.rule: A recalled problem: ask about its result, its method and an auxiliary element.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Recall of a related problem has failed. Which moves does the book favour next? Select all that apply.
options: Repeat the same recall attempt unchanged, more slowly
Restate the problem, or go back to definitions
Wait quietly until an idea arrives of its own accord
Solve first a more accessible related problem
optionExplain: Repetition feels like persistence, but the book advises varying the means, not repeating them.
Right: restating and returning to definitions are the book's first variations.
Waiting clumsily for an idea is itself named as a planning fault.
Right: the list says to solve some related problem first if the proposed one resists.
questions.explain: When recall fails the book turns to variation: restating the problem, going back to definitions, or solving a related problem first. Unchanged repetition and idle waiting are the two moves it warns against.
questions.rule: When recall fails, vary the problem; do not repeat the recall.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In the book's box-diagonal problem, how did the second approach make contact with the pupils' knowledge?
options: Through the data, by matching each edge of the box to a known right triangle in a figure
Through the conclusion, by recalling a theorem with a similar conclusion
By analogy, asking for a simpler plane problem about a rectangle's diagonal
Through letters, by solving in a, b and c and inserting numbers last
optionExplain: The first approach went through the unknown; the second did not start from the data.
That is the move for a problem to prove; the box problem asks to find a length.
Right: the analogue led to a plane section of the box through two opposite edges.
Working in letters is a useful habit, but it is not how contact was made.
questions.explain: The first approach reached known knowledge through the unknown, a segment. The second reached it through analogy with the plane, so two routes gave essentially the same idea.
questions.rule: Two different approaches can lead to the same plan.
questions.teaches: In the box-diagonal problem the teacher could also proceed by analogy instead of through the unknown: a simpler plane problem about the diagonal of a rectangle leads to the diagonal of a plane section of the box through two opposite edges.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An analyst has hundreds of past reports on file. Why does the book narrow the recall question to those with the same unknown?
options: Problems with the same unknown must share the same method, so the recalled one is sure to work on the new problem
It insists on one particular common point, which narrows the search among many related problems
It is the more general suggestion, so it covers more of what she has solved
It lets her skip the question whether the condition can be satisfied
optionExplain: No such guarantee is claimed; the recalled problem is only a lead.
Right: related problems share something, while the unknown names one definite point of contact.
It is the narrower suggestion; Do you know a related problem? is the more general.
The two questions do different jobs; one does not replace the other.
questions.explain: Do you know a related problem? is general, and many problems are somewhat related. Look at the unknown insists on one particular common point, so the search is cheaper.
questions.rule: Narrow the recall by the unknown.
questions.teaches: Do you know a related problem? is the more general suggestion; Look at the unknown insists on one particular common point, the same kind of unknown, so it narrows the search among the many problems that have something in common with yours.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You are halfway through a plan and the next step fails again. What would you guess the author advises?
options: Repeat the step more carefully, since repetition builds skill and the step may succeed next time
Drop the problem for good, because the plan has failed
Vary the means: restate the problem, specialise, or try a related problem
Wait for inspiration without working further on it
optionExplain: Careful repetition feels virtuous, but the author warns that the same trial tends to fail in the same way.
A failed plan is not a failed problem; the author expects you to change the approach.
Right: the author says to try again, but differently.
The author treats inspiration as something deserved by work, not a substitute for it.
questions.explain: The author's advice is the old try, try again with a twist: vary the problem. The card next adds the signs to watch and when to rest.
questions.rule: Try again, but differently.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: When an attempt fails, do not repeat it unchanged: ____ the problem and try another way in.
questions.explain: The book's remedy for a failed trial is variation of the problem, which opens a new way in.
questions.rule: Vary, do not repeat.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A technician's repair attempt fails. Sort each next move: does it vary the attempt, or repeat it?
groups: Varies the problem or the road

items.t: Test a smaller version of the fault that she can fix
Restate the fault in terms of what the part is defined to do
Set one input to zero and see what the part does
Try the same patch again with more force
Rerun the identical test hoping it passes this time
Reread the same error log in the same order for a third time

questions.explain: The first three change the problem or the aspect under view. The last three repeat; the book says plain repetition teaches little and tends to fail where it failed before.
questions.rule: Change something when an attempt fails.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A solver meets one sign, then another, then a third along her plan. According to the author, what happens to her hesitation?
options: It stays unchanged, because signs prove nothing at all about the plan
It grows, since many signs suggest a trap
It turns into certainty that the plan will succeed
It fades, and she moves on with growing confidence
optionExplain: Signs are not proof, but the author lets them set how boldly to proceed.
Nothing in the text reads a run of signs as a warning.
Signs support a probable conclusion only; certainty needs the strict argument.
Right: as signs multiply, hesitation fades and confidence grows.
questions.explain: The author describes a solver who starts cautiously, hesitates when signs are rare and gains confidence as they multiply. The confidence is still only probable.
questions.rule: More signs, more confidence; never certainty.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sam has worked hard on a pricing model for hours without success. Before he stops for the night, what does the author advise?
options: Settle some small point, so that he leaves with a sense of achievement
Delete the model completely, so that tomorrow's attempt starts fresh with no old ideas
Work on until it is solved, because stopping loses momentum
List the reasons the plan cannot work and sleep on them
optionExplain: Right: the author wants the problem set aside with the impression of some achievement.
Nothing in the text asks for starting over; a small gain is worth keeping.
The author says there is a limit beyond which forcing conscious effort does not pay.
The advice is to settle a point, not to rehearse failure.
questions.explain: A problem put aside after a small success is returned to more gladly. Rest is for problems already worked hard, and the small point keeps the working mood.
questions.rule: Before you rest, settle one small point.
questions.teaches: Before setting a problem aside, settle at least some little point so that you do not leave it without the impression of some achievement, and an interval of rest may then give you more tomorrow with less effort.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A founder bases her launch on one supplier. What do the book's proverbs advise, and what warning goes with it?
options: Stay with the first supplier whatever happens, since changing schemes midway only wastes time and money
Have another scheme in reserve from the outset, but changing schemes too often wastes time
Switch supplier at the first sign of trouble, since signs prove the plan wrong
Wait for luck to decide, since the proverbs rank luck above preparation
optionExplain: The proverbs warn that changing can be overdone, not that it should be ruled out.
Right: the proverbs say to be ready for failure with a second scheme, and they mock overdoing the change.
Signs only support a probable conclusion, and the proverbs warn against too much changing.
The proverbs say luck is deserved by diligence, not that it replaces a reserve plan.
questions.explain: The book's proverbs advise being prepared from the outset for a possible failure of the scheme, with another in reserve, yet they poke fun at changing from one scheme to another too often.
questions.rule: A second plan in reserve, but do not overdo the switching.
questions.teaches: The book's proverbs advise being prepared from the outset for a possible failure of the scheme and having another one in reserve, but they warn that changing from one scheme to another can be overdone and lose time.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A task that asks you to show conclusively that a statement is true, or else false, is a problem to find.
questions.explain: That is a problem to prove. A problem to find asks for an object, the unknown. The card next shows how the list's questions change with the kind.
questions.rule: The aim decides the kind.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each question for a problem to find with its counterpart for a problem to prove.
pairs: Did you use all the data?
Did you use the whole hypothesis?
Look at the unknown and recall a problem with a similar one
Look at the conclusion and recall a theorem with a similar one
questions.explain: The counterparts swap unknown for conclusion and data for hypothesis and keep the rest of the question.
questions.rule: Unknown to conclusion, data to hypothesis.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which task calls for Look at the conclusion rather than Look at the unknown?
options: Find the shortest ladder that reaches a given window
Construct a square with the same area as a given rectangle
Find how many handshakes occur among ten people
Show that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular
optionExplain: It asks for an object, a length, so the unknown is the thing to look at.
It asks for a figure, which is an unknown of a problem to find.
It asks for a number, so it is a problem to find.
Right: it asks for a proof, so the conclusion is the thing to look at.
questions.explain: Only the rhombus task asks to show that an assertion holds, so its principal parts are hypothesis and conclusion. The other three ask for an object.
questions.rule: Proofs have a conclusion to look at; finding problems have an unknown.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statement overstates how the list carries over to problems to prove?
options: Look at the unknown has a counterpart that looks at the conclusion
Every theorem splits cleanly into hypothesis and conclusion, so the swap works on all of them
Did you use all the data? has a counterpart that asks about the whole hypothesis, not only part of it
Several questions, such as drawing a figure, need no change for proofs
optionExplain: This is accurate: the book states that counterpart.
Right: the book gives a theorem that does not split naturally, the infinity of primes.
This is accurate: the question becomes Did you use the whole hypothesis?
This is accurate: only the questions tied to the unknown, data and condition need rewording.
questions.explain: The correspondence is a guide. The book itself names a theorem, that there are infinitely many primes, which has no natural hypothesis and conclusion.
questions.rule: The swap is a guide, not a table.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, problems to prove are more important than problems to find in elementary mathematics.
questions.explain: The author says problems to find are more important in elementary mathematics and problems to prove in advanced mathematics, which is why his list is built for finding and must be revised for proving.
questions.rule: Elementary: mostly finding. Advanced: mostly proving.
questions.teaches: Problems to find are more important in elementary mathematics and problems to prove in advanced mathematics, so a reader moving to advanced work should expect to meet more problems to prove.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An auditor must show that a claim follows from the ledger but cannot derive it. Which question from the book's list for proofs fits?
options: Could you think of another hypothesis from which the conclusion follows easily?
Could you think of other data appropriate to determine the unknown?
Can you check the result by comparing it with observed numbers or a commonsense estimate?
Is the condition sufficient to determine the unknown?
optionExplain: Right: it is the counterpart of asking for other data appropriate to determine the unknown.
This is the question for a problem to find, so the wording does not fit a proof.
She has no result to check yet, so this does not help her find a derivation.
A proof has no unknown; this question belongs to a problem to find.
questions.explain: For a proof the list's question about other data becomes a question about another hypothesis from which the conclusion follows easily.
questions.rule: Proof stuck: look for another starting hypothesis.
questions.teaches: For a problem to prove, the list also asks whether you could think of another hypothesis from which you could easily derive the conclusion, the counterpart of asking for other data appropriate to determine the unknown.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A report must be on the table, printed, by 9 a.m. and nothing is prepared. Which first thought would you guess the book favours?
options: Start with the first task on the list, do it well, and see where that leads you next
Wait until the right ideas for the report arrive
Picture the printed report on the table and ask what must come immediately before
Check each task in the order they were given
optionExplain: Forward trial from the data is the usual first attack, but the book says it tends to succeed only by accident.
The book does not recommend waiting for ideas to arrive on their own.
Right: starting from the goal as reached is the book's working backwards.
Checking steps belongs to carrying out a plan, which does not yet exist.
questions.explain: The book recommends beginning at the end: picture the goal reached and ask what precedes it. The card next gives the full procedure.
questions.rule: Begin at the end and ask what comes immediately before.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put the steps of working backwards and its sequel in the order the book gives them.
items: Assume the goal is already reached
Ask from what situation it could be obtained
Repeat that question until something known or doable appears
Carry out the steps in the reverse order of discovery
questions.explain: Analysis assumes the goal and works back through antecedents to something known; synthesis then retraces the steps forwards.
questions.rule: Assume, ask what precedes, repeat, then reverse.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Starting from 1, you may add 3 or double. To reach 22 in four moves, working backwards from 22, which sequence of moves is right?
options: Double, add 3, double, add 3
Add 3, add 3, add 3, double
Add 3, double, double, add 3
Add 3, double, add 3, double
optionExplain: This gives 1, 2, 5, 10, 13, so it ends at 13.
This gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 20, so it ends at 20.
This gives 1, 4, 8, 16, 19, so it ends at 19.
Right: working back, 22 came from 11 by doubling, 11 from 8 by adding 3, 8 from 4 by doubling, and 4 from 1 by adding 3. Forward, 1 to 4 to 8 to 11 to 22.
questions.explain: Working back from 22: the move before 22 must be doubling 11, because 19, the other candidate, cannot be reached from 1 in three moves while 11 can. Reversing the chain gives the forward sequence.
questions.rule: Chain back from the goal, then run the chain forward.
questions.hint: From which number could 22 be reached in one move? Try each, then repeat.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student squares \(x+2=\sqrt{x+14}\) and reports \(x=2\) and \(x=-5\). What is the slip?
options: Working backwards is unsound for equations, so the method should be dropped
Squaring cannot be undone, so the backward chain needs checking forward; -5 fails
Squaring is not allowed in equations like this, so the equation must be solved by guessing instead
Both answers are right, since each satisfies the squared equation
optionExplain: The method is sound when each step can be reversed or checked; the slip is a step that cannot.
Right: a backward step must be reversible. Squaring gives 2 and -5, but at -5 the left side is -3 and the right side is 3.
Squaring is allowed; what matters is checking that the steps run backwards.
They satisfy the squared equation, but the original equation is the one to be solved.
questions.explain: Squaring a true statement can create false roots. The book states the proviso that derivations be convertible; here the forward check shows x = 2 works (4 = 4) and x = -5 does not (-3 is not 3).
questions.rule: Check that the backward steps can be reversed.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The book regards assuming the problem already solved as self-deception, tolerated only because it does no harm.
questions.explain: The book defends the assumption as provisional, harmless, useful and natural. It is made only to start the analysis, and if no object satisfies the condition the analysis ends in a problem with no solution, which shows the original has none.
questions.rule: Assume the goal reached: it is provisional and harmless.
questions.teaches: Assuming the problem solved is provisional, harmless and useful, because if no object satisfies the condition the analysis must end in a problem that has no solution, which shows the original has none; it is also natural, as in imagining oneself already across.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A community group plans a fundraiser by starting from the closing event. How does the book describe their planning and their doing?
options: Planning and doing are the same steps in the same order, the first only done aloud and the second in practice
Planning is synthesis and doing is analysis, since doing comes first in time
Planning is analysis in thought and doing is synthesis in action, with the order reversed
Only mathematical plans can be analysed; a fundraiser has no analysis
optionExplain: The book stresses that the order is reversed between the two.
Analysis comes first, as invention; synthesis follows, as execution.
Right: in the creek example the analysis consists in thoughts, the synthesis in acts, and the order is reversed.
The book offers a nonmathematical creek-crossing example for exactly this reason.
questions.explain: The book's creek example shows that the same objects fill analysis and synthesis, in thoughts for the first and in acts for the second, in reverse order. A fundraiser planned from the closing event fits.
questions.rule: Plan backwards in thought; act forwards in deed.
questions.teaches: In a practical problem the same objects fill the analysis and the synthesis: the analysis consists in thoughts and the synthesis in acts, and the order is reversed, so what is the first desire in the analysis is the last act of the synthesis.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A problem has so many variable parts that you cannot see where to begin. What would you guess the book suggests?
options: Ask for a more special problem, such as one datum set to a trivial value
Add more detail to the problem so that every one of the many cases is covered at once
Wait for the parts to sort themselves out as you work
Replace the problem at once by a much broader one
optionExplain: Right: an extreme or simple special case can give an entry into a problem with too much variety.
More detail adds to the variety instead of reducing it.
The book prefers a deliberate change of the problem to waiting.
Widening is tried when a special case offers no foothold, not as the first answer to too much variety.
questions.explain: Too much variety is the book's cue for a more special problem. The card next sets this beside the other variations.
questions.rule: Too much variety: specialise.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each blocking difficulty to the variation the card suggests.
pairs: Too much variety to cover at once
Specialise, for example with a trivial datum
A simpler system with similar relations exists
Use analogy and a simpler analogous problem
The special case gives no foothold
Try a wider problem that contains it
A recalled result needs a part your figure lacks
questions.explain: Each difficulty has a variation that fits it best. The pairing is our reading of the book's cases, not a rule the book states.
questions.rule: Match the variation to what blocks you.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A coach cannot schedule a 12-team tournament with many pitch and time restrictions. Which variation matches the advice for too much variety?
options: Generalise to any number of teams and any number of venues
Schedule 2 teams, then 4, and look for the pattern
Copy the draw of a tournament in a different sport as it stands
Add an auxiliary pitch to every fixture and see what happens
optionExplain: Widening adds variety; it suits a special case that gives no foothold.
Right: fewer teams is a more special problem that can give an entry.
Analogy is useful when the systems share relations, but copying unchanged ignores the restrictions.
Adding an element needs a purpose such as making a known result usable, not an arbitrary addition.
questions.explain: With too much variety the book looks for a more special problem, so a small tournament is the foothold, to be linked back to the full one afterwards.
questions.rule: Shrink the case first when there is too much variety.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statements about auxiliary problems does the book support? Select all that apply.
options: Its time and effort are taken from the original, so choose with judgment
Following the list's questions guarantees finding the right one
Ask which of its result and its method you expect to use
Any auxiliary problem easier than the original is worth solving
Looking at the unknown and varying the problem often help to find one
optionExplain: Right: the book warns that the effort given to it is lost if the investigation fails.
The book says there is no infallible method, only questions that frequently help.
Right: the book asks whether you will use its result, its method or both.
Ease is one reason, but the cost to the original and the use of its result or method must be weighed.
Right: the book names both as frequently helpful.
questions.explain: The book offers helpful questions, never a guarantee, and it asks you to weigh cost against what you expect to take from the auxiliary problem.
questions.rule: Questions often help; none guarantees an auxiliary problem.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A vague pattern claim resists proof. Restating it as an exact formula in n makes proof possible. Why does the book say this can happen?
options: The stronger statement is more precise and testable, so it can be checked step by step
The exact formula is a weaker statement than the vague claim, so it asks for less to be shown than the vague claim does
Any exact formula is easier to prove than any claim in words
The vague claim was false, so no proof of it could exist
optionExplain: Right: the book calls this the inventor's paradox, and its example gained a testable step from n to n + 1.
The precise statement is stronger; it implies the vaguer one.
The book says only that the more ambitious plan may succeed, not that it always does.
Nothing says the vague claim was false; it was less accessible to testing.
questions.explain: In the book the second, more precise assertion implied the first, and its exactness allowed a step from n to n + 1 to be tested. The stronger theorem was easier to master.
questions.rule: A sharper statement can be easier to prove than a vague one.
questions.teaches: The book calls it the inventor's paradox that the more ambitious plan may succeed: the stronger, more precise statement implies the vaguer one and, being more explicit and more accessible to testing, can be easier to master.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two cyclists ride straight roads at constant speeds. The case of one standing still is solved. How can that serve the general case?
options: Use the standing case as the answer, since the general case adds nothing that the special case lacks
Double the speed of the second cyclist and repeat the standing case
Give both a common motion that brings one to rest and leaves their distance unchanged
Ignore the standing case and solve by trial and error from the start
optionExplain: A special case is a stepping stone; the book says a remark is needed to carry it back.
Changing one speed changes the distances; it does not turn the general case into the special one.
Right: this is how the book links the ship at anchor to the general case of two moving ships.
The book uses the special result by finding a link, rather than discarding it.
questions.explain: In the book's ships problem, imparting a common motion to the whole system reduces one ship's speed to zero without changing the distance between the ships, so the special solution applies.
questions.rule: A special result serves the general case once you find the link.
questions.teaches: In the book's ships example the special problem of one ship at anchor is used for the general case by imparting a common motion to both ships that reduces one ship's speed to zero, which leaves the distance between them unchanged.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: While devising a plan you reason from a few cases and a guess. Where does the book say such reasoning belongs?
options: Nowhere in mathematics, since only strict proof counts
In the final argument, as long as it is stated confidently
In checking the result, where a plausible argument can replace the derivation itself
In devising the plan, like scaffolding removed from the finished proof
optionExplain: The book calls heuristic reasoning good in itself and often necessary.
Confidence does not turn a plausible argument into a proof; the book warns against mixing the two.
A plausible argument raises or lowers credibility but cannot replace the derivation.
Right: provisional reasoning helps to build the proof but the proof must stand without it.
questions.explain: The book likens heuristic reasoning to scaffolding: needed while building, not part of the finished structure. The card next sets out the standards for each phase.
questions.rule: Plausible while building; strict when finished.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Heuristic reasoning is needed to construct a strict proof as ____ is needed to erect a building.
questions.explain: The book compares provisional reasoning with scaffolding: it supports the work and is taken down when the proof stands.
questions.rule: Scaffolding comes down when the building stands.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A tiling cost is claimed as \(T=p(w+l)\), p being price per unit area. Which tests expose the error? Select all that apply.
options: Test by dimension: the formula multiplies a price per area by a length, not by an area
Shrink w to 0: the floor vanishes, yet T stays p times l
Check symmetry in w and l: swapping them leaves T unchanged
Check growth: T increases when w or l increases
optionExplain: Right: price per area times length is not a price, so the formula cannot be correct.
Right: a floor of no area should cost nothing, so the formula fails this limiting case.
This holds for the wrong formula and the right one (T = p w l) alike, so it exposes nothing.
This holds for the wrong formula and the right one alike, so it exposes nothing.
questions.explain: The correct cost is p times w times l. The wrong formula breaks the dimension test and the limiting case w = 0, but it passes symmetry and growth, which the correct formula also passes.
questions.rule: Choose tests that the wrong answer can fail.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A formula that passes the dimension test and two special cases is thereby proved correct.
questions.explain: Passing raises confidence but does not prove. The dimension test cannot see pure numbers such as one half, and a formula can pass a few special cases and still be wrong elsewhere.
questions.rule: Tests raise confidence; they do not prove.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A tax tool shows a monthly fee of 40,000 pounds for a corner shop. Which check does the book offer first for a numerical result?
options: Run the test by dimension on the fee, to see that the units agree
Compare it with observed numbers or a commonsense estimate
Show the fee is symmetric in the shop's figures
Rederive the fee in the same order, step by step
optionExplain: A pure number in pounds has no dimension error to find; letters make that test possible.
Right: the book says numerical results can be tested against observed numbers or a commonsense estimate.
Symmetry is a test for a formula in letters, and it will not catch a wild number.
Plain repetition teaches little and repeats the same stumble; a sanity check is faster.
questions.explain: A result in numbers can be set against the world. A fee far above any plausible charge for a corner shop fails that check at once; formulas in letters allow further tests such as dimension, symmetry and limiting cases that numbers do not.
questions.rule: Set a numerical answer against the real world first.
questions.teaches: Numerical results can be tested by comparing them with observed numbers or with a commonsense estimate of observable numbers, yet teachers find students untroubled by absurd answers such as a boat 16,130 feet long, and problems in letters allow tests that problems in numbers do not.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A pupil finishes a problem and the answer matches the book's. What would you guess the author wants next?
options: To move on to the next problem at once, to keep up speed and avoid dwelling
To memorise the answer so that it can be repeated in a test
To ask the teacher for a harder hint on the same problem
To re-examine the result and the path, and ask what else follows
optionExplain: The author names closing the book at this point as what good students tend to do, and as a loss.
The author values the connections and the method more than the answer alone.
Nothing in the text asks for more hints after a solution is complete.
Right: the author says that looking back consolidates knowledge and develops ability.
questions.explain: The author wants a real look back at the result and the path. The card next lists what it adds.
questions.rule: A matching answer is the start of the look back.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each looking-back move by what it mainly adds.
groups: Connects the solution to other problems

items.t: Derive the result a second way
Recheck the touchy points of the argument
Recheck the argument in a different order of steps
Ask whether the method fits another problem
Give the result a concrete interpretation in a new setting
Derive a new problem by specialising the old one

questions.explain: The first three test or tighten the solution. The last three link it to other problems, which is what turns one solution into usable knowledge.
questions.rule: Check it, then connect it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An analyst solves a tough pricing problem. Which next step is looking back as the book describes it?
options: File the answer in the shared folder and begin the next task on the list
Ask a colleague to recheck the arithmetic once more and then regard the matter as closed
Ask whether the method prices other products and whether a shorter argument exists
Repeat the same steps in the same order to confirm the total
optionExplain: This is the habit the book criticises: closing the book on a finished solution.
A check is part of looking back, but stopping there leaves out simplifying and connecting.
Right: it asks about the method for other problems and about a shorter argument, both named in the look back.
Plain repetition teaches little; the book asks for a different route or a different order.
questions.explain: Looking back asks whether the method serves other problems and whether the argument can be simplified. Filing the answer or repeating the steps leaves most of its value unused.
questions.rule: Ask what else the method and result can do.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Among problems derived from a solved one by generalisation, specialisation and analogy, all can be solved at once with the old solution.
questions.explain: In the book's example only the problem obtained by specialisation could be solved immediately from the old solution; the generalised and analogous problems were interesting but needed more work.
questions.rule: New problems from variation are not all easy.
questions.teaches: In the book's example of deriving new problems by generalisation, specialisation and analogy, only the one obtained by specialisation could be solved immediately on the basis of the solution of the original problem.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A teacher wants practice problems derived from a solved one. Easy ones are dull and interesting ones too hard. What does the book say?
options: Finding one both interesting and accessible takes experience, taste and luck
Derive many from one solved problem, since the process is easy to carry far
Use only specialisations, since any other variation is a waste of time
Avoid deriving problems at all, as looking back should only check the answer and nothing more
optionExplain: Right: the book says the derived problems tend to be inaccessible and the easy ones uninteresting.
The book says the process is unlimited in theory but seldom carried far in practice.
Specialisation is easy to solve but not the only useful variation; the others bring interest.
Deriving new problems is one of the book's suggestions for looking back.
questions.explain: The book warns that the problems we obtain by variation are apt to be inaccessible, and the easy ones apt to be uninteresting. A problem that is both takes experience, taste and good luck.
questions.rule: Interesting and accessible together is hard to find.
questions.teaches: Problems obtained by varying a solved one are apt to be inaccessible, while easy new problems are apt to be uninteresting, so finding one that is both interesting and accessible takes experience, taste and good luck.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A teacher wants students to learn to solve problems alone. What would you guess is the best use of a hint?
options: Give the exact step needed, so that no time is wasted
Offer a general question first and go more specific only if needed
Show a full worked solution first, then set the same problem for the student to copy
Hold back every hint until the student has asked twice
optionExplain: An exact step gives the secret away and leaves little for the student to learn.
Right: the student keeps as much of the work as possible and may find the idea himself.
The book wants the student to find the idea with help, not to copy one.
Too little help can leave the student with no progress at all.
questions.explain: The book asks for help in measure: general first, specific later, so the student does the thinking. The card next gives both aims.
questions.rule: Help in measure; general before specific.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The teacher's two aims are to help the student solve the problem at hand and to develop his ____ to solve future problems by himself.
questions.explain: The second aim is the student's ability to solve later problems alone; the first success adds a little to it.
questions.rule: Solve this problem; grow the ability for the next.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A coach tells a stuck student, Use similar triangles. What does the author say is wrong with such a hint?
options: It is too general to help anyone, so the student learns nothing from it
It makes the student think too long about the problem
It gives the secret away and teaches nothing for later problems
It shows the coach does not know the answer
optionExplain: The fault is the opposite: it is too special.
The objection is that it removes thinking, not that it adds it.
Right: a special hint leaves little for the student and cannot be repeated on other problems.
The text raises no doubt about what the coach knows.
questions.explain: The author's objections to a hint such as Could you apply the theorem of Pythagoras? are that it gives the secret away, is too special, and is not instructive.
questions.rule: Prefer a general, natural question to a special hint.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: When a teacher solves a problem before the class, he should hide his own questions so that the solution looks effortless.
questions.explain: The teacher should dramatize his ideas a little and put to himself the same questions that he uses when helping the students, so the class can imitate them.
questions.rule: Show the questions you ask yourself.
questions.teaches: When the teacher solves a problem before the class, he should dramatize his ideas a little and put to himself the same questions which he uses when helping the students, so that they can imitate them.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: A teacher who puts the same list question at every step, whatever the problem, shows the mastery the book wants.
questions.explain: That is pedantry: applying a rule rigidly, in cases where it fits and where it does not. Mastery applies it with ease and judgment and notices where it fits.
questions.rule: Ask a question when the problem calls for it, not by habit alone.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A manager hands an analyst a ready-made plan, and the analyst soon loses the thread. By the book's account, why does this happen more easily?
options: He was given too much freedom to adapt the plan
He did not check the final result of the plan
He asked too many questions of himself while carrying it out, and lost the thread of the plan
He took the plan from outside, on authority, not working for the idea himself
optionExplain: The book describes the opposite: the plan came from outside rather than from his own work.
Checking the result is a different phase; the book's point concerns holding on to the plan.
Questions asked by the solver do not cause forgetting in the book's account.
Right: the book says a plan received from outside is easily forgotten, unlike one the student worked for.
questions.explain: The main danger when carrying out is that the student forgets the plan. If he received it from outside on the teacher's authority he forgets it easily; if he worked for it himself, even with help, he does not lose it easily.
questions.rule: A plan you worked for is a plan you keep.
questions.teaches: In carrying out the plan the main danger is that the student forgets it, which may easily happen if he received the plan from outside and accepted it on the authority of the teacher, whereas an idea he worked for himself, even with help, is not easily lost.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, Main divisions, main questions
questions.q: In the diagram, the shaded right triangle has the box diagonal as hypotenuse and edge c as one leg. What is its other leg?
options: The edge b, the front edge of the box's bottom face
A second copy of edge c at the far side of the box
The diagonal of the box's base rectangle, whose sides are a and b
The edge a, the side edge of the bottom face running back from the front
optionExplain: Edge b is one side of the base, but the leg that closes the right triangle with c runs diagonally across the base, not along a side.
A copy of c is parallel to c and cannot form the second leg of a right triangle with it.
Right: the leg in the base joins the lower end of the box diagonal to the foot of c, so it is the diagonal of the a-by-b base rectangle.
Edge a is also a side of the base, not the segment that closes the right triangle with c.
questions.explain: The vertical edge c stands at right angles to the base, so the other leg lies in the base. It joins the two ends of the base diagonal, which is the diagonal of the a-by-b rectangle.
questions.rule: To use a right triangle for a box diagonal, find the vertical edge and the base diagonal.

media.alt: A rectangular box drawn in perspective. Edge a runs back along the left of the bottom face, edge b runs along the front of the bottom face and edge c stands upright at the right. The long diagonal x runs from the far left bottom corner up to the near right top corner. A shaded right triangle has x as hypotenuse, the upright edge c as one leg and a diagonal across the bottom face as the other leg.

questions.unitTitle: Part I: In the Classroom, More examples
questions.q: In the diagram of the two angles, which statement belongs to the hypothesis rather than to the conclusion?
options: Each side of one angle is parallel to the matching side of the other and points the same way
The angle at A equals the angle at A prime
The two angles lie together in one common plane
The two figures are triangles with equal base segments
optionExplain: Right: the parallel, equally directed sides are given, so they belong to the hypothesis.
The equality of the two angles is what must be proved, so it is the conclusion.
The problem says the two angles lie in different planes, so a common plane contradicts the hypothesis; it is not what is given.
The figure shows no triangles at all; they appear only if an auxiliary element is added.
questions.explain: The parallel, equally directed sides are given, and that is the hypothesis. The equality of the two angles is the conclusion to be shown.
questions.rule: Read the hypothesis off what is given in the figure; the conclusion is what you must reach.

media.alt: Two separate angles, each drawn as a pair of rays from a vertex. The upper one has vertex A' with rays toward C' and B'; the lower has vertex A with rays toward C and B. Matching rays slope the same way, as if parallel and equally directed. No triangle or joining line is drawn.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Analogy to Bright Idea
questions.q: In the diagram, the shaded median plane passes through M, the midpoint of edge AB. Which edge does it also contain?
options: Edge AD, joining A to the apex
Edge BD, joining B to the apex
Edge AC, joining A to the far vertex
Edge CD, the edge opposite AB
optionExplain: AD meets the plane only at A, since A lies off the line through M and CD.
BD meets the plane only at B, for the same reason.
AC meets the plane only at A, so it is not contained in it.
A median plane joins the midpoint of one edge to the opposite edge, so it holds M and the whole edge CD.
questions.explain: The solid's counterpart of a median is a plane through the midpoint of an edge and the opposite edge. For AB that opposite edge is CD.
questions.rule: A median plane of a tetrahedron joins the midpoint of an edge to the opposite edge.

media.alt: A tetrahedron drawn with vertices A, B and D visible and a fourth vertex C hidden at the right. M marks the midpoint of the base edge AB. A shaded planar region joins M, the apex D and the opposite edge, showing a median plane of the solid, the counterpart of a median of a triangle.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.section: Could You Derive Something Useful from the Data?
questions.q: In the diagram, short segments run from the line through A to the dots for B and C. Why are they drawn at right angles?
options: A line equally far from two points must cut the segment joining them at right angles.
The distance from a point to a line is measured along the perpendicular, so each segment shows that point's distance.
Right angles make the line pass exactly through the midpoint of the segment joining B and C.
Perpendicular segments are the only ones that can be drawn from a point to a line on paper.
questions.explain: The book says the figure is suggested by the definition of the distance of a point from a line, which involves right angles. The segments show the two required equal distances.
optionExplain: The picture does not say the line cuts BC at right angles; equal distances do not require it.
Correct: the definition of distance from a point to a line uses the perpendicular.
The condition asks only for equal distances; it does not put the line through the midpoint of BC.
Oblique segments can be drawn; they just do not give the distance.
questions.rule: Draw the figure the definition suggests.

media.alt: A long horizontal line starts at the dot A. Two short segments stand at right angles to it, one rising above the line toward the upper side and one dropping below it further right; each ends in a dot for B and C. It shows the unknown line with perpendicular distances.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Can You Check the Result? to Decomposing and Recombining
questions.q: In the diagram, the problem is now to find the apex A. Which items are the data of this new problem?
options: The base length a and the height h, with both B and C left unknown
The three vertices of the triangle, with the angle at A as the unknown
The angle at A and the point A, with the base BC as the unknown
The points B and C in position, the height h and the angle at A
questions.explain: The new unknown is the point A. The data are the two points B and C, the line h and the angle at A, so some data are shared with the old problem while the unknown has changed.
optionExplain: That was the old problem's datum, a length a; in the new problem B and C are fixed points, so they are not unknown.
A is the unknown, so the vertices are not all given.
A is what is sought, and the base BC is part of the data.
Right: the new problem gives B and C in position, the line h and the angle at A, and asks for the point A.
questions.rule: After changing unknown and data, restate which are which.

media.alt: A triangle with horizontal base BC and apex A at the top. A solid vertical segment h falls from A to the base, which carries the letter a. Dashed lines join A to B and to C, and a small arc at A marks the angle between them. The apex is the unknown point.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: If You Cannot Solve the Proposed Problem to Look at the Unknown
questions.q: The picture shows n = 4: a rectangle 4 by 5. Drawn for n = 5, the rectangle has area 5 times ____.
questions.explain: The rectangle has sides n and n + 1, so for n = 5 its sides are 5 and 6. Each staircase is half of it, 15.
questions.rule: Rectangle sides are n and n + 1.

media.alt: Two copies of a rectangle side by side. In the first, a zigzag stair-step line splits the rectangle into two equal staircase-shaped halves. In the second, one staircase half is shown as columns whose heights rise one unit at a time, four steps in all.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the diagram, which angle at A equals the angle at B?
options: The angle between the line and side AB, on the left of A
The angle between the two sides of the triangle at A itself
The angle between the line and side AC, on the right of A
The straight angle formed by the whole line through A
optionExplain: Correct: alternate angles between the parallel line and BC are equal, so the angle at B reappears at A on the left.
The angle inside the triangle at A is the third angle, not a copy of B.
That angle matches the angle at C, not the one at B.
The whole line gives the two right angles that the three angles together fill.
questions.explain: The line through A is parallel to BC, so alternate angles are equal. The angle at B reappears on the left at A and the angle at C on the right.
questions.rule: Alternate angles between parallels are equal.

media.alt: A triangle ABC with A at the top and BC as the bottom side. A horizontal line through A runs parallel to BC. Matching angle arcs mark the angle at B and the angle at A on the left side, and the angle at C and the angle at A on the right side.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the diagram the big pail is full at 9 quarts and the level marks are 5 and 1. Two equal pours of the small pail take the level from 9 to 1, so the small pail holds ____ quarts.
questions.explain: The level falls 9 to 5 to 1, so each pour removes 4 quarts, the capacity of the small pail, which is emptied into the river twice.
questions.rule: Pouring the small pail away twice leaves 1 quart.

media.alt: The tall pail is full and hatched up to a mark labelled 9. Dashed level lines mark the water heights 5 and 1 inside it, so the level falls in two equal drops. The short pail beside it is empty.

questions.unitTitle: Dictionary: Why Proofs? to Working Backwards
questions.q: In the diagram, what must the dog do to reach the food?
options: Turn away from the food and leave through the open side, then curve round
Run straight at the food and push through the dotted fence
Stay where it is and wait for the food to come nearer
Run along the closed top side until it finds a gap there
optionExplain: Correct: the only way out is the open side, which lies away from the food, so the dog must first move away from it.
The fence blocks the direct path, so a straight run fails.
Waiting does not solve the problem.
The top side is closed, so no gap can be found there.
questions.explain: The food lies beyond the closed side, so the way to it starts by turning away through the open side. That is the going-round the entry describes for the dog.
questions.rule: Turn away from the goal to go round the obstacle.

media.alt: Three sides of a rectangular fence drawn with dots: top, left and right, with the bottom side open. Inside the fence is a dog D; outside, beyond the closed top side, is food F directly above the dog.

cover.alt: Book cover: a pale background with two line drawings of triangles above the title How to Solve It, subtitled a new aspect of mathematical method, with the author's name George Polya beneath.
